Theodore Roosevelt is born in Manhattan

At 7:45 in the evening, after a labor that began late in the afternoon, Mittie Roosevelt gives birth to her second child, Theodore Jr., at the family's East 20th Street home. Both of the baby's grandmothers are on hand, and Dr. Markoe attends.
The day after the birth, Mittie jokes that baby 'Teedie' resembles a terrapin crossed with Dr. Young.

Parents mark five years of marriage
Theodore Sr. and Mittie celebrate their fifth anniversary. They wed on December 22, 1853, after Dr. Hilborne West, whose sister Mary was Weir's wife, brought them together.
A background note: soon after their marriage the couple settled in 1854 at 28 East 20th Street, the house where Theodore was born.

Roosevelt's big sister Bamie celebrates her fourth birthday. Bright beyond her years, she lives with Pott's disease, a tubercular illness of the spine, and is strapped into a stiff steel-and-leather brace that pins her in place and chafes her back.
The note on Bamie continues: the rigid brace rubs until it opens a painful sore on her back.

Oregon is admitted as the nation's 33rd state while the Roosevelt baby is not yet four months old.

Around now Bamie comes under the care of the orthopedist Dr. Charles Fayette Taylor, who is trying a fresh 'movement cure' of therapeutic exercise. She is among his first patients and gets a smaller, lighter brace that lets her move. Theodore Sr. later founds an orthopedic hospital with Taylor in charge.
New York Orthopedic Hospital and Dispensary
Off to the country with Mother

Mittie, Grandmother Bulloch, the baby and nursemaid Dora Watkins head out of the city for the country, while Theodore Sr. and Bamie remain at home. The same day Charles Carow weds Gertrude Tyler in Norwich, Connecticut; they will become Edith Carow's parents.
A follow-on note identifies the newlywed Carows as the future parents of Edith Kermit Carow, Roosevelt's second wife.

Roosevelt's mother Mittie celebrates her 24th birthday.
By this point the infant Theodore is going by the family nickname 'Teedie.'
Grandmother Bulloch writes to Susan West that little Teedie is still bothered by a milk crust and by teething, but is not really ill.
The same letter goes on to praise Teedie as about the brightest small child the writer has ever known.

Theodore Roosevelt Sr. marks his 28th birthday.

John Brown goes to the gallows
The abolitionist John Brown is executed at Charlestown, Virginia, a sign of the crisis building over slavery.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark six years of marriage.
Big sister Bamie celebrates her fifth birthday.
Writing to Mittie, Theodore Sr. says he misses the help Teedie gives him at bedtime.
The letter explains just what Theodore Sr. misses: the toddler's eager help as he undresses each night.
Gertrude and Charles Carow welcome their first child, a boy, who dies at six months.
Abraham Lincoln gives his address at Cooper Union in New York City, not far from the Roosevelt home.
A new son is born to Theodore Sr. and Mittie in New York, giving Teedie a little brother.

A photograph is taken of the toddler in a dress and a hat, as was customary for small boys of the day.

The Roosevelts are living in New York City; the record lists only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Big sister Bamie has her sixth birthday.
A new state, the 34th, is admitted to the Union.
Little brother Elliott, called Ellie, turns one.
A house divided over the Union
Writing to Mittie on the eve of war, Theodore Sr. wishes the two of them saw eye to eye on the great national question that splits his Northern loyalties from her Southern ones.
Abraham Lincoln is inaugurated for his first term.
A quiet stretch in New York City

Confederate batteries open on Fort Sumter, and the Civil War begins.

The Roosevelts are living in New York City; the record lists only the family's whereabouts for this date.
In Boston, Alice Hathaway Lee is born. She will become Roosevelt's first wife.

Edith Kermit Carow, Roosevelt's future second wife, is born at her mother's family home, the Tyler house in Norwich, Connecticut. The Carows are comfortable: Charles has inherited more than $36,000 and stock in rail lines, canal and bank companies, and gas utilities, and they live on Livingston Place near East 14th Street.
A note on the Carow home places it close to the Manhattan mansion of Cornelius Van Schaack Roosevelt, Teedie's grandfather.
A soldier laddie at the fitting

Aunt Anna writes Mittie about the struggle to fit the squirming Teedie for a Zouave shirt. When told the shirt was for a soldier, the toddler asked if he was one; she said yes and named herself his Captain.
The letter concludes: with his new rank settled, Teedie stood still long enough to be measured.
A baby sister, Corinne, joins the Roosevelt household.
Father heads to Washington; asthma begins

Theodore Sr. goes to Washington to push for a law letting Union soldiers set aside part of their pay for their families, and serves as one of three allotment commissioners with Theodore B. Bronson and William E. Dodge. He hires a substitute to serve in the army. About now Teedie's asthma starts. When Port Royal falls to the North, Grandmama weeps for three days.
Grandmama Bulloch's lament continues: she would sooner lie in a common grave than see the South rejoin the Union.
Full of mischief and a cold
Mittie tells her husband that Teedie is loving and sweet but getting into everything and in need of his father's firm hand. He also has a bad cold.
North and South under one roof
With Theodore Sr. loyal to the Union and Mittie's family devoted to the South, the Roosevelt home is split by the war.
Teedie informs Bamie that he has two fathers, his Papa and one in Heaven. Asked by Mittie how he knew, he points to the prayer his father says each morning.
A long night with a sick boy
Mittie writes Theodore Sr. that Teedie was ill overnight and she got up to him six or seven times; she plans a dose of magnesia if he does not improve.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark 8 years since their wedding.
Theodore Sr. tells Mittie it pains him to be away from the children so often, yet without the allotment work he feels he ought to be gone entirely, in the army.
In a long New Year's letter to Mittie, Theodore Sr. lays out his allotment commission work in detail.
Source note on the allotment letter
This date carries only the citation for the previous day's letter.
Teedie comes down in the morning looking glum and announces a toothache in his stomach. His frailty has relatives fearing he may not survive the year.
Writing from an army camp, Theodore Sr. frets over Teedie's illness and wonders whether the house furnace is keeping the children from good health, pinning hopes on summer.
An evening at the White House
Theodore Sr. receives an invitation to Mrs. Lincoln's ball and goes.
Brother Ellie has his second birthday.
Two-year-old Ellie speaks more plainly than Teedie. Elsewhere, Edith Carow's grandfather Daniel Tyler becomes a brigadier general of volunteers and is sent to the Army of the Mississippi.
Theodore Sr. accompanies Mrs. Lincoln on a shopping trip as the Battle of Shiloh opens in Tennessee.
The Roosevelts are living in New York City; the record lists only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Theodore Sr. comes back to New York from his rounds of the army camps.

The children grow up on Mittie's, Aunt Anna's and Grandmama's tales of plantation life at Roswell and the Br'er Rabbit stories, and act out tableaux. Teedie bites Bamie's arm, then hides under the kitchen table with dough from the cook. His father finds him, chases him to the stairs and punishes him.
Alice Lee, Roosevelt's future first wife, has her first birthday in Boston.
The Roosevelts are living in New York City; the record lists only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Edith Carow, Roosevelt's future second wife, has her first birthday.
Union and Confederate armies clash at Antietam Creek in Maryland.
Theodore Sr. turns 31 on the day Lincoln issues the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, set to take effect on New Year's Day, 1863.
Baby sister Corinne has her first birthday.
A birthday supper and a big laugh
For Teedie's fourth birthday the family gives a supper party. He announces that he likes chicken, roast beef and all good things more than salt water, and the laughter leaves him puffed up for days.
Union and Confederate armies collide at Fredericksburg, Virginia.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark 9 years since their wedding.

The children go to Sunday school at the Madison Square Presbyterian church led by Dr. Adams. With Theodore Sr. away, Mittie and Aunt Annie have them fill parcels of small comforts meant to slip through the Union blockade to the South.
Aunt Annie Bulloch teaches the children at home in return for her room and board. Teedie finds a glass prism that has dropped from the chandelier and hides it away as a prize.
Teedie starts to read, poring over David Livingstone's African travels.
Far from the Roosevelt nursery, armies meet at Chancellorsville, Virginia.
Summer by the shore at Long Branch
The family heads to Long Branch, New Jersey, for the summer, where Mittie undergoes ether treatments for her health.
West Virginia is admitted, bringing the count of states to 35.
Teedie is rushed to the city and then on to Saratoga in hope of easing his illness.

Looking back years later, Roosevelt recalls his asthma-ridden boyhood: trips in search of air he could breathe, and nights when his father paced the room carrying him while both parents tried to help him breathe.
The decisive battles of Gettysburg in Pennsylvania and Vicksburg in Mississippi rage through July 4.
Violence against the military draft breaks out in New York City.
Alice Lee has her second birthday.
The Roosevelts are living in New York City; the record lists only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Edith Carow has her second birthday.
Theodore Sr. turns 32 as the Battle of Chickamauga is fought in Georgia.
Teedie stands for a portrait holding a fur hat, dressed in billowing Zouave trousers, a tie and a dark cutaway coat, his longish hair parted down the middle.
Theodore Sr., Mittie and Aunt Anna go to New York's 'Russian Ball,' given for the Russian ambassador.
At the dedication of the soldiers' cemetery in Pennsylvania, Abraham Lincoln gives his Gettysburg Address.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark 10 years since their wedding.

Roosevelt's later memory of Christmas mornings: stockings borrowed from the grown-ups, opened before dawn on his parents' bed, and each child's larger gifts waiting on a separate table in the drawing room after breakfast.

When Theodore Sr. emptied his pockets the children got to play with whatever came out. Roosevelt later remembered the family's morning prayers, and the race at the stair foot to claim the snug spot beside Father on the sofa.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie host a large party to welcome 1864.

A Bible verse from John, chapter 2, about zeal for God's house eating one up frightens Teedie, who imagines the 'zeal' as a beast hiding in churches. He later tells the story in his third Earl Lecture in March 1911, printed in Realizable Ideals (1912). Edith's grandmother, Emily Lee Tyler, dies.
The best man he ever knew
In later life Roosevelt sums up his father as the finest man he knew, strong and brave yet gentle and generous, and intolerant of selfishness, cruelty, idleness, cowardice or lying in his children.
The Roosevelts are living in New York City; the record lists only the family's whereabouts for this date.
The Roosevelts spend the summer at Loantaka in New Jersey. Roosevelt later remembered how the children adored the country, disliked the city, and hated the autumn move back to town.
Alice Lee has her third birthday.
Union ships fight their way into Mobile Bay.
Edith Carow has her third birthday.
Union forces under William T. Sherman occupy Atlanta.
Roosevelt's grandmother, Martha Bulloch, dies at 65. Nevada is admitted as the 36th state.
Anniversary as Sherman reaches the sea
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark eleven years of marriage while William T. Sherman's army arrives at Savannah, Georgia, Mittie's home ground.
A new top floor at home
Decorator Leon Marcotte remodels the family house at 28 East 20th Street, adding a fourth story.
The Roosevelts are in New York City; the record gives only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Abraham Lincoln is sworn in for a second term.
Union troops enter Richmond, the Confederate capital.
Confederate General Robert E. Lee gives up his army at Appomattox Court House, Virginia.
An assassin kills Abraham Lincoln in Washington, and Andrew Johnson becomes President.
Emily Carow, Edith's younger sister, is born.
Watching Lincoln's funeral from the window

Lincoln's funeral cortege rolls past Grandfather Roosevelt's Union Square mansion, and a Brady photograph catches Teedie and Ellie at an upstairs window. When little Edith Carow begins crying, scared by the black mourning drapery everywhere, the boys shut her in a closet.
Mary Ledwith, known as 'Mame,' is the nurse in the Carow household.
The last Confederate army gives up
The final Confederate army surrenders at Shreveport, Louisiana, and the Civil War ends.

At Loantaka, New Jersey, the Roosevelts host Aunt Lucy Elliott with her children Maud and Johnny, who spent the war in Georgia. Lucy's husband Dan Elliott died of tuberculosis during the war; years before, he had killed a man in a duel.
P. T. Barnum's American Museum on the corner of Broadway and Park Place is destroyed by fire.
Alice Lee has a birthday, turning 4.
Edith Carow has a birthday, turning 4.
The Confederate cruiser Shenandoah sails into Liverpool. Her sailing master is Irvine Bulloch, Mittie's brother and Teedie's uncle.
The Shenandoah is surrendered to British authorities.
Barnum's replacement museum opens its doors on Broadway at Prince Street.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark 12 years since their wedding.
School, a wedding and Kipling-style tales

Teedie and Ellie have a brief spell at a 20th Street school run by Professor McMullen. Aunt Anna Bulloch marries James K. Gracie. Teedie entertains Ellie and Corinne with animal yarns of his own making.
The Roosevelts are in New York City; the record gives only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Ellie celebrates his sixth birthday at home in New York.
A quiet stretch in New York City
The Roosevelts are in New York City; the record gives only the family's whereabouts for this date.
A seal skull starts a museum

Spotting a dead seal at a Broadway market, Teedie is given its skull, the first prize of his 'Roosevelt Museum of Natural History.' He writes nature essays, including one on the 'Foregoing Ant' after misreading 'foregoing' in a book as the name of a species.

A Shetland pony called Grant arrives for the children. When Theodore Sr. asks who will ride first, Ellie and Teedie hang back and Conie leaps on, so the pony becomes hers. At Loantaka, the Elliott cousins and their mother come to stay.
Aunt Lucy and her children pay another visit.
Readers, magazines and a shared classroom

The children love the McGuffey Readers and 'Our Young Folks' magazine. Aunt Annie teaches the Carow children alongside the Roosevelts; the Carows, cutting costs, now live with Aunt Ann Eliza, widow of Robert Kermit, whose house backs onto Cornelius Van Schaack Roosevelt's on Union Square.
Alice Lee has a birthday, turning 5.
Edith Carow has a birthday, turning 5.

Uncle Irvine Bulloch, the former Confederate officer, quietly enters New York and meets his sisters, Mittie and Anna, for a rendezvous in Central Park. At home, Mittie refreshes the 20th Street house with new wallpaper and upholstery, and dresses almost always in white. The Roosevelt children spend many hours playing at the Carows'.
The Roosevelts are in New York City; the record gives only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark 13 years since their wedding.
Birthdays with Father; a new portrait

Theodore Sr. makes each child's birthday a day of special attention, riding with Corinne and reading poems with her. Teedie sits for another photograph beside the fringed chair from his portrait at five, now shorter-haired in a dark suit and hat.
Nebraska is admitted as the 37th state.
Congress passes the Reconstruction Act, splitting the former Confederacy into five military districts.
The Roosevelts are in New York City; the record gives only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Summer on the Hudson; a second pony

The family rents John Aspinwall's house at Barrytown-on-Hudson for the summer. Teedie writes to his old nurse Dora Watkins that a second pony has arrived, which Ellie rides, and that he himself nearly took a spill. New York opens its first elevated line on Greenwich Street, and the Carows summer with Grandfather Tyler at Red Bank.
Alice Lee has a birthday, turning 6.
Edith Carow has a birthday, turning 6.
A quiet stretch in New York City
The Roosevelts are in New York City; the record gives only the family's whereabouts for this date.
The Roosevelts are in New York City; the record gives only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark 14 years since their wedding.
A garbled note on Louisa May Alcott
The record's only line for this date names Louisa May Alcott, but the text is too garbled to say what it reports.
Stevens brings impeachment to the Senate
Representative Thaddeus Stevens carries the House's impeachment of President Andrew Johnson to the Senate.
The impeachment trial of President Andrew Johnson gets under way.
Barnum's Broadway showplace at Prince Street goes up in flames, less than three years after the first one was lost.
Lessons and pickles at Aunt Annie's

School for Teedie, Ellie, Conie and the Carow girls Edith and Emily moves to Aunt Annie Gracie's furnished rooms on Fourth Avenue, where she sets out open-air meals of green pickles and cold lamb. Late in April Mittie heads to Savannah with Theodore Sr. and Conie and visits Roswell, the plantation where she grew up.
The oldest Roosevelt letters still in existence date from today: notes from Teedie to his mother, to Conie and to his father, who are away in the South.
Already drawn to animals, Teedie keeps four mice, two white and two brown.
Teedie writes his father asking for 'supple jacks' and reports that one of the brown mice has been crushed.
The Senate votes to acquit President Andrew Johnson.
The family again spends the summer at John Aspinwall's house in Barrytown-on-Hudson.

Teedie devours Robinson Crusoe, Mayne Reid's adventures, Little Women and Little Men, Swiss Family Robinson, Homes Without Hands, The Saga of King Olaf and the magazine 'Our Young Folks', and writes his own book, 'Natural History on Insects.'
Alice Lee has a birthday, turning 7.
Edith Carow has a birthday, turning 7.
At Barrytown, Teedie opens his first diary. He notes that his aunt and Uncle Jimmy Gracie left that evening, and records a bout of asthma.
A wet day. Dora Watkins, the children's nurse, has to go into New York City.
Teedie rides the pony Grant both before and after breakfast.
Teedie's diary reports that nothing worth mentioning took place.
Teedie rides Grant. The cart horse Billy collapses in the shafts.
The children play store and 'baby,' and Teedie spends time writing, reading and drawing.
Sunday: Teedie goes to church and, by his own account, does nothing at all after lunch.
A hidden house in the woods
Exploring the woods, the children stumble on a small house.
Teedie rides Grant six miles to Cruger's Island.
The children spend the day playing in the brook.
Teedie makes a six-mile ride before breakfast, and Annie Platt arrives.
Brook by day, games by night
Another day of splashing in the brook, followed by games after supper.
Teedie heads to the brook and studies the animals around a pond.
A lost book and talk of birds
Teedie loses his book, which turns up again by September 4, and writes about birds.
Teedie's diary records a cold, rainy day and some 75 swallows in the house as they gather to fly south. Cousin Jimmy arrives back from Niagara Falls and the boys play fort for the rest of the day.
Tracking a weasel and a fox
Teedie and Cousin Jimmy find a weasel's hole and a fox's den, then take a long walk.
Teedie's first diary closes on this date.
Without the knowledge of his wife, Aunt Lizzie Ellis, Uncle Robert Roosevelt maintains a mistress, Minnie O'Shea, under the name 'Mrs. Robert F. Fortescue,' just down the street.
Voters send Ulysses S. Grant to the White House.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark fifteen years of marriage.
Mittie brings Teedie to Philadelphia to visit her half-sister Susan and Susan's husband, Dr. Hilborne West.
The Roosevelts are in New York City; the record gives only the family's whereabouts for this date.
Ellie turns nine; Central Park done
Ellie celebrates his ninth birthday, and work on Central Park is finished.
Ulysses S. Grant is inaugurated as the 18th President.
A charter for the museum in the parlor
Around now a charter is approved for the American Museum of Natural History, an institution born in the front parlor of the Roosevelts' East 20th Street house.
Forty pages on bugs and fish
Teedie fills about 40 pages with natural history notes under the title 'About Insects and Fishes.'

As the family readies for Europe, Aunt Anna, now married to James Gracie, will stay behind. Bamie counts as a grown-up even in the eyes of her siblings, and Teedie explains his shorthand: the three younger children versus the adults.
The transcontinental railroad is completed at Promontory, Utah, while the Roosevelts prepare in New York for their voyage.
The family is still in New York City on the eve of departure.
Sailing for Europe on the Scotia

Teedie's travel journal begins as the family boards Cunard's paddle-wheeler Scotia, then the fastest ship to Europe. He weeps a good deal on the way to the docks. With nursemaid Mary Ann the party numbers seven, and by bedtime he is seasick.
Sick at breakfast, bored at sea
Teedie spots two ships and some fish, is ill at breakfast, finds the voyage dull, and spends the day reading and playing with Ellie and Conie.
Three ships and a school of porpoises pass by; Teedie fills the day with play, reading and writing.
Dolphins appear and two ships are spotted.
Teedie is sick and homesick and misses the Sunday service. Mittie writes of a steward feeding him on deck, and of grubby carpets on an otherwise tidy ship.
Teedie sees two ships and lots of fish, and makes friends with some boys on board.
The Scotia crosses the Gulf Stream, and Teedie gets to know a West Indian passenger, Mr. St. John.
A day of reading and play, with two ships, a shark, fish and gulls to watch.
The steamer Tunis is sighted, and Teedie talks again with Mr. St. John.
At 4 a.m. the ship calls at Queenstown, Ireland, then crosses the Irish Sea to Liverpool. Mittie marvels that amid the bustle of customs, Teedie sits reading a book.
Teedie meets his Bulloch cousins, and the children race around the hotel.
The Roosevelts attend church with the Sears family and walk in the Botanic Park. Ella Sears is engaged to 27-year-old Uncle Irvine Bulloch.
Out to Waterloo on the Queen's birthday
The family travels about five miles to Waterloo, home of Uncle James Dunwoody Bulloch, on Queen Victoria's 50th birthday.
The children play in the park, and Teedie sees a canary.
Teedie plays with his cousins and passes time reading, writing and drawing, while Papa visits the Darbys.
Sharp words with Jefferson Davis's son
Visiting his cousins' school at Waterloo, Teedie meets a son of Confederate president Jefferson Davis, and the boys trade sharp words.
Parents to Chester, children to the park
Theodore Sr. and Mittie go to Chester while the three younger children visit Princes Park and trade funny rhymes.
Donkey rides and a cut leg
At Southport with his cousins, Teedie rides donkeys and gashes his leg vaulting a fence.
Teedie goes to church, nursing the leg he cut the day before.

The family takes the train some 80 miles to Chatsworth, the Duke of Devonshire's estate, in company with Ella Sears and Uncle Irvine, stopping at the Peacock Inn and the Edensor Hotel. Conie has a fright. Back home, the Alabama claims dispute simmers as the U.S. seeks damages from Britain.
A walk with Conie and a castle visit

Ten-year-old Roosevelt strolls with his little sister Conie, stops to admire some puppies, and sees Haddon Hall, an old castle dating to the 11th century, before the family returns to the Chatsworth Hotel in Liverpool.
By rail to the ruins of Furness Abbey
The family rides the train to the ruined Furness Abbey, getting in after nightfall. The diary names the Roosevelts' hired valet, Noel Paovitch.
Exploring the abbey, then on to Ambleside
Roosevelt pokes around the abbey ruins and an old water tower, then the family travels by rail and carriage to Ambleside in the Lake District.
Lake Windermere, a dancing bear, and asthma
At Ambleside, Roosevelt visits Lake Windermere, watches a dancing bear, and goes to church. That night his asthma flares.
Through the rain the family takes a coach to Keswick and then the railway cars to Edinburgh. Roosevelt notes in his diary that they "romped."
Sunday church and a climb on the crags
Roosevelt goes to church in Edinburgh on Sunday and later scrambles up the crags above the city.
Climbing Arthur's Seat with his parents
The family drives to Arthur's Seat, and Roosevelt climbs the hill with his father, his mother Mittie, and his older sister Bamie. He buys himself a sweet cracker.
A visit to Sir Walter Scott's home
Roosevelt, his parents and Bamie take the train to Abbotsford, the house of the novelist Sir Walter Scott, and also see the ruins of Melrose Abbey.
Roslin castle, chapel and a solo lunch
From Edinburgh the family heads out to Roslin, where Roosevelt sees the castle, its dungeons and a chapel, then buys his lunch and eats it on his own.
The family takes the train to Stirling and its castle.
Roosevelt travels through the Trossachs pass and past Loch Katrine and Loch Lomond on the way to Glasgow. The scenery calls to mind Scott's poem "The Lady of the Lake."
A long, grimy train ride to York
An eight-hour rail trip of roughly 140 to 160 miles brings the family to York. Worn out and grubby, Roosevelt leaves the cathedral before seeing all of it.
Bible reading and York's Roman walls
Skipping church, Roosevelt reads the Bible indoors, then walks along York's old Roman walls and crosses the River Ouse by ferry.
Rowing on the Ouse and rock candy
Roosevelt and his brother Ellie row on the River Ouse. Later he and Conie visit a museum by themselves, and two shillings go to rock candy.
A long rail day to Leamington
The family spends six or seven hours on the train to Leamington, and Roosevelt picks up a book at a station along the way.
Warwick Castle and its Saxon giant
From Leamington, Roosevelt visits Warwick Castle, with its legend of a Saxon giant.
Back to Warwick with the valet
Roosevelt, Ellie and Conie return to Warwick with the family valet and play in a garden.
It rains in Leamington, and in the afternoon Roosevelt plays outside in the garden.
The family travels by train to Oxford, where Roosevelt sees an archery match and the university's colleges.
Headache and a squabble in Oxford
Roosevelt goes to church in Oxford with a headache. When Conie and Ellie make a racket to annoy him, Bamie puts a stop to it.
Arriving in London by hansom cab
The family moves on to London, the three younger children traveling ahead with the valet. Roosevelt, still nursing a headache, gets a ride in a hansom cab.
Let down by the London zoo
At the Zoological Gardens in London, Roosevelt is disappointed to find mostly the same creatures he could see at any other menagerie.
Roosevelt goes back to the London zoo and this time is pleased, finding some rarer animals.
Fishing in Hyde Park and Punch and Judy
In Hyde Park, Roosevelt and Conie haul tiny fish out of the lake. He and Ellie then go to a riding school, and the children catch a Punch and Judy show.
Roosevelt spends the morning at the zoo and the afternoon at riding school, and is troubled again by a headache.
Healthy lungs, then thrown at riding school
A London doctor examines Roosevelt and pronounces his lungs sound. At riding school the same day, he is thrown from his mount.
Roosevelt attends church at Westminster Abbey and looks at the tombs.
The three youngest Roosevelts play in Hyde Park and then visit a waxworks exhibit.
Another day of play in Hyde Park
Roosevelt spends the day playing in Hyde Park.
Boats in Hyde Park, then the British Museum
Roosevelt watches boats on the water in Hyde Park and then goes to the British Museum. A letter his mother wrote around this time survives in print.
Separated from the nursemaid in Hyde Park
Roosevelt, Ellie and Conie head to Hyde Park in the care of Mary Ann, lose track of her, and make their own way home.
Indoor play and the British Museum
Roosevelt plays inside the hotel, spends time in Hyde Park, and then visits the British Museum with the valet.
Asthma sends him to the seaside at Hastings
Roosevelt's asthma grows so severe that his father takes him to Hastings on the coast, where they walk the beach and see the castle.
A gloomy Independence Day by the sea
In Hastings, Roosevelt goes to church and walks along the cliffs, but it is a dreary Fourth of July. His asthma is so bad he lacks the breath to blow out his candle.
Breakfast alone and a croquet win
Roosevelt has breakfast by himself in Hastings, goes out with his father to a spot he calls "Roar valley," and wins a game of croquet.
A paper knife and the trip back to London
His father buys Roosevelt a paper knife before they return to London. A visit to the museum in Hyde Park is foiled because it is closed.
A trip to the Crystal Palace
Crystal Palace again on Mittie's birthday
The three younger children return to the Crystal Palace. It is their mother Mittie's 34th birthday.
Richmond outing and a sibling quarrel
Roosevelt, Ellie and Conie go out to Richmond, and Ellie and Conie get into an argument.
Head on the block at the Tower of London
The whole family tours the Tower of London with a guide in old warder's dress. Roosevelt looks over the armor, lays his head on the executioner's block, and glimpses the Princess of Wales.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at home reading the Bible, then goes to Kensington Gardens.
Blind man's buff and the zoo
Roosevelt plays blind man's buff at the hotel in the morning and goes to the zoo in the afternoon.
The family sails down the Thames and across to Antwerp, and Roosevelt is seasick on the way.
First to step onto the Continent
Roosevelt is the first of the family ashore on the European mainland. In Antwerp he sees a church and the town hall.
Botanic gardens, then on to The Hague
In Antwerp's botanical garden the children play at bear hunting. A rail and boat journey then carries the family to The Hague.
Chinese curios and a glimpse of the queen
At The Hague, Roosevelt visits a museum with Chinese objects and the summer palace, sees the Dutch queen, and notices that the city has horse-drawn streetcars.
A Dutch farmhouse and stories from Father
A carriage ride takes the family to a Dutch farmhouse, where they eat fruit. They go on by train to Amsterdam while his father tells stories.
Roosevelt tours the museum of paintings in the palace and a privately owned gallery in Amsterdam, then the family drives to Delft, a spotless town where he sees wooden figures.
Seven hours by rail to Cologne
The family enters Germany, riding the train for seven hours to Cologne.
Up the Rhine by boat from Mainz
After a train ride to Mainz, the Roosevelts spend eight or nine hours on a boat traveling up the Rhine.
In Frankfurt, Roosevelt sees a museum, a cemetery, the Kaiser Hall and the promenade, eats at an outdoor restaurant, and goes to the zoo with the valet.
The family passes through Heidelberg and continues by rail to Baden.
Donkeys and a hike to the old castle
At Baden, Roosevelt and his father hike up to the old castle while Ellie and Conie ride donkeys.
Verses, the Black Forest, and a letter to Edith
Roosevelt stays in on Sunday to learn verses and read the Bible, then walks in the Black Forest. He also writes to his childhood friend Edith Carow.
The family drives among rocky hills, then takes the train to Strasbourg, where Roosevelt sees the cathedral.
Feeling ill on the way to Basel
Roosevelt is sick as the family takes the train to Basel, Switzerland.
The family heads into the Jura Mountains and stops for the night at Münster around 8 p.m.
Roosevelt spends two and a half hours crossing the Jura, sees a lake and the walled village of Auberg, and buys shoelaces. Back in America, Alice Lee turns eight.
A brook, Bern, and a view of the Alps
After playing in a brook, the family travels by carriage and rail to Bern. Roosevelt sees the cathedral, eats ice cream, takes in the Alps from a hilltop, and tours two museums.
Wildflowers and a ride to Ouchy
Roosevelt and Conie gather wildflowers. After a drive around Bern, the family takes a three-hour train ride to Ouchy on Lake Geneva.
A black cat and a sculptor's shop
Roosevelt wanders around town, spots a black cat, looks in at a sculptor's shop, and reads the Bible.
A rainy day in the grotto
His parents go off to Geneva while rain falls all day in Ouchy, and Roosevelt plays in a grotto.
From Ouchy, Roosevelt travels by steamer and rowboat to the Castle of Chillon and explores its dungeons.
Down Lake Geneva and uphill toward Mont Blanc

The family sails down Lake Geneva to Geneva, sees Mont Blanc, and sets out for Chamonix in a four-horse wagon. On a long climb an extra mule and horse are hitched on; Roosevelt, suffering a sharp pain, walks up himself and arrives at 7.
Climbing Mont Blanc on his own legs
At Chamonix, Roosevelt climbs to about 8,000 feet on Mont Blanc and does it without riding a mule. Back home, Edith Carow turns eight.
Roosevelt goes out on the glacier again, spends time at the hotel, and buys specimens for his museum.
The family hikes to a waterfall along a trail squeezed between steep cliffs, and Roosevelt notes passing a pair of drunks.
Sick on the trail, riding a mule
On an outing Roosevelt writes as "the Shapo," a stomach pain and nausea force him to ride a mule rather than walk.
Drawing birds on a rainy day
Rain keeps the family indoors. Roosevelt draws birds, plays with Ellie and Conie, and listens as Bamie reads aloud to the three of them.
Nineteen miles over the Tête Noire

Crossing the Tête Noire pass, the family logs its mileage: his father 22, Roosevelt 19, sister Bamie 18, brother Ellie 12, mother Mittie 9 and little Conie 3. At the border he stands with a foot in each country.
The family takes the train and then a carriage to Visp, stopping at a waterfall where Roosevelt throws stones.
By mule and on foot to Zermatt
Riding mules part of the way and walking the rest, the family reaches Zermatt.
Roosevelt climbs on foot to a chalet high on the mountainside.
Roosevelt spends Sunday learning verses from the Bible.
Roosevelt walks 13 miles as the family returns to Visp.
Snow at the top of the Eggishorn

The family heads for the Eggishorn by way of Fiesch, with Ellie and his father walking while Roosevelt rides a horse. He reads "Henry of Greece," reaches the frigid summit, and plays in the snow before coming down.
Roosevelt sees the Rhône Glacier, and the family pushes on to Andermatt through a snowstorm. He has a bad toothache.
Roosevelt hikes up a peak the diary calls "Ardorne."
Twenty miles through the Grimsel Pass
The family crosses the Grimsel Pass on foot, Roosevelt covering 20 miles to his father's 22.
Roosevelt labels his crystal collection, plays with Ellie in the park, and attends the English church.
Roosevelt gets his hair cut, goes shopping, plays indoors, and pelts the waiter and chambermaid with balls of paper.
A fall on the Grindelwald glacier
At Grindelwald, Roosevelt buys a tiny butter churn and takes a 20-foot fall on the glacier.
Roosevelt goes up to the Wengernalp and hears two avalanches.
The three younger children stay behind, take a galloping donkey ride, and see a poisonous snake that goes after the chambermaid.
The family moves to Lucerne and goes out on the lake. Roosevelt feels very homesick.
Souvenirs and getting lost with Conie
Roosevelt and Conie buy keepsakes, including picture frames and candy, lose their way, and find their way back to the hotel.
Sick in bed, with stories from his parents
Ill, Roosevelt spends the whole day in bed eating arrowroot, while first his mother and then his father tell him stories.
Still sick in the morning, Roosevelt is left on his own in the afternoon. He draws a landscape and a church, then rips it up.
Croquet, an island row, and homesickness

The children go to Brunnen to play croquet and climb on rocks, and row out to an island. Roosevelt is homesick. A letter from Edith, undated, tells of a pulled tooth and laughing gas and encloses a leaf for him.
Exploring the house in the rain
Ellie is sick and it rains in Lucerne. Roosevelt and Conie explore the house and are spooked by a gurgling noise.
Roosevelt goes on a donkey ride in Lucerne and is again homesick.
A cold day on the Rigi
The family goes up the Rigi, where it is bitterly cold.
Walking most of the way to Zurich
Traveling to Zurich, Roosevelt and his father cover most of the distance on foot.
Church and a bath in Zurich
Roosevelt goes to church and has a bath.
The family travels to Ragaz, close to Liechtenstein. There is talk that Mary Ann may soon be let go.
Pfäfers gorge and a solo castle hike
After visiting the gorge at Pfäfers, Roosevelt and Conie climb trees back at Ragaz, and he walks three miles alone to the castle of Wartenstein.
Picnic high above the Rhine at Splügen
At Splügen the family picnics, and a man drops a stone into the Rhine some 200 feet below.
Roosevelt and his father hike out of Switzerland at 10:30, and he straddles the Italian border. At Chiavenna the journal he has kept ends; he finds Italy cold, gloomy and foul-smelling.
At Cadenabbia on Lake Como, the family is rowed across the water under the moon.
Lakeside villas as the weather clears
Roosevelt sees the Villa Carlotta and Villa Melzi. Rain gives way in the afternoon to what he calls "True Italy of the poets." His mother writes that he is ill with asthma.
After church, Roosevelt visits another villa on Lake Como and sits alone by a waterfall writing in his journal.
Lizards and a moonlit row to Lugano
The family travels by rowboat on Lake Como toward Lugano. Roosevelt catches two lizards, the party steams down Lake Lugano, and they row under the moon.
Isola Bella and a bad night
Sick at Stresa, Roosevelt rides by carriage to Lake Maggiore and Isola Bella and eats lemons. That night he is very ill.
A lost watch and The Last Supper
Roosevelt loses his watch. The family takes the train to Milan, where he sees Leonardo's Last Supper in what he calls "barracks."
Early to the cathedral, rough play
Roosevelt rises at six to see Milan's cathedral. Later the children play "hotel," and Conie gets hurt in a rough game.
Roosevelt, Ellie and Conie stay inside playing games, then get ice cream after dinner.
The family takes the train to Venice. Roosevelt figures he has gotten through some 50 novels since the family sailed, and they ride a gondola after dark.
Gnats, sleeplessness and collapse in Venice
Kept awake all night by gnats, Roosevelt is sick. While the family goes out, he later makes it to St. Mark's but collapses from exhaustion.
Roosevelt stays inside reading and drawing, then takes a gondola ride late in the afternoon.
Feeling better, Roosevelt sees the churches of Santi Giovanni e Paolo and the Frari, the Doge's Palace, and a glassworks. It is his father's 38th birthday.
His watch is found and sent on to him. Roosevelt climbs the Campanile, visits the Lido, and sees a prince and princess glide by in a gondola.
Asthma in Venice on Black Friday
Sick with asthma, Roosevelt still visits a gallery, St. Mark's Square and the Ducal Palace. Across the ocean, the Black Friday gold panic hits Wall Street.
Roosevelt sees St. Mark's Square, the basilica and the glassworks while Mittie and Bamie shop. At midnight the family boards a boat for Trieste.
Asthma, and a cigar as remedy
Asthma keeps Roosevelt up for four hours, and he is made to smoke a cigar for it. The boat reaches Trieste by six; he rests, walks alone and sleeps.
At Adelsberg, Roosevelt walks alone for two hours up a steep hill to a castle. The lane reminds him of Madison, New Jersey.
Twelve hours by rail to Vienna
The family spends twelve hours on the train to Vienna.
Roosevelt is ill and stays inside all day.

Recovered, Roosevelt sees the imperial treasury and the crowns of Charlemagne and Rudolf II, and goes with his father to the natural history museum. Conie turns eight and is honored with a formal outdoor supper at a château.
Schönbrunn, the opera, and no more "baby"

In Vienna the three younger children give up their game of "baby," meet their father at Prince Eugene's palace, and look without success for a riding school. Roosevelt drives out to Schönbrunn with his parents and Bamie and sees the Parliament buildings. Mittie writes that he has suffered two weeks of stomach trouble and near-asthma.
A country rest at Bad Vöslau
Sick again, Roosevelt goes with his father to Vöslau in the countryside, which he thinks resembles Hastings, and has Sunday school in the woods.
Back in Vienna, Roosevelt visits a museum with his parents and Bamie and then sees a doctor with his father.
Roosevelt, Ellie and Conie go to the Ambras collection and see suits of armor.
Letters from home on the way to Ischl
During an eight-hour train ride toward Bad Ischl, Roosevelt reads newly arrived letters from America. Four hours by carriage follow, and the family stays at a German inn.
A six-and-a-half-hour carriage ride, with fourteen horses changed in relays, carries the family to Salzburg.
A nightmare and illness on the way to Munich
Roosevelt has a bad dream about the devil and comes down with what he calls "cholera morbus" during an eight-hour train ride to Munich.
Riding school on a rainy day
It rains in Munich, and the boys go to riding school.
Sick, then a walk at Starnberg
Very ill, Roosevelt is soothed by his mother's stories and rubbing. In the afternoon he, his father and Ellie take a walk at Starnberg.
The royal palace and two galleries
Feeling better, Roosevelt returns to Munich and tours the royal palace and two picture galleries with Bamie and his parents.
Five months gone, seven to go
After a bad night, a homesick Roosevelt counts five months away from America with seven still ahead. The family rides five hours by train to Nuremberg.
Roosevelt sees the churches of Nuremberg.
Twelve hours by rail to Dresden
The family spends twelve hours on the train to Dresden in Saxony.
A harsh chest rub in Dresden
Roosevelt's chest is rubbed so hard that it bleeds. He also sees forests, gets a haircut, and visits the picture gallery.
Roosevelt visits a Dresden china shop and buys Christmas presents.
After church, Roosevelt lies by the fire feeling homesick.
Roosevelt helps Ellie and Conie pick out souvenirs and plays with a "Miss Wolf."
Roosevelt visits the historical museum in Dresden.
Counting animals at the natural history museum
Roosevelt goes alone to the natural history museum and tallies 101 animals, then visits Miss Wolf. His journal for this period ends.
The three children travel five hours to Berlin, in Prussia, with the adults following six hours behind.
A pulled tooth and the royal palace
The whole family visits the dentist, and Roosevelt has a tooth pulled. He also sees the royal palace, the stock exchange and a synagogue.
Roosevelt and Brilliot, a servant, walk four or five miles to Charlottenburg.
The family visits two churches to hear their organs and then attends the American church in the rain.
Sick, with a stop at riding school
Roosevelt is sick, goes to riding school, and otherwise stays indoors.
Illness cuts the Berlin stay short
Sick, homesick and suffering a headache, Roosevelt still goes to riding school and the zoological museum. The family leaves Berlin because he is ill.
After seeing an aquarium, the family rides the train twelve and a half hours to Cologne, where they had been four months earlier.
Eleven presents for his eleventh birthday
In snowy Cologne the family celebrates Roosevelt's eleventh birthday. He receives eleven presents, including a writing desk, and Mittie dresses in full evening attire for his party.
The family takes a six-hour train ride to Brussels.
Rain keeps Roosevelt inside, where he plays with Ellie.
Roosevelt spends the day at the house.
To the market with the valet
Roosevelt walks to the market and plays with the valet.
Shoemaker, then the train to Paris
After a stop at the shoemaker's, the family rides six hours by train to Paris. Another journal volume closes.
In Paris the family settles into pleasant rooms, and Roosevelt rides a merry-go-round.
On a wet day that grows dark early, Roosevelt plays in the hotel and beside the Seine.
Out shopping for Christmas gifts, Roosevelt rubs the phosphorus off matches onto his hands and makes them glow.
On a rainy day Roosevelt visits a fruit market and makes sugar candy.
Mittie pokes fun at Roosevelt for constantly saying "pretty Papa, Pretty Mama."
A sore toe and the Vendôme Column
Despite a corn on his toe, Roosevelt climbs the Vendôme Column with the valet.
A riverside walk and a steam bath
Roosevelt walks by the Seine with the valet and takes a steam bath.
Steam bath with Mother and a new stamp book
Roosevelt takes a steam bath with his mother and buys a stamp album.
Roosevelt marks the halfway point of the trip abroad with a cheer. He and Ellie visit a Russian steam bath.
Roosevelt and Mittie take steam baths, and he sees a doctor with his father. His stamp album now holds 30 stamps.
Sick, and sharing the stamp album
Roosevelt is ill and takes a steam bath. He, Mittie and his father look over his stamp collection together.
Pillow fight and a letter to Edith
Still sick and taking steam baths, Roosevelt gets into a pillow fight and writes to Edith Carow.
Roosevelt stays in, plays with Johnny Lampson, and gets into a scuffle with the chambermaids.
A walk instead of a bath
Roosevelt skips his bath and goes walking with his mother.
His father goes to London while the rest of the family stays in Paris. Roosevelt explores the house with Johnny Lampson and takes a walk.
While Mittie takes a steam bath, Roosevelt and Ellie do gymnastics, and he buys a pop gun. At home in America, Edith Carow writes Conie that she misses her.
Roosevelt and Ellie do gymnastics and go to a little theater. Their rough play with Johnny Lampson gets them told to stop.
Staying in, Roosevelt listens as his mother tells about her 13 siblings and what became of them; four are still living.
In the evening Mittie shows Roosevelt a portrait of Edith Carow, and the sight of her face fills him with longing for home and the past.
Wooden horses and the Arc de Triomphe
After a doctor's visit, Roosevelt plays with Johnny Lampson, sees a theater, rides the carousel, and visits the Arc de Triomphe.
With a stiff neck and headache, Roosevelt writes two letters and feels worse as the day goes on. Edith writes him from America.
The doctor calls and changes Roosevelt's medicine for the third time. He has no appetite and eats only tea and toast.
Roosevelt spends the day indoors again.
Still confined to the house, Roosevelt starts to feel better.
On his sixth straight day indoors, Roosevelt has a visit from Johnny Lampson but is too worn out to enjoy their evening games.
Tears of homesickness on the way to Dijon
The family travels to Dijon. Roosevelt cries from homesickness, wishing to escape a land of people who cannot speak his language.
A cold walk and a night train
In bitter cold, Roosevelt walks around Dijon, and the family spends the night on a train to Marseille.

Ellie is sick, so Roosevelt and his father explore Marseille: the exchange, the harbor and docks, the cathedral, the forts and the old town. He closes his second journal book with a roll call of the children's ages.
Leaving Marseille, the family rides the train until 6:30 and Roosevelt sees the Mediterranean. His father calls the three youngest "bothers," and Roosevelt takes his medicine.
Coins and reading on a rainy day in Nice
It rains in Nice. Roosevelt plays with his coins and reads. The family's two servants are the valet, called "B," and Mary Ann.
Donkey on the beach and Revolutionary ancestors
On the beach at Nice, the adults walk, the two younger children stand by, and Roosevelt rides a donkey. Mittie tells of family ancestors who served in the American Revolution.
Beach, hillside and a far view of the Alps
Roosevelt plays on the beach, as do Mittie and Bamie, runs up a hill, spots the Alps in the distance, and plays with his coins.
Roosevelt goes to the post office with the valet and buys Ellie a knife to replace the one he lost the day before.
Talking over the trip with Mother
On a wet day, Roosevelt plays with tin animals, eats at an English restaurant, and talks with Mittie about the journey so far.
Rowing out to the U.S.S. Sabine
The three youngest play a chasing game, buy gifts for Mary Ann and the valet, and row out to see the American warship Sabine anchored in the harbor.
After a trip to the post office, Roosevelt visits Monaco and its casino, then plays on the hotel steps.
Conie pretends to be sick. Roosevelt goes to church and on a walk, finds the Roman amphitheater dull, and notices painted scenes on the houses.
Along the Corniche to San Remo
Behind four horses and a mule, the family climbs the steep Corniche road 37 miles to San Remo. Roosevelt straddles the French-Italian border, and another journal volume ends.
Roosevelt walks with his mother as the family continues by carriage into Italy. At Finale his father buys cakes, and he and the children toss them to beggars.
The three youngest buy mementos; Mittie and Bamie admire them while their father makes fun of them. Roosevelt goes to church and watches a pageant in Savona.
After a morning romp, the family reaches Genoa and takes a long walk around the sights.
Roosevelt tours Genoa and then goes by train to Chiavari. Ellie loses his knife, Roosevelt gets four coins, and their parents are still behind.
Walking beside the carriage to La Spezia
On a climb over a high mountain, Roosevelt, Ellie and his father walk alongside the carriage past many beggars. From La Spezia they take the train to Pisa.
Roosevelt goes to church in Pisa, sees the Leaning Tower and the cathedral, and attends Sunday school.
Roosevelt climbs the tower and returns to the cathedral. His diary notes the "League of the Cross" for the first time.
A flooded rail trip to Rome
A long train ride through flooding from heavy rain, by way of Livorno, takes the family to Rome.
Rome in the rain on an anniversary
Rain keeps Roosevelt in the hotel, playing and looking at coins; he finds Rome dirty and dreary. It is his parents' 16th wedding anniversary.
Coins, books and a rainy walk
Roosevelt plays with his coins, plays with Conie and Ellie, and reads. After dinner he and Conie go walking in the rain.
Excited about Christmas, Roosevelt plays in the hotel and hangs up his stocking.
Christmas morning and the Pope at St. Peter's
Before six the children burst in on their parents to open their stockings. Later Roosevelt visits St. Peter's and sees Pope Pius IX.
Temple of Vesta and St. Paul's
Roosevelt attends church and sees the Temple of Vesta and the Church of St. Paul.
Roosevelt writes a story, reads and plays.
An eight- or nine-hour train trip in hail takes the family past Albano, Roman ruins, Velletri, Segni and Cassino to Naples. Roosevelt and Mittie read about the mountains along the way.
With Vesuvius in sight, Roosevelt visits the church of San Martino and sees a Pietà.
On a sunny day the family rides two carriages about two hours to Pompeii and sees the House of Diomedes.
Roosevelt climbs Mount Vesuvius, sees lava still smoking, and joins a snowball fight.
Old Naples, Sorrento, and a letter to Edith

Roosevelt sees the old quarter and market of Naples before going on to Sorrento. Answering Edith Carow's letter, he tells her that the day before he poked an alpenstock into the volcano and it caught fire.
Rocks by the sea and a letter to Aunt Annie
Skipping church, Roosevelt goes to the seaside and plays on the rocks. He writes to Anna Gracie.
Back to Naples and the museum
In the rain, the family returns to Naples, where Roosevelt visits the museum.
Volcanic ground and a Roman vase
Two carriages take the family to Lake Agnano, the Grotto of Posillipo, the Solfatara crater and Roman temples. His father gives Roosevelt a Roman vase and coin.
Sick in the night with a cough, Roosevelt is dosed with ipecac. He and Conie stay home while the others go to Pompeii.
Roosevelt reads, plays, buys journal books, rides a donkey and plays on the roof.
On a rainy day, Roosevelt buys a charm, plays with coins, and fishes from the rocks.
On the train, the family stops at Caserta and its villa, and Roosevelt and Ellie play baby.
Meeting an American boy in Rome
Back in Rome, Roosevelt skips church and walks with Ellie. They meet an American boy and invite him to dinner on Thursday.
Rainy-day soldiers and a costume party
Rain falls all day. Roosevelt and Ellie play soldiers and then donkey, and their father throws a dress-up party.
Roosevelt plays with tin soldiers and vaults over posts.
Roosevelt plays by a fountain and is embarrassed by how dirty his clothes get.
Roosevelt goes to a hunt meet and plays with lances.
Roosevelt goes to the post and buys a Roman coin, and he is enjoying Rome.
Roosevelt buys a present for Bamie, then he, Ellie and a boy named Charlie play soldier roughly.
A pleasant Sunday at the Villa Borghese
Roosevelt goes to church, walks in the Villa Borghese gardens, has supper with Mittie and attends Sunday school, and has a very good time.
Roosevelt, Ellie, Conie and George Cromwell go out on the Pincian Hill, meet priests and chase dogs.
Caps, ancient tombs and Bamie's birthday
Roosevelt and Ellie buy caps, shoot at dogs and play soldier. With his mother he goes to see some old tombs. Bamie turns fifteen.
Roosevelt buys a gun and a bugle and plays soldier with George Cromwell.
After a poor night, Roosevelt plays soldiers and chases dogs on the Pincio. His father hosts a grand dinner for 22 guests.
Coffee for a sleepless night, then Albano
Awake for two or three hours in a very bad night, Roosevelt is given coffee. After a visit to the Pincio, he, Ellie and his father ride the rail line out to Albano, where they stay overnight.
His father returns to Rome while Roosevelt and Ellie go on a donkey ride in the rain. The rest of the family arrives.
Roosevelt skips church, plays baby with Ellie and Conie, and explores caverns that fascinate him.
Monte Cavo and the Appian Way
Riding donkeys, the family climbs Monte Cavo and visits Rocca di Papa, dines at Albano, and rides by carriage to Rome along the Appian Way.
George is chosen captain of the boys' soldier company. Roosevelt climbs a tree, plays with coins and has supper with Mittie.
Roosevelt and Charlie Cromwell go to the Pincio to play soldiers; someone ends up pushed into the fountain. Tea and coins round out the day.
Roosevelt buys caps, runs races and plays horse on the Pincio. A guest recorded as T. Bronzen comes to dinner.
The three youngest go to the Pincio and play brigands.
Roosevelt plays coachman and looks over his coins.
Church, Villa Borghese and the Pincio
Roosevelt attends church and Sunday school, visits the Villa Borghese and the Pincio, and plays with coins.
Kissing the Pope's hand on the Pincio

While the children play leapfrog, Pope Pius IX passes in his sedan chair. Young "Teedie" has just boasted that no true American believes in popes, yet when the pontiff holds out his hand, Roosevelt kisses it, as Conie later recalled and his diary confirms.
Prisoner's base on the Pincio with Conie

Roosevelt and his little sister Conie head up to the Pincio gardens in Rome and join a crowd of other children in a game of prisoner's base, then take their supper with their mother, Mittie. Back home, young Edith Carow writes Conie that she has been ordered to set her books aside.
Jostled in the crowd at St. Peter's
After hide-and-seek on the Pincio, the family goes to St. Peter's hoping to see the Pope. In the packed crowd a monk shoves young Theodore, and his father pushes the man back, hard.
A birthday party for Ellie in Rome
It is Ellie's birthday. Roosevelt plays horse on the Pincio, and at five o'clock a crowd of friends arrives for the party, where a girl named Elliese Van Schaack gives him a kiss.
A full day of games on the Pincio: fort, coins, horses, tag, and robbers-and-gendarmes, with Roosevelt leading the gendarmes as their captain.
Another afternoon on the Pincio, this time spent playing bull, tag, and hide-and-seek.
Two brothers go to church alone
Roosevelt and his younger brother Ellie attend church on their own. The diary also names two boys, Theodor Bronzen and Elliott de Briskey, apparently playmates.
On the Pincio, Roosevelt buys his sister Conie a ball.
Rainy day of books and sisters
Rain keeps the children indoors. Roosevelt reads about travel and geography and plays with his sisters Bamie and Conie.
Ball and horse despite the weather
The weather is poor, but Roosevelt still gets out to the Pincio for games of ball and horse.
From the Pincio to the Vatican Loggia
After time on the Pincio, Roosevelt visits the Vatican and its Loggia.
The family drives out by carriage to Tivoli, with Roosevelt perched on the driver's box in the bitter cold. They see the waterfalls and Hadrian's Villa.
Ancient Rome while Ellie stays in bed
With Ellie ill at home, the rest of the family rides by carriage through ancient Rome: the Forum, Trajan's Column, the Colosseum, and the Baths of Caracalla.
A Sunday of church and Sunday school, with battle games in between.
Roosevelt goes to the Vatican to look at its paintings.
A morning on the Pincio, then paintings at the Farnese palace.
Horse and Indian on the Pincio
Roosevelt spends the day at the Pincio playing horse and Indian.
After the Pincio, Roosevelt sees the Castle of St. Angelo.
Goodbyes in Rome as Father falls ill
On a last day at the Pincio, Roosevelt plays horse and bids farewell to the friends he has made in Rome. His father is unwell, and guards go through the family's luggage.
Now in Florence, Roosevelt plays in the garden while his father lies very sick.
Father rallies; Mittie tells old stories
His father is much improved. Roosevelt goes to church with Bamie and Ellie, plays coins and baby in the garden, and listens as his mother tells stories about her own girlhood.
Muddy games and San Marco's paintings
Roosevelt plays baby in the garden and ends up covered in mud, then visits the paintings at the convent of San Marco.
A chilly trip up to Fiesole
The family makes a cold outing to Fiesole, in the hills above Florence.
Roosevelt plays in the garden and looks at paintings in a Florence gallery.
In the garden Roosevelt plays soldiers and coins, and he spends time reading history.
A bit under the weather, Roosevelt still plays soldiers and reads Greek history.
In the garden Roosevelt lays out tiny roads, palaces, and catacombs. He also visits the zoo, has tea, and reads.
Headache keeps him from Sunday school
Roosevelt is sick with a headache and misses Sunday school.
Roosevelt goes back to building little roads in the garden as his brother Ellie celebrates his tenth birthday.
A visit to Mr. Elliott by the river
Roosevelt and Ellie call on a Mr. Elliott, then play in a park along the river in Florence.
Watching the bears at feeding time
With his father sick again, Roosevelt gets a haircut at the barber and visits the zoological garden, where he watches the bears being fed.
The Uffizi and the Ponte Vecchio
Roosevelt looks at pictures in the Uffizi, crosses the Ponte Vecchio, and plays in the garden.
In the garden, Roosevelt, Ellie, and Conie each tend a miniature city of their own.
The family travels to Bologna, passing through eighteen tunnels along the way, while Roosevelt reads Greek history.
Church is held at the hotel in Bologna. Roosevelt watches the pigeons and sees the carnival.
Galleries, then a night train to Turin
After visiting the art galleries in the rain, the family boards a train for Turin following dinner, and Roosevelt plays with his father.
In Turin, Roosevelt sees the armory, the royal palace, and animal skeletons at a museum.
Fourteen hours by rail into France
A fourteen-hour train ride carries the family over steep mountains into France. This is the last entry in this volume of the boy's journal.
After four more hours by train the family reaches Paris. Roosevelt is sick but still finds time for his coins.
In Paris, Roosevelt plays in the Tuileries, visits the shoemakers, and plays coins.
A day of play with boats and toy soldiers in Paris.
Snow falls on a Sunday of church and Sunday school, with coins for play.
A frozen fountain and the Lampsons
Roosevelt sails his boats, finds the fountain frozen over, and spends time with the Lampson family's Johnny.
The fountain is still iced over. Roosevelt plays soldiers and hide-and-seek.
On a rainy day Roosevelt plays soldiers and reads. The diary also mentions a dark closet.
Johnny Lampson comes to dinner after a day of soldiers and boats, and Roosevelt catches sight of Emperor Napoleon III.
Roosevelt and Ellie spend the day sailing their toy boats.

Feeling a little sick, Roosevelt goes by train to Fontainebleau to see the palace. The family inspects Les Ruches, Mlle. Marie Souvestre's private school, where Bamie will remain when the rest go home to America.
Roosevelt goes to church in Paris.
A wet day passed with toy soldiers and boats.
Rain again, and more games with toy soldiers.
Roosevelt takes a walk and plays with his soldiers.
Roosevelt plays with his boat, a ball, and his soldiers.
While Roosevelt plays ball in a Paris garden, his uncle Silas Weir Roosevelt dies back in the United States.
Time in the garden and with the toy soldiers.
Roosevelt and Bamie go to church together, followed by a walk, coins, and Sunday school.
Forty-five minutes locked in a closet
Roosevelt spends three-quarters of an hour shut inside a closet, and plays soldiers.
Roosevelt plays boat and marbles and gazes at the toy soldiers in a shop.
Outdoors in the garden for tag, then time with his stamps.
Roosevelt is taken to the Louvre.
After the Tuileries garden, Fanny Lampson comes over to play and stays for tea.
Roosevelt tours the tombs of Pere Lachaise cemetery and the Pantheon.
Another day of play in the Tuileries garden.
Roosevelt goes to see animals in Paris.
The family drives by carriage to Sevres and tours the china factory.
Roosevelt has his photograph taken and takes a French lesson.
A visit to the Tuileries, then French class.
Roosevelt buys himself a helmet and a bow and arrows.
Sunday brings church and a walk.
Emperor and Prince Imperial review troops
Roosevelt watches Napoleon III and the young Prince Imperial review the French troops in Paris.
The family travels an hour and a half to Versailles.
Nine boys and an army indoors
Nine boys fill the house for a game of soldiers.
During a day of soldiers, Roosevelt gets into a fight.
Roosevelt plays soldiers, with ten of them noted, and ball.
A sick boy goes to Fontainebleau
After a rough night, Roosevelt goes to Fontainebleau and plays in the garden, though he is ill.
The best Easter of his life
At Fontainebleau, Roosevelt walks in the woods and hunts Easter eggs, and calls it the happiest Easter he has known.
Parents and Bamie head to Paris
His father, mother, and Bamie go up to Paris while Roosevelt stays at Fontainebleau playing in the garden.
Roosevelt returns to Paris by train.
Still sick, Roosevelt reads in the shade.
A French lesson and time in the garden.
Roosevelt takes the train to Fontainebleau and scrambles over the rocks.
A day in the park at Fontainebleau among the rocks.
Back in Paris, Roosevelt visits the Tuileries and the Champs-Elysees.
A full day of lessons and play
Garden, soldiers, a French lesson, reading, and play fill the day.
Tag and coins in the rain
Despite rain, Roosevelt plays tag and coins and has a French lesson.
Roosevelt plays horse and fort and reads.
Tearful goodbye to Bamie; on to London

The family leaves Bamie behind at school and everyone cries. After five hours on the train and a slightly queasy Channel crossing from Boulogne to Folkestone, they reach London. Years later Roosevelt said plainly that he disliked the whole trip.
Sent from the table in London
There is no church today. Roosevelt goes to Hyde Park, and at a meal he dips his fingers into the butter dish and is dismissed from the table.
A gift of stamps from a stranger
Roosevelt goes to Wells and to a bank, where a kind gentleman hands him some stamps.
A train ride to Windsor Castle, where Roosevelt sees the farm, stables, and castle, then a stop at Eton before heading home.
A day at the London zoo
Roosevelt visits the zoo in London.
Roosevelt works on his stamps and returns to the zoo.
Roosevelt travels to Liverpool, with his parents coming along after, and meets his uncle Irvine Bulloch. Coins round out the day.
Church and a walk in Liverpool.
Cousins, the beach, and rare stamps
Roosevelt sees his cousins, goes to the beach, and comes across some rare stamps.
At Waterloo, near Liverpool, with Aunt Hattie, Roosevelt digs burrows and trenches.
Rain at Waterloo, and Roosevelt reads.
A cave in the sand hills
Roosevelt plays in the sand hills and finds a cave, then rides into Liverpool in the afternoon.
A visit to the waxworks, then goodbyes to the Liverpool cousins.
The family sails on the screw steamer Russia across the Irish Sea. It rains, but Roosevelt does not get seasick.
With no church aboard, the ship lies at Queenstown, Ireland, for nine hours. Sunday school is held.
The first days at sea are rough and Roosevelt gets seasick, but he recovers fast, makes friends, and plays on deck.
The Russia steams on across the Atlantic; the diary records only that the family is at sea.
The Russia steams on across the Atlantic; the diary records only that the family is at sea.
The Russia steams on across the Atlantic; the diary records only that the family is at sea.
The Russia steams on across the Atlantic; the diary records only that the family is at sea.
The Russia steams on across the Atlantic; the diary records only that the family is at sea.
Church and Sunday school at sea, a fight in the morning, then tag, hide-and-seek, and a game of Colosseum with sixteen children.
The ship takes on a pilot, and Roosevelt sees whales, one of which sprays him with water. His travel journal ends here.
America comes into view. The Russia passes Sandy Hook into New York Bay, and friends meet the family at the pier.
Back in New York, Roosevelt goes round to a neighbor's for breakfast, sees his friend Jimmy, and looks over a collection.
Home all day with Jimmie and Dora
Roosevelt spends the whole day at home playing with Jimmie and chatting with Dora.
The rest of the family goes to the country
While the others head out to the country, Roosevelt stays in the city with his parents and has Jimmie over to play.
Off to Philadelphia with Aunt Susy
No church today. Roosevelt walks with Evelen and reads, then sets off with Aunt Susy on a four-hour train trip to Philadelphia, reading and writing along the way.
China animals and strawberry ice cream
In Philadelphia Roosevelt buys little china animals, shares strawberry ice cream with Aunt Susy, and sees the U.S. Mint. His father arrives that night and goes to the Union League Club.
Roosevelt begins collecting every kind of wild creature he can find, launching a boyhood natural history collection.
Out of the city to Riverdale
After only a few hours back in New York, the family heads up to the country at Spuyten Duyvil in Riverdale for the summer.
Roosevelt scrambles over the rocks and plays in the brook at Spuyten Duyvil.
Tin armor, six nests, and haying
Roosevelt fashions a suit of armor from tin, finds six birds' nests, and helps make hay.
Roosevelt calls on the Dodge family and goes to the beach.
A Sunday of church, photographs, and Sunday school in Riverdale.
Roosevelt builds a hut and spots a bird's nest.
On a rainy day Roosevelt visits his aunt Annie Gracie, climbs trees, and reads.
Croquet, woods, and a ride with Conie
Roosevelt and Conie go riding, play by the brook and in the woods, and finish with croquet.
Roosevelt goes to the dentist and has a tooth filled, then turns to his coins.
Swollen gland sends him to the doctor
A swollen gland takes Roosevelt to the doctor and into New York, where he visits 14th Street and stays the night with his friend Jimmie.
Steamboat game, then back to the country
In rainy New York, Roosevelt plays steamboat, then takes the train back to Riverdale and drives to Yonkers.
A morning in bed, a cow in the afternoon
Sick, Roosevelt stays in bed through the morning. In the afternoon he takes a walk and watches a cow being milked.
Showing off coins; Jimmie and Frank visit
On a rainy day Roosevelt shows an aunt his coins. Jimmie and Frank come up for croquet and hide-and-seek.
Roosevelt builds a fire in his hut.
Aunt Annie visits; the hut is done
Aunt Annie comes to call, and Roosevelt finishes his hut.
All the cherries he can eat
At Aunt Annie's, Roosevelt climbs a cherry tree and eats until he is full.
The diary notes only that it is very hot.
An oriole's nest for the collection
After Sunday school, play, and reading, Roosevelt gets hold of a Baltimore oriole's nest.
Roosevelt goes to see the doctor.
Ill again, Roosevelt goes into the city.
Candy and a walk with Father
In New York Roosevelt walks with his father, has candy, reads, and plays, then returns to Riverdale with his mother.
Roosevelt helps the gardener pull weeds.
A garden, a swim, and a festival
Roosevelt plants a garden and goes swimming while Ellie goes yachting. There is a Sunday school festival.
Church and a Sunday school meeting
Roosevelt attends church and a Sunday school meeting.
Roosevelt swims and is feeling better.
Roosevelt finds two hens' nests and sells the eggs to his father.
Roosevelt works through an hour and a half of French, rides his pony, and swims.
Heat wave brings back his asthma

Roosevelt swims and plays among the woods and rocks. A punishing heat wave strikes New York, and after a healthy stretch since Europe his asthma returns; his family begins moving him from place to place hoping to ease it.
Roosevelt plays croquet and rides his pony.
A letter to Bamie in France
Nineteen people turn out for Sunday school despite the rain, and Roosevelt writes to his sister Bamie.
Roosevelt celebrates the Fourth by setting off torpedoes, firing them at his toy soldiers, and enjoying fireworks.
Roosevelt goes looking for birds' nests.
Chasing a cow and building a fort
A busy day: a swim, a cow chase, a new fort, riding, play, and a bath.
Roosevelt tramps through the woods down to the creek and on to the river.
Roosevelt buys fishing tackle and goes swimming on his mother's 35th birthday.
Roosevelt rides out with his father and goes swimming.
After Sunday school, Roosevelt plays on the hill and climbs trees.
His friend Johnny Elliott leaves, and Roosevelt learns how to swim.
Roosevelt swims again and notes that he is improving.
Roosevelt plays, swims, and rides horses with his father.
War in Europe, worry for Bamie
Roosevelt has lessons, a ride, and a swim. As the Franco-Prussian War breaks out, the family grows anxious about Bamie, still at school in France.
Nests and a swim in the rain
Roosevelt searches for birds' nests and swims, though it rains.
Roosevelt attends Sunday school, writes a letter, and plays around.
Roosevelt spends the day on coins and swimming as France formally declares war on Germany.
Roosevelt is ill and goes to the city.
After playing indoors in New York, Roosevelt and his parents ride six hours by train to Saratoga. Covered in grime, he takes a bath.
In Saratoga, Roosevelt goes to church and to Aunt Lucie's.
A bow from the Indian camp
Roosevelt visits an Indian encampment at Saratoga and buys a bow and arrows.
Roosevelt reports that the day was much the same as the one before.
Roosevelt leaves Saratoga for New York.
Back in Riverdale, Roosevelt plays and hunts birds' nests.
Bow and arrow on the rocks
Roosevelt plays on the rocks and shoots his bow. In Massachusetts, Alice Lee, his future first wife, turns nine.
Roosevelt and Conie go riding with friends.
Roosevelt goes to Sunday school and plays; the record also places him at Richfield Springs.
Boat, train, and coach to Oyster Bay
Though sick, Roosevelt makes the trip out to Oyster Bay, changing from boat to train to coach.
Boats and swimming at Oyster Bay
At Oyster Bay Roosevelt plays with boats, swims, reads, and plays.
Roosevelt returns to Riverdale by boat.
School, archery, and a lost journal
Roosevelt has school, shoots arrows, and plays soldiers. He later notes that his journal went missing for the next several weeks.
Edith Carow, a childhood playmate and later Roosevelt's second wife, celebrates her ninth birthday.
Roosevelt suffers an attack of asthma.
Off to Long Island to breathe easier
The family takes Roosevelt to Oyster Bay in hopes the change will help his breathing.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay and thrilled to be there.
A rainy walk to Otsego Lake
At Richfield Springs, Roosevelt walks to Otsego Lake and back in the rain, with nothing to read.
From Richfield Springs Roosevelt writes Bamie about the long trip from Oyster Bay, ten hours by train and two by boat, and proudly reports that he can now swim.
Bamie is out of the war zone, staying in Liverpool with Uncle Jimmy Bulloch. At Richfield Springs, Roosevelt is with his mother and a crowd of relatives.
The record notes the Battle of Gravelotte between French and German armies, part of the Franco-Prussian War.
The family returns to its New York house on East 20th Street.
Worse in the city, back to Richfield
Mittie brings Roosevelt back to New York, but his health declines, so the two return to Richfield Springs.
A hard night after another attack
Roosevelt has another asthma attack at Richfield. The spasm eases, but he spends a wretched night.
Mother and son return to New York
Roosevelt and Mittie travel back to New York City.
Roosevelt is in New York City.
Roosevelt is back at Riverdale; the record notes only the place.
Roosevelt is back at Riverdale; the record notes only the place.
Roosevelt is back at Riverdale; the record notes only the place.
Roosevelt spends the whole day playing hunt the stag, and meets John Hay, his father's friend and once President Lincoln's private secretary. This journal ends here.
The family moves back into the city house on East 20th Street.
His sister Conie celebrates her ninth birthday.
Roosevelt's father tells the sickly boy that he has a fine mind but lacks the physical strength to match, and that he must make himself strong. Within days the boy starts regular gymnasium work.

Daily trips to John Wood's gymnasium begin, with Mittie bringing Roosevelt and Ellie and patiently watching as Wood teaches them the equipment. The children also begin lessons at Mr. Dodsworth's dancing school on Fifth Avenue, alongside Fanny Smith and Edith Carow.
The record notes a French capitulation to the Germans, entered here as the end of the Franco-Prussian War.
A home gym on the piazza
John Wood helps fit out a gymnasium on the piazza of the family's house on East 20th Street, where Roosevelt begins the dull, repetitive work of building up his chest.
His father and mother mark seventeen years of marriage.
For Christmas, his father presents young Teedie with William Bailey's Our Own Birds.
Bamie home; Uncle Rob to Congress
Bamie comes back from Liverpool, and Roosevelt's uncle Robert B. Roosevelt has been elected to Congress on the Democratic ticket.
Bamie celebrates her 16th birthday, which she spends, like every Saturday, riding horseback with her father. The record also mentions museum visits.
The family is at home at 28 East 20th Street in New York.
His brother Ellie has his 11th birthday at the family home on East 20th Street.
The family remains at 28 East 20th Street.
Roosevelt is in New York City.
Twelve years old in New York
Roosevelt, now 12, is in New York City.
Roosevelt is in New York City.

At 77, Roosevelt's grandfather Cornelius Van Schaack Roosevelt passes away in New York, leaving TR's father at least a million dollars. The same day, rioting involving Irish immigrants breaks out in the city.
Alice Lee, Roosevelt's future first wife, has her tenth birthday.

A family party forms for the Adirondacks: Uncle Cornelius Roosevelt and Aunt Laura, Uncle Hilborne West and Aunt Susy, and cousin West Roosevelt, a boy close to Roosevelt's age. The Carows leave for Renovo, Pennsylvania.
North by rail and stage to Lake George
The party rides the train to Glens Falls, then a stagecoach to Lake George, where they stay at the William Henry Hotel.
Fort ruins, specimens, and a mountain
Roosevelt and two other boys explore the ruins of Fort George, gather specimens, see an Indian encampment, row to an island, swim, and climb a mountain.
Roosevelt tries an airgun, takes a steamboat ride, and goes up a mountain.
Up the lake to Ticonderoga's ruins
The party steams up Lake George aboard the Minnehaha, then takes a stagecoach past the ruins of Ticonderoga. Roosevelt picks up a cannonball the record links to the Battle of Plattsburgh.
Quizzing the stage driver about animals
A train ride of an hour and a half and a stagecoach bring the party to Paul Smith's, sixty miles in all. On the way Roosevelt talks with the driver about wild animals.
After church, Roosevelt kills a snake to keep as a specimen. Back home, Edith Carow turns ten.
Off into the woods with Father
His father, Uncle Hilborne, and the three boys set out by boat on an excursion to Upper St. Regis, practicing with a revolver and landing on an island.
Camped in the woods by Lake St. Regis, the party shelters under their boats in a thunderstorm. Roosevelt describes the animals, and his father reads to the boys by the campfire.
Out fishing, Roosevelt is carried into the stream, and a guide tells the boys a panther story.
Last of the Mohicans by the fire
The party moves back upstream to its starting point. The boys chase the guide around, and his father reads them The Last of the Mohicans.
The party crosses the lake by boat to Paul Smith's.
Roosevelt climbs St. Regis Mountain and watches the wildlife.
Sunday church and a row on the lake.
Roosevelt goes by boat to Martin's on Lower Saranac Lake while most of the party takes the stagecoach.
After a stagecoach ride to Lake Placid, Roosevelt goes hunting for fungus specimens.
The Ausable River and its falls
Near Plattsburgh, Roosevelt sees the Ausable River and its falls.
Roosevelt visits Ausable Glen and rides a steamboat.
A lost hat and a tame bear
The party crosses Lake Champlain and takes the train to White River Junction, Vermont. Roosevelt loses his hat and sees a tame bear.
By train through Wells River and Littleton, the party reaches the Profile House in New Hampshire's White Mountains.
With no church service, Roosevelt climbs Cannon Mountain.
Riding to the Flume with West
Roosevelt and his cousin West ride to the Flume and its waterfall, then climb Bald Mountain twice.
Warned to go easy on the horses
Roosevelt is told to stop riding the horses so hard.
A full day on Mount Lafayette
