Roosevelt, West, and Ellie spend a whole day on the tough climb up Mount Lafayette, watching for wildlife along the way.
A 27-mile stagecoach trip brings the party to the Crawford House, and they go up Mount Willard by carriage.
By mountain car up Mount Washington
From the foot of Mount Washington the party rides the mountain railway to the top. Roosevelt bathes in an emerald pool.
At North Conway, Roosevelt bathes at Diana's Falls and explores a cave.
Roosevelt goes to church in North Conway.
The party crosses Lake Winnipesaukee on the way to Worcester.
Roosevelt arrives in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, by train and tours a glass factory.
The party reaches New Haven without seeing the Springfield Arsenal.
Home again, and a first museum gift

Roosevelt lingers in New Haven, driving about, before following his father, Conie, and Ellie home to Riverdale. That season the young collector gives New York's American Museum of Natural History a bat, 12 mice, a turtle, a red squirrel skull, and four bird eggs. The Carows settle at 200 West 44th Street, and Edith enters Miss Comstock's School.
His sister Corinne has her 10th birthday.
Back on East 20th Street, Roosevelt works out every day and studies English, French, German, and Latin with private tutors. A Mr. Bell begins teaching him taxidermy.
The Great Chicago Fire breaks out, a national disaster noted here for context; the record places nothing of Roosevelt's own on this day.
Thirteen and at home in New York
Now thirteen, Roosevelt is living with his family in New York City; no particular events are recorded.
Parents mark eighteen years of marriage
Roosevelt's parents, Theodore Sr. and Mittie, celebrate their eighteenth wedding anniversary.
Year closes with the family in New York
The year ends with Roosevelt in New York City. The record also flags two items of the moment: Jules Verne's novel Around the World in Eighty Days and the coming creation of Yellowstone in March.
Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her seventeenth birthday.
Roosevelt spends the month at home in New York City; the record notes no specific events.
Roosevelt's younger brother Elliott, called Ellie, celebrates his twelfth birthday.
Taxidermy lessons from Audubon's old companion

Around this time young Roosevelt begins learning to stuff and mount specimens from Mr. Bell, an elderly taxidermist who had once worked alongside John James Audubon. Roosevelt later recalled the lessons in his own words.
Congress establishes Yellowstone as the first national park, noted here for context; the record ties no Roosevelt activity to the day.
March at home in New York
Roosevelt, thirteen, passes March at home in New York City; no particular events are recorded.
April at home in New York
Roosevelt, thirteen, passes April at home in New York City; no particular events are recorded.
May at home in New York
Roosevelt, thirteen, passes May at home in New York City; no particular events are recorded.
Summer at Dobbs Ferry and a first gun

The family settles in for the summer near Dobbs Ferry, where Uncle Hilborne West helps tutor the children and sparks fresh interests. Roosevelt receives his first gun, a 12-gauge Lefaucheux double-barrel, but keeps missing everything he aims at; he admits to his father he can't even make out the letters on a big billboard.
Roosevelt's mother Mittie celebrates her thirty-seventh birthday.
Writing Aunt Annie about the Fourth
Roosevelt writes to his aunt Annie Gracie describing the family's Fourth of July.
The record for this day carries no legible entry.
Roosevelt's mother Mittie is sick through the night with severe nausea, a doctor at her side until dawn.
Still unwell, Roosevelt's mother Mittie spends the whole day in bed after a hard week.

Mittie writes her sister Annie Gracie that she has been laid low by a long bout of dyspepsia. She describes Theodore Sr. teaching Sunday school on the porch while young Teedie sprawls on a blanket with a religious tract, now and then letting out his odd, squeaky laugh. Uncle Hilborne West is visiting too.
Alice Hathaway Lee, the Boston girl Roosevelt would marry eight years later, celebrates her eleventh birthday.
Roosevelt sends Aunt Annie Gracie a funny, illustrated letter poking fun at her upcoming trip to Europe.
Bullied on the way to Moosehead Lake
After an asthma attack, Roosevelt is sent to Moosehead Lake in Maine. Along the way two boys taunt him and knock him around, and he vows to build up his body and learn how to box.
Edith Carow, Roosevelt's childhood playmate and future second wife, celebrates her eleventh birthday.
The record for this day survives only as unreadable OCR, so nothing can be said with confidence.

The entry is badly garbled but appears to place Roosevelt in Maine, likely around Moosehead Lake.

Writing to his father from Philadelphia, Roosevelt asks to stay on until Saturday because he is enjoying himself so much. He visits the Academy, whose library he notes holds 38,000 books.
Roosevelt's father celebrates his forty-first birthday.
Roosevelt's younger sister Corinne, known as Conie, celebrates her eleventh birthday.
Shortly before the family's second trip abroad, Roosevelt finally gets eyeglasses. He later wrote that they revealed a world he had never seen, and his fascination with birds takes off.
Sailing for Liverpool aboard the Russia

The family boards the steamer Russia bound for Liverpool. Once past Sandy Hook, Roosevelt turns seasick and heads to bed. He has packed ready-made pink labels for the specimens he plans to collect. His mother describes him as tall, gangly and bespectacled, with his squeaky laugh.
Crossing the Atlantic on the Russia, Roosevelt is badly seasick all day.
Crossing the Atlantic on the Russia, Roosevelt is badly seasick all day.
Crossing the Atlantic on the Russia, Roosevelt is badly seasick all day.
Crossing the Atlantic on the Russia, Roosevelt is badly seasick all day.
Crossing the Atlantic on the Russia, Roosevelt is badly seasick all day.
Feeling better at last, Roosevelt spends time playing up on deck.
Shipboard life carries on much as it did the day before.
A gale keeps him in his berth
A gale hits the ship, and a sick Roosevelt stays in his bunk.
Rough water in the Irish Sea
The Russia pushes through a rough Irish Sea toward Liverpool.
Landing in Liverpool, hunting for arsenic

The family comes ashore at Liverpool and checks into the Adelphi Hotel, where Uncle Irvine Bulloch, Aunt Ella and cousins greet them. Roosevelt sets out to buy arsenic for preserving specimens, only to meet a wary druggist, and local boys pester him in the street.
Roosevelt turns fourteen in Liverpool and goes to church.
Roosevelt buys birds and skins them, then celebrates his birthday. His gifts: a bag, two pens, two pencils, an inkwell and two penknives.
Roosevelt and his sister Conie browse Liverpool's bookstores, and he spends more time skinning birds.
Roosevelt and his brother Ellie head out to Waterloo, near Liverpool, to play football and read.
Still in Liverpool, Roosevelt goes swimming and spends the day playing.
Arthur Dean and Jimmy call on the family. Roosevelt visits an old bookshop, and the day ends with tea at Waterloo.
At Waterloo, Roosevelt reads Audubon from a copy belonging to his Aunt Hattie.
Roosevelt goes to church in Liverpool; the diary also mentions heavy boots.
Roosevelt and Ellie travel to London with Antoine, the family's courier, and put up at a Brunswick hotel; they will meet the rest of the family in Paris.
In London Roosevelt calls on Arthur Dean and walks the Strand trying to find books. Back home, Ulysses S. Grant wins a second term as President.
Roosevelt takes the train to Dover, gets seasick on the hour-and-a-half steamer crossing to Calais, then rides the rails to Brussels.
Train to Bonn and a cousin visit
Roosevelt travels by train to Bonn, where he sees his cousin West and Frankie Roosevelt at their school.
In Bonn, Roosevelt buys rabbits and birds so he and his cousin West can skin them.
Rainy day of talk and dissection
On a wet day in Bonn, Roosevelt talks and dissects specimens. He is lodging at the Golden Star.
Roosevelt attends church, then spends the day talking at the hotel.
With rain falling and nothing to do in Bonn, Roosevelt finds the day gloomy.
Another day much like the last in Bonn, brightened when West and Frankie come over.
Roosevelt rides the train from seven in the morning until eleven at night to reach Paris, where he stays at the Hotel du Jardin.
Larks, buntings and a changed Paris
Roosevelt buys larks and buntings to skin and takes a walk in the rain. He notices how Paris has been altered since the war of 1870. His parents arrive.
On another rainy day, Roosevelt buys and skins a bunting, shops for Christmas presents and stops at a café.
Roosevelt skins birds through a rainy day in Paris, dines with the Theodore Bronsons, and writes to his uncle Hilborne West.
Church and specimens in the rain
Roosevelt goes to church in Paris and works on bird skins while the rain continues.
Rain is the only thing recorded for the day in Paris.
Roosevelt visits a Paris market, skins specimens and reads.
The whole family leaves for Turin
All the Roosevelts board a train out of Paris, heading for Turin.
The family is in transit toward Italy, the next leg of a journey that will carry them on to Egypt; the record gives no details.
The family stays at a hotel in Turin.
The family takes the train to Bologna, where they visit the churches of San Domenico and Santo Stefano.
After seeing San Pietro and Bologna's market square, the family rides the train down to the port of Brindisi.
The family boards a steamer for Alexandria, and Roosevelt is seasick again.
The steamer carries the family past Greece.
Out on the Mediterranean, the family sees only a handful of other vessels.
At eight o'clock Alexandria comes into view. Roosevelt writes a lively account of coming ashore, including a customs house where bribes changed hands, and the family checks into the Hotel Abbat.
Roosevelt walks around Alexandria and describes what he sees.
Train across the delta to Cairo

A six-hour train ride through the Nile delta brings the family to Cairo and Shepheard's Hotel. Each day after breakfast, Bamie gives Roosevelt, Ellie and Conie two hours of lessons. Theodore Sr. will spend about $2,000 on the Egyptian part of the trip.
Roosevelt attends the English church in Cairo and roams about the city.
Roosevelt and Ellie explore Cairo's bazaars on donkeyback.

A two-hour trip takes the family to the pyramids, where Roosevelt notes the animals along the way and sees the Sphinx. Only the men climb the pyramids, but Theodore Sr., Conie, Bamie and Roosevelt venture inside one.
Roosevelt visits gardens and goes for a donkey ride, delighted that his new spectacles let him see.
A group photograph at the mosque
At the Mosque of Muhammad Ali, a photograph is taken of the Roosevelts together with the Clift family and a party of Harvard men.
Roosevelt misses the howling dervishes but sees the old obelisk at On, also called Heliopolis.
Roosevelt watches the procession of the cloth for Mecca. His father admires a Circassian woman glimpsed in a window.
Roosevelt attends the English church, visits gardens and talks with a Dr. Grant.
While the others outfit the dahabeah, the Nile houseboat named Ibis, Roosevelt wanders and skins birds.
The day is spent shopping in Cairo.
Roosevelt and his father make some purchases, perhaps including the book on Egyptian birds that Roosevelt later mentions in his Autobiography.
In the afternoon the family settles onto the dahabeah, which Roosevelt finds snug and pleasant.
Out shooting with his father near Cairo, Roosevelt brings down the first bird of his life. He also sees the howling dervishes.
A white wagtail and fifteen species
Roosevelt and his father go shooting and bag a white wagtail; on an hour's walk he counts fifteen kinds of birds.
Roosevelt goes to church, pays visits and takes a walk.
After a morning's shooting, Roosevelt visits the museum at Boulaq with its collection of ancient Egyptian objects.
Conie sick, the men out shooting
Conie is ill, while Roosevelt and his father spend the morning shooting.
Theodore Sr. and Bamie go into Cairo and friends call. Out shooting with his father, Roosevelt spots an uncommon white-tailed plover.
A yellow wagtail in five shots
Roosevelt and his father go shooting, and it takes him five shots to get a yellow wagtail.
Three boats start up the Nile
That afternoon a small flotilla heads upriver: four Harvard men aboard the Rachel, the Clift family on the Gazelle, and the Roosevelts on the Ibis.
Aground near Tura, full game bags
Near Tura the boat runs onto a sandbar. Roosevelt and his father shoot in a palm grove and come back with bulging game bags.
A Sunday pelican near Beni Suef
Near Beni Suef the men of the Rachel shoot a pelican on the Sabbath. Roosevelt watches birds, and his parents mark their nineteenth anniversary.
Skinning a pelican aboard the Rachel
Roosevelt skins the pelican on the Rachel and goes shooting. The American consul calls.
Roosevelt skins birds, then rides horses with his parents. Mr. Clift pays a visit.
Christmas gifts are opened in his father's cabin, and Roosevelt's is a double-barreled shotgun. He promptly shoots four doves and calls on the American consul.
Four miles above Beni Suef, Roosevelt and his father go shooting.
An ibis, a lark and a collision
At Fechtan Roosevelt shoots an ibis and a lark. The Ibis bumps into the Rachel, which stays behind, and Mr. Waitman appears on the Water Lily.
About fifteen miles beyond Fechtan the party goes shooting, and local people complain.
The Ibis sails on, and Roosevelt watches the birdlife along the river.
The boat sails and stops at Golosna, where the family buys live doves.
New Year's Eve party on the Ibis

At Minich, Roosevelt and his father shoot eighteen birds, and the Rachel catches up. That night about twenty people from all three boats crowd onto the Ibis to sing, drink eggnog, toast midnight with champagne and dance the Virginia reel.
The Ibis sails on, about seven miles past Roda.
The boat grounds on a sandbar and the crew must haul and pole it free. Roosevelt hears jackals.
Bumps and groundings on the Nile
The day's excitement comes from collisions, groundings and similar mishaps on the river.
Becalmed below the cliffs of Abu Feda
With no wind opposite Abu Feda, the crew tows and poles the boat. The day closes with a splendid sunset over the cliffs.
At Asyut the Ibis breaks its tiller, and Roosevelt sees a mirage.
Donkeys to the tombs of Asyut
Above Asyut, Roosevelt rides a donkey out to ancient tombs covered in hieroglyphs, and he scorns the scrawls left by modern visitors.
The Ibis sails on below Girga.
Good wind and a sketch of the ibis
With a good breeze above Girga, Roosevelt goes shooting and writes a description of the ibis.
The boat makes good time with a strong wind above Qena.

At Thebes Roosevelt walks ashore past the temple of Medinet Habu and the two seated colossi, hands resting on their knees. The boat ties up beside the Temple of Luxor, and that night he sees Karnak under the moon.
Across the river to the Valley of the Kings
Roosevelt crosses the Nile, sees temples on the Valley of the Kings side, and collects several birds.
Roosevelt spends the day walking around Luxor.
Roosevelt visits the tomb of Ramesses III and Belzoni's tomb, and on the way back shoots a wolf.
The boat is tracked upstream to Armant, where Theodore Sr. shoots a hawk.
At Sharuna Roosevelt makes a long hike across a sandbank.
Doves and a misfire near Edfu
Above Edfu Roosevelt walks along the shore and gets some doves, though his gun misfires once.
A full day's sail to Aswan
The Ibis sails from morning to evening to reach Aswan.
Philae by moonlight on Bamie's birthday
Roosevelt hunts in the desert outside Aswan. Everyone dines aboard the Ibis, and by moonlight he sees the ruins at Philae. It is Bamie's eighteenth birthday.
Elephantine Island and Philae by day
After sleeping through much of the morning, Roosevelt visits Elephantine Island and returns to Philae to see it in daylight.
Hunting in the desert near Aswan, Roosevelt sees a jackal.
Roosevelt visits the Nile cataracts at Aswan.
Roosevelt spends the day hunting in the desert.
After one more desert hunt, the Ibis heads downstream in the afternoon. The family has to turn around because Theodore Sr. must be in Vienna by May 1.
Roosevelt hunts along the river and sees the ruins of Kom Ombo at sunset; the boat sails through the night.
A cheerful letter to Aunt Annie
Near Kom Ombo Roosevelt visits a ruin and writes to Aunt Annie Gracie that he is having a fine time.
Roosevelt tours the temple at Edfu in the morning and shoots in the afternoon.
El Kab's tombs and on to Isna
Roosevelt sees the temple and tombs of El Kab, and the boat reaches Isna in the afternoon.
At Isna Roosevelt sees the temple of Khnum and goes shooting.
Returning to Thebes, Roosevelt spends the day shooting.
On a daylong shooting trip at Thebes Roosevelt takes fifteen birds and visits Medinet Habu. He has shot up so much on the journey that his clothes no longer fit.
At Thebes Roosevelt tours Karnak and collects some specimens. His sister Corinne writes to Edith Carow back home.
The family holds Sunday services, and Roosevelt returns to Karnak.
Roosevelt goes out shooting and brings back a crane, snipe and pigeons, while his father and Ellie visit a tomb on the far bank.
Stopping two days at Qena, the family visits the Temple of Dendera, and Roosevelt goes shooting.
Roosevelt spends the day shooting at Qena.
The boat is rowed downstream to El Balyana, and Roosevelt shoots.
Roosevelt sees the temple at Abydos and kills sixteen pigeons.
After a morning of shooting, the crew rows all day, and the Ibis falls in with the boat Zingara.
Father preaches to the Rachel's party
The passengers of the Rachel come aboard to hear Theodore Sr. read a sermon. Roosevelt writes to Aunt Annie Gracie.
Roosevelt goes shooting and later takes tea.
At Beni Hasan Roosevelt heads out to shoot.
Rowing Ralph Waldo Emerson to lunch

After touring the Beni Hasan tombs and shooting an owl, Roosevelt helps host Ralph Waldo Emerson and his daughter Ellen for lunch, rowing them over to the family boat himself. Ellen later wrote home describing the ruddy-cheeked, blue-eyed boy at the oars.
Roosevelt shoots with his father near Beni Suef. The Ibis runs into another boat, the Moorkat, which smashes the front cabin.
The boat sails all day toward Memphis, with choppy water in the afternoon.
The Serapeum and back to Cairo
At Memphis Roosevelt sees the Serapeum and the Apis pits, kills two ibises and arrives back in Cairo in the afternoon.
The family goes to church in Cairo and continues living on the boat.
Still on the dahabeah, Roosevelt kills birds on a rainy day.
The family leaves the boat for Shepheard's Hotel; it rains.
Roosevelt idles about the city in the rain.
On another rainy day Roosevelt visits Dr. Grant's.
First look at the Suez Canal
At Ismailia, Roosevelt sees the Suez Canal and stays at the Hotel Pagnon. The women of the family go by way of Alexandria to Port Said, where the men will meet them.
Up the canal to Port Said
Roosevelt takes a steamer up the canal to Port Said and stays at the Hotel de France. His asthma flares.
On board the steamer Alphe, Roosevelt and the men rejoin the rest of the party.
Landing at Jaffa, a night in a monastery
The party lands at Jaffa and rides three hours to Ramleh, lodging in a monastery. Theodore Sr. persuades the monks to let the women stay as well.
Roosevelt shoots a kestrel and a lark, then rides to Jerusalem, outracing Mr. Jay on horseback. He finds the city surprisingly small; the family stays at the Damascus Hotel.
Roosevelt visits the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Garden of Gethsemane.
Roosevelt sees the Mosque of Omar.
After a morning hunt, Roosevelt goes to the Wailing Wall and the tombs of the judges and kings. Ellie turns thirteen.
Roosevelt visits a convent, buys photographs and goes riding.
Roosevelt sets out on horseback for the Dead Sea over a rough road. The caravan counts some 35 pack animals and 25 people, with Bedouin guards, and camps near Jericho.
Roosevelt bathes in the Jordan, which strikes him as no bigger than a creek, then swims in the Dead Sea and finds he can't sink.
After a convent visit, the party rides to Bethlehem by way of the Pools of Solomon. Theodore Sr. pays guards to let them into the site of the Nativity.
Roosevelt rides to Hebron, sees Abraham's Oak and the mosque, and goes shooting.
Back in Jerusalem, the day is rainy.
Farewell to a horse named Grant
Roosevelt rides to Jaffa and boards ship, where he is seasick. He is sad to say goodbye to the horse he rode and named Grant.
The family sails to Beirut and stays at the Hotel d'Orient. Roosevelt rides a horse and suffers an asthma attack.
In Beirut the party tests horses for the overland trip.
A ride of about seven hours brings the party to Ain Tufeh. Roosevelt and Ellie are stuck with poor mounts.
Off the Diligence Road to Abla
The party follows the Diligence Road until lunch, then turns off and meets people at Abla.
A three-hour canter from Abla brings Roosevelt to the grand ruins of Baalbek, where he shoots a finch.
After shooting several birds in the morning, the party rides to Syrahayi and spends a bitterly cold night in tents.
The party rides to Sukr El Wady. That night Roosevelt is struck by a severe asthma attack along with cholera morbus.
On a showery day Roosevelt hunts and spots jackals that had killed a goat; he gives chase but they escape. The party reaches Damascus.
Roosevelt sees the horse market in Damascus and bargains in the bazaars for a suit.
Roosevelt tours the Mosque of St. John, climbs a 220-step minaret for the view, and goes shooting with the British consul.
Roosevelt goes shooting and brings back several birds.
After another day of shooting, men from the British consulate dine with the family.
Ten changes of horses to Beirut
On the road back to Beirut, Roosevelt sees gazelles; the party switches horses ten times.
In Beirut, Ellie is sick; Roosevelt goes to church.
Roosevelt and Conie dine with Mr. Bliss and his family while Ellie remains ill.
The family sails from Beirut at seven aboard an Austrian steamer; Ellie is still sick.
The steamer passes Cyprus. Ellie is still unwell.
Far from land, birds alight on the ship, and Roosevelt pays to have them so he can skin them. Ellie is still ill.
Specimens from the sailors off Rhodes
The sea is too rough to land at Rhodes, but sailors catch specimens for Roosevelt. In the afternoon the ship runs along the coast of Asia Minor, and Ellie improves.
The steamer reaches Smyrna, where the family transfers to another ship.
Candy and tag on a paddle steamer
On a small paddle-wheeler bound for Athens, Roosevelt buys candy, gets seasick and plays tag.
Seasick still, Roosevelt reaches Piraeus and takes a carriage up to Athens, where he sees the Acropolis. The men and women of the party lodge at separate hotels.
By carriage, Roosevelt tours the ruins of the Olympieion, a Greek theater, the Acropolis and the Parthenon, in the rain.
Areopagus, then a ship for Constantinople
Roosevelt goes back to the Acropolis and climbs the Areopagus, then drives to Piraeus to board an Italian steamer for Constantinople.
The steamer reaches Smyrna in the afternoon, and Roosevelt walks through the town.
The steamer does not get under way until six in the evening.
The ship passes through the Dardanelles and the Sea of Marmara while Roosevelt plays on deck.
At Constantinople the family rows ashore, walks to the Hotel d'Angleterre, and attends church.
Candle fight with the Lawrence boys

Roosevelt rides out with Frank and Tom Lawrence, who stay for dinner and games of muggins. He, Ellie and Tom end up in a candle fight, flinging hot wax at each other. He writes Edith Carow, mentioning that he has lost his gun.
Roosevelt visits the ancient walls and towers of Constantinople.
Sightseeing on horseback while the others ride in carriages, Roosevelt is thrown. He sees the Süleymaniye Mosque and Hagia Sophia and is sick that night.
The Lawrences and Roosevelts go together to the Sultan's palace, and Roosevelt sees the Sultan.
The Lawrence family leaves for Brindisi.
Midnight sailing into the Black Sea
The family boards a steamer at ten in the evening and sets out at midnight across the Black Sea toward Romania.
Seasick, Roosevelt reaches Varna at six in the evening and transfers to a riverboat on the Danube.
The riverboat steams up the Danube all day through green, rolling country, and Roosevelt suffers a severe asthma attack.
Between Serbia and Austria the family changes boats and then boards a train.
The family reaches Pest around one o'clock, stays at the King of England Hotel, visits a picture gallery and climbs the hill.
The family checks into the Grand Hotel in Vienna. Theodore Sr., who sits on the exposition's board of directors, prepares for its opening.
Nothing in particular fills the day.
Cousin West Roosevelt, Frank, Aunt Mary and the Misses Tiny and Gertrude Roosevelt pay a visit. Roosevelt buys a rabbit, dissects it, and plays.

Roosevelt sums up the past week in Vienna in his diary as pleasantly uneventful, spent skinning birds or rabbits. West leaves for Bonn, and Ellie and Theodore Sr. go to Dresden.

Edith Carow writes a school essay called 'Port Washington,' arguing the virtues of Oyster Bay over Long Branch, New Jersey. Her family summered at both.

Back in New York, Roosevelt prepares for college under tutor Arthur Hamilton Cutler, sharing lessons with his cousin West and brother Elliott. He shines in science, history, geography, German and French, but lags in Greek, Latin and math.
Six to eight hours of study a day
Roosevelt is putting in between six and eight hours of schoolwork each day.
Theodore Sr. and Mittie mark twenty years of marriage.
The boys' own Roosevelt Museum of Natural History holds a meeting; its minutes were later published by historian Paul Russell Cutright.

Corinne, Edith Carow, Fanny Smith and eleven other girls start a club called P.O.R.E., first the 'Paradise of Ravenous Eaters,' later the 'Party of Renowned Eligibles,' and the D.L.A.C. writing club carries on. The Roosevelts are now truly wealthy: Theodore Sr. does charitable work and handles the reins of a four-in-hand coach, and the mansion hosts formal dinners often.
Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her 19th birthday.

Roosevelt goes out to Oyster Bay with his mother and Conie. Everything there reminds them of his father, which makes the start of the stay painful.
Roosevelt rows his skiff around Centre Island, kills an oldsquaw duck and shoots two muskrats in a brackish pond.
One more muskrat, then the city
Roosevelt bags a muskrat in a tiny brook before returning to New York, where Bamie is just back from Denver.
A hymn from Conie, thoughts of a wife
Conie copies out a hymn of consolation for Roosevelt. He writes that he has lost the one person he told everything, and wonders who the wife will be who might one day fill that place.
Home in New York, nothing noted
Roosevelt is home in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
The chronology places Roosevelt in New York and notes no events.
Roosevelt is in New York City with his family; the day has no entry.
Mother sees him off to Boston
Roosevelt boards the overnight boat for Boston, with his mother coming down to say goodbye. On board he is homesick and grieving for his father.
Roosevelt settles back into his small room in Cambridge, and his friends give him a hearty welcome.
Roosevelt notes that a month of hard study stands between him and the end of term.
Easier at college than at home
Roosevelt writes that the sharpest grief is passing, though nights are still hard. College holds fewer reminders than home, and the Bible chapters his father loved bring him both joy and sadness.
Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; the record notes nothing else for the day.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Cambridge and logs no letters or events.
Roosevelt teaches what he expects to be his final Sunday school class until October.
Strong grades, a proud father remembered
Roosevelt's marks are excellent, and he recalls how proud his father was of his progress.
Roosevelt shaves off his whiskers and takes no end of ribbing from his friends. He also takes up lawn tennis.
Kept indoors by gloomy weather, Roosevelt thinks about his father at length, and for once the memories bring him only happiness.
Roosevelt is sorry to learn that his friend Hal Minot has left college, remembering how kind Minot was during his worst days of grief.
Off to Minot Weld's for the weekend
Roosevelt heads to Minot Weld's home for the evening, planning to stay until Monday.
Roosevelt and Minot Weld poke around the farmyard in the morning, then drive over to visit Dick Saltonstall.
Roosevelt hears a brief sermon he likes and reflects on how widely his father was loved.
Roosevelt gets back to Cambridge early in the day.
Roosevelt keeps working hard but admits his marks matter less now, since he valued them most for his father's pride in them.
Roosevelt and the friends who share his club dining table have their picture taken.
Three months on, a boat to New York
Three months after his father's death, Roosevelt and Harry Chapin catch the evening Fall River line boat to New York.
Arriving in New York at dawn, Roosevelt takes a morning train to Oyster Bay to join his mother. He finds the countryside lovely, collects a warbler and spends the night.

After noting plenty of warblers at Oyster Bay and shooting two squirrels, Roosevelt goes into the city and straight out to Uncle Corneil's place in Orange, New Jersey, where the whole family and the Gracies make a fuss over him.
Roosevelt spends a quiet Sunday in Orange, New Jersey, where he last stayed years ago with his father. Being with the family lifts his spirits.
Roosevelt goes into the city early and takes the overnight boat to Boston.
Roosevelt reaches Cambridge early in the morning.
Roosevelt is deep in exam preparation.
Missing Father's advice on his future

On a walk into town with Jack Tebbetts, whom he calls a rough diamond, Roosevelt is moved by his friend's words about his father. He writes how lost he feels without his father's guidance on what to do after college.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Cambridge and logs no letters or events.
No entry for the day at college
Roosevelt is at college in Cambridge, with no activity written down.
Roosevelt spends Sunday with the George Minot family, hears a sermon on finishing whatever one starts, and takes a long afternoon walk.
Back in Cambridge, Roosevelt is putting extra effort into French, which he despises, amid poor weather.
Roosevelt is keeping fit with lawn tennis and the occasional row on the river in a racing shell.
Dick Saltonstall comes to the Delta Kappa Epsilon theatricals, and Roosevelt is pleased he will join their table next year. Several students, Pellew among them, drink far too much.
Feeling ill and feverish, Roosevelt has a vivid dream about his father that leaves him sad and lonely.
Bob Bacon flies at Beacon Park
At the Harvard Athletic Association's foot races at Beacon Park, Robert Bacon turns in an impressive time.
French exam, a loss to Yale
Roosevelt sits his French midyear exam, and the Harvard baseball team is badly beaten by Yale.
With his exams piling up, Roosevelt studies on a Sunday and feels ashamed of it.
Roosevelt takes his year-end anatomy exam.
Roosevelt helps about six classmates prepare for the next day's exam.
Roosevelt sits his annual rhetoric exam.
Roosevelt takes his year-end German exam.
Cool weather helps Roosevelt study. His sophomore marks average 89, from a 96 in German I down to a 51 in French, and the year at Harvard cost him $2,049.
Roosevelt takes his annual French exam after a week of feeling poorly. Harvard's freshman nine trounces Yale's class of 1881.
With the spring's hard work behind him, Roosevelt catches himself still imagining his father's pleasure at each success.

Roosevelt credits his Boston friends' hospitality with brightening college life. Jack Tebbetts invites him to Schooner Head for a month and Harry Shaw for a Sunday. With his club table disbanded, he now eats at Memorial Hall beside Gorham Peters.
Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; the record notes nothing else for the day.
Botany exam, then off for summer
Roosevelt finishes his botany final and leaves Cambridge that evening, heading for Oyster Bay as the term ends.
Roosevelt reaches Oyster Bay around noon and finds every corner of the house tied to memories of his father.
Warblers, a ride and a cry for Father

Roosevelt collects a parula warbler and a grasshopper sparrow in Fleets Woods and takes a fine ride on Lightfoot. Annie Murray is visiting Conie, the Gracies are in town, and his grief breaks through again.
Roosevelt sands and varnishes his boat. He is grateful for his family's affection but wishes his mother and Bamie would stop quarreling.
Four months after his father's death, Roosevelt spends the sermon picturing him in his familiar corner of the family pew.
Roosevelt is up with the sun for a long hike, back by nine, and spends the rest of the day building his boathouse.
Rainy day of chores, a petted son
On a wet day Roosevelt divides his time among the boathouse, his gun and his rowboat, and worries that his doting family will spoil him.
Roosevelt and Annie Murray ride out to Syosset and back through Laurel Hollow, then takes her rowing. He finds her sweet, pretty and clever; she leaves the next day.
Pine Island and the season's first swim
Roosevelt rows to Pine Island, collects a pine warbler and takes his first swim of the year. He notes that all the Roosevelt young men but him are now in business.
Fanny Smith has come to visit, and cousin West Roosevelt, who has loved her for three years, comes for tea. Roosevelt rows her to Cooper Bluff, where they race down the slope like children.
Roosevelt picnics at Yellow Banks with Fanny, Conie and West, and in the afternoon takes Fanny on a long ride. The Gracies arrive for a stay of several weeks.
After church Roosevelt sets out for Harvard to take his last two exams, stopping for tea at the family's New York house, which feels empty and desolate.
After a botany exam, Roosevelt explains that he did badly on French three weeks earlier because asthma kept him awake the night before. He shrugs it off.
After his final German exam, Roosevelt is surprised to be elected to the A.D. Club. He judges his second Harvard year happy and useful, and boards the night boat for New York.
Roosevelt visits Cassin in New York before going out to Oyster Bay. He recalls his father pacing the floor for hours carrying him through childhood asthma attacks.
Roosevelt shoots poorly with the rifle, rows to Plum Point and goes riding.

Roosevelt describes his days of riding, tramping after specimens and rowing or sailing, gun in hand. He resolves not to be gloomy, since his father was always cheerful, and gallops twenty miles on Lightfoot.
Sailing to Lloyd Neck with Alfred
Roosevelt rows to Plum Point and back, then sails with Alfred to Lloyd Neck for lunch and some shooting. In the afternoon he rides with two girls; the day's bag is two herons and two sandsnipe.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; nothing else is recorded for the day.
A chickadee nest and a sunburn
Roosevelt finds a chickadee nest on Pine Island and takes Nellie Beekman riding. His sunburned face, he jokes, looks like an undercooked lobster, and he frets about Elliott's friends.
Roosevelt rows around Centre Island in two hours, shooting along the way and taking on water in a heavy sea. A long gallop on the flat Long Island roads follows; he bags two sandpipers.
Water lilies and a supper sail
Roosevelt rides to Brookville and Glen Cove, walks Fleets Woods with his mother, drives Conie to Cold Spring for water lilies, rows to the marsh, and sails with Elliott at dusk, eating dinner aboard.
At New London for the boat race
Roosevelt travels to New London for the Harvard-Yale race, staying at Harry Chapin's with Minot Weld and Jackson.
Harvard wins the race handily and Roosevelt shouts himself hoarse. He takes the night boat to New York that evening.
Back at Oyster Bay, Roosevelt buys a Sharps rifle, and Harvard takes the baseball championship.

A sermon line strikes Roosevelt, who credits his faith with carrying him through his grief; the family spends the evening singing hymns. Meanwhile President Hayes removes Chester A. Arthur and puts Edwin A. Merritt in charge of New York's customhouse.
Target practice and a tan at Tranquility

Summering at the family's Oyster Bay house, Roosevelt tests a new rifle and scores 67 of 100, calling himself a poor marksman. Rowing has bronzed his upper body, his horse has gone slightly lame, and the swimming is a delight.
Rifle practice, then a farewell visit in town
Roosevelt improves to 71 of 100 at the rifle, then heads into New York City to see Annie Murray, who leaves for Europe the next day, and spends a pleasant evening calling on her.
Seeing Annie off, then a night sail

At seven in the morning Roosevelt boards the steamer Russia to bid Annie Murray goodbye, finding her pretty but a touch cross. He accompanies Aunt Susie on the trip to Oyster Bay, and that night he and his brother Elliott sail Elliott's 21-foot Daphne across to Rye Harbor, dropping anchor at 1:30 a.m.
Fourth of July sail home from Rye

Roosevelt and Elliott pass the morning and have dinner at the Bulkleys' near Rye, then set off for home at 4:15 p.m., not reaching their Oyster Bay mooring until eleven. The long sail calls up memories of the brothers' many earlier cruises together.
A tender talk with his mother
Roosevelt and his mother Mittie talk at length, sweetly and sadly, about his late father. Uncle Jimmie Gracie stays over from the city, and he and Roosevelt spend time sailing and rowing.

Roosevelt rows eight miles around Centre Island, logging each landmark against the clock, though low tide forces a half-mile detour and the portage eats 14 minutes. In the afternoon he outshoots Alfred at the rifle, 54 to 18.

Roosevelt writes that he is heartsick for his father. At evening singing the family cannot get through a hymn they last sang together on the Sunday he died, and Roosevelt reads Isaiah 55, one of his father's favorites, at prayers.
Winning a rifle match on Mittie's birthday
On his mother's 43rd birthday, Roosevelt wins a shooting match against his cousins West and Emlen, 57 to their 48 and 49. His horse has nearly recovered from its lameness.

Marking five months since his father's death, Roosevelt reflects that he feels much older and must now solve his own problems instead of bringing them to his father, whose words and gestures he still recalls with startling clarity.
Stuck in the mud at Lloyd Neck

Rowing around Lloyd Neck, Roosevelt bogs down in the mud flats while carrying his boat across the isthmus and struggles to free himself. On the way home a thunder squall catches him in a stiff southwest wind. Fifteen miles, two plover and two gulls.
Roosevelt sails with West and Alfred, picnic lunch aboard, and splits the rest of the day between riding and rowing. In his diary he frets that so remarkable a father deserved a worthier son.
Rained in, sizing up his friends

Rain keeps Roosevelt indoors for the first time all summer. He takes stock of his five closest friends: Elliott and Jack Elliott think too well of him, West and Emlen too little, and Alfred judges him about right.
A daily run through the woods
Roosevelt runs a mile flat out through the woods and plans to make it a daily habit.
Pascal and doubts at Communion Sunday

On Communion Sunday Roosevelt copies out a line from Pascal warning against both excluding and relying only on reason, and writes that he finds materialism and superstition equally distasteful. During church he broods on feeling less useful than his father, yet ends on a note of faith.
Hot row and a long gallop
In dead calm and fierce heat at high tide, Roosevelt rows around Centre Island again, the portage this time taking only five minutes. Later he and Emlen gallop out beyond Wheatley and around it.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

Roosevelt and West ride out on a cool, cloudy morning, reach Smithtown by 10:45, push on to Lake Ronkonkoma for supper, and return to Smithtown to sleep. About 35 miles, and his horse finishes as fresh as it began.
Back from Smithtown in the heat
Roosevelt rides home from Smithtown to Oyster Bay in two and a half hours on a very hot day.
Twenty-five miles by oar to Rye

Leaving at 5:15 a.m., Roosevelt rows across to Rye Beach by way of Rocky Point and Oak Bluff, then rows home that evening, a round trip of more than 25 miles in calm, heavy heat. He spots a stormy petrel.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.
Roosevelt's diary for this Sunday holds a single line of scripture, a plea from the Gospel of Mark.
Roosevelt hikes far through woods and fields with his shotgun and brings back four woodcock and two doves.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.
Visiting the sick, then the Dickeys

In New York City Roosevelt calls on his ailing friend Cassin, then spends the evening with the Dickey family, whose warmth he loves. Young Charles Dickey will enter Harvard next year, and Roosevelt promises himself to help him.
Roosevelt heads back out to Oyster Bay from his stay near the city.
Rigging a sail on his skiff
Roosevelt fits his small outrigger skiff with a leg-of-mutton sail on a seven-foot mast and takes her out. She points poorly into the wind but holds steady and moves briskly downwind.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.
Marsh shooting on Alice Lee's birthday

On the day Alice Lee, his future wife, turns 17, Roosevelt rows to Lloyd Neck and paddles the winding marsh channels at high tide, taking shots at herons and snipe. A southerly breeze lets him sail several miles out into the Sound. Elliott leaves on a three-week holiday.
Rainy woods, then a fine ride
Despite rain, Roosevelt roams the woods with his gun in the morning, bagging a dove and a wild pigeon, and enjoys a splendid ride in the afternoon.
Roosevelt borrows Alfred's boat and circles Centre Island in an hour and 24 minutes.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.
Starting at ten, Roosevelt rows around Lloyd Neck past the Huntington Harbor lighthouse and is home by 1:45. A dead-high tide trims the portage to four minutes.
Aiming for Greenwich, landing in Darien

Roosevelt and Emlen sail across the Sound meaning to reach Greenwich but misjudge which side of Shippan Point to pass and end up at Darien. Roosevelt notes he has ridden his horse every day he has been home this season.

Roosevelt admires the scripture carved over his church door and writes that he puts no stock in faith without deeds. He has been reading the published memorial to his father and resolves to live as his father would have hoped.

Roosevelt hunts woodcock over some 25 miles of rough country, where the birds now hide in dense brush. He misses more than half his shots and comes home with seven, he and the dog both worn out by the heat.
A birthday gift for Edith Carow
For Edith Carow's 17th birthday, Roosevelt sends her a bonbonniere. His sister Corinne also writes Edith an affectionate letter about her future.
Roosevelt's good friend Jack Elliott arrives at Oyster Bay for a visit of five or six weeks.
Sail, oar and paddle to Lloyd Neck

With a following wind, Roosevelt and Jack Elliott make good time to Lloyd Neck using sail, oars and paddle together. They hunt the lagoons, lunch, fight their way out of the marsh at dead low tide and row home into a headwind, with two yellowlegs and two herons.
Six months gone, a glorious sail

Roosevelt and Jack sail in a near-reefing breeze without shortening canvas. He calls Oyster Bay the ideal place for young men and wonders if anyone could be happier, while noting it has been six months since his father died.

Roosevelt's Harvard rank list comes, showing an average near 85, a ten-point gain over the year before, with his best marks in German and natural history. He is pleased and thinks his father would have been too, though he is laid up with cholera morbus.
Still ill, Roosevelt misses church for nearly the first time that year. With idle hours, a rarity for him, his thoughts keep returning to his father.
Mosquito portage and a note from Edith

Roosevelt and Jack row to Plum Point, haul the boat 200 yards over miserable, mosquito-thick ground into the big marsh behind Centre Island, then hunt, lunch and sail home. Edith Carow has sent a sweet thank-you for her birthday gift.
Riding the tide through Lloyd Neck marsh
Roosevelt and Jack row to Lloyd Neck, going into the marsh as the tide rises and coming out as it falls. A stiff southerly holds them out until late afternoon. One yellowlegs, one sand snipe.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

Roosevelt hunts woodcock from eight to five without stopping to eat or rest, testing new knickerbockers, gaiters and hunting shoes. The cover is so thick he misses two shots in three, yet he takes six birds and feels completely fresh.
Edith visits; caught in a squall
Edith Carow arrives for a two-week stay with Corinne. Roosevelt, Emlen and Jack sail to the Connecticut shore and run into a heavy rainstorm on the way back.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.
Roosevelt, Edith, Corinne, Jack and Emlen sail out for a picnic lunch at Yellowbanks. He starts teaching Jack to box, gets the better of Emlen in a bout, and loses to him at the rifle.
Roosevelt rows Edith out toward Lloyd Neck and spars with Jack and West. Riding with West, he hears all about his cousin's devotion to a young woman named Fanny and is touched by how smitten West is.
Roosevelt drives Edith to Cold Spring to gather water lilies, a lovely morning together. In the afternoon Elliott sails in on the Waterwitch with cousin Jack Roosevelt after a three-week cruise.
Family sail and tea at West's

Roosevelt, Elliott and Jack take their mother, Edith and Corinne sailing. That evening a large family party has tea at West's, after which Roosevelt and Edith walk up to the summer house. He worries his hard ride that day may have hurt his horse.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.
Having warned a dog's owner after the animal harassed him on horseback, Roosevelt carries out the threat while riding with West, killing it with his revolver as it runs beside his horse.
Roosevelt notes how much he values the family habit of morning and evening prayers on Sundays.
A dawn gallop, then off on the Addie

On a crisp, clear morning Roosevelt rides twenty miles at a gallop with Emlen. Around noon he, Emlen, West and Jack board the Addie for a short cruise, reaching New Haven about ten that night in light air.
Lazy day under sail to New London
Light winds keep the Addie under way until 8 p.m. before she reaches New London. The young men swim, read the New Symposium, climb the rigging and play whist.
The party sails on to Greenport in fitful breezes. With hundreds of cartridges aboard, they fire their revolvers at anything that surfaces, from bottles and buoys to sharks and porpoises.

In a steady breeze the Addie sails all day along Long Island's low, sandy shoreline. Roosevelt spends long stretches up in the crosstrees; the rest goes to whist and arguments about materialism and politics.

The Addie reaches Oyster Bay at 1 a.m. and the crew comes ashore for breakfast. Roosevelt has loved the cruise, and in the afternoon he goes sailing again with Jack and Alfred. Corinne writes Edith that her visit was worth another painful goodbye.
Roosevelt and Jack row nearly twenty miles after sea coots without seeing a single one. George Minot arrives for a few days' visit.

Roosevelt talks with Uncle Jim about what he will do with his life and admits he has no idea what follows college. Missing his father's guidance keenly, he decides his job for the next two years is plain: study hard and live as a brave Christian gentleman.

A strong westerly sends two boats across to Rye and back: Roosevelt and Alfred in the Meteor, with Elliott, Jack and George Minot crewing the Daphne. They lunch with the Bulkleys, where Roosevelt meets Miss Lee Berry.
Racing a squall to Rocky Point

Roosevelt and Jack plan a night out in the skiff, but heavy rain sends them home. After lunch at Matinecock Point a fierce northwest squall hits off Oak Bluff, and they run before it under sail to Rocky Point, taking on a lot of water.

George Minot tells Roosevelt that his brother Hal, a close friend, has lost his reason and been placed in an asylum. Roosevelt grieves for the gentle, bright young man and his family. Later Uncle Hill and Aunt Susie come to stay.
Sad news, then dinner at the Union League

Overnighting in New York, Roosevelt visits Cassin, who is slowly dying, and learns that Cousin Sam Roosevelt has died. Still low about Hal Minot, he dines that evening at the Union League Club with Jack Roosevelt and Emlen.
Roosevelt, West and Emlen board an early-morning train to Boston, bound for three weeks in the Maine woods. Writing of Hal Minot, he says his father's death has dulled his ability to grieve.
After an overnight train to Mattawamkeag, the party rides a buckboard to Island Falls, arriving at 8 p.m. Roosevelt is suffering a bad bout of asthma and misses his horse.
Roosevelt walks, reads his Bible and memorizes Psalm 19. With no church in Island Falls, he attends a Methodist meeting in the schoolhouse. Thoughts of Hal Minot bring back his grief for his father.
Seven months after his father's death, Roosevelt spends the whole day after partridges without seeing one.

The party heads downstream to camp at the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake, the others in a bateau with guide Sewall while Roosevelt goes ahead by canoe with guide Dow. He enjoys the paddling and woods walking but misses every shot at pigeons and ducks.
A loon at long range and a quiet ramble

Roosevelt and Emlen canoe the lake; Roosevelt fires at a loon over a hundred yards away and nearly hits it. In the afternoon they hike about ten miles after partridge, taking one ruffed grouse, and he praises Emlen as a loyal companion.

Rain keeps the party under canvas with books, cards and gun cleaning, eating duck, partridge, trout and pickerel. Roosevelt and Emlen sit three hours in the wet waiting for ducks and come back empty-handed.
Another wet day of reading, euchre, whist and rifle practice in camp. Roosevelt waits for ducks again with one long miss, and kills a bat and a nighthawk.
When the rain stops at noon, Roosevelt hikes fifteen miles with Sewall and comes back with nothing. He misses two foxes at about sixty yards and is fed up with his week of poor shooting.
Roosevelt reads his Bible in the morning, then fills the afternoon cleaning guns and labeling specimens before a swim in the mill race.

After a frosty night, Roosevelt and Sewall hike thirty miles near the Mattawamkeag River, on the move from eight to seven save a half-hour lunch. He gets only four shots, bagging a rabbit, a merganser and two grouse, but loves the walk.
Roosevelt, West and guide Dow paddle to the head of the lake and hunt the sloughs and bogs with middling luck, taking two ducks. The three camp overnight in a wigwam on a meager supper.

Up before dawn, the three hunt ducks and see none. Back at the main camp, Roosevelt walks about ten miles with Will Dow for four shots, a merganser and three grouse, and decides moccasins are the best footwear for the woods.
Roosevelt hikes about fifteen miles, three of them through some of the hardest swamp walking he has known. He takes a spruce partridge among the cedars and a ruffed grouse up on a hemlock ridge.
On a ten-mile walk with Sewall, Roosevelt stalks and kills a duck on a small lake. The others then trick him with a dead duck propped up to look alive in a pond. He has bathed in the mill race daily.
Autumn color in the Maine woods
Roosevelt and Emlen hunt in the afternoon; Emlen never fires, and Roosevelt misses a duck but drops a partridge. The leaves are turning, and he counts the trip a real success.
Roosevelt passes Sunday much as he did the week before.

The party breaks camp and heads back to Island Falls in the clumsy bateau: Sewall paddling, Roosevelt and Dow at the oars, Thompson trolling, and West and Emlen in the bow watching for game. Roosevelt spends the afternoon in the woods with West.
Roosevelt hikes 25 miles with Dow, taking a woodcock and two partridges. Game has been scarce all trip, but he has loved it, and the party has not had one quarrel.
Roosevelt rides around all day in a buckboard, Will Dow at his side, climbing down each time they spot a partridge. He gets five grouse and sees a fox.
The party drives by wagon to Mattawamkeag and boards the night train for Boston. His companions will continue to New York; Roosevelt is bound back to Harvard.
Back at Harvard, a surprise invitation

Roosevelt returns to Cambridge for his junior year to a warm welcome. To his astonishment the Porcellian Club asks him to join, and he feels he must decline because he belongs to the A.D. Club, though he wishes otherwise. His sister Corinne turns 17.

Roosevelt finds his classes and lab work will fill about twenty hours a week, with an 8 a.m. recitation daily, Saturdays included. Harry Shaw and Dick Saltonstall each invite him for Sunday, and his club table at Mrs. Wilson's serves excellent meals.
Roosevelt goes to church and plans to resume teaching Sunday school in a week or two.
Down to work and the rifle club
Roosevelt starts studying in earnest and joins the rifle club, meaning to shoot regularly this year. In New York the cables for the Brooklyn Bridge are finished.
Roosevelt is voted into the Harvard Glee Club.
At the D.K.E., but not drinking

Roosevelt attends the first D.K.E. meeting of the year. He finds its drinking tiresome as a steady diet, though fun now and then; he does not drink there, drinks very little anyway, and will not smoke before he is 21.
First meeting of the Art Club
Roosevelt goes to the opening meeting of the Art Club and enjoys it.
Roosevelt ranks his courses: philosophy and political economy come first, natural history is engaging if less so than last year, and the rest interest him little.
Roosevelt spends the morning shooting at the range.
Roosevelt is studying hard, but his strong average last year earns him optional recitations, so he expects some three weeks of winter holidays.
Roosevelt starts up again with his boxing teacher and writes his mother an affectionate letter saying his studies take six or seven hours a day.

After two drunk club men argue about him and reveal his preference for the Porcellian, the A.D. members vote to let Roosevelt choose between the clubs, since he never formally joined theirs. Knowing either choice will hurt someone, he spends a miserable day weighing what honor requires.
Roosevelt is at Cambridge; no activities are recorded.
Roosevelt settles it and joins the Porcellian, listing classmates on each side: Weld, Shaw, Trimble, Morgan and Griswold among the Porcellian men; Bob Bacon, Billy Hooper and others in the A.D.
Roosevelt records that Arthur Hooper has left Harvard and that Brooks and Peters have been dropped. He has warmed to Charley Ware and Harry Shaw, and calls Harry Chapin a perfect trump.
Charley Dickey under the same roof
Roosevelt is glad to have Charley Dickey living in his house and feels he has helped him. He writes Bamie that more than half his college career is behind him.
One of Roosevelt's natural history courses demands heavy laboratory work, which he enjoys though it devours his time.
Sparring and gratitude to the A.D.
Roosevelt has been boxing with several classmates and writes that the A.D. men have handled the club episode very decently.
Roosevelt lists his dining-table companions: Weld, Chapin, Ware, Washburn, Ellis, Peters and Saltonstall.
Roosevelt enjoys dinner at the Hoopers' and is pleased to meet Miss Jeannie once more.
Off to Chestnut Hill with Dick Saltonstall
After boxing Tucker Burr to a standstill, Roosevelt rides in Dick Saltonstall's buggy to the Saltonstall home at Chestnut Hill, where the family's kindness makes him feel completely at home.

Roosevelt rambles through the woods alongside Dick, Dick's sister Rose and their cousin Alice Lee, whom he finds sweet and pretty. The group dines and takes tea at the Whitneys', dancing and singing until they drive home around eleven. He would marry Alice in 1880.
After church, Roosevelt spends the afternoon gathering chestnuts with Alice Lee.
Back to Cambridge and the Glee Club
Roosevelt returns by carriage to Cambridge early in the day and that evening hears some lovely singing at the Glee Club.
A political meeting for Benjamin Butler and Denis Kearney sets off a brawl between students and townspeople, and Roosevelt enjoys watching the crew pile in.
Arguing with Mill, tiring of Ferrier
Roosevelt finds political economy absorbing even though he does not fully accept John Stuart Mill, and is losing patience with Ferrier's philosophy.
A long walk and a family scandal
Roosevelt hikes with Jack Tebbetts, who has grown on him. Then a letter brings word that his cousin Cornelius has married a French actress, which Roosevelt condemns harshly in his diary.
Roosevelt takes the night boat to New York for a break, admitting he has not studied as hard as he should in some subjects and vowing to buckle down on his return.
Home with family at Oyster Bay

Roosevelt breakfasts with West, who is upset over Cornelius's marriage, visits Aunt Annie, lunches with West and Alfred, and reaches Oyster Bay in the afternoon, happy to be with his family. All look well except Elliott.
Roosevelt marks his 20th birthday at Oyster Bay with his mother and sisters, but the day is shadowed by longing for his father. He also shoots two gray squirrels.
In a stiff north wind Roosevelt rows around Centre Island through seas that half-fill his boat, then sails home fast from Pine Island. An afternoon walk with his gun turns up nothing.
Sailing for ducks in light, shifting wind, Roosevelt finds few birds but plenty of fun: he drops two coots from a flock, runs down a loon after a lengthy pursuit, and misses an old squaw.
A southeaster with steady rain squalls soaks Roosevelt on a duck-hunting sail, and he comes home with nothing after missing a grebe.
Rain again. Roosevelt grumbles that his whole break has been spoiled by weather: too rough one day, too calm the next, then two days of rain.
Roosevelt returns from Oyster Bay to Harvard.

Roosevelt serves as a steward at the athletic association's field meeting, and that evening is initiated into the Porcellian Club. He admits the wine left him tipsier than ever before, vows it won't happen again, and notes that drink makes him combative.
Morning after, back to Sunday school
Feeling the effects of the previous night, Roosevelt nonetheless resumes teaching his Sunday school class, whose pupils are delighted to have him back.
A sample day, hour by hour

Roosevelt begins logging a typical week: chapel at 7:45, study nearly all day, a walk before dinner, then an evening with the University crew and a couple of hours lounging at his club after midnight.
A surprise visit from Mother and Elliott

Between chapel and study, Roosevelt is astonished when his brother Elliott and their mother arrive for the day. He shows Elliott his club and lunches in Boston with Mittie, then studies, boxes, plays whist and works until eleven.
Study, then a walk with friends
Roosevelt studies from 8:30 to 4, goes walking alongside Dick Saltonstall and Jack Tebbetts, spends the evening at the club and studies again until eleven.
Another full study day, broken up by boxing and a game of billiards.
Partridge and burgundy at the club
After a day of study, Roosevelt joins eight or ten friends for a late supper of partridges and burgundy at the club, not getting to bed until nearly 2 a.m.
Football, then a weekend at Minot Weld's
Roosevelt breakfasts late at the club, drives with Harry Chapin to watch a football game, and in the afternoon heads to Minot Weld's home to stay through Monday.
Moonlit drive home from the Saltonstalls'

Staying with Minot Weld in Jamaica Plain, Roosevelt attends church and walks home with Miss Wheelwright, then rides in Minot's tilbury to the Saltonstalls' for tea, where Alice Lee is as lovely as ever. He writes to Corinne and Bamie, telling Bamie how much he enjoys the Porcellian.

Roosevelt sits his political economy exam and in the afternoon goes out to George Minot's to stay the night.
Back in time for Sunday school
After Sunday dinner Roosevelt drives back to Cambridge to teach his Sunday school class.
Facing three exams this week, Roosevelt has been studying flat out.

When scarlet fever is suspected among the Richardson children in his lodging house, Roosevelt moves out at once and bunks for now with Harry Jackson, since his roommate Bob Bacon is home nursing a sore throat.
Roosevelt goes into town for a pleasant dinner at Harry Shaw's.

Roosevelt dines with the Hoopers; Miss Jeannie Tuckerman is among the company.
After lunch Roosevelt rides out with Dick Saltonstall to spend Thanksgiving at Chestnut Hill. He feels nearly at home with the family and admires Mr. Saltonstall as an old-fashioned gentleman.

Roosevelt spends Thanksgiving dancing, walking and playing lawn tennis with Alice Lee and Rose Saltonstall. He calls Alice as sweet and refined a girl as he has met, and the household now calls him by his first name.

Roosevelt enjoys the club's regular Sunday breakfast around 9:30, praising the food and the company.

Roosevelt moves into the room shared by Charley Ware and Charley Washburn, likely staying through Christmas, and is grateful for friends' offers of space. Teddy Baylies celebrates turning 21 with a club breakfast.

Roosevelt boxes more than half an hour with Sharon, taking the worse of it but making him work. His hour exams are going well, and he grows fonder of the Porcellian, especially of Otho Williams.
Roosevelt sends Alice Lee a letter for the first time, planning an outing to have tintypes made on Saturday.

Honoraries at breakfast, dinner in town
Several honorary members join the Porcellian Sunday breakfast. After teaching Sunday school, Roosevelt dines pleasantly in Boston with Jack Tebbetts.
Routine thrown off by the move

Living away from his own room has upset Roosevelt's schedule, cutting into study and exercise. Grateful as he is to his two hosts, he admits he is spending too much time at the club on whist, billiards and late suppers.
Roosevelt and classmates launch a Finance Club, which he expects to be valuable, and he and Bob Bacon begin a paper on city taxation.

Busy as Harvard keeps him, Roosevelt writes at length about his father: dreading a Christmas without him, recalling being called his dearest child, and resolving to live in a way he would never be ashamed to confess. The entry ends under an ink blot.

A child's funeral stirs old grief
Roosevelt's whole Sunday school attends the funeral of one of its pupils. Seeing the coffin carried in brings back his father's funeral so sharply that he fears breaking down in church.

Roosevelt finds the D.K.E. theatricals surprisingly clever and clean, stays until midnight, then plays billiards at the club until 2 a.m. with Otho Williams, the other weakest player there.
Roosevelt does poorly on his Italian exam but notes good marks overall. He names Minot Weld and Harry Chapin as his closest college friends, and lists several others he is fond of.

Roosevelt travels to New York for Christmas break. Much as he loves college, he is always glad to be home, and he calls these his golden years.

Though cheerful, the family cannot help thinking of his father. Roosevelt senses the sweet now outweighing the bitter in their memories, and finds he has been very happy these past six months despite his loss.
Mission school visit and cousins in love

Roosevelt visits his former mission school pupils and learns that his friend Cassin has died. Among his cousins, romance is everywhere: Emlen confesses his love for Miss Parish, West is devoted to Fanny, and Alfred is courting Miss Tuckerman.
Jack Elliott arrives, a touch of fever
Jack Elliott comes from Philadelphia, as delightfully absent-minded as ever, and Roosevelt is relieved to find one friend not in love. He is slightly unwell with what West calls an 'ephemeral fever.'
Christmas is a sad one for Roosevelt, the first without his father, whom he remembers as the heart of every family celebration. His gifts are mostly books.
Kept indoors by fever, Roosevelt writes that he seems headed for a career as a naturalist, which would mean three years of study abroad, a prospect that depresses him.
Still housebound, Roosevelt listens to Emlen's heartfelt talk about Grace Parish and wishes him well. Elliott is doing well, and Roosevelt marvels at his relatives.

Roosevelt heads out to Oyster Bay, Jack Elliott along with him, for a long cold tramp. Amid redpolls and crossbills he shoots an Ipswich sparrow, a rarity, and the evening goes to philosophy talk and double-dummy whist.

Roosevelt goes to church, then takes a long walk with Jack, whom he calls the best partner for such outings. He loves these winter trips: thin shooting but a warm supper and roaring fire at day's end. Snow falls overnight.

In snow and wind, Roosevelt and Jack smash through shore ice in the rowboat, sail to Plum Point and lunch on Pine Island. Finding West Harbor frozen, they are swamped twice launching through heavy surf, soaked in icy water, then fight their way to Rocky Point before racing home under sail.
Twelve hours afield on New Year's Eve

Setting out at 7:30 with a local gunner and no dog in four inches of snow, Roosevelt covers about 25 miles without food or rest, home twelve hours later. He calls it one of his best days ever, shooting six quail, five rabbits and a squirrel.

The family, joined by Uncle Jimmie and Aunt Annie Gracie, has come out to Oyster Bay for a merry New Year's. After they leave in the afternoon, Roosevelt and Jack Elliott take their guns into the snowy woods.
Rabbit tracks lost in the snow
Roosevelt hunts through a heavy snowfall, taking three rabbits before fresh snow buries the tracks. In the afternoon he returns to New York City.
Usher twice over, confidant to cousins

Tom Ludlow and cousin Jack Roosevelt both ask Roosevelt to usher at their weddings, to his puzzlement. West, Emlen and Alfred all confide their romances to him, and Elliott brings two friends to dinner, one named Russell whom Roosevelt likes.
Roosevelt dreads leaving his family even though Cambridge suits him so well. He calls on Annie Murray and praises his brother Elliott.
Tea with Hal Chapin, a talk with Bamie
Hal Chapin comes to tea, and Roosevelt has a heartfelt talk with his sister Bamie, wondering whether any man has two better sisters. That evening he leaves for Harvard.
Arriving in Cambridge early, Roosevelt dives into his studies with fresh resolve.

A poor exam and two writing projects
Roosevelt fears he did badly on a natural history exam, and later notes that he did. He is also writing on city taxation for the Finance Club and compiling a list of Oyster Bay's bird species.

Harry Shaw's cutter takes Roosevelt from the Porcellian to the Saltonstalls', where Dick, Minot Weld, Alice and Rose are gathered, on a perfect cold, clear day. He sees Mr. Saltonstall about Dick joining the Porcellian, then plays whist and billiards that evening. He writes Hal Minot that he misses having someone to share his interests with.
Roosevelt picks up his Sunday school class again after the holidays.

Roosevelt takes the night boat to New York for Tom Ludlow's wedding.
Arriving in New York, Roosevelt attends the rehearsal for Tom Ludlow's wedding, where one of the bridesmaids is Helen White, an old sweetheart.

Despite bad weather Grace Church is packed for the Ludlow wedding, where Roosevelt ushers the middle aisle with Livingston, Rutherford and Cruger. Heading for the night train back to Harvard, his cutter overturns.

On Bamie's 24th birthday, half the Porcellian rouses Roosevelt late at night to tell him he is fifth man of the Hasty Pudding's first group of nine, and parades him around until 6 a.m. That evening a Porcellian dinner draws many graduates and ends in rowdy drinking by some.

Old papers and theology at Chestnut Hill

After a three-hour exam, Roosevelt goes to Chestnut Hill for the weekend. He spends the evening going through Mr. Saltonstall's family papers, swapping stories of travel in Egypt and Syria. Tom Lee arrives and they argue theology.

After an engaging sermon, Roosevelt joins about 25 people sledding on double runners and has the time of his life. He likes Rose and especially Alice more each visit; the family now calls him 'Thee.' Alice comes in for tea and stays the evening.

Roosevelt joins a toboggan party at Chestnut Hill with Alice, Rose and several other young women and friends, sharing a sled with Alice, Miss Whitney and Dick. He writes Bamie that he likes the two girls more daily, Alice most of all.
Roosevelt heads to Worcester for a Sunday visit with Charley Washburn, has tea at the Tiffanys', meets a pretty Miss Cross, and enjoys a sleigh ride behind Charley's trotter.
Roosevelt spends a pleasant Sunday much like those he spends at home.
Roosevelt sets to studying hard and writes to Corinne about the January 31 sledding party.

On the first anniversary of his father's death, Roosevelt asks God for the strength to honor his father's hopes. Writing to the family has been hard; heavy study and Sunday school keep him busy, but evenings and nights are sad.

With the semiannual exams over, Roosevelt plans to rest after steady work since Christmas.

About forty honorary members join the 18 active members at the club's big midwinter supper. Many older men knew his father or of him, and Roosevelt wishes he could someday honor that name. George Upham joins the club along with three other sophomores.

Roosevelt boards an evening train north toward Island Falls, Maine, planning a two-week stay.
A winter sleigh ride to Island Falls

Bill Sewall meets Roosevelt's train at Mattawamkeag with a sleigh, and the two travel 36 miles over half-broken roads, reaching Island Falls near ten at night. The air is bitter but still, and well bundled, Roosevelt loves the ride. Elliott turns 19. His notes on Oyster Bay birds are dated to this period.
First try on snowshoes in Maine

Roosevelt straps on snowshoes for the first time and covers about six miles checking lynx traps with Will Dow. The traps are empty, but he marvels at the snow-heavy evergreens and drops a porcupine from a hemlock with his rifle.
Bible reading and a winter tramp

A quiet Sunday: Roosevelt reads his Bible in the morning, then walks the snowy pine and spruce woods in the afternoon. He finds the cold easy to bear among the trees but harsh in the wind, and notes how little life stirs in the forest.
Eight hours in the woods with Dow

With Will Dow, Roosevelt hikes to Dyer Brook and then strikes off cross-country through hardwoods and tangled spruce and cedar swamps. Over an eight-hour tramp he logs an arctic woodpecker, chickadees, two gray jays at lunch, and the tracks of hare, lynx and spruce grouse.
A ruffed grouse after a long hunt

Roosevelt spends the day in the woods with Bill Sewall. Tracks of a dozen kinds of animals are everywhere, yet they see only chickadees and a woodpecker until they trail a partridge, flush it from a fallen birch and Roosevelt brings it down.
Asthma at night, grouse by day

Another day of snowshoeing with little game to show for it, though Roosevelt is having the time of his life. Asthma keeps him awake at night. After lunch at a logging camp he shoots a partridge from a spruce top and a porcupine; the traps have so far yielded a lynx and a fox.
Thirty miles by pung to a logging camp

Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow set out with a box sleigh and a scrawny horse for a logging camp thirty miles off, arriving after dark. It is ten below at the start and the roads are terrible. Along the way he spots a red crossbill, flocks of snow buntings and some unusually tame grosbeaks.
On the trail of a caribou

Through a heavy snowstorm Roosevelt and Dow hunt all day, finally jumping a caribou in thick spruce. He glimpses it at under thirty yards but cannot shoot, and they track it until dark, then spend a cold, hungry night by a big fire with no blankets.
Caribou chase ends without a shot

Before sunrise, in subzero cold, the hunters take up the caribou's trail again through swamps, ledges and open cranberry bogs. Roosevelt studies how the animal trots and bounds in snow over three feet deep. By midday they quit and are back at the logging camp at sunset.

Worn out from two days after the caribou, Roosevelt rests. His asthma has not troubled him since reaching camp, and he warms to the rough, generous lumbermen, especially one named Charley Brown. Rain followed by frost has coated every tree in ice.
A buck, rabbits and a venison feast

Roosevelt and Sewall find a small deer yard. He trips and misses his first shot at the buck, then runs it down over a mile and kills it with his rifle. After an afternoon of rabbit hunting, venison replaces the usual pork and beans. He writes his mother that he has stored up health enough to last into summer.
Dragging the sleigh back to Island Falls

The return trip is miserable: sleet and rain, wretched roads, and a horse that keeps floundering into drifts until the men unhitch it and haul the sleigh themselves. Wet, chilled and hungry after walking the whole way, Roosevelt still notes snow buntings singing, and reaches Island Falls by teatime.
A raccoon and a camp on Mattawamkeag Lake

After another empty seven-mile trap round, Roosevelt follows a raccoon's track and shoots it from a dead tree. The party then snowshoes to Mattawamkeag Lake and camps at its foot, picking up two spruce grouse on the way in the best snow conditions of his stay.
Long-range rifle practice on the ice

The party breaks camp and returns to Island Falls by dinner, traveling over the frozen lake and river. Seeing no game, they pass the time shooting at targets 300 to 500 yards off, and all three do well with a Sharps rifle.
Counting trophies from two happy weeks

A last morning hunt turns up no partridges and empty traps, but Roosevelt is content. He sums up the trip as his pleasantest two weeks ever, with skins of fox, lynx, raccoon and buck to take home, plenty of game eaten and many specimens collected.
Leaving Maine to catch up on studies
Roosevelt leaves by sleigh at five in the morning for Mattawamkeag and boards the night train to Boston. He resolves to work double time until Easter to make up for the holiday.
Back at Harvard, too late for church
After a train held up six hours, Roosevelt reaches Cambridge late Sunday morning and writes his mother from the Porcellian Club that he arrived too late for church.

Roosevelt boxes in the Harvard lightweight competition, beating W. W. Coolidge before losing to the champion, C. S. Hanks. He weighs in at 135 pounds. He also notes he has nearly caught up on the work missed in Maine. Owen Wister later made this bout famous.
Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne that he placed second in the sparring contest and had a fine time in Maine.

Roosevelt goes out to Chestnut Hill to dine and sleep at the Saltonstalls', who make him feel like family. He spends the evening at the Lees' with Alice Lee and plans to give Alice and Rose Saltonstall rugs made from his Maine fox and lynx skins.
Roosevelt takes in the Delta Kappa Epsilon club's theatricals, which he rates as very good, followed by a convivial night.
Hasty Pudding show and a gift of poems

Roosevelt calls the Hasty Pudding theatricals the best he has seen, and enjoys the singing that follows in the club room and the Yard. He mails his sister Corinne a little volume of verse, Charles Fletcher Lummis's Birch Bark Poems.

Roosevelt ducks out of the start of a Porcellian supper to join Jack Tebbetts' party with Alice Lee, Rose Saltonstall and other young women, then returns around eleven for the rowdy end of the club evening, where a tipsy Otho Williams asks him to be his second in a mock duel with Charley Sprague.
At his Sunday school class Roosevelt shows the boys a batch of photographs from the East, which makes for an unusually lively session. In the evening he calls on Jeannie Hooper and Mrs. Jude.

Roosevelt drives to Minot Weld's for amateur theatricals, sitting beside Alice Lee and later spending much of the evening with Nana Rotch. Back around one, he stays up singing and talking at the Porcellian until three.
Roosevelt shares a game supper at the Porcellian Club with Otho Williams, Jim Wright and Charley Sprague.
A lunch party and gifts of fur rugs

Roosevelt hosts a luncheon in his rooms, with Mrs. Saltonstall as chaperone, for Alice Lee, Rose Saltonstall and a dozen friends, then shows them the Porcellian and Pudding clubs. He gives Alice the lynx rug and Rose the fox; Alice is making him slippers. That night he sails for New York with Minot Weld and Dick Saltonstall.

Home in New York for vacation, Roosevelt shows Minot Weld and Dick Saltonstall the city. At Aunt Annie's that evening he sees Fanny Smith, Margie Tuckerman and Edith Carow. He announces to his sister Corinne that his side-whiskers are gone.
Christine and Lucy Kean come to lunch, and Roosevelt likes them both. His mother has fallen ill, which leaves him feeling wretched.
Elliott's dinner at the Jockey Club

Elliott hosts a dinner at the Jockey Club. Roosevelt travels in Harold Haddon's dog cart while the rest of the party, including Grove Porter and Ike Iselin, comes by drag, and he takes a strong liking to Haddon.
Roosevelt's cousin Emlen has been turned down by Grace Parish, and the two have a long talk. His mother is still unwell.
Emlen treats the group to a successful lunch at the Down Town Club, and they dine at cousin West's before an evening at the theater.
Dog show, then the night train north

Roosevelt visits the dog show, lunches with Lizzie Moran and escorts Annie Murray to a rehearsal for the Fancy Dress Ball before catching the night train to Boston. His guests loved the holiday, and his mother is nearly recovered.
Roosevelt is back in Cambridge and picks up his studies again.

Roosevelt spends the afternoon at Nana Rotch's, teaching her the five-step waltz.
