Roosevelt, Alice, Rose Saltonstall and her brother Richard board the night train for Mount Desert, Maine, transferring to the boat at 11 p.m. The same day Commander Henry Gorringe delivers the ancient obelisk known as Cleopatra's Needle to New York, bound for Central Park.

The party lands on Mount Desert after midday. Alice and Rose lodge with the Weld family at Bar Harbor, while Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall are put up by Jack Tebbets at Schooner Head, about three and a half miles off.
From his base at Schooner Head, Roosevelt rides over to Bar Harbor twice, and fits in tennis and bowling besides.
Roosevelt plays tennis through the morning and spends the afternoon walking around to the local sights, marveling at the grandeur of the Maine scenery.
A stomach illness keeps Roosevelt indoors. He writes his sister Corinne to ask after Douglas Robinson and jokes about how awkward it is for a suitor to be sick.
Recovered enough to get around, Roosevelt is driven by Jack Tebbets over to Otter Creek in the afternoon.
Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall leave Schooner Head and take rooms with the Weld family in Bar Harbor, under the same roof as Alice and Rose.
Roosevelt plays tennis all morning, then spends the rest of the day with Alice exploring the Bar Harbor woods and the rugged shoreline.
A buggy ride and a party
Roosevelt takes Alice for an afternoon spin in a buggy and goes to an enjoyable party that evening.
On Alice's 19th birthday, Roosevelt marvels in his diary at his luck in winning her, promising to repay her love with lifelong care and tenderness.
Roosevelt falls ill again. His 'Big Six' friends rally around him, and Alice gives up her own fun to look after him, which leaves him more devoted to her than ever.
Alice wins the ladies' tennis prize
Roosevelt is on the mend, and Alice carries off first prize in the women's tennis tournament.
Roosevelt attends church and hears what he judges an excellent sermon.
Roosevelt praises the Welds' kindness. When rough weather keeps them off the rocks at night, he and Alice slip away to the kitchen to be alone.
Roosevelt hikes up Newport Mountain in the morning.
Wet weather does not stop Roosevelt from spending most of the day beside Alice, and there is a dance in the evening.
Roosevelt drives Alice over to Schooner Head for dinner.
The Mount Desert party breaks up. Roosevelt and Alice travel with Shaw, Chapin and the Saltonstalls and reach Chestnut Hill late at night. It is also Edith Carow's 19th birthday.
Glad to be among the Lees
Back at Chestnut Hill, Roosevelt says how fond he is of the whole Lee family and spends the entire day with Alice.
Alice drives Roosevelt out for a carriage ride, and he records how happy he is.
Roosevelt stays close to Alice, already miserable at the thought of the six-week separation that begins in two days.
Roosevelt spends another full day with Alice, reading to her from Hawthorne and Thackeray. Both love poetry, especially Longfellow and parts of Shelley and Swinburne.
Farewell to Alice, night train south
After a last happy day together, Roosevelt says goodbye to Alice for what he expects will be six or seven weeks and boards the overnight train to New York.
Shopping, then out to Oyster Bay
Roosevelt spends the day shopping in New York and goes out to Oyster Bay that evening, finding his mother there along with Aunt Susie, Uncle Hill and two members of the Locke family.
Roosevelt plays tennis with Frank and goes out paddling in his cousin Emlen's canoe.
Roosevelt gets his gear ready for a western hunting trip, and also walks in the woods and takes his mother out in the light wagon.
His brother Elliott turns up while the family is at church. Roosevelt confesses he is painfully lonely for Alice and thinks of her constantly.
Roosevelt and Elliott board the overnight train for Chicago to begin a western hunting trip.
The brothers ride all day across Pennsylvania's forested hills and Ohio's prairies. Roosevelt delights in traveling with Elliott, noting that the two of them keep their tempers and get things done.
Sweltering Chicago, and a guide found
In Chicago, a big Freemasons' gathering makes rooms scarce and the heat is fierce. That evening the brothers meet a man named Wilcox and agree to go to his farm until September.

At Wilcox's farm near Huntley, sixty miles out of Chicago, the brothers hunt prairie chickens across the open fields. Elliott misses his bird; Roosevelt drops his. He finds the open-country shooting new and fun, though the farm food is coarse.
The brothers spend four hours walking the fields after prairie chickens. Elliott outshoots Roosevelt, four grouse to one.

Roosevelt and Elliott set out by wagon, stopping wherever the cover looked good to hunt stubble and pasture for chickens and the sloughs for ducks, snipe and plover. He calls it one of his most pleasant days.

Roosevelt admits Elliott is the better shot but says he is getting better. He likes the farm men despite the plain pork-and-potatoes fare, misses Alice terribly, and that night joins everyone in singing hymns. He writes Corinne and Bamie about it.
On a full day's wagon hunt, Roosevelt shoots worse than ever while Elliott seems to hit nearly everything he aims at.
A wet dawn with few birds
The brothers head out before sunrise through soaking prairie grass, but birds are scarce and both shoot poorly.
Rained in with a rowdy crew

Rain keeps the brothers indoors. Two farmhands, a Texan and an Irish youth, get roaring drunk and Roosevelt braces for a brawl that never comes. He tells his mother in a letter how shabbily dressed he and Elliott are.
Poor luck, constant thoughts of Alice
A day of shooting yields little. Roosevelt writes that Alice is his first thought on waking and his last at night.
A morning on foot turns up no game at all. Roosevelt decides the area has been shot clean and plans to leave the next day.
Back to comfort at the Sherman House
The brothers return to Chicago and check into the Sherman House, which feels like a palace after the rough farmhouse.
Roosevelt goes to a Methodist church and admires the earnest, if startling, preacher, noting that most of the congregation are men, unlike the usual crowd.
Stuck in Chicago until Wilcox is ready to head west with them, the brothers take in the city's sights.
Turkish bath, theater and a hunting portrait

Still waiting for Wilcox, Roosevelt fills the day with a drive, reading, whist, the theater, a long walk and a Turkish bath. He and Elliott sit for a studio photograph in their hunting clothes, but his longing for Alice keeps growing.
Wilcox at last shows up, and the brothers expect to head west within a couple of days.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that Chicago is a remarkable city, huge and wealthy.
The hunting party sets out from Chicago: Roosevelt, Elliott, an engineer and a former Confederate soldier.

Arriving at Carroll, Iowa, before dawn, the party heads straight out by wagon over the open, unfenced prairie and does not return until 9 p.m. Birds are plentiful and Roosevelt shoots his best yet, despite colic and asthma.
Twenty-five miles south over treeless hills

After breakfast the party drives about 25 miles south through low, bare, thinly settled hills and spends the night at a rough farmhouse. Birds are few and skittish, but Roosevelt shoots as well as Elliott or better.
A lame horse and a near upset

The party works back over the prairie, the dogs mixed in quality. They return after dark with a horse lame and the wagon nearly overturned in a mudhole. Roosevelt loves the cross-country driving and outshoots Elliott.

Driving toward Wall Lake, Roosevelt shoots chickens in tall grass, then wades hip-deep in mud to retrieve snipe and is bitten by a snake as he climbs out. The night is spent at a tidy little farmhouse.
Sunrise and pelicans on Wall Lake

Roosevelt hunts yellowlegs along the lakeshore at dawn and admires the sunrise, a big flock of pelicans and thousands of yellow-headed blackbirds. He shoots badly later, while Elliott excels. Asthma bothers him, yet he can walk all day.
In crisp fall weather the party bags some two dozen chickens before dinner. Paddling the lake with Elliott in an old flat-bottom boat, Roosevelt's second gun breaks, leaving him without one.
On the drive back to Carroll the wagon nearly overturns on a large rock, pitching Roosevelt and the driver out headfirst, though neither is badly hurt. He catches the overnight train to Chicago.
Roosevelt arrives back in Chicago without mishap.

Roosevelt takes communion at a Methodist church. He reflects that the trip has helped his health but cannot make up for being away from Alice. He writes Corinne, poking fun at Elliott's eating and drinking, and tells his mother the sport has been decent.

Roosevelt and Elliott buy new guns, split from their two companions, whom they dislike, and take the night train toward St. Paul. Their goal is a reunion in Moorhead, Minnesota, with their cousin Jack Elliott.
To Moorhead with a bobtailed pointer
Armed with two new guns and an old short-tailed pointer, the brothers leave St. Paul in the evening for Moorhead, on the Dakota line, to see Jack Elliott.

At Moorhead the brothers drive out to vast stubble fields and hunt a new kind of grouse until the old pointer tangles with a skunk. Back at their poor hotel they find cousin Jack Elliott and talk late into the night.
Roosevelt spends the day with Jack Elliott, whom he has not seen in almost two years, and says he feels strong and healthy.

A serious old German drives the brothers north past the Buffalo River to hunt grouse and ducks. Roosevelt sees jackrabbits for the first time, and they ride five miles by full moon to a settler's house for the night.
The brothers find countless grouse, but Roosevelt, up much of the night with asthma and plagued by colic and rain, shoots badly while Elliott excels. He longs to get back to Alice.
Lost on the prairie in the rain
In cold, lashing rain the party drives more than thirty miles, loses its way more than once, and ends at a Norwegian settler's home. When the sky clears near sunset they bag ducks and grouse.

Roosevelt beds down on a settler's floor beneath a buffalo robe while a gale howls outside, then hunts ducks in the cornfields and chickens across the fields all day in wind and rain. He says he feels in superb health.

On a cold, clear day the brothers cross country by wagon, nearly bog down in a slough, shoot grouse and ducks, and drop two geese from a passing flock while hiding behind wheat sheaves. They camp in the timber by the Buffalo River and dine on roast duck and chicken by a big fire.

Another day of hunting stubble fields for chickens and sharp-tailed grouse, with both brothers shooting well. They again sleep on the ground by the river, with no tent or proper outfit, not even a frying pan.
Head over heels in a mudhole

Roosevelt has great fun wading after ducks in a big slough until he tumbles headfirst into a mudhole, gun and all. That evening the brothers are back in Moorhead with Jack Elliott. He calls it his best hunt ever, though he aches to see Alice.
Roosevelt spends the day with Jack Elliott and totals the trip's game in his diary: 203 for himself and 201 for Elliott, 404 in all, mostly grouse, with ducks, plover, yellowlegs and much else.
The brothers leave Moorhead for St. Paul. Roosevelt has loved the trip, but is gladder still that it is over and Alice is near.
Roosevelt arrives in Chicago on the way east.
Roosevelt departs Chicago heading east. At home, his sister Corinne turns 19.
Roosevelt breaks his journey east with a stop at Niagara Falls.
Roosevelt reaches New York, collects a suitcase Bamie packed for him at the family home on West 57th Street, and hurries on to Chestnut Hill that evening to be reunited with Alice.
Reunited with Alice, Roosevelt writes that she is unchanged yet somehow even more charming, and that he cannot bear to have her out of his sight.
Roosevelt spends the whole day at Chestnut Hill with Alice.
Roosevelt says his days with Alice feel like a dream of happiness.
Roosevelt reluctantly returns to New York in the evening, comforted that this is the final separation: the wedding is just over three weeks away.
Staying with Aunt Annie and Uncle Jimmie Gracie in their snug New York house, Roosevelt busies himself with wedding gifts and preparations. He also enrolls at Columbia Law School.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is recorded.

Roosevelt begins classes at Columbia Law School, where he will spend about six hours a day. He plans Alice's gifts, a diamond crescent, ruby bracelet and sapphire ring worth about $2,500, and vows to be thriftier once married. His wedding gifts alone ultimately cost $3,889.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt goes out to Oyster Bay and is glad to find Elliott, Corinne, Bamie and his mother at home. There is much to discuss about the wedding.
Beating Elliott and Fred Weeks at tennis
Roosevelt spends the day outdoors, defeating both Elliott and Fred Weeks at tennis. Cousins Emlen and Alfred, with Griswold, arrive to spend Sunday.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; nothing else is recorded.
Back in New York, Roosevelt says he enjoys law school so far. His cousins have been generous with wedding presents for Alice, including a pearl ring from Emlen and a bracelet from West.
The record places Roosevelt in New York City and Boston but gives no details.
Two weeks before the wedding, Roosevelt dines at the home of his childhood friend Edith Carow, joined by Fanny Smith and Grace Potter, all of whom will attend. Fanny finds him wild with excitement.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt travels from New York out to Oyster Bay.
Woods and tennis with the Weeks boys
Roosevelt walks in the woods and plays tennis with Johnny and Freddy Weeks.
Last bachelor Sunday at Oyster Bay
Knowing his next visit to Oyster Bay will be with his bride, Roosevelt prays he can make Alice happy and resolves to be as unselfish and cheerful as she is.

Roosevelt heads into New York to wrap up business before leaving for Boston on Friday. He records the wedding party: Corinne, Rosy Lee, Rose Saltonstall and Fanny Peabody as bridesmaids, and ten ushers including cousins Emlen and West Roosevelt.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record is otherwise silent.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.
Roosevelt takes the night train to Boston for his wedding.

Roosevelt hurries out to Chestnut Hill in the morning to embrace Alice, who has received some 250 wedding presents. In the afternoon he goes with his friend Cottie Peabody to the Peabody estate, Kernwood, in Salem, and admires both the place and the bright, well-read family.
Church in Salem and tea with Fanny Peabody

Roosevelt and Cottie walk into Salem for church, then he calls on old 'Grandma Lee.' They take tea at Fanny Peabody's, and he meets Frank Peabody's fiancée, Rosamund Laurence, whom he finds handsome and cultivated.

Roosevelt settles the last wedding details and in the evening cuts down trees and fools around with Cottie Peabody. Elliott checks in at Boston's Brunswick Hotel, bringing Fanny Smith, Grace Potter and Edith Carow.

Roosevelt comes into Boston, lunches with both families at the Lees', and dines and sleeps at the Brunswick. Elliott will be his best man. At dinner he tips Fanny Smith's chair so far back she fears a backward somersault.

On his 22nd birthday, Roosevelt marries Alice Hathaway Lee at noon in Brookline's Unitarian church, with Elliott as best man. After a reception at the Lee home, where Edith Carow dances the evening away, the couple leave around 4 p.m. for a suite in Springfield.
The newlyweds travel from Springfield through New York to Oyster Bay for a two-week stay, with the house to themselves apart from two servants and a groom.
Alice spends the day recovering from the trip.
Roosevelt's horse is in fine shape for lovely drives, the tennis court is marked out and his rowboat is afloat. The couple breakfast at ten, dine at two and take tea at seven.

Instead of church, Roosevelt reads the Bible aloud, and the couple walk among hills turned red and gold. While Alice sews he reads to her from Quentin Durward, The Pickwick Papers and The Newcomes. He writes his mother that the honeymoon at Tranquility is a joy.

Roosevelt sketches honeymoon life at Oyster Bay: wood fires, the servants Mary Ann and Kate, the coachman Davis, a collie named Dare, a calf and a gloomy cat. He adores Alice at the tea table in her pink and gray dress, and their days run to drives, walks, tennis, reading aloud and cards.

Roosevelt drives to Norwich to cast his first-ever vote for president, choosing Republican James A. Garfield. Garfield wins the White House over Winfield Scott Hancock, with Chester A. Arthur as vice president.
Roosevelt and Alice are at Oyster Bay; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes that he and Alice are almost never apart and he wishes the honeymoon could go on forever.
Roosevelt notes another wholesome, contented day at Oyster Bay.

Rain keeps the couple inside. Roosevelt loves talking with Alice about everything from politics to poetry and reading to her from history, novels or the daily paper, their only link to the wider world.

Roosevelt reads the Bible aloud, then takes a long autumn walk with Alice, who strides well and climbs fences nearly as easily as he does. His hunter keeps them in woodcock and partridge. Elsewhere, James Roosevelt and Sara Delano marry and sail for Europe on the Germanic, the ship carrying Elliott toward India.
Drive to the brush plains past Syosset
The couple take a long carriage ride out past Syosset onto the brush plains, returning through the Cold Spring valley, Laurel Hollow and Oak Openings, then play lawn tennis.
On a fine Indian summer day Roosevelt plays tennis and reads Manzoni's The Betrothed aloud on the piazza, then rows Alice around Centre Island and watches the sun set over the water.
The couple drive toward Locust Valley and Glen Cove. Roosevelt doubts any honeymoon has been happier.
Rain keeps them in all morning, but they go driving after lunch.

On a cross-country walk toward Syosset, Alice stops to pet every animal but flees bulls and turkey cocks, while the collie trots along. Roosevelt is sorry to see the honeymoon end but eager for the life ahead.
The couple leave Oyster Bay and drive into New York to an enthusiastic welcome, settling at the family home at 6 West 57th Street with his mother, Bamie and Corinne. Elliott is away in the East.
Sunday lunch and the Newsboys' Home

Roosevelt notes that Alice plans to join the Presbyterian church. After services he hosts the family's customary Sunday lunch, and in the evening he goes to the Newsboys' Home. He and Alice will spend the winter living with his mother.
Roosevelt shows off his smart cart on an afternoon drive with Alice through the park. That night they go to the opera in Hilborne Roosevelt's box.
Alice holds her afternoon at-home for visitors.

Roosevelt describes his routine: walk downtown to Columbia Law School on Great Jones Street at 8:30 to study under Professor Theodore Dwight, read Blackstone, research his naval history of the War of 1812 at the Astor Library, then hurry uptown so he and Alice can go driving.
St. Andrew's Society and Whitelaw Reid
Roosevelt attends a lively gathering of the St. Andrew's Society and has a long conversation with newspaper editor Whitelaw Reid.
Roosevelt drives Alice up through Riverside Park and takes her to the opera that night.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no entry survives for the day.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing more.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are recorded.

Roosevelt notes that even on nights at home, callers pour in, though he and Alice still find quiet time together. He drives her out every afternoon he can, or his mother or a sister when Alice cannot go.
After a heavy snowfall Roosevelt takes Alice on a sleigh ride. He finds his law studies absorbing.
Roosevelt and his cousin Emlen host a big Thanksgiving dinner for about a hundred newsboys. That evening the family gathers for its own feast.
Aunt Annie Gracie gives a dinner for the newlyweds. Roosevelt is seated next to Annie Murray and meets a bright young man named Archie Alexander.
The Lees come to New York
Alice's parents and her sister Kitty arrive in New York, to Roosevelt's delight, and dine with the family.
Alice decides to join the church
The Lees and others come for tea. Roosevelt records that Alice has made up her mind to join the church, and he speaks to the newsboys as he does every Sunday.
Villamof, a member of the Russian legation whom Roosevelt finds very clever, dines with the family. Roosevelt also takes Kitty Lee for a drive.

Roosevelt buys the first of three Cove Neck parcels near Oyster Bay from Thomas Youngs; together they total 155 acres. When his mother reads Elliott's letters from India aloud, he paces restlessly, longing for the wilds and a rifle.
A drive and the theater with the Lees
Roosevelt takes Alice on a long drive and goes to the theater with the Lees that evening.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded for the day.

While Corinne, Alice and Edith Carow make a trip to Morristown, New Jersey, Roosevelt goes to a large dinner party, sitting between Mrs. Newbold and Mrs. Astor and chatting with Mrs. Cutting and Mrs. Potter. He takes a liking to Astor and Cutting.
Roosevelt drives his mother through Riverside Park and notes how much he likes his law studies.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no entry survives.
Alice grumbles that New York keeps her forever hurrying and running after things, such as the horsecars.
A dull dinner at the Millers
Roosevelt attends what he considers a rather boring dinner at the Millers', seated by a Miss Duncan.
Grand ball for Alice and Corinne
The Roosevelts throw a great ball at home for Alice and for Corinne's debut, drawing some 500 guests including Mrs. William Astor and the Vanderbilts, Dodges, Harrimans and Iselins.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record is silent.
Roosevelt attends the preparatory service held before Alice joins the church.
A reception, and pride in Alice

At a grand reception at home Roosevelt enjoys roaming and chatting freely. He confesses he is not much for society, though he likes some married women such as Mrs. Astor, Mrs. Cutting and Mrs. Newbold, and is proud that everyone admires Alice.

Roosevelt describes a perfect Sunday: late breakfast, church, dinner, an afternoon with Alice, tea with West, Hilborne, Uncle Jimmie and Aunt Annie, then the newsboys. Alice formally joins the church, and he feels they are now united in all things.
Roosevelt goes to a cheerful small dinner at the Iselins'.
Roosevelt attends a Mendelssohn concert and thinks it excellent.

With his horse in high spirits and lovely weather, Roosevelt relishes driving Alice up Riverside Park beside the Hudson, or his mother when Alice cannot come, and marvels at his luck in their home life.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt makes the rounds of big afternoon receptions at the Iselins' and the Morans'. He likes these teas because he never lingers with any one girl long enough to run out of talk.

At Alice's suggestion Roosevelt hosts a whist club of young men including Douglas Robinson, Ike Iselin, Bob Sedgwick and his cousins West and Emlen. He likes them all, especially Doug, who may join the family.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no entry is recorded.
At the Patriarchs' Ball, Corinne is a belle and Alice is much sought after. Roosevelt enjoys some splendid waltzes, partnering Lucy Tuckerman, Emily Post and Miss Livingston.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing further.
When the streets are icy Roosevelt swaps the cart for the buggy. He loves driving Alice up Riverside Park, with the snow-covered Palisades set against gray skies above the ice-choked Hudson.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt and Alice travel to Chestnut Hill to spend Christmas with the Lees, happy to see everyone again.
Roosevelt watches the young Lees open their presents, goes sledding, and joins the whole Saltonstall family at Christmas dinner.
Roosevelt attends the little Chestnut Hill church in the morning and goes coasting after lunch.
Crashing a sled into a tree
Roosevelt's sledding ends with a smash into a tree. In the afternoon he takes Rosy Lee for a long sleigh ride in excellent conditions.
Returning from errands in Boston, Roosevelt and Alice learn that Rosy has the measles and move at once to the Saltonstalls, who welcome them warmly.
Roosevelt laments the measles outbreak, feels for Mrs. Lee, half fears going home, and praises the Saltonstalls' kindness.
Roosevelt is at Chestnut Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt and Alice decide to head home the next day. He calls 1880 by far his happiest year because he won Alice, and closes his diary with a month-by-month cash account and notes on his shooting tallies.
Roosevelt and Alice return to New York from Chestnut Hill.
Roosevelt goes to the Newsboys' Home in the evening as he does each Sunday, after his cousin West and others come to tea. He and Alice likely spend the day paying calls on their return.
On the holiday Roosevelt takes Alice on a 30-mile sleigh ride in splendid snow. They dine with Hill and Frank and go to the theater.
Roosevelt resumes classes at law school, walking both ways as always. He takes his mother sleighing and plays whist at the Robinsons'.
After a long sleigh ride with Alice, Roosevelt dines at James Roosevelt's and then attends Mrs. King's ball at Delmonico's.
Roosevelt dines at the Astors' and works with college friends to organize a free trade club. Every minute of his time is spoken for.
Two Rathbone sisters come to stay, and there is a pleasant small party at Aunt Annie Gracie's.
Roosevelt takes Alice Rathbone out in the sleigh.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no entry survives for the day.
Sleigh ride and a dinner at home
Roosevelt takes his mother sleighing. At a dinner at home he sits between Grace Rathbone and Lucy Tuckerman.
Fanny Smith and dinner at the Delanos'
Roosevelt takes his friend Fanny Smith sleighing, then dines at the Delanos', seated between Mrs. Astor and Mrs. Drayton.
In superb sleighing weather Roosevelt drives Alice out beyond Harlem. The evening brings a lively theater party and supper at the Tuckermans'.
Roosevelt attends a grand ball given by the Astors.
Roosevelt, Alice, Corinne and Bamie set out in a party of fifteen young people, riding a special railroad car bound for Niagara Falls, a jaunt he calls tremendous fun.
The party views the falls, rapids and whirlpool, takes long sleigh rides, and finishes with a dance. Roosevelt says they took the hotel by storm.
The group goes to church by sleigh and ventures beneath the falls, a grand sight. Riding the night train back to New York, they swap ghost stories and songs.
Cousin John visits on Bamie's birthday
Cousin John Elliott comes to stay, and Roosevelt takes Flora Grant out in the sleigh. It is Bamie's 26th birthday.
Checking on the newsboys' night school
Roosevelt takes his mother sleighing and goes downtown to look in on the newsboys' night school.
Roosevelt takes Alice out in the sleigh.
Roosevelt argues a case in the law school's moot court and prevails.
Roosevelt takes Harriet Lawrence for a sleigh ride.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded.
The Roosevelts give a dinner at home for Lowell, a Miss G. and Miss Lawrence.
Roosevelt enjoys a cheerful dinner at Rosy Roosevelt's.
Roosevelt says the sleighing is the best he has ever seen and he takes Alice out every day.
A sleigh outing and a party at home
Roosevelt takes a Miss Peabody out in his sleigh, and the family hosts a party that evening.
Roosevelt dines with the Moran family.
Roosevelt goes to an evening party at Hilborne Roosevelt's featuring a juggler.
The family's Sunday tea draws its usual crowd of callers.

Roosevelt takes Fanny Peabody sleighing and spends the evening with a group he calls the F.C.D.C. His days run to a three-mile walk to law school under Theodore Dwight, lectures and library study, the walk home, a sleigh ride and a social evening.
Dinner at the Keans' and a coffeehouse
Roosevelt dines at the Keans' and goes downtown with John Fernan to look over a coffeehouse.
Rosy and Rose come to visit
Alice's sister Rosy and Rose Saltonstall arrive to stay.
Sleigh ride and a theater party
Roosevelt takes Rosy sleighing and goes to a theater party in the evening.
Roosevelt takes Rose Saltonstall out in the sleigh and attends a dinner that night.
Roosevelt takes his mother for a sleigh ride and goes to a small party in the evening.
Corinne says yes to Douglas Robinson
After much wavering and distress, Corinne agrees to marry Douglas Robinson, a wealthy young man whose family fortune is in real estate. Roosevelt is delighted and calls Douglas a splendid fellow.
Roosevelt takes Aunt Annie Gracie sleighing and dines at the Leavitts'.
Roosevelt takes Rosy sleighing and joins a rollicking party at the Robinsons'.
Roosevelt enjoys a tea at Julian Weir's and a dinner at the Griswolds', and finds both great fun.
Roosevelt attends a preparatory communion lecture given by Dr. Hall and goes sleighing with his mother.
Roosevelt dines with the Weekes family.
Roosevelt is in New York City; his diary entry for the day is a single unclear mark.

After a drive with Rose Saltonstall, Roosevelt goes to a political meeting before the Patriarchs' Ball. It is the first mention of the 21st District Republican Association, run by boss Jake Hess from Morton Hall on 59th Street; Roosevelt probably joined the previous fall.
Roosevelt attends a Mendelssohn concert. Edith Carow writes Corinne to share her joy at the engagement and hopes to like Douglas Robinson.
Roosevelt goes to a tea at Percy King's and a small party at Aunt Annie Gracie's.
A Republican primary at Morton Hall
Roosevelt attends a primary of the Republican Association at Morton Hall, drives Alice in the buggy now that the snow has melted, and sees Rosy and Rose off to Chestnut Hill.
Roosevelt attends a musical evening at the Betts' home and takes Corinne for a drive.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no entry survives.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded.

The Niagara travelers reunite for a party at the Betts', with tableaux, waxworks and lively dances from the Virginia reel to the Highland schottische. Alice's piano playing is loud enough that cousin Emlen's family hears it through the wall next door.
Alice, with Roosevelt in tow, chaperones a small group of young people on an overnight visit to the Keans' country place.
Roosevelt returns to New York and takes Missy Robinson for a drive.
Political club, then the Bachelors' Ball
Roosevelt stops at the Primary Political Club at Morton Hall, then goes on to the very stylish Bachelors' Ball.
A long drive and dinner guests
Roosevelt takes Alice on a long drive; Mr. and Mrs. Meusing come to dinner.
Roosevelt drives his mother and dines with the Stuyvesant Fish family.
Roosevelt spends Sunday evening with the newsboys, as is his custom.

Roosevelt spends the evening with the F.C.D.C. Far away in India, Elliott turns 21. Around this time Roosevelt writes 'Sou' Sou' Southerly,' a story about how he and Elliott nearly drowned in a boat; it was never published.
Law books by day, a party by night
Roosevelt spends an evening at a party given by the Johnsons and notes in his diary that his legal studies have been demanding.
A long carriage ride with Alice
Roosevelt takes his wife Alice out for a lengthy drive around the city.
Dinner guests, then a Republican primary
The Thayer family dines with the Roosevelts, and afterward Roosevelt heads to Morton Hall for a Republican primary meeting.
A night at the theater as Garfield takes office
Roosevelt joins John and Nannie Roosevelt and Walter Suydam for an evening at the theater. In Washington, James A. Garfield becomes the twentieth President.
A quiet Saturday in New York
Roosevelt is in New York City; no particular activities are recorded.
Sunday at home in the city
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Spring arrives for a cart ride
With the first real taste of spring in the air, Roosevelt takes his wife Alice out in the cart.
A blank Tuesday in New York
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.
Along the Hudson by Riverside Park
Roosevelt drives his wife Alice up through Riverside Park, a ride he remembers as a lovely one.
Roosevelt's diary notes a modest dinner gathering.
Politics and opera in one evening
Roosevelt fits both a Republican primary meeting and a night at the opera into a single evening.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the day has no recorded details.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing further is recorded.
Speaking up on the city charter
After dinner at the Free Trade Club, Roosevelt gives a talk to the Republican Association about the proposed new city charter.
Roosevelt takes his younger sister Corinne for a long drive.
Up Riverside Park again with Alice
Roosevelt and his wife Alice take another extended drive through Riverside Park.
Roosevelt visits the Newsboys' lodging house and then a reception at the Tuckermans'. He also writes his sister Corinne to give his warm approval of her coming marriage to Douglas Robinson.
Roosevelt is chosen as a trustee of both the Orthopaedic Dispensary and the New York Infant Asylum, an honor he notes comes with real work attached.
New York Orthopedic Hospital and Dispensary
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted for the day.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the day passes without recorded detail.
Back to the law after some loafing
Roosevelt drives Alice, vows to buckle down on his law studies after a lazy stretch, and spends the evening dining with Hilly before joining him in his opera box.
Driving Fanny Smith on Alice's at-home day
Because his wife Alice keeps Tuesdays for receiving callers, Roosevelt takes family friend Fanny Smith out for a drive instead.
Six miles on foot each day
Roosevelt drives his sister Bamie through the park and notes that his daily walks to and from downtown, about six miles, plus park drives, make up all his exercise.
Law school and stalled writing projects
Roosevelt reports a daily drive with Alice, hard work at law school, and a couple of literary projects that are not going well.
Lunch with Lord and Lady George Campbell
Roosevelt lunches at the Kennedys' to meet Lord and Lady George Campbell. That evening Uncle Jimmie arrives.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no specific events are recorded.
Church, the newsboys, and family tea
Roosevelt and his wife Alice attend Dr. Hall's church in the morning, he spends the evening with the newsboys, and the extended family gathers for the usual Sunday tea.
Roosevelt's wife Alice departs for two weeks at Chestnut Hill with her family, and he admits he misses her badly. He takes Uncle Jimmie out driving.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded for the day.
Hitting the law books, Tod and Bigelow to dinner
Roosevelt reports intense study at law school, and friends Tod and Bigelow join him for dinner.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt takes his childhood friend Edith Carow out for a drive.
The best dinner party of the winter
At a dinner party Roosevelt is seated between Maria Potter and Christine Kean and later chats with Lulu McAllister; he rates it the most enjoyable such evening of the season.
Roosevelt is in New York City. His only diary entry, apparently about a dinner party, was crossed out in the original.
Roosevelt gives his older sister Bamie a drive.
Aunt Annie's drive and an evening of whist
Roosevelt drives his Aunt Annie and later hosts a whist party for friends including Beekman, Sedgwick, Iselin, and Colgate.
Roosevelt takes his sister Corinne out for a drive.
A houseguest and a dogcart ride
George Minot is staying with the Roosevelts. A dinner party fills the evening, and Roosevelt takes Lizzie Moran out in the dogcart.

Roosevelt drives his mother, then goes to a rowdy Republican primary at Morton Hall, where he speaks for a street-cleaning bill the party machine opposes. He calls it hopeless, then visits the John Taylor Johnstons.
Reunited with Alice at Chestnut Hill
Roosevelt travels to Chestnut Hill and is overjoyed to see his wife Alice and the Lee family again.
Sunday chapel and tea with the Saltonstalls
Roosevelt worships in the little chapel at Chestnut Hill, has tea with the Saltonstalls, and goes walking with Georgie and Bella.
Roosevelt goes over to Cambridge, stops at the Porcellian Club, and visits his friend Endicott Peabody, later the headmaster of Groton.
A lazy day with the children
At Chestnut Hill Roosevelt plays with the children and takes it easy all day.
Back in New York, Roosevelt catches a con man and holds him for arrest after a real scuffle.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the day has no entries.
A drive and a dinner party
Roosevelt takes his wife Alice for a long drive, and a dinner party follows in the evening.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt attends a meeting of the executive committee of the Young Men's Republican Association.
The swindler goes before a grand jury
Roosevelt secures an indictment from the grand jury against the con man he caught, and enjoys fine spring driving weather.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is noted.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record is blank.
Roosevelt watches his sister Corinne perform in private theatricals with Paul Tuckerman, which he praises, followed by dancing.
Mamie Saltonstall and Hattie Lee arrive to stay for a few days, and Roosevelt says he is keeping at his law studies reasonably well.
Last Sunday with the newsboys until fall
Roosevelt makes his final visit of the season to the Newsboys' lodging house and praises his future brother-in-law Douglas Robinson.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no details survive.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt heads downtown for the annual Newsboys' dinner and has a grand time.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are listed.
Roosevelt delights in the spring driving and says his horse has never performed better.
Six months for the swindler; doubts about law

Roosevelt sees the con man he caught sent to the penitentiary for six months. He is growing disenchanted with law school ethics. Angered by a Garfield appointment, Roscoe Conkling and Thomas Platt give up their U.S. Senate seats.
Rose Lee, Alice's sister, is a guest in the Roosevelt household.
Naval History at the Astor Library
Alongside his law studies, Roosevelt is spending most of his free hours in the Astor Library researching the book that becomes The Naval War of 1812.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt reports that he takes his wife Alice out driving each afternoon, usually up Riverside along the Hudson.
Roosevelt goes to another brawling Republican primary, where his street-cleaning bill draws only a handful of votes out of several hundred.
Roosevelt's old friend Dick Saltonstall comes to stay with the family.
A small party at the theater
Roosevelt takes Rosy, Dick, Fanny Smith, and Romy Colgate to the theater.
A good sermon and packing headaches
Roosevelt hears a fine sermon at Dr. Hall's church while the household struggles with packing for the coming trip to Europe.
Roosevelt sits in on a meeting of the Orthopaedic Dispensary's directors.
New York Orthopedic Hospital and Dispensary
Roosevelt notes gorgeous weather and wonderful drives.
Roosevelt finishes his law school term, signs his will, and sends his horse off to the country. His luggage weighs in at about 1,000 pounds.
Sailing for Europe aboard the Celtic
Roosevelt and his wife Alice board the Celtic for England at 3 p.m. on a hot day, with a crowd of friends seeing them off for a summer abroad.
On the first full day of the crossing Roosevelt feels fine while Alice is badly seasick.
Alice's seasickness worsens. Roosevelt tries to feed her, but she cannot keep food down and stays bedridden for days.
Alice is worse than ever while Roosevelt stays perfectly healthy.
Roosevelt and Alice are crossing the Atlantic; nothing is recorded.
The crossing continues with no diary entry for the day.
Worn out from caring for his seasick wife, Roosevelt vents in his diary, though he himself has stayed well.
Roosevelt and Alice remain aboard ship; no details are recorded.
The voyage continues; the record is blank.
The Roosevelts land at Queenstown, where Alice recovers almost immediately, and steam up the river to Cork to stay at the Imperial Hotel. Back home, the American Red Cross gets its start that day.
After church, Roosevelt and Alice hear the bells of Shandon and drive out to the ivy-draped ruin of Blarney Castle. He writes Rose Lee about the voyage and Ireland.
The couple take the train to Killarney, ride a jaunting car to Muckross Abbey, Ross Castle, and Torc waterfall, and return by boat.

Alice rides a pony while Roosevelt walks the wild Gap of Dunloe, then they boat across the Upper Lake. Finding a man collapsed from hunger, Roosevelt has him fed, gives him ten shillings, and sends him to Cork.
On to Dublin, counting his luck
Roosevelt and Alice take the train to Dublin. He declares her the best traveling companion he has ever had.
The Roosevelts visit Bray and Powerscourt and walk the wooded glen of the Dargle, enjoying a life of ease.
Across the Irish Sea to Liverpool
The couple sail to Holyhead and go by rail to Liverpool, where they stay with Aunt Hattie Bulloch.
Roosevelt and Alice are in Liverpool; no activities are recorded.
Roosevelt spends the afternoon with Uncle Irvine Bulloch and Aunt Ella at their charming small house.
The Roosevelts remain in Liverpool; no details are given.
Roosevelt and Alice go on to London and check into the Queen's Hotel, where Harry Shaw, Minot Weld, and Harry Chapin call on him.
At the National Gallery Roosevelt admires Rembrandt and Murillo but dismisses Turner, then visits the Zoological Gardens, where Alice wonders who shaves the lions.
Crown Jewels and an evening of opera
Roosevelt escorts Jenny Tuckerman to the Tower of London to see the Crown Jewels and armor, then hears Christina Nilsson sing at the Haymarket.
A coach ride to the Epsom races
Along with Shaw, Weld, Chapin, and the Lawrences, Roosevelt takes a coach out to Epsom for the races, and finishes the day at the theater.
South Kensington and Gilbert and Sullivan
Roosevelt tours the South Kensington Museum and catches Gilbert and Sullivan's latest comic opera, probably Patience.
Roosevelt hears fine music at St. Paul's in the morning and, in the afternoon, a sermon by Dean Stanley at Westminster Abbey.
Robinson relatives and the British Museum
Roosevelt lunches with relatives of Douglas Robinson, admires the sculptures at the British Museum, and dines with the Kingsfords.
Roosevelt rides out to Windsor Castle by coach despite the rain and dines with Chapin, Weld, and Shaw.
Roosevelt visits the Grosvenor Gallery, goes shopping, and has Shaw and Chapin over for dinner.
Roosevelt admires the Doré Gallery, buys gifts, and is fitted for new clothes.
Roosevelt shops and returns to the British Museum.
Across a calm Channel to Paris
Roosevelt and Alice cross a smooth English Channel and settle into the Hotel Bellevue in Paris.
After church, Roosevelt walks to the Place de la Concorde and along the Champs-Élysées.
Sights of Paris and a letter to Conie
Roosevelt shops, tours the Bois de Boulogne, the Vendôme Column, and the Arc de Triomphe, and writes Corinne about London, its art, and the Channel crossing.
Roosevelt tours the Louvre, admiring the Venus de Milo and works by Rubens and Murillo.
Roosevelt and Alice are in Paris; nothing is recorded.
From the Hotel Bellevue on the Avenue de l'Opéra, Roosevelt writes Corinne with his opinions of the art at the Louvre.
Roosevelt and Alice leave Paris by morning train, bound for Venice.
Grimy and tired, but enchanted by Venice
After a few mishaps on the way, the couple arrive in Venice dirty and weary. Roosevelt calls it the loveliest place of the trip so far.
A palace hotel and the waterways
The Roosevelts take rooms in the old palace that is the Hotel Danieli, facing San Giorgio Maggiore and the Lido, and in the evening glide through the canals by gondola with Giuseppe Beppo at the oar.
Titian, the Doge's Palace, and music on the piazza
Roosevelt views a Titian masterpiece, tours the Doge's Palace, rides a gondola to the Lido, and ends the night listening to music in Piazza San Marco.
San Marco by day, canals by night
Roosevelt visits San Marco and rows through Venice again after dark. He is able to read the Italian papers aloud to Alice.
Roosevelt and Alice travel from Venice to Milan, which is very hot.
Roosevelt sees Milan's cathedral before moving on to Lake Como. He writes Bamie about Venice.
The Roosevelts are at Lake Como; no details are recorded.
Roosevelt finds Nicholas Fish and his wife at the lake, and drives with Alice to the town of Como to see its cathedral.
The Roosevelts remain at Lake Como; nothing is recorded.
Hiring Lombardino and a three-horse carriage
The couple steam up the lake to Colico, then hire a carriage with three horses and a driver named Lombardino for a two-week tour, reaching Chiavenna that night.
Roosevelt and Alice cross the Splügen Pass, stopping for a poor lunch at Campodolcino, and spend the night at a decent inn in the village of Splügen. They walk the hills among Swiss cows and sheep.
The couple drive through the dramatic Via Mala, lunch at Thusis, climb to a Rhaetian castle, and follow a gorge to Tiefencastel.
Roosevelt and Alice leave the valley by the treeless Julier Pass, descending into the Upper Engadine and on to Samedan.
At Samedan, Roosevelt takes his wife Alice out riding donkeys.
Alpine climb as Garfield is shot
Alice rides and Roosevelt hikes up Muottas Muragl for a fine view and a good workout. In Washington, Charles Guiteau shoots President Garfield at a train station.
From Samedan, Roosevelt writes to his sister Bamie.
The couple cross the Bernina Pass by carriage, lunching at the hospice amid deep snowdrifts, and continue to Le Prese, where Roosevelt rows Alice on the Lago di Poschiavo after dinner.
Word of Garfield reaches the Alps
Roosevelt travels up the Valtellina to the Baths of Bormio, where he learns that Garfield has been shot and calls it a dreadful blow to the country.
Fresh reports tell Roosevelt that Garfield has survived, and he writes that the crisis means work ahead for every man who wishes his country well.
Roosevelt and Alice cross the snowy Stelvio Pass, but heavy rain washes out the road beyond the summit and they retreat to spend the night at Trafoi.

The couple descend into the Adige valley, lunch at the Haidersee with a curious German landlady, and stop at Hoch-Finstermünz above a deep gorge. Roosevelt interprets for their driver. It is his mother Mittie's 46th birthday.
Driving down the Inn valley through rain and sun, Roosevelt and Alice stop for the night at a traditional Tyrolean inn in Imst.
The couple follow the Inn valley on to Innsbruck.
After sightseeing in Innsbruck, Roosevelt and Alice go on to Munich.
Roosevelt tours the picture gallery and other sights in Munich.
Roosevelt and Alice travel on to Lucerne.
A bundle of letters from home
In Lucerne, a refuge from the heat, the couple collect a stack of mail: two letters from Oyster Bay and nine from Chestnut Hill.
Roosevelt and Alice hike up Mount Pilatus from Alpnach and down the other side to Hergiswil, outpacing their guide halfway up. Roosevelt chats with German students along the way.
Convinced it is Sunday, Roosevelt and Alice ask about church services until they discover their mistake in the afternoon; their puzzled waiter takes them for Jewish.
Roosevelt attends the English Church in Lucerne and finds the sermon weak.
Roosevelt climbs the Rigi Kulm and watches a magnificent sunset.
Up at three for the sunrise
Roosevelt rises at 3 a.m. to see the sunrise from the Rigi, descends to Lucerne, and writes Bamie.
The Roosevelts drive across the Brünig Pass to Interlaken.
Roosevelt and Alice are at Interlaken; nothing is recorded.
The couple drive through the rain to Grindelwald and lodge at the Schwarzer Adler.
With Alice riding and Roosevelt walking, they make a round trip to a lookout near Grindelwald.
Roosevelt leaves Grindelwald at 8:15 a.m. with guides Peter Egger and Hans Baumann, whom he rates highly, and reaches the Bergli hut at 4:45 p.m. to spend the night.
Starting at 3:15 a.m. into wind and cloud, Roosevelt crosses the Mönchjoch and the Jungfraufirn and stands on the Jungfrau's summit at 8:55. He enjoys the descent and is back in Grindelwald by 6 p.m.
Roosevelt is at Grindelwald after the climb; no events are recorded.
Alice is carried in a sedan chair while Roosevelt walks to the Upper Grindelwald Glacier; in the afternoon they drive back to Interlaken.
The Roosevelts hire a carriage and drive to Kandersteg.
Gemmi Pass and a surprise reunion
The couple cross the Gemmi Pass to Leuk and go on to Visp, where they are astonished to run into Charley Alexander.
Alice rides and Roosevelt walks from Visp to Zermatt in the company of Charley Alexander, whom he finds a fine companion.
Glacier walk and dinner for friends
After yet another weak sermon, Roosevelt walks to the glacier with Alexander and hosts a small dinner for friends he has met at Zermatt.
Roosevelt and Alice, still traveling with Alexander, climb to the Gornergrat and spend the night at the Riffel.
Alexander departs; friends gather at Zermatt
Back in Zermatt, the Roosevelts reluctantly part with Alexander. The Gardiners, the Baylies, and the Kennedys are also in town.
At 9 a.m. Roosevelt and a pair of Taugwalder-family guides head toward the Matterhorn and reaches the climbers' hut by seven. The peak had first been summited only sixteen years before.
Roosevelt leaves the hut at 3:45 a.m., reaches the Matterhorn's summit at seven, and is back in Zermatt by 3:30 p.m., hard and risky going, but he is in top condition.
Telling Bamie and Bill Sewall about the climb
Roosevelt and Alice leave Zermatt for Stalden, Alice and the bags on two mules. He writes Bamie and his Maine guide Bill Sewall about the Matterhorn ascent.
Leaving at 4:30 a.m., the couple go by mule to Visp, by train to Martigny, and by a shaky wagon to Chamonix, arriving under a bright moon.
Roosevelt finds the Chapmans staying at Chamonix and is unimpressed by the church service.
The Roosevelts ride the stagecoach from Chamonix to Geneva.
Roosevelt and Alice are in Geneva; no events are recorded.
The couple travel on to Basel.
Roosevelt is fascinated by the Basel Minster and especially its medieval collection before going on to Strasbourg.
Roosevelt admires Strasbourg's cathedral, above all its exterior, and buys some fine antique silver.
The Roosevelts continue to Mainz on the Rhine.
On the Rhine, Roosevelt notes a gymnastic society, the Turnverein, out in great numbers.
Roosevelt and Alice take a Rhine steamer to Cologne.
Cologne Cathedral ranks second only to Milan
Roosevelt visits Cologne Cathedral and prefers it to every cathedral he has seen except Milan's.
Roosevelt enjoys the company of General and Mrs. Cullum in Cologne, then travels to Amsterdam.
Roosevelt tours Amsterdam and its picture galleries, then drives out in the afternoon to the spotless village of Broek.
The Roosevelts continue to The Hague.
Art and a long walk at The Hague
Roosevelt visits the picture gallery and the Dutch Museum and walks all over town.
Working on his naval history abroad
From The Hague, Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is at work on The Naval War of 1812.
Roosevelt goes to Antwerp and sees its cathedral.
The couple move on to Brussels.
Roosevelt spends the morning in a Brussels picture gallery and writes Corinne that he admires Rembrandt but dislikes Rubens.
Roosevelt and Alice return to Paris.
The Roosevelts are in Paris; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt and Alice remain in Paris; the day is blank.

Roosevelt is in Paris; no events are noted.
Roosevelt's diary notes a visit to the Hôtel de Cluny.
Roosevelt visits the tomb of Napoleon.
Roosevelt and Alice return to London and take rooms at the Bath Hotel.
The Roosevelts are in London; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt and Alice are in London; the day is blank.
Roosevelt writes Bamie about Napoleon's tomb and tells Bill Sewall that a summer in Europe has only deepened his gladness at being an American.
Roosevelt shops and returns to the Doré Gallery.
Dinner and a theater box from Captain Thompson
Captain A. Thompson treats the Roosevelts to dinner and a box at the theater.
Roosevelt returns to the National Gallery.
Roosevelt visits Colonel Sawler at the Tower of London.
Naval lessons from the Bulloch uncles
Roosevelt and Alice go to Liverpool to stay with the Bullochs. Uncle Irvine and Uncle James give him expert help with nautical terms for his naval history.
The Roosevelts are with the Bullochs in Liverpool; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt and Alice remain in Liverpool; no events are noted.
The couple are in Liverpool; the day is blank.
Days with the old sea captain
Roosevelt spends most of the day with his uncle James Bulloch. He writes his mother that the Doré pictures no longer appeal to him and that he is very fond of Uncle Irvine.

While Roosevelt is in Liverpool, President Garfield dies in the United States from the wound he suffered on July 2, and Chester A. Arthur takes office.

Roosevelt and Alice are in Liverpool on the eve of sailing; no details survive.
Roosevelt and Alice board the Britannic for America and find Bob Grant good company on board.

Alice takes to the sea this time
Unlike the miserable outbound crossing, Alice is genuinely enjoying the trip home. It is Corinne's 20th birthday.
The Britannic continues west with Roosevelt and Alice aboard; nothing is recorded.

The record points to Joe Murray's later account of how Roosevelt won his Assembly nomination, published in Lawrence Abbott's Impressions of Theodore Roosevelt.
Roosevelt and Alice are still at sea aboard the Britannic; no details survive.
The Britannic reaches New York, and the Roosevelt and Lee families turn out in full to welcome the couple home.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt resumes law school and starts working the primaries at Morton Hall, determined to block the renomination of William Trimble, who opposed the street-cleaning measure in Albany that spring.

Law, politics, and above all the book
Roosevelt sums up his life: moderate effort at law, real effort at politics, and the most effort of all on his naval history, which he hopes to publish this winter.

Roosevelt's diary for this date records his Assembly nomination and platform, but he struck it out; it belongs to October 28.
A misplaced diary line, belonging to October 29, notes that Uncle Jim, Emlen, and Al strongly oppose his running for office.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded for the day.
At Morton Hall, Roosevelt lodges a formal objection to William Trimble's renomination for the State Assembly.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded for the day.
Joe Murray talks him into running
Republican district leader Joe Murray persuades Roosevelt to run for the State Assembly himself. A crossed-out diary line here, belonging to November 2, says friends are backing him loyally.
Roosevelt turns 23 and marks his first wedding anniversary with Alice.
Roosevelt, surprised, wins the Republican nomination for the Assembly from the 21st District, which Joe Murray engineers over the head of district boss Hess in place of William Trimble.

The record marks this as the day Roosevelt wins his first election.
Running for the Assembly as his own man

A week before the vote, Roosevelt faces Dr. W. W. Strew, lately dismissed as head of the Blackwell's Island asylum. He tells the New York Herald he belongs to no one, and after a tense saloon stop where he scolded the owner about license fees, the district men Murray, Hess and Bullard step in to run things.
Roosevelt is in New York City in the closing days of his Assembly race; no other details survive for the day.
Roosevelt is in New York City in the closing days of his Assembly race; no other details survive for the day.
In his diary Roosevelt boils his stance down to one line: a Republican, but free to break ranks on city affairs.
Roosevelt is in New York City as the Assembly race nears its end; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City as the Assembly race nears its end; nothing more is recorded.
Evening Post backs the young candidate
On the eve of the vote, the New York Evening Post endorses Roosevelt, pointing to his late father's record of civic service and to the high regard people who know the son hold him in.
Elected to the New York Assembly
Roosevelt wins his first election, taking the 21st Assembly District seat 3,490 votes to 1,989 over Democrat William Strew. The job pays $1,200 a year.
Roosevelt is in New York City the day after winning his Assembly seat; nothing else is noted.
Joking that he is now a politician
Roosevelt writes to college friend Charles Grenville Washburn with a wry note on his new status, and thanks lawyer Joseph Choate for his part in the win.

Naval War of 1812 goes to Putnam's

Roosevelt hands his finished manuscript of The Naval War of 1812 to the Putnam publishing house. He also buys a stake in the firm and takes a desk there, where he is not shy about offering advice on how the business should be run.

Roosevelt writes that New York's winter round of dinners and balls is now in full swing, and everyone is joining in.

Roosevelt drives the tenement cigar-making bill to passage. He had toured New York's tenements with Samuel Gompers and seen for himself the sweatshops and child labor bred by rolling cigars at home.

The great bridge linking Manhattan and Brooklyn is formally opened.
Free trade talk, and a hunting idea

Guest of honor at a Free Trade Club dinner at Clark's Tavern, Roosevelt speaks on "The Tariff in Politics," predicting free trade will come in time. There he meets Henry H. Gorringe, who sparks the idea of a hunt on the Little Missouri.

Alice is expecting. Roosevelt starts planning the house he will call Leeholm, and he headlines a Garfield Club meeting with a talk on "The Political Situation."
Roosevelt's brother Elliott proposes marriage to Anna Hall.

On doctor's orders Roosevelt heads to Richfield Springs to recover. He and Alice make the trip by buggy.

At Richfield Springs Roosevelt learns that Elliott is engaged and is thrilled. He writes Conie that Alice and the horse both got sick on the hilly drive, and that he chafes at the idle spa routine of waters, baths and ailing elderly guests.

Roosevelt sets out for the West on his hunting trip. Henry H. Gorringe, who had first proposed it, drops out at the last moment. Roosevelt writes Bamie to tell her he is leaving for Dakota.
Roosevelt reaches Chicago and writes his mother that he feels full of fight.
Roosevelt is on the rails, heading for the Dakota Badlands.
Roosevelt switches trains to the St. Paul Express for the run west.
A 2 a.m. arrival in Little Missouri
Roosevelt steps off the train at Little Missouri in Dakota Territory and rouses the owner of the Pyramid Park Hotel at two in the morning. He is given a bed in a fourteen-bed bunk room.
Joe Ferris signs on as guide

Roosevelt hires 25-year-old Joe Ferris to guide him. Buffalo have been hunted hard in the Dakotas lately. They overnight at the Maltese Cross Ranch, which Sylvane Ferris, 24, runs with Bill Merrifield, 28; all three men came from Canada. Roosevelt also writes his mother.
A mare named Nell and the Lang cabin

Roosevelt buys a mare called Nell from Ferris, then rides 45 miles south to the cabin of Scotsman Gregor Lang and his son Lincoln, 16. Lang, sent by an English firm to scout cattle country, talks with Roosevelt past midnight about the region and the cattle trade.
A missed buck in the rain

Up at six on a soaking day, Roosevelt hunts with Joe Ferris. Ferris drops a blacktail buck at long range after Roosevelt misses it, to his own annoyance. That night Roosevelt again talks cattle with Gregor Lang late, while Ferris sleeps.
Mud and an empty game bag
Roosevelt and Ferris hunt the whole day in the rain, bag nothing, and come back caked in mud. While Ferris sleeps, Roosevelt and Gregor Lang talk cattle, America and politics.
Another wet day: Roosevelt hunts from morning to night and then talks late into the evening, just as before.
Rain again. Roosevelt's party spots a band of wandering Cree, but otherwise the day repeats the last two.
A wounded buffalo and a bloody brow

Roosevelt hits a buffalo too far back and it gets away. In the chase the animal charges, his pony knocks his rifle into his head, and he bleeds from the cut. That night the horses bolt. Ferris hears him exclaim he is having fun.
In cold rain, Roosevelt gets a shot but misses with water streaming into his eyes, and spends another drenched night outdoors.
Hard luck, and a choice to invest

On a hot day Roosevelt tumbles down a cliff, is thrown from his horse, and nearly loses the horse to quicksand. After two days on biscuits and rainwater, he resolves to put money into the Badlands, and talks late with Gregor Lang again.
More rain, and more hunting for Roosevelt.
With Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield at the Lang cabin, Roosevelt hands them a $14,000 check to run his stock and purchase 450 cattle. The sum tops his entire income for the year, $13,920.
At the Lang cabin Roosevelt writes out a ranch contract. Ferris and Merrifield head to Minnesota to be released by their employers, Wadsworth and Halley, so they can partner with him.
Riding into Montana with Joe Ferris, Roosevelt finally brings down a bison bull. He celebrates with a whooping dance and hands Ferris $100 then and there.
Roosevelt skins the bison he shot the previous day and then rides back to Little Missouri.
Roosevelt is at the Maltese Cross, the cabin of Ferris and Merrifield.

Roosevelt is at the Pyramid Park Hotel in Little Missouri. Across the river the French Marquis de Mores has been building Medora since April, named for his wife, with grand plans to ship beef east in refrigerated rail cars.
Roosevelt remains at the Pyramid Park Hotel in Little Missouri.
In Bismarck, Roosevelt arranges to have his bison head mounted.
With Ferris and Merrifield back, Roosevelt's first contract with them is completed. It is also his sister Conie's 22nd birthday.

Roosevelt starts back to New York while Ferris and Merrifield travel to Iowa to buy 300 head of cattle.

Roosevelt is still traveling east. Mittie writes a friend that Alice's pregnancy is now plainly showing. The family, above all Uncle James Roosevelt, head of Roosevelt and Son, frowns on Roosevelt's Badlands investment.

Speakership slips away to Titus Sheard

The Republican caucus picks Titus Sheard, not Roosevelt, for Speaker. Members break pledges as machine men and corporate lobbyists close ranks, and Senator Miller wins over John O'Brien. Stung, Roosevelt moves to make Sheard's nomination unanimous. His year-end notes also tally his Dakota game and his 1883 income.

The New York Sun greets the year with a jab, predicting no happy new year for "the exquisite Mr. Roosevelt."

Roosevelt files three anti-machine bills: steeper liquor license fees, a halt to city borrowing, and more power for New York's mayor to name department heads without the aldermen. Newspapers start backing him in the clerk dispute.

Heading a probe of city corruption

Roosevelt chairs a special committee probing corruption in New York City, joined by Republicans William O'Neil and Erwin and Democrats Hartford D. Nelson and Thomas V. Welch. Sheard lets him replace the Cities clerk with his own pick.

Alice waits out her last weeks
Close to giving birth, Alice feels neglected. Roosevelt has let their 55 West 45th Street house to his brother Elliott and Anna, and Alice is staying with Mittie and Conie on West 57th Street.
Roosevelt's investigation of New York City government claims a scalp: the city's Undersheriff, fresh off the witness stand, is taken into custody and indicted for misusing public money.
Back at the hearings in New York City, Roosevelt is once more exasperated by how the Sheriff responds to the committee's questions.

Speaks up for the aldermanic bill
Roosevelt makes a speech backing his bill on the powers of the mayor and aldermen, then heads up the Hudson to Albany.
A bloody nose in the sparring ring
In Albany, Roosevelt boxes hard enough to draw blood from his sparring partner. He writes his pregnant wife Alice that he aches to be home with her by Friday evening.
Roosevelt dines with the Rathbone family in Albany.
Home to New York; his mother has a cold
Roosevelt travels down to New York City. His mother, Mittie, is laid up with a cold.
Saturday at home in New York

The Sheriff hands over his books
A win for Roosevelt's committee: the Sheriff of New York gives up his account books for examination. The committee then breaks for a week.

A daughter, Alice, is born at 10 a.m. Roosevelt has already left for Albany. With Conie away and Mittie fighting a bad cold, his sister Bamie is the one tending the new mother, while Alice's parents wait at the Brunswick Hotel for their first grandchild.

Under a thick fog that has shrouded the Hudson Valley for days, Roosevelt receives one telegram, then another, and races to New York. When he reaches home at half past ten that night, Alice has slipped into a coma from Bright's disease. That same day, a Cooper Union rally backs his aldermanic bill.
His mother and his wife die

Valentine's Day brings a double blow. At 3 a.m. Roosevelt's mother, Mittie, dies of typhoid fever at 48. At 2 p.m. his wife Alice, just 22, dies too. In his diary he marks the day with a single line. He wires the news to Dora Watkins.
Out of sympathy for Roosevelt's double loss, his Assembly colleagues vote to adjourn for the day.
Mittie and Alice are mourned together at the Fifth Avenue Presbyterian Church and laid to rest in Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn. Observers describe Roosevelt as dazed and childlike in his grief.
Baby Alice christened, given to Bamie
The infant Alice is baptized, and her aunt Bamie takes charge of her care.
Four days after the funerals Roosevelt is back in Albany. He writes Andrew D. White to thank him for his sympathy.
Roosevelt is in Albany; no further events are noted.
On the floor for the aldermanic bill
Roosevelt rises in the Assembly to argue for his aldermanic bill.
Writing to Carl Schurz, Roosevelt explains that he has thrown himself back into his duties because staying busy is what keeps him sane.

Roosevelt questions a New York Department of Correction official about improper fees for moving prisoners.
In the Assembly, Roosevelt presses colleagues to pass his measure capping how much debt cities can run up.
Roosevelt amends a bill to aid Black orphans and sends four bills out of his Committee on Cities.
Seven more bills, and Elliott turns 24
Roosevelt reports seven more bills, among them measures on protecting mechanics and laborers and on Brooklyn's sewers and drainage. It is also his brother Elliott's 24th birthday.
An inheritance, and good news from Dakota

Roosevelt is back in New York for his investigations. He receives $62,500 from his mother's estate, and his ranch partners in Dakota report the cattle came through a hard winter in good shape. Bamie rents 422 Madison Avenue and raises Baby Alice there; Roosevelt throws himself into Assembly work through the spring.
Jail testimony and a contract for Leeholm

Roosevelt's committee hears witnesses describe drinking and sexual misconduct inside New York's jails. The same day he signs a $16,975 contract to build Leeholm, his house on Long Island, designed by the architects Lamb and Rich and to be built by a Lawrence, Long Island, firm, John A. Wood & Son.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is recorded.
At 10 o'clock the investigating committee sits again in New York City.
A sister worries about sleepless nights
Roosevelt reads the Banking Committee's bill on the Assembly floor. In New York, Conie writes Bamie that their brother is pacing through the nights and barely sleeping.
Liquor speech and a debt-limit victory
Roosevelt delivers an important address about the Liquor License Bill and his committee reports a dozen fresh bills. His bill capping municipal debt passes.

Seven more bills leave the Cities Committee. Roosevelt also files his Tenure of Office Bill: it would cut short every New York City department head's term on January 15, 1885, keep the current mayor from naming replacements for four years, and badly complicate the aldermanic bill.
The committee opens its final weekend of testimony at the Metropolitan Hotel in New York City.

Roosevelt's Cities Committee reports another 14 bills to the floor.

After reporting 15 bills in the morning and six more at night, Roosevelt reads the committee's official report on New York City and finds it buries his strongest findings. He carries all 1,054 pages of testimony to the Delavan House and begins dictating and drafting a report of his own.

Roosevelt finishes his own 44-page report, feeding pages to the printer as he goes, and lays it before the Assembly with nine reform bills. Democrats led by Assemblyman Littlejohn object; his bid to force three bills out by Tuesday loses 21 to 60, though the inquiry wins more time.

In the Commercial Advertiser, Roosevelt responds wryly to colleagues who call him arrogant for driving his bills so hard.

The Assembly approves Roosevelt's bill to put the Parks Commission under a single head, along with six of his other bills, while two more go down. He also issues his second report on corruption in New York City.

Picked as a delegate to Utica

His Bureau of Elections and Tenure of Office bills move to the full Assembly sitting as a committee. Roosevelt then heads to New York City, where a reform slate chosen at Morton Hall for the special state convention at Utica includes him.

Harper's Weekly runs a Thomas Nast cartoon picturing Governor Cleveland signing bills that Roosevelt hands him. Back at the hearings, a plumber named Michael O'Malley testifies about prostitution in the city.

For a second time Roosevelt appears before Governor Cleveland asking him to remove Alexander Davidson as Sheriff of New York City.

Roosevelt checks into Bagg's Hotel in Utica for the special Republican state convention and works the back rooms. His goal: win all four of New York's at-large seats at the national convention for independents who, like him, oppose James G. Blaine.

At the Grand Opera House in Utica, Roosevelt outmaneuvers Senator Warner Miller, breaks with his friend Hunt, and leads the voting for delegate-at-large with 472 votes, ahead of Andrew D. White, John J. Gilbert and Edwin Packard. He waves a fist at Miller, crowing over revenge for his loss of the Speakership race to Sheard.
A hero's welcome in the Assembly
Roosevelt returns to Albany and his allies greet him as a conquering hero; newspapers liken the chamber to a reception room in his honor.

Roosevelt writes Simon North of the Utica Morning Herald that machine politicians dislike him and that he is eager to get out West and leave politics. The family houses at 6 West 57th and 55 West 45th Streets are emptied and sold, and Bamie answers condolence letters from 422 Madison Avenue, next door to the Clarence Day family.

After a hearing, Roosevelt heads to Albany. He invites Henry Cabot Lodge, a Massachusetts delegate-at-large, to spend the weekend of May 17 at the family house on West 57th Street despite the household being packed up, and writes Louis T. Michener of Indiana about the coming national convention.

Third report: take the police out of politics

Two of Roosevelt's bills need last-minute rewriting because of sloppy errors. He also delivers a third report on graft in the city, proposing that police jobs come under civil service rules and that the four-member police board be scrapped.
The Legislature adjourns for the year, and Roosevelt heads home to New York City.
The start of a lifelong friendship

Roosevelt hosts independent delegates bound for the national convention. Henry Cabot Lodge is his houseguest, likely their first long stretch together and the beginning of a friendship for life. Together they confer with Edwin Godkin, who edits the Evening Post.
Roosevelt and Lodge travel to Washington to talk with Senator George F. Edmunds of Vermont, their pick for the presidential nomination.
In an interview with the New York World, Roosevelt regrets how many of his bills were blocked in the Albany session just ended.
