Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is noted.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the day carries no entries.
Roosevelt boards the Pennsylvania Limited for Chicago, riding in a private car alongside Carl Schurz and George William Curtis.

In Chicago for the Republican National Convention, Roosevelt backs Edmunds. He and Curtis take rooms at the Grand Pacific Hotel, New York's headquarters, while Lodge settles at the Leland House with Massachusetts. Roosevelt sports a bamboo cane and a straw boater lined in blue.
With the Republican National Convention about to open, Roosevelt watches more delegates stream into Chicago, and the newcomers lean heavily toward James G. Blaine.
Fighting Powell Clayton's bid to chair
Roosevelt teams up with his friend Henry Cabot Lodge to block Powell Clayton, a machine politician they consider corrupt, from being named temporary chairman of the convention.
Speaking up for John R. Lynch

On the convention's sunny first day, the New York delegates take the front center rows. Roosevelt rises to back John R. Lynch of Mississippi, a Black Republican, for temporary chairman, and Lynch wins. All day he pushes hard against Blaine.
Rain and routine at the convention
A damp day in Chicago brings ordinary convention business, while supporters of Senator George F. Edmunds scheme to hold off the nomination.

Rain falls again as the delegates receive women's suffrage petitions and hear William McKinley present the party platform. Sixteen nominating speeches fill the evening, and the hall doesn't empty until 1:45 in the morning.
Blaine wins on the fourth ballot

Voting starts and Blaine gains ground on every roll call. After the third ballot Joseph Foraker moves to recess and Roosevelt leaps up shouting in support, but the motion fails in the uproar. Blaine takes the nomination on the fourth ballot with 541 votes.
Off to the Badlands after defeat
Beaten at the convention, Roosevelt leaves Chicago and heads west for Dakota, and the papers note his retreat to the wilds.
A gloomy letter from St. Paul
Traveling west, Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie from St. Paul that the reformers have been crushed, and he judges Blaine the worst choice of anyone the convention weighed.

Roosevelt steps off the train in Medora, where Joe and Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield greet him and talk over the convention at the newspaper office. A St. Paul Pioneer Press interview quotes him saying he will stay with the party ticket.
Riding out to the Maltese Cross
Roosevelt saddles up and rides from town to his Maltese Cross Ranch.
A day at the Maltese Cross
Roosevelt is at his Maltese Cross Ranch; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt signs a second deal with Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield, paying $26,000 for a thousand head of cattle. Back East, his refusal to bolt Blaine has made the news, and New York's Union League Club blackballs him for it.
Staying at Gregor Lang's, Roosevelt bags a jackrabbit and a curlew with his heavy express rifle and is itching to go after antelope. Mrs. Maddox takes his measurements for a buckskin outfit.
At the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt drops two curlew with his rifle, one in flight, and is pleased with the shooting. Harper's Weekly declares against Blaine.
Roosevelt prepares to leave the Maltese Cross on a four-day antelope hunt.
A badger run down on horseback
Roosevelt spots a badger far from its burrow, gallops up and kills it with his revolver, then watches a cattle roundup.

Roosevelt tells Bamie the St. Paul interview was made up, delights in the June weather after thirteen hours on horseback, and says ranching will be his real business. He means to bring Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow out from Maine. To Lodge he admits he has heard no news since the convention.
A fine buck antelope at full gallop

Riding alone on the prairie, Roosevelt races his pony across the path of a small band of antelope, jumps down and drops a big-horned buck. From a cattleman's shack he writes Lodge asking to see him soon and insisting they cannot bolt the party.
Roosevelt is away hunting; no details survive for the day.
Another day afield for Roosevelt, with nothing further recorded.

Rounding a knoll, Roosevelt sees two antelope watching from far off. He gets down, aims high and breaks one's neck at a measured 300 yards, the longest shot he has ever made. He spends the night in the trees.
Roosevelt comes back to the Maltese Cross Ranch from his hunting trip.
After shooting two plover for the cook pot, Roosevelt tells Bamie he has spent a week alone on the plains, sleeping out under the sky, and has two antelope and a deer to show for it.
The Maltese Cross sits right on the main trail, so cowboys drop by every day to visit, and Roosevelt manages little writing.

After a mallard for the pot, Roosevelt scouts the river north of Medora for a new ranch site. He buys a squatter's claim for $400, and a pair of locked elk antlers found on the ground gives the place its name: the Elkhorn.

Roosevelt travels by rail with the Marquis de Mores and a man named Jameson, to Mills City in Montana, hoping to join a vigilance group formed to stamp out horse stealing. The vigilantes turn all three down because they come from prominent families.
Back at the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt shoots a sharp-tailed grouse cock with his rifle for the table.
Roosevelt is at his ranch; the day has no further record.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at the Maltese Cross; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt boards an eastbound train at Medora for New York.
Roosevelt is on the train, making his way from Dakota toward New York.
Roosevelt's eastbound journey to New York continues.
Roosevelt reaches New York and settles in with his sister Bamie at her home on Madison Avenue.
A Dakota paper on his reform work
Roosevelt is in New York as the Mandan Pioneer, back in Dakota, runs a piece on him and the reform fight in New York City politics.
Roosevelt meets with Republican leaders in New York and finds that every prominent reformer wants no part of Blaine.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing more.
Another unrecorded day for Roosevelt in New York City.
Roosevelt writes his old Maine guides Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow, asking them to join his Dakota ranching venture, and encloses a $3,000 check to clear a mortgage.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.
Roosevelt remains in New York City with nothing further on record.

The Democrats name New York's governor, Grover Cleveland, as their presidential candidate, with Thomas A. Hendricks as his running mate. Roosevelt loathes Hendricks as a Copperhead, a Northerner who sided with the South during the Civil War.
Roosevelt goes to Orange, New Jersey, to see his younger sister Corinne.
Roosevelt stays on in Orange, New Jersey.

Roosevelt takes his baby daughter Alice to Chestnut Hill to visit her mother's parents. Old college friends in Boston give him the cold shoulder, since many reform Republicans, the Mugwumps, have broken away to back Cleveland, along with a long list of major newspapers.
Roosevelt is staying at Chestnut Hill; nothing more is recorded.
Another quiet day for Roosevelt at Chestnut Hill.
Roosevelt remains at Chestnut Hill with no other details noted.
A porch talk with Lodge at Nahant
Roosevelt visits Henry Cabot Lodge's summer place at Nahant, and the two talk late on the porch. Lodge, who took the brunt of the Blaine backlash alone while Roosevelt was out West, is feeling low.
From Chestnut Hill, Roosevelt writes the Boston Herald to say publicly that he will vote for the Republican presidential ticket.
Roosevelt writes Lodge's wife, Nannie, joking that he has been tangling with Boston's Mugwumps.
Bad press and a Cleveland scandal
Newspapers criticize Roosevelt and Lodge for sticking with Blaine, and the story of Grover Cleveland's child born out of wedlock breaks.
Roosevelt is back in New York City; no details survive.
Roosevelt is in New York City with nothing else on record.
Talking ranch life with the Tribune
At Bamie's Madison Avenue home, Roosevelt gives an interview to a New York Tribune reporter and speaks warmly of the West and cattle ranching.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.
Roosevelt spends a quiet, unrecorded day in New York City.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is known.
Roosevelt meets Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow in New York and the three set off for Medora. He tells Lodge that friends seem startled he has not sprouted hooves and horns.
On the way to Dakota, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow pick up a traveling companion at Harrisburg, an Englishman named Messiter, whom Roosevelt judges no great thinker but a gentleman.
Roosevelt and his party are still on the train heading west.
Passing through St. Paul on the trip west, Roosevelt sits for a newspaper interview.

Roosevelt's cattle operation now runs on two spreads: the Maltese Cross, seven miles south of Medora and run by Merrifield and Sylvane Ferris, and the new Elkhorn, thirty miles north, placed under Sewall and Dow. Together they carry about 4,500 head.
Roosevelt pulls into Medora with his Maine men. Bill Sewall takes one look around and is unimpressed by the place as cattle country.
Roosevelt dispatches Sewall and Dow downriver to the Elkhorn with a hundred head. While he was away, Merrifield and Sylvane Ferris had driven in a thousand cattle from Iowa.
Roosevelt rides to Gregor Lang's ranch, with the Englishman Messiter along. Lang's wife has just come over from Ireland to join him.
Roosevelt remains a guest at Gregor Lang's ranch.
Roosevelt is at the Maltese Cross on the 23rd birthday of Edith Carow, his childhood friend and future wife.
Roosevelt rides north from the Maltese Cross to look in on Sewall and Dow and their progress at the Elkhorn.
While Roosevelt is at the Elkhorn, the Mandan Pioneer muses that he could win a seat in Congress the moment Dakota becomes a state.
Roosevelt spends the day after grouse near the Elkhorn.
At the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt completes his written memorial to his late wife Alice and mails it East to the Putnam firm to be printed.
At the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt writes of his growing affection for the stark Badlands landscape.
Sombrero and a house under way

Roosevelt writes Lodge that he would laugh to see him in his wide sombrero. To Bamie he recounts traveling out with his Maine friends and asks her to keep the builders moving on Leeholm, the new house she is overseeing at Oyster Bay.
Facing down a gunman in Mingusville

This is the likeliest date for Roosevelt's run-in at Nolan's Hotel in Mingusville. A drunk waving two pistols mocks him as a bespectacled dude; Roosevelt knocks him down, the shots go wild, and the man hits his head on the bar. The tale races across the Badlands.
Roosevelt writes W. L. Hubbell confirming the facts in a Tribune letter concerning the state legislature.
Roosevelt is on the Little Missouri; no details are recorded.

Roosevelt plans a two-month overland hunt to Wyoming's Bighorn Mountains with Bill Merrifield as hunting partner and a seasoned plainsman named Lebo as teamster and cook. His diary lists ponies, clothes, food and an arsenal of guns. That day he covers 72 miles in the saddle.
From Chimney Butte, Roosevelt tells Bamie about the coming hunting expedition and how much he has come to love the place.
Hailstorm on the first day out

The Bighorn trip gets a slow start. Roosevelt and Merrifield leave the wagon and ride to Lang's for the night, ducking into a washout when a hailstorm hits so hard the ponies won't face it. Their slickers keep them dry, and his new Winchester performs well.
Rain all day, roast duck at night

In a steady downpour Roosevelt leaves Lang's, shoots ducks and grouse in the sloughs and skips lunch, then catches up with the wagon at Lake Station on the old Keogh Trail. They burn the old station's logs for a fire, eat fried duck and sleep in the wagon.

Under gray skies the wagon struggles through soaked ground. Roosevelt drops a whitetail buck at a hundred yards and two sage grouse, all with his Winchester. They make only twelve miles and camp early at a muddy pool to dry out, crossing from prairie into rough Badlands.

After a frosty night, a big herd of beef steers that had bedded nearby passes the camp; all night Roosevelt heard the riders singing around it. The party's greyhound dies, and they make 25 miles past countless buffalo skulls. He sketches his companions Lebo and Merrifield in his diary.

A fierce night storm drenches the tentless party. Following a cattle trail southwest about twenty miles, Roosevelt misses two good shots at blacktail bucks. They camp beside a lovely natural park dotted with pine-topped sandstone pillars.

The party crosses the Little Beaver onto wide brown-grass plains, where Roosevelt notes that cattle herds have replaced the buffalo. He misses a doe, shoots two young sage grouse through the head for the evening meal, and they camp in the Powder River Badlands to the howl of coyotes.
Letters written on a water keg

The party follows a creek down to the Powder River and pushes on through sagebrush bottoms to a dry camp. Using an upturned keg as a desk, Roosevelt writes Bamie and Lodge and hands the letters to a passing cowboy. To Lodge he mixes trail news with talk of Cornwallis and the Puritans.
A pony tumbles down a cliff

Moving up the Powder to where the Little Powder joins it, Roosevelt shoots grouse, doves and teal for the pot. Merrifield misses a cougar, the pair nearly bog down in a swamp, and Merrifield's pony somersaults twice down a thirty-foot sandy bank.
Night with the N Bar outfit

A short day's travel. Roosevelt shoots eight prairie chickens and buys a fine young horse from a cowboy for $100. They stop at the N Bar Ranch, where thirty men and some three hundred horses are gearing up for the beef roundup, and he admires the cowboys' style.
A yearling buck in the swamp

The Powder valley narrows between bold, pine-dotted bluffs. Roosevelt fills the bag with sage hens and prairie chickens, and at dusk, kneeling in a marsh, he shoots a young whitetail buck through the heart at fifty yards.
Heading up the Powder, the party fords the river nine times, the wagon nearly sinking in quicksand once, and camps just short of Clear Creek.

Climbing Clear Creek over barren sagebrush country, the wagon sticks three times and the team nearly gives out. In the afternoon Roosevelt breaks the backs of two blacktail bucks with a single shot at 431 paces and keeps the bullet.
The party makes about twenty miles up Clear Creek and crosses from Montana into Wyoming, passing many cattle and a Cheyenne camp. Roosevelt notes that he has been bathing in the river daily.

Camped a few miles from Buffalo with the snowy Bighorns in view, Roosevelt nearly halves a jackrabbit at 75 yards. Near a Cheyenne village, Merrifield proposes a shooting match, and the two hunters easily beat the Cheyenne marksmen.
The hunting party reaches Buffalo, which Roosevelt sizes up as a genuine frontier settlement.
Trading the wagon for pack ponies
At a Crazy Woman Creek sawmill the party leaves its wagon behind and sets up a pack string of seven horses, with the wagon cover doubling as a tent, for the climb into the mountains.

Balky ponies and a faint trail delay the start until ten. The party grinds up the steep climb to the Bighorn plateau, camps on Willow Creek, and Roosevelt shoots two blue grouse out of a tree for supper. Ice forms overnight.
First elk in the high country

The party works up to about 8,000 feet into green park country of glades, lakes and clear streams and camps by a rushing creek. Hunting on foot, Roosevelt trails a band of elk and kills a cow and a calf; Merrifield takes two more.

With the ponies worn out, they stay put to dry meat and stretch hides. A bull elk calling near camp the night before lures Roosevelt out alone all day, but he never sees it, coming home with only a rabbit and a grouse.

Snow covers the camp by morning and rain and sleet fall all day, so the men stay in the tent before a roaring log fire. In the afternoon Roosevelt takes a brisk three-hour ride on his horse California through the mist.

Roosevelt and Merrifield ride out at dawn on Blackie and Splitear and hunt until dusk over rough burned timber. They find three bull elk and wound all of them, give chase on foot, and bring down two; Roosevelt also kills a blacktail doe. He is fascinated by the bulls' bugling in the rut.

Out alone, Roosevelt lets a doe and two fawns pass since camp has plenty of meat, then shoots a dozen blue grouse for variety. Meanwhile Merrifield chases a black bear up a tree and kills it, to Roosevelt's regret at missing it.
The party moves camp about six miles to a fork of the Ten Sleep. Snow falls off and on, and Roosevelt finds the scene lovely by moonlight. He reports the bear meat tasty and his health never better.
A long, fruitless still-hunt with Merrifield turns up only a few deer tracks amid snow and frozen ponds. The silent pine and spruce forest reminds Roosevelt of the woods of Maine and the Adirondacks.
Fifty trout and a weary hike
Roosevelt and Merrifield ride and hike most of the day to reach a mountain lake, catch about fifty trout, and return exhausted to a trout feast in camp.
A great bull elk at 75 yards

Finding no game, they move camp six miles toward the foothills. Hunting on foot that afternoon, Roosevelt kills a big bull elk with a superb rack facing him at 75 yards, and picks off two grouse for supper.

Roosevelt shoots a spike blacktail in the morning, wearing moccasins for silence. That afternoon he and Merrifield trail a grizzly through thick forest to its bed, and Roosevelt kills it with one shot to the brain from 25 feet. He is very proud of his first bear.
A sow grizzly and her cub

After skinning yesterday's grizzly, Roosevelt rides to a scenic canyon and needs six shots to kill a blacktail buck. While skinning it at dusk, he and Merrifield spot a mother grizzly and a big cub, chase them a mile on foot, and kill both.

The men haul the bears into camp. That afternoon they find a big grizzly feeding on the bull elk carcass, and Roosevelt has Merrifield take the shot, since he has yet to kill one on his own. Four blue grouse make supper.
All three men beat the woods for bear all day with no luck. When Lebo misses a bull elk, it crosses Roosevelt's path; he wounds it, sprints after it in his moccasins, and drops it with a second shot.
The party breaks camp and starts down, three pack ponies loaded with hides and antlers, and camps again on the creek they used coming up.
The party reaches the Crazy Woman Creek sawmill where the wagon waited. Roosevelt's horse California is worn out after falling into a creek.

With the wagon back in service, the party rolls to Fort McKinney, where Roosevelt dines at the post. He jots down a Dr. Tyrell's account of two 8th Cavalry soldiers killed by a grizzly in New Mexico in 1872.
The party makes a decent day's travel, camping above Piney Fork, and Roosevelt bags a jackrabbit and two ducks. He writes Bamie about his bears and elk as they head home.
A long day on the trail brings the party back to its August 30 lunch spot beneath a big balm tree, where they camp.
The party follows Clear Creek to within six miles of the Powder, then stops under two big cottonwoods so the spoiling bear hides can be scraped and dried. The horses are in poor shape.
The bear skins are still drying, so the party stays put. Roosevelt hunts the north side of the creek and sees nothing.
Teal and chickens by the river
With the hides still damp, Roosevelt hunts south of the creek without luck, then takes the shotgun along the river and bags two teal and five sharptail grouse.
An off day with the rifle
After a long day's travel the party camps where the Powder curves. Short of fresh meat, Roosevelt goes hunting but misses three whitetail shots, and Merrifield misses two.
Rain soaks the men overnight despite the wagon cover. They travel well and camp a few miles upriver from the N Bar Ranch, and Merrifield brings down a whitetail doe.
Camp by the S H ranch
The party pastures its horses near the S H ranch, and it rains again overnight. Back East, Roosevelt's sister Corinne turns 23.
Traveling down the Powder, the party camps near Powderville. Roosevelt shoots two blue-winged teal with the rifle and ten more ducks with a right-and-left from the shotgun.
Cold rain falls through the night and all the next day. The party travels until dark and camps near White Clay Buttes with poor grass and muddy water, the team nearly spent.
Pitch-pine fire at the Medicine Buttes

After a hard frost, Roosevelt shoots seven sharptail grouse. On a cold, windy day one team horse gives out and Splitear goes into harness. They camp after dark among the Medicine Buttes beside a blazing pitch-pine fire under a sandstone cliff.
Pinned in camp by a gale
On the trail back from his Wyoming hunt, Roosevelt and his party sit out a day of howling wind and rain squalls rather than risk the open prairie.
Strayed horses and a mare in the mud
Wet bedding, wandering horses and a team mare stuck in a mud hole cost Roosevelt's party the day; it takes two hours to haul her out, and she is too weak to travel.
Out of meat, he shoots supper
After two days without meat, Roosevelt takes his shotgun out from camp on the big sand and brings back three teal and two sharp-tailed grouse.

Roosevelt drives to Muddy Creek, shooting a jackrabbit and two grouse along the way. Then he and Bill Merrifield ride all night under the moon, 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., covering fifty miles to the Chimney Butte ranch. He later recalled the hoofbeats and coyote cries of that ride in print.
Home from Wyoming with a big bag
Back at Chimney Butte from the Bighorn country, Roosevelt tallies a season's take of more than a hundred birds and small animals, plus three grizzly bears, six elk and seven deer.

At Elkhorn, Sewall and Dow tell Roosevelt of threats against him and his men, of lynchings while he was away, and of the Marquis de Morès's hired gunmen stopping in for a meal. As the story was later told, Roosevelt rode to E. C. Paddock's cabin, told him that if there was to be killing it could start now, and warned him off his men and his claim.
Roosevelt departs Medora for New York City.
Roosevelt is on the way to New York City.
Roosevelt reaches New York City and goes to his sister Bamie's house on Madison Avenue.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
Backing Blaine; a niece named Eleanor

At 422 Madison Avenue, Roosevelt tells reporters he will support Blaine in November and voices anger that Governor Cleveland never removed Sheriff Davidson. His brother Elliott and Elliott's wife, Anna, welcome a daughter, Anna Eleanor.
Roosevelt works through a pile of letters in New York City.
Roosevelt is offered the Republican nomination for Congress in New York's First District, which includes Oyster Bay, and turns it down.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.
Roosevelt is in New York City with nothing logged.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing further appears.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are recorded.
Speaking to Brooklyn's Young Republicans, Roosevelt campaigns for Blaine and lands a stinging line on the Democratic running mate, Thomas A. Hendricks.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is noted.

In Malden, Massachusetts, Roosevelt rallies Republicans for Henry Cabot Lodge's congressional race, arguing Blaine won the nomination honestly and the party will keep him in check. He also writes William Clapp of Boston denying a remark newspapers pinned on him after Chicago.
Roosevelt speaks in Melrose, Massachusetts, on Lodge's behalf.
A warm crowd at Chickering Hall
Roosevelt gives a strong speech at Chickering Hall in New York City, and the partisan audience receives it well.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are listed.
Newark speech; a letter to the Globe
Roosevelt speaks at the Grand Opera House in Newark, New Jersey, and writes the Boston Globe's editor to deny that on June 6 he vowed not to support Blaine.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt is in New York City with no recorded events.
A literary birthday dinner in Boston
Roosevelt turns 26 in Boston and dines at Henry Cabot Lodge's home with three celebrated writers: the novelist William Dean Howells, the poet Thomas Bailey Aldrich, and Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes.
Roosevelt campaigns for Lodge in Winchester, Massachusetts.

While Roosevelt is in Boston, Blaine's campaign blunders in New York: a minister brands the Democrats the party of "rum, Romanism and Rebellion," Blaine fails to disown the insult to Catholics, and a showy dinner with wealthy backers at Delmonico's after a big parade sours voters further.
From Boston, Roosevelt writes Francis Scott to commend him for supporting William R. Grace in the New York mayoral race.
Roosevelt answers Richard R. Bowker of Publishers Weekly, who had accused him in the Brooklyn Eagle of double-dealing over Blaine, and tells Charles H. Knox he is backing Grace for mayor.
Roosevelt speaks in Elmira, New York, for Jonas Van Duzer.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events listed.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing noted on the eve of the election.
Roosevelt casts his vote in New York City as Democrat Grover Cleveland narrowly defeats Republican James G. Blaine for President. The race is so tight that Blaine waits two weeks to concede.
Roosevelt promises Walter Hubbell his help in the race for Speaker of the State Assembly.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded.
Writing Lodge, who has lost his race for Congress, Roosevelt reports that New York is in turmoil after the election.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events noted.
Roosevelt is in New York City with nothing logged.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the day has no entries.
Cheering Lodge; a talk at the Nineteenth Century Club

Roosevelt writes again to Lodge, beaten by fewer than 300 votes, trying to lift his spirits and inviting him and his wife Nannie for a visit in midwinter. He also gives a talk at the Nineteenth Century Club about what the campaign revealed of Republican principles; he had seen Blaine as the lesser evil.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt sets out for Dakota Territory.
Roosevelt is still on the way to Dakota.
A third day of travel toward Dakota.
Roosevelt reaches the Little Missouri and heads out to his Chimney Butte ranch.
A cold night alone on the way to Elkhorn

Roosevelt helps Sylvane Ferris and Merrifield move a small beef herd, then sets out mid-afternoon from Medora for Elkhorn as the Badlands turn wintry. Darkness and cold stop him; he shelters in an empty shack with nothing but tea for supper.
Felling logs for the Elkhorn house

Roosevelt shoots grouse from the trees for breakfast and joins Sewall and Dow, who are cutting logs for the Elkhorn ranch house. In ten-below cold, Sewall drops 53 trees, Dow 49, and Roosevelt 17. Final returns show that a shift of just 575 votes in the city would have made Blaine President.
Roosevelt picks the spot for the Elkhorn ranch house and pitches in on construction.
Riding the range with Captain Robbins

Roosevelt rides his range with Captain Robbins and shoots seven grouse. Back East, his childhood friend Edith Carow has dinner with a Mr. Stratton at his Aunt Annie Gracie's. Roosevelt is weighed down by his political setbacks and family losses.

With Sewall and Dow, Roosevelt rides from Elkhorn up to Chimney Butte through snow at 20 below zero. He is thinking about a stockmen's association to settle fights over range rights and strayed cattle.
Roosevelt rides out to persuade nearby ranchers that a stockmen's association is worth joining. He shoots six grouse and rides to town and back with Sewall at 20 below.
Roosevelt shoots five cottontails and writes Bamie about the cold and snowstorms, sending love to his little daughter and asking for a few blank checks.
Roosevelt watches for beaver and shoots three grouse.
Roosevelt and Sewall ride to Gregor Lang's place, then return to the Maltese Cross. Temperatures hover around 20 below.
Up at five in the cold
Rain at the Maltese Cross. Roosevelt is up by 5 each morning for ranch chores in brutal cold.
Card games and books by the fire
Roosevelt rides home. At night the ranch hands play chess and checkers, deal hands of casino and old sledge, or read.
Another rainy day at the Maltese Cross, part of a stretch of heavy labor.
Roosevelt shoots two grouse, then rides into Medora for lunch with the Marquis de Morès.
Roosevelt sends Sewall and Dow back to Elkhorn.
Roosevelt hikes all around Square Butte looking for deer without luck, but shoots five grouse out of a tree.
Roosevelt and Merrifield spend the whole day hunting mountain sheep and see none.
Running a fever, Roosevelt stays inside. In his diary he crosses out a planned sheep hunt.
A whitetail doe near the house
Hunting the river bottom close to the ranch, Roosevelt drops a whitetail doe at 40 yards and shoots four grouse.
After another fruitless search for sheep with Merrifield, Roosevelt brings down three blacktail deer, a doe and two bucks, to stock the ranch for winter.
Sylvane Ferris arrives from Spearfish driving 52 unbroken cow ponies, and Roosevelt joins the hands in breaking them in the bitter cold.
Roosevelt sends word for Sewall and Dow to come get ponies for Elkhorn.
Roosevelt spends the day hunting bighorn sheep.
Sewall and Dow arrive to help
Sewall and Dow ride in from Elkhorn to help with the ponies. Roosevelt shoots a cottontail.
A day spent breaking horses at the Maltese Cross.
Setting out on a sheep hunt

Roosevelt and Merrifield ride while George Myers drives the buckboard on a three-day hunt for bighorns. Over brutally rough country they see nothing and bed down in an unheated shack on the Oxbow at ten below.
Roosevelt hunts all over Bullion Butte and sees no sheep; he does get a grouse. Temperatures swing from 25 above to 10 below.
His bighorn ram, ahead of a blizzard

After a ride and a mile on foot over terrible ground, Roosevelt shoots a bighorn ram at about 90 yards. With a blizzard brewing he races back to Chimney Butte, arriving just as the storm hits, and writes Bamie about his trophy.
Bitter cold grips the Maltese Cross: 20 below zero in daylight and 50 below after dark.
Another day of fierce cold at the ranch.
A whitetail buck in the snow
Hunting through snowy brush, Roosevelt shoots a whitetail buck and a prairie chicken.
Roosevelt is at the Maltese Cross; no events are noted.

At an 11 a.m. meeting in Roberts Hall in Medora, Little Missouri cattlemen elect Roosevelt chairman. The Marquis de Morès and Gregor Lang attend; eleven outfits are represented and eight more send word they approve.
Roosevelt leaves Medora for New York City.
Roosevelt is on his way to New York City.
A frontiersman in a Chicago lobby
Passing through Chicago, Roosevelt turns heads in the Grand Pacific Hotel lobby, according to the New York Times, bundled in a coonskin coat and fur cap with a rifle and shotgun in hand.
Roosevelt reaches New York and carries his hunting trophies to Bamie's house on Madison Avenue.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt spends Christmas Day in New York City.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events noted.
Roosevelt is in New York City with nothing logged.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events listed.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the day passes without recorded events.
Writing the West; posing in buckskin

Roosevelt starts putting his Western adventures on paper, the beginning of Hunting Trips of a Ranchman, a book that will run about 95,000 words. He sits for a New York studio portrait in his buckskin suit, and the Century carries his article on three years in the Assembly.
Roosevelt begins 1885 at 422 Madison Avenue in New York City.
Roosevelt travels to Albany to work for Walter Hubbell's bid to become Assembly Speaker.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt is in Albany with nothing logged.
Roosevelt is in Albany; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Albany; nothing appears.
George Z. Erwin is chosen Speaker of the Assembly without opposition.
Roosevelt is back in New York City; nothing is noted.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events listed.
Roosevelt is in New York City with nothing recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing appears.

Back in Albany, Roosevelt works to send William M. Evarts to the U.S. Senate in place of Elbridge G. Lapham. The Stalwarts, led by Thomas C. Platt, favor Levi P. Morton; Senator Warner Miller is for Evarts.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt is in Albany with no recorded events.
Roosevelt is in Albany; the day is blank.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing logged.
Roosevelt is in Albany; no events are listed.
Roosevelt is in Albany on his sister Bamie's 30th birthday.

His illness behind him, Roosevelt catches a train in New York City bound for the Dakota Badlands.

Passing through St. Paul, Roosevelt draws a newspaper sketch that pokes fun at him as a boyish New York dandy, with a little lisp, a reddish mustache and spectacles.
A fallen boulder delays his arrival
Roosevelt finally reaches Medora, hours behind schedule: his westbound Pacific Express, due that evening at 6:47, ran seven or eight hours late after a huge rock tumbled onto the line.

Roosevelt rides north to the Elkhorn, where his new cabin is almost finished. He is pleased to find his cattle in good shape.

On his sister Corinne's third wedding anniversary, Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie about forcing a swollen river and then picking his own way across rough country, wet through, before he reached home.
Elkhorn house done, cattle buying sent east

Roosevelt dispatches Merrifield, Sewall and Dow to Minnesota with a $12,500 check to buy about 1,000 more cattle. Alone, he takes three trips to explore the country, and at the Mingusville hotel he turns away a drunk cowboy, warning he will shoot anyone who forces his door. Sewall and Dow finish the Elkhorn ranch house.
Between two ranches, mostly on horseback
Roosevelt is at Elkhorn this spring, shuttling between his two ranches. He fits in some writing and reads proofs of his new book, but he spends most of his days riding the country.
Roosevelt is at his Elkhorn ranch.
New herd arrives; drive north begins
Roosevelt's newly bought cattle, valued at $39,000, come in at Medora, and he starts trailing them north to Elkhorn with a crew of just six riders.
Roosevelt is on the trail with the new herd, pushing north toward Elkhorn.

The heat is fierce and the cattle go without water. After dark they stampede, and Roosevelt and his small crew need more than an hour to settle them.

From Medora, Roosevelt tells Henry Cabot Lodge that he leaves for the spring roundup in the morning, fresh from trailing a thousand cattle north.

Roosevelt sets out for Montana alongside the cowhands of his Maltese Cross outfit, bound for the spring roundup.

On the way to Montana, Roosevelt answers his sister Bamie, who had asked whether his heavy spending on cattle would pay off, and writes Jonas Van Duzer to learn when the state Republican convention meets.

Roosevelt reaches Box Elder Creek in Montana for the Badlands spring roundup, which gathers outfits from across the Little Missouri country: about 100 riders and 1,000 horses working 10,000 square miles. Days start with breakfast at 3 a.m., and he puts in 16 hours wrestling calves, riding the long circle and standing herd day and night.

Roosevelt leaves the roundup on the Little Missouri after 32 days, outlasting most of the cowhands and logging more than 1,000 miles on horseback.

Traveling east, Roosevelt tells Henry Cabot Lodge that New York Mayor William R. Grace wants him as the city's Health Commissioner. A St. Paul paper marvels that the Eastern dude is gone: the drawl has vanished and he now looks every inch a Westerner.

Dow's wedding; a motto over the door

Out in Dakota, Wilmot Dow, newly married, brings his bride, Mrs. Sewall and the Sewall baby to Elkhorn, which Sewall later remembered as one big contented household. At Leeholm, the Roosevelt family motto, Qui plantavit curabit, is carved above the front door.
Edith Carow, Roosevelt's childhood friend, celebrates her twenty-fourth birthday. Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay.

The Leeholm household travels into New York City for Ulysses S. Grant's funeral procession, and Captain Roosevelt marches in it with his regiment. Some 60,000 marchers stretch seven miles, taking five hours to pass President Cleveland's reviewing stand while about a million people look on.
Roosevelt heads to Nahant, Massachusetts, to stay with Henry Cabot Lodge and his family.
Roosevelt is a guest of the Lodges at Nahant.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay, far from Dakota, when a Morton County grand jury meeting in Mandan charges the Marquis de Mores with killing Riley Luffsey back in June 1883.
West again on the Chicago Limited
Roosevelt leaves New York City aboard the Chicago Limited, bound for Dakota.
'Brown as a berry,' says a Pittsburgh paper
On the way to Dakota, Roosevelt is spotted aboard the Chicago Limited by the Pittsburgh Dispatch, which marvels at his deep tan and the 30 pounds he has put on.
Roosevelt is still traveling to Dakota.

Roosevelt reaches Medora and talks over the murder charge against the Marquis de Mores with Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow.
Elkhorn full of family; feud with De Mores

At Elkhorn Roosevelt finds the women from Maine settled in with Sewall and Dow, and Sewall's baby Lucretia, nicknamed Kitty. Bismarck and St. Paul papers report bad blood with the Marquis de Mores: when the Marquis paid half a cent a pound under the agreed price for cattle, Roosevelt tore up the check and drove his cattle home.
Rocking chair, birdsong, a meeting called
At Elkhorn, Roosevelt likes to settle into his rocking chair on the porch with a book and the sound of birds. He sends out notice of a Stockmen's Association meeting for September 5.

De Mores surrenders; Roosevelt hunts elk

Back from the East, the Marquis de Mores turns himself in to the sheriff at Mandan, convinced Roosevelt has been working to see him convicted for Luffsey's death. Roosevelt, meanwhile, rides out with Wilmot Dow to hunt elk.
A bull elk on the hunt
Out hunting, Roosevelt brings down a bull elk.
Elk hunt over, back to Medora
Roosevelt wraps up the elk hunt and returns to Medora.
A hot-tempered letter from De Mores

From his jail cell in Bismarck, the Marquis de Mores writes Roosevelt, who is in Medora, accusing Joe Ferris of stirring up witnesses against him, asking whether Roosevelt is behind hostile newspaper stories, and hinting that gentlemen can settle such matters directly.
At the Stockmen's Association meeting in Medora, Roosevelt is chosen chairman again. The members settle the date and route of the fall roundup and pick a foreman to run it.
A firm answer to the Marquis
Roosevelt replies to De Mores that he is no enemy, but that he will not be cowed by any threat and stands ready to answer for anything he has said or done.
Roosevelt heads back north to Elkhorn.

Out hunting, Roosevelt is followed for a while by five Indians who wave their weapons at him; he stands them off and they leave.
Roosevelt is at Elkhorn as the Marquis de Mores goes before a jury in Bismarck on the murder charge.
Calling on De Mores in his cell
Traveling through Bismarck, Roosevelt stops to see the Marquis de Mores in jail, then continues on toward New York.
Roosevelt is on the train to New York.
Roosevelt continues his journey to New York.
Home to New York; De Mores acquitted
Roosevelt reaches New York City. In Dakota, a jury clears the Marquis de Mores of murder, along with his three co-defendants: E. G. Paddock, Richard Moore and Frank Miller.

At the New York Republican convention, Roosevelt backs Cornelius N. Bliss for governor, but Ira Davenport wins the nomination, and William O'Neil, his choice for the secretary of state slot, loses to Anson B. Wood. His mark shows instead in the party platform, through his work on the resolutions committee.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her twenty-fourth birthday. He is at Oyster Bay.

Roosevelt's article on the President's policies appears in the North American Review, likening Jefferson Davis unfavorably to Benedict Arnold and branding him an "unhung traitor." Davis fires back a letter telling Roosevelt he must know little of American history.

Roosevelt joins the crowd at the Republican State Committee meeting in New York City and tells a Tribune reporter he is ready for orders. By chance he meets Edith Carow at Bamie's, begins calling at her 36th Street home, and asks her to Leeholm's Hunt Ball. The house is now renamed Sagamore Hill for the Sagamore Mohannis, who signed the land away two centuries before.
Riding to hounds at Oyster Bay
Roosevelt joins the Oyster Bay hunt and comes away delighted with his old horse, which carried him up close enough to finish second at the kill.
Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill, where a game of polo is on the program.

A note of praise for Lodge
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes to his friend Henry Cabot Lodge, cheering a recent Lodge speech and his return to the political fray.
Calling on Davenport, standing firm with Davis

In New York, Roosevelt joins the many visitors paying respects to Ira Davenport, the Republican nominee for governor. He also answers Jefferson Davis, who objected to being likened to Benedict Arnold, and makes clear he will not take the comparison back.
Roosevelt is again at his Oyster Bay home; nothing else is recorded for the day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
A Saturday at Sagamore Hill, with no other entries in the record.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the first birthday of his niece Eleanor, daughter of his brother Elliott.
Volunteering to stump for the party
Roosevelt heads back to Republican headquarters in New York City and once more puts himself forward as a campaign speaker.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; no further activity is set down.

Lodge visits and rides to hounds
Henry Cabot Lodge is Roosevelt's houseguest at Sagamore Hill, and the two friends ride out with the hunt together.
Picked as a county convention delegate
Republican primaries in New York City select delegates for the county convention, and Roosevelt wins a seat representing the 21st Assembly District.
Brooklyn speech on reform and rights

Roosevelt delivers a major address to Brooklyn's Young Republican Club, making the case for civil service reform and defending the rights of Black citizens in the South. Henry Cabot Lodge shares the platform.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at his Long Island home; no events are noted.

County convention at the Grand Opera House
Roosevelt divides the day between Sagamore Hill and Manhattan, where the New York County Republican Convention meets in the hall of the Grand Opera House.

A broken arm cannot stop the hunt

The hunt gathers at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt, mounted on Frank, takes a hard fall that badly breaks his left arm. Bloodied, the arm dangling, he rides on to the finish, then chases little Alice around the house and hosts the Hunt Ball that night. Edith Carow is at the ball.
Setting Lodge straight on the papers
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes to Henry Cabot Lodge to deny reports that have been running in the newspapers.
Roosevelt marks his 27th birthday at home at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Another day at home in Oyster Bay, with no events in the record.

Roosevelt thanks Henry Cabot Lodge and his wife for their concern over his hunting fall. He insists the whole episode was more funny than grim, says he can dress himself again, and regrets only losing the rest of the hunting season.
Last day of October at home
Roosevelt closes out the month at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing else.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay as November begins; nothing else is recorded.
Eve of the election at home
The day before the state election, Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with no other activity noted.
Roosevelt casts his ballot at Oyster Bay on Election Day. Statewide, Democratic Governor David B. Hill wins a new term, defeating the Republican Ira Davenport.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill the day after the governor's race; no other events are noted.

Roosevelt stays at his Long Island home; the record notes nothing more.

With his arm still in a sling, Roosevelt proposes to his childhood friend Edith Carow, and she accepts. His gifts to her include a pearl necklace, a watch and an engagement ring. The two agree to tell no one for now.
Telling the Bowery about ranch life
Roosevelt gives a lecture on the Bowery in New York City titled "Ranching in the West," drawing on his years in Dakota.
Roosevelt, now 27, is in New York City; the record gives no other details.
Roosevelt spends Christmas Day in New York City.
A harsh lecture on the West

Lecturing in New York City about the West, Roosevelt makes sweeping, disparaging remarks about American Indians, ranking even a vicious cowboy above them in moral character. The words reflect prejudices common among white Americans of his day and are recorded here as he spoke them.
Roosevelt rings in 1886 in New York City; his diary notes a dinner at "G.K.L."
Harper's Weekly publishes a piece by Roosevelt on ranching, and that evening his diary records a dinner party in New York.

Roosevelt's diary lists two appointments in New York: Fanny Dana in the afternoon and Lizzie Cary in the evening.
Roosevelt's terse diary points to a Civil Service Reform meeting at noon and an engagement on 31st Street that evening.

Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her 31st birthday. His diary notes a dinner along with names that are hard to make out.
The diary for this day holds a theater engagement that Roosevelt later struck through; the transcription is too garbled to read reliably.

Roosevelt takes on a new book: a life of Missouri senator Thomas Hart Benton for the American Statesmen series. That evening he dines at his sister Corinne's.
Roosevelt's diary notes a dinner at Lizzie's, probably Lizzie Cary.

Writing to Henry Cabot Lodge, Roosevelt admits the Benton biography he has just agreed to write leaves him a bit overwhelmed.

Roosevelt goes to the theater with E.K.C., his secret fiancée Edith Carow.
Roosevelt's diary lists a dinner "at Kean."
On daughter Alice's second birthday, Roosevelt is booked to speak at Morton Hall. He also writes a Wisconsin historian asking for diaries and other records of America's westward push.
Roosevelt's diary notes he is to speak at "O.R."
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York, with no diary entry for the day.
Roosevelt dines at the Lexington Avenue home of newspaper publisher Whitelaw Reid. A small drawn mark appears in his diary for the day.

Roosevelt is in the city; the diary is silent.
A fawn-skin gift for Nannie Lodge

Roosevelt sends Nannie Lodge a footmuff made from a fawn skin he brought back from Dakota, and mentions that the one or two beaver he trapped had poor pelts. He tells her that, apart from family, she and Cabot are the only people he truly cares for.
Roosevelt's diary notes the Eastlake engagement, then that he skipped it, followed by an "E" for Edith.
Roosevelt gives up his commission in New York's National Guard.
In New York City, Roosevelt's younger brother Elliott turns 26.
Bamie heads west with the James Roosevelts
Roosevelt's sister Bamie sets off for California and Mexico with their cousins Sara and James Roosevelt, the future parents of Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Roosevelt's diary reads "Centry E." — likely the Century club and a meeting with Edith.

Roosevelt is in the city with nothing recorded.
Once more Roosevelt's diary carries only an "E," signaling time with Edith.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is noted.
A speaking engagement appears in Roosevelt's diary but is crossed out.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are recorded.
On his final full day before heading west, Roosevelt's diary notes Edith, a lunch, and Beekman Place.
Roosevelt leaves New York for Medora and a summer on his Dakota cattle ranch, saying goodbye to Edith.
The train carries Roosevelt on to St. Paul.
Roosevelt's diary records his arrival in Medora.
In Medora Roosevelt meets Joe Ferris's new bride, then drives down the valley to his Elkhorn Ranch.
Grouse for supper, ice on the river

At Elkhorn, Roosevelt shoots four sharp-tailed grouse for supper and finds the ranch in better shape than he feared. An ice jam has formed on the Little Missouri right in front of the house, as he tells Bamie in a letter.
A muddy hike to Tomkins Ranch
Roosevelt walks across the hay plateau to the Tomkins ranch through deep mud.
Roosevelt hikes out to collect four deer carcasses that Sewall and Dow had hung in a tree, only to find that cougars have eaten them.
Roosevelt's diary notes four prairie chickens shot at Elkhorn.
Roosevelt discovers that thieves have made off with the ranch boat. Sewall and Dow set to work building a new one so the three can chase them down the river.
Boat building on a swollen river
Work on the new boat goes on while Roosevelt hunts deer without luck. The river runs high, with ice heaped several feet up its banks.
The diary for the day is two words: boat building.
The new boat is finished, but it is too cold to set out. Roosevelt shoots four chickens, completes the first chapter of his Benton book, and tells Lodge that writing comes very hard for him.
In bitter cold, Roosevelt writes to Bamie that life at the ranch has fallen back into its usual routine. He is reading and pressing on with his Benton biography.
Blizzard at Elkhorn; news of the Carows
A furious blizzard sweeps the ranch. Back east, Roosevelt's sister Corinne writes Bamie that the Carow family has sold its house and will go abroad in late April for perhaps a year and a half.
With milder weather, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow push off in the new boat to hunt down the men who stole theirs. They camp below Eaton's and shoot three prairie chickens.
Temperatures drop below zero as the pursuit of the boat thieves goes on. Roosevelt bags four prairie chickens.

Far downriver, north of Elkhorn, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow find their stolen boat and catch the three thieves completely off guard. Rifles leveled, Roosevelt orders hands up, and the men surrender without a shot. Earlier he brings down a whitetail doe at 75 yards.
Guarding prisoners on an icy river

With the captives aboard both boats, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow start the slow trip back toward Medora until an ice jam stops them. The prisoners cannot be tied up for fear of frostbite, and supplies dwindle until only flour is left. To pass the long watches, Roosevelt reads Anna Karenina cover to cover.
The boats are held fast by river ice, Roosevelt's diary reports.
For a second day, ice keeps Roosevelt's party and its prisoners from moving.
The boats inch a couple of miles downstream before ice stops them once more.
To the tail of the jam
Another couple of miles brings the party to the lower end of the ice jam.
The boats make it to the C Ranch, and Roosevelt shoots two prairie chickens.
On a borrowed horse, Roosevelt rides to the Killdeer Mountains and hires a wagon and driver, and lays in supplies for the overland leg.
Forty-five miles on foot behind the wagon

While Sewall and Dow carry on downriver with the boats, Roosevelt marches the prisoners overland to the Killdeer Mountains. The captives ride in the wagon; he trudges behind through sticky gumbo mud, Winchester in hand, and goes without sleep.
Roosevelt drives his captives by wagon to Captain Brown's ranch.
Handing the thieves to the sheriff
Roosevelt delivers the three prisoners to the sheriff in Dickinson, about 40 miles east of Medora, ending the chase. While in town he has Dr. Victor Hugo Stickney treat his blistered feet.

Roosevelt returns from Dickinson to Medora and writes his sisters. To Bamie he tells the boat-thief story and shares his verdict on Anna Karenina; to Corinne he asks, pretending not to know, when Edith leaves for Europe. Local elections also fill county offices.

Roosevelt chairs the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association at its spring session in Medora, keeping strict parliamentary order. The members pick him to represent them at the Montana stockmen's gathering in Miles City.
Roosevelt and Bill Merrifield ride down the valley to Elkhorn Ranch.
On a rainy day at Elkhorn, Roosevelt writes Corinne about political campaigns and arranges for a card to go with flowers for Edith when she sails.
Roosevelt rides up to Medora and sends Henry Cabot Lodge an account of how he ran down the boat thieves.
Roosevelt rides out to his Chimney Butte ranch.
Roosevelt and Sylvane Ferris travel to Miles City to represent the local ranchers at the Montana Stock Growers meeting, taking rooms at the MacQueen House.
Parade of cowmen in Miles City
The stock growers' meeting opens in Miles City with a morning parade from the MacQueen House: the 5th Infantry band, mounted cowboys and some 150 cattlemen marching four abreast.
The stock growers elect Roosevelt to their executive committee as Dakota Territory's representative, taking the seat once held by the Marquis de Mores.
Roosevelt attends a session of the stock growers' executive committee in Miles City.
Back in Medora, Roosevelt writes Bamie about the stockmen's convention and pokes fun at dull society people.
Roosevelt and Bill Merrifield head out from Medora on a weeklong antelope hunt.

While Roosevelt hunts in Dakota, Edith Carow leaves for Europe with her sister Emily, their mother Gertrude and their nurse Mame Ledwith. Short of money, the Carows plan to live abroad where costs are lower. Not even Edith's mother or sister knows of the engagement.
Roosevelt is still out with Merrifield on the antelope hunt.
The hunt goes on; the record says only that Roosevelt is hunting.
Roosevelt remains in the field after antelope.
Last days of the antelope hunt
Roosevelt and Merrifield are still hunting.
Back in Medora after a week chasing antelope with Merrifield, Roosevelt writes Bamie. It is also his sister Corinne's fourth wedding anniversary.
Roosevelt is in Medora; nothing further is recorded.
Roosevelt is in Medora working on his Benton biography, splitting his nights between the ranch and a room above Joe Ferris's store. Far to the east, Chicago workers strike for an eight-hour day.
Roosevelt is at his Elkhorn Ranch; nothing else is recorded.
Another day at Elkhorn with no events set down.

A bomb explodes during a labor rally at Haymarket Square in Chicago, killing eight. From Elkhorn, Roosevelt says his ranch hands would gladly turn their rifles on the rioters, and that he feels the same.
Roosevelt is at Elkhorn Ranch; the record notes nothing more.
Another Elkhorn day with no events recorded.
Roosevelt remains at his ranch on the Little Missouri; nothing else is noted.
The record places Roosevelt at Elkhorn and says no more.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at Elkhorn Ranch, with nothing recorded.
Roosevelt is at the ranch; no details survive for the day.
Another day at Elkhorn without any recorded events.
Writing from Medora, Roosevelt thanks Corinne for sending soap. He misses his family, he admits, but genuinely enjoys life on the range.
Roosevelt is at Elkhorn Ranch; the day is otherwise blank.
Roosevelt stays at Elkhorn; nothing more is recorded.
From Medora, Roosevelt writes Bamie about his civil service article for the Princeton Review and asks her to send toys for the Sewalls' baby.
Roosevelt is at Elkhorn Ranch; nothing is noted.
Another quiet day at the ranch.

From Medora, Roosevelt reports to Henry Cabot Lodge that the Benton biography is about half written.

Roosevelt is at Elkhorn the day before the spring roundup gets under way.
The roundup gets under way at Medora. Roosevelt later recalled the scene: a string of chuck wagons and some sixty riders splashing through the river ford as they set off.
Roosevelt works the roundup, mounting up before sunrise in the cool prairie air.
Another day on the roundup, crossing open prairie in the early light.
Roosevelt spends the roundup morning sweeping the range in a wide loop alongside the hired riders, threading single file through the buttes.
Afternoons on the roundup mean working the gathered cattle, separating animals at a gallop with sudden stops and turns.
The roundup's hardest work comes next: roping, throwing and branding the half-wild calves.
Calves are branded in a corral or inside a circle of riders, and after dark the men bed down in whatever shelter the camp offers, or none at all.
Roosevelt is out with the roundup; nothing more is noted.
A White House wedding back east
As Roosevelt rides with the roundup in Dakota, President Grover Cleveland weds Frances Folsom in a White House ceremony.
Roosevelt is out on the range with the roundup; no specifics are recorded.

Mail day: roundup, Tolstoy and Benton

In from the roundup, Roosevelt writes Bamie that two weeks of range work have been a real pleasure and urges her to fill Sagamore Hill with friends. He is deep in War and Peace. He also asks Lodge to find someone to research Benton's life after 1850, the last gap in a nearly finished book. A letter from Edith arrives from London.
Roosevelt is back at Elkhorn Ranch; nothing else is recorded.
Another day at Elkhorn with no events noted.
Roosevelt sets out from Elkhorn with Sewall and Tompkins on a 70-mile hunting trip. Before it ends he takes two elk and six antelope.

Roosevelt rides his horse Sorrel Joe up the valley to Medora.
Roosevelt joins the roundup with the Maltese Cross wagon. He writes Bamie that work has paused briefly, offers his opinions on War and Peace, and mentions the cheerful gatherings at Sagamore.
The roundup works its way down to South Heart.
The roundup pushes on to Rocky Ridge.
A brutal day to Davis Creek
The roundup reaches Davis Creek after an enormous day: Roosevelt later wrote that he was mounted at 2 a.m. and kept at it past 8 in the evening.
Rounds at the saloon, then back to camp

Up at 3:30, Roosevelt works down to Andrew's Creek, then rides into Medora for his mail. He buys the cowboys a round at the saloon and herds them back to camp before things get out of hand. A quick note to Lodge reports hard work as the roundup crosses to the west divide.
The roundup moves to Gardiner Creek.
The roundup arrives at Bullion's Creek.
The outfit works its way down Bullion's Creek.
The roundup comes to Chimney Butte.
Roundup over, an offer from New York

Roosevelt rides into Medora with the roundup finished. He tells Bamie the cattle have fared well and thanks her for the Sewall child's toys. To Douglas Robinson he says he is weighing Mayor Grace's offer to make him New York City's health commissioner, and that only 30 pages of the Benton book remain.
Roosevelt and Bill Merrifield ride from Medora back to Elkhorn Ranch.
Benton, and a bare, overgrazed range
At Elkhorn Roosevelt works on Benton. He worries about the range, too crowded with cattle: by June 10, he notes, nothing green was left anywhere he had ridden.
Writing, then branding with Bill Rowe
After a stint on Benton, Roosevelt rides out with Bill Rowe to round up and brand calves.

Roosevelt completes his biography of Thomas Hart Benton at Elkhorn, where he has been writing every morning from first light until noon. He then rides out with Bill Rowe on his little black horse to corral and brand calves.
Roosevelt rides his horse Manitou up to Medora.
Roosevelt is in Medora on the Fourth of July; the record gives no other details.
Fourth of July oration at Dickinson

Roosevelt is the featured speaker at Dickinson's Independence Day celebration in a town of about 700, urging listeners to use America's blessings wisely. Western Starr gives the public reading of the Declaration. Back at Elkhorn, Roosevelt tells Corinne it would break his heart to give up ranch life. Corinne gives birth to a daughter, also named Corinne.
Roosevelt is at Elkhorn Ranch; nothing further is noted.
Roosevelt is in Medora, about to leave for New York; no other events are recorded.

Heading east, Roosevelt talks with a Bismarck Tribune reporter over coffee in the dining car. The paper paints him as an eager, quick-talking young man with a toothy grin and squinting blue eyes, a New York reformer turned Dakota ranchman.
Roosevelt is on the train bound for New York City.
The journey east to New York continues.
Roosevelt is in New York City after his long trip from Dakota.
Checking Benton at the Astor Library

Roosevelt begins some three weeks of fact-checking his Benton manuscript at the Astor Library. Around this time, he brings two big ranch dogs from the Badlands to Sagamore, and young Alice long remembers being bowled over by them.

Roosevelt reaches Medora. Out at Elkhorn, Bill Sewall's family welcomes a newborn son the same day.
Roosevelt is in Medora on Edith Carow's 25th birthday; she is traveling in Europe.
Books, and love for the ranch
From Medora Roosevelt writes his sisters. He tells Bamie about two books on his reading pile and tells Corinne how deeply he cares for ranch life.
Roosevelt is in Medora; no other activity is recorded.
Off to court, manuscript in the mail
Roosevelt heads to Mandan, where Mike Finnegan and the men who stole his boat face trial, and mails his Thomas Hart Benton biography to the publisher.
Guest of the Selmes, eager for a fight
In Mandan Roosevelt stays with the Selmes family. He writes Lodge proposing to raise a cowboy regiment if the trouble along the Texas–Mexico border turns to war.
Writing Bamie from Mandan, Roosevelt reports on the boat thieves' trial, praises Mrs. Selmes, and returns to his idea of a cowboy regiment for the Mexican border.
Back to Elkhorn; Dow becomes a father
Roosevelt returns to the Elkhorn Ranch, where Wilmot Dow's son is born.

Guilty verdict for the boat thieves
In Mandan the jury convicts the men who stole Roosevelt's boat. Finnegan and Burnsted each get three years; charges against Pfaffanbach are dismissed because of his mental condition.
Scouting for a mounted rifle unit
In Bismarck Roosevelt explores whether he could raise a body of mounted riflemen for service in Mexico.
Roosevelt is back at the Elkhorn Ranch.
From Elkhorn Roosevelt writes Bamie admiring Mrs. Selmes, and tells Lodge he hopes the uninsured Benton manuscript reached the publishers, warning that revisions must wait.
Stockmen re-elect him, then off to the mountains

Roosevelt is kept on as president of the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association at its fall meeting, then leaves with Merrifield to hunt in Idaho's Coeur d'Alene range. At Thompson Falls, Montana, he meets hunter John Willis.
Roosevelt, Merrifield and Willis go after mountain goats and pitch camp on Vermilion Creek.
Struggling to keep up with Willis
Willis drives the hunting party hard over jagged rock and treacherous mountain slopes.
The hunt goes on, but the party spots no mountain goats.

While Roosevelt hunts in the mountains, The New York Times society column reports that he is engaged to Miss Carow.

Goat country with Willis and Merrifield
Roosevelt is deep in the Idaho mountains, hunting with John Willis and Bill Merrifield.

Times takes back the engagement story
With Roosevelt still hunting, The New York Times retracts its August 29 report of his engagement, a correction Bamie likely arranged.
Roosevelt is still out on the mountain goat hunt.

Aiming at what would be his first mountain goat, Roosevelt slips and plunges some 40 or 50 feet down the slope, crashing through a pine into a thick balsam. He comes away with only scratches; Willis asks if he is hurt, hears no, and tells him to come on. Roosevelt climbs back up.

Back in Medora, Roosevelt counts two white goats from the long Idaho hunt but admits the trip gave him little pleasure.
Annoyed that the secret is out
At Elkhorn Roosevelt is vexed to learn New York society knows of his engagement. Bill Sewall, meanwhile, is unhappy in Dakota and fears he is wasting Roosevelt's money.
From Medora Roosevelt confirms to Bamie that the newspaper was right: he will sail to marry Edith before Christmas. Uneasy about remarriage, he says Bamie may keep his daughter, Baby Lee.

Settling up with Sewall and Dow

Roosevelt closes his accounts with Sewall and releases him and Dow, on good terms, from a ranching deal that was losing money. He then hands cattle to Merrifield and Sylvane Ferris to run on shares for four years.
Roosevelt is at Elkhorn; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at Elkhorn on his sister Corinne's 25th birthday.

Roosevelt visits the Selmes in Mandan. Back in the Badlands a white haze hangs in the air, birds head south early, and the range holds too many cattle. The Marquis de Mores has closed his packing plant and leaves for good after heavy losses; Roosevelt's own stake has reached about $85,500.
Near Mandan Roosevelt rides out after prairie game with a pack of hounds.
Roosevelt is back in Medora before heading east.
Roosevelt leaves Medora for home on Long Island.

Roosevelt is on the train toward New York.
Roosevelt arrives at Oyster Bay. His sister Bamie now lives in a newly acquired house, 689 Madison Avenue.
Riding to hounds on Long Island
Roosevelt joins the hunt with the hounds at Oyster Bay. Meanwhile both the Sewalls and the Dows start home to Maine.
Roosevelt writes Lodge listing his western bag: three white goats, plus elk and deer.
Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay on the second birthday of his niece Eleanor, Elliott's daughter.

At the Union League Club Roosevelt takes the Republican nomination for mayor of New York and talks campaign with reporters. He also gets a look at the Statue of Liberty, still headless while workers finish it.
What the city needs in a mayor
From Oyster Bay Roosevelt writes Elihu Root and William Bellamy that New York needs a mayor of strong character who owes nothing to party bosses.
Roosevelt tells Lodge that many Republicans pressed him to run before he said yes.
Roosevelt is in New York City in the thick of the mayoral race.
Roosevelt is in New York City in the thick of the mayoral race.
Roosevelt writes Lodge that he sees essentially no chance of being elected.
Roosevelt writes Frances Dana, later Mrs. Parsons, that he took the nomination very unwillingly.
Firing back at the Labor Party
Roosevelt publishes a scornful open letter to Labor Party official Denis Donohue Jr., angry at being painted as a 'landlord' candidate, and insists America has no fixed classes.
Bamie writes Edith that Roosevelt is spending nearly all his time at campaign headquarters in the Fifth Avenue Hotel.
Roosevelt is in New York City in the thick of the mayoral race.
Roosevelt writes Charles P. Miller rebutting critics who call him a mere stand-in candidate.
Roosevelt is in New York City in the thick of the mayoral race.
A birthday rally at Cooper Union
Roosevelt turns 28 the day his nomination is formally ratified at Cooper Union, where he calls for sweeping reform.
Liberty unveiled; no time to hunt
President Cleveland dedicates the Statue of Liberty in the harbor. Roosevelt writes Lodge that the campaign has kept him from hunting.

After a rushed 8 p.m. dinner Roosevelt races by hansom cab between rallies: Black voters at the Grand Opera House, immigrants at Concordia Hall, then Ward Hall on Third Avenue, and finally the 24th Ward in the Bronx. He is done by 10:30.
Roosevelt says the breakneck campaign schedule has not worn him out at all.
Newspaper coverage dwells on how young and green the Republican candidate is.
An article, a secret booking, a note to Lodge
The Century runs Roosevelt's 'Machine Politics in New York City.' On a foggy day he books two berths on the Etruria as 'Mr. and Mrs. Merrifield' and tells Lodge he sails Saturday to marry Edith.
Democrat Abram Hewitt wins the mayor's race with 90,552 votes. Labor's Henry George finishes second at 68,110, and Roosevelt runs third with 60,435.
After sleeping late, Roosevelt goes to his now-abandoned campaign rooms.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt and Bamie stay up almost until dawn finishing the engagement announcements. He also writes his cousin Laura Roosevelt with the news.
At 1 p.m. the Etruria leaves New York for Europe with Roosevelt and Bamie aboard.
At sea Roosevelt and Bamie meet Cecil Spring Rice, 26, who had served on Lord Rosebery's private staff, heading home after a visit to his brother in Canada.
While Roosevelt is at sea, the formal announcement of his engagement to Edith Carow goes to the newspapers.

The Etruria docks at Liverpool and Roosevelt and Bamie catch the first London train, where he and Edith are together again. He takes rooms at Brown's Hotel; she is staying at Buckland's Hotel.

Roosevelt marries Edith Kermit Carow at St. George's Church in London on a day so foggy the mist fills the church. His new friend Cecil Spring Rice stands as best man; the groom sports bright orange gloves.
Roosevelt and his wife Edith leave London for Dover to begin their honeymoon.
Roosevelt and Edith are traveling on their honeymoon; the record notes letters but gives no details for this day.
Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie from his honeymoon travels.
Roosevelt and Edith reach Hyères on France's Mediterranean coast. He writes Bamie happily of walks and drives over hills and shore, and of their rooms overlooking the bay.

Roosevelt and Edith are in Spezia on the Italian coast.

Roosevelt and his wife Edith greet 1887 on the island of Capri during their Italian honeymoon.

From Florence Roosevelt tells Bamie that Edith and her sister Emily treat him wonderfully, and that he is drafting six long Century magazine pieces about ranch work and the hunt, work that later became a book.
A change of heart about Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he has weighed selling Sagamore Hill yet loves the place. He and Edith stroll the Boboli Gardens and shop for dining room furniture for the house.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that he and Edith have resolved to raise his daughter, Baby Lee, themselves. Edith had pressed for it.
Roosevelt and Edith reach Naples traveling with Edith's family.
Pompeii, almost for the first time
The party drives to Pompeii. Roosevelt had been there as a boy but recalls so little that it feels nearly new.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie celebrates her 32nd birthday back home.
In Sorrento Roosevelt has walked his shoes to pieces. He writes Corinne that he is surprised to enjoy doing nothing for so long, and glad Edith would no more want a long stay abroad than he would.
From Sorrento Roosevelt thanks Cecil Spring Rice for his London hospitality and asks him to visit Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Bamie from Sorrento that revisiting Italy has been a joy.
In Rome Edith says a tearful goodbye to her mother Gertrude and sister Emily.
St. Mark's Square and a wry letter
In Venice Roosevelt and Edith visit the Piazza San Marco. He sends Corinne some teasing remarks about Italians and his 'charitable' view of foreigners.
Milan, and plans for a private study
On Alice's third birthday Roosevelt writes Bamie from Milan about the cathedral and his plan to turn Sagamore Hill's top-floor room into a study open only to invited guests.
From Paris Roosevelt writes Lodge, pleased that his friend approves of the Benton biography.
Roosevelt and Edith are back in London, where Edith feels ill; she is expecting their first child.

Roosevelt gathers fellow hunters, among them Elliott, cousin West and George Bird Grinnell, to found the Boone and Crockett Club, devoted to outdoor life, hunting and protecting big game.
