Roosevelt's niece Eleanor, Elliott's daughter, has her fourth birthday.
Hunting stories and a mayoral endorsement

From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt writes Lodge about the fun of his western hunt and says Lodge's political standing is now secure. He also issues an open letter to New York City voters backing Joel Erhardt for mayor; Erhardt would lose.
Benjamin Harrison, the candidate Roosevelt campaigned for, defeats President Grover Cleveland, and Republicans carry both houses of Congress too.
Publisher George Haven Putnam and Rebecca Putnam sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Henry Cabot Lodge is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Thanks to Spring-Rice for rare prints
Roosevelt thanks Cecil Spring-Rice for some uncommon prints and fills him in on polo and the Kootenay hunt.
A Mrs. Halsey signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

Roosevelt's six Century magazine pieces come out between hard covers as a single book on ranching and the hunt, with drawings by Frederic Remington. Before Christmas he will complete the first volume of The Winning of the West.
Roosevelt and Edith mark two years of marriage.
Roosevelt writes Thomas Lounsbury to admire his life of James Fenimore Cooper and to discuss the Battle of Lake Erie.
John Wallace Riddle and Bob Ferguson, noted as "The Hieland Laddie," sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
At the Federal Club in New York, Roosevelt speaks in favor of Maine Republican Thomas B. Reed for Speaker of the House.
Roosevelt asks Lodge whether his uncle James Bulloch could draw a pension for service in the Mexican War.
The record for this day is blank.
A full house on Christmas Eve
Family fills Sagamore Hill for Christmas Eve: the Gracies, Douglas and Corinne Robinson with young Theodore Douglas Robinson, and Elliott and Anna with Eleanor.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about where he stands on civil service reform.
Uncle James and Aunt Anna Gracie are guests at Sagamore Hill again.
Roosevelt moves the family to 689 Madison Avenue for the winter while Bamie is abroad in Europe, and he sets up an office at Putnam's on West 23rd Street.
Roosevelt's older sister Bamie, traveling in Europe, has her thirty-fourth birthday.
Roosevelt writes Baltimore lawyer Charles Bonaparte that he shares his outlook on civil service reform.
Roosevelt is at the family's winter home, 689 Madison Avenue in New York.
Roosevelt goes to a meeting of the Civil Service Reform Association.
Roosevelt asks Bamie to let Nannie and Cabot Lodge know he would like to see them.
Roosevelt tells Charles Bonaparte he plans to speak at a reform gathering in the capital.
Roosevelt's daughter Alice celebrates her fifth birthday.

President Cleveland signs the law opening the way for the two Dakotas, Montana and Washington to join the Union, which will bring the count to 42 states. Roosevelt's Badlands ranch country is about to become North Dakota.
Roosevelt joins fellow reformers at their conference in Washington.
Roosevelt's brother Elliott has his twenty-ninth birthday; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Benjamin Harrison is sworn in as President.
Advice for a John Jay biographer
Roosevelt offers George Pellew some suggestions for his John Jay volume in the American Statesmen series.
Roosevelt subscribes for two years to the Civil Service Chronicle and writes Lodge that he will throw himself into writing, keeping to the share of politics any decent citizen owes.
Roosevelt dines with William C. Whitney.
Roosevelt sends Lodge a short note about political appointments.
Roosevelt pays a call on Frederick Grant, the late President Grant's son.
Roosevelt writes to Lodge from New York.
Lodge lobbies for a State Department post for Roosevelt as assistant to Secretary James G. Blaine, but Blaine turns him down.
Roosevelt completes Volume Two of his frontier history, The Winning of the West.
Roosevelt urges Spring-Rice to see the need for stronger American coastal defenses, with Germany in mind as a possible attacker.
Roosevelt complains to William Dudley Foulke that Harrison's New York appointments are strengthening Thomas Platt's organization.
Lodge comes up from Washington bearing word from the White House: President Harrison wants Roosevelt on the Civil Service Commission at $3,500 a year. Roosevelt says yes.
Corinne and Douglas Robinson mark seven years of marriage.
Only a fragment survives for this day, a note that the Civil Service Commission was created to end the spoils system of rewarding party loyalists with jobs.
Roosevelt's cousin Dr. West Roosevelt and his wife Laura sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
President Harrison signs Roosevelt's commission as a Civil Service Commissioner.
Miss Rose Lee is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt arrives in Washington and bunks at the Lodges' Connecticut Avenue house while they are away. The Commission's offices sit in the west wing of City Hall on Judiciary Square.
Roosevelt calls on President Harrison and meets the Cabinet, Postmaster General John Wanamaker among them. To Bonaparte he admits he was reluctant to accept the post.
Roosevelt encourages Cecil Spring-Rice to pursue a diplomatic career.
Roosevelt sends two letters on Commission matters to Indiana reformer Lucius Swift.
While Roosevelt works in Washington, Bob Ferguson signs the guest book at Sagamore Hill.
Back in New York, Roosevelt learns that civil service exam questions were being peddled to favored applicants for $50 apiece, and drafts a report calling for three men to be dismissed.
Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about rebuilding Indianapolis's corrupt local civil service board.
Governor Thompson is a guest at Sagamore Hill. In Pennsylvania, the Johnstown Flood strikes the same day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt heads for Washington, writing Bamie on the way that he came down hard on the New York customs officials.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Report blasts the New York customs exams
The Civil Service Commission issues its findings on the New York Custom House, condemning the local board's entrance examinations as sloppy and crooked.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
While Roosevelt works in Washington, Cabot and Nannie Lodge stay at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
A new week at the Commission
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt thanks Lodge for letting him stay in his Washington home and mentions dinner with the Thompsons.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt starts a ten-day swing through the Midwest.

With fellow commissioners Lyman and Thompson, Roosevelt tours major western cities to check how the civil service law is being followed, starting in President Harrison's home town of Indianapolis at Postmaster William Wallace's invitation. He tells reporters the law must be treated as binding.

In Indianapolis Roosevelt confers with his old friend Lucius Swift, who edits Indiana's reform paper, the Civil Service Chronicle, removes three employees who were hired against the rules, and sends Swift a note.
Roosevelt is traveling on the Commission's western tour.
In Milwaukee, postal clerk Hamilton Shidy gives evidence against Postmaster George H. Paul. Roosevelt also writes Swift twice about civil service matters.
Back in Washington, Roosevelt tells Lodge the trip was short but shook things loose.
The Commission recommends that George H. Paul be removed as Milwaukee's postmaster.
Newspapers nationwide give Roosevelt flattering coverage.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt dines with the Herberts in Washington, while Bob Ferguson and Nellie Tyler sign the guest book back at Sagamore Hill.
Making the Commission a living force
Roosevelt tells Lodge he has turned the Commission into a real power and will enforce the law without fear or favor. He also writes Silas Burt that the reform law will be upheld.

The Commission's first annual report appears, and critics warmly greet the opening two volumes of his frontier history. In Milwaukee, Postmaster Paul fires Hamilton Shidy, and Postmaster General Wanamaker will not give him his job back.

At Sagamore Hill, where Bob Ferguson signs the guest book, Roosevelt praises Lodge's life of George Washington, takes Lodge's kind words about his own book, and says of the Commission that he has made a difference.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded.
A guest named Foster, Frank Roosevelt and S. Van Fleet sign in at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt jokes to Lodge that, with the Midwest cases done, the Commission will slip back toward a sleepy state, and he writes Swift on civil service matters.
A telegram brings Roosevelt and his fellow commissioners to the White House, where President Harrison says he approves of their work.
Roosevelt reports to Lodge that the President is backing the Commission.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes historian Francis Parkman, delighted that Parkman admires The Winning of the West.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt tells Lodge the Milwaukee report comes out tomorrow and that it hits Paul hard.
Elliott and Anna Roosevelt and their daughter Eleanor are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt warns Swift that powerful people are leaning on the President to keep Paul in office.
Roosevelt complains to Bamie, only half in jest, that desk life is making him soft.
Polo ponies sold, a newspaper attack

Roosevelt tells Corinne his life keeps getting more sedentary and that he is selling his polo ponies. He tells Lodge that Washington Post editor Frank Hatton, a foe of reform, has accused him in print of winning his job through machine politicians. Two visitors, W. H. Russell and a Charles A. Ul, sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Swift on civil service business.
Answering Hatton; a job for Shidy

Roosevelt publicly rebuts what he calls falsehoods in Hatton's editorial and writes Brander Matthews on civil service. Through Roosevelt, Hamilton Shidy lands a post at the Census Bureau. Washington is hot and drowsy, with most officials away.
Hatton strikes again; Harrison won't budge

A second Hatton editorial insults Roosevelt. A chance encounter with President Harrison goes badly: the President declines to act against Paul. Roosevelt files a report on the western trip with the Commission and writes Lodge.
Roosevelt charges that an unnamed Cabinet member has been dragging his feet on the Paul case.
Frank Hatton attacks Roosevelt yet again, mocking him as a reformer with only a thin coat of virtue.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Summoned to the White House, Roosevelt learns that Harrison has let Paul resign rather than removing him. Roosevelt takes it as a defeat.
Edith marks her twenty-eighth birthday; Roosevelt is in Washington.
Roosevelt sets off for a vacation in the Rocky Mountains and writes William Clapp about civil service reform.
Passing through St. Paul, Roosevelt writes Lodge about politics.
Roosevelt is in St. Paul on his way west.

At Elkhorn Ranch, Roosevelt writes Bamie that next year he means to bring the whole family out to Elkhorn. On this trip he survives a fierce fight with a grizzly, which becomes his most prized hunting trophy.
Edith begs him to be careful
Edith writes Roosevelt that she is trying not to worry while he is in the wilds, but finds it hard.
Vincent Rowe signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
From Helena, Montana, Roosevelt tells Lodge his month off is over, he is headed home, and he feels terrific.
Missing him; Elliott hurt; a big bag

Edith, expecting a baby, writes that she misses Roosevelt terribly and counts the weeks. Elliott breaks an ankle that is misdiagnosed, then rebroken and reset. Roosevelt reports a haul of two moose, a mountain bison, two bears and a cougar, one bear charging him.
Roosevelt writes Edith that he has never felt fitter, misses her badly, hopes to be home before the 20th, and wants her with him at Yellowstone next year.
Roosevelt's son Ted celebrates his second birthday.
A New York Sun review of The Winning of the West claims Roosevelt had help writing it. Suspecting James R. Gilmore wrote the review, Roosevelt fires back a long, cutting reply to him and the paper.
Roosevelt wishes Bill Merrifield success in his race for the North Dakota legislature, and writes Charles A. Dana and the editor of the New York Sun.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt congratulates Lodge on the planks adopted at the Massachusetts Republican convention. Corinne turns 28.
Elliott and Anna Roosevelt welcome a son, Elliott Roosevelt Jr.
Nothing is recorded beyond a stray word carried over from the day before.
Gilmore replies by accusing Roosevelt of plagiarism, and Roosevelt's second rebuttal cuts him down even further.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the Knights Templar reunion filling Washington.
Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

Roosevelt fires a last shot at Gilmore, saying he takes no joy in beating down a weakling. Then a telegram from Sagamore Hill brings news that his son Kermit has been born prematurely, with Bamie helping at the birth.
Arriving at Long Island City after the last train has gone, Roosevelt hires an engine of his own and pulls in at home around 4 a.m. It is also niece Eleanor's fifth birthday.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Money worries, and thanks to Bamie
Roosevelt confides to Bamie his worries about money and job security, and passes on Edith's heartfelt thanks for Bamie's help at the birth.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt urges Lodge to make a speech going after the Mugwumps.
At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt writes the Commission's annual report to President Harrison.
Roosevelt gives Lodge his frank views of the strengths and flaws of various politicians.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt marks his thirty-first birthday at Sagamore Hill and writes Carl Ernst on civil service matters.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt dines with the Cruger family and Frank Hiscock.
Roosevelt dines with former Senator Warner Miller and writes Lodge.
Roosevelt returns to Washington, to quarters off Connecticut Avenue.
Baby Kermit is baptized at home, in Edith's sitting room at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt tells Swift he has finished a rough draft of the Commission's annual report.
Roosevelt sends historian William Poole a long letter on military affairs on the western frontier in the 1700s.
The Commission's annual report is delivered to the White House. The same day, New York World reporter Nellie Bly leaves New York to race around the globe.
Backing Reed; the budget grows; Edith arrives

Roosevelt sides with Thomas B. Reed over William McKinley in the contest for Speaker. Harrison signs off on the Commission's yearly report and asks Congress to give it more money. Edith sets up the Washington household and explores the city while the children stay at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt and Edith mark three years of marriage, and Thomas B. Reed, the man Roosevelt backed, becomes Speaker of the House.
Roosevelt writes editor Edwin Godkin on civil service matters.
No help for a San Francisco examiner
Roosevelt tells J. G. Underwood, an examiner at the San Francisco customs house, that the Commission cannot assist him, and writes Charles Fingard on civil service.
Roosevelt writes William Merville about the papers applicants need for federal jobs.
Roosevelt writes James Sexton, the postmaster of Chicago.
Philadelphia customs and a special commission
Roosevelt reports to the Commission on Collector Cadwalader and the Philadelphia Custom House, and writes Charles Bonaparte about setting up a special panel.
Christmas with Edie and the bunnies
The Roosevelts spend Christmas at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's 'Blessed Bunnies' (the children) all together with Edith.
Roosevelt reads a paper on the westward movement during the Revolution to the American Historical Association.
Elliott, still in pain from his foot, goes south, taking laudanum and morphine and drinking hard. Edith's household budget for the year shows clothes, groceries, a staff of ten and fuel.
New Year's at the White House
Roosevelt and Edith go to a White House reception to welcome 1890.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Theater and supper with John Hay
Roosevelt takes in the theater and has supper with John Hay, and writes Curtis Guild Jr. to endorse his platform.
Roosevelt tells Bamie, who has the grippe, that the new house is coming together, and that Germany's Baron Speck von Sternberg came for tea.
Roosevelt writes Bamie about her coming move to London.

Roosevelt asks Charles Collins for more Congressional funding for Commission staff, writes George Putnam about Volumes III and IV of The Winning of the West and the New York book, and sends civil service letters to James Warner, William Lyall and Brander Matthews.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie has her thirty-fifth birthday.
Roosevelt wants Congress to look into the Commission itself, apart from the Lyman inquiry, so the agency can be cleared of the accusations against it.
Nellie Bly completes her trip around the world, nearly 25,000 miles covered in just 72 days, outpacing Jules Verne's fictional traveler; the New York World tells her story.
The House opens a full inquiry into Roosevelt's Commission, chaired by Representative Hamilton Steward of South Carolina with Frank Hatton assisting.
Roosevelt describes for Bamie a banquet at Vice President Levi P. Morton's mansion.
The Washington social season keeps Roosevelt and Edith out five evenings a week. The Century publishes his article on the merit system versus patronage.
Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews he has written about a fourth of his New York City history.
Roosevelt's daughter Alice celebrates her sixth birthday.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Washington hostesses balance their guest lists with care, mixing power, intellect and pedigree, and that Edith is enjoying society more than ever.
House hearings on the Commission open with twelve charges. One accuses Roosevelt of placing Hamilton Shidy at the Census Bureau though Shidy broke his oath at the post office.

On Elliott's thirtieth birthday, Shidy takes the stand and concedes he would falsify records again. Around this time Roosevelt's Washington circle includes John La Farge, Clarence King, the Chanlers, Speaker Reed, Spring-Rice, the Lodges, John Hay, Henry Adams, Augustus Saint-Gaudens and the Camerons.
Newspapers savage Shidy's testimony, branding him both dishonest and foolish.
Holding his own at the hearings
Census Superintendent Robert Porter testifies at the House hearings, and Roosevelt defends himself skillfully.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt tells Isaac Sharpless he is buried in work and cannot come speak for him.
At the House hearings Roosevelt demolishes George H. Paul under questioning.
Roosevelt and Paul clash again at the hearings.
The House hearings wrap up after a final day of Roosevelt against Paul.
Roosevelt delivers a speech in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Roosevelt writes Century editor Richard Watson Gilder about articles by himself and Lodge and offers a piece on his grizzly fight.
Jacob Riis's Theodore Roosevelt, the Citizen tells of a speech Roosevelt gave at Chicago's Madison Street Theater; the date of that speech is not given.
Hard words to Bamie about Anna Hall Roosevelt
Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie a blunt judgment of his sister-in-law Anna, saying a life given over to frivolity has worn away her character.
Veterans' preference in the new bill
Writing from Washington, Roosevelt explains to Lucius Swift that the pending Civil Service bill would favor former soldiers when filling government jobs.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that he and Edith miss her badly and that their evenings have grown quiet without her.
Roosevelt writes William Potts about Civil Service matters and sends Brander Matthews a letter on copyright law.
Roosevelt is in New York City tending to business.
In a note to Bamie from Washington, Roosevelt reports that young Ted has recovered.
Trouble at the New York Customshouse
Roosevelt writes John Comstock about irregular practices at the New York City Customshouse.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne marks eight years of marriage to Douglas Robinson.
Writing New York, shelving the West

Roosevelt pushes ahead on his overdue New York City history yet cannot find time for The Winning of the West. Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan's sea power book appears this season, and Edith's butcher bill comes to $119.
Roosevelt urges Bamie to act firmly on their brother Elliott's drinking, warning that delay only deepens the danger and the risk of scandal. The same day, Oklahoma land opens to settlers.
Roosevelt writes A. W. Greely about Civil Service matters and commiserates with Brander Matthews over the copyright bill's defeat.
A pause in the press attacks

Hatton's stinging editorials against Roosevelt go quiet while a House committee prepares its verdict on the Civil Service Commission. Roosevelt writes Swift on reform and William Miller about the New York customs service.
Roosevelt meets with President Benjamin Harrison, whom he finds colorless, then dines with the Davises.
Lodge hears about the Dudley case
Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge about the Dudley case and Civil Service affairs.
Roosevelt picks up Alfred Thayer Mahan's new study of sea power and history.
Roosevelt tells Mahan he has given half of two busy days to his book and read it from cover to cover.
Answering a critic of his West
Roosevelt asks historian Lyman Draper for material to rebut Butterfield, whose book on Simon Girty faults The Winning of the West.
Edith takes the children to Sagamore
Edith brings Alice, Ted and Kermit to Sagamore Hill for the summer.
Roosevelt firmly rejects A. W. Greely's claim that the reform commission had wrecked the Signal Corps.
Ferguson and Spring Rice at Sagamore
Roosevelt tells Swift that the merit rules govern only six or eight percent of yearly federal hires and firings. Bob Ferguson and Cecil Spring-Rice sign the guest book.
A House committee files its report clearing Roosevelt's Civil Service Commission of the charges against it.
Roosevelt assures A. W. Greely that he does not think him guilty of wrongdoing.
Roosevelt writes Herman Lehlbach defending the Civil Service Commission as fair and honest.
Elliott sails to Europe for a cure
Roosevelt's brother Elliott leaves for Europe to sober up, taking his wife Anna, daughter Eleanor and son Elliott Jr.
Idaho enters the Union as the 43rd state.
Wyoming enters the Union as the country's 44th state.
E. Willard Reby signs the guest book
A visitor named E. Willard Reby is recorded in the Roosevelt guest book.
Promising Gilder an essay on reform
Roosevelt tells Century editor Richard Watson Gilder that his reform article for the magazine should be done within a few days.
Nellie Tyler's name appears in the guest book.
Isaac Iselin and Charles P. Dickey Jr. sign the guest book.
Roosevelt mails Horace Scudder of the Atlantic Monthly his review of Mahan's book on sea power.
Roosevelt completes his book on the history of New York City.
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about the work of writing his New York history.
Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 29th birthday.
Rachel Sherman, H. Marquand and Frank Roosevelt are entered in the guest book.
Clearing the desk at the Commission
Back in Washington, Roosevelt works through his pile of Civil Service Commission business and writes Lodge about reform and a visit from Bryce.
Writing Lodge from Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt boasts that he has thoroughly demolished his critic Grosvenor.
Family party heads for the Badlands

Roosevelt, Edith, Bamie, Conie, Douglas Robinson, Bob Ferguson and Lodge's 16-year-old son Bay set off for a week at Medora and Elkhorn and two weeks in Yellowstone. His essay on college graduates in public life runs in the Atlantic Monthly.
Roosevelt's party rolls west by train while, far off in Vienna, his brother Elliott falls back into drinking. Edith's meat bill comes to $29.
Back to Elkhorn with the family

Roosevelt's party steps off the train at Medora at 4:30 in a hard rain and rides 33 roadless miles to Elkhorn, fording the river 23 times, the women jolting along in a springless wagon. By noon they are at the ranch, where Roosevelt shows them around and a prairie dog town.
Edith writes her sister Emily Carow and includes her own drawing of the Elkhorn cabin.
Edith now weighs 131 pounds, six above her usual.
Roosevelt's party leaves the Badlands and heads west by rail to Livingston, Montana.
Roosevelt's son Ted celebrates his third birthday.
The chronology lists this date with no legible entry.
A letter to Emily Carow reports that the party has finished seeing Yellowstone: frosty nights, geysers, and a fall from a horse that left Edith bruised.
Roosevelt writes Lodge twice from Medora, announcing that he has just arrived.
Congress sets aside Sequoia, the nation's third national park.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 29th birthday.
Roosevelt and Edith return to Washington and rejoin the family.
Yosemite and General Grant parks created
Congress creates Yosemite and General Grant national parks in California.
Roosevelt pitches in to battle a prairie fire.
Roosevelt goes hunting with his friend Bob Ferguson.
Writing from Elkhorn, Roosevelt tells Lodge that President Harrison has lost all interest in Civil Service reform. He also writes Bamie.
Roosevelt's niece Eleanor, Elliott's daughter, celebrates her sixth birthday.
Roosevelt tells his mother-in-law Gertrude Carow how much Edith enjoyed her days at Elkhorn and shares news of the three growing children.
A chilly meeting with the President
Roosevelt reports to Lodge that his interview with President Harrison was brief and frosty.
Roosevelt writes Rufus Dawes on Civil Service business.
Whistling to work, branding toy cattle

Roosevelt walks to the office in grey trousers and a boyish hat, whistling. At home he heats hairpins into tiny branding irons and marks the children's toy herds: the Elkhorn brand for Ted, the Maltese Cross for Kermit, a triangle for Alice. Elliott's family is in Venice.
Midterm elections hand Democrats a commanding majority in the House, 255 seats to 88.
Roosevelt confesses to Lodge that the election results left him too gloomy to write.
Roosevelt's college friend Henry (Hal) Minot dies in a train wreck near New Florence, Pennsylvania. Minot headed the Eastern Railroad of Minnesota.
The chronology continues the account of Hal Minot's death, placing the wreck near New Florence, Pennsylvania.
The chronology finishes its note on Hal Minot, president of a Minnesota railroad.
Roosevelt and Edith mark four years of marriage.
Sitting Bull is shot dead by Indian police.
Christmas morning at 1820 Jefferson Place: the children dive into their stockings and cheer each new find.
Roosevelt sends Bamie holiday greetings and insists she spend next Christmas with them.
Troops of the 7th Cavalry kill more than 300 Sioux at Wounded Knee.
Boone and Crockett rallies for Yellowstone

Roosevelt plays host to his Boone and Crockett friends over dinner at the Metropolitan Club, where members agree to back laws shielding Yellowstone from exploitation. Edith, pleased, is expecting again; the year's grocery bills total $550.
The chronology completes its note on the Boone and Crockett Club's pledge to defend Yellowstone.
Elizabeth Cameron is startled that Edith is pregnant again and frets about the Roosevelts' modest income.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie celebrates her 36th birthday.
Roosevelt agrees that Bamie should travel to Europe to help Elliott.
Bamie takes Elliott to a sanitarium at Graz in the Austrian Alps. In New York a servant, Katy Mann, is carrying a child she says is Elliott's, and an angry Roosevelt resolves to pay to keep it quiet.
Proud of his work, grieving for Bamie
Roosevelt tells Bamie he is glad to serve as Civil Service Commissioner and believes he has done good work, and says he and Edith wish they could stand beside her through her ordeal with Elliott.
Roosevelt reports to Bamie that the main battle in Congress is now over free silver.
Roosevelt replies to Joseph Thorp's proposal to bring the Indian Bureau under Civil Service rules.
Alice turns seven as Grosvenor strikes
On his daughter Alice's seventh birthday, Congressman Grosvenor goes after the Civil Service Commission's funding.
With the Commission's budget under attack, Roosevelt tells William Potts he will not leave Washington.
A compromise amendment passes, keeping money flowing to the Civil Service Commission.
Roosevelt gives a speech in New Haven, Connecticut.
After a letter arrives from Elliott, Roosevelt writes Bamie that the situation is horrible, like a nightmare that will not lift.

Edith reads Grimm and the Arabian Nights to Alice, who is surprised to learn Edith is not her father's sister; only Bamie speaks to her of her mother, Alice Lee. Roosevelt romps with Ted and Kermit, playing bear. A forest reserve law, pushed by the Boone and Crockett Club, passes.
Roosevelt writes Senator Arthur Gorman to rebuke him for attacking Civil Service reform.
Off to New York with the Lodges and Reed
Roosevelt and Edith travel to New York City together with Tom Reed and the Lodges, Cabot and Nannie.
Roosevelt and Tom Reed both give speeches at a Federal Club dinner and afterward go to Chase's studio to watch the dancer Carmencita.
Roosevelt lunches with his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson.
Roosevelt writes Bamie from Washington; the chronology gives no details.
Roosevelt and Edith dine at the Camerons' with a group of Italian diplomats.
Itching to return to the West
Roosevelt tells Bamie he is eager to resume The Winning of the West and is mapping out its next two volumes.
John C. Rose of Baltimore brings Roosevelt evidence of Civil Service abuses; Roosevelt asks him to keep it quiet for now.
Rose hands over his findings on vote buying, and Roosevelt takes them to John Wanamaker, who declines to do anything.
On election day Roosevelt turns up unannounced in Baltimore, walks the wards, and sees open lawbreaking at the polls.
At dinner at the Pellews', Roosevelt meets Judge Brown, newly named to the Supreme Court.
Newspapers turn on Roosevelt for his Baltimore foray.
Patronage politicians call on President Harrison to demand Roosevelt's removal.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Bob Ferguson has been very ill and is recovering at Mrs. Cameron's.
Back to Baltimore to build his report
Roosevelt returns to Baltimore while drafting his election report, and writes old Albany friend Frederick Kruse about his books and Lucius Swift about Commission business.
Roosevelt tells Lucius Swift he is hard at work investigating matters in Baltimore.

Back in Baltimore, Roosevelt gets help from local lawyer Charles J. Bonaparte, later a member of his Cabinet. He also tells W. T. Huff that public ownership of railroads and telegraphs could not work here.
At a riding academy jumping contest, Lodge's son Bay wins every weight class aboard Toronto.
Roosevelt is back in Baltimore pursuing his election inquiry.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that English reviewers have welcomed his New York history, and sends love to Elliott and Anna.
Rock Creek runs and a question from Ted
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he takes walks and runs through Rock Creek Park, and that young Ted has asked whether God is a fairy.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne and Douglas Robinson mark nine years of marriage.
Elliott denies it; the book appears
Still in Europe, Elliott writes Roosevelt denying he fathered Katy Mann's child, and Roosevelt takes him at his word. Roosevelt's New York history comes out to mixed notices.
Roosevelt's 146-page report on the Baltimore elections is released.
Ever closer to Edith and the children
Roosevelt tells Bamie his ties to Edith and the children grow stronger every day.
With the Lodges and his own family gone for the summer, Roosevelt and Cecil Spring-Rice move into Lodge's house. Roosevelt writes Charles Peters about a faulty appointment letter.
A ride with Speck von Sternberg
Roosevelt and Spring-Rice dine in, and he rides out with Speck von Sternberg. He writes Theodore Babcock about New York customs exams, and tells Bamie he is leaving for Indianapolis and St. Louis.
Trip to Indianapolis and St. Louis
The chronology finishes its note that Roosevelt is setting out for Indianapolis and St. Louis.
Roosevelt writes G. Garbet about the Republican Party.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Elliott's troubles have become a waking nightmare for him.
With two fellow commissioners away, Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is enjoying handling the Commission's work by himself.
Roosevelt writes John F. Victory about the Letter Carriers Association.
Roosevelt writes John Clarke about party politics inside the New York Custom House. Speck von Sternberg stays at Sagamore Hill.

Edith takes the children to Sagamore Hill, where Bob Ferguson visits, while Roosevelt and Spring-Rice share bachelor rooms in Washington. In Europe, Elliott drags his wife, children and Bamie off to Paris and takes a mistress.
In a painful letter, Roosevelt tells Bamie that for the sake of Anna and the children, Elliott must be left to destroy himself with drink.
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Lodge about restricting immigration.
Douglas Robinson's Orange, New Jersey, polo team falls to Meadowbrook of Long Island.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he still wants to believe Katy Mann's claim about Elliott is false.
A letter from Bamie tells Roosevelt that Elliott is suffering delirium tremens. Roosevelt writes Clarke and praises Lodge's Boston history, built on the same plan as his New York book.
Roosevelt judges his brother as unbalanced in morals as in mind. That evening he hosts the British Minister and the Secretary of War for dinner.
Roosevelt hosts the British Minister and the Secretary of the Navy at dinner.
Roosevelt tells Lodge that Spring-Rice has read his history of Boston.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he and Spring-Rice are enjoying their time together in the heat, though Elliott's troubles have him at his wits' end.
Roosevelt sends a letter to his brother Elliott.

Spring-Rice reports to Elizabeth Cameron on his housemate's quirks: pacing in creaking boots while he thinks, and attacking chicken like a wild animal. Roosevelt urges Lodge to come for polo week at Oyster Bay.
Elliott and Anna Roosevelt's son Hall is born in Paris.
Roosevelt consoles Lodge on his defeat for Harvard Overseer and praises Carl Schurz's Atlantic article on Lincoln.

Roosevelt and Spring-Rice move to 1721, where Springy, lost in the dark, climbs to the third floor, finds a bare bed and calls out in alarm. At Sagamore Hill, Bob Ferguson and Gertrude and Emily Carow visit, and Alice rents out trees in her orchard to her siblings.
Roosevelt meets President Harrison about the Civil Service and finds him disagreeable from start to finish. He tells Lodge he is busy on the Commission's annual report.
Roosevelt advises Bamie that Anna should keep her distance from Elliott as a husband until he has proven himself through three years of abstinence, given his affair with Katy Mann and others.
Roosevelt rides the train to New York and stages a fireworks display for the children.
Roosevelt crosses Long Island Sound to bury his cousin Alfred, killed beneath the wheels of a train.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Katy Mann is demanding $10,000 to stay quiet, and no settlement looks close.
Roosevelt writes Bamie; no details survive in the chronology.
Cecil Spring-Rice is recorded in the guest book.

Roosevelt reports to Bamie that an investigator, judging by the baby's looks, believes Katy Mann. Bamie writes that Elliott is confined in a Paris asylum for inebriates and that Anna will sail home without him.
Roosevelt and Douglas Robinson go to see Katy Mann's infant. She receives a payment and drops from the record.
Roosevelt sends Bamie a letter; its contents are not described.
Anna and the children come home
Bamie returns to America with Anna and her three children.
Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 30th birthday.
After a long, hard labor at Sagamore Hill, Edith gives birth to a daughter, Ethel, with Dr. West Roosevelt in attendance. The baby is so big that her father dubs her Elephant Johnnie.
Spring-Rice complains to Elizabeth Cameron that Edith's sister Emily Carow bores him with endless tales of romance in Rome.
Roosevelt's Baltimore report goes to the newspapers and lands on page one.
Newspapers report that Roosevelt has sought a court ruling declaring his brother Elliott insane.
Writing Taft on choosing civil servants
Roosevelt writes Charles Wilby on Civil Service and Solicitor General William Howard Taft on how to select government workers.
William Howard Taft dines with Roosevelt.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that the ordeal is beyond belief but the only course is forward. Elliott, quoted in the Paris Herald, insists he is sane.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Elliott's letters read as perfectly rational yet utterly lacking in conscience.
Roosevelt writes E. B. Livingston about family history and life in Southern California, and Joseph Mulvey about the Letter Carriers Association.
Roosevelt rents a house at 1215 19th Street in Washington. Out west the Merrifields leave for Montana and Roosevelt shuts up the Elkhorn ranch house.
Wilmot Dow dies; west to Medora
Roosevelt writes Bamie that his old Maine guide and ranch partner Wilmot Dow has died, and sets out for Medora.
Roosevelt's son Ted celebrates his fourth birthday.
Roosevelt's hunting tally reaches nine elk in four weeks.
Roosevelt hunts with Bob Ferguson at Two Ocean Pass in the Shoshone Mountains of northwest Wyoming.
The chronology completes the location of the hunt: Two Ocean Pass in the Shoshones of northwest Wyoming.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 30th birthday.
Revolution grips Chile. An American minister shelters the ousted president, enraging Chileans, and the U.S. seizes the rebel steamer Itata. Nellie Tyler is staying at Sagamore Hill.
At Sagamore Hill on Kermit's second birthday, Roosevelt tells Lodge he has come home once more to talk of his own removal.
Roosevelt's niece Eleanor celebrates her seventh birthday.
A mob in Valparaiso, Chile, assaults sailors from the cruiser Baltimore on shore leave, killing two; Chile later pays the U.S. $75,000 in reparations.
Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about the Civil Service system.
A form for the railway mail
Roosevelt sends James White a sample form for the railway mail service.
Roosevelt writes Daniel Griffin about the Commission's handling of Civil Service violations.
Roosevelt sends Lodge a typewritten letter applauding one of his speeches.
Headed to New York to dig into abuses
Roosevelt tells Lucius Swift he is going to New York to look into abuses.
The Carows head back to Europe
After five months in America, Edith's mother and sister sail for Europe, and Edith is glad enough to have them gone.
Americans vote in the 1891 off-year elections.
Roosevelt writes Herbert Welsh about the Civil Service and Indian matters.
Roosevelt goes to New York City, planning to see Bamie at Sagamore Hill, and takes tea with Mrs. Jones and the Greens.
Roosevelt hosts a ten o'clock breakfast for a table of writers and editors: Charles Dudley Warner, William Dean Howells, Richard Watson Gilder, Brander Matthews, Green and Lodge.
Edith writes her mother that she will come to Europe for about a week once their investments recover.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that a bad case of bronchitis has left him very ill.
Worn out and sent to bed
Roosevelt rallies for a time, but exhausted in body and spirit he breaks down in December, and Edith confines him to bed for eight days.
Roosevelt and Edith mark five years of marriage.
Roosevelt writes Bamie; the chronology gives no details.
Roosevelt writes Bamie and sends Herbert Welsh a letter on Civil Service matters.
Roosevelt writes Stuart Wood about Civil Service reform in Philadelphia.
Roosevelt writes Richard Henry Dana about merging three Civil Service reform magazines into a single publication.
Angry over the two American sailors killed in Valparaiso, Roosevelt wants the United States to go to war with Chile.
The federal immigration station on Ellis Island opens its doors.
Roosevelt writes Bamie; no details are given.
Roosevelt sends George W. Jolley a letter about the merit system.
Roosevelt leaves New York by ship for Europe to face his brother Elliott.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie celebrates her 37th birthday.

Roosevelt writes Bamie in triumph: Elliott has accepted his terms, signing over two-thirds of his property, including a $60,000 trust, to a fund for his wife and children, and agreeing to two years' probation away from his family.
Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice that he and Edith miss him very much.
Roosevelt sails from Le Havre for home.
Elliott boards a different steamer for America, leaving his mistress, Mrs. Evans, in France.
No petitions for a federal officer
Roosevelt tells Joseph Mulvey he cannot sign a petition while holding a government post.
Roosevelt's daughter Alice celebrates her eighth birthday.
Roosevelt writes Bamie; no details are given.
Firings at the Cincinnati post office
Roosevelt writes Charles Wilby about removals at the Cincinnati post office.
Elliott spends five weeks in Dwight, Illinois, taking Dr. Keeley's gold cure for alcoholism.

With 25 tainted officials still drawing federal pay in Baltimore despite his findings, Roosevelt goes to a New York Civil Service Reform Association meeting and blasts John Wanamaker as the root of many abuses.
Roosevelt is in New York City.
Roosevelt remains in New York City.
Roosevelt joins Archibald D. Russell, Bob Ferguson and Douglas Robinson in organizing the Elkhorn Stock Company.
Baltimore probe and a Texas hunt

Roosevelt asks the House to investigate the Baltimore affair. He then takes Elliott south, stopping at Owensboro, Kentucky, before going on to a Texas ranch on the Nueces River, where he brings down a sow and a boar.
Roosevelt writes John Clarke about Civil Service matters.
Roosevelt is in Chicago looking into Civil Service abuses reported by Oliver T. Morton.
The House votes to have its Civil Service Reform Committee investigate the Baltimore affair.
Edith tells her mother that their uncle John Carow, who had no children, has left her and her sister Emily $32,000 apiece.
At a special hearing before the Postmaster General, which Roosevelt does not attend, Wanamaker has an excuse for every charge. Roosevelt writes Oliver T. Morton about the Civil Service.
Roosevelt writes his fellow Civil Service commissioners about his Chicago investigation.
Roosevelt tells Thomas Lounsbury he enjoyed his Chaucer study and has reread the Canterbury Tales.
Corinne and Douglas Robinson mark ten years of marriage.
Roosevelt goes before the House committee looking into corruption in Baltimore.
A gift and a peccary hunt
Roosevelt thanks Spring-Rice for a present and describes the peccary he hunted in Texas not long ago.
Roosevelt and Edith are Henry Adams's dinner guests.
Roosevelt tells Oliver T. Morton the Chicago report is complete, and writes Osborne Howes about Americanizing immigrants.
Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about a report on wrongdoing at the New York customs office.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the Baltimore investigations and Wanamaker.
Roosevelt sends Wanamaker a registered letter holding him responsible for the abuses, with a copy to President Harrison.
Sending Harrison a copy of his Wanamaker letter, Roosevelt says he never sought a fight with the Post Office Department but was drawn into one by pressing for the inquiry.
Roosevelt thanks historian Francis Parkman for two books.
With no answer from Wanamaker, Roosevelt attends the House committee's last session and sets the facts beside Wanamaker's account.
Roosevelt is applauded for his House testimony.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that once forced to fight, he chose to hit hard. He also writes Horace Johnson that he stands behind his report.
Roosevelt writes John Andrew reviewing the history of the Wanamaker matter back to March 23, 1891, and learns that Brander Matthews has the measles.
Roosevelt writes James T. Beach about irregular Civil Service appointments in Missouri, and tells N. B. Pearce why his son was not hired.
Gertrude Carow writes Edith that she is deeply grateful her daughters received such a generous inheritance.
The investigating committee's majority report calls Wanamaker's testimony evasive and garbled, a clear win for Roosevelt.
The Democratic Party names Grover Cleveland as its presidential nominee.
Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about Civil Service and books.
Roosevelt writes W. C. Kenyon about the Civil Service.
Elliott takes a job with the Robinson family's holdings near Abingdon, Virginia, and stops drinking.
Dr. and Mrs. Paul Thorndike and Henry Cabot Lodge sign the guest book.
The Homestead strike erupts in Pennsylvania; 13 die in the fighting and mobs control the town for five days.
Militia arrive at Homestead, Pennsylvania. Governor Hugh S. Thompson and his wife sign the Roosevelt guest book.
J. Hallett is entered in the guest book.
E. Willard Ruby and Bronson Winthrop sign the guest book.
J. Hallett again appears in the guest book.
Edith writes her sister Emily that baby Ethel is sturdy and headstrong.
Harper's Weekly describes Roosevelt as a polo player.
Edith tells Emily she has set aside her shares in the Elevated Railroad to pay for the boys' schooling.
Roosevelt tells Lodge that both Cleveland and Harrison have poor records. Most afternoons he plays tennis with Wharton at the Legation.
Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 31st birthday.
Dr. West Roosevelt and his wife are recorded in the guest book, along with a Laura Roosevelt.
At Elkhorn, Roosevelt writes Bamie that he finds little to hunt and the deserted cabin weighs on him. The Independent publishes his article on President Harrison's foreign policy.

Roosevelt rides south alongside Sylvane Ferris and Hell-Roaring Bill Jones, swapping cowboy talk, and reaches Deadwood. Edith writes Emily that Kermit would rather sit with her in a dim room than go walking with anyone else.
Opening the Harrison campaign in Deadwood
At the Deadwood Opera House, Roosevelt kicks off the Republican campaign for Harrison. He tells Bamie he has shot pronghorn and prairie fowl.
Touring Pine Ridge and Crow Creek
Roosevelt visits two Sioux reservations, Pine Ridge and Crow Creek. A speech he gave on Indian affairs is reprinted in a later biography.
Roosevelt's son Ted celebrates his fifth birthday.
At a Sioux City press conference, Roosevelt ridicules the South Dakota Republican Central Committee's assessments on officeholders.
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Lodge he has a good shot at the Senate. He and Edith go riding on polo ponies.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 31st birthday.
Roosevelt writes Lodge and Seth Low about the coming elections.
Gertrude Carow writes Edith that she sometimes weeps for her when unwell, and that her life would be empty without Edith, the children and Theodore.

Roosevelt sends his mother-in-law a lively report: he rides Pickle and Edith rides Diamond; Edith walks him to the office each day and reads Marbot's memoirs by the fire while he writes; Alice dotes on Edith and the little ones; Ethel is a handful; and Ted totes a tin sword everywhere.
From Virginia, Elliott sends his daughter Eleanor a birthday message.
Roosevelt's son Kermit celebrates his third birthday.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about a new editor at the Cosmopolitan and shifts among Republicans before the election. Niece Eleanor turns eight.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he has just returned from an Indian conference at Lake Mohonk that he found ridiculous yet worthwhile.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the Harrison-Cleveland race.
Roosevelt writes Bamie; no details are given.
Roosevelt offers Lucius B. Swift his help proving that federal workers in Indianapolis were pressed for political money.
Roosevelt tells Swift that Commissioner Lyman will reach Indianapolis on Wednesday.
First Lady Caroline Harrison, wife of President Benjamin Harrison, dies.
Roosevelt tells Swift his papers will help prosecute John K. Gowdy, chairman of the Indiana Republican committee. Anna Roosevelt has surgery and asks Elliott to stay in Virginia.
Coon hunting with Ted at home
Roosevelt and his son Ted track a raccoon to a hollow tree near Sagamore Hill and take it.
Cleveland wins back the White House
Election Day: Grover Cleveland beats President Benjamin Harrison, returning to the presidency after four years out, the only president to serve two terms that do not follow one another.
Taking the election loss in stride

Writing to Lodge from Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt admits the Republican defeat disappoints him but did not catch him off guard; only the scale of the New York margin surprised him. Nellie Tyler signs the guest book.
From Washington, Roosevelt tells Lodge that every one of his election forecasts proved accurate.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Asking Swift about a blue book

In Washington Roosevelt writes to Lucius Swift about obtaining a "blue book," the federal register of government employees. The same day, the long Homestead steel strike against Carnegie and Frick collapses.
An essay on Parkman in print
The Independent runs Roosevelt's essay on the historical writings of Francis Parkman.
Roosevelt writes to William Dudley Foulke; the subject is not recorded.
The United States begins taking steps to annex the Hawaiian Islands.
Roosevelt and his wife Edith travel together to Washington, D.C.
Anniversary, and a cool first meeting
Roosevelt and Edith mark six years of marriage. He also meets the celebrated war correspondent Richard Harding Davis, and the two do not hit it off at first.
Proud of four years enforcing the law

Roosevelt tells William Dudley Foulke about meeting Richard Harding Davis over dinner at the British Legation, and that he did not care for him. Expecting to leave office in March, he says he can at least claim he never backed away from enforcing the law.
Roosevelt sends Brander Matthews tips on a cowboy tale Matthews is writing. Meanwhile his brother Elliott pleads by letter with Mrs. Hall to know why he is kept from seeing his wife Anna.
Anna Hall Roosevelt, wife of Roosevelt's brother Elliott, dies of diphtheria at 29. A telegram to Elliott in Virginia tells him to stay away; he comes anyway.
Roosevelt sends the Civil Service Commission a report on improper conduct by the Democratic Committee in Indianapolis.
Christmas greetings, and spectacles for Ted
Roosevelt sends holiday wishes to Cecil Spring-Rice, reporting that young Ted now wears glasses and that Henry Adams is back in town, hosting his usual pleasant dinners.
Urging Schurz to write on Lincoln
Roosevelt asks Carl Schurz for a talk in New York about civil service matters and says he wishes Schurz would take on a life of Lincoln for the American Statesmen series.
No events are recorded for this day; the source page holds only bibliography notes.
Roosevelt asks Carl Schurz to serve as his go-between with President-elect Cleveland on civil service questions.
Roosevelt takes the children out sledding,, joined by Ted and several Black boys.
Dinner at Blair Lee's; eyeing Remingtons

Roosevelt dines at Blair Lee's and asks his sister Bamie to find out what two Frederic Remington paintings would cost. Edith writes her sister Emily that Elliott was merry and singing comic songs at his late wife's sister's home barely two weeks after the funeral.
Roosevelt travels to Philadelphia to look into the workings of the post office there.
Lunch with Corinne; Boone and Crockett dinner
In New York Roosevelt has lunch with his sister Corinne and her husband Douglas Robinson, then joins 28 members at a Boone and Crockett Club dinner.
Writing, then dinner at the Players
Roosevelt puts in time writing, then dines with Brander Matthews at the Players club in New York.
Back in Washington, dinner at Mrs. Slater's
Roosevelt returns to Washington and has dinner at the home of Mrs. Slater.
Rides with Cabot, romps with the children

Roosevelt tells Bamie he rides with Lodge whenever he can and that Willie Phillips joined him that morning for a rough-and-tumble outing with the children. He is weighing parting with most of the Sagamore Hill land, keeping just 20 acres, with Uncle Jim or Bamie as possible buyers.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is noted for the day.
Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her 38th birthday.
Roosevelt gives a speech in Buffalo, New York.
A Boone and Crockett book appears
The Boone and Crockett Club publishes American Big-Game Hunting, edited by Roosevelt and George Bird Grinnell. His own contribution is a story titled "Coursing the Prongbuck."

Roosevelt tells Bamie of Elliott's latest misadventure in Abingdon, where he knocked over a lamp and burned himself badly, and says he sees no point in trying further to steer his brother onto a better path.
Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about literary matters.
Battle of Mobile Bay in the sickroom
With every child in the house sick with measles, Roosevelt builds model warships, an ironclad ram and a monitor, and refights the Battle of Mobile Bay alongside Ted and Alice.
Roosevelt dines at the home of Secretary of the Navy Benjamin Tracy.

Alice celebrates her ninth birthday in leg braces doctors thought she needed; years later she believed her legs had been fine all along. Roosevelt dines at Cochrane's and writes Bamie about Edith's and Lodge's love of belles lettres.
Seeking more money for the Commission
Roosevelt presses Senator Edward Wolcott for bigger appropriations for the Civil Service Commission, which now oversees 43,447 federal jobs.
The Atlantic turns down a review
Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews that the Atlantic has rejected his review of books by Matthews and Lodge.
On Elliott's 33rd birthday, with his brother back in Virginia, word reaches Roosevelt of new bouts of hard living.
Writing up the Boone and Crockett Club
Harper's Weekly publishes Roosevelt's article about the Boone and Crockett Club.
On Inauguration Day for Democrat Grover Cleveland, Roosevelt submits his formal resignation from the Civil Service Commission, assuming the new President will want his own party's man in the seat.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.
In a talk with President Cleveland, Roosevelt learns, to his astonishment, that the new President wants him to remain as Civil Service Commissioner.
Edith glad to stay in Washington
Edith writes her sister Emily that she is happy Roosevelt will keep his post and spare them from leaving their Washington life.
Nothing new is recorded; the entry finishes Edith's letter from the day before.
Writing to the Pine Ridge agent
Roosevelt writes to George Brown, the Indian agent at Pine Ridge in South Dakota; the contents are not recorded.
Subscribing to the Chronicle; staying on
Roosevelt mails Lucius Swift a dollar for a subscription to the Civil Service Chronicle along with reform business, and tells Carl Schurz about his decision to remain on the Commission.
Roosevelt writes his childhood friend Fanny Dana, who has sent him her popular field guide to wildflowers, about plants as they turn up in literature.
Roosevelt is appointed to Harvard's Board of Overseers and placed on a three-member committee to review the zoology department and suggest improvements. He visits Cambridge during the month.
Roosevelt proposes to Richard Watson Gilder a joint article with Lodge on immigration drawing on the 1890 census, plus one on Lincoln's speeches.
Roosevelt and William Dudley Foulke trade views on Indiana's local civil service boards.
Roosevelt writes ornithologist William Brewster about his report to the Harvard Overseers on the zoology department.
Nothing new is recorded; the entry finishes the note on the previous day's letter to William Brewster.
Roosevelt writes William Dudley Foulke on civil service business.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Roosevelt tells James Clarkson he favors a bigger navy and hopes one day to see every European power pushed off the American continent.
Cleveland wants him a while longer

Roosevelt tells Bamie that President Cleveland recently asked him to remain another year or two. His letter covers the Boone and Crockett Club's log cabin exhibit too, planned at Chicago's world's fair, where Bamie sits on the organizing commission.
Corinne marks 11 years of marriage. In Washington, Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift on civil service.
A council of war on the Navy
Roosevelt, Lodge, Henry Davis and Admiral Stephen Luce gather for what they call a "council of war" on the U.S. Navy and why it must grow.
At Sagamore Hill; loss in Elliott's family
Roosevelt's record places him at Sagamore Hill. The entry also notes that Elliott's young son, "Little Ellie," will die of scarlet fever before May is out.

Chicago throws open the gates of the World's Columbian Exposition, marking 400 years since Columbus reached the Americas. In Washington, Roosevelt writes Alfred Thayer Mahan about the Navy and expansion.
Fighting a stall on free delivery

Roosevelt writes William Dudley Foulke about Senator Daniel Voorhees's charges, aimed at holding up civil service classification of the free postal delivery service. He also writes Lucius Swift on reform business.
Roosevelt calls on Bamie in New York and writes Brander Matthews about the American Revolution.
A political dinner in New York
Roosevelt attends a political dinner in New York.
Roosevelt is on the train to Chicago.
At the fair with family and the Lodges
Roosevelt reaches Chicago accompanied by Edith, Senator Lodge and his wife Nannie, and they join Bamie, who helps manage the world's fair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Club cabin dedicated at the fair
The Boone and Crockett Club's log cabin is dedicated at the Chicago world's fair.

Edith writes Emily that the fair feels like fairyland: a night gondola ride on the canals, and daytime rambles through the Midway's Javanese, Egyptian, Turkish, Japanese and Eskimo exhibits, where she found a fur-clad doll for Kermit. Roosevelt sends Lucius Swift two letters on the Terre Haute affair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.
Back to Washington from the fair
Roosevelt leaves Chicago and returns to Washington.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Edith opens Sagamore Hill for summer
While Roosevelt stays in Washington, Edith opens the house at Sagamore Hill for the season, noting the date in the guest book in her own hand.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz about the report on the Terre Haute investigation.
Cowboy Land in print; Aunt Annie dies
The Century publishes Roosevelt's article "In Cowboy Land." The same day his aunt Annie Bulloch Gracie, his mother's sister, dies.
Mrs. George Cabot Lee, mother of Roosevelt's late first wife, signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Dr. Alexander Lambert signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt asks Carl Schurz whether he received the Indian agent report and requests it be returned when Schurz is done.
Mr. and Mrs. W. Whitmore sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt writes John N. Bogert on civil service matters.
Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews that the Chicago trip was well spent and that the fair's buildings may be the finest architecture ever put on display. He also writes Carl Schurz.
Bob Ferguson signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt urges Alfred Thayer Mahan to take up a history of Lord Nelson.
Roosevelt writes C. Gaushell about civil service.
Roosevelt writes William Brewster again about the Harvard Overseers' report.
Appealing to Cleveland on free delivery
Roosevelt writes President Cleveland about obstacles being thrown in the way of the free postal delivery service now run under civil service rules.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt gives a talk at Groton, Massachusetts, and writes to Bamie.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt tells Bamie the Civil Service Commission keeps him extremely busy, and writes Carl Schurz on reform business.
A financial panic sweeps the country. At the Chicago world's fair, Frederick Jackson Turner gives his lecture on the frontier's significance in American history.
To Sagamore Hill; Cleveland's secret surgery
Roosevelt heads to Sagamore Hill. The same day President Cleveland undergoes a secret operation to remove a cancer from his mouth.
Roosevelt tells Lodge that as far as his own work goes, there is little to choose between the Harrison and Cleveland administrations.

Roosevelt writes Bamie that Uncle Jimmy is terribly lonesome and that Kermit wanted to make a meal of firecrackers on the Fourth, Alice wants short hair and trousers, and Ted is riding the pony Grant.
Dr. Alexander Lambert signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Grace Potter signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
A new guard for the Commission
Roosevelt asks Interior Secretary Hoke Smith to send a replacement watchman for the Commission's building now that the old one has quit.
Dr. Alexander Lambert signs the Sagamore Hill guest book once more.
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 32nd birthday.
Cleveland calls Congress back on silver
President Cleveland summons Congress into emergency session and pushes for repeal of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act.
A desk instead of a table

Roosevelt complains to Interior Secretary Hoke Smith that he asked for a meeting table and got an old desk. He also tells Carl Schurz that Harper's Weekly is unfair to attack Postmaster General Wilson Bissell, whom he rates well above John Wanamaker.
Ethel turns two, a cheerful toddler who waddles along at a run. Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz about Bissell and irregularities in the Post Office.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Corinne has helped Elliott when no one else in the family could, and that Cabot has done well in the Senate.
Thanking Schurz for his reform work
Roosevelt tells Carl Schurz how much he values Schurz's energetic work for civil service reform and honest government.
Roosevelt writes Charles Lyman on civil service matters.
Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz on civil service and sends Brander Matthews a lighthearted letter about how American women are educated.
Silver act repealed; TR heads west
Congress repeals the silver purchase law, and Roosevelt sets out for the West.
Roosevelt meets Seth Bullock in the West.
Roosevelt leaves on a hunting trip. Corinne Robinson II signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Helen B. "Nellie" Tyler signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt speaks to Buffalo's Liberal Club in New York State, warning against letting a dishonest man stand for his party.
Nothing new is recorded; the entry finishes the quotation from the Buffalo speech of the day before.
Ted turns six; a troubled dream
Ted celebrates his sixth birthday. Edith writes Roosevelt, who is away, about a bad dream in which he turned away from her.
Nothing new is recorded; the entry finishes Edith's letter of the day before.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt's son Kermit celebrates his fourth birthday.
Roosevelt's niece Eleanor, Elliott's daughter, turns nine.
Mr. and Mrs. Percy Roberts sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt tells William Dudley Foulke the Interior Department has not improved and that Josiah Quincy has outdone everyone as a dispenser of patronage.
Roosevelt marks his 35th birthday in Washington and writes Lucius Swift about Indiana post offices.
James King Gracie, the uncle the family calls Uncle Jimmy, signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Edith sends a letter to her sister Gertrude Carow.
On Election Day, a visitor recorded as Lord Ara signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
A Commission fight comes to a head
Roosevelt tells Carl Schurz he is genuinely relieved that a dispute inside the Civil Service Commission has finally come to a head.
Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz on civil service business.
Roosevelt's book The Wilderness Hunter is published.
Roosevelt and Edith celebrate their seventh wedding anniversary.
Roosevelt calls on the Whites, finds them out, and buys a volume of Keats for Bob Ferguson.
Bamie sails to keep house for Rosy

From New York Roosevelt tells Bamie of plans to host Commission representatives at dinner at 689 Madison Avenue. Bamie, having nursed Bob Ferguson through scarlet fever, is leaving for London to run the household of their widowed cousin James "Rosy" Roosevelt, the embassy's First Secretary, and his two children. Roosevelt then returns to Washington.
Edith tells Bamie that Roosevelt fears they are headed for the poorhouse.

Roosevelt takes Alice, Ted and Kermit to Rock Creek Park and the zoo, and that evening he and Edith are Henry Adams's dinner guests. He tells Bamie his spending outruns his income by $2,500 and he may have to give up Sagamore Hill.
A non-partisan dinner is held for Navy Secretary Hilary Herbert.
Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about literary affairs and college athletics.
Making the case for outdoor sport
Harper's Weekly publishes Roosevelt's article on sports, in which he argues that games played outdoors beat indoor ones.
Roosevelt writes to Bamie from Washington.
Exercise, a stalled book and a fur collar

Roosevelt exercises in Rock Creek Park. He sends Bamie a note from Alice and admits The Winning of the West is going slowly; he praises Brander Matthews's article on Andrew Lang. Elliott has sent him a coachman's fur collar for Christmas, and he is baffled that Edith's sister Emily has become a Catholic.
Revolt in Hawaii; New Year's calls begin
American settlers revolt in Hawaii. In Washington Roosevelt and Edith begin a round of calls at the White House and on cabinet families.
New Year's dance at the British envoy's
Roosevelt and Edith finish their round of cabinet calls and go to Sir Julian Pauncefote's annual dance.
Roosevelt attends a goodbye dinner at Henry Adams's house before Adams leaves for Europe.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Dinner with the Reeds, Storers and Taft
Roosevelt hosts Tom Reed and his wife, the Bellamy Storers, and Judge William Howard Taft, a family favorite.
Playing bear; Edith sizes up Lt. Cowles

Roosevelt plays bear with the children, spins them Indian stories, and pushes ahead with his Winning of the West, now on its third volume. Answering Bamie's question about Navy Lieutenant William Cowles, Edith writes that she saw him now and then in Washington but formed no strong opinion of him.
Roosevelt writes Bamie about a new fellow commissioner named Proctor.
Roosevelt sends Congressman Alexander Dockery a letter about Commission business.
To New York for a club audit
Roosevelt travels to New York for an audit of the Boone and Crockett Club's books.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
