The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews that Alice and Ted are delighted with the fairy tale Prince Prigio, and writes Lemuel Quigg about appointments.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Roosevelt writes the Civil Service Commission about the Gaddis case.
Roosevelt and Brander Matthews exchange literary news. Edith, expecting a baby, is ill.
First dinner at Cleveland's White House

Roosevelt and Edith dine at the White House for the first time. President Cleveland welcomes them in the East Room at 7:15; Roosevelt takes Mrs. Cleveland in to dinner, while Century editor Richard Watson Gilder escorts Edith, who is seated between Gilder and the President. He also writes Lucius Swift on civil service.
Edith on the White House dinner
Edith describes the White House dinner to Bamie: as the only Republicans at the table, she and Roosevelt felt like outsiders and watched every word.
Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about the investigation into Indiana post offices.
Laying out his Post Office battles
Roosevelt writes Case Broderick a letter that gives the clearest single account of his running fights with the Post Office Department.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Frederick Jackson Turner to praise his essay on the frontier in American history. He also tells William Dudley Foulke that the Commission should control removals as well as hiring.
A long ride along the Potomac
Roosevelt and Lodge ride for three hours across fields and along the Potomac. He tells Bamie that Uncle Jim wants to buy a ten-acre parcel of his Sagamore Hill land.
Alice turns ten, a sociable girl who brings home tales from school every day.
Roosevelt dines at the home of Alan Johnstone.
Roosevelt writes William Dudley Foulke on civil service.
Dinner with the Lodges and Chanlers
Roosevelt and Edith share dinner with the Lodges and Winthrop Chanler's family. Kermit has chicken pox. Roosevelt writes Bamie.
Hosting lawmakers on reform and Hawaii
Six members of Congress dine at Roosevelt's home, where talk turns to civil service reform and the Hawaii question.
Roosevelt dines at Miss Gwynn's, where Tom Reed is a fellow guest.
Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about President Cleveland's nomination of Peckham to the U.S. Supreme Court.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Lecturing, editing and paying in gold

Around this time Roosevelt starts lecturing for pay, edits another collection of writing for the Boone and Crockett Club, writes volumes three and four of The Winning of the West and plans two more he will never finish. The first money from John Carow's estate arrives; with paper currency scarce, he pays his servants in gold.

Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about the Treasury's Gaddis case, writes Madison Grant about the Boone and Crockett Club and deer of the world, and tells Carl Schurz that Treasury Secretary John Carlisle is stonewalling the Gaddis matter.
Roosevelt writes Bamie, newly presented at the English court, and grumbles that Cleveland and the Democrats have made a mess of governing.
Roosevelt writes Henry White, First Secretary of the U.S. Embassy in London, hoping to see him when he visits Washington.
Rudyard Kipling and his wife dine with the Roosevelts, along with Brooks Adams, Samuel Langley, Miss Pauncefote, Willie Phillips and Emily Tuckerman.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Congressman Alexander Dockery about how to stand up for the Commission when the House holds hearings.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
A Rock Creek scramble and a land sale

Roosevelt, Edith (nine months pregnant), Ted, Alice and friends clamber up Rock Creek. He sells six acres to his uncle James Roosevelt at $400 an acre, so that just 30 acres remain of the land he first bought at Sagamore Hill. Elliott is living in New York under a false name with his mistress. The Forum publishes "What Americanism Means."
Roosevelt teases Bamie about his money troubles, suggesting she buy a postal scale since her letters keep arriving with postage due.
Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews he has been coughing for two months.
Roosevelt writes Interior Secretary Hoke Smith opposing any shrinking of Yellowstone National Park and proposing that the Sequoia and Yosemite regions become national parks.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

The chronology logs Archibald Bulloch Roosevelt's birth under this date, and again under April 16, but Archie was born on April 9, 1894. The entry describes a midnight delivery so easy and quiet that Roosevelt has to wake the nurse, Mame; he writes Bamie that Edith suffered less than ever, then brings Alice and Ted in to meet their brother.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Roosevelt writes C. P. Connolly about his Forum article "What Americanism Means."
Roosevelt teases Bamie about his money troubles, suggesting she buy a postal scale since her letters keep arriving with postage due.
Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews he has been coughing for two months.
Thomas Edison's Kinetoscope peep-show viewer goes on public display at 1155 Broadway in New York.
Roosevelt writes Interior Secretary Hoke Smith opposing any shrinking of Yellowstone National Park and proposing that the Sequoia and Yosemite regions become national parks.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

Archibald Bulloch Roosevelt arrives around midnight. Roosevelt writes Edith's sister Gertrude that the baby came at 12:35 after Edith's shortest, easiest labor and will carry his great-great-grandfather's name; he tells Bamie Edith is happy. He brings Alice and Ted, rag dolls in arms, to see the baby.
Roosevelt writes C. P. Connolly about his Forum article "What Americanism Means."
Thomas Edison's Kinetoscope peep-show viewer goes on public display at 1155 Broadway in New York.
Roosevelt jokes to Bamie that his branch of the Roosevelt family is now large enough.
Edith writes Bamie about their niece Eleanor's visits to Sagamore Hill, calling her plain but predicting the ugly duckling may yet become a swan.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Answering Pearson in the Sewanee Review

Roosevelt writes Francis Stetson about filling a classified job in the Sub-Treasury office in New York. In the Sewanee Review he publishes an upbeat rebuttal to Charles H. Pearson's gloomy book National Life and Character.
Washington sees a scuffle with Coxey's Army of unemployed marchers; Jacob Coxey draws a fine for stepping onto the Capitol lawn.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

Roosevelt writes Corinne, who is ill and grieving Aunt Annie Gracie, their mother's sister and early teacher to the Roosevelt and Carow children; her little Stewart is sick as well. He and Edith ride in Rock Creek Park, and he discovers he has lost a $130 check.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about literary business.
Roosevelt writes Bamie about bimetallism and the tariff.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The Pullman strike begins. Roosevelt writes Charles Pearson about his book National Life and Character.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Roosevelt writes William Dudley Foulke about investigating the free postal delivery service.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Edith sends a letter to Bamie.

With Edith and the children away, Roosevelt meets the newly seated senators from Michigan and California over dinner and keeps writing his frontier history. The entry also notes a Nicaragua interocean canal.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he has met Frank Cushing, explorer of the American Southwest. He dines at the Camerons' and tells Brander Matthews he likes his exam papers.
Roosevelt writes Congressman Alexander Dockery about civil service.
Winning a House fight on reform
Roosevelt tells Bamie he has come out on top in a hard-fought House battle over civil service reform.
Edith notes in the guest book that she has opened the Sagamore Hill house for the season.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Bob Ferguson signs the Sagamore Hill guest book. In Washington, Roosevelt writes A. C. Bernheim about falsehoods spread during the 1886 New York mayoral race.
Roosevelt passes along to Bamie that Alfred Thayer Mahan is now visiting London.
Roosevelt congratulates John Fox Jr. on publishing A Cumberland Vendetta, his latest novel.
Roosevelt goes up to New York and spends the night at Chamberlain's.
Guinea pigs, a rabbit and a pony
Roosevelt reaches Sagamore Hill in the afternoon and is introduced to the children's guinea pigs, their rabbit and the pony Nellie.
Corinne Robinson II signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Mr. and Mrs. Bellamy Storer sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Baby Archie is christened at 5 p.m. in Edith's parlor at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt reports to Bamie.
Miss Alice Lee signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt dines with Henry Adams and Henry Cabot Lodge.
Roosevelt writes John Fox Jr. again about his book. Fox would later ride with the Rough Riders and write The Trail of the Lonesome Pine.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he is in his usual civil service fights and calls Treasury Secretary John Carlisle worse than Wanamaker. Bamie has ear trouble, and Kermit's knee is bothering him.
Roosevelt explains how the U.S. civil service works in a letter to James Young, and writes Carl Schurz on reform business.
Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews on literary matters and floats the idea of a piece about the Culloden campaign, centered on the Stuart claimant or on Cumberland.
Swimming lessons and a windmill mishap

Roosevelt teaches his niece Eleanor to swim while Kermit, in a knee brace, watches from the side. After a run-in with the Sagamore Hill windmill, Roosevelt comes in cut and bleeding, and Edith sends him upstairs to bleed in the bathroom, not on the carpet. Bamie is still abroad.
Henry Adams and Cecil Spring-Rice sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
The Pullman strike erupts into violence.
Mrs. George Cabot Lee, Alice's grandmother, signs the Sagamore Hill guest book while the Pullman strike goes on.
From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt tells Carl Schurz his trouble with Treasury Secretary Carlisle continues. The Pullman strike drags on.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Union leader Eugene Debs is arrested, and the Pullman strike peters out.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Roosevelt writes Fanny Dana that he admires her poem but faults its lines about birds, whose calls and habits she has gotten wrong.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt gives a lecture at Chautauqua.

Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Bamie in London: Douglas is mending after a polo fall, Spring-Rice is visiting, and Kermit chafes in his knee brace. He answers Fanny Dana's defense of her poem, takes Kermit to Dr. Schaeffer about the knee, and notes Ethel and Kermit fight furiously. W. P. Trent visits.
Roosevelt, Cecil Spring-Rice and W. P. Trent travel from Sagamore Hill to Philadelphia, where Roosevelt gives an address.
After Elliott crashes his carriage into a lamppost and is thrown, Roosevelt writes Bamie wishing his brother could have died in place of Anna.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.
Horses and a hideaway at Sagamore Hill
Summer at Sagamore Hill: Roosevelt rides a horse named Diamond and Edith rides Pickle. A small gazebo called the Nest, about 200 yards north of the house, serves as Edith's private retreat.
Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 33rd birthday.
United States recognizes the Republic of Hawaii
In Washington, President Grover Cleveland extends American recognition to the new Republic of Hawaii.

Edith writes to her sister Emily that she lives in fear of Elliott's behavior bringing scandal down on Roosevelt. To her mother Gertrude she adds that she is glad her husband never went into business, where worry would have driven him wild.
A note of praise to J. W. Fox
Working in Washington, Roosevelt writes J. W. Fox to say he enjoyed Fox's latest book.
Tennis, talk, and worry over Elliott

Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie from Washington about his busy days with Lodge: tennis, shared dinners, long political conversations. He also tells her that their brother Elliott has started drinking again.
Ethel turns 3 as bad news arrives

Daughter Ethel celebrates her third birthday; she is a strong-willed little girl who bosses her mother. The same day a telegram reports that Elliott is gravely ill in New York City, where he lives with Mrs. Evans on West 102nd Street. Fanny Sturgis visits.
Elliott Roosevelt dies in New York

Roosevelt's younger brother Elliott, after trying to leap from a window of his apartment, suffers a last seizure and dies. Roosevelt is crushed by grief. Mrs. Evans, the woman Elliott lived with, receives $1,250 to stay silent. Roosevelt also sends a civil service letter to Lucius Swift.
Conie mourns Elliott in a letter
Roosevelt's sister Conie writes Bamie about seeing Elliott after his death, describing how the swelling had left his face and the gentle look that brought her to tears.
Elliott laid to rest in Brooklyn
Roosevelt weeps at his brother Elliott's funeral; Elliott is buried at Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn. Writing to Bamie, Roosevelt likens his brother in his last days to a hunted animal.
Back at work in Washington, Roosevelt writes Senator Arthur Gorman about the Civil Service Commission and a congressional committee, and sends Lucius Swift a letter on commission affairs.
From Washington, Roosevelt writes the Swifts again on civil service business.
Writing to his sister Conie, Roosevelt says he now wants to hold only happy memories of Elliott, recalling the boy who explored hotels with them and went to dancing class.
Turning down a run for mayor
New York City reformers urge Roosevelt to run for mayor. Edith objects, preferring their settled life and his steady post in Washington, and Roosevelt, against his own wishes, says no.
A gift for a pony cart
Alice's Lee grandparents send Roosevelt money for a pony cart that Alice and the younger children can share.
A. P. Jones signs the guest book
A. P. Jones is recorded as a visitor at the house.
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Lodge a wide-ranging letter about the civil service, politics, and books.
Roosevelt sets out for the Badlands and his ranch country around Medora.
Roosevelt's son Ted turns seven. He reads all the time, but he squints and his eyesight is poor.
Douglas and Corinne Robinson, Teresa Houghton, Mr. Peel, Mr. Morris, and Uncle James K. Gracie all appear in the guest book.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 33rd birthday.
Edith is upset to learn how much Roosevelt had wanted to run for mayor and how readily he treated her objection as final. She writes Bamie that she had not understood his feelings at all.
Roosevelt returns home from his trip to the Dakota ranch country.
Home at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Lodge that his ranch visit lasted just two weeks and that he shot five antelope.
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Lodge he will explain his side of the mayoral episode in person.
Back to Washington; family to Vermont
Roosevelt returns to Washington. Meanwhile his sister Bamie carries Edith and the youngsters off to Vermont for a two-week holiday.
Kermit turns 5; plans for a Bronx zoo

Son Kermit turns five, a self-contained boy with a curious mind who does little schoolwork. In Washington, Roosevelt writes Swift on the civil service and tells Madison Grant about plans he and others are making to found the Bronx Zoo.
Election talk and feeling against Platt
Roosevelt writes Lodge from Washington about the coming elections and the mood against New York party boss Thomas C. Platt. The record also notes a birthday for his niece Eleanor.
Roosevelt confides to Swift that he wishes he could leave office briefly just to say some things publicly. He also writes T. T. Hudson about resisting anti-Catholic societies.
In Washington, Roosevelt sends Swift another letter about the civil service.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.
Roosevelt writes Bishop John Keane to assure him the Republican party holds no prejudice against Catholics.
From Washington, Roosevelt writes Swift about the approaching elections.
Roosevelt writes Swift from Washington about the civil service.
No money to run for mayor
Writing Bamie, Roosevelt explains that he lacked the money for a mayoral campaign. He also writes Swift about post offices in Indiana.
Roosevelt writes J. W. Fox from Washington about the history of Scotland.
"I would have given my right arm"

Roosevelt pours out his regret to Lodge over the mayoral race he passed up, calling it a chance that would not come again. He takes the blame himself rather than putting it on Edith, and says the matter is best left behind.

Roosevelt marks his 36th birthday in Washington and writes Lodge about politics and the civil service.

Month's end; Strong's mayoral win noted
The page closing October lists Sagamore Hill, Massachusetts, and Washington among Roosevelt's stops, and notes that reformer William L. Strong wins election as mayor of New York City.
Voters go to the polls across the country on Election Day.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Groton, Massachusetts.

Roosevelt and Edith mark eight years of marriage.
Connecting Riis with the new mayor
From Washington, Roosevelt writes Swift about the civil service and urges Jacob Riis to meet Mayor-elect William L. Strong.

The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
Laid up with bronchitis in Washington, Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about cowboys and lumbermen in fiction and the failings of writers.

Books and politics with Brander Matthews
Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews again from Washington, mixing literature with politics.

Strong offers the street cleaning post
New York's Mayor William L. Strong offers Roosevelt the job of Street Cleaning Commissioner, and Roosevelt declines. He also writes Henry Merwin about Harvard and athletics.
On Christmas Day, Roosevelt takes his horses over jumps.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he has, after long wavering, refused the street cleaning post in New York. He also writes Carl Schurz turning the job down.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
In bitter cold Washington weather, Roosevelt tells Bamie he is trying to get Volume IV of his frontier history, The Winning of the West, under way.
At year's end the household has its share of troubles: Kermit and Alice both wear leg braces, baby Archie is being weaned, and Edith suffers from migraines.
From Washington, Edith tells her sister Emily that Roosevelt has turned down New York's street cleaning commissionership.
Roosevelt writes Jacob Riis that he ought to become an adviser to Mayor William L. Strong.
From Washington, Roosevelt writes editor Horace Scudder about literary matters.
Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her 40th birthday.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is anxious about Edith, who will not look after her own health no matter what he tries.
Edith writes her sister Emily that a fortnight at Corinne's home in Orange, New Jersey, gave her a needed break from family cares.
Roosevelt writes Edward Porritt comparing the American civil service with Britain's.
With Edith in Orange to have Alice's ankle braces adjusted, Roosevelt tells Bamie he is caring for the four younger children at home in Washington.
President Grover Cleveland sends Congress a message about a $45 million drain on the Treasury.
A Boone and Crockett book appears
The Boone and Crockett Club publishes Hunting in Many Lands, edited by George Bird Grinnell, with Roosevelt's piece "Hunting in the Cattle Country" among its stories.
Roosevelt writes William Fitch, customs collector at the Texas border town of Eagle Pass, about having mounted officers draw up civil service examinations.
Cleveland and Morgan confer on gold
At the White House, President Cleveland meets J. Pierpont Morgan to deal with the gold crisis. Roosevelt is in Washington.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.
Roosevelt writes F. Doremus standing up for the civil service statute.
Winthrop Chanler and his wife join Roosevelt for dinner in Washington.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.
Alice celebrates her 11th birthday in Washington with her grandfather George Lee visiting. Edith calls her a right hand and companion, and of the children Alice is closest to Ted.
Roosevelt writes Senator Francis Cockrell about a proposed pay cut for the Civil Service Commission's secretary.
Snow covers Washington, and Roosevelt tells Bamie he has been trying out Norwegian snowshoes, as skis were then called, and riding with Lodge.
Nothing is recorded for this day beyond a page heading.
Roosevelt writes Hugh McKittrick defending civil service reform.
Cuban rebels launch an uprising against Spanish rule.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Henry White and his wife came to dinner, along with the young architect Grant LaFarge, son of artist John LaFarge.
Writing Lucius Swift, Roosevelt says he is disgusted with Postmaster General Bissell.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about Doyle's appropriation, keeps teaching himself to ski, and works alongside Lodge on their book of Hero Tales for young Americans.
Roosevelt tells General James R. O'Beirne he has written Mayor Strong on his behalf.
Roosevelt travels to Cincinnati to inspect the city's post office and federal revenue office. He gives a speech, with William Howard Taft making the introduction.
Edith sends a letter to her mother, Gertrude Carow.
Roosevelt meets Rudyard Kipling again, and the two argue over a great many things, America above all.
New York politics and Joe Murray
Edith visits the Tylers. Roosevelt writes Charles Parkhurst about Joe Murray and city politics, writes Murray about politics and obeying civil service rules, and dines at the Shoreham.
A sketch of Kipling for Bamie
Roosevelt sends Bamie an account of his week, including a less than flattering description of Kipling's face.

Roosevelt writes Walter Camp about a book of football facts and figures. He argues Americans need sport and exercise, names football his favorite, scorns critics who call it too rough, and notes he boxed and wrestled at college but was too nearsighted for football.
Roosevelt writes Joseph Sears, who edits Harper's Young People, the magazine where portions of his Hero Tales book were appearing.

Roosevelt sends a flurry of letters: to Parkhurst vouching for Joe Murray's character, to Lemuel Quigg and Governor Levi Morton backing New York school reform that Platt opposes, and to Brander Matthews about Kipling. He tells Morton he would want a commission if troops went to Cuba, though he expects no war.
Roosevelt writes Lemuel Quigg about a subcommittee's report on the school bill.
Surprised by a police board push
Roosevelt tells Lemuel Quigg he had not expected Quigg to actually urge the mayor to name him a Police Commissioner.
Lodge to meet Quigg about the police job
Roosevelt wires Lemuel Quigg that Lodge will see him in New York, a meeting meant to arrange Roosevelt's appointment to the city's Police Board.
Roosevelt writes to the unnamed critic who reviewed the third volume of his frontier history; the reviewer turns out to be historian Frederick Jackson Turner.
Yes to the New York Police Board

Roosevelt agrees to become one of New York City's four police commissioners, at $6,000 a year, and wires Quigg his acceptance. To Lodge he admits he still feels unsure about the job and what lies ahead.
A dinner full of writers and diplomats
Roosevelt hosts a dinner for a lively company: novelist Owen Wister, Kipling, Tom Page, John Hay, and Austin Wadsworth, along with Merriam, Procter, and Rockhill.
Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews he now shares Matthews's view of Kipling, and mentions dining with the Brooks Adamses.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that spring has arrived and takes the children out to Rock Creek.
Baby Archie celebrates his first birthday.
Turner unmasked; Edith on a bicycle
Roosevelt writes Frederick Jackson Turner, now known to be his reviewer, about western history. Edith tells her sister Emily she has taken up bicycle lessons and finds them hard going.
Rock Creek scramble and police news
Roosevelt tells Bamie about the family's regular Sunday afternoon romp in Rock Creek and shares news of his New York police appointment.
Roosevelt's appointment as a New York police commissioner is confirmed for a six-year term. He writes Quigg about the post.
Roosevelt informs Mayor William L. Strong that he will take up his police duties on May 1, 1895.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.
Roosevelt writes President Grover Cleveland proposing two candidates for his Civil Service Commission seat: Bellamy Storer and William Wharton.
With Corinne and Douglas Robinson visiting, Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is sorry to be leaving Washington after six years.
In Washington, Mary Leiter, whose parents are friends of Roosevelt's family, weds Lord Curzon.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.
Word of a death in the family
Edith's aunt Mary Moore writes to tell her that her mother has died.
Roosevelt sends President Cleveland his resignation from the Civil Service Commission and writes fellow police commissioner Avery Andrews about the New York force.
Questions about the Police Board's powers
Roosevelt asks Quigg to clarify the laws governing the Police Board, and tells Frederick Jackson Turner their views on western history line up.

A telegram brings word that Edith's mother, Gertrude Carow, has died abroad at 59 after a mix of illnesses; she had been dependent on morphine. Roosevelt writes Bamie about beach rights at Sagamore Hill and thanks Lucius Swift for a letter.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.
Corinne and Douglas Robinson mark 13 years of marriage. Roosevelt writes Judson Grenell about civil service examinations.
The police world Roosevelt is entering

On the eve of the move, the chronology sketches New York's police: headquarters on Mulberry Street, reporters Lincoln Steffens and Jacob Riis keeping watch from across the street, board meetings twice a week, a powerful and wealthy chief in Thomas Byrnes, and corruption throughout the ranks.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.
A goodbye lunch with Henry Adams
Roosevelt is honored at a goodbye lunch in Washington, with Henry Adams among those present.
Roosevelt's six years on the U.S. Civil Service Commission formally come to an end as his resignation takes effect.

At City Hall, Roosevelt takes the oath as a New York police commissioner, then walks north to Mulberry Street, where his fellow commissioners Frederick D. Grant, Avery Andrews, and Andrew Parker choose him board president. Hurrying into his new office with reporters Steffens and Riis, he asks what they should do first.
In New York, nothing more recorded
The chronology places Roosevelt in New York City but notes nothing else for the day.
Albany trims the board president's power
The State Legislature passes a bill that reduces the authority of the Police Board's president, the post Roosevelt now holds.
In New York, nothing more recorded
The chronology places Roosevelt in New York City but notes nothing else for the day.
Roosevelt lands in the headlines as patrolmen accused of corruption go on trial. He writes Charles Saxton about the veto of the Ainsworth bill.
Roosevelt hires Minnie Gertrude Kelly, the first woman to serve as a secretary at police headquarters.
Roosevelt's routine: at headquarters by 8:30, striding fast and taking the stairs at a bound, and gone at 6:00. He writes Lodge about the new job.
Roosevelt rents his sister Bamie's house at 689 Madison Avenue and writes her in London that his first six days were the hardest work of his life.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the page cites a source on his move from the civil service to the police.
In New York, nothing more recorded

The New York World runs a portrait of Roosevelt. He writes Quigg about Police Chief Thomas Byrnes.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he plans to act against Chief Byrnes right away and does not trust him at all.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he now runs the most important and most corrupt department in New York.

Roosevelt passes along to Lodge Brander Matthews's idea of ending Hero Tales with a chronology.

At Lincoln Steffens's urging, Roosevelt pushes the notoriously brutal Inspector Alexander "Clubber" Williams into resigning.
Edith records in the guest book that the house was opened for the season on May 25.
Facing an investigation, with a generous pension waiting, Chief Thomas Byrnes resigns. Peter Conlin becomes the new chief.
Roosevelt writes Seth Low that removing Byrnes was essential.
In New York, nothing more recorded
The chronology places Roosevelt in New York City but notes nothing else for the day.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill for Decoration Day and delights in the children. Edith's sister Emily Carow arrives to stay for six months; the two sisters are mourning their mother.
In charge of the Police Board
Roosevelt tells Bamie he spends the work week alone in New York City and now has the Police Board firmly under his control.
Henry White and M. Maxwell visit
Henry White and M. Maxwell are guests at the house.

At 2 a.m. Roosevelt and Jacob Riis set out from the Union League Club and walk to Third Avenue and 27th Street without meeting a single policeman. Second Avenue proves a bit better. Roosevelt tracks down the missing men and sends them back to their beats, though he punishes no one. Every paper headlines the patrol.
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Bamie he rides a bicycle between the station and 689 Madison Avenue.
Grant LaFarge and Dr. Morris visit
Grant LaFarge and Dr. Morris appear in the guest book.
Order to close saloons on Sunday
Roosevelt directs the police captains to enforce the law keeping the city's saloons shut for the full 24 hours of Sunday, beginning at midnight Saturday.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
Another night patrol, with steak at 3 a.m.

Roosevelt goes out again by night with writer Richard Harding Davis and Commissioner Avery Andrews. He praises a sergeant on the well-covered Lower East Side, catches Patrolman Rath, eats steak at Mike Lyons's all-night place on the Bowery at 3 a.m., then finds the West Side poorly patrolled.
Roosevelt is at his New York City house on Madison Avenue.

Roosevelt tells Bamie he has little time to write and misses the children during the work week; at home he romps with Archie in the evening and plays with baby Ethel at her crib. He also writes Lodge about Jessie the dog.
A patrolman stands up to "King" Callahan

The closing law is enforced in New York: Patrolman Bourke makes saloonkeeper Pat "King" Callahan shut his bar and is assaulted for it. Roosevelt writes Bamie that he relishes his late-night walks for the force.
Patrolman Bourke is vindicated at the Tombs Police Court in the Callahan case.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
Roosevelt attends his Harvard class dinner, 15 years after graduating, the only one he ever went to. He is elected a Harvard Overseer, leading the poll.
Marshal at Harvard, then to Nahant
Roosevelt serves as a marshal under Roger Wolcott, then goes with Lodge to Lodge's home at Nahant.
Roosevelt returns to New York City.

Sunday closing is enforced again, and the papers call it the driest Sunday in years. Roosevelt sends Bamie a letter from Alice with a joke about Edith's efforts to get it written. His review of Benjamin Kidd's Social Evolution appears in the North American Review.
Winthrop Chanler, William Astor Chanler, Cecil Spring-Rice, and Lt. Von Hornell sign the guest book.

A cable reaches Sagamore Hill: Bamie, 40, is engaged to William Sheffield Cowles, 49, a Navy commander serving as naval attaché at the American embassy in London. One snag is that New York does not recognize his divorce.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that the news of her engagement stunned the family, but that they are truly happy for her.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
John Elliott appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Bars find back doors; Ethel's narrow escape

Saloonkeepers dodge the Sunday law with side doors and hidden liquor. Roosevelt writes Bamie that her engagement is the family's main topic and that he approves her choice, and reports that Ethel swallowed a bottle of nitre and a toadstool without harm.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.

A New York judge rules that the closing law covers every drink, including milk and lemonade. Roosevelt writes Swift about his work on the Police Board.
Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz about the makeup of the police force by ethnic background.
Keeping the peace at a parade
Roosevelt tells Lodge he turned out the police to guarantee order at a New York parade of Protestant Irish.
Speaking at the Good Government Club on East 115th Street, Roosevelt persuades German-Americans, angered by the closing law, that his intentions are good.
Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz about events in the city and his Good Government Club speech.
The New York Times puts the saloons' average weekend loss from the closing crackdown at $20,000.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he has asked New York lawyers about Will Cowles's divorce problem; Cowles could seek relief in court or settle in a more tolerant state.
Roosevelt gives Lodge a full account of his struggles enforcing the liquor law.
On Sunday, at least half a million New Yorkers head to saloons in New Jersey and on Long Island to escape the closings.
W. Hallett Phillips appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
On another midnight prowl, Roosevelt finds every policeman where he should be, and calls the night walks great fun.
Mr. Mantins appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Mr. Parker appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
New York has its driest Sunday yet; Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the free silver question.
A pink shirt and a Scribner's article

Roosevelt is seen in an English straw boater, pink shirt, and black silk cummerbund with tassels hanging to his knees. Scribner's Magazine publishes his article looking back on his years fighting the spoils system. Mrs. James Lowndes visits.
Roosevelt writes editor Charles A. Dana on the subject of Indian words. Avery Andrews, Grant LaFarge, and Mr. Smalley are guests at Sagamore Hill.
A bomb mailed to Roosevelt is opened by a wary post office clerk; it fails to go off.
On Edith's 34th birthday, Roosevelt writes Horace Scudder introducing Lincoln Steffens to the Atlantic, and writes Carl Schurz about false stories in the German press.

At Carnegie Hall, Roosevelt addresses the national convention of the Catholic Total Abstinence Union. Mayor Strong, Archbishop Corrigan, Commissioner Parker, and State Senator "Big Tim" Sullivan share the stage. He argues that no man's Sunday pleasures should cost his family his week's pay.
Roosevelt writes Lodge, who is traveling in Europe, that he enjoyed his letter.
Dan Tyler Moore appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
Ethel turns four, everyone's favorite and a little girl who loves the water.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.
Mrs. Clifford Richardson appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt inspects the precincts by day, and the Liquor Sellers Association declares its support for the Sunday closing law.
Clifford Richardson and Morton Procter appear in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Speaking in steaming East Side halls
Roosevelt tells Lodge he has spoken repeatedly through the summer in crowded, sweltering East Side halls before heated audiences.
Mrs. Alexander Moore appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
James King Gracie appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Lodge sees a large kingdom ahead

Dr. and Mrs. Alexander Lambert visit. Lodge writes Roosevelt predicting that his swift rise will soon bring him great things. Roosevelt sometimes lunches with Conie at the Vienna Bakery at 10th and Broadway. The page also lists the Roosevelt cousins summering near Sagamore Hill.
New York sees its driest Sunday so far under the closing law.
Roosevelt tells Bamie the last four months have been the most successful of his life.
Roosevelt gives a speech in Buffalo, New York.
Fanny Shenges appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Ted turns eight. Edith finds him more like his father all the time, though he is growing slowly.
All his time for the Police Board
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Henry White that the Police Board has consumed every hour he has.
A relic of Stuyvesant's pear tree
Roosevelt writes Mayor Strong about a piece of the historic pear tree planted by Peter Stuyvesant, and writes W. Hallett Phillips about the Lenox Library matter.
Roosevelt tells W. Hallett Phillips he will not interfere with New York's private clubs over Sunday closing.
Roosevelt writes Phillips again about the Sunday closing fight.

Opponents of the Sunday law stage a two-hour parade through Yorkville and mockingly invite Roosevelt, who shows up and enjoys the floats lampooning him. When a spectator calls out in German asking where Roosevelt is, he answers in German that he is right there. Bob Ferguson visits Sagamore Hill.
Corinne celebrates her 34th birthday; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt tells Bamie the political outlook is bleak but he means to fight it out to the end.
Roosevelt and Edith learn that from now on they must pay rent for the house at 689 Madison Avenue to Bamie and her husband-to-be, Will Cowles.
A day in New York City
Roosevelt is in New York City, where his work as president of the Police Board keeps him through the autumn election season. The record notes nothing else for the day.

Too busy for politics, he tells Lodge
Writing from New York City to Henry Cabot Lodge, who is traveling in Spain with his family, Roosevelt says he has little time to spare for politics.
Roosevelt tells Carl Schurz he followed Schurz's advice in reviewing a Yorkville parade, and assures him he bears German-Americans no ill will.
A day in New York City
Roosevelt is in New York City, where his work as president of the Police Board keeps him through the autumn election season. The record notes nothing else for the day.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at home at Sagamore Hill, a short break from the city.

Kermit turns six; Leslie's sizes up TR

Kermit Roosevelt celebrates his sixth birthday, described as a funny, loving little boy very much his own person. The same day Leslie's Weekly runs a piece weighing Roosevelt and the task facing him at police headquarters.
Few true friends, he confides to Lodge
On his niece Eleanor's eleventh birthday, Roosevelt pours out his feelings to Henry Cabot Lodge, saying that outside his family he counts only one or two people as real friends.
Speaking to a huge political crowd
Roosevelt addresses a giant political rally in New York City with Joe Murray, his old political sponsor, in the chair.
Sunday home, and a rent offer for Bamie

Home at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells his sister Bamie he spends the week in the city, speaking nightly, and gets only a few hours at home on Sundays. Edith writes Bamie offering $1,800 to rent her townhouse from January through April, promising to keep it clean and treat her things with care.
Roosevelt travels to Boston and gives a speech there.
Hard at work on the stump
Roosevelt writes Seth Low that he is working hard and giving speeches, even though Republicans are distancing themselves from him.
Roosevelt speaks to four Republican mass meetings in Baltimore and has a talk with Tom Reed.
Roosevelt writes Lodge from New York City about the small-bore local politics consuming his days.
Roosevelt takes the platform at a New York City political gathering.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he has quarreled with Lemuel Quigg. His wife Edith wishes her husband had held back his jab that the good-government reformers had turned foolish.
Answering criticism from Preble Tucker, Roosevelt defends backing the Republican ticket over the Independent one and explains his nickname for the reformers, "Goo-Goos."
The guest book records two visitors: Mr. White and Mr. Versehoyle.
A 37th birthday, a week from the vote
On his 37th birthday Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is grateful only one more week remains before the election.
Roosevelt tells Henry White the fates seem to be running against his side in the coming election.
Roosevelt reports to Lodge that his campaign speeches have taken aim at many people, and the backlash against him is loud.
Roosevelt writes editor Charles Dana about a newspaper attack on him by Ashbel P. Fitch, and writes Maria Storer about appointing Catholics, among other matters.
Roosevelt may be pushing himself too hard in the campaign's last days; he is noted as very tense.
Roosevelt's brother-in-law Douglas Robinson signs the guest book.
Republicans lose the city, and TR is blamed
On Election Day Republicans carry upstate New York but fall to the Democrats in New York City, a defeat laid at the feet of Roosevelt's unpopular crusade to enforce the law.
No letup, he tells police captains
The day after the election, Roosevelt summons the police captains and makes clear the Board expects the laws to be enforced as strictly as ever.
Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt rides, chops wood and walks with Edith and the children. He also writes Lemuel Quigg that plenty of people are hoping the two of them will split.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he expected all along to be blamed for the election loss.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt tells Lemuel Quigg that crime is running below 1894 levels and the city has been notably calm.
Roosevelt predicts to Bamie that lawmakers will abolish his job within a couple of months.
At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt works on the fourth volume of his frontier history, The Winning of the West.
Roosevelt writes Bamie, about to marry in London, marveling that she will be a wife by the time his letter arrives. He and Edith send the couple $500.
Wishing he could be at the wedding
From 689 Madison Avenue Roosevelt tells Bamie how much he longs to be with her and her new husband.
Roosevelt takes offense at Mayor Strong's banquet quip, aimed at him, that a Dutchman could be turned into a Puritan.
Conie writes about the wedding plans
Roosevelt's sister Conie sends him and Edith news of the preparations for Bamie's wedding.

Roosevelt's older sister Bamie marries naval officer William S. Cowles in London, at Westminster's St. Andrew's Church. Conie and Douglas Robinson are there, cousin Rosy Roosevelt walks her down the aisle, and Bob Ferguson is an usher. Roosevelt himself stays in New York.
Roosevelt tells Henry White he is being driven hard, with the papers trying to steer him off his course at the Police Board, and says how badly he misses Bamie and her new husband.
If only he could buy Remingtons
Roosevelt tells Frederic Remington he wishes he were rich enough to buy a number of his paintings, and they swap notes on "ganglio," a Western word unknown back East.
Roosevelt keeps at his fourth Winning of the West volume.
From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt tells Bamie he would love a break.

Roosevelt endorses Lodge's resolution in the Anglo-Venezuelan boundary dispute, arguing that an attack on Venezuela should count as an attack on the United States. He also writes Brander Matthews about books and Kipling.
Roosevelt reports to Lodge that Governor Levi Morton is furious that Roosevelt favors Tom Reed for the 1896 presidential nomination.

Dinner with the city's department heads
Roosevelt dines at the Crugers' home and meets the heads of the city's departments.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the race for the 1896 Republican nomination between Tom Reed and Platt's man, Levi P. Morton, and tells W. Hallett Phillips he could not place Phillips' article.
Roosevelt has an article in the Outlook. He also writes W. Hallett Phillips that he was unable to get Phillips' piece published.
Roosevelt writes William S. Cowles that he hopes the government holds firm on Venezuela, and tells Bamie he spent the money she sent on Christmas presents for the children at Schwarz's toy store.
Volume IV done, and a lonely Christmas note

Roosevelt completes his fourth Winning of the West volume. In a holiday letter he tells Lodge he misses their usual Christmas dinner together, complains that even Quigg is playing him false, vows to keep fighting, and notes Hero Tales is coming out in an edition for blind readers.
Roosevelt is at home with his family at Sagamore Hill over the holidays.
Roosevelt spends Christmas Day with Edith and the children at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at home with his family at Sagamore Hill over the holidays.
Angered by calls for peace in the Venezuela crisis, Roosevelt writes Lodge that the clamor has persuaded him the nation needs a war.
Roosevelt is at home with his family at Sagamore Hill over the holidays.
Bob Ferguson visits; the children thrive
Bob Ferguson is a guest at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt writes Bamie that the children are rosy-cheeked, healthy and happy.
Bram Stoker, the author of Dracula, records his impression of Roosevelt as a man who cannot be flattered, scared or bought, and predicts he will one day be President.
Back to Bamie's house for the winter

The family moves into Bamie's house at 689 Madison Avenue for the winter, now as paying tenants. Ted and Alice start dancing lessons with Mr. Dodsworth, who once taught their father. Roosevelt writes Lodge about machine support for Parker, and the Harvard Crimson faulting campus opposition to the firm Venezuela policy.
The first printing of Hero Tales from American History, written by Roosevelt with Henry Cabot Lodge, is sold out.
Corinne and Douglas call; Utah becomes a state
Conie and Douglas Robinson visit Roosevelt. Nationally, Utah becomes the nation's 45th state.
Missing Bamie in her own house
Roosevelt tells Bamie it feels odd to live in her house without her there, and mentions a Republican Club dinner for Cornelius Bliss.
Steering clear of fights with Parker
Roosevelt tells Lodge he is working to avoid clashes with fellow commissioner Andrew Parker, whom The Sun is now championing against him.

Roosevelt writes Albert Bushnell Hart about the Monroe Doctrine, the Venezuela dispute and those who want peace whatever the cost.

In world news, the Spanish government pulls General Arsenio Martínez Campos out of Cuba.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie celebrates her 41st birthday while he is in New York City.
Platt says his job is doomed

At the Fifth Avenue Hotel Roosevelt meets Thomas C. Platt, the "Easy Boss," who tells him the Greater New York bill will pass and cost him his post, shifting hiring and firing to Roosevelt's enemy Governor Morton. Roosevelt tells Bamie a foreign war would be welcome.
Roosevelt speaks to the Methodist Ministers' Association at 150 Fifth Avenue and brings them firmly to his side; they will not stand by while politicians remove him. Edith writes to Bamie.

The New York Times prints the full text of the bill aimed at ousting Roosevelt, and the measure is then pulled. Roosevelt stays loyal to the party.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he and Edith are staying with the Lodges in Washington and have seen Tom Reed.
Roosevelt and Edith travel back to New York City.
A scorching rebuke to Alphonse Major
Roosevelt sends Alphonse Major a blistering letter condemning his hostility toward Catholics on the police force.

While Roosevelt is in New York, General Valeriano Weyler arrives in Havana from Spain to take over from Campos.
Weyler takes a harder line in Cuba
In Cuba, the newly arrived General Weyler begins a tougher campaign against the rebels. Roosevelt is in New York City.

Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan and Colonel Greene dine with Roosevelt, and his sister Conie is staying with him. He tells Will Cowles he expects to be legislated out of office and is racing to rebuild and toughen the force before then, and writes Francis Scott about police spying.
On his daughter Alice's twelfth birthday, Roosevelt congratulates William Rockhill on being named Assistant Secretary of State.

Roosevelt writes to Swift about the civil service. In Cuba, rebels sever every telegraph line into Havana.
Roosevelt orders the police station lodging rooms shut for good, the outcome of a long campaign he waged with Jacob Riis against the filthy overnight shelters.
Busy at the board; Mame is ill

Roosevelt tells Bamie he is swamped with Police Board work, and that with the nurse Mame sick, Edith is worn out caring for the children alone. He also writes Assistant Secretary of State William Rockhill.

Roosevelt gives a University of Chicago talk titled "Manly Virtues." In Cuba, 48 civilians are slaughtered at Guatao.
Roosevelt lays out the strains of his job for Bamie and weighs the drawbacks of Long Island's country schools. He sends Lodge two letters on police business and national affairs.
More Spanish soldiers land in Cuba to put down the rising. Roosevelt is in New York City.

Roosevelt warns Bamie that Platt's camp wants him and his allies out of office. He is reading proofs of the fourth Winning of the West volume and says he would welcome fighting Spain if it ended the chaos and bad rule in Cuba.

The Police Board calls in Chief Peter Conlin to break Commissioner Parker's deadlock over promotions. Conlin declines, and insists every promotion be sent to him first.

The board orders Conlin to give his answer in writing. That evening Roosevelt hosts Parker at 689 Madison Avenue along with Charles Parkhurst, Joseph Bucklin Bishop and others. Walking home, Parker grumbles to Bishop about how much Roosevelt talks; Bishop replies that Roosevelt says whatever he thinks the moment he thinks it.
Parker repeats to Roosevelt only the unflattering half of Bishop's remark about his "boy's mind." Roosevelt confronts Bishop, hears the full story, and concludes that Parker bears close watching.

Roosevelt and fellow commissioners persuade the legislature to replace the state's bipartisan police board law with one more to his liking. He tells Bamie the U.S. ought to push Spain out of Cuba, and admits the board is wearing on him. He tells Henry White that Edith is still mourning her mother.

Roosevelt dines at Aunt Lizzie's and afterward stops by the Century Club.
Writing Bamie and Will Cowles, Roosevelt talks battleship guns and his job, and reports that the Greater New York bill will not cost him his post.
Both houses of Congress adopt resolutions recognizing a state of war between Spain and the Cuban rebels and affirming American neutrality.

Edith writes Bamie that Roosevelt's cousin James West Roosevelt has died, his weak lungs worsened by drinking and morphine.

On Archie's second birthday Roosevelt travels to Albany to give evidence to the state Senate's cities committee. Parker has doctored records to suggest Roosevelt shuts Democrats out of promotions; Roosevelt's testimony falls flat and the bill fails.
Roosevelt writes Ed Lauterbach a formal denial of Parker's claim that he favors Republicans in police hiring.
Roosevelt tells Lodge that fellow commissioner Frederick Grant now simply follows Parker and Conlin.
Roosevelt writes to Bamie from New York City.
Roosevelt writes Lemuel Quigg about Police Board matters.
Another bomb sent through the mail to Police Headquarters is defused.
Roosevelt writes Lemuel Quigg about the two-faced maneuvering on the Police Board.

Harvard's president scolds TR and Lodge

On Corinne's 14th wedding anniversary, Roosevelt writes Lodge about Le Bon's book on socialism. Harvard president Charles Eliot has branded them both degenerate sons of Harvard for their expansionist views; both men want every European power out of the Americas.
Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz about Police Board appointments. Uptown, a string of break-ins hits the area around 156th Street and Union Avenue.
At a Police Board meeting Parker asks for a yearly vote on the board presidency, then puts Roosevelt's name forward.

At City Hall Roosevelt quarrels with Comptroller Ashbel Fitch and goes so far as to challenge him to a duel.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about building up the Navy, and owns up to losing his temper with Fitch the day before.

Roosevelt is in New York City, where his fight at the Police Board goes on. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Officers Ryan and Reid arrest the burglars behind the 156th Street break-ins.
At work in New York City
Roosevelt is in New York City, where his fight at the Police Board goes on. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he was guest of honor at a Naval Reserve dinner, and sends Mayor Strong a statement on how disorderly houses are being closed.

Roosevelt tells Bamie he has met Earl Spencer, complains of petty quarrels with Fitch and Parker, and describes lunch on Harry Davis' ship Montgomery off Staten Island. The guest book notes the house opened for the season.
Parker has won over Commissioner Frederick Grant, who now stays away from board meetings too.
Roosevelt uncovers graft by Parker and takes it to Mayor Strong, who writes Parker. Parker will not step down.

Roosevelt paints Bamie a picture of the boys' outfits, above all Kermit in blue overalls Edith sewed to look just like the hired man's, plus a cap, battered tennis shoes and gloves over poisoned hands, tumbling head over heels.
Nothing is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt dines at the Hotel Claremont.
Roosevelt reviews the yearly police parade from Fifth Avenue at 40th Street as some 2,000 officers march. Word reaches the papers that Parker was told to quit.
In New York Roosevelt tells Bamie he cannot vouch for Commissioner Parker's honesty with money.
At work in New York City
Roosevelt is in New York City, where his fight at the Police Board goes on. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt attends the regular meeting of the Police Board.
Mrs. Clifford Richardson signs the guest book.
Commander Davis is recorded in the guest book.
Roosevelt prepares formal charges against Commissioner Parker.
The trial of Commissioner Parker opens, with Elihu Root prosecuting, General Benjamin Tracy for the defense, and Mayor Strong sitting as judge.
Proceedings continue in New York City in the case against Commissioner Andrew Parker.
Nothing is recorded for this day.
Edith stayed in town for him

Roosevelt heads out to Sagamore Hill only to learn that Edith had remained in the city to keep him company. He confides to Bamie his worries about national politics and his distrust of McKinley's backbone.
Republicans open their national convention in St. Louis, with William McKinley, Tom Reed and Governor Levi Morton in the running.
McKinley wins on the first ballot
In St. Louis the Republicans make McKinley their nominee in a single ballot, with 661½ votes. Roosevelt is in New York City.
Proceedings continue in New York City in the case against Commissioner Andrew Parker.
At Sagamore Hill the family takes its first swim of the season, and Alice trots and canters on her horse Diamond. Roosevelt writes Will Cowles.
Grace Potter is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Bamie he is fairly pleased with how the convention turned out.
Proceedings continue in New York City in the case against Commissioner Andrew Parker.
Roosevelt writes Bellamy Storer that the party platform is excellent and that McKinley will make both a strong candidate and a good President.
Children in the hired man's garb
Roosevelt tells Bamie how hard his job has become, then turns to the children: Ted and Kermit dressed like farmhands and happily dirty, Ethel chubby, Archie sweet, and Alice the best of big sisters.
The Parker trial continues, and Roosevelt finds it deadly boring.
Roosevelt and Edith travel to Austin Wadsworth's in Geneseo, New York, where riding leaves him aching all over.
Riding at Geneseo, Roosevelt goes over a fence and falls.
Proceedings continue in New York City in the case against Commissioner Andrew Parker.
The case against Commissioner Parker comes to a close.
Bryan nominated; TR on his nerves

The Democrats in Chicago nominate William Jennings Bryan for President. Roosevelt writes Fanny Parsons about the nervousness she, Edith and Corinne noticed in him before the Mayor's committee and in Albany.
Nellie Tyler signs the guest book.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Mayor Strong has not yet ruled on Parker, and that Strong hopes Parker has learned from the episode.
Architect Grant La Farge appears in the guest book.
Roosevelt tells Lodge Parker keeps his seat, and scoffs at the wild scene at the Democrats' Chicago convention.
Roosevelt writes S. J. Pryor to correct a false London Daily Mail story about New York police and visitors to the city. Bob Ferguson is a guest.
Jacob Riis visits Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt rows Edith out on the bay, and the family throws a delayed Fourth of July party with the children and fireworks.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that their friend Riis is passing Sunday with the family at Sagamore Hill.
Hallett Phillips and Roosevelt's niece Corinne Robinson are listed as guests.
Dinner with Riis and Stephen Crane
Colonel Andrews is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Bamie he had dinner the week before with Stephen Crane and Jacob Riis, and sizes up the McKinley-Bryan race.
Roosevelt calls on Mark Hanna, McKinley's campaign manager, at the Waldorf, and that evening has a private dinner with Hanna and two executive committee members.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about politics and literature.
Roosevelt advises Lodge that Hanna needs careful handling, and hopes Lodge's son Bay will publish "The Wave."
Roosevelt tells Tom Reed he wishes Reed, not McKinley, were heading the ticket.
The Storers come to Sagamore Hill
Bellamy and Maria Storer, friends of Roosevelt's from his Washington years, arrive as houseguests at Sagamore Hill.
Rowing the Storers around Oyster Bay

Roosevelt takes his guests out on the water and confides to Maria Storer, a well-connected Washington lobbyist close to McKinley and Mark Hanna, that he wants the Navy's number-two job. He also writes Bamie about meeting Hanna.
The Storers remain at Sagamore Hill. The record notes that William McKinley owes the couple $10,000.

From the city, Roosevelt sends Cecil Spring-Rice a long letter: Ted is picking up shooting, Alice has grown as tall as Edith, Kermit is out of his brace and squabbling with Ethel. He also muses at length on race and nationality.
Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 35th birthday.
John Elliott signs in as a guest at Sagamore Hill.
A Mr. Gordon Cummings is the day's guest at Sagamore Hill.
Ready to take the Navy post
Roosevelt writes both Bellamy and Maria Storer that, if the Navy's assistant secretaryship comes his way, he should take it.
Bryan's Garden rally goes badly for police
William Jennings Bryan launches his presidential bid at Madison Square Garden, and the city police, Roosevelt's department, handle the crowd poorly.
Roosevelt's daughter Ethel celebrates her fifth birthday.
Heat wave and plans to head west
Roosevelt tells Bamie he is going west while Edith and the children summer at Lake Champlain. The city is sweltering, horses are dying in the streets, and police are handing out ice to the poor.
At Madison Square Garden, Bourke Cockran argues for gold, and this time the police manage the crowd well after the Bryan fiasco. Roosevelt writes Lodge about the anti-Platt Republicans.
A police board session turns into an open clash, with Roosevelt and fellow commissioner Andrew Parker yelling at each other.
Off to Medora with a new rifle
Roosevelt heads west for the Badlands, carrying a new Winchester that fires smokeless powder.
Roosevelt is away in the West; the record gives no details for the day.

Li Hung-chang arrives in New York
While Roosevelt is still out west, the Chinese statesman Li Hung-chang visits New York and is greeted by Police Commissioner Frederick Grant.
Roosevelt is still in the West; no specifics are recorded.
Antelope hunting on the open prairie

Roosevelt writes Kermit from the prairie: six hours out after pronghorn, dinner eaten in the wagon's shade, his gun cleaned, a bath in a pool nearby, and nights spent fully dressed inside a buffalo-hide sleeping bag.
Roosevelt is in the West; the record has nothing more for the day.
Ted starts at the Cove School
Back home, nine-year-old Ted enrolls at Oyster Bay's single-room Cove School, where most classmates are children of local gardeners, groundskeepers and valets.
Roosevelt is hunting in the Dakota country.
Roosevelt remains on his western hunting trip; no details survive for the day.

Roosevelt gets back to New York City after his time at his Dakota ranch.
Speech to the Sound Money League
Roosevelt addresses the Sound Money League and, in a letter to publisher George Haven Putnam, wishes people would see him more broadly as a historian.
Ted's ninth birthday and first gun

For Ted's ninth birthday, Roosevelt presents the boy with a Flobert rifle, his first firearm, and tries it out by shooting into the ceiling. He tells Bamie the western cattle are struggling and that he bagged five antelope.

Roosevelt writes Lodge that the Republican nominee for governor, Frank Black, belongs to Platt, and describes his battles with Parker and the Grand Army veterans. British reviewers, he adds, have bristled at his remarks about Britain in volume four of his Winning of the West.
Send-off dinner for Emlen and Christine
Uncle Jim and Aunt Lizzie host a farewell dinner for their son Emlen Roosevelt and his wife Christine.
Roosevelt sends Bamie a campaign update, noting McKinley is running his race from his Ohio front porch, and reports romps with the children in the old barn.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne marks her 35th birthday. He writes Bamie, who is in Scotland.
Roosevelt campaigns for McKinley across upstate New York, from Utica to Buffalo.
Roosevelt and Lodge travel to Canton, Ohio, to see McKinley at his home.
Packed halls and a cool reception
Roosevelt boasts to Bamie that his upstate rallies overflowed, but admits McKinley, though friendly, does not count him and Lodge among his favorites.
Roosevelt writes diplomat Henry White on political matters.
Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice about Bryan and the silver question that splits the 1896 race, with Bryan for silver and McKinley for gold.
Roosevelt's son Kermit celebrates his seventh birthday.
Roosevelt's niece Eleanor has her 12th birthday, and he writes to Bamie.
Full house at the Chicago Coliseum
Roosevelt fills the Chicago Coliseum with a speech for McKinley and sound money, part of a swing across the Midwest.
First color comics in the Journal
The New York Journal runs the first color comic strips. Nothing is recorded for Roosevelt himself.
Morristown rally and an election forecast
Roosevelt speaks at Morristown, New Jersey, then back in New York writes Lodge about how the election looks.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he expects the Republicans to carry the election.
Wilmington speech in a busy week
Roosevelt speaks in Wilmington, Delaware, one stop in a week of McKinley rallies across Maryland, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.
Dr. Alexander Lambert and his wife are guests at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt writes Bamie.
Bread, coins and a copycat speech

Roosevelt makes the case for gold using loaves of varying size plus gold and silver coins to make his point. At Sagamore Hill, Ted copies his father with an unplanned speech to the household staff on the back porch.
Roosevelt's uncle James K. Gracie is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

McKinley takes the White House by more than 600,000 votes, and Republicans capture both houses of Congress. With no telephone at Sagamore Hill, the news comes by carriage, while Alice creeps out of bed to listen from the stair landing.

Roosevelt tells historian Frederick Jackson Turner he enjoyed Turner's review of his Winning of the West, while standing by the book's criticism of Jefferson. He also writes editor Albert Shaw of the Review of Reviews.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Bamie of his relief at the Republican victory.
Another quiet day at Sagamore Hill with nothing further noted.
Victory party with the money men
Roosevelt joins Mark Hanna and wealthy Republicans to celebrate the win, though he is disgusted by how McKinley was marketed to voters.
James K. Gracie is once more a guest.
Roosevelt chides Bamie for sending so few letters and urges her to come home to the United States before long.
Bertha Potter is a guest. Roosevelt asks Bellamy Storer whether he ought to visit President-elect McKinley in Canton.
Roosevelt's friend Bob Ferguson is a guest.
Jacob Riis and family friends visit
Jacob Riis and his wife are guests, along with Morton Procter.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie marks one year of marriage.
On Thanksgiving, Roosevelt, Bob Ferguson and Ted shoulder axes for a ten-mile tramp, cutting the bridle path clear as they go.
Lodge pleads his case in Ohio
Roosevelt reports to Bamie that Lodge has met McKinley in Ohio to push for him, and that McKinley hopes Roosevelt has no fixed ideas about appointments.
Roosevelt and Jacob Riis look into a burlesque show by the dancer known as Little Egypt at Clarendon Hall, which had drawn many complaints over her skimpy costume.

Roosevelt and Edith celebrate their tenth wedding anniversary. Edith tells Spring-Rice that Ted is thriving among his Cove School classmates and will miss them once Alice's governess takes over in town.
Lunch with Dana; Hawaii and Cuba
Roosevelt lunches with General Wilson and editor Charles A. Dana, and writes Lodge hoping McKinley will act firmly on Hawaii and Cuba.
Roosevelt writes Maria Storer about the assistant secretaryship of the Navy.
Maceo killed; help for an honest officer
Spanish forces kill the Cuban rebel general Antonio Maceo, and Americans clamor for intervention. Roosevelt asks Dr. Matthew Beattie to testify for an honest policeman facing trial.
Roosevelt tells Elihu Root that Boss Platt wants a meeting.
President-elect McKinley sends Roosevelt a courteous reply acknowledging Storer's visit on his behalf, and Roosevelt thanks Lodge for working to land him the Navy post.
Roosevelt tells Maria Storer he has decided against a visit to McKinley in Canton.
Board meetings and Edith's Christmas letter

Roosevelt attends a meeting with the mayor and a police board session. A letter from Edith to Bamie paints the family's Christmas morning: Archie bundled in her blue shawl, Bob in a sofa blanket, Theodore in his old brocade robe, and big presents opened in the Gun Room.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about an interview on Cuba.
The police board holds its final meeting of the year.
The source page for this date holds bibliography and editorial notes rather than any account of Roosevelt's day.
A Review of Reviews essay and a book review

Roosevelt's article "How Not to Better Social Conditions" runs in the Review of Reviews, and he reviews Brooks Adams's The Law of Civilization and Decay. Meanwhile newspapers fault the reform police board as powerless.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he backs Cuban independence and would like to see Spain driven out. A thaw at Sagamore Hill has ended the skiing.
Roosevelt writes Albert Shaw defending his opposition to Platt and praising departing Governor Levi Morton.
Roosevelt declares he will stop joining the police board's quarrels, and sends Bamie his frank views of diplomat Henry White.

During a city cab strike, Roosevelt tells Jacob Baucsh that peaceful strikers have nothing to fear from police. He also hears via Lodge that Cornelius Bliss would take him as assistant if Bliss gets the Navy.
New York Republicans nominate Thomas Platt for the U.S. Senate by 147 votes to 7. Platt asks who backed Joseph Choate and later makes those men pay; Roosevelt had stayed in Platt's camp.
The family is at 689 Madison Avenue in New York; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Thomas Lounsbury and Alfred Thayer Mahan came to tea, and that he dislikes John Sherman as McKinley's pick for Secretary of State.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie has her 42nd birthday.
The legislature sends Thomas Platt to Washington as New York's U.S. Senator.
Roosevelt gives an address at the U.S. Naval Academy.
Roosevelt writes Lodge that he has set the New York Sun straight after it claimed he favors open immigration.
Dancing class, Selous, and a campfire story

Roosevelt tells Bamie the children are taking dancing lessons in the city, Ted is staying with Corinne, and Kermit dreads his father ending up a street sweeper. A letter has come from the hunter Frederick Selous, and a Boone and Crockett Club volume edited by George Bird Grinnell appears with Roosevelt's piece "On the Little Missouri."
Roosevelt's letter to William Sanger defending the board's hiring and other practices is printed in the New York Sun.
Roosevelt's daughter Alice has her 13th birthday.
Yes to the Navy, no to London
Roosevelt tells Bamie he would take the Navy post if offered, and that a visit to her in London is impossible.

Roosevelt tells Bamie that John Hay will be ambassador to Britain and that his own police work has grown almost unbearable amid new fights, corruption flare-ups and resignation threats. His board record includes tougher fitness standards for recruits, a lower age limit, civil-service exams, a standard .32 Colt revolver, and required courtesy from officers.
Mayor Strong now regrets putting Parker on the board but has no authority to remove him. Roosevelt sends Thomas Lounsbury a letter on spelling and books.
William McKinley takes the oath as the 25th President in Washington.
Too busy to think of the Navy
Roosevelt tells Henry White that board fights consume him and leave scant time to dwell on the Navy job.
Roosevelt vents to Lounsbury about fellow commissioner Frederick Grant, likening his mind to some tree-dwelling forebear.
Roosevelt writes Lodge that Parker and Grant have stalled all board business, and he sees no hope for the Navy appointment.
Roosevelt thanks Henry White for helping his bid for the Navy post.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he thinks Grant and Parker are tangling police business on orders from the Republican machine.
Mayor Strong removes Commissioner Parker for neglect of duty, based on charges from the previous summer, pending the governor's approval.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about socialists and anarchists.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he doubts the appointment will happen, plans to leave 689 Madison by late April, and wants her home. He reports to Lodge that Platt will not stand in his way.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he will write John D. Long, McKinley's choice to run the Navy, about the assistant's job.
A way to get him out of New York
Roosevelt writes Lodge that machine politicians see the Navy job mainly as a means of removing him from New York.
Roosevelt shares his worries about the police board's future with Lodge.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he has discussed his own successor on the police board with Mayor Strong.

Lodge and others press Roosevelt's case in Washington. Platt drops his resistance, reasoning Roosevelt will do less harm there than in New York, while McKinley, anxious to avoid war, worries about Roosevelt's hawkish talk on Cuba.
McKinley picks Roosevelt to be the Navy's assistant secretary, at a salary of $4,500, and sends the nomination to the Senate. Roosevelt crows to Lodge with a line from the Arabian Nights.
The Senate approves Roosevelt for the Navy post. Parker laughs long over what he calls Roosevelt's retreat. Roosevelt writes Lodge about remarks linking him with John Altgeld printed in the Sun.
Roosevelt's son Archie celebrates his third birthday.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is delighted by the appointment, though sorry it means he cannot join her in London.
Japan sends a cruiser to Hawaii
Japan dispatches a cruiser toward Hawaii, a hedge against the United States moving to annex them.
Roosevelt is chosen again to chair the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association.

Roosevelt writes Henry White that he is relieved to leave the police board, having done all he could. Frank Moss becomes board president. Parker was never removed and later resigned, the one opponent Roosevelt never bested.

At Roosevelt's final police board meeting, Parker and Grant stay away, so there is no quorum and no vote of thanks; Chief Conlin leaves without a farewell. Roosevelt sends Mayor Strong his formal resignation.
Roosevelt writes Jacob Riis a warm thank-you for two years of support.
First day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt starts work as the Navy's second-in-command under Secretary John D. Long, 58, and moves in with Lodge in Washington. He thanks Captain Bowman McCalla for his congratulations.
Roosevelt answers well-wishers William Mantius, Governor Hugh Thompson and William Fitch, and lets William Trent know he has gone through Trent's study of Southern leaders.
Roosevelt is in Washington at his new Navy post; nothing specific is recorded.
Roosevelt alerts President McKinley that Japan has sent a cruiser to Hawaii and lists the American warships nearby.

Roosevelt writes a memorandum on fleet preparedness that tucks in four warnings about trouble over Cuba, and writes both McKinley and Long about sending ships to the Mediterranean.
A summer away from the family
Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice, now posted with the British diplomats in Germany, lamenting that he will see little of Edith and the children this summer.

The guest book marks the opening of Sagamore Hill for the season. In Washington, Roosevelt writes Lincoln Steffens about the police board, Speck von Sternberg about his new job, and Frank Moss praising his early work as board president.
In Washington, Roosevelt notes his sister Corinne's 15th wedding anniversary.

Roosevelt writes Bamie, Hamlin Garland, Henry White and Francis Lowell; Will Cowles has a berth on the cruiser Topeka through his help. His article on scientific naming appears in Science. With the old Henry Adams circle scattered, he starts dining nearly every day at the Metropolitan Club with Mahan, Dewey, Wood and other expansionists.
Roosevelt digs up the Civil War desk of an earlier assistant secretary, Gustavus Fox, carved with Monitors, warships and flags, and has it moved into his office. Bamie's ship arrives in New York.

Roosevelt tells Alfred Thayer Mahan he would take Hawaii at once if it were up to him. He also writes John Hay that he misses him and is waiting for Lodge to come by for a walk.

Roosevelt tells Bamie he enjoys Will's letters and longs for Sagamore Hill, Edith and the children. Mrs. Hilborne Roosevelt and Miss Dorothy Roosevelt are recorded as guests.

At the Biological Society of Washington, Roosevelt debates C. Hart Merriam of the Biological Survey over how to classify species and subspecies. He writes Richard Henry Dana opposing stacked turrets on new battleships and tells General James Wilson he won't raise Wilson's case with McKinley today, having pestered the President enough lately.

Torpedo boat trip and a baby on the way
Roosevelt rides a torpedo boat and writes Taft that Willie Phillips died in a boating accident. Edith tells her sister Emily to expect a new niece or nephew in early December.

Roosevelt promises Mahan to push their naval ideas as far as he can, and tells Jacob Riis how much he values their friendship.
Roosevelt writes Henry Fairfield Osborn about his quarrel with Merriam, and briefs the hunter Frederick Selous, who is planning an American trip, on the West and elk hunting.

A war game for the War College
Roosevelt sends Caspar Goodrich a problem for Naval War College students: an imagined American clash with Japan over Hawaii. He also backs Avery Andrews on police board business.
Roosevelt sends Spring-Rice news from home and family, along with a critique of Brooks Adams's new book on the decline of civilizations.

Mahan urges Roosevelt to seize Hawaii first and sort out the questions later. Roosevelt's wider wish list includes Hawaii, a canal through Nicaragua, Spain out of Cuba, and European islands in the hemisphere. Film from 1897 shows him leaving the State, War and Navy Building, the earliest known footage of him.
Big speech at the Naval War College

At Newport, Roosevelt urges a stronger Navy before the Naval War College, citing George Washington on preparedness as the surest path to peace. It is the first major speech of his career; it makes headlines and wins praise.

Roosevelt thanks Charles A. Dana for an editorial on his Newport speech, cautions J. M. Wall about Americans who lean toward Britain, agrees with Hawaiian agent Alfred Hartwell that America should take the islands now, and introduces his friend Proctor to Ambassador John Hay.
Roosevelt advises President McKinley to annex Hawaii.

Roosevelt tells Mahan that Secretary Long disagrees with him about expanding the battleship fleet, and recommends Charles McCawley and William Rockhill to Richard Olney for government posts. Nellie and Hope Tyler are guests.

Roosevelt writes torpedo-boat builder Nathaniel Herreshoff, tells Brander Matthews he is tied to Putnam's and cannot publish his essays elsewhere, and sends Putnam's the essays for the book that becomes American Ideals.
Fourth of July invitation for Franklin
Roosevelt invites his young cousin Franklin, then at Groton, to spend the Fourth of July at Sagamore Hill.
