The immigration station buildings on Ellis Island in New York harbor burn down. Roosevelt is in Washington.
McKinley signs off on Hawaii treaty

President McKinley approves a treaty to annex Hawaii. Roosevelt writes Will Cowles about Goodrich and the Metropolitan Club, defends Senator Platt's bid to join that club in a letter to its governors, and discusses readiness against Japan with Captain Goodrich.

Secretary Long heads home to Hingham, Massachusetts, for a vacation, and Roosevelt runs the department with vigor and care. He writes Lodge, editor William Courtney about his "Books on Big Game" article, and Admiral Montgomery Sicard about August squadron maneuvers.
Dinner for senators and the Cuba envoy
Roosevelt brings several influential senators and America's envoy to Cuba together for dinner at the Metropolitan Club, and assures Long that Washington is calm and he need not rush back.

Roosevelt writes Admiral John Walker for a report on the 1894 events in Hawaii.
Roosevelt writes Congressman Charles Boutelle about drydocks, and tells Long about torpedo boats and uniforms, encouraging him to visit the Portsmouth yard rather than come back to Washington.
Admiral Walker on Hawaii; backing Low
Admiral Walker meets Roosevelt about Hawaii. Roosevelt tells Long that Japan is unhappy over the islands, and writes Seth Low to support his campaign to become Greater New York's first mayor.

Roosevelt writes Boutelle on Navy matters. Mr. and Mrs. Clifford Richardson are guests.

Roosevelt writes Charles Davis about Navy matters and William Fullam about lobbying.
Roosevelt writes Seth Low about the approaching New York elections.
American Ideals appears; war plans drawn

Roosevelt's essay and speech collection American Ideals is published. He lunches at the Metropolitan Club as the Navy Department prepares a war plan for a possible fight over Cuba that would also target the Philippines. Around now he first meets William Allen White. With Edith expecting their sixth child, Sagamore Hill fills with 16 children counting cousins.
Backing Procter at the Civil Service Commission
Roosevelt asks Richard Gilder and Seth Low to support Procter's place on the Civil Service Commission, and writes Putnam's about his essays.
Roosevelt heads to Sagamore Hill, where young Franklin Roosevelt is a guest.
Long is back at his desk
Secretary Long returns from vacation while Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Sagamore Hill hosts an Independence Day party, and Franklin joins the fun.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt thanks Avery Andrews for a report.
Grant LaFarge is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt's nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson is a guest, and Roosevelt writes Bamie.
Roosevelt travels by torpedo boat from Oyster Bay to Newport, Rhode Island.

Roosevelt is in New York City.
Roosevelt sets out to inspect naval militia stations around the Great Lakes, stopping at Mackinac, Detroit, Sandusky and Chicago.
In Sandusky, Roosevelt declares that America need not ask Japan or anyone else what territory it may acquire. The press reacts badly, and Secretary Long is furious.
Roosevelt tells novelist John Fox Jr. that he and Edith both liked The Kentuckians.
After ten days spent putting the household in order, a return to Sagamore Hill is recorded.

Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.

With Secretary Long off on another vacation and McKinley out of town too, Roosevelt is left running the Navy through the summer heat. He sends George Bird Grinnell comments on a hunting story Grinnell wrote.
Spain, Japan and Germany as rivals

Roosevelt writes Captain Bowman McCalla about a big navy and the nation's likely foes, Spain, Japan and Germany. He sends William Laird Clowes Navy business and tells Lodge that Edith is visiting Washington, Procter keeps his Civil Service seat, and Cuba should be free.
Roosevelt writes General James H. Wilson.
Roosevelt sends Secretary Long his report on the naval militia.
Edith turns 36 while visiting Roosevelt in Washington.
Moonlit drive from the Overlook Inn
Roosevelt has dinner out at the Overlook Inn and enjoys a lovely drive home by moonlight. He writes Long about torpedo boats and other Navy matters.
Cool weather and a navy yard probe
Roosevelt tells Lodge the weather has turned cool, Edith has had a fine time in Washington, and Davis is investigating the Brooklyn Navy Yard.
Roosevelt promises Secretary Long he will stop sending him complicated papers, since Long needs a break.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
No mayoral nomination from the machine
Roosevelt tells his old political mentor Joe Murray that New York's organization Republicans would never agree to nominate him for mayor.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.

On Ethel's sixth birthday, Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice about using a strong fleet to bar Germany from the Western Hemisphere, the Kaiser, and Russian views of the U.S. He also writes Senator Cushman Davis about an appointment and Long about Navy business.
Roosevelt tells Uncle Jim Roosevelt that New York City is his official residence, and mentions photographs of the children.
Roosevelt writes Long about drydocks, torpedo boats and other department business.
Roosevelt asks Paul Dana of the New York Sun about sending reporters to the naval maneuvers, insisting the Navy must keep growing, and writes Noble Butler about red tape.
Roosevelt urges Secretary of War Russell Alger to bring back the Army-Navy football game, and writes Bamie, Naval Academy superintendent Philip Cooper, and Lodge.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells Bellamy Storer how much he is enjoying running the department, and tells Long he is very busy.
Dr. Alexander Lambert and his wife are guests.
Roosevelt assures Bamie that Washington's heat isn't bothering him and that the Navy work fascinates him. He writes Boutelle about practice maneuvers.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells General James H. Wilson the U.S. cannot match Britain at sea but should outrank Germany.
Roosevelt writes George Bird Grinnell about the forest reserves President Cleveland created and a Boone and Crockett Club publication.
Watching from the Fern; Conlin out
Roosevelt tells Will Cowles he plans to watch September's maneuvers from Cowles's ship, the Fern, and tells Avery Andrews that Conlin has lost his post as New York police chief.

Roosevelt asks Lodge to proofread a Navy article, congratulates John McCullagh as New York's new police chief, and sends Long photos of the children taken by Emily Carow, agreeing to soften his big-navy rhetoric.
Roosevelt tells Will Cowles he will have to observe the maneuvers from the Dolphin instead of the Fern.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Grinnell about Boone and Crockett articles and sends President McKinley his compilation of past presidents' words in favor of preparedness and a large navy.
Police essay and a naval anthology

Roosevelt's article on running the New York police appears in the September Atlantic Monthly, and the Government Printing Office issues his collection of presidential statements on naval power by Washington, Jackson, Lincoln and Grant. He writes Long about the Dock Department.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Jacob Riis about the police and Parker, and invites him along on the upcoming maneuvers as a reporter.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Seth Low about the New York mayoral contest and Long about dry docks.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
On Labor Day, Roosevelt writes Long about department business.
Aboard the Iowa for target practice

Roosevelt joins Captain William Sampson on the battleship Iowa as a seven-ship squadron holds gunnery practice off the Virginia capes. Frederic Remington, two newspapermen and his aide Lieutenant Sharp come along.
Roosevelt is still out with the squadron for its maneuvers.
Roosevelt is still out with the squadron for its maneuvers.
Back in Washington, Roosevelt writes Long on Navy business, Francis Tiffany Bowles about dry dock No. 3, and James Bryce that work has kept him from his family for six weeks.
Three good days with the fleet
Roosevelt thanks Bowles for information, tells Lodge he loved his three days at sea with the squadron, and writes Seth Low about the elections.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
Ted celebrates his tenth birthday. Roosevelt writes French Chadwick about Navy business.
Roosevelt rides out with McKinley for the afternoon, and the President compliments his Sandusky speech and his Navy work. He writes Henry Fairfield Osborn about the Merriam dispute.

Roosevelt writes Long about Navy business in the September heat, and tells Lodge that McKinley likes his work and will permit a naval buildup. Other letters go to William Weaver on electric turrets, Colonel Francis Greene on possible war with Spain, Frederic Remington, and General Wilson about the drive with McKinley.
Roosevelt writes Congressman Charles Boutelle on Navy matters.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he is dining at the White House that night and that McKinley is pleased with his work.
Roosevelt writes William Kimball about the Navy and urges Long not to cut his vacation short, since all is running smoothly.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Long on armor plate, the danger over Cuba, Hawaii and other Navy matters.
On another drive with McKinley, Roosevelt lays out a plan for fighting Spain that closely forecasts what later happens. He writes Lodge on war plans and John Hay about returning the ship President.
Roosevelt writes Avery Andrews about the New York police and William Kimball about the Navy and the newspapers.
Roosevelt writes Senator William E. Chandler about the Navy.
By now Roosevelt has met privately with McKinley three times. He writes Ira Hollis on the Navy and Lodge on Long and his own heavy duties.
A day at the Navy Department
Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.
A Rock Creek scramble with Leonard Wood
Roosevelt tells Bellamy Storer he has befriended Army Captain Leonard Wood and the two went scrambling in Rock Creek.

On Corinne's 36th birthday, Roosevelt sees a request to give Commodore Howell the Asiatic Squadron and steers George Dewey to enlist Senator Redfield Proctor, who gets McKinley to suggest Dewey instead. He sends Senator Chandler a private Navy letter.
Long returns from vacation irritated by Roosevelt's maneuvering, but Dewey is named to command the Asiatic Squadron anyway.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he will spend the next two weeks at Sagamore Hill, and compliments Arlo Bates on his book of talks about studying literature.

Roosevelt heads for Sagamore Hill and presses Long to build up the fleet. At Groton he keeps the boys laughing for over an hour with police stories, as cousin Franklin records. He also meets Kansas editor William Allen White.
Bamie's lease on her Madison Avenue apartment in New York runs out, and from now on Roosevelt counts Washington, D.C., as his place of residence.
Roosevelt is with the family at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted for the day.
Another Sunday with the family at Sagamore Hill, with no further events on record.
Roosevelt remains at Sagamore Hill; the record is otherwise blank.
Corinne and Douglas visit Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt's sister Corinne and her husband Douglas Robinson sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing more recorded.
A day at Sagamore Hill with no other entries.
Roosevelt stays on at Sagamore Hill; no events are listed.
Still at Sagamore Hill, with the record otherwise empty.
Roosevelt's son Kermit celebrates his eighth birthday at Sagamore Hill. Far to the south, newspaperman Karl Decker spirits the imprisoned Cuban Evangelina Cisneros out of Havana.
At Sagamore Hill on the birthday of Eleanor Roosevelt, whom the record lists as turning 43.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is noted.
Another day at Sagamore Hill with nothing more on record.
The last full day of the summer stay at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

Roosevelt brings the family back to Washington, where Kermit and Archie start at a public school. Their rented home at 1810 N Street faces the British Embassy. He tells Seth Low he wishes he could lend a hand in the New York mayor's race.
Relief at staying out of the race
Writing to Henry Cabot Lodge, Roosevelt says he is glad not to be caught up in New York's mayoral contest.
Roosevelt tells his sister Bamie he will make speeches for local Republican candidates in Massachusetts and for Senator Mark Hanna in Ohio.
Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz that, as a federal official, he may not back party candidates in the New York City mayor's race.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
McKinley keeps him out of New York politics
Roosevelt lets Jacob Riis know that President McKinley has specifically ordered him not to take sides in the city's elections.
Dry docks, books and a gift

A busy day of letters: Roosevelt writes Senator William Chandler about the dry dock board, praises Stanley Waterloo's novel The Story of Ab, thanks Frederic Remington for a book, and mails William Allen White a copy of American Ideals.
Roosevelt marks his 39th birthday in Washington.

Roosevelt tells Bamie he walked the two little boys to their public school himself. He also urges more target practice for the Navy, and tells Lodge that Henry George's death has upended the New York mayor's race.
Roosevelt heads to Ohio to campaign for Senator Mark Hanna.
Roosevelt is in Ohio on his speaking trip for Senator Hanna.

Roosevelt is in Ohio. In Cuba, Marshal Ramón Blanco takes over from Valeriano Weyler and eases Spanish policy. Around this time Roosevelt and Leonard Wood take long hikes in Rock Creek Park, talking over Cuba under Spanish rule.
Too busy for the next volumes
Roosevelt tells publisher George Haven Putnam he would like to push on with his frontier history, The Winning of the West; Navy work, however, leaves him no time.
On election day in New York City, Democrat Robert Van Wyck beats Seth Low and the rest of the field for mayor. Roosevelt follows the result from Washington.
A board to study naval operations
Roosevelt writes Ira Hollis about a board to look into naval operations.
Taking stock after the city defeat
Roosevelt writes John Hay about the Republican setback in New York, French Chadwick about the Cuban rebellion, and Lodge with sharp words about Boss Platt.
Roosevelt writes Senator Joseph Foraker about Hawaii, tells Lodge he is happy to be in Washington, and discusses New York politics with Curtis Guild.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
A Sunday tramp with the children
Roosevelt takes the children for a cross-country hike in Rock Creek Park.
Roosevelt tells Henry White the family is settled in Washington, and writes Lodge that Platt's machine politics cost the Republicans the elections.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt proposes to editor Walter Hines Page an article on the terror the Mongol and Tartar hordes once spread.
Roosevelt recommends to Frederic Remington some early books that describe fights with Native Americans.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Harvard president Charles Eliot about a speech he will give at Harvard, and defends President McKinley's conduct in the New York elections to Alderman Philo Sherman.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

The Roosevelts' youngest child, Quentin, arrives at the house in Washington, catching everyone by surprise. Roosevelt writes Bamie the news and notes that Archie is not pleased, though the other children adore the baby. He also argues for war with Spain in a letter to William Kimball.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt comments on a cowboy story by Edwin Godkin and congratulates Harvard football captain Norman Cabot on a strong season.
Roosevelt writes Captain Arent Crowninshield about ram ships and other Navy matters.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie marks two years of marriage to William Sheffield Cowles.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Orders for the North Atlantic Squadron
Roosevelt writes Admiral Montgomery Sicard about the North Atlantic Squadron.

A newly described Olympic Mountains elk is named Cervus roosevelti for the founder of the Boone and Crockett Club. Edith falls ill with the grippe after Quentin's birth and stays sick into February. Roosevelt joins a board on line-versus-staff friction in the Navy and writes Bamie, Selous and James Bryce.
Roosevelt declines a dinner invitation from Augustus Gardner, explaining he is pinned down by work.
Roosevelt and Edith mark their 11th wedding anniversary.
Roosevelt writes Admiral Montgomery Sicard on Navy matters.
Invited to give the Lowell Lectures
Roosevelt writes Augustus Lowell about an invitation to lecture at the Lowell Institute in Boston.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt accepts the Lowell lecture invitation, and hears from his ranch partner Sylvane Ferris that the herd is dying off; the plan is to quit the cattle business next year.
Commodore George Dewey has set out for the Far East, where he will take command of the Asiatic Squadron.

Roosevelt turns in the Navy Personnel Board's report, some 8,000 words long, earning praise from Secretary Long and the newspapers. He writes Mahan on annexing Hawaii and thanks C. Hart Merriam for naming a new wapiti for him.
A police case from the old days
Roosevelt writes Frank Moss about putting an officer back on the New York City police force.
Roosevelt writes Alfred Thayer Mahan once more about Hawaii.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Mahan again on Hawaii and praises Owen Wister's new book, Lin McLean.
Roosevelt urges Mahan that they must do their utmost for the country, and writes Charles Lummis about getting the cowboy term 'horse wrangler' into the dictionary.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Coffee instead of beer for sailors

Roosevelt writes William Kimball on military readiness and George Zurcher about serving sailors coffee in place of beer. He also asks editor William Laffan to let him review Mahan's latest book on American sea power.
Roosevelt writes William Chanler that the Democrats are lining up against annexing Hawaii.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt sends his old friend Bob Ferguson a photograph involving Edith and firecrackers.

Roosevelt offers John Merritt ideas for new stamp designs, writes Chanler again on Hawaii, writes Richard Wainwright about a picture of himself, and tells C. Whitney Tillinghast he is ready to fight Spain.

On Christmas Eve Roosevelt writes Captain Charles Sigsbee about the Navy giving up sail power for good, and Carl Schurz on civil service. He again tells General Tillinghast he will go to war if it comes.
Roosevelt and Edith bring Alice, Ted and Kermit to Christmas dinner at the home of Henry Cabot Lodge.
Roosevelt compliments Frederic Remington on his writing about the West.
Roosevelt thanks Navy Secretary John D. Long for a supportive note and covers Navy business.

The year-end record notes Roosevelt's eleven articles on American game animals for a British sporting encyclopedia, on subjects ranging from the bison and wapiti to the puma, peccary, pronghorn and wolf.
Roosevelt thanks Bamie for a gift book that was just what he wanted, reports that Edith is starting to look well again, and tucks in notes from Ted and Kermit.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt assures Secretary Long that he means to be 'good' and avoid saying or doing anything embarrassing.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt discusses the Navy personnel legislation with Edwin Godkin and Senator Eugene Hale on Navy matters, and sends Rudyard Kipling news of the New York police, politics, the Navy and the family.
Edith falls ill with the grippe once more. The younger children are sent to stay with friends, and a trained nurse comes into the house.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Missing the Boone and Crockett dinner
Because Edith is ill with neuralgia pains, Roosevelt tells Grant La Farge he must miss the yearly dinner of the Boone and Crockett Club.
Advice for the new police chief
Roosevelt discusses the pending Navy personnel legislation with Ira Hollis and offers guidance to John McCullagh, newly named chief of the city's police force.
Roosevelt writes Francis Higginson about the Personnel Bill and retirement rules for naval officers.

Rioting erupts in Havana, and the battleship U.S.S. Maine is sent from Key West toward Cuba. Roosevelt writes Admiral William Kirkland about admirals and tells Captain Caspar Goodrich he gives his weekends to the children.

Secretary Long brushes off Roosevelt's warnings about war with Spain. With Edith still ill, possibly with typhoid, Roosevelt writes Francis Greene and Adjutant General Tillinghast about getting a commission if war comes.
Roosevelt urges Secretary Long to get ready for war with Spain by pulling the battle fleet together, and Long goes along.
Roosevelt tells Captain Bowman McCalla that Charles Boutelle, who chairs the House Naval Affairs Committee, dislikes him.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Ted worn down; dreaming of the hunt

Roosevelt tells Bamie that Ted has broken down from nervous strain and that he cannot attend the Boone and Crockett dinner. He writes Speck von Sternberg on Cuba, confesses to Selous he longs to slip away after big game, and discusses naval moves against Spain with Charles Davis.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
A sick household and a tax tangle

Roosevelt tells Bamie that Ted and Edith are worse and Kermit is sick too. He writes Emlen Roosevelt, C. Rockland Tyng and Douglas Robinson about his taxes: a steep Oyster Bay assessment pushed him to claim New York City residence, where the bill came in even higher. By evening Edith is better, though Ted is not.
Planning more Winning of the West
Roosevelt writes George Haven Putnam about adding two more volumes to his frontier history.
Roosevelt confides to Captain Robley Evans his fear that the McKinley administration is following the previous one's line on Cuba.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
The U.S.S. Maine steams into Havana harbor on an official 'courtesy call'; no welcome is offered, but the rioting has ended. Roosevelt writes Bamie that Edith is so ill she must wean the baby.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt has breakfast with the Lamberts and Avery Andrews.
Roosevelt writes Franklin Hall about his tax bill at Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

Edith's temperature stays at 101 degrees and Ted is too sick to be moved. Lodge warns that Cuba could blow up any day. Roosevelt writes his cousin James Roosevelt about his taxes and the illnesses at home.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells Frederick Selous about the cold snap in Washington and confesses he has taken up skiing, which he finds great sport.
Setting the bar for club membership
Roosevelt writes the London firm Rowland Ward about hunting books, and spells out for William Wadsworth what it takes to join the Boone and Crockett Club.
In a letter to Frank Moore, Roosevelt names Germany as the European power most hostile to the United States, with France and England not far behind.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Thomas R. Woodrow about why educated college graduates belong in public life.
Roosevelt writes Secretary Long about fitting battleships with torpedo tubes, and Robert Johnson about ironclads and monitors.
The de Lôme letter sets him off

Hearst's New York Journal prints a private letter from Spanish minister Enrique Dupuy de Lôme that mocks President McKinley as weak. Roosevelt is furious and eager for war. At a dinner party he lectures Mark Hanna and a Miss Adler so energetically that one sweeping gesture tears her dress.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt's daughter Alice celebrates her 14th birthday in Washington.
Alice is sent off to New York City to live with her aunt Bamie.
Roosevelt writes Charles Moore about possible alliances with Russia, England or Germany, cautioning especially against Germany.

At 9:40 that night the battleship Maine explodes in Havana harbor; 260 of her crew die at once and six more later. The sensational papers clamor for war while much of the country seems unmoved. Roosevelt calls it treachery. He also writes Selous, wishing he could get away, and Edith writes her sister Emily Carow.
The day after the Maine disaster, Roosevelt writes Secretary Long about deploying American warships, and writes Benjamin Diblee about Harvard's Porcellian Club.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Secretary Long about torpedo boats.

Doctors find that Ted's nervous exhaustion comes from being pushed too hard by his father. Roosevelt tells Bamie that Edith is still very ill and vows not to press Ted again. He also writes Long about the Maine inquiry and calls for more battleships.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt fires back at J. E. Myers, who had argued that the country should do away with its Navy altogether.
Edith notices a swelling low in her abdomen.
Roosevelt writes his brother-in-law Will Cowles about the Maine and Edith's illness, discusses books with William Trent, and asks Bamie whether he should ship Alice's piano and bicycle to New York.
Roosevelt writes Assistant Secretary of State William R. Day about a made-up 'interview' with him printed in New York newspapers.

With Secretary Long away for the afternoon, Roosevelt runs the Navy Department and cables Commodore Dewey to gather his squadron at Hong Kong, keep coaling, and be ready to strike the Spanish in the Philippines if war comes. He orders ships everywhere to fill their bunkers. He also brings in Dr. William Osler to examine Edith.
Secretary Long comes back to work, grumbling in his diary that Roosevelt nearly set off a bigger blast than the Maine in his absence. Still, Long cancels none of the orders Roosevelt sent.
Dr. Osler finds Edith critically ill with an abscess in the psoas muscle and advises operating at once, but Roosevelt wants further opinions first.
Alice and the boys of Washington

Roosevelt writes Charles O'Neil about the Maine inquiry. Alice, who had been leading a crowd of admiring boys around Washington, frets at first at Bamie's in New York, then takes to the city's social life so well she refuses to come back.
Roosevelt compliments Ernest Bruncken on his pamphlet How Germans Become Americans.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells Douglas Robinson that Edith remains seriously sick, and goes over his tax troubles.
Roosevelt writes naval historian William Clowes, then in Switzerland, about the Maine disaster and readiness for war.
A gynecologist examines Edith and agrees with Dr. Osler's diagnosis.
Roosevelt tells Douglas Robinson the country is moving toward war, though McKinley will try to avoid it. He writes Bamie about Edith's planned operation and Bradley Johnson about the Navy.
Roosevelt at last agrees to surgery, and doctors successfully remove the abscess near Edith's hip.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

At McKinley's request Congress votes $50 million to build up the armed forces. Roosevelt writes John Roosevelt about moving his legal residence to Washington for tax reasons, tells Charles Davis he will fight if war comes, asks Tillinghast about raising a regiment, and writes Henry White about the Maine.
Edith's surgical wound is left open to drain, and she stays very sick for weeks. Roosevelt writes Mahan about Hawaii.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Secretary Long about the Navy Department's budget.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Fake photos and a hunting invitation
Roosevelt tells Bradley Johnson he hopes to join him for some hunting, writes Mahan on war preparations, and writes wildlife photographer A. G. Wallihan about faked pictures.
Roosevelt tells Senator William Chandler he will be miserable if kept at a desk while others fight, and writes General Francis Greene that he hopes to see combat.
Roosevelt fears to Bamie that McKinley is set on peace. He writes Robley Evans on the Navy and lays out a plan of campaign against Spain for Mahan.

Back from Cuba, Senator Redfield Proctor of Vermont tells the Senate what he saw and calls for American armed intervention. Roosevelt writes journalist Walter Wellman about Robert Peary's Arctic plans.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
President McKinley learns that the Maine inquiry will conclude the ship was destroyed from outside.

Roosevelt signs an affidavit that he is a Washington resident to escape New York City taxes. He tells Brooks Adams that Edith is slowly recovering and that it is not too late to intervene in Cuba, and sends Mahan ideas on war with Spain.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
The Navy orders its ships repainted from peacetime white to battle gray. Roosevelt writes Mahan about warships.

Spain's minister is told his country's rule in Cuba can no longer be tolerated. Roosevelt asks Long about resigning, and tells him of Professor Samuel Langley's flying experiments on the Potomac, which fascinate him.
Challenging Hanna at the Gridiron Club

Speaking after dinner at Washington's Gridiron Club, Roosevelt openly takes on Senator Mark Hanna's caution about Spain. He asks William Chanler if he can raise a regiment, and tells Tillinghast that trouble with Spain is near.
Roosevelt writes Ted, now with Bamie and Alice in New York, about a hard walk with Dr. Leonard Wood spent figuring out how they might both join the army bound for Cuba.

The Maine report is made public. Roosevelt objects to Paul Dana about false stories in the Journal, tells his sister Conie he is worked to the limit, and writes William Tudor that America's inaction since the explosion is humiliating.

In a reflective letter to William Sturgis Bigelow, Roosevelt considers the consequences of war. He tells Will Cowles he is disgusted with foreign policy and hopes the Senate, led by men like Lodge, will demand Cuban independence. He also writes Dr. Alexander Lambert about not pressing Ted.
Telling the President to his face

Spain accepts every point of McKinley's ultimatum except an armistice. Roosevelt reports to Will Cowles that he urged armed intervention in front of the President and Cabinet. He writes Henry White and Douglas Robinson on Cuba, and Long about Langley's flying machine.

Roosevelt applauds Senator William Frye of Maine for his work on Cuba, writes John Roosevelt about his legal residence, and tells James Bryce that Spain should be pushed out of the Western Hemisphere.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he would give anything for two days in full charge, and tells Dr. Alexander Lambert, Ted's physician, that he must fight if war comes.

Douglas Robinson has urged Roosevelt not to join the fighting, but Roosevelt answers that duty tells him to go. He also tells P. Lee Phillips he will not need maps and writes Long about men seeking to return to service.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Edith surprises him at the club

McKinley drafts a war message. Roosevelt writes William Wadsworth about getting into a regiment and General Benjamin Tracy on why war must come. Edith, much improved, hires a carriage to the Metropolitan Club and has Leonard Wood call him outside; Roosevelt is overjoyed to see her up.
Roosevelt writes Robert Bacon, William Tudor and Elihu Root about the looming war, scorning those who want peace at any cost.
Roosevelt tells Dr. Henry Jackson that diplomacy has done all it can and rejects Jackson's call for peace at any cost.

Roosevelt wants Cuba freed from harsh Spanish rule. McKinley meets envoys of six major powers and makes clear he will not accept interference over Cuba. Roosevelt writes Wadsworth about a volunteer regiment.
Roosevelt urges Robert Bacon to support a fight for Cuban independence that would drive Spain from the Americas.
Fitzhugh Lee, the American consul general in Cuba, is called home. In Washington, Archie celebrates his fourth birthday.
President McKinley sends Congress his message on Cuba, calling for American intervention.
Roosevelt writes Robert W. de Forest about a Yale newspaper clipping de Forest had sent him.
Roosevelt tells Lodge that a resolution for war ought to come from Congress.
The first orders go out to mobilize America's army and navy.

In his diary Roosevelt mocks McKinley's continued efforts for peace, credits himself with having the Navy ready, and despairs of the Army and the War Department. He presses Long for a blockade of Cuba before Spain can mobilize.
Roosevelt's diary is unimpressed by Secretary of War Russell Alger and the Army's commanding general, Nelson Miles.

After long debate Congress passes the intervention resolution in the small hours of April 19. Roosevelt explains to Paul Dana why he wants to fight, writes General Tracy on the Navy, and scoffs in his diary at Alger and Miles's boast of 100,000 men in Tampa within a day.

Roosevelt's diary accuses Speaker Thomas Reed, with Joseph Cannon and Charles Boutelle, of blocking war preparations. Congress adopts joint resolutions recognizing Cuban independence and telling Spain to get out.

McKinley signs the Cuba resolution. Spain's minister leaves Washington and U.S. minister Stewart Woodford leaves Madrid. Roosevelt writes Captain Robley Evans about the Marines, confident of beating Spain even with damaged battleships.

The United States formally breaks diplomatic relations with Spain. Roosevelt's diary praises the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. He tells General Tracy the country must strike now, and writes William Chanler about Army volunteers.
The Atlantic Squadron leaves Key West for Caribbean waters.
A volunteer cavalry post in sight

McKinley asks for 125,000 volunteers to bolster a regular army of about 28,000, among them three regiments of frontier horsemen and crack shots. Roosevelt is in line for second in command of the first of these cavalry regiments, under his friend Leonard Wood.

Spain formally goes to war with the United States. Secretary Long cables Dewey to go after the Philippines. Roosevelt writes his old ranch partner Sylvane Ferris about the cavalry regiment he is raising.

Congress declares war on Spain, and Dewey gets orders to go after Spain's ships. Roosevelt's commission dates from today; friends think he has lost his mind. He writes Chanler, John Fox, Wadsworth and Will Cowles about the volunteer regiments.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Bags of applications start pouring in for Roosevelt's new regiment; some 23,000 arrive in all. He writes John Moore about horses for the unit.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne marks her 16th wedding anniversary with Douglas Robinson.

Roosevelt hands his Elkhorn ranch over to Sylvane Ferris and buys life insurance. Bamie, now expecting, still has Ted and Alice. Wood leaves for San Antonio to build the training camp, and Roosevelt lands Krag carbines with smokeless powder and khaki uniforms for the men. He later said he would have left even a deathbed to answer this call.
Commodore Dewey destroys Spain's Pacific squadron in Manila Bay in about seven and a half hours of action, without losing a single American life.

Roosevelt wires his congratulations to Dewey. McKinley and Long approve Roosevelt's plan for a combined naval and military attack on Cuba. He wires Guy Murchie to recruit Harvard men and orders a blue cravenette lieutenant colonel's uniform from Brooks Brothers.
A watch and the last cattle
Roosevelt thanks Douglas Robinson for a watch; Douglas is buying up the few cattle Roosevelt still owns.

Roosevelt thanks his old Maine guide Bill Sewall for caring about how the new unit fares, and wires Lincoln Steffens about Eastern college men joining up. Among them are polo star Joseph Sampson Stevens, quarterback Dudley Dean, tennis champion Bob Wrenn, Columbia oarsman Hamilton Fish and the fashionable Woodbury Kane.

Roosevelt tells Bamie he has stayed in Washington to cut through red tape. He has signed up about 40 men from Harvard, Yale and the Knickerbocker Club, Bob Ferguson among them, signing up at the 1814 G Street office. Edith keeps gaining, though worry about him wears on her. He thanks Conie for a watch.

Roosevelt's diary records his commission as lieutenant colonel with Wood as colonel, by his own choice, after he had been offered the top post. He sends to McKinley, by way of Long, his resignation from the Navy's second-ranking post, and writes Bamie, Douglas Robinson and Fitzhugh Lee.
Roosevelt vents in his diary about delays in the Army's ordnance office and a War Department without leadership.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Edith is well and that the two of them have gone out to dinner a few times. He tells Conie that Douglas Robinson's cousin Kenneth has joined the Rough Riders.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells Colonel Wood that the Krag carbines he obtained are being shipped to San Antonio.
Roosevelt takes Edith for a drive through the countryside in bloom.
At 10 p.m. Roosevelt boards a train for San Antonio. Kermit, who stayed up to see him off, writes that his father has gone to war. Roosevelt sends Bamie a goodbye note and thanks Conie for a poem.
Roosevelt is on the train bound for San Antonio.
Roosevelt's journey to San Antonio continues.
Roosevelt reaches the regiment's camp at San Antonio, about 500 tents holding some 1,000 men.

Roosevelt judges Major Alexander Brodie a good man and settles into camp routine: reveille before dawn, watering horses in the river, mounted drill and bronco busting he oversees, skirmish practice, dress parade, officers' school at night, then taps. Afterward he writes letters, while many troopers slip into town.
Kenneth Robinson writes Conie that Roosevelt has been putting the men through drill for several days.

Bob Ferguson tells Douglas Robinson that Roosevelt already has a firm grip on the men. Around now Roosevelt buys the troopers a round of beer; Wood rebukes him for blurring the line between officers and men, and Roosevelt promptly admits the mistake.
Roosevelt's diary marvels at the regiment's progress under constant drill, and he tells Lodge they are hard at work getting it into shape.
Roosevelt notes in his diary that the Harvard and New York recruits are getting along well with the cowboys.

Roosevelt's diary blasts the Ordnance Bureau for sending what the regiment doesn't need by express and its rifles by slow freight, and he lays the ultimate blame on the President. He writes Robert Bridges about writing an account of the coming campaign.
Roosevelt is with the regiment in San Antonio; nothing further is recorded.
The regiment's training continues at San Antonio, with no other entries.
Roosevelt remains at the San Antonio camp; no other events are noted.
The Rough Riders get their name
Roosevelt assures President McKinley the regiment is in fine form and eager for Cuba, and describes for Lodge the 'Rough Riders,' as the newspapers now call them.

Roosevelt's diary notes the regiment is almost at full quota and praises Wood's tireless work. The mounted drill is excellent, but restless troopers have taken to shooting up San Antonio on nights in town.
Roosevelt is in camp at San Antonio; no other events are recorded.
The regiment is ordered to Tampa, Florida, and sits for its regimental photograph. Edith writes Roosevelt about Ted.
At 5 a.m. Camp Wood comes down, and loading the horses onto the train takes until midnight. Roosevelt takes charge of the rear four of the train's seven sections.
The train finally pulls out at 6 a.m. Roosevelt's diary complains of a rail system breaking down, endless delays, and no proper places to unload, water and feed the horses.

The regiment rolls on toward Tampa in a long train of passenger, baggage, box and livestock cars, loading and unloading horses through each night. Roosevelt carries a dozen pairs of spectacles stitched into his clothes and hat.

On a long, sweltering, crowded train ride to Florida, Roosevelt lets his troopers drink but comes down hard on anyone who gets drunk. In spare moments he reads a French book on Anglo-Saxon superiority.
Hot coffee on a hungry train
With no hot meals aboard, Roosevelt arranges hot coffee for his troopers. At station stops along the way, townspeople hand the soldiers watermelons and beer.

The regiment arrives at Tampa to find the railroads in a snarl; the troopers ride the last six miles and Roosevelt and Wood hunt for their campsite after dark in 90-degree heat. Edith has come down to the Tampa Bay Hotel, and he spends the night there with her.
The horses are worn out from the trip, so the regiment drills on foot. Roosevelt rides into Tampa, and Edith writes home to the children.
A diary cry over Tampa's disorder
Roosevelt pours his frustration into his diary, blaming the mess at Tampa on a collapse of both the rail and military systems. Edith writes her sister Emily about her journey to Florida.

The Rough Riders show off a sharp mounted drill on the flats, watched by foreign military observers, Richard Harding Davis and Edith. Then word comes that only officers' horses will ship to Cuba, and just eight of the regiment's twelve troops will go.
Edith heads home; orders to embark
Edith starts back to New York. Drinking coffee in the hotel, Roosevelt hears the troops will ship out right away, and he dashes off notes to his sisters brimming with eagerness to go.
Seizing a coal train and a ship

When no train shows up, Roosevelt commandeers a coal train going the wrong way and has it backed down to the docks with his men aboard. Wood grabs the transport Yucatan, meant for two other regiments, and the Rough Riders hold it. Two Vitagraph cameramen come along; the fleet sails but halts on reports of ships in the Gulf.
The troopers sit crammed aboard the Yucatan in the heat, waiting without complaint while the food goes bad. Roosevelt fumes in his diary about the bungling.
The transports move out into the channel. Sharks prowl the water, but some overheated men go swimming anyway. Roosevelt tells Lodge the disorder is beyond words.
Another day stalled in Tampa harbor. Roosevelt notes in his diary that the tropical sun is hard on his men.
Sixth day aboard the sweltering ship

Still stuck in the bay, Roosevelt writes Bamie about a small ship carrying a thousand men, warns Edith the wait is hurting morale, and asks Lodge to carry word of the Tampa mismanagement to the President.
In the afternoon the transports finally raise anchor, move down the bay and drop anchor once more.
At last, the fleet sails for Cuba
The transports clear the Tampa Bay lighthouse and steam for Cuba that evening, every ship lit up while the bands play the national anthem together. Roosevelt sends Douglas Robinson a quick note.

Late in the evening Roosevelt spots the lights of the Tortugas and Key West. The 31-ship convoy stretches 25 miles and straggles, and General Shafter brushes off the Navy's plea to darken the ships at night.
The convoy crawls along, slowed by a schooner and a scow under tow. By day the officers hold classes and the men drill on deck.
Another day aboard ship on the way to Cuba; the record notes nothing more.
Sent back to guard a straggler
Shafter orders the Yucatan back to escort a transport towing a schooner. Roosevelt calls the order idiotic: his ship has no towline and only gives the rear gunboat Bancroft one more vessel to watch.
The Yucatan plods along beside the towed schooner while the rest of the fleet disappears over the horizon.
The fleet turns southwest and the destination becomes clear: Santiago. The ships stop some 20 miles to the east of Morro Castle after a day hugging the Cuban shore.
Battle orders and a war dance
Orders for the landing are read out to the troops, and Roosevelt celebrates with a war dance and a rousing Irish-American song.
Ashore in Cuba with a toothbrush

After a 3:30 a.m. reveille and a morning naval bombardment, the landing begins. Officers' horses are pushed overboard to swim; Roosevelt's Rain-in-the-Face drowns while Texas reaches shore. The Yucatan sails off with the baggage, leaving him only a toothbrush and a yellow mackinaw. By midnight 6,000 troops are on the beach.

After General Lawton seizes Siboney that morning, the regiment sets out at 3:45 p.m. under General Joseph Wheeler and cover seven steamy miles by sundown, Roosevelt on foot beside his men. Movie cameras catch pack mules on the trail toward Santiago.

Before dawn the regiment pushes toward Las Guasimas, and Spanish snipers open up from cover, killing Sergeant Hamilton Fish and Captain Allyn Capron. Roosevelt, splinters in his eyes, leads three troops on a flanking fire that opens the way for the charge. In two hours the Spanish fall back, and he pockets three Mauser cartridges for his children.
A day of rest after the fight
The regiment rests. Roosevelt writes Edith an account of the Las Guasimas fight.

The regiment moves three miles. Told the commissary's beans are for officers only, Roosevelt orders 1,100 pounds of them as an officer, feeds his whole regiment, and hauls one sack himself over eight miles of jungle road.

The regiment stays put while Roosevelt goes out scouting. Back home the newspapers praise the Rough Riders and ignore the other units at Las Guasimas. Letters pass between him and Edith, and he writes Lodge about the battle.
The Rough Riders remain on the Las Guasimas ridge. In New York, people are already talking about making Roosevelt the next governor.
Back to the coast for supplies
Roosevelt heads back to the coast to push ammunition and food forward. General Shafter at last reaches the Las Guasimas ridge.

Shafter surveys the heights of San Juan from El Pozo and holds a war council; the advance on Santiago begins as Wheeler falls ill with fever. The regiment marches late and camps at 9 p.m. At Sagamore Hill, Edith buys a horse she names Cuba and fills scrapbooks with clippings.
The charge up Kettle and San Juan hills

Roosevelt's 'crowded hour.' With Wood moved up to brigade command, he leads the Rough Riders. After hours pinned down by fire at Bloody Ford, he rides Little Texas up Kettle Hill, takes a graze on the elbow, and finishes on foot. He then rallies the men across to San Juan Hill, where the flag is already up. The regiment suffers the heaviest losses of any unit there.

Before dawn a shell lands near Roosevelt, who keeps striding the San Juan ridge under rifle and artillery fire. His diary lists officers of the regular cavalry. Bob Ferguson writes Edith that he now believes nothing can kill her husband.
Truce, and the Spanish fleet is gone

A truce takes hold at noon. Off Santiago, the Navy under Sampson and Schley destroys the Spanish squadron as it runs for the open sea. Roosevelt's men dig in through daily rain, and he writes Edith and urges Lodge to get more troops and supplies sent.
A grim Fourth in the trenches

The truce holds, but men in the trenches suffer from wounds, dysentery, malaria and hunger. Army bands play for them, and the Rough Riders ask for 'Fair Harvard.' Across the Pacific, the U.S. takes Wake Island. Roosevelt sends Wood a report on what has happened since the July 1 battle.

Outside Santiago, Roosevelt writes Lodge that General Shafter is criminally incompetent and describes the hardship and disorder of the siege. Bob Ferguson tells Edith her husband is reveling in the fight.
The siege of Santiago continues. In Washington, Congress votes to annex Hawaii. Roosevelt writes to President McKinley.
Hoping for the Medal of Honor
Still in the lines outside Santiago, Roosevelt tells Lodge he believes he has earned both a higher rank and the Medal of Honor, should General Wheeler recommend him.
Another day in the trenches outside Santiago; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt and the regiment remain in the lines outside Santiago; the day passes without other notes.
The guns open again outside Santiago, as the dynamite gun and the Colt guns fire on the Spanish lines. Roosevelt tells Lodge that Shafter ought to be removed from command.

Roosevelt is formally commissioned colonel. The regiment shifts a mile to the right taking its Gatling gun along to cover the road to El Caney, and the hardest rain yet falls that night. Stephen Crane later praised how hard he worked for his men during the siege.
The siege goes on outside Santiago, with rain pouring down until midday.
Outside Santiago, American and Spanish officers meet to discuss the city's surrender.
The regiment holds its lines outside Santiago, and a letter arrives from Edith.
A face-saving deal; Uncle James dies

Negotiators agree the Santiago garrison will give up within two days, after a token bombardment aimed harmlessly over the houses to preserve Spanish honor. Roosevelt writes Ethel about the endless rain. At home, his uncle James Alfred Roosevelt dies that evening on the Long Island Rail Road near New Hyde Park.
Roosevelt and the regiment spend the day in the lines outside Santiago, with the surrender close at hand; nothing more is noted.
At noon the American flag rises over Santiago as 17,000 Spanish troops give up the city.
Half the regiment out of action
Roosevelt shifts his camp across the ridge to the foothills west of El Caney as yellow fever cases mount. He notes that half his men are dead, wounded or sick.

Roosevelt writes a burst of letters: to Edith on victory and the collapse of transport, food and hospital services; to Douglas Robinson thanking him for supplies; to Lodge describing San Juan; to General Bradley T. Johnson on his pride in the men; and to Bamie with news.
With more officers falling sick, Roosevelt takes command of the 2nd Brigade. He reports on bad conditions near Santiago to General Wood and writes Ethel about Cuba's lizards and birds.
The regiment remains in camp near Santiago; no events are recorded.
Feeding the men from his own pocket

Roosevelt tells Douglas Robinson he is paying for the Rough Riders' food himself and that half the regiment is out of action. He writes Lodge about bad organization and fears of yellow fever, though none of his men actually has the disease.
Fresh meat finally reaches the sick-ridden camp. Roosevelt writes Secretary of War Russell Alger asking that his men be sent on to fight in Puerto Rico.
A service is held in camp, and Roosevelt notes a slight improvement in the men's health.
Roosevelt jots down camp anecdotes in his diary, including a lost hat, troopers Pollock and Paunce, and a man who refused to grow his hair long in wartime.
Another day in camp in Cuba with nothing recorded.

Roosevelt tells Douglas Robinson he never expected to come through unhurt, discusses a possible run for governor with John Lewis Childs, and praises the young Harvard men serving as troopers in a letter to President Charles W. Eliot.

Roosevelt records troopers' stories in his diary, including Crockett's wound and the parson who ground coffee. He thanks Bamie for Red Cross supplies she arranged and calls the regiment thoroughly American.
Roosevelt's diary names two bronco busters in the regiment, Darnell and Smoky Moore.

Roosevelt formally accepts his colonelcy. General Shafter calls all officers together to discuss the army's health crisis. In his diary Roosevelt recalls Happy Jack, a former lightweight boxer sure he could not catch fever.
Pleading to bring the men home
Roosevelt tells Lodge he would much rather take on national politics than New York's sewers and police boards, and he writes Seth Low that his men must leave Cuba before sickness kills them.
The regiment stays in camp in Cuba; the record is blank.
Nothing is recorded for the day in Cuba.

Roosevelt writes two letters warning that disease will destroy the army unless it leaves Cuba: one under his own name and a 'round robin' signed by many officers around Santiago. Both go to the Associated Press for publication at home.
Roosevelt's warnings appear in American morning newspapers, and both the President and Secretary Alger are furious.
Roosevelt is still in Cuba while Bamie and Winthrop Chanler stay at Sagamore Hill.
Washington orders Shafter's army to Montauk on Long Island. It is Edith's 37th birthday.
Roosevelt remains in Cuba while Douglas Robinson signs the guest book at Sagamore Hill.
The Rough Riders sail out of Santiago harbor aboard the troopship Miami. Wood stays behind as the city's military governor.
The Miami steams north toward home.
Still at sea aboard the Miami. Jacob Riis signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Another day aboard the Miami heading for Long Island.
While Roosevelt is at sea, the United States and Spain sign a peace protocol, and Hawaii is formally annexed.
U.S. forces capture Manila in the Philippines. At home, Ethel celebrates her seventh birthday.
Platt cool on Roosevelt for governor
Boss Thomas Platt pushes back against the talk of nominating Roosevelt for governor. At sea, Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about an article he hopes to write for Macmillan's.

Tugs bring the Miami in at noon as a big crowd waits on the Montauk shore. Roosevelt, looking fit beside his gaunt troopers, tells reporters he feels ashamed to be so healthy but that it was a bully fight; he will talk only about the regiment. The men go into quarantine at Camp Wikoff, and he slips out to see Edith.
Edith in a Montauk boarding house
Roosevelt is at Montauk, where Edith has taken a room in a grubby boarding house nearby.
Roosevelt wires Lemuel Quigg, Platt's lieutenant in the state Republican organization, that he will be discharged early from quarantine.
John Jay Chapman, who leads an independent effort to draft Roosevelt for governor, visits him. Roosevelt notes in his diary the tale of Ballard, a former sheriff who broke up the Black Jack gang.
Telling Quigg he wants the job
Lemuel Quigg calls on behalf of the Republican organization, and Roosevelt admits he would like to be their candidate for governor. His diary recalls surf baths with his troopers.
A hero's welcome at Oyster Bay

Roosevelt and Edith leave camp for a five-day family visit at Sagamore Hill, and some 1,500 people turn out in Oyster Bay to greet him. Little Archie, not quite sure who he is, greets him cheerfully as 'Colonel.'
In the evening Roosevelt puts on a tuxedo and sips madeira on the piazza while guests fill the house, among them Grant La Farge, Corinne and Douglas Robinson, and Speck von Sternberg.
Driving Edith to the Red Cross
Roosevelt takes Edith by carriage to a meeting of the Red Cross.
Sagamore Hill hums with visiting delegations and photographers, and Lodge stops by. Roosevelt tells Charles W. Eliot his letter to Alger was written in a spirit of 'calculated imprudence.'
A fallback deal with the independents
Chapman returns alongside Isaac Klein, a Citizens Union leader, and Roosevelt agrees to run as an independent for governor if the Republicans pass him over.
Roosevelt returns to camp at Montauk. Bamie signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt is at Camp Wikoff; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt tells Seth Low he is 'running' for governor the way Low once did, by letting things unfold. He assures Quigg he has said nothing to reporters.
A quiet day in camp. Dan Tyler Moore appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt travels to Newport, Rhode Island, to attend William Tiffany's funeral.
Roosevelt tells Quigg he will go before the Republican convention if the organization wants him, whether or not Governor Black fights back.
The record lists honorary Rough Riders: correspondent Richard Harding Davis, British military attaché Arthur Lee, and regular Army artillery Lieutenant Parker.

Platt lets it leak that he backs Roosevelt for the Republican nomination for governor. Alarmed, Chapman and Klein rush to Montauk, and Roosevelt calms them. He also congratulates John Hay on becoming Secretary of State.
A quiet day at the Montauk camp with nothing recorded.
Roosevelt writes Francis E. Leupp that he has not fretted over the nomination at all, and that in party politics one has to work with the machine.

President McKinley and Secretary Alger visit the troops at Montauk. Roosevelt tugs his glove off with his teeth before he shakes the President's hand. He tells Lodge that Edith is cross with him for not writing and that Alger should go.
Roosevelt is in camp; the day is blank in the record.
Edith brings Alice, Ted, Kermit and Ethel to Montauk for a 24-hour stay. Ted and Kermit bunk in the tent on a cot and an air mattress, and their father sleeps on a table.
Another camp day at Montauk with nothing noted.
Roosevelt tells Quigg the Rough Riders will soon be mustered out.
A quiet day in camp. Bob Ferguson signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt says he will accept the Republican nomination for governor but will not go after it. He visits with Colonel L. H. Jerome.
Edith tells her sister Emily that the Rough Riders raised a new flag in her honor. Roosevelt wires Quigg that the regiment will muster out Thursday or perhaps Friday.
Yes to the nomination, with reservations
Roosevelt writes both Quigg and Chapman that he wants the nomination, but tells Quigg he does not accept every condition Platt has set.

On Ted's 11th birthday, bugles call the 900 surviving Rough Riders together one last time. They form a square around a hidden gift, Frederic Remington's bronze The Bronco Buster, and present it to their colonel. Roosevelt, choked up, shakes every man's hand.
Home with an eagle named Teddy
Roosevelt heads to Sagamore Hill with a few Rough Riders, his horse Little Texas, and the regiment's bald eagle mascot, Teddy.
Several Rough Riders sign the Sagamore Hill guest book, among them Gordon Johnston, Jack Greenway, Bob Ferguson, Hal Sayre, David Goodrich and Charles Ballard.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt goes into New York City for a talk with Senator Platt, held at the Fifth Avenue Hotel, before the convention and accepts the Republican nomination.
Rough Riders Quaid, Kuoblach and McGinty stop at Sagamore Hill for breakfast on their way from Montauk to New York.

Roosevelt sends John Jay Chapman a 'Dear Jack' letter turning down the independents. Chapman does not think Roosevelt lied but still feels cheated. Roosevelt tells Lodge he cannot leave New York just now.
In New York City, Roosevelt confers with Chauncey Depew at the Union League Club along and Benjamin Odell.
Roosevelt is at home; the record is otherwise blank.
A letter held back three days

Roosevelt writes Chapman a second letter, then sets it aside for three days, and drafts a similar one to Leupp, declining the independent nomination. He tells Chapman his name will likely go before the Republican convention at Saratoga.
Edith hopes he loses the nomination
Edith writes her sister Emily that she would be relieved if her husband were not nominated for governor.
A stormy night and a residency scandal

Chapman storms out to Sagamore Hill and argues hard with Roosevelt, then misses the last train and has to stay the night. Meanwhile the press reports that Roosevelt is legally a resident of Washington, not New York. He offers to withdraw; Platt asks if he is a coward, and Roosevelt vows to run. Elihu Root finds a legal way through.
Chapman catches a morning train back. Roosevelt takes a walk with Edith and has dinner with the children.
Roosevelt writes Platt, Lodge and Nicholas Murray Butler about the residency issue.

The Republican convention at Saratoga nominates Roosevelt for governor, 753 votes to 218 for the sitting governor, Frank Black, whose administration was tarnished by Louis Payn's evasion of civil service law and George Aldridge's handling of Erie Canal funds. It is also Corinne's 37th birthday.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about his residency trouble and wires Quigg his thanks for helping him win the nomination.
Roosevelt goes into New York City in the afternoon and sends Seth Low two letters of thanks for his help with the nomination.
A secretary for a flood of mail

Roosevelt writes Quigg about party unity and tells Butler a tough, aggressive campaign lies ahead. Alice refuses to go to boarding school, so the family must find her a governess. He hires Amy Cheney as secretary, and she, Edith and Alice tackle the mail in the Gun Room.
Roosevelt meets in New York City with Benjamin Odell, who chairs the state Republican committee, then is home at Sagamore Hill by late afternoon.
Roosevelt spends the evening at a Republican Club reception in New York City and writes President McKinley that the shifts in the race look good for their side.
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt pays his taxes: $995.28.
Leading Republicans travel to Sagamore Hill to formally notify Roosevelt that he is their nominee for governor. His Democratic opponent will be Augustus Van Wyck.

Roosevelt launches his race for governor with a Carnegie Hall address titled 'The Duties of a Great Nation,' telling the crowd the country must meet its destiny with courage. He asks Lodge to come speak in the city.
President McKinley congratulates Roosevelt on his nomination. Odell, uneasy with the Rough Rider escort and the noise, decides the campaign should be low-key.

The Erie Canal deepening scandal, which ensnares Governor Black, becomes a central campaign issue, and Roosevelt must stand apart as the honest choice. Edith tells her sister Emily that the Carnegie Hall crowd was so excited she forgot to be nervous.
Roosevelt goes to an evening meeting at Brooklyn's Union League Club.
A Sunday at home with nothing recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City on Kermit's ninth birthday.
Roosevelt gives an evening speech in Manhattan's Lyric Hall and writes Lodge, who liked the Carnegie Hall speech. His niece Eleanor turns 14.
Roosevelt is in the city; no events are recorded.
Another day in New York City with nothing noted.
A wild goose chase to Troy

Pressed into speaking at the Rensselaer County Fair, Roosevelt rides the train to Albany and on to Troy in a steady drizzle, without Governor Black. Only about 300 people show up, he stays in his carriage, and back at the station his train has left. That night he and Corinne attend a meeting of Black voters in New York City, which also falls flat.
Still angry over the previous day's fiasco, Roosevelt decides to run his own campaign from now on. That night he addresses a crowd at the Lenox Lyceum.
Roosevelt writes Quigg about organizing Jewish voters in New York City and tells Lodge the Republicans are weak statewide this year.

At 10:02 a.m. Roosevelt's train pulls out of Weehawken with six uniformed Rough Riders and six reporters aboard. Along a 212-mile run through the Hudson Valley he makes 17 stops, from West Nyack and Newburgh to Albany, Saratoga and Glens Falls.

Roosevelt swings north toward the Adirondacks, going after Democratic boss Richard Croker at stops from Whitehall and Plattsburgh to Ogdensburg and Malone. In Oyster Bay, Bamie and Will Cowles welcome a son, William Sheffield Cowles Jr.
Rain-soaked crowds along the St. Lawrence

Moving down the St. Lawrence country, Roosevelt warns that Croker will corrupt the courts. He gives ten-minute talks at Potsdam, Canton, Gouverneur, Carthage, where 3,000 stand in the rain, Lowville and Boonville, then speaks in Brooklyn that evening on state and national issues.
Roosevelt speaks in the evening at Durland's Riding Academy and at the Grand Central Opera House.

Roosevelt addresses seven big meetings and confers with Republican district leaders before heading to Poughkeepsie for an evening speech and an overnight stay. He urges Quigg to enlist Jacob Riis in the city campaign.
The 'Roosevelt Special' makes a fast run up the Hudson and Mohawk valleys, with speeches at Little Falls, Johnstown and Gloversville.
A Sunday break in the city; nothing recorded.
Roosevelt speaks across the southern edge of the state, from Suffern and Middletown to Port Jervis, Binghamton, Cortland and Elmira.
Touring central and western New York, Roosevelt makes 16 speeches across Steuben, Allegany and Livingston counties, including Corning, Hornellsville and Warsaw, and ends the day in Buffalo.
Nineteen stops and a talk on labor
Roosevelt gives 19 speeches, at Niagara Falls, Lockport, Tonawanda, Medina, Palmyra, Fairport and elsewhere, and in Rochester speaks on the interests of labor.
Roosevelt marks his 40th birthday with 14 speeches, among them Canandaigua, Seneca Falls, Geneva, Auburn and Syracuse.
Roosevelt speaks 15 times, working from Phoenix and Oswego north to Watertown and back down to Rome and Utica.
Making farmers laugh, then Cooper Union
In 11 speeches through the Mohawk Valley, from Herkimer to Schenectady, Roosevelt gets farmers laughing with nothing more than a certain look. That evening he speaks at Cooper Union in New York City.
Roosevelt wraps up the swing with 15 more speeches and a dozen impromptu talks, 102 in all on the tour, and speaks that evening at Harlem River Park.

Roosevelt speaks at the Lenox Lyceum and stumps Long Island and the southwest of the state. Sergeant Buck Taylor of the Rough Riders introduces him with an unfortunate promise to lead voters 'like sheep to the slaughter.' J. P. Morgan gives $10,000 to the campaign. At home Roosevelt dictates The Rough Riders, which will earn $1,000 per magazine installment.
Roosevelt addresses crowds at Cooper Union, Cosmopolitan Hall and Morrisania Hall, then gives an evening speech in Yonkers.
Roosevelt tours Long Island, with stops from Jamaica and Flushing out to Babylon, Islip, Patchogue and Southampton.
Roosevelt speaks in Albany and Troy.
Unsure how the fight is going
Roosevelt speaks in Brooklyn and then at Chickering Hall in Manhattan. He admits to Lodge he cannot tell how the race is going and fears 'Blifil and Black George' might come out ahead.
From the Bowery to Wall Street
Roosevelt attends a Cooper Union meeting and speaks on the Bowery and on Wall Street at the Sub-Treasury. His current reading is a German study of Polybius.
Roosevelt spends the last Sunday before the election at home; nothing else is noted.
Last swing through the Southern Tier
On the eve of the election Roosevelt speaks in Olean, Jamestown, Salamanca, Hornellsville, Wellsville and Kennedy.

Roosevelt wins the governorship by 17,794 votes, 661,715 to Augustus Van Wyck's 643,921, with Timothy Woodruff elected lieutenant governor. He and Alice are reading and Edith is at her needlework when two reporters arrive at Sagamore Hill with the news.
Roosevelt writes Andrew Powell, making clear he stands against anti-Catholic bigotry of the kind Powell represents.
The governor-elect is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.
Another quiet day at home after the election.
Roosevelt confers at Republican headquarters in the Fifth Avenue Hotel.
A Sunday at home with no entries.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day is blank.
No events are recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt sets out from New York for Boston to lecture at the Lowell Institute.
An evening with Lodge in Boston
In Boston, Roosevelt passes the evening in the company of George Lyman and Lodge.
Roosevelt is back in New York City; nothing else is recorded.

Quentin turns one. In Boston, opponents of overseas expansion form the Anti-Imperialist League, with members such as Senator George F. Hoar, Carl Schurz, Moorfield Storey, Gamaliel Bradford and Edward Atkinson.
A Sunday at home; nothing recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record is blank.
Roosevelt appears before the War Department investigating committee to report on conditions the army faced in Cuba.
Roosevelt gives the committee a second report on what troops endured in Cuba.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is noted for the day.

On Bamie's third wedding anniversary, Roosevelt tells Cecil Spring-Rice of his luck in getting into the war, getting out alive, and winning the governorship. He reviews the year for James Bryce and tells Arthur Lee that Britain and America must stand together.
Bound for Boston, Roosevelt is stopped by snow at New London, Connecticut.
Still stuck at New London, Roosevelt gives up on Boston and heads back toward New York City.
Roosevelt travels back to New York City.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing else is recorded.

Before Christmas Roosevelt gives eight Lowell lectures, earning $1,600 in all. Kermit, sick with erysipelas, has to wear a protective face mask; his father takes Alice and Ted tobogganing. Edith makes a trip to Albany, where Mrs. Black shows her the Governor's Mansion.
No to a machine man for Public Works
Roosevelt tells Lodge he does not want machine politician Francis Hendricks as Superintendent of Public Works, and asks about his chances for the Medal of Honor.
Theodore and Edith mark 12 years of marriage at Sagamore Hill.
Edith writes her sister Emily in Italy, telling her not to come home and explaining that the new responsibilities of a governor's wife demand all her attention.
Roosevelt holds meetings in New York City about state appointments.
'I want it': the Medal of Honor
Roosevelt continues meetings on state appointments and tells Lodge plainly that he has earned the Medal of Honor and wants it.
Roosevelt goes to Boston for an evening Lowell Institute lecture and takes the night train back to New York.
Roosevelt holds further meetings on state appointments in New York City.
Roosevelt is in the city; nothing is recorded.
The United States and Spain sign the Treaty of Paris. Roosevelt lectures that evening at the Lowell Institute in Boston and tells S. C. Harriott he will appoint only the best people.
Roosevelt is in Boston; nothing else is noted.

Roosevelt tells Susan B. Anthony he has always favored votes for women, saying the obstacle lies in women's own attitudes rather than in government. He tells Lodge he is unhappy with the peace treaty's terms.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; the day is blank.
Roosevelt meets in New York City on state appointments.
Nothing is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt is in the city; the record is blank.
Roosevelt tells Lodge it now looks unlikely he will receive the Medal of Honor.
Speaking to schoolchildren on Sullivan Street
Roosevelt gives a speech at the Children's Aid Society school on Sullivan Street.
Roosevelt is home for the holidays; nothing is recorded.
Christmas gifts at Cove Neck School

At 3 p.m. on Christmas Eve the governor-elect arrives at Cove Neck School with Edith and Alice, hands out presents and gives a short talk. Ted and Kermit are pupils there, and Kermit recites a nursery rhyme.
Christmas visitors at Sagamore Hill include Speck von Sternberg, Mrs. James B. Leavitt, John Elliott, Grace and Bertha Potter, Helen Cutting, Miss Le Morine and Mrs. Alexander Moore.
Feeling wronged by the War Department
Roosevelt complains to Lodge that the War Department has not dealt fairly with him over the Medal of Honor.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.
The family's last quiet days at home before Albany.
Roosevelt and his family travel to Albany and settle into the Governor's Mansion. Generals Sumner and Wood nominate him for the Medal of Honor.

With New Year's Day on a Sunday, Roosevelt and other state officers take the oath before Secretary of State John Palmer. He and Edith attend a quiet ball at the State Armory. Ted and Kermit start at the Albany Military Academy, Gertrude Young becomes governess to Alice and Ethel, and the first part of The Rough Riders appears in Scribner's.
Locked out of the Governor's Mansion

Roosevelt dines with his old friend Fanny Smith Parsons, now living in Albany, while Edith and the children stay in bed sick. Returning at midnight, he finds himself locked out of the mansion and breaks a window to get in.

In bitter subzero cold, with band instruments frozen silent, Roosevelt is inaugurated governor in the Assembly Chamber and sends lawmakers his yearly message. He is the first governor to serve in the newly finished Capitol, at a salary of $10,000 a year.

Roosevelt starts meeting reporters twice a day for 15 minutes, winning them over with an open, friendly manner and plenty of off-the-record talk. He writes Odell about Erie Canal appointments. Edith tells Emily the inauguration so moved her she could barely watch.

Roosevelt confers with Odell and with Syracuse politician Francis Hendricks, the machine's pick for Superintendent of Public Works. He writes William Ferguson about appointing Black men to state jobs and asks Max Keyes, a witness, to support his Medal of Honor claim.
A promise to do his duty
Roosevelt assures Herbert Welsh that he intends to act honorably and meet his responsibilities in office.
Roosevelt heads to Manhattan that afternoon for the Century Association's Twelfth Night dinner.

Roosevelt meets Platt, Odell and Root about the Public Works post and whether a man named Hill can serve as Erie County district attorney. It is the first of the Saturday morning breakfasts Corinne later described.

Roosevelt praises Trevelyan's American Revolution volumes and young Bay Lodge's poems in a letter to Lodge, writes Captain William Llewellyn about the Medal of Honor, and takes up the army's bad beef with General Nelson Miles.
Roosevelt confers with Elihu Root on the Public Works post and writes Helen Johnson that women are wronged by being denied equal treatment.
Roosevelt confers with Lou Payn, the insurance superintendent. He tells General Francis Greene that Secretary Alger opposes his Medal of Honor and tells Wood he wishes he could come to Albany.
Platt picks from an honest list

Having refused Platt's choice, Hendricks, Roosevelt sends the senator four honest candidates for Superintendent of Public Works. Platt chooses John N. Partridge. Roosevelt also writes Lodge about the medal.

Roosevelt sends John Partridge's nomination for Public Works to the state Senate. He writes Root about his tax and residency troubles, and tells Edwin Whitehead he wants boys to be tough and athletic yet gentle with the weak.

A special commission of the Workingmen's Federation of Labor holds a hearing on pending labor bills. Roosevelt writes Paul Dana and General Miles about spoiled meat fed to soldiers in Cuba, and Seth Low about the Partridge appointment.
A Sunday in Albany with nothing recorded.
Roosevelt convenes his cabinet for the first of its weekly meetings. He writes Odell about appointments and tells George Trevelyan how much he admires his American Revolution volumes.

Roosevelt meets the state's Civil Service Board. He writes Colonel Dibble about the Navy and Dewey at Manila, Odell about appointments, John P. Clarke on legislative matters, and Martha Selmes a chatty letter on how his life has changed in a year.
National Guard speech on Bamie's birthday
Roosevelt addresses the National Guard Association on Bamie's 44th birthday. He writes Winthrop Chanler about the army and politics and Platt about appointments.

Roosevelt signs the Ellsworth-Allds appropriation, Chapter 1 of the session's laws, covering legislators' contingent expenses. He writes John E. Roosevelt about his residency and asks Lodge to drop the Medal of Honor campaign altogether.
In New York, Roosevelt goes to an Irish-American Historical Society reception and a Union League Club dinner, and reviews the 23rd Regiment in Brooklyn.
Roosevelt holds meetings with Riis, Butler, Choate, Sloane, Slicer, Doty and Clarke, then goes to dinner with the Boone and Crockett Club.
A Sunday in the city with nothing recorded.
A police bill for the city

Republicans announce they will bring in a bill reshaping the city's police. Roosevelt writes a batch of political letters, including to Riis, Chauncey Depew, Senator Joseph Foraker, Seth Low, and Lodge about Lodge's book on the war.
