At a cabinet meeting, Austen Fox is named to probe the canal frauds as special counsel, assisted by Wallace MacFarlane. Roosevelt also confers with Quigg and Hotchkiss on changing the primary law.
Roosevelt writes Elihu Root about changes to the primary law.
Roosevelt writes Quigg about the primary law and tells Lodge his work in Albany seems to be going smoothly.
Roosevelt confers with Odell on the police bill. In the Philippines, Emilio Aguinaldo proclaims a Philippine Republic. Roosevelt tells Root that one of Root's jokes has upset the governor's staff.
Primary law talks and a CCNY dinner
In New York, Roosevelt confers with Root and Platt about the primary law and speaks at a City College dinner.
A Sunday in the city with no recorded events.
Roosevelt tells H. R. Caraway that a claim in the magazine Arena is false: he would never think of using troops to keep William Jennings Bryan from being inaugurated.
A plan for the city police

Roosevelt lays out his plan to overhaul the city's police force in a letter to Frank Moss. He writes William Wharton about Colonel Lay's dismissal and describes his duties as governor to William Howard Taft.
Declining a dinner for Carl Schurz
Governor Roosevelt writes Sherman Rogers from Albany that he will skip a dinner honoring Carl Schurz, citing the political gulf between the two men.
Chosen to lead a war veterans' order

In Albany, Roosevelt is chosen to command the Naval and Military Order, a society of Spanish-American War veterans. He also writes about appointments and the press, and sends Tiffany's a note sharing his thoughts on young Ted.
Letters on state police and a dismissal
From New York City Roosevelt takes up the idea of a state police force with Frank Moss, tells Bellamy Storer how busy he is, and writes former Governor Levi P. Morton about Colonel Lay's removal.
Roosevelt sits down to breakfast with Thomas Platt, Benjamin Odell and Elihu Root at his sister Corinne's house at 422 Madison Avenue.
A quiet Sunday; the record places Roosevelt in Albany with nothing further noted.

As the U.S. Senate approves the peace treaty with Spain, the United States takes Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines for $20 million and fighting breaks out with Emilio Aguinaldo's Filipino forces. In Albany, Roosevelt writes Root on politics and Lemuel Quigg on appointments.
Roosevelt sits in on a hearing on the Ambler dairy bill, writes Lodge about the Philippine treaty, and teases Count von Götzen about which nation the world dislikes most.
Teaching his children to admire courage
Roosevelt thanks General Bradley Johnson for meeting his children, writes Jacob Riis about the condemned Martha Place, and opens a long tug-of-war with Senator Platt over appointments.
In the afternoon Roosevelt attends a trustees' meeting for the state home for old soldiers and sailors at Bath.

Roosevelt tells his old ranch partner Sylvane Ferris he wishes he could get back to Medora. The rest of the day's mail is politics: appointments, Platt's objections to his picks, police and election bills, and a commission to improve the canals.
A note to a military novelist
Roosevelt writes General Charles King, author of army novels, that he enjoyed Trials of a Staff Officer.
On his daughter Alice's fifteenth birthday, Roosevelt speaks to the state YMCA gathering in Albany.
Lincoln Day speech on America's role
In New York City Roosevelt gives a Lincoln Day address at the Republican Club on the share of the world's labor that falls to America.

Roosevelt writes his friend Cecil Spring-Rice, then in Persia, that he wishes they could meet, and compliments Colonel George Henderson on his Civil War book. He continues to support former slaves of the Roswell plantation that belonged to his mother's family.

Roosevelt names James Varnum to be the county's Surrogate in New York and writes about the Civil Service Commission and garment workers. Edith, meanwhile, warns her sister Emily away from an unpromising suitor.
Roosevelt lays out his appointment choices for Joseph Bucklin Bishop, the newspaperman who would become a close friend, and writes ornithologist Frank Chapman about protecting birds.
Roosevelt goes to New York City for a dinner in honor of Ambassador Joseph Choate and reviews the 7th Regiment.
Platt breakfast and a word on police

Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt and Odell, writes explorer Walter Gordon-Cumming about the war and how the U.S. runs its new territories, and tells William Rainsford he will not meddle in police matters.
A Sunday in New York City. Edith writes her sister Emily offering last year's gowns, since a governor's wife shouldn't wear the same clothes two seasons running.
Hearing in the Martha Place case
Roosevelt holds a hearing on Martha Place, a convicted murderer facing execution. No woman had yet been put to death in New York State.
Roosevelt tells Francis Jones he will not halt Martha Place's execution, adding that he could not respect anyone who traded away principle for the hope of higher office.
Roosevelt addresses the Syracuse Chamber of Commerce and writes Frank Moss on politics.
Roosevelt confers with Root, Odell, Mazet, Stranahan and Raines on the police bills.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing more.
Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no details are recorded.
In Washington Roosevelt spends time with his close friend Henry Cabot Lodge.
Hunting books and a mediation board

Roosevelt writes his publisher about book sales and the coming Big Game Hunting, which joins two of his earlier hunting books. He also asks Charles Fairchild to sit on the state Board of Mediation and Arbitration; Fairchild says no.

Roosevelt writes about the Army beef inquiry, thanks Lodge for his stay, and tells Bellamy Storer he can't sway the choice of an American cardinal. Alice later remembered the Albany mansion as big, shabby and gloomy; Edith becomes a member of the Friday Morning Club and takes botanical walks with Fanny Parsons.
Roosevelt meets Platt about the Astoria gas bill, corresponds about the British edition of his Naval War of 1812 and other publishing matters, and stands up for Leonard Wood.
Roosevelt speaks at an evening dinner of the state's newspaper editors and writes Lodge about what Navy armor plate costs.
In New York City Roosevelt speaks at the Yale alumni dinner about Yale's part in the war with Spain.
Roosevelt meets his cousin Emlen Roosevelt to go over his personal taxes and property.
Roosevelt spends Sunday in New York City; no details survive.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.
Going after a crooked canal man
Roosevelt writes Adam Smith about ousting a dishonest canal superintendent in Herkimer County.
A commission to probe the canals

Roosevelt names a commission to investigate the state canals. He tells Leonard Wood he hopes the Senate will confirm him to a regular Army brigadier generalship, and outlines his canal policy for General Francis Greene.
Roosevelt complains to Lodge that Congress has been stingy with the Army and Navy, and remarks on General Shafter's coarseness.
Roosevelt speaks on good citizenship to the West Side Republicans in New York City, and writes Nicholas Murray Butler about the school bill.
Roosevelt meets Root, along with Coleman, Clarke and Ford, about the Amsterdam Avenue bill.
A Sunday in New York City with nothing more recorded.

Roosevelt turns down a settlement of the state's suits against Armour & Co. over butter-law violations. Pressed by the Storers, he reluctantly writes McKinley about their hope that Archbishop Ireland be made a cardinal, and tells George Gunton his labor bills are a hard sell.
Roosevelt signs a charter change that pools Greater New York's county funds into one general fund and lets the comptroller borrow against expected revenue. He writes Root about the Astoria gas bill.
Roosevelt signs a law requiring new fire and marine insurance companies to start with at least $200,000 in capital, and books a Saturday breakfast with Platt.
Roosevelt gives a speech at Bleecker Hall and writes about the Place execution and the fight against sweatshops.
Consulting Platt on transit and gas
Roosevelt meets Fallows about the Amsterdam Avenue bill and asks Platt's views on the tunnel, rapid transit and Astoria gas bills.
After breakfast with Platt, Roosevelt backs the Ford bill, sent to the Legislature that day, to tax corporations on the public franchises they hold, then heads back to Albany.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is noted.
Martha Place is put to death, the first woman executed in New York State. Roosevelt sends Emily Carow a Rough Rider pin and tells her he is enjoying being governor.
Roosevelt writes Lucius Littauer about letting an appointee go and Seth Low about the bridge bill.
Birds and a new national park
Roosevelt writes Frank Chapman about saving New York's bird species. The same day Congress creates Mount Rainier National Park, the nation's fifth.
Dairy hearing and the Ireland question
Roosevelt hears more on the Ambler dairy bill and writes Bellamy Storer about Archbishop Ireland, Winthrop Chanler with word for Platt, and Platt about the Greater New York bill.
Roosevelt addresses the Citizens Union in New York City and writes Stafford Mosher about the canal.
Platt balks at the Ford bill
Over breakfast at his sister Bamie's home, 689 Madison Avenue, Roosevelt learns that Platt opposes the Ford franchise tax bill. Edith tells Spring-Rice the family likes life in the governor's office.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the day is otherwise blank.

Roosevelt gives way to Platt on the Ford bill, asking the Legislature instead for a joint committee to study franchises and corporate taxes. He signs the Ambler dairy law against selling dyed oleomargarine, and Edith turns the mansion's third floor into a gym for him and the children.
Roosevelt attends a dinner held for Senator Platt in Albany.
Help for an old Rough Rider
Roosevelt meets legislative leaders and confers on the Ahearn school bill, and sends former Rough Rider William Proffit $75.
Roosevelt writes T. Thomas Fortune about race relations and internal quarrels in the Black community.

American troops take Malolos and Aguinaldo's forces retreat north. In Albany Roosevelt writes about savings bank, sweatshop and streetcar bills, and recommends Israel Fisher to McKinley for the post of General Appraiser in New York.
A landmark day for labor laws

Roosevelt signs a burst of reform laws: the Costello act policing sweatshop work in tenements, broader powers for factory inspectors with caps on hours for women and minors, canal repair money, and racing revenue for agriculture. He writes Bamie about the dispute over James Roosevelt's will.
Roosevelt is in Albany; no activities are noted.
Grade crossings and a book critic
Roosevelt signs a law helping cities get rid of railroad grade crossings, listens to arguments over the Ahearn school bill, and answers John McBlaine, a critic of The Rough Riders.

Roosevelt signs a law barring elected city officials from also holding a city-paid appointed job. A compromise Ahearn school bill goes to the Assembly, and he writes Platt about lengthening the session.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes John Sleicher about the Ford franchise tax and tells Douglas Robinson he will name Will Osborne to the Lunacy Commission.
Ready to sign the Ford bill
Roosevelt tells Paul Dana he now thinks the Ford franchise bill is sound and will gladly sign it.
Roosevelt sets out for Chicago, writing Douglas Robinson about the Osborne nomination and complaining to Joe Bishop about Goodman Brown as a Lunacy Commission pick.
Union League dinner on Archie's birthday
In Chicago Roosevelt is the guest at a Union League Club dinner; back home it is his son Archie's fifth birthday.

In Chicago Roosevelt speaks at the University of Chicago and the Harvard Club, then delivers his famous call to effort and courage, "The Strenuous Life," at the Hamilton Club's Appomattox Day gathering.
Roosevelt speaks at University Hall in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and starts back to Albany.

The state Senate approves the Ford bill by a vote of 33-11. Roosevelt signs the Raines-Mazet act letting the governor launch election-fraud probes through the attorney general, and vents to Franklin Moulton about the 'goo-goos.'
Roosevelt signs a change to the Beet Sugar Act offering a bounty to makers of sugar from New York-grown beets.
Roosevelt says the Ford bill will help the public and urges the Assembly to send it to him quickly, but Platt has it shelved there. He also explains his 'goo-goo' jab to Joe Bishop.
Roosevelt is in Albany; no details recorded.
Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt at Bamie's home on Madison Avenue and returns to Albany that afternoon.
Roosevelt signs a law against selling adulterated juice as pure, issues a statement favoring limits on rapid transit franchises, and writes about a Rapid Transit Commission and the police bill.
Opening the books of membership groups

Roosevelt signs a law letting Supreme Court officers inspect the accounts of membership corporations, sits through a rapid transit hearing, and writes William Cutting about killings of prisoners in the Philippines.
Roosevelt signs the Civil Service Act overhauling state and local merit systems, Ford and Fallows's Amsterdam Avenue act, and a ban on women and minors working at emery polishing wheels.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt signs the Krum act limiting what savings banks may invest in and a revised local-option procedure under the liquor law. He congratulates Bellamy Storer on his new post as U.S. minister to Spain.
Roosevelt urges the Legislature to move fast on the rapid transit bill and writes about the savings bank bill and a meeting with labor leaders.
Roosevelt is in Albany; no activities are noted.
Roosevelt sits with the Board of Regents and meets labor representatives about rapid transit. He writes Wood about errors in The Rough Riders and Maria Storer about Spain.
Roosevelt signs the Ahearn school act. A committee hears arguments on the Ford franchise tax, and he writes Assembly Speaker S. Fred Nixon about it.
Roosevelt goes down to New York City for the evening to attend the Commerce Commission's dinner for Senator William Frye.

Roosevelt signs a Poor Law change on relief for Civil War veterans. Having lined up enough Assembly votes for the Ford bill, he sends an emergency message to free it from committee; Speaker Nixon refuses to read it, rips it up, then collapses in an anteroom.

Learning at 7 a.m. that Nixon destroyed his message, Roosevelt writes a second one and threatens to deliver it in person. It is read, and the Assembly approves the Ford franchise tax, 109-35, as the session ends. He also signs carriage and election-registration laws.
Roosevelt takes the family on a trip into Rensselaer County outside Albany. It is his sister Corinne's seventeenth wedding anniversary.
The Roosevelts picnic on the bank of the Hudson. Edith writes Emily that a new Cyrano de Bergerac suffered in translation, and that she has watched Ellen Terry and Henry Irving perform.
Platt fumes over the Ford bill
Roosevelt tells Bamie that Platt is angry the Ford bill got through the Assembly, and writes others about the bill, the cardinal question and the primary bill.

Roosevelt signs an improved primary election law building on Root's 1898 measure, money for more natural history and geography teaching in public schools, and funding to keep the Commerce Commission's inquiry going.
Roosevelt writes Odell about the tax reform bill.

Roosevelt signs laws outlawing poisonous food coloring, authorizing a Cohoes canal with locks linking the Erie and Champlain canals, and enlarging the forest preserve in four Catskill counties. He invites Odell to Albany to talk taxes.

Roosevelt signs the Raines-Mazet police act forbidding officers to sway votes, raise political money, or hire and promote for partisan reasons. He also toughens penalties for corrupt practices and lets the governor deputize train conductors and steamboat crews as police.
Roosevelt takes a trip to the Helderberg hills near Albany. Platt writes asking him not to sign the Ford bill, and Roosevelt himself has some doubts about it.
Roosevelt is near Albany; the rest of the entry is unreadable.
Standing firm, and the Buffalo strike

Roosevelt tells Platt the Ford bill must pass this session, promising to recall the Legislature to strip out the objectionable assessment clause. At the Buffalo mayor's request he agrees to send militia into the dock strike.
Roosevelt goes to New York City for an evening speech at the City Club.
Roosevelt sends General Bradley Johnson news and his thinking on the franchise bill.
Capping city franchises; special session called

Roosevelt signs a charter amendment holding street franchises in Greater New York to 25 years (tunnels 50) and requiring good service at fair rates, a step toward the Atlantic Avenue tunnel. He wires Odell that he is calling the Legislature back on May 22 for the Ford bill.

Roosevelt signs the Sabine act tightening enforcement of the eight-hour day for state workers at local wages, and a broad reworking of second-class city government. He writes Platt about the Ford bill and the coming session.
Explaining the Ford bill to Garfield
Roosevelt writes Riis that he is rethinking the drug bill, sends Gherardi Davis notes on bills, and lays out the Ford bill for James R. Garfield, a Cleveland lawyer and son of the late President.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.
Property and its uses in Buffalo
After meeting Odell about the Ford franchise tax, Roosevelt speaks that evening in Buffalo to the Independent Club about property and the state.
Roosevelt again meets Odell about the Ford franchise tax.
Roosevelt formally summons the Legislature into special session and writes Frank Higgins about the Ford bill.
By telegram Roosevelt tells John Raines he will approve the franchise measure unchanged if the Legislature is withdrawn, and tells Odell some parts are objectionable while others are fine.
In New York City Roosevelt confers with Platt, Odell, Quigg, Boardman and Cohen, and speaks at the City Club.
Roosevelt leaves New York City for the Adirondacks.
Roosevelt spends the day in the Adirondacks; no details survive.
Lawmakers return for the special session
Senators and Assemblymen are back in Albany as the special session opens.
Roosevelt signs an election law setting rules for poll officers, especially in New York City, and a law letting large cities build tuberculosis hospitals beyond their limits.
Roosevelt asks Hobart Krum to examine one part of the franchise bill that may be unconstitutional.

With the Legislature's revisions to the Ford bill done and awaiting his approval, Roosevelt signs bans on slot machines and on monopolies in everyday goods. He tells William Allen White he liked his article.
The Ford franchise tax becomes law

Roosevelt signs the Ford franchise tax, making corporations pay taxes on their public franchises. He also signs a ban on transportation rate-fixing pools and a law keeping state fish hatchery waters clean.

Roosevelt opens an inquiry into Insurance Superintendent Louis F. Payn. He tells Bamie and Lodge how pleased he is with the Ford bill win, praises Lodge's new Spanish-American War book, and says he hopes to rest this summer.
Roosevelt is in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; no details are recorded.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt joins the Decoration Day parade in New York City and speaks to the Grand Army of the Republic.
In New York City, Roosevelt addresses the Hungarian Republican Club.
Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing more.

Over breakfast Roosevelt talks Tax Commission appointments with Platt and Odell, then spends the night at Cortlandt Park with Andrews and Treadwell, bound for the militia camp at Peekskill. He writes Speaker Nixon about naming Lester Stern a tax commissioner.
Roosevelt heads for the Peekskill militia camp, with stops at Sing Sing and Nelson Park.
Roosevelt is at the Peekskill camp; no details are recorded.
Roosevelt is at West Point; no details survive.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is noted.
Columbia gives Roosevelt an honorary Doctor of Laws. He writes Odell about the city district and tells Kansas editor William Allen White he would very much like to meet him.

Back in Albany Roosevelt approves new Civil Service Commission rules. He asks Harvard's Charles Eliot whether Leonard Wood will get an honorary degree, and writes McKinley once more for the Storers on the cardinal question.
In Rochester Roosevelt is on hand as the Frederick Douglass monument is unveiled. Ted and Kermit finish the school year at the Albany Military Academy.
Family heads to Sagamore for summer

Roosevelt travels from Rochester to Peekskill while Edith takes the family home to Oyster Bay for the summer. James K. Gracie visits, and Roosevelt writes Seligman, Straus and Peters about Dreyfus's acquittal in France.
Roosevelt is at Peekskill; nothing more is recorded.
From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt arranges trains for a trip west with Paul Morton and asks John Hay whether Parker is leaving the Civil Service Commission.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Sagamore Hill guests include Nicholas Murray Butler, Colonel Arthur Lee, Captain Andrews and Winthrop Chanler.
Bob Ferguson visits. Roosevelt tells McKinley he is dropping the cardinal question, writes Hay about resistance to civil service reform, and writes Bruno Hermann about German Americans.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is in New York City; no details survive.
Roosevelt speaks at Cornell University's graduation in Ithaca.
Roosevelt passes through Chicago on his way west.
Roosevelt is on the train to Las Vegas, New Mexico.
Roosevelt reaches Las Vegas, New Mexico, as the first reunion of the Rough Riders gets under way. Mr. and Mrs. Clifford Richardson are listed as guests.
The Rough Rider reunion continues in Las Vegas with memorial services and a parade.
Roosevelt heads east again toward Chicago.
Roosevelt travels from Chicago to Milwaukee, speaking along the way at Fort Madison and Galesburg.
Roosevelt speaks to the Milwaukee Chamber of Commerce, then starts east.

With newspapers boosting him for President in 1900, Roosevelt returns to New York City via Albany and declares he is not running. He dines with Generals Wood and Greene, talking over Cuba and the Philippines. Mrs. Regis Post is a guest.
Romps with the children; Lee courts Ruth Moore

Arthur Lee is staying at Sagamore Hill, where he courts Ruth Moore. Roosevelt plays hard with the children: 'stagecoach' on the float, running down Cooper's Bluff, racing through the old barn, and tennis with Alice.

Lodge is urging Roosevelt to join McKinley's 1900 ticket, with Vice President Hobart ill. Roosevelt tells Corinne he plans to spend the month writing a life of Oliver Cromwell, and writes about his western trip, his rift with Tom Reed, and worries over U.S. colonial policy.
Roosevelt is down with the fever he picked up in Cuba the summer before, an illness that would return throughout his life.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Fireworks, grass fires and a giant TR

Firecrackers wake Roosevelt and Edith at 4 a.m. and go on all day; he helps stamp out grass fires on the lawn and gives an Independence Day speech in Oyster Bay. The night ends with a fireworks portrait of him. He invites Admiral Dewey to Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt thanks John Gansey for a kind letter and says he will seek neither the presidency nor the vice presidency in 1900.
Fourth of July news for Bamie
Roosevelt writes Bamie about the Fourth of July fun, the presidential talk swirling around him, and Emlen's lawsuit over James Roosevelt's will.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
White House talks on a new War Secretary

Roosevelt goes to Washington to confer at the White House with McKinley and others on choosing a Secretary of War, and urges Francis Greene for a Philippine command. He shares with Bill Sewall how hard it is to choose when right and wrong are mixed.
Roosevelt leaves Washington for Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt updates Greene on his push to make him military governor of the Philippines, and tells Wood that McKinley disagreed with his view of the islands, calling things there good.
Platt meeting and lunch with Greene
In New York City Roosevelt confers with Platt, then has lunch with Douglas Robinson and General Greene.

Attorney General Davies visits Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Bamie he had a fine talk with McKinley but little time for vacation, writes General James Wilson about Cuba's troubles, and thanks McKinley for a pleasant White House dinner.
Roosevelt writes Thomas Slicer about removing Asa Gardiner as New York City's district attorney.
Woodruff, Nixon, Bender and Youngs visit Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.
Corinne's children Corinne and Teddy Robinson arrive as guests. Roosevelt writes James Reynolds about factory inspector appointments.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Corinne that her son Teddy, at sixteen, is not enjoying his summer: too old for the children's games and without friends his own age.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Slicer about removing Fellows and says he would decline the Secretary of War post if offered. He writes Benjamin Shove about removals.
Bamie and her husband Captain Will Cowles come to Sagamore Hill. The canal investigators, Fox and MacFarlane, publish their findings.
Rowing every day; Root to the War Department
Roosevelt tells Lodge he rows nearly every day, and writes about the Philippines, Cuba and Wood. Alger is out, and Root will become Secretary of War.
At Manhattan Beach Roosevelt calls on Platt, who is staying at the Oriental Hotel, and sends news of New York to General Frederick Funston, serving in the Philippines.
Roosevelt is at Manhattan Beach; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt visits the quarantine station on Barren Island.
Caspar Whitney and Miss LeMorine visit. Roosevelt praises Root's choice as Secretary of War in letters to Greene and Wilson, and wishes Root luck.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Edith tells Emily she mixes her own toothpaste from cuttlefish bone, dragon's blood, alum, orris root and spices. Roosevelt writes Edward Brown about his record on labor as governor.
Senator Frank Higgins is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
C. J. Sage of Melbourne, Australia, visits Sagamore Hill.

Russell Alger leaves the War Department and Elihu Root replaces him, while Vice President Hobart signals he means to remain. The Quiggs and General Avery Andrews visit, and Roosevelt sends Bradley Johnson a copy of The Rough Riders with notes on Remington's San Juan painting.
Roosevelt writes Austen Fox and Wallace MacFarlane, the canal investigators, regarding a Tribune editorial on their inquiry.
Roosevelt completes his life of Oliver Cromwell, sold for magazine serialization at $5,000 plus 15 percent royalties, and writes Robert Bridges about publishing it.

At Asbury Park, New Jersey, Roosevelt speaks at the theological school on practical and decent politics, then spends the night at Norwood Park with Vice President Hobart. He also writes Caspar Whitney on the editorship of Harper's Weekly.
Grant La Farge is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

Bob Ferguson and David Goodrich are at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about civil service and the effort to keep Proctor, and sends General James Wilson recommendations for government posts.
Roosevelt is in Utica on his wife Edith's birthday.
Roosevelt tells Hermann Kohlsaat he is putting off his trip west and asks about the Republican position on trusts.
Roosevelt writes Harry Newcomb, naming New York's delegates to the Chicago conference on trusts.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Dr. and Mrs. Alexander Lambert and Colonel Dick visit. Roosevelt writes Charles Scribner about Oliver Cromwell and tells Lodge he lunched with Root and that Edith will join him touring county fairs.
Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice about Irish and German Americans, the Alaska boundary dispute with Canada, Russia, and the waning of the 'old Americans.'
Robert Bridges of Scribner's comes to Sagamore Hill to proof Oliver Cromwell. Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice again, and wires McKinley that he will speak in Ohio in October.
Ethel celebrates her eighth birthday at Sagamore. Edith writes Emily she hopes TR wins a second term so Alice can make her debut at the Executive Mansion.
Roosevelt writes Root about particular Rough Riders who served under him.

Roosevelt speaks to a firemen's convention in Yonkers, dines with Littauer, Odell and Platt, and leaves for Buffalo that night. He asks Charles Scott for guidance on trusts, admitting he is unsure what stand to take.
Roosevelt reaches Olcott by way of Buffalo and sets out for the Niagara County Fair. Edith tells Emily her heart had become 'enlarged' while he was in Cuba, then recovered when he came home safe.
Roosevelt is at Niagara Falls; no details are recorded.
Roosevelt is at Silver Lake; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt is at Chautauqua; no details survive.
With McKinley and Hobart at Plattsburgh
At Plattsburgh Roosevelt spends time with McKinley and Hobart, the President and Vice President.
From Plattsburgh Roosevelt tells Platt his speaking tour has gone well and sends General Wilson ideas for military appointments.
Avery Andrews and Judge Parkhurst are guests at Sagamore Hill.
George Haven Putnam is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt spends six straight hours in a rowboat. Baron Speck von Sternberg and Mrs. Rose are guests.
Roosevelt sends Lodge news, tells May Youngs that William Loeb is serving as private secretary, and writes Wood about Cuba.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt speaks at the fair in Hornellsville and stays the night in Olean.
Bound for Watertown, Roosevelt speaks at Little Valley and stops at Buffalo, continuing his round of county fairs. He writes William Archer about the Germans.
Canals at the Jefferson County Fair
In Watertown Roosevelt talks about canals and how they should be run at the Jefferson County Fair, then leaves for New York City.
John Fox Jr. visits Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt thanks Root for hearing him out and sends Arthur Lee his thoughts on reorganizing the U.S. Army.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Wood privately about Army matters and urges Root to make him a brigadier general in the Regular Army.
Roosevelt speaks at the county fair in Ogdensburg.
Fulton County Fair and Philippine geology
Roosevelt addresses fairgoers in Johnstown, Fulton County, and stays the night in Utica. He writes geologist George Becker about his intriguing study of Philippine geology.
Roosevelt addresses fairs in both Norwich and Delhi and spends the night in Syracuse.
Roosevelt travels from Syracuse back to Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt dines in New York City with Odell, Platt and Cohen. He tells Bellamy Storer his five oldest children can all swim, and writes his last letter to Lodge while Lodge is in England.
Roosevelt speaks at the Orange County Fair in Middletown and writes W. Forbes Murray about a heckler he faced in Hornellsville.
Roosevelt addresses the fair in Walton, Delaware County, on Ted's twelfth birthday. The Chicago conference on trusts opens.
Roosevelt addresses the fair at Lowville in Lewis County and stays in Utica, while the Chicago trust conference goes on. He tells Will Cowles he is swamped with speeches.
Roosevelt addresses the fair at Lyons in Wayne County as the trust conference in Chicago continues.
Brooklyn veterans and a parade outfit

After breakfast with Youngs, Roosevelt speaks to Brooklyn veterans. The Robinsons and Bob Ferguson visit. He writes on political pressure, backs Mazet, asks Avery Andrews what a governor should wear riding in Dewey's parade, and writes Nixon about charges against officials.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Nicholas Murray Butler and Mr. Hollis visit. Roosevelt writes Frank Moss about the Ramapo water scandal, Grant La Farge about the canal scandal, and Samuel Young about the Philippines.
Roosevelt addresses the fair at Riverhead in Suffolk County and tells Lemuel Quigg he backs Mazet in organization politics.
Roosevelt tells Bradley Johnson he is reading Johnson's biography of Nathan Bedford Forrest, and writes George Heins about civil service reform and the Miss Frost complaint.
After stopping in Albany, Roosevelt arrives in Otsego County and speaks at the Cooperstown fair.
Roosevelt speaks at Richfield Springs, goes on to Utica, and leaves for Akron, Ohio.
Roosevelt stops in Cleveland to confer with Mark Hanna, then speaks in Akron to launch the Ohio Republican campaign before heading back to New York. He writes Grant La Farge about the canal scandal.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt tells Root that General Otis is a drag on the American campaign in the islands and that what is needed there is a fighter.
Mrs. Alene, Grant La Farge and Mr. McNaughton visit. Roosevelt sends Arthur Lee good wishes on becoming engaged to Ruth Moore.

Roosevelt addresses the fair in Mineola, Queens County, on his sister Corinne's 38th birthday. Admiral Dewey's flagship Olympia anchors off Staten Island, his first time home since Manila Bay. Roosevelt tells Thomas Slicer he is battling machine politics.
Roosevelt makes an official call on Admiral Dewey aboard the Olympia, while giant letters on the Brooklyn Bridge spell out a welcome. With Admiral Sampson he also tours the Indiana and New Hampshire.
The Olympia sails up the bay and on into the Hudson River, trailed by hundreds of ships in a line five miles long. General Avery Andrews is a guest.

Roosevelt rides at the head of Admiral Dewey's homecoming parade, 35,000 marchers strong, with McKinley and Hanna also taking part; it passes beneath a victory arch where Fifth Avenue meets 23rd Street. His article on Dewey appears in McClure's, and Bamie and her husband take a new home on N Street in Washington.
Canada's Governor General at Sagamore Hill
Governor Roosevelt plays host at Sagamore Hill to Lord Minto, the Governor General of Canada. Robert C. Pruyn signs the guest book.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more.
Dining in honor of Admiral Dewey
In Washington, Roosevelt joins a dinner honoring Admiral George Dewey, hero of Manila Bay. The guest book lists Lord and Lady Minto, Captain Lascelles, Mrs. Leonard Wood and Colonel Arthur Lee.
In New York City, Roosevelt sits down with Benjamin Odell, the state Republican chairman.
Roosevelt is in Binghamton, New York.
Roosevelt addresses crowds in two southern-tier New York towns, Elmira and Waverly.

Roosevelt writes a stack of letters from Albany. He asks H. H. Kohlsaat not to launch a Roosevelt-for-President movement, tells Henry White he is readying for the coming elections, and argues that Leonard Wood has earned a promotion.
Kermit Roosevelt celebrates his tenth birthday. His father writes George Gunton about the franchise tax, Henry Nelson about the Navy, and Martha Selmes a chatty update.
Roosevelt is in Albany on the fifteenth birthday of his niece Eleanor Roosevelt, daughter of his late brother Elliott.
Roosevelt is back at Sagamore Hill.
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's closest political friend, Henry Cabot Lodge, lands back in the United States after a trip to Europe.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
A letter on race and crime
From Albany, Roosevelt writes John William Fox about questions of race, including the crime of rape.
Roosevelt is in Albany as his sister Bamie's son, Sheffield Cowles, turns one.

In New York City, Roosevelt speaks in support of the Fusion slate opposing Tammany Hall. He also presses Elihu Root on reorganizing the Army and doubts to William Chandler that Admiral Howell should lead the Asiatic Squadron.
Breakfast with the bosses, then west
Roosevelt breakfasts in New York with Senator Thomas Platt and Benjamin Odell before boarding a train for Cincinnati. He writes Lodge, whose mother is ill.
Talking Philippines at Cincinnati's Music Hall
On the campaign trail in Ohio, Roosevelt speaks at Cincinnati's Music Hall about American policy in the Philippines.
Roosevelt gives another campaign address in Cincinnati.
Crediting good timing for the governorship
Back in Albany, Roosevelt admits to Charles Wood that coming home from Cuba just as a governor's race opened had much to do with his election.
Special court term to tackle Tammany
After meeting Platt and Odell in New York, Roosevelt orders an extraordinary term of the Supreme Court to hear cases of lawbreaking tied to Tammany Hall. He then heads for Baltimore.

Roosevelt barnstorms western Maryland for Governor Lloyd Lowndes's re-election, from Barton and Frostburg to Cumberland and Hagerstown, with a stop across the line in Piedmont, West Virginia. He assures Lodge the Presidency holds no interest for him.
Frederick by day, Baltimore by night

Roosevelt keeps up the Maryland swing, speaking in Frederick and stopping at Union Bridge, Westminster and Bruceville before an evening address in Baltimore. Grant La Farge and a Mr. McNaughton appear in the guest book.
A forty-first birthday on the stump
Roosevelt marks his forty-first birthday with a speech at Elkton, Maryland, then catches a train home toward Albany.
Guinea pigs and a special prosecutor

A busy letter day in Albany. Roosevelt tells Philemon Sherman he backs expansion, admires Maria Storer's 'goddess' pictures of Edith, and reports that Ted and Kermit are raising guinea pigs. He also names Ansley Wilcox to prosecute the Gardiner case.
Roosevelt thanks General Bradley T. Johnson for a pet possum sent to the Roosevelt children, takes aim at Carl Schurz in a letter to F. B. Cunz, and writes House Speaker David B. Henderson.
Roosevelt speaks to a Republican dinner in Boston. The same day The Century runs his essay on military preparedness.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.
Roosevelt spends Election Day at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt remains at Sagamore Hill the day after the election.
From Albany, Roosevelt tells General Leonard Wood he is still working to win him a brigadier general's rank in the Regular Army, and notes that his own expansionist views are drawing fire.
Roosevelt turns down Albert Mills's invitation for his Boston trip to the Harvard-Yale game, and grumbles to John Rose that papers like the Evening Post are printing falsehoods about him.
In two letters, Roosevelt invites Harper's Weekly editor John Finley to Albany to watch state government up close, and hopes Finley can dig up facts on the canal scandal to answer the Evening Post.
Roosevelt meets legislators Stranahan, Frank Higgins and Jotham Allds in Albany to discuss a special commission on taxation.
Odell, and a state police idea
Roosevelt confers with Odell and asks Nicholas Murray Butler to talk over a bill to create a state constabulary.
Roosevelt takes in the Harvard-Yale football game in Boston.
Roosevelt is in Boston on his youngest son Quentin's second birthday.
Roosevelt addresses students at Yale in New Haven and dines with the university's president, Arthur Twining Hadley.

In New York City Roosevelt holds a hearing on charges against District Attorney Gardiner, huddles with Platt, Odell, Quigg, Slicer and Davies, and addresses the Chamber of Commerce. That same day Garret Hobart, the Vice President, dies, leaving open the office that will soon shadow Roosevelt's future.
Breakfast, then home to Oyster Bay
Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt and Odell in New York and heads out to Oyster Bay that afternoon.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the fourth wedding anniversary of his sister Bamie and William Sheffield Cowles.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
Wilcox named; Dewey's bid frowned on

Back in Albany, Roosevelt names Buffalo lawyer Ansley Wilcox to hear the Gardiner charges and meets the Education Commission. He tells Bamie the fuss around Admiral Dewey, who is angling for the Democratic presidential nomination, is beneath dignity.

Roosevelt urges the state's conservation commission to hire game wardens and protectors among other reforms. He also writes Finley Peter Dunne, whose Mr. Dooley teased that The Rough Riders should have been titled 'Alone in Cuba,' and invites him to visit.
Roosevelt hears arguments on a Supreme Court appointment and writes G. Stanley Hall about bringing children up with firmness and manliness.
No appetite for the Vice Presidency
Roosevelt writes Lemuel Quigg about the police bill and says he will talk with him about the Vice Presidency, a job he does not want.

On their thirteenth anniversary Roosevelt gives Edith a costly watch with a blue face, the gift she liked best of any he had given. He also writes Secretary John D. Long, thanking him on Ted's behalf for a guinea pig named Admiral Dewey that started the boys' brood.
Talking taxes and trusts with economists
Roosevelt confers with economists Jeremiah Jenks and Edwin Seligman, along with Senator Stranahan, about taxation and the trusts.
Roosevelt asks Secretary of State John Hay to consider moving Bellamy Storer from Madrid to Paris or Rome, and writes Leonard Wood about the men backing his promotion.
Lodge presses the Vice Presidency again

In New York, Henry Cabot Lodge once more urges Roosevelt to go after the Republican vice presidential nomination. Roosevelt tells Hugh Leonard, author of a wrestling book, that he has taken up the sport himself.
In New York City, Roosevelt meets with the state's canal commissioners.
Charter revision and the second spot
Over breakfast with Platt and Odell, Roosevelt talks through naming charter revision commissioners and the question of the vice presidential nomination.

Senator Platt tells Roosevelt he officially favors renominating him for governor. Roosevelt's letters range over the Raines liquor law, the Astoria Gas Company, a court vacancy, a breakfast invitation to Butler, and the Vice Presidency.

Roosevelt resolves to let Insurance Superintendent Louis Payn go when his term ends in February, though Boss Platt wants him kept and Payn vows to stay. He sizes up Francis Hendricks as a replacement.
Roosevelt reminds Senator Platt of their breakfast on December 23 at Douglas Robinson's house.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he enjoyed Mr. Dooley's spoof of his book, while marveling at how neatly Dunne finds the weak spots.
Edith writes Cecil Spring-Rice that she misses the old Washington days, and Roosevelt writes Elihu Root about the trusts.
Roosevelt writes Odell about Nicholas Murray Butler and Payn's reappointment, and answers both C. C. Kohlsaat and George Lyman about the vice presidential question.
Saying no to the Vice Presidency

Roosevelt tells Bamie he will turn down the vice presidential offer and mourns the war in South Africa between the British and the Boers. In New York, Edith greets her sister Emily Carow, just home from Italy.
Letters to Conie, Platt and Riis
Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne, Senator Platt about Hissock and Payn, and Jacob Riis about a bill on drug clerks.
Annual Message: clean streams, safe birds

Roosevelt meets with Mazet and wraps up his Annual Message, sending a copy to Platt. The message takes a hard line on big corporations and calls for ending pollution of Adirondack streams and protecting birds and deer.
Roosevelt goes down to New York City and dines at seven at his sister Corinne's home, 422 Madison Avenue. His essay 'Expansion and Peace' appears in the Independent.
Roosevelt is in New York City.
At Corinne's home, Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt and Odell and they discuss removing Louis Payn.
Roosevelt is in Albany for Christmas Eve.
Stockings and present tables at the Mansion

All six Roosevelt children are at the Governor's Mansion for Christmas, with Emily Carow, Bob Ferguson and Speck von Sternberg as guests. The family keeps its yearly routine: stockings first, then breakfast, then a separate table piled with gifts for each child.
Roosevelt writes the Land Office about the Astoria grant and Andrew White about pardons. He tells Lodge that Platt still backs his refusal of the vice presidential slot, though he cannot see why.
Roosevelt thanks his sister Bamie for her generous Christmas presents, a handsome table and a set of knives.
Another breakfast with Platt and Odell
Roosevelt breakfasts again in New York City with Platt and Odell.
Platt wants no fight over Payn

Roosevelt reports to Lodge that Platt is against a battle over Payn. He also writes Bamie, George Lyman about the Vice Presidency, Platt about Payn and Mazet, and Austen Fox about the canal section of his message.
Roosevelt tells John Williams he must dismiss factory inspector O'Leary, and reports to Lodge that Platt now says he should accept the vice presidential nomination.
Platt skips the New Year's reception
Roosevelt holds the customary New Year's Day reception in Albany. Senator Platt stays away to show his displeasure with the governor's course.
Roosevelt writes Platt and Lodge about publisher L. A. Coolidge, and sends New Year's wishes to his friend Cecil Spring-Rice.
Message calls for forest parks and trust curbs

Roosevelt's Annual Message is read to the Legislature. It urges saving the forests, creating preserves in both the Catskills and the Adirondacks, and bold legislation to rein in the trusts. He scolds the Mail and Express for printing the text early.
The Regents Commission releases its report while Roosevelt is in Albany.
Labor law and a leaky newspaper
Roosevelt writes George Gunton about the labor law and asks Frank Mack, an Associated Press man, how to deal with the Mail and Express.
Roosevelt asks Elihu Root for the testimony from an 1895 trial involving Louis Payn.
Roosevelt travels to Concord, New Hampshire, to speak at St. Paul's School.
Roosevelt tells Cuthbert Pound he would name him Superintendent of Insurance if he were sure the Senate would confirm him.
In a letter to William Kimball, Roosevelt names Germany, under its current Kaiser, as the likeliest serious rival of the United States.
Roosevelt informs Cuthbert Pound that he has settled on Judge Charles Saxton as his nominee for Superintendent of Insurance.
Investigation ordered; a funeral in Schenectady

Armed with evidence against Louis Payn, Roosevelt directs Adjutant General Avery Andrews to investigate. He goes to Schenectady for the funeral of Samuel Dana Greene and his wife, then on to New York City that night to see Andrews at his hotel on Fifth Avenue.
Roosevelt writes J. P. Clarke that he very nearly named him to investigate the State Trust Company.
The investigation of Payn is finished. Roosevelt tells James Sheffield that a successor's name is going to the Senate shortly and writes Lyman Abbott about politics.
Roosevelt updates Thomas Slicer on the Payn fight, writes George Holls about merging the state's Regents bodies, and thanks Avery Andrews for his report.
A fan of Mr. Dooley on Dreyfus
Roosevelt tells Finley Peter Dunne how much he enjoys some of his pieces, singling out those on the Dreyfus affair.
State senators confer in Albany over who should follow Payn as insurance chief.
Roosevelt is in Albany on his older sister Bamie's forty-fifth birthday.
Toasting the University of the South
That evening Roosevelt speaks in New York City at an alumni dinner for the Sewanee school, the University of the South.

Over breakfast Roosevelt tells Platt and Odell that Payn must go; Platt rejects Judge Saxton and every name on a list. Roosevelt gives him until January 23 or he will go public. Platt then tells reporters he backs Roosevelt for Vice President. That night Roosevelt speaks at the Union League and Boone and Crockett clubs.
Corinne and Douglas come to Albany
Roosevelt's sister Corinne and her husband Douglas Robinson ride back to Albany with him for a visit.
Ribs caved in by a wrestler

Roosevelt confesses to Will Cowles that he has had too much of the strenuous life lately: a hefty wrestling partner has caved in his ribs. He also writes about the Payn fight, the Vice Presidency, and a scrap young Ted got into at the Albany Academy.

Platt still insists on Payn, so Roosevelt offers Francis Hendricks. Odell holds the bluff to the last moment, then accepts Hendricks. Roosevelt also talks with Robert Bacon about the State Trust Company and tells Bamie he is weighing the Philippines governor-generalship.
Francis Hendricks agrees to become Superintendent of Insurance. Roosevelt writes Platt and Hendricks about the nomination.
The New York Commerce Commission's report is sent to the Legislature. Roosevelt writes Seth Low about the Payn affair and George Lyman about his vice presidential chances.
Speak softly and carry a big stick
Roosevelt announces Hendricks's appointment to the press. Writing to Henry Sprague, he quotes the proverb that would become his best-known motto. He also sends Platt good wishes for his ailing wife.
Roosevelt writes William Sanger about Army reserves, and three correspondents, including Spring-Rice, about the war in South Africa.

Roosevelt crows to Thomas Slicer about winning the Payn fight, tells Captain Bowman McCalla of his pride in the armed forces, and praises Sanger and Young's Philippine work to President McKinley and Elihu Root.
Weighing the Vice Presidency with Lodge
Roosevelt holds a conference on the Regents Bill, writes Arthur Lee about the Boer War, and lays out for Lodge the arguments for and against the Vice Presidency.
The state Senate confirms Francis Hendricks as Superintendent of Insurance, closing Roosevelt's fight over Payn. He writes General Francis Greene about the canals and sends Platt a report.
Vice presidential rumors in the papers

Stories turn up in the newspapers, from no clear source, claiming Republicans will put Roosevelt on the national ticket. He admits to Platt he has thought hard about the Vice Presidency and tells Odell it looks worse the longer he considers it.

Roosevelt holds talks on the trusts with Jenks, Higgins, Stranahan and Nixon, and on the Regents Bill with Seth Low. He tells Lodge, the party committee and Butler plainly that he would rather stay governor than run for Vice President.
Insurance men want him kicked upstairs

Furious over Payn's ouster, New York's big insurance firms team up with other corporations to lean on Platt to be rid of Roosevelt, even by promoting him to the Vice Presidency. Roosevelt writes Lodge about the forces lined up against his staying on.
Roosevelt tells Bamie his opponents want him in the Vice Presidency because they think he can do no harm there, and adds thoughts on the Boer War. He assures L. J. Moore he has no plan to run.
Calling for a stronger Army and Navy

In New York, Roosevelt and Odell meet at the Fifth Avenue Hotel about the Vice Presidency. He then speaks to the state bankers' association and at Carnegie Hall in favor of building up the armed forces, and compliments William Allen White on a Scribner's story.
Roosevelt tells Platt he would sooner teach history at a college than serve as Vice President. He also praises William Howard Taft and writes the hunter Frederick Selous about the Boer War.
Rapid transit for Greater New York

Roosevelt signs the Davis Rapid Transit Act, letting Greater New York's municipal assembly grant franchises for rapid transit lines, and writes about the Backus matter, appointments and city investigations.
Roosevelt writes Grant La Farge about the Fisheries and Forests commission, Lodge about the Vice Presidency, and George Priest about the franchise tax.
Roosevelt lunches with Platt and Odell in the Fifth Avenue Hotel's famous 'Amen Corner,' still insisting he wants another term as governor rather than the Vice Presidency.
Roosevelt meets George Holls and Shaw in Yonkers about the Regents Bill and announces his opposition to the proposed Nicaraguan canal arrangement.

Roosevelt issues a public statement ruling out the vice presidential nomination. It is also his daughter Alice's sixteenth birthday; she has grown nearly as tall as her father. He tells Lyman Powell he is drafting a bill to regulate trusts.
Roosevelt's letters cover the Philippines, Puerto Rico, Long Island coastal land and his refusal of the Vice Presidency. He also advises Robert Bacon on whether to go into politics.
After meeting Odell, Roosevelt writes Josephine Shaw Lowell about errors he may have made, and tells Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan he considers the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty a mistake.

Roosevelt signs the Ahearn School Act, which pays New York City teachers and school workers the salaries they are owed. He writes Butler about the Unification Bill and the game commission, and Albert Shaw about his canal treaty statement.

Roosevelt objects to Will Cowles and Finley Peter Dunne about the plan, favored by McKinley and Hay, for an isthmian canal left open and unfortified. He also writes about his renomination, a forest commission and the state of New York politics.
Roosevelt confers with Limburger, lawyer for the Ramapo water company, and writes Butler. In Washington, Secretary of State John Hay signs an agreement with Nicaragua securing rights for a canal.
Roosevelt writes John Hay himself, laying out his objections to the Nicaraguan canal treaty.
A landmark forest, fish and game law

Roosevelt signs a sweeping law protecting New York's forests, fish and game, rewriting Chapter 31 of the General Laws. It caps his conservation work as governor. He also meets Greene and Hill on canal funding.

Roosevelt confers with Odell about the fish, game and forest preserve boards and speaks to the Foreign Missionary Conference. In a long letter to Josephine Shaw Lowell, he defends his entire term as governor.
In New York City, Roosevelt speaks at three dinners: the Harvard Club, the Buyers Association and the Press Club. He writes Quigg about bills and about backing Platt.

In Buffalo, Roosevelt speaks to the Daughters of the American Revolution and then to the Saturn Club on Washington and what is ideal versus practical in politics. He complains to Bamie of fighting the machine on one flank and reformers on the other.
Roosevelt sees Woodruff and invites Harvard president Charles Eliot to stay with him at the Governor's Mansion.

The Canal Commission's bills go to the Legislature. Roosevelt repeats his case against an open Nicaraguan canal to Will Cowles and explains to Maria Storer why he cannot get involved in naming an American cardinal.

Roosevelt tells Bamie he believes he has run the governorship better than anyone in his lifetime, Grover Cleveland included. He says sorry to Josephine Shaw Lowell for how sharp his previous letter sounded, and tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler he hopes future historians will also write well.

Roosevelt lunches with Odell in Newburgh and speaks on good citizenship at Trinity Episcopal Church. Meanwhile, both McKinley and Senator Hanna are cool to having him as running mate. The six Roosevelt children sit for a group photograph.
Roosevelt writes Ray Tompkins about two appointments, those of Van Duzer and O'Neil.

Roosevelt signs a Penal Code amendment barring anyone from asking a candidate for money in return for a newspaper's or publication's backing. His letters touch city water, the fleet and coastal forts, and the Boer War and Nicaraguan canal.
Roosevelt goes from Albany to New York City for an evening address to the Ohio Society, and tells William O'Neil his financial dealings have blocked his appointment.
Roosevelt is in New York City.

Roosevelt writes Elon Brown about quail hunting, General Greene about the canal bill, and John D. Long about the ship Merrimac, which he bought as Assistant Secretary of the Navy and which the press is now criticizing.
Roosevelt warns Grant La Farge of a determined push to defeat his nominees.
Edith sets off to see San Juan Hill

Edith and her sister Emily leave for Cuba; Edith wants to judge for herself how steep San Juan Hill really is. Roosevelt writes Seth Low about the Ramapo water bill and tells La Farge that lumbermen and cold-storage interests are lobbying against him.
Roosevelt sends Lodge sympathy on the death of his mother, and writes Frederick De Berard about the Ramapo bill, a disputed plan involving upstate land for a New York City reservoir.
Roosevelt is the dinner speaker for West Side Republicans at their club in New York and writes A. J. Sage about Australian troops in the Boer War.

Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt and Odell in New York and tells William O'Neil he will not get the appointment. In Cuba, Edith and Emily arrive by ship at Havana, where Governor General Leonard Wood meets them.
Roosevelt is in New York City.
Edith finds San Juan Hill gentler than expected

Edith writes Ethel that San Juan Hill is less steep and imposing than she imagined. Roosevelt promises General Henry Evans he will help the family of Marshall, his Rough Rider aide, and writes Spring-Rice, James Carter and Lodge.
Roosevelt asks Princeton professor Woodrow Wilson to suggest someone who could assist him with appointments, and writes about Puerto Rican sovereignty and the Ramapo charter.

Roosevelt signs a change to the Stock Corporation Law requiring companies to keep complete stock books open to shareholders and creditors. He writes George Bird Grinnell about conservation appointments.
Hoping for a state trust bill
Roosevelt tells Henry Lincoln he would like New York to take up legislation on trusts, and compliments J. M'Carthy on his books.
From Cuba, Edith writes Spring-Rice about bright flowers and pastel houses. Roosevelt applauds an article by Francis Cabot Lowell about political bosses.

Roosevelt speaks to the Irish-American Friendly Sons society on St. Patrick's Day, and his essay 'The Best and the Good' appears in The Churchman. He writes about objections to his forest bill, volunteer factory inspectors and the Ramapo charter.
Roosevelt explains to James C. Carter why New York City politics is so difficult, and writes Frederick Selous about the Boer War and South Africa's troubles.
Roosevelt tells Butler that the Morgan Bill was not submitted in proper form.

Roosevelt signs the Davis Palisades Act, providing land, money and a managing commission for a park shared with New Jersey along the Hudson's Palisades. He also writes family members after the death of Aunt Laura.
Roosevelt signs a law requiring Indian children on the Cattaraugus and Allegany reservations to attend school, and writes Joe Bishop and George Lyman about getting the Ramapo Bill passed.
Canal foes and a book on trusts
Roosevelt writes General Greene about feeling against the canal bill around the state, and tells George Gunton he is interested in his book Trusts and the Public.
Roosevelt tells Congressman Lucius Littauer that being governor counts for more than being Vice President, and asks Lyman Abbott to talk over the Ramapo Bill.

Roosevelt goes down to New York City that evening to review the Military Athletic League's show at Madison Square Garden. He writes Odell about the mortgage tax bill and tells Stephen Thayer he supports the Morgan Bill.
A free hand on the Bath home
Roosevelt thanks Platt for letting him handle the Bath Soldiers' Home question as he sees fit.
Roosevelt tells S. Fred Nixon he opposes the Bath Home Bill, calling it thoroughly vicious.
Roosevelt tells Eugene Ware he enjoyed his book of verse, Rhymes of Ironquill.
Roosevelt's essay 'Character and Success' appears in The Outlook.

Roosevelt signs a law outlawing commercial prize fights. In his letters he again declines the vice presidential nomination, discusses the Elsberg bill and the power of Platt and Odell, and complains about the New York Times man in Albany.

Admiral Dewey declares himself a candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination, to the amusement of a doubtful public. Roosevelt invites Seth Low to lunch and writes Mark Hanna about convention tickets.

Roosevelt signs the Tenement House Commission Act, letting him name an unpaid panel to study tenement conditions and propose a housing code. He speaks at an Assembly memorial for former Governor Roswell Flower and hurries bills along before adjournment.
Roosevelt signs the Fallows Anti-Ramapo Act, which bars New York City's water commissioner from signing water contracts without approval from city boards and both the mayor and comptroller.
On the session's last day, Roosevelt signs a cap of six percent a year on loan interest and the General City Act. He writes Interior Secretary Ethan Allen Hitchcock about the Hudson Palisades.
Breakfast and lunch in New York
Roosevelt breakfasts at the Fifth Avenue Hotel with Platt and Odell, then lunches with Seth Low and Hammond at Corinne's house on Madison Avenue.

It is Archie's sixth birthday. Roosevelt signs another bill to promote sugar beet growing, tells Lodge he has run an honest, efficient administration, and writes Leonard Wood about Dewey, Cuba and Wood's new baby.
Roosevelt writes Truman Backus about charges made against him and tells James H. Wilson he has no wish to be Vice President.

Roosevelt signs a law creating a state hospital for crippled and deformed children. Angry at Admiral Dewey's switch to the Democrats, he scorns him to Lodge, and writes about corporate danger, appointments and the Vice Presidency.
Roosevelt signs a bill funding surveys and cost estimates for improving three state canals: the Erie, the Oswego and the Champlain. He tells Joe Bishop the machine wants him out as governor.
Roosevelt hears arguments on a compromise school bill and meets Ellsworth and Nixon. He writes Conie about the meals with Platt and Odell held at her house.
Hours for drug clerks; Cromwell in waiting

Roosevelt signs laws chartering the state medical association and setting hours and working conditions for pharmacists and drug clerks. He asks Robert Bridges when his Cromwell will come out as a book.

Roosevelt signs a bill letting him appoint a commission to study New York City's government. He writes and wires about a strike by Italian immigrant workers at the Croton dam, and writes Robert De Forest about the Tenement House Commission he chairs.

The Republican State Convention picks Roosevelt, with Platt, Depew and Odell, as a delegate-at-large to the national convention in Philadelphia. Editor Dana of the Sun advises him to accept if the party wants him. He writes about the Croton riots and strike.

Roosevelt signs a law that no child may be barred from a New York public school because of race or color, repealing local authority to run separate schools for Black children. He tells Greene that skipping Philadelphia would look like running away.

Roosevelt signs a Labor Law change requiring employers to provide seats for waitresses and women in factories and let them use them. He writes Lincoln Steffens about his McClure's article on Roosevelt.
Roosevelt spends the evening in Schenectady and writes Avery Andrews, Seth Low about the street railroad bill, and Elihu Root about the Turks.
Roosevelt holds a hearing on the Remsen bills in Albany, then goes to New York City for an evening at the Ecumenical Mission Conference.
Roosevelt breakfasts with Senator Platt in New York City.

Roosevelt signs a truth-in-labeling law for linen. Flooded with letters urging him to run, he tells Lodge he will accept the vice presidential nomination or the Philippine governorship, yet tells Senator Redfield Proctor the same day he will refuse.

Roosevelt signs a bill letting New York City repair and expand its county courthouse under contract safeguards. He thanks his old Maine guide Bill Sewall for maple sugar and writes about the Boer War and the family.

Roosevelt signs a batch of laws on Fifth Avenue stages, transfer-tax appraisers, pharmacies and municipal civil service, and announces who will serve on the commission to revise New York City's charter. That evening he leaves for Chicago.
In Chicago Roosevelt gives speeches, saying he can serve the country best by staying governor of New York.
Roosevelt speaks about General Ulysses S. Grant in Grant's hometown of Galena, Illinois.
Roosevelt travels from Chicago back to Albany.

Roosevelt tells Bamie he has no wish for the Vice Presidency despite Lodge's view, and fears to Brander Matthews he may lose the governorship. He contributes $50 to a fund for a soldier who died in the Croton riots and praises Root for upholding the Monroe Doctrine.
Writing for boys; dinner with young Churchill

Roosevelt's essay 'The American Boy' runs in St. Nicholas. He sends John Burroughs a copy of Hunting Trips of a Ranchman and tells Platt he has appointed the Charter Commission. Around this time, Corinne later recalled, he dined at her house with General Joe Wheeler and a young Winston Churchill, talking mostly about the Boer War.
Roosevelt signs the Hallock Bird Protection Act. His letters cover sweatshops, a pardon he refuses, mistreatment at Elmira prison, and his plan to sign the Soldiers' Home Bill.
Roosevelt signs the Davis School Act over New York City's objection, and writes Ansley Wilcox about the Democrats' choice for governor and Bird Coler's chances.
Roosevelt signs the Elsberg City College Act and two Remsen acts to open and improve Bedford and Remsen avenues in Brooklyn. He attends a dinner for the city's Charter Commission.

Roosevelt signs the Platt Act, freeing the veterans' home at Bath from oversight by the State Board of Charities. He tells John Burroughs that Ted is staying with him, and writes Charles Skinner about prison-made furniture for schools.
Roosevelt writes Paul Dana about the vice presidential nomination and Platt about the street railroad bill.
Roosevelt and Edith head to Washington. Before leaving he writes about sweatshops, hunting, attacks on him, a wildlife bill and the nomination.
In Washington, Roosevelt and Edith call on John Hay, John D. Long and Elihu Root, and visit the White House.
Fort Myer and a full dinner table
Roosevelt lunches with Arthur Lee and visits Fort Myer. At dinner he is with the Roots, the Hays, the Cowleses, the Longs, the Thomas Nelson Pages and Mrs. Tuckerman.

Roosevelt tours Congress with Lodge and is guest of honor at a White House dinner given by President McKinley. Talking with Senators Foraker and Chandler, Root, Long and the President, he learns they do not want him as Vice President, which only makes him want it more.
Roosevelt's article 'The Eighth and Ninth Commandments in Politics' appears in The Outlook while he is in Washington.
Roosevelt and Edith return home to Oyster Bay.
Diplomat Henry White is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Alford Cooley about civil service appointments and Joe Bishop about the Charter Commission.
Roosevelt speaks to the Hungarian Republican Club in New York. He turns down a speaking date in Ottawa and congratulates General Samuel Young on regaining his rank as major general of volunteers.

Roosevelt again tells Maria Storer he cannot step into church politics, informs William Allen White he has signed the Davis Bill, and writes George W. Perkins of New York Life about the Palisades Park Commission.

Roosevelt tells Frank Scott he is getting The Strenuous Life ready to publish. Other letters cover civil service exam exemptions, the convention, the attorney generalship, and uniform colors with Speck von Sternberg.
Roosevelt is in Albany while Ted continues his stay with naturalist John Burroughs.
Roosevelt writes about controversies in Cuba and the Civil Service Act, and thanks John Burroughs for hosting Ted.
Roosevelt spends the day between Sagamore Hill and Albany.

In the evening Roosevelt goes to New York City to speak about municipal finance at a Merchants' Association dinner for William King. His letters touch civil service, the Vice Presidency, ranching and the West.
From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt writes thirteen letters, on topics from citizenship for Indians, Cuba and labor to the Vice Presidency and an honorary degree from Harvard.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
Rough Rider friend Bob Ferguson is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes William Polk of Louisiana about New York's civil service.
Roosevelt is in New York City for the Memorial Day parade.
Guided by Jacob Riis and Reynolds, Roosevelt tours New York sweatshops, then joins his old regiment for a Rough Riders reunion dinner held at the Union League Club.
Governor Roosevelt spends the day in New York City walking through garment sweatshops alongside his friend Jacob Riis, the reformer and reporter.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Roosevelt receives Major H. H. Llewellyn as a guest at Sagamore Hill.
A day of letters in Albany
Back at his desk in Albany, Roosevelt sends off a stack of letters ranging from New York tenements and Cuba to Cromwell, civil service, and Spanish cannon taken in the late war.
Going over the Ice Trust case
In Albany, Roosevelt and Attorney General John C. Davies examine the Ice Trust case together, and he writes friends about fish and game law and the men who should run that commission.
Off to Oyster Bay after a busy morning

Roosevelt writes a flurry of letters on civil service, labor and the Philippines, among them one urging Platt to accept Professor Cuthbert Pound for the Civil Service Commission, then heads for Oyster Bay. He also writes his sister Corinne, whose son Ted Robinson is ill with diphtheria.
Roosevelt addresses the students of St. Paul's School in Concord, New Hampshire, then dines in New York City with Senator Platt and Benjamin Odell.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Sagamore Hill opens for the season

The guest book marks the opening of the house for summer. Roosevelt tells Charles Wheeler he has settled on Professor Pound for the Civil Service Commission and writes Lodge about Platt and the Ice Trust.
Sunday visit from Butler and Holls
Nicholas Murray Butler and George Holls spend Sunday with Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.
Lunch at the Union League, letters on the vice presidency

Mrs. Dean Sage is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt lunches in New York with Greene, Butler, Holls and a Mr. Elisberg, then takes the evening train to Albany. His letters weigh the governorship against the vice presidency and pass Lodge some ideas for a labor plank.

After an interview on the Ice Trust in Albany, Roosevelt travels to Rochester and gives an address titled "Promise and Performance" at the university. He tells General Greene the corporate-backed party organization still badly wants him on the ticket.
Roosevelt travels from Rochester to Caledonia, New York, to dedicate a monument to the town's soldiers, then returns to Rochester.
Roosevelt lunches with Benjamin Odell at the Union League in New York and goes out to Oyster Bay that afternoon.

Roosevelt and Edith head to the Republican National Convention in Philadelphia and check into the Hotel Walton. Reporters crowd Platt's room asking if he will run. When the Kansas delegation's leader calls on him, Roosevelt gives in and says he will take the nomination.
Delegates from Pennsylvania and California seek Roosevelt out in Philadelphia. He warns Hermann Kohlsaat that a fight is ahead.
Mark Hanna reaches Philadelphia furious that nobody has asked President McKinley about the choice for vice president.
After lunch with Lodge and Edith, Roosevelt offers to pull his name from the vice presidential contest, and Edith approves. He softens the statement, however, and the nomination still looks certain.
A dramatic entrance at the convention

The Republican National Convention opens with Mark Hanna as temporary chairman. Roosevelt, in his black hat, strides slowly into the hall as heads turn. He sits as one of New York's four delegates-at-large with Platt, Odell and Chauncey Depew.
Thucydides after a day of maneuvering

Roosevelt walks Lodge, the newly chosen convention chairman, to the podium. Out of view, Platt's ally Matthew Quay rewrites the rules to clear the way for Roosevelt. That night in his hotel room he reads Thucydides.

Pressed by the Platt machine and by Roosevelt backers across the country, Hanna yields. McKinley is renominated with 926 votes, and Roosevelt is named his running mate with 925. Roosevelt lunches with General Greene, addresses the convention, and wires the President.
Home, and a visit to Riis
Roosevelt and Edith leave Philadelphia for Oyster Bay. He calls on Jacob Riis, who is sick.
Writing Seth Low about the machine
From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt tells Seth Low he had turned the state machine upside down and made it act against what he wanted.
Roosevelt writes Senator Platt to ask whether he is turning his back on General Greene.

Roosevelt writes a string of letters on the nomination, telling Bamie he could not have avoided it and is moved by how it came about. In the evening he goes into New York to attend a gathering of the AAAS, the national science association.
Roosevelt goes to Cambridge for his class's twentieth reunion at Harvard and writes that his campaign is now under way.

Back at Oyster Bay from Cambridge, Roosevelt offers himself to Mark Hanna for the campaign, saying he is fit and ready to be worked hard. Other letters cover the Philippines, the governorship and a pending case.
At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt lunches with Seth Low, sees Ansley Wilcox, and dines with Greene and Goddard. He writes John McDonough about Germany.
Roosevelt writes Frank Travers to arrange the Oyster Bay committee for his July 12 notification ceremony, then goes to New York for the afternoon.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill; nothing further is recorded.
Whistle-stops on the way to Oklahoma
Heading for Oklahoma City, Roosevelt's train pauses at Newkirk in Oklahoma Territory and at a string of Kansas towns: Newton, Peabody, Florence, Emporia, Osage City, Lawrence and Holliday.
Rough Riders reunite in Oklahoma City
Roosevelt joins his old regiment for the Rough Rider reunion in Oklahoma City.
The Rough Rider reunion wraps up in Oklahoma City and Roosevelt boards a train for Chicago. Bob Ferguson is with him.
From Chicago Roosevelt goes to Galesburg, Illinois, for an afternoon speech.
Hanna, Canton and dinner with McKinley
Traveling east, Roosevelt confers with Mark Hanna in Cleveland, speaks at Canton, Ohio, and sits down to dinner with President McKinley.

Roosevelt gets back to Sagamore Hill in the afternoon to find the children still waiting to celebrate the Fourth. A thunderstorm holds things up, but at eight o'clock the first rocket climbs, and the fireworks run until ten. His letters plan the notification ceremony and tell Hanna he prefers set speeches to train tours.
A quiet day at home; nothing more is noted.
Dr. Alexander Lambert and his wife are guests. Roosevelt's letters range over Rough Riders appearing with him in South Dakota, Black regiments in Cuba, the merchant marine, and Bryan.
Writing Adelbert Moot about speaking engagements in the West, Roosevelt says he believes the region likes him.
Roosevelt's sisters, Corinne Robinson and Anna Cowles, come to Sagamore Hill.
At Sagamore Hill a committee led by Senator Edward Wolcott officially tells Roosevelt he is the Republican choice for Vice President.

Roosevelt speaks in Mineola as the cornerstone is laid for Nassau County's first courthouse. Lodge is a guest at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt promises Leonard Wood he will raise a brigadier general's star with McKinley.

Roosevelt writes Odell and Arthur Cosby about removing Gardiner, tells Harvard's Charles Eliot that his nephew Ted Robinson will enroll, and explains to Silas Burt why he accepted the nomination. He also sends a letter to Alice Lee, cousin to his late first wife.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill in the evening, bound for St. Paul, Minnesota.
Roosevelt spends the day on the train to Minnesota.
Addressing Republican clubs in St. Paul
That evening Roosevelt speaks to the convention of the National Republican League in St. Paul.
From Milwaukee Roosevelt continues to Chicago and shares dinner with Hanna at the Chicago Club.
Back east to Greene and Odell
Arriving in New York, Roosevelt dines with General Greene and Benjamin Odell at the Union League before heading home to Oyster Bay.
Writing about China and the Boxers
Roosevelt tells Odell he will not campaign in the Northeast, and writes Root, Speck von Sternberg and Spring-Rice about the Boxer uprising in China, the Boers and his candidacy.
Roosevelt writes William Rockhill to congratulate him on his new diplomatic post in China.
Roosevelt is at home; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt addresses the Jewish Chautauqua Society in Atlantic City, New Jersey, and stays that night at the Union League in New York.
Breakfast with Wood, worries about his voice

Roosevelt breakfasts in New York with Leonard Wood, Alford Cooley and Gherardi Davis, then returns to Oyster Bay. He confides to Odell that his voice may not hold out, and passes on grumbling from Buffalo.

Colonel and Mrs. Alexander Brodie are among the guests. Roosevelt writes Root that the army's blue shirts are impractical, writes Paul Dana about trouble at Elmira prison, and tells Arthur Lee about his hopes for British-American unity.
Austin Wadsworth visits Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Odell about the governorship, tells Winthrop Chanler that Bryan has to lose, and writes William H. Lewis about race relations.

Roosevelt confers with Attorney General Davies about both the Gardiner matter and the Ice Trust. Bellamy Storer offers to rent him his Washington house should he become Vice President, and Roosevelt urges McKinley to make Wood a brigadier general in the regular army.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's "Promise and Performance." Walter Goodwin and Bob Ferguson are at Sagamore Hill.
On the Brockway case and a military aide
Roosevelt writes Platt about the Brockway case and Lord Minto about Colonel Kitson as a military aide.

In New York Roosevelt sees Hanna, has lunch at the Union League with Odell and calls on General Greene before going home. He asks John Hay to name Lodge's son Bay to the consulship at Venice. Butler and William Dudley Foulke visit.
Naval reserve camp, a throat doctor
Roosevelt stops by the camp of Brooklyn's naval reservists on Centre Island. He tells George Holls that all the speaking has worn on his throat, and he is seeing a doctor.
Joseph Bucklin Bishop is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes William Byrne about Cuba and sends G. H. Putnam word of Ansley Wilcox's report on the Gardiner case.
