Weak spots in the Democratic campaign
Roosevelt points out to Robert Burch where the Democrats' campaign is faltering and writes Ansley Wilcox about his report on Gardiner, the Buffalo district attorney accused of corruption.
Roosevelt goes into New York in the afternoon to meet Odell. His letters touch on Cuban marriage law, Platt and the governorship, and his speaking schedule.
Roosevelt writes Jacob Riis to thank him for the piece on him that Riis published in the Review of Reviews.
A day at home with nothing else on the record.
On his wife Edith's 39th birthday, Roosevelt is in New York calling on Hanna and lunching with Odell and Platt. He writes William Howard Taft about the nomination.
Andrew D. White and George Holls visit Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill. He shares his political outlook with Alfred Thayer Mahan and tells Lodge he will not speak in Boston.
Roosevelt takes his sons off on a fishing trip and writes Hanna about German-American voters.
Back from fishing, a pick for governor
Home from the fishing trip, Roosevelt suggests Judge Charles Andrews to Platt as Republican candidate for governor and answers false charges made against him in the campaign.
In New York Roosevelt confers with Attorney General Davies and with Hanna, then returns to Oyster Bay, where Nicholas Murray Butler is a guest. He tells Odell he will not speak at the State Fair.
Ferdinand Becker, Bob Ferguson and a Mr. Goodrich visit Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is recorded.
Van Wyck charges and a campaign route
On Ethel's ninth birthday, Roosevelt is in New York, going over charges against Augustus Van Wyck with Davies, mapping his campaign tour with Hanna, and lunching with Odell before heading home.
Douglas Robinson's son Monroe is a guest. Roosevelt compliments Robert Grant on his novel Unleavened Bread and writes Henry Purroy about the Ice Trust and Van Wyck.
Sizing up the election for Platt
Roosevelt writes Platt about cannon and how the coming election looks.

Roosevelt speaks at a church fair in Oyster Bay. With opponents attacking his military service, he asks Root for documents on his record and tells Charles Burke he will answer with the letters that recommended him for the Medal of Honor.
Roosevelt meets Mark Hanna in New York.

Roosevelt goes fishing again. In Boston, Lodge's son Bay marries Matilda Davis. Roosevelt confides to Bamie his worries about the election and party feuds, and tells Henry Payne he must ration his speeches to save his voice.
"I shot him in the left breast"
Answering Democratic charges that he shot a Spanish soldier in the back on San Juan Hill, Roosevelt writes Henry Turner that the man was hit from the front.
A night at the White House

Roosevelt sleeps at the White House in Washington. He writes Platt that either Root or Charles Andrews would make a fine choice for governor, insisting the next governor must be more than an agent of the organization.
Roosevelt returns to Oyster Bay, where Speck von Sternberg and Dr. Alexander Lambert are guests.
Roosevelt spends time with Speck von Sternberg, writes David Sickels backing Root for governor, and tells Wood he has raised the brigadier general question with McKinley.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Arthur Lee and his wife visit Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt spends the afternoon in the city. He tells Butler that Root has refused to run for governor, leaving Odell as the choice.

Mrs. Leonard Wood, her daughter Luisita and Bob Ferguson are guests. Roosevelt assures Whitelaw Reid that Odell is honest and will be a good governor, and writes Seth Low and George Holls in the same vein.
No activity is recorded beyond a day at home.
Roosevelt confers in New York with Hanna and Greene. He warns Lodge that voters in the West are indifferent and that Odell will get the nomination for governor.
Letters on Cuba, China and a wedding
Roosevelt writes on Cuba to Indianapolis News editor Charles Williams, turns aside an offered judgeship with Wheeler Peckham, and sends Lodge his thoughts on Bay's wedding and on Odell and Platt.
Roosevelt asks Adjutant General Henry Corbin for reports backing up his military record and writes Wood again about Cuban marriage law.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.
Off to Albany as the campaign takes shape
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Albany. The battle lines of 1900 are drawn: Democrats run against imperialism and the trusts, while Republicans point to good times and a full dinner pail.

The hearing on charges against Buffalo prosecutor Gardiner takes place in Albany. To George Van Ness, Roosevelt writes about expansion and the Philippine question, and answers Louis Viereck's charge that he is hostile to German-Americans.
Roosevelt joins Chicago's Labor Day parade and gives a speech titled "The Labor Question."
At the state convention in Saratoga
Roosevelt addresses the Republican state convention of New York in Saratoga.
Roosevelt gives a speech in Detroit.
Roosevelt speaks eleven times in a single day in Michigan, with stops at Lansing, Owosso, Saginaw, Bay City and Grand Rapids among others.
Toward Chicago as Galveston is struck
On his way to Chicago, Roosevelt speaks at Holland, Michigan, and at Madison and South Bend, Indiana, with Bob Ferguson along. That day a hurricane hits Galveston, Texas, killing some 7,000 people.
Chicago speech and lunch with Payne
Roosevelt speaks in Chicago and lunches with Henry Payne.
Roosevelt gives speeches at La Crosse, Wisconsin.
Roosevelt campaigns across South Dakota, speaking in Yankton and Sioux Falls with shorter stops in Canton, Vermillion, Madison and Flandreau.
Two South Dakota towns, Brookings and Huron, hear Roosevelt speak.
Ted turns 13 while his father campaigns
Roosevelt speaks at Watertown, Redfield and Aberdeen, South Dakota, on his son Ted's 13th birthday.
Into North Dakota; Ted off to Groton
Roosevelt speaks at Ortonville and Wheaton, Minnesota, then at Webster and Fargo, North Dakota. Back east, Edith takes Ted to begin at Groton School in Massachusetts.

Roosevelt speaks at Casselton, Tower City and Bismarck, North Dakota. He writes Senator Edward Wolcott his formal letter accepting the vice presidential nomination, including a history of American expansion.
Roosevelt speaks in the North Dakota towns of New Salem and Mandan and in Miles City, Montana, then spends the afternoon in Medora, his old ranching town. That evening he gives a speech in Dickinson.
Roosevelt makes stops across Montana and speaks that evening in Helena.
Roosevelt speaks in Butte, Montana, and in the mining towns around it.
Roosevelt campaigns in northern Utah, speaking in Ogden, Brigham City and Logan.
Roosevelt speaks in Salt Lake City and rides in a parade there.
Roosevelt speaks at Evanston and Green River, Wyoming, and again at Ogden, Utah. James K. Gracie is recorded as a guest.
Roosevelt's Wyoming stops include Laramie, Rawlins and Medicine Bow.
Roosevelt speaks at Boulder and Denver. He writes Corinne that Cabot and Nannie Lodge have joined him, with a little horseback riding between the speeches.

At Cripple Creek, Colorado, a hired gang of "muckers" attacks Roosevelt's train, and Rough Riders step in to protect him. He goes on to speak at Victor. George Fred Williams later claims Roosevelt was drunk there, a charge without any truth.
Roosevelt campaigns through Pueblo, Florence, Salida and Granite in Colorado. It is his sister Corinne's 39th birthday.
Roosevelt makes seventeen stops in Kansas in a single day.
Roosevelt speaks his way across Kansas from El Dorado to Kansas City.

Roosevelt leaves Kansas City for Nebraska in the evening, and The Century prints his essay "Civic Helpfulness". While McKinley stays home on his front porch, Roosevelt crisscrosses the country; one typical day runs from a 7 a.m. breakfast to midnight, with a dozen speeches broken up by reading Scott, history and ornithology, dictating letters and meeting the press.
Roosevelt speaks thirteen times across Nebraska, at McCook, Fairmont, Hastings, Tecumseh and Beatrice among other towns.
Roosevelt campaigns at Lexington and in Bryan's hometown of Lincoln, Nebraska.
Roosevelt speaks at Deadwood in the Black Hills and at Alliance.
After stops all over Nebraska, Roosevelt gives an evening address in Omaha.
Roosevelt speaks in the Iowa cities of Cedar Rapids, Waterloo and Davenport, then crosses to Rock Island, Illinois.
After speeches at Elgin and Chicago, Roosevelt writes Lodge disputing reports that he was drunk on the stump in September, and assures William Walton he holds nothing against Quakers.
Roosevelt gives a Sunday talk to the congregation of Chicago's Trinity Dutch Reformed Church and is the dinner guest of the party's national campaign chiefs at the Chicago Club.
Roosevelt gives a speech in Joliet and stops in towns all over Illinois.
In St. Louis Roosevelt addresses the city's Merchants Exchange, then joins an evening rally parade.
Roosevelt speaks at Fort Wayne and Lafayette, Indiana, as his son Kermit turns 11 back home.
Roosevelt speaks in Indianapolis. His niece Eleanor Roosevelt turns 16.
Roosevelt speaks at Evansville, Indiana, and writes Donald Dickinson about Bryan and the Ice Trust.
Roosevelt speaks in Louisville and at stops around Kentucky. Finley Peter Dunne's "Mr. Dooley" lampoons his campaign.
A Kentucky Sunday with Colonel Alexander

Near Lexington, Kentucky, Roosevelt visits Colonel A. J. Alexander. He tells Lodge that a round-robin letter has been published attacking George Fred Williams, who had charged Roosevelt with drunkenness.
Roosevelt makes ten speeches in a day, including at Lexington and Covington. Nellie and Hope Tyler appear in the guest record.
Roosevelt is in Dayton and gives a speech at Columbus, Ohio. He writes Bamie, with whom Edith and the children are staying.
Roosevelt speaks in Toledo and Cleveland.
Roosevelt speaks at Canton, Ohio, then at Wheeling and Parkersburg in West Virginia. It is the second birthday of his nephew Sheffield Cowles.
Roosevelt's train stops across West Virginia, and he speaks at Hinton.
Roosevelt speaks at the Music Hall in Baltimore and leaves for New York City.
Back home between campaign swings, Roosevelt has his niece Corinne Robinson as a guest.
Roosevelt opens his New York swing with speeches at Newburgh and Kingston.

Roosevelt's train leaves Kingston at 9 a.m. and works through the Catskills and the upper Susquehanna, with stops from five minutes to an hour at Phoenicia, Pine Hill, Fleischmanns, Arkville, Roxbury, Stamford, Bloomville, Oneonta, Unadilla, Sidney and others, ending at Norwich at 6:20.
Roosevelt speaks in Auburn and Syracuse.
After speeches at Little Falls and Schenectady, Roosevelt dines at the Fifth Avenue Hotel in New York and addresses a rally at Madison Square Garden.
Roosevelt turns 42 making train stops across New York and speaking at night in Binghamton. He writes Odell about Mayor Van Wyck's reply to the Ice Trust charges.
From Binghamton Roosevelt sends Odell a telegram on the Ice Trust and the mayor.
Roosevelt speaks at Cortland, Ithaca and Elmira, and wires Odell again about Van Wyck.
Corning to Rochester in one day

Opening the day with 45 minutes in Corning, from 8:25 that morning, Roosevelt works west through Bath, Wayland, Livonia, Avon, Geneseo and Mount Morris to Rochester, loops through Canandaigua, Geneva and Penn Yan, and is back in Rochester by 8 p.m.
Into Buffalo, and the campaign by the numbers

Roosevelt works west through Brockport, Medina, Albion, Lockport, North Tonawanda and Niagara Falls, reaching Buffalo at 4 p.m. By November 3 his tally will be 673 speeches in 567 towns across 24 states, 21,209 miles traveled, and an estimated three million listeners.
Roosevelt speaks at Batavia and Jamestown and telegraphs Attorney General Davies about how the election is to be run.
A rain-soaked finale at the Garden

In New York Roosevelt breakfasts at the Lawyers Club and is received at the Produce Exchange. After a parade, a mass meeting with fireworks is held for him at Madison Square Garden in a downpour. Edith, Alice and Kermit are there; Ted is away at Groton.
As Roosevelt rests at Sagamore Hill, New York police chief William Devery tells his men to ignore the governor's orders for honest elections.

Roosevelt speaks at a reception and sends sharp letters to District Attorney Asa Bird Gardiner and Mayor Van Wyck: cancel the police chief's order, or face the consequences. He also writes the county sheriff. The order is withdrawn, and New York City votes fairly.

Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay. McKinley and Roosevelt beat Bryan decisively, 292 electoral votes to 155, with about 7.2 million popular votes to the Democrats' 6.36 million. Benjamin Odell wins the governorship of New York.
Edward Marshall of the New York World drives out to Sagamore Hill early in the morning to tell Roosevelt he has won.
Oyster Bay's townspeople come to Sagamore Hill to serenade their newly elected Vice President.
Bamie and Margaret Roosevelt visit. Roosevelt thanks Democrats who crossed over to vote for him and tells his uncle James Bulloch he has received more than 1,000 congratulatory telegrams.
With John McIlhenny as a guest, Roosevelt writes McKinley and Hanna on the question of church lands in Cuba, Hay on politics, and George Lyman on the election returns.
Roosevelt moves between Sagamore Hill and New York City; no details are recorded.
Roosevelt lunches at the Union League with Odell, Riis, Seth Low, Butler, Holls, Albert Shaw, Brander Matthews, Arthur von Briesen and others, then leaves for Albany.
In Albany Roosevelt goes over the Ice Trust prosecution with Davies, then goes to Syracuse for an afternoon speech.

Roosevelt writes Charles Eliot about the Philippine fighting, tells George Smalley he opposes Hearst and Croker, writes Lyman Abbott against Coler, and sends letters on the Ice Trust and the police bill.
Roosevelt confers with Hayes, attorney for the New York World, and writes the board of the Long Island State Hospital about the Backus investigation.
Unable to attend the National Irrigation Congress, Roosevelt sends regrets along with ideas on replanting forests and building dams. Helen Cutting is a guest.
Helen Roosevelt is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is noted.

Quentin turns three. West Virginia's congressmen have sent Alice a pet bear, which she calls Jonathan Edwards in honor of the famous preacher in Edith's family tree. Roosevelt writes friends abroad about Anglo-German relations, China and hunting, and praises Sienkiewicz's novels.
Roosevelt issues a statement that the telegram the New York World ran early was not the version he meant to release. He writes Joe Bishop about the Ice Trust.
Roosevelt writes Philip Garrett about citizenship for American Indians.
Ted the fighter, Kermit's guinea pigs

Roosevelt tells Edward Martin that Ted sings in the Groton choir, captains his dormitory football team and is a scrapper, and that Kermit has named guinea pigs after Admiral Dewey, Dr. Johnson, Bishop Doane and Fighting Bob Evans. Other letters treat free silver with Grover Cleveland and the constabulary bill.
Clearing Van Wyck, and "fat and stiff"

Roosevelt dismisses the Ice Trust charges against Mayor Van Wyck. In a pile of letters he congratulates Arthur Lee on winning a seat in Parliament, praises Selous's new book, and confesses to the old hunter that he is getting "fat and stiff."

Roosevelt goes from New York to Philadelphia and speaks that evening at a Union League dinner honoring President McKinley. He writes old Rough Rider H. K. Love, now in the Philippines, about the governor-generalship there.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the fifth wedding anniversary of his sister Bamie.
Roosevelt writes Edward Sanford Martin a long, largely autobiographical letter about Ted's scrapes at Groton, and sends Anna Davis sympathy on the death of her husband, Senator Cushman Davis.
A Washington house and a lion hunt

Roosevelt meets Platt and Odell in Albany and goes to Oyster Bay that afternoon. He assures Bellamy Storer he bears Mrs. Storer no grudge and works out rent for their Washington house, and tells Philip Stewart he wants to plan a mountain lion hunt.
Lieutenant Crimmins and Bob Ferguson are guests.
Roosevelt divides the day between Sagamore Hill and New York City.
Roosevelt and Edith go to and fro between Sagamore Hill and Albany, while the children stay home with their nurse Mame and Miss Young, who is Alice's governess.
Bob Ferguson, Mr. and Mrs. Grant La Farge, Jennings Cox and John Elliott are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt and Edith mark fourteen years of marriage at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt insists to Andrew D. White that he is no candidate for President and that the topic should be dropped. He also turns down a pardon for a man named Emmons.
Roosevelt tells his nephew Ted Robinson to put schoolwork ahead of athletics. Other letters cover his charitable interests, Indian citizenship, and a favor he will not ask of Odell.
A baby named for Leonard Wood
Roosevelt asks Root to come to a dinner honoring J. P. Morgan and tells Wood that a son born at Sagamore Hill to the family coachman has been named Leonard Wood Hall in his honor.

Roosevelt writes about inauguration seats, an Annapolis appointment and hunting gear, asks Major James Pond about meeting Winston Churchill, and tells Edith's sister Emily how Edith disciplined Kermit, who wants his own room.

The family moves out of the Executive Mansion in Albany; Edith writes Emily how happy they have been there. Roosevelt writes on photographs of the children, the Boer War, the scandal and the state's forest and game commission.

Writing Emily, Roosevelt reports that Kermit and Archie attend the little Cove School and go wood-chopping with him, that with Ted off at Groton, Kermit is angling for a room of his own, and that he and Ethel team up against Archie.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
Eager for the hunt, Roosevelt tells Philip Stewart he will send his bags by stagecoach but drive himself out in a rig.
Roosevelt writes Bradley Tyler Johnson, who hopes to get his grandson into the Naval Academy.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt attends the Senatorial Dinner in Washington.
Roosevelt speaks in New York at a dinner of the national league of civil service reformers.
A soldiers' monument on Riverside Drive
Roosevelt comes down from Albany for the afternoon ceremony laying the cornerstone of a monument to soldiers along Riverside Drive. New immigration buildings open at Ellis Island that day.
Roosevelt is at home; no details are noted.
What a Vice President can't do
Roosevelt tells Austin Wadsworth he has doubts about him joining the western trip, and reminds Lyman Abbott that as Vice President he will not be able to introduce bills.
Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing further is recorded.
Roosevelt visits a Sullivan Street school run by the Children's Aid Society in New York.
Wise removed from the Lunacy Commission
After a hearing in Albany, Roosevelt removes Peter Wise from the State Lunacy Commission for misconduct.
Roosevelt writes Frederic Harrison about the American turns of phrase in his biography of Cromwell, such as saying Cromwell "whipped the Welsh."
Gardiner removed for defying election orders

After conferring with Hammond and Gardiner, Roosevelt removes Gardiner from office for ignoring his November election orders and appoints Eugene A. Philbin. The Fergusons, George and John Kean Roosevelt, and Monroe and Stewart Robinson are guests.
Roosevelt is in Albany; no details are recorded.
On Christmas Eve Roosevelt writes William Llewellyn about how often former Rough Riders end up in shootings and killings.
The Roosevelts celebrate Christmas at home.
Nephew Ted Robinson and his band of friends come to Sagamore Hill.
Helen Cutting, James Jackson and Courtlandt Nicoll are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.
A medical college and a Morgan dinner
Roosevelt speaks as Cornell's medical college opens in New York, then goes to the Union League's dinner honoring J. P. Morgan.
Roosevelt speaks at the YMCA in New York on "Christian Citizenship."

Roosevelt's two years as New York's governor close with a farewell dinner in Albany given by Woodruff; he judges he has been the best governor of his era. He tells Charles Hasbrouck no reporters will join his western hunt and tells Philip Stewart he will hunt on his own. Edith starts keeping a daily diary.
Roosevelt writes former Governor David B. Hill that Chief Justice Alton Parker has praised the way he treated the courts as governor.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is recorded.
Frederick Holls, Nicholas Murray Butler and Albert Shaw are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt goes to a dinner of the Boone and Crockett Club, the hunters' conservation group he helped found.
Roosevelt spends the day between New York City and Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at home on the eve of his western trip.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Colorado on a hunt for mountain lions.
Roosevelt's train reaches Chicago in the afternoon.
Roosevelt rides the train toward Colorado Springs.
Leaving the railroad, Roosevelt drives fifty miles overland to reach Meeker, a remote frontier settlement,, arriving at 8 p.m. The hunter John Goff meets him and takes him to his ranch.
On horseback all day after mountain lions and lynx, Roosevelt watches the hounds actually climb a tree. He shoots an 18-pound bay lynx the dogs have treed and spends the night at Goff's ranch.
Roosevelt rides for ten hours. The pack runs down and worries another lynx but is baffled by an old cougar trail. He spends the night at the Keystone Ranch.
A cougar killed with a knife

After a chase of more than two hours, Roosevelt kills a cougar with his knife while the hounds hold it; four dogs are hurt. The cat is fully grown but small, six feet long and just over 80 pounds. He writes Ted all about it.
Roosevelt knifes a second cougar as the dogs hold her. She is 6 feet 7 inches and 118 pounds, and has three kittens only days old in a cave in a cut bank. The pack is worn out.
On his fifth straight day of riding, Roosevelt shoots a 21-pound lynx in the piñon pines after a fine run. Edith writes him recalling the European honeymoon they took after marrying in 1886.
Riding from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. over very rugged mountains, the party has two good lynx chases, and Dr. Webb shoots a 29-pound cat. Roosevelt notes a big lynx had killed an eight-month-old fawn.

Stewart is sick. Webb kills a 107-pound cougar in a small tree on a cliff face with the dogs just six feet off, and Roosevelt takes a 25-pound lynx. He writes Ethel about the hounds that climb trees. It is Bamie's 46th birthday.
On the eighth day of riding, Stewart kills a young cougar of about 47 pounds. Roosevelt notes that two animals killed in the open had been dragged, not carried, beneath the trees.
The hunters rest. Roosevelt nails up skins, does some target shooting and has a bath.
After another full day in the saddle, Stewart shoots a 22-pound bobcat on a rock.
Roosevelt rides all day without success after a light snowfall overnight.
A second straight day of riding turns up nothing.
Stewart shoots an 11-pound lynx the dogs have treed, and the hunters kill a 108-pound cougar holed up in a cave by smoking it. One dog dies and five are wounded.
It snows all day, and Stewart and Webb leave the camp.
Snow falls through the morning at the Keystone Ranch.

In thirteen hours in the saddle, Roosevelt runs down a 164-pound cougar, 7 feet 8 inches long. The chase lasts four hours; the cat runs three miles once jumped, and he shoots it by moonlight on a cliff. Edith writes Emily that being at the center of things is interesting but changes nothing essential.
Roosevelt kills the mate of the cougar taken the day before, a reddish one where the other was gray, shooting it in a tree after seeing it get up ahead of the dogs.
A big lynx and a lost dog

Roosevelt kills a 31-pound lynx after a run of more than an hour. One dog goes into a hole after another lynx and never comes back out. He writes Ethel about the ranch animals, among them a pig named Maude.
Roosevelt rides from the Keystone to Mathers Ranch.
Roosevelt kills a cougar in a spruce tree. He later wrote about hunting mule deer on this trip in The Deer Family, recalling bitterly cold days.
Searching for strayed hounds in Colorado
On his winter lion hunt in western Colorado, the Vice President-elect spends a snowy day at Mathers Ranch tracking down hunting dogs that had gone missing.
Roosevelt recovers the strayed dogs at Mathers Ranch as the snow keeps falling on his Colorado hunting camp.
An empty day in the hunting country
Roosevelt's diary records no game sighted at Mathers Ranch. The guest book lists Mr. Furguson and Mr. and Mrs. Clifford Richardson.
A big storm buries the Colorado ranch where Roosevelt is hunting, and his diary notes little else.
First cougar of the Colorado trip
Roosevelt kills a mountain lion in the pinyon after the hounds chase it for two hours, then makes a tough climb back up on foot.
Another snowy day at Mathers Ranch passes without Roosevelt sighting any quarry.
A repeat of the day before
Roosevelt's one-word diary line simply marks the day as a copy of the last: snow at Mathers Ranch and no game.
Roosevelt moves over to Foreman's ranch and brings down another mountain lion in the pinyon below a mountain his diary calls Colo Row.
A blank day at Foreman's ranch
Roosevelt hunts from Foreman's ranch but sees nothing worth a shot.
Roosevelt rides from Foreman's ranch back to his base at Mathers Ranch.
Roosevelt shifts his hunting party from Mathers Ranch to Keystone Ranch. The guest book lists Mr. Furguson and Mr. Hutchinson.
Lynx and two lions on Alice's birthday
At Keystone Ranch Roosevelt kills a lynx and two cougars, finishing them with a knife while the dogs held them. Back east, his daughter Alice turns 17.
A cougar after a long cold trail
Roosevelt follows an old track for three hours before the hounds bring a cougar to bay, and he gets a fine look at the chase.
The biggest cougar of the hunt
Roosevelt shoots and knifes a huge mountain lion, about 8 feet long and 227 pounds, after a three-hour chase on a track the party had nearly given up as stale.
The hunt winds down as Roosevelt rides into the town of Meeker.
Roosevelt leaves Meeker and heads for Rifle in a wagon, starting the long trip home.
Roosevelt is in Colorado Springs on his way back east.
Greeting the public in Colorado Springs
Colorado Springs turns out for a public reception honoring the Vice President-elect.
Roosevelt boards a train in Colorado Springs bound for home.
Roosevelt spends the day traveling eastward by rail.
Roosevelt's homeward route takes him through Chicago.
Back in New York by way of Albany
After a stop in Albany, Roosevelt reaches New York City.
Home to Sagamore Hill with lion skins promised
Roosevelt sees E. A. Philbin in New York City and then reaches Sagamore Hill for the night, his Colorado hunt over. He writes Bamie that her little boy Sheffield will get a mountain lion skin.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt remains at Sagamore Hill with nothing further noted.
Brushing off tall tales of the hunt
Roosevelt tells Lodge he has no wish to give speeches, and dismisses the wild newspaper yarns about his Colorado lion hunt as pure invention.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more.
Two articles out and a Washington house rented

Roosevelt and his wife Edith take the Storers' house in Washington for the coming term. Two Roosevelt pieces appear, in Outing and McClure's. The same day, J. P. Morgan buys out Hill and Rockefeller interests to create U.S. Steel, capitalized at $1.4 billion.
Last days at home before the inauguration
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as the inauguration draws near; nothing else is noted.
A family party sets out for Washington
Roosevelt heads to the capital with his wife Edith, his sister Corinne and her husband Douglas Robinson, Uncle James Gracie, Bob Ferguson, his Albany secretary William Loeb, and his valet, Pinckney.
Lunch with family and a Depew dinner
On the eve of the inauguration Roosevelt stops by the White House, lunches with the Cowleses, the Lodges and Senator Kean, and goes to a dinner hosted by Chauncey Depew.

Roosevelt takes the oath as Vice President while McKinley begins his second term, with Edith and the children, Ted down from Groton, looking on. That night at the ball the First Lady seems ill, rain falls outside, and young Ted gulps champagne he takes for fizzy water.
First day in the presiding chair
Roosevelt takes up his new job running the Senate, which he finds dull, while Edith and the family head back to Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt chairs the Senate and answers office seekers: he tells Maria Storer the vice presidency carries no say over appointments, and declines to use a gavel Ferd Brother sent because the Senate keeps its own traditional one.
Roosevelt again presides over the Senate in its special session.
A busy desk of letters from the Senate chair

Between Senate sessions Roosevelt writes friends at home and abroad about Britain and America, hunting, soldiering and China, and tells John Goff to ship all twelve cougar skins from the Colorado hunt to a New York furrier.
The Senate's special session adjourns, ending Roosevelt's first stint in the chair.
Roosevelt is in Washington; no activity is recorded.
Roosevelt compliments Owen Wister on his Grant biography, answers a question about his neckwear, and tells Maria Storer he has raised with McKinley the idea of a Vienna post for her husband.
Letters on the Philippines and San Juan

Roosevelt writes William Allen White about a piece on Croker, Taft about the Philippines, General Young about a West Point appointment for Howze, and Major Brown about the islands and the Spanish soldier he shot at San Juan.
A good word for Philip Stewart
Roosevelt writes Dr. Alexander Lambert with warm praise for Philip Stewart.
Roosevelt leaves Washington for home, passing through New York City on the way to Oyster Bay.
The Sagamore Hill guest book records a visit from Mr. Holls.

Roosevelt confides to Spring-Rice that he would like more to do, tells Bayard Taylor painting is not to his taste, writes Caspar Whitney on Alaska game laws, and congratulates General Chaffee on his command in China.
Roosevelt is at home on Long Island with nothing else recorded.
Public opinion and the limits of leadership

Writing to Mahan, Roosevelt argues that leaders can only carry the public as far as opinion has been readied, and that Americans know little of affairs in China. Other letters cover military matters, reform, Washington and Anglo-American ties.
Roosevelt is at home; the record notes nothing further.
Poultney Bigelow visits Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt writes William Collier steering him away from the Civil Service Commission.
Roosevelt praises Booker T. Washington's new book and asks James Lowndes about studying and practicing law in Washington, an idea he was weighing for life after the vice presidency.
Roosevelt goes into New York City for the dinner of the 2nd Battery of the New York National Guard.
Breakfast, the Lotos Club and Legal Aid
In New York City Roosevelt breakfasts with J. P. Clarke and Nicholas Murray Butler, attends the Lotos Club's dinner for Governor Odell, and gives a speech at the Legal Aid Society's banquet.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
A military tournament and a stack of letters
Roosevelt takes in a military tournament held at the Garden and writes about Civil Service Commission seats, New York police, and why he cannot get to Albany. The Walter Palmers are guests.
Roosevelt urges President McKinley to name William Foulke to the Civil Service Commission, and writes Joe Bishop about Platt and Odell and James Field about Harvard.
Aguinaldo captured; advice on German sea power

News comes that General Funston has seized Aguinaldo in the Philippines. Roosevelt writes Lodge about Germany's navy with blunt frontier advice, and sends a flurry of letters on appointments, false press reports, Morgan and Gunton, and praise for Leonard Wood.
Roosevelt tells Jacob Riis to keep calling him Colonel rather than using his new title, and writes Matthew Quay about an appointment and B. F. Koons about elk.
Books, law school and Buffalo plans

Roosevelt answers Annie Meyer's request for a critique, discusses Huxley's memoir with Florence LaFarge, tells Louisa Schuyler he will open the Pan-American Exposition, and writes on law school and military matters.
Roosevelt sends praise to Frederick Funston for capturing Aguinaldo, and tells Charles Bonaparte that Governor Odell has done well so far.
Ted is back at Sagamore Hill on a week's break from school. Hector and Bob Ferguson are guests.
Roosevelt travels to Yonkers for dinner with Frederick Holls.
Talking with Riis at the Robinsons'
In New York City Roosevelt sits down with Jacob Riis at his sister Corinne's home.
No backing from Platt for Joe Murray

Roosevelt writes the Postmaster General, discusses the police bill and state jobs with Clarence Esty, and lets his old friend Joe Murray know that Senator Platt will not support him for the post he wanted.
John Kendrick Bangs and Mr. Rodgers visit, and Roosevelt thanks Hamlin Garland for sending his novel Her Mountain Lover.
Roosevelt writes John Oskison about Oklahoma statehood and Buffalo Bill, Charles Bonaparte about Proctor, and Frederic Remington about flatboats.
Roosevelt tells George Gunton he has not yet persuaded J. P. Morgan to fund an Institute for Social Economics, and lets Philip Stewart know he will miss this year's Rough Rider reunion.
Roosevelt is at home with nothing else noted.
Species debates and a preface promised

Roosevelt compares his time as governor with Odell's, argues species and subspecies with naturalist C. Hart Merriam, agrees to write a preface for Camera Shots at Big Game, and discusses literacy tests with Bonaparte.
On Archie's seventh birthday Roosevelt lunches with Joe Bishop and writes Ted that bear-play right before bed is now banned, and that little Quentin is sore that Archie gets presents and he doesn't.
Philander Knox replaces John Griggs as Attorney General. Roosevelt defends Funston's Philippine conduct to Lyman Abbott and writes on bay-bird shooting and speeches.
Roosevelt writes Clarence Esty about the weekend breakfasts he shared with Platt and Odell during his governorship.
Roosevelt writes S. E. Furry about the Women's Industrial Home Society, sends notes to George Lyman and Meyer, and writes Cleveland Dodge about Proctor.
Roosevelt writes Senator George Hoar about his upcoming speeches.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no activity is recorded.
An odd mix of dinner guests

Roosevelt teases his sister Corinne about the strangely matched guests invited to a dinner at her house, writes Joe Bishop about a speech and the tariff, and answers William Llewellyn about Rough Riders who shot women.
A western job for Riis's son
Roosevelt asks Gifford Pinchot whether Jacob Riis's son might go west, and tells Riis he has written on the boy's behalf.
The Evening Post is out to get him
Roosevelt writes the Storers about his relations with McKinley, tells Ted about a bay-bird hunt, and warns Leonard Wood that the New York Evening Post wants to ruin him.
Lunch with writers and a talk to newsboys
In New York Roosevelt lunches at the Robinsons' with Gilder, Butler, Brander Matthews and Rainsford, then speaks to the boys at the Newsboys' Lodging House.
Cousins Jack and Margaret Roosevelt are guests at Sagamore Hill.
An article that came out too soon
Bob Ferguson visits. Roosevelt writes William Rideing about his piece "The Essence of Heroism" in the April Youth's Companion, which was not meant to run while he was Vice President.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Nicholas Murray Butler about speaking dates, George Terry about the Union League Club's Black staff, and George Lyman to arrange a May 1 dinner in Boston.
Keeping the lion skins out of the papers

Henry White and Mrs. Cadwallader Jones visit. Roosevelt asks Edward Martin to keep reporters away from his Colorado skins, writes the furriers about them, and corresponds on newsboys' dinners and bay birds.
Made a Mason in Oyster Bay

Roosevelt is raised to the third degree in Oyster Bay's Masonic lodge. He writes Arthur Lee that the Alaska boundary must be settled and on a neutral Nicaraguan canal, and discusses Byzantium and Alexander with Frederic Harrison. Curtis Guild and Attorney General Davies visit.
Roosevelt writes William Caruthers about corporate stockholders, and tells Maria Storer he has urged John Hay to find her husband a better post.

Roosevelt tells Taft about the Philippines and describes his easy spring at home: riding and rowing with Edith, playing with the children and walking the countryside. Helen Cutting and Jack Roosevelt visit.
John Elliott is a guest, and Roosevelt writes Abbott Lawrence Lowell about a lecture.
Bob Ferguson is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt leaves for Boston to stay with George Lyman. It is his sister Corinne's 19th wedding anniversary.
Harvard, the Home Market Club and plans for law

Roosevelt speaks at Harvard, lunches with Dean Briggs, and addresses the Home Market Club in Mechanics Hall that evening. He also arranges to study law in the fall with Justice Edward White of the Supreme Court.
Roosevelt breakfasts in Boston at the Somerset Club with Groton headmaster Endicott Peabody and with Francis Cabot Lowell, then heads for Groton.
Roosevelt spends time with his son Ted at Groton School, then returns to New York City and stays the night with his sister Corinne.
Roosevelt is in New York City, where the guest record lists a Miss Wood.
A note to the British military attaché
Roosevelt writes Gerald Kitson of the British Embassy about military matters.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is recorded.
Young Kermit tries out the horse Diamond and handles him well; one of his guinea pigs goes by Dewey Jr. Roosevelt writes about McKinley and about the Rough Riders.
Cherry blossoms and a thrown block

Roosevelt sends Ted the news from home: the cherry trees are blooming, Quentin hurled a block at his mother, and Ethel is weeding the path to earn money for an art magazine. He also writes on Harvard's psychology lab, praises Josephine Daskam's writing, and compliments Groton.
General James Wilson is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
The guest book records a Mr. Willard at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Thomas Gaffney on questions of nationality.
Roosevelt confers with Marcus Braun in New York City. Fanny and Jim Parsons arrive to stay the weekend.
Roosevelt is at home on Long Island with nothing else recorded.
A post office for Bill Sewall
Roosevelt writes Senator Eugene Hale of Maine backing his old Maine guide and Dakota partner Bill Sewall for postmaster of Island Falls.
Roosevelt writes Catherine New about Harry New.
Roosevelt writes Judge Alton Parker on legal matters, sends news to Bamie, and answers encyclopedia editor George Aiton on the relationship between Jews and government.
Picturing life as a history professor
Stewart and Helena Elliott visit. In a letter Roosevelt guesses that once his term as Vice President ends he will likely end up teaching American history.
Christine Kean Roosevelt is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt goes to East Norwich for the laying of a new church's cornerstone.
Roosevelt, his wife Edith and daughter Alice ride to Buffalo to open the Pan-American Exposition, arriving at 8 p.m. Reporter Oscar King Davis shares the train.
Roosevelt gives the opening address at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo and talks with American Indians on the grounds. Alice rides a camel and takes in the midway's notorious dance show.
Roosevelt joins Senator Mark Hanna at a reception at Buffalo's Merchants' Exchange.
Roosevelt remains in Buffalo; nothing further is noted.
From the Indian camp to Geneseo
Roosevelt visits the Indian encampment at the exposition, then leaves for Geneseo.
Roosevelt calls on the Wadsworth family at Geneseo.
At Geneseo, Alice goes riding from the Wadsworth stables.
The Roosevelts remain in Geneseo; nothing more is recorded.
Meeting Mr. Dooley on the train home

Heading home, Roosevelt shares the train with Augustus Saint-Gaudens and Finley Peter Dunne, creator of Mr. Dooley, whom he meets for the first time. Edith stops in Albany, Emily continues to Boston, and Kermit is waiting to greet his father when he gets home at 10 p.m.
Roosevelt is at home after the Buffalo trip; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Richard Derby about plans for a dinner for young college men.
Roosevelt attends the dedication of a sanatorium in Bedford, New York, and writes President McKinley hoping the First Lady is feeling better.

Roosevelt is hard at work on The Deer Family, a book on American deer he is writing with three co-authors. He tells Ted that Quentin and the dog Black Jack are always underfoot, and writes on the Boers, Saint-Gaudens's sculpture, law school and the Rough Rider reunion.
Roosevelt writes Elihu Root with high praise for Augustus Saint-Gaudens's statue of General Sherman and asks him about Cuba.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.
Cuba, and an invitation to Butler
Roosevelt writes Nicholas Murray Butler about Cuba and asks him to come stay at Sagamore Hill, and responds to Hugo Munsterberg's article on American women.
Booking a speech a year out
Roosevelt writes John C. Linehan about a speaking date in 1902.
John Riddle visits. Roosevelt tells Thomas Grindell he doubts Chicago is the right spot for the next Rough Rider reunion.
Roosevelt gives a speech in Huntington, Long Island, and writes Eugene Philbin about detectives on the police force and civil service reform.
The Supreme Court and the territories

Mrs. Clifford Richardson, Captain and Mrs. Howze and Nicholas Murray Butler visit. Roosevelt writes Frederick Fincke about the Court's rulings on laws in the new territories, and Caspar Whitney about animal books and hunting.
Clifford Richardson and Alvord Cooley are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing else noted.
Don't hold the reunion for me

John McIlhenny visits. Roosevelt urges Philip Stewart not to push back the Rough Rider reunion on his account, and invites William Osborne, who is touring Princeton, Yale and Harvard, to Sagamore on June 29.

Roosevelt speaks from his own piazza to members of the Long Island Bible Society. He writes McKinley hoping the First Lady is better, and withdraws his backing from S. E. Furry's home for 'fallen women'.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Chicago publisher Hermann Kohlsaat about his chances for the presidency in 1904, and Arthur Brown about nature pamphlets.
Roosevelt is in New York City, where the guest record lists Clifford Richardson.
Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt is back at home with nothing else recorded.
A Rough Rider's job and a rail car

General Young, the Younghusbands and Howard Townsend visit. Roosevelt asks Secretary Hay to help Rough Rider Henry Bardshar, arranges a rail car with Paul Morton for his western trip, praises William Allen White to Knox, and writes about the cougar hunt.
Grant LaFarge visits. Roosevelt writes George Lyman defending his part in the San Juan Hill fight.
Foreign affairs with Lodge; a skin for Bamie
Roosevelt sends Lodge two letters, noting McKinley will skip commencement and weighing relations with Britain and Germany. He is pleased that Bamie liked her mountain lion skin.
Bob Ferguson is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

The Van Rensselaers and the Lamberts visit. Roosevelt vents to George Lyman about General Nelson Miles, plans a Boston trip with Lodge, praises Robley Evans's book, and writes Bellamy Storer about Catholics holding public office.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is recorded.
Roosevelt writes John Hammer Jr. about patronage for Rough Riders, and tells historian Walter McCaleb he thinks Wilkinson's earlier plot mattered more than the Burr conspiracy.
At Harvard's commencement in Cambridge, Roosevelt lunches with Lodge and Lowell and gives a talk at the class dinner.
Novelist Owen Wister is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Harvard, history books and the press

Roosevelt writes about President Eliot's view of him and of expansion, thanks Henry Higginson for giving Harvard its new Union, praises Eleonora Kinnicutt's ideas, and discusses Revolutionary War books and newspaper campaigns.
College men talk decency in public life
Roosevelt hosts students from Harvard and Yale at Sagamore Hill for a discussion of his theme "Applied Decency in Public Life." David Sandrich and Philip Stewart are guests.
A new horse, poison ivy and a mothball

Edith gets a horse called Yagenka and comes down with poison ivy, while Quentin gets a mothball stuck up his nose. Abroad, Germany asks Venezuela to send its debt dispute to the Hague tribunal; Venezuela says no.
A visit to Orange, New Jersey
Roosevelt is in Orange, New Jersey, where the guest record lists a Miss LeMoine.
Roosevelt remains in Orange, New Jersey; nothing more is noted.

Roosevelt tells Frederic Coudert that America should not extend its rule over a people able to govern themselves unless they wish it. He also writes Spring-Rice on civilization and Dr. Elmer Capen about speaking at Tufts.
Taft takes charge in the Philippines
On Independence Day William Howard Taft is installed as civil governor of the Philippines. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Rough Rider marksmanship with the Krag
Roosevelt advises Albert Lenoir Key never to hit without hitting hard, writes about Sagamore Hill, and tells James Parker the Rough Riders outshot other units in Cuba with their Krag carbines.
Roosevelt is at home with nothing else recorded.
Roosevelt writes George Becker about the Philippines, China and American expansion.
Lunch with Platt; plans for the South
Roosevelt lunches with Senator Platt at the Lawyers' Club in New York, and tells Booker T. Washington he hopes to visit Tuskegee and his mother's hometown of Roswell, Georgia.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing further noted.
Planning a bay-bird trip with six boys

Roosevelt arranges with Regis Post to take six boys shooting on Great South Bay, tells Endicott Peabody about his June evening with college men, and discusses Russia, Winston Churchill, battlefield tactics and Britain's army with Sternberg.
Roosevelt suggests to William Llewellyn that the Rough Riders hold reunions less often, and says he is unhappy they delayed this year's so he could come.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.
Lining up an August trip west

Roosevelt discusses books and studies with Lyman Abbott, praises Taft and muses on the presidency, sets up an August western hunt with Paul Morton, and invites William Allen White to ride his train to Colorado.

Roosevelt tells Philip Stewart it is fine for Ted to gather some birds' eggs and the odd bird, but that he should avoid wasting wildlife, recalling that as a boy he himself collected specimens to the point of needless killing.
Roosevelt divides the day between Sagamore Hill and New York City; his sister Bamie is a guest.
The Henry Marquands visit, and Roosevelt writes his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson about what lies ahead for him politically.
Roosevelt spends time at Sagamore Hill and in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
Reviewing novels by Churchill and Norris

Monroe and Stewart Robinson and Nicholas Murray Butler visit. Roosevelt writes Douglas Robinson again about his future, comments on American novelist Winston Churchill's The Crisis, and gives Owen Wister his take on Frank Norris's The Octopus.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt takes Ted, Kermit and several of their cousins with Regis Post on a cruise and shooting trip across Great South Bay, sailing by yacht from Babylon.
The Great South Bay party puts in at Fire Island.
Roosevelt and the boys are cruising Great South Bay; his sister Corinne appears in the guest record.
Last day on Great South Bay
The cruise on Great South Bay continues; nothing else is noted.
Princeton professor Woodrow Wilson, Professor Trent and Dr. Seymour Abbot are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Dr. and Mrs. Alexander Lambert are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill and in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt leaves New York City in the evening, bound for Chicago.
Chicago stop on the way west

In Chicago Roosevelt sees Governor Yates and Charles Fairbanks and has lunch at the Union League Club with Paul Morton before heading for Colorado Springs. At home, Alice is out dancing often and secretly smoking, and the younger children have colds.
On the way to Colorado Springs, Roosevelt's train stops at Kansas City and Emporia.

Roosevelt gives a speech, "Manhood and Statehood," at Colorado Springs for the 25th anniversary of Colorado statehood, praising work and scorning idleness. William Allen White later described a gathering at Philip Stewart's home during the visit.
Roosevelt attends a reception in Colorado Springs.
Roosevelt is in Colorado Springs; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt heads into the Colorado backcountry on a hunt with his friend Philip B. Stewart.
Roosevelt is out hunting in Colorado on his wife Edith's 40th birthday.
Still hunting in Colorado, Roosevelt writes Lincoln Steffens that he has always felt more at home in the West than in the East.
Roosevelt tours the mines at Victor and Cripple Creek.
Back in Colorado Springs, Roosevelt helps lay the cornerstone of a YMCA building.
Roosevelt is in Colorado Springs; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt leaves Colorado Springs with Philip Stewart and others for a fishing trip on the White River.
Roosevelt is fishing on the White River while back home his daughter Ethel turns 10.
Heading home with a Kansas speech
Roosevelt starts back east from Colorado and gives a speech along the way in Hutchinson, Kansas.
Roosevelt is on the train heading east.
Alice, whose jaw started aching during an Adirondack outing, is brought to New York's Roosevelt Hospital with an abscess.
Roosevelt goes to see Alice at the hospital every day she is there, splitting his days between Oyster Bay and the city.
Roosevelt divides his time between home on Long Island and the city.
Back and forth to the city
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill and in New York City; nothing else is noted.
Colds at home, Russia with Holls

Roosevelt confers with Frederick Holls about Russia. He tells Lodge the whole family has colds and writes about the Sampson-Schley dispute and his popularity out west, and notes a former Rough Rider's appointment as a forest ranger.
Roosevelt writes Interior Secretary Ethan Hitchcock, a former envoy to Russia, that he is still fondly recalled there.
Now young Quentin is admitted to Roosevelt Hospital. Roosevelt writes Robert Cornell about reappointing W. C. Church, a Black officeholder.
Doctors operate on an abscess in Quentin's ear. Alice and Ted befriend the interns and roam the hospital.
Roosevelt tells Paul Morton he will write William Allen White, then writes White about a possible run for president in 1904.
Sunday between Sagamore and the city
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill and in New York City; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt praises a Finley Peter Dunne piece and invites him to Sagamore Hill, and tells E. M. Reily, who sent him whiskey, that he does not drink.
A run of small family misfortunes

Roosevelt praises George Gunton's writing on labor unions, discusses next year's speeches with Senator Foraker, writes on bosses and New York politics, and tells Charles Dawes about the string of minor troubles at home.
Between Long Island and New York
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill and in New York City; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Springfield, Illinois, stopping in Chicago.
Roosevelt is honored with a reception and a dinner at Springfield's Camp Lincoln, then goes back to Chicago.

In Chicago Roosevelt reviews the naval militia and visits Solomon Bethea and Graeme Stewart. Edith takes the children to the Adirondacks for two weeks, while Alice stays at the Robert Pruyns' camp some distance away.
Roosevelt is in Chicago; nothing else is recorded.
"Speak softly and carry a big stick"
At the Minnesota State Fair Roosevelt delivers "National Duties," using in public for the first time the West African saying that became his trademark for foreign policy.

Roosevelt leaves Minneapolis for Vermont and sends William Allen White his read on the political scene. In Macedonia, revolutionaries kidnap a party of missionaries that includes American Ellen M. Stone.

Roosevelt reaches Rutland, Vermont, for a round of speeches while Edith and the children stay in the Adirondacks and McKinley heads to the Buffalo fair. Stone's kidnappers free all but her and Katerina Tsilka and take them into the mountains.
Marble quarries and the heroic virtues
Roosevelt tours a mill and the marble quarries with Senator Redfield Proctor and gives a speech titled "Brotherhood and the Heroic Virtues." Film made the same day shows President McKinley.

Roosevelt is at a Fish and Game League luncheon on Vermont's Isle La Motte when a telephone call brings word that President McKinley was shot at 4 p.m. in Buffalo by anarchist Leon Czolgosz. Roosevelt is hurried indoors at Nelson Fisk's home, then leaves for Buffalo, where he stays with Ansley Wilcox.
With doctors upbeat about McKinley, Roosevelt writes Bamie and William Allen White that the President is mending, and writes Paul Morton about political support and Albert Cummins about an Iowa trip.
Hanna advises him to leave Buffalo

At the Wilcox house Roosevelt and Mark Hanna agree that his departure from Buffalo would reassure the nation the danger is past. He wires Edith that he may head to the Adirondacks to be with the family if the President keeps gaining.
Roosevelt writes Lodge that the shooting was an assault on free government itself. Edith, writing her sister Emily, guesses the gunman must be an anarchist.
Cleared to leave; Ted's first buck

Told McKinley is doing well enough, Roosevelt heads home to Long Island. Edith and the children are staying near Mount Marcy at Camp Tahawus, where Ted shoots his first deer. Letters go to Bethea, George Smalley on jingoism, and Curtis Guild predicting the President's recovery.
Roosevelt sees E. T. Brackett and Alton B. Parker at Saratoga, then sets off to join his family in the Adirondacks.

Roosevelt hires two guides for a climb of Mount Marcy. With Edith, Kermit, Ethel, James McNaughton, a governess and three friends, he hikes to Lake Colden, about 3,500 feet up, and camps there in the rain.

On Ted's 14th birthday, Roosevelt and a guide climb Mount Marcy in cold, misty weather while the others turn back. Lunching at Lake Tear of the Clouds, he is handed a telegram at 1:25 p.m.: McKinley is failing. A frantic 50-mile night ride takes him to the North Creek rail station and on toward Albany. By early the next morning McKinley is dead.
Sworn in as President in Buffalo

Arriving in Buffalo at 1:30 p.m. to find McKinley dead, Roosevelt takes the oath as the 26th President at 3:15 p.m. in Ansley Wilcox's library, the furniture still under summer dust covers. Judge John R. Hazel swears him in, wearing borrowed clothes that don't fit, with most of the Cabinet present. He asks Booker T. Washington to meet with him.

Roosevelt stays at the Wilcox house, attends a service for McKinley, and confers with Root, Knox, Odell and Littauer as McKinley lies in state at Buffalo City Hall. Edith brings the children home to Sagamore Hill, where a doctor finds a pebble in Quentin's sore ear; Archie has tonsillitis.
Riding the funeral train to Washington

Roosevelt travels to Washington aboard the train carrying McKinley's body, arriving at 8:30 p.m. Edith and Bamie follow on another train and stay at 1733 N Street, where Corinne and Douglas join them. Edith's diary says he looked grave and older.

McKinley's body rests in the White House, where Grover Cleveland is among thousands of mourners. Roosevelt and Edith follow the hearse to the Capitol with Will Cowles; there the crowd bursts through barriers and police and soldiers force it back. That evening he holds a Cabinet meeting at 1733 N Street.
McKinley laid to rest in Canton
Roosevelt accompanies McKinley's body to Canton, Ohio, for the funeral and burial. Edith goes home to Sagamore Hill and writes Emily that Quentin has put black armbands on his dolls.
Roosevelt returns from Canton to Washington and sits down with William Allen White at Bamie's house.
Roosevelt meets with Hay, Long, Wood and Root, chairs a Cabinet meeting, lunches with Hay over reciprocity treaties, and sees Senators Cullom and Proctor.
Callers, a Taft profile and school worries

Roosevelt sees Leonard Wood, Carroll D. Wright, Binger Hermann, Representatives Livingston and Dayton, and Senators Elkins and Scott. His article on Governor Taft runs in The Outlook. Edith writes that people are anxious about how the children will be schooled in Washington, and Roosevelt writes Gilder about a proposed biography.

Roosevelt begins work in the White House, signing papers all day on what would have been his father's birthday, which he takes as a good sign. His only dinner guests are his sisters, Bamie and Corinne, with their husbands.

Roosevelt formally settles in and receives Gage, Postmaster General Smith and Senators Penrose, Cockrell and Pritchard. Edith readies five family bedrooms and clears out decades of clutter; only Kermit and Ethel are there so far. He tells Lodge it would be worse to be morbid than to accept how he came to office.
Roosevelt declares that posts in the new island territories will be filled without regard to politics.
Standing by his words on Paine
Roosevelt defends to Owen Wister his famous put-down of Thomas Paine.

Ellen Stone's captors send word that she and the pregnant Katerina Tsilka will be killed unless 25,000 Turkish pounds, about $110,000, arrives within 20 days. Roosevelt writes about Colorado appointments, about Cuba, the Philippines and territorial governors, and about politics.

On Corinne's 40th birthday, Roosevelt says he will honor McKinley's pledged appointments, tells Brooks Adams the U.S. must help balance European trade or risk war, and opposes a government-owned Pacific cable.
The Congregational missionary board refuses to pay Ellen Stone's ransom, hoping to discourage terrorism. Roosevelt writes Root about inspecting coastal forts.
Edith writes Emily that the White House has no space for the children's old nurse, Mame, and confides her fear that Roosevelt could be assassinated.

Roosevelt keeps McKinley's entire Cabinet and meets Admiral Schley and Senators Proctor, Mitchell and Foraker. He writes Hay about an isthmian canal and tells Foraker he cannot campaign for him. Kermit and Archie start at Force public school, Ethel boards at the Cathedral School, and his article "With the Cougar Hounds" appears in Scribner's.
Inviting old friends to the White House

Two weeks into his presidency, Roosevelt writes to diplomat friends Cecil Spring-Rice in Cairo and Speck von Sternberg in Calcutta, wishing each could come stay with him at the White House. Edith tells a friend her husband is carrying the new job with ease.
No government rescue for Ellen Stone
Roosevelt writes Alvey Adee at the State Department that Washington cannot be expected to free Ellen Stone, the American missionary held captive in Macedonia.
Setting the record straight on deer
Roosevelt asks editor Caspar Whitney to make clear that his chapters for The Deer Family were written while he was still Vice President.
Roosevelt tells Maria Storer he is working to find a post for her husband Bellamy, and writes his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson about trust policy and Bleistein, a horse from Buffalo.

Missionary leaders Samuel Capen and a colleague named Smith call about Ellen Stone; Roosevelt tells them the government will not pay her ransom but urges a public subscription to raise it. He dines with McDougall Hawkes and writes John Hay about the canal treaty.
Roosevelt sits down with Senator Thomas C. Platt to sort out federal patronage for New York City.

Roosevelt announces Thomas G. Jones as his choice for federal judge in Alabama, bypassing Mark Hanna. He confers again with Platt, wishes Seth Low luck in the mayor's race, and tells Sarah Leavitt he tries to raise his children as his own father raised him.

Roosevelt confers with Henry C. Payne on appointments in the South and issues a statement on the Philippines. He sends John Hay instructions for the Pan-American conference and writes Governor Odell, William Sanger, and Mark Hanna.

Roosevelt sees Senators Mason and Cullom and lunches with the New York Merchants Association's Secretary Mead. In a busy day of letters he tells Joseph Choate the Isthmian treaty delights him and thanks John Burroughs for looking after Ted.
Booker T. Washington at the President's table

A short overnight announcement reveals that Booker T. Washington dined with Roosevelt the evening before, the first Black guest at a White House dinner. Racist outrage erupts across the South. Roosevelt writes Douglas Robinson about his trust policy and the appointments fight.
Pillow fights and a forest plan

Roosevelt tumbles on the bed first with Archie and Quentin and afterward with Kermit and Ethel. His nephew Sheffield Cowles turns three. He tells Gifford Pinchot he will put forest work under Agriculture rather than Interior.

The official mourning period for McKinley closes. Roosevelt confers with Platt and Treasury Secretary Gage, names William D. Foulke to the Civil Service Commission, learns Ted has broken his collarbone, and turns down a Rough Rider bodyguard.
Roosevelt meets with Senator Platt and Governor Odell, the two power brokers of New York Republican politics.
Roosevelt leaves for Farmington, Connecticut. He writes David Starr Jordan about Hawaii and tells Seth Low where he will be on the eve of the city election.
At the Cowles home in Farmington, Roosevelt lunches with Connecticut Senators Joseph Hawley and Orville H. Platt, then dines with Governor George McLean.

Yale's 200th anniversary brings Roosevelt to New Haven to accept an honorary Doctor of Laws, followed by a reception, a banquet, and a speech. His daughter Alice comes along and finds herself seated beside Mark Twain.
Back in Washington, Roosevelt writes Lucius Littauer that his dinner with Booker T. Washington was simply a gesture of respect for a man he admires, and that he treats Southern attacks with contempt.

After meeting Congressman Moody and Senators Wolcott and Pritchard, and a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt jokes to Philip Stewart that the quiet dinner with Booker T. Washington has gone global. J. C. Greenaway is a White House guest.
Roosevelt writes naval Lieutenant Percival Werlich about his promotion and asks him to promise to give up drink.
Roosevelt turns 43 and spends his birthday drafting his first annual message to Congress.

Roosevelt receives judges of the Court of Claims and lunches with Senator Nelson Aldrich. He tells Curtis Guild he will keep inviting Booker T. Washington, and writes Lodge about appointments and Senator Hale's opposition to a bigger Navy.
A post for the St. Louis fair
Roosevelt tells Senator Platt that Thomas Cridler has agreed to represent the planned St. Louis Exposition overseas.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Edith takes charge of the household

Alice moves into the White House. Edith does away with the housekeeper's job and runs the house herself, hiring Belle Hagner as social secretary at $1,400 a year. Her days settle into a rhythm: breakfast with the family, mail and menus, afternoon rides with her husband in Rock Creek Park, and evenings with the children.
Dinner with Hay and James J. Hill

Roosevelt dines with John Hay and railroad builder James J. Hill. He tells Nicholas Murray Butler of four open Army second-lieutenant slots, asks Jacob Riis when he'll be in town, and tells Ted he hoped for better class standing.
Keep the family out of print
After a conference with Senator Wolcott, Roosevelt writes William Chandler that he wants a stronger Navy, and asks Owen Wister to leave Edith and the children out of his writing about him.
Roosevelt sends young Sarah Schuyler Butler an illustrated letter about Eli Yale, the big blue macaw kept in the conservatory as one of his children's pets.
Roosevelt leaves Washington to cast his ballot in Oyster Bay, stopping in New York at his aunt's house on West 57th Street. He writes Philip Stewart about appointments.
Election Day: Low wins New York
Roosevelt is in Oyster Bay on Election Day, when reformer Seth Low is chosen mayor of New York City.

Back in Washington, Roosevelt meets Joseph Choate and lunches with Choate, Hay, Myron Herrick, and Major Webb Hayes. He tells William Allen White he is battling senators over Kansas patronage and quizzes Secretary Hitchcock on forest reserves.

Roosevelt confers with Platt on New York patronage, writes Elihu Root about the friars' lands in the Philippines, and urges John Hay to see Speck von Sternberg named Germany's ambassador in Washington.

Roosevelt dines with Mark Hanna and John G. Milburn, and in letters to Albion Tourgée and another correspondent defends the Booker T. Washington dinner. He also writes Richard Welling about helping the Republican ticket.

Roosevelt talks patronage with J. G. Capers and finance bills with Senator Burrows, and receives Senator Quay and the British envoy, Lord Pauncefote. Letters go to William Frye, Speck von Sternberg, Archbishop Ireland and Booker T. Washington.
Roosevelt is in Washington; no activities are recorded.

Roosevelt meets R. C. Morris and a National Business League delegation. He invites humorist Finley Peter Dunne, creator of Mr. Dooley, to dinner, thanks Russell Harrison for his late father's article, and writes Leonard Wood about Cuba's economy.
After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt lunches with E. A. Bond, Senator James McMillan and Lucius Littauer, then dines with editor Paul Dana, the poet Bay Lodge and Charles Gleed.

Roosevelt meets Lemuel Quigg and talks Canadian reciprocity with Isidor Straus, then dines with Lodge and Spooner. He writes Governor Odell about his tussle with Platt over who will be customs collector in New York.
Roosevelt lunches with J. N. Partridge, J. C. Davis and J. T. McDonough, dines with Lodge, August Belmont and Lyman Abbott, and writes William Allen White about appointments.

Roosevelt lunches with Senators Hopkins and Lorimer and dines with Lodge, while New York's mayor-elect Seth Low spends the night at the White House. He writes Root on military posts and sends a letter to Senator Orville H. Platt, an ally on trusts.

Roosevelt meets the canal commissioners and Nevada Stranahan, hosts a Cabinet dinner, and names Herbert Peirce Third Assistant Secretary of State. He tells Governor Odell he is glad Odell and Mayor-elect Low have come to terms.
Roosevelt lunches with J. W. Brock and receives Secretary Hitchcock and the American novelist Winston Churchill and his wife. Dinner guests are the Cowleses, Lodge, Peirce and J. H. Sears.

The United States and Britain sign the second Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, clearing the way for an American canal across the isthmus. Roosevelt works on his annual message with Root and Speaker Henderson, receives Irish parliamentary leaders and the German ambassador, and spars by letter with Aldrich and Paul Dana over reciprocity and trusts.

On Quentin's fourth birthday, Roosevelt lunches with Robert Bridges, greets the Italian ambassador, and dines with the Roots, the Lodges and Finley Peter Dunne. He urges Seth Low to meet with Platt and tells Platt so.
Roosevelt lunches with the Woodruffs, the Cowleses, and Abner McKinley, brother of the late President.
Roosevelt confers with Senator William Allison and Governor Hunt.
Down the Potomac on the Sylph
After a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Archbishop Michael Corrigan, Roosevelt boards the presidential yacht Sylph for a cruise toward Norfolk, Virginia, dining at Quantico.
Roosevelt spends the day on the presidential yacht Sylph.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded for the day.
On Bamie's sixth wedding anniversary, Roosevelt hears a Cuban delegation ask for tariff cuts, lunches with Aldrich, and writes Charles Gleed opposing St. Louis boss Richard Kerens.
Roosevelt hosts an evening musicale with Senator Redfield Proctor, Lodge, Francis Leupp and others.
Roosevelt writes Joseph Bucklin Bishop about Philadelphia appointments and George Matthews about moving DeBarry out of Buffalo.

The Roosevelts keep Thanksgiving simple: turkey with all the trimmings and an evening together in the Red Parlor. Joining the family at table are the Lodges and Robinsons, along with Captain Davis and Brooks Adams.

Roosevelt talks Cuban reciprocity with Leonard Wood and meets his Cabinet. He writes Alice, visiting the Lees in Boston, that he has been playing bear with the little ones, Quentin has a touch of asthma, he has been riding Bleistein, and Edith looks young and lovely.

Roosevelt cheers at the Army-Navy football game in Philadelphia with Secretaries Long and Root and George Cortelyou. He writes Henry Higginson that he backs the gold standard but will be flexible on currency, and his article on photographing wild animals runs in World's Work.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.
Roosevelt and Edith mark their 15th anniversary. They dine with the Woods, William Rockhill and the Cowleses, and he confers with Senator Orville H. Platt.

Roosevelt's first message to Congress goes up in printed form, some 30,000 words. It calls forest and water questions among the nation's most pressing internal problems; John Hay ranks it with Lincoln's writing for individuality. Lawmakers begin organizing a reclamation bill, and Roosevelt dines with congressional leaders.

Roosevelt lunches with a large party including Seth Low, Chauncey Depew, Hay, Root, Knox and Choate, and sends Congress the Isthmian Canal Commission's report, which favors Nicaragua over Panama on cost.
Roosevelt writes his Colorado friend Philip Stewart about appointments.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.
Roosevelt confers with Secretary of State John Hay and General Leonard Wood.
Nicholas Murray Butler stays at the White House, and Roosevelt confers with Henry C. Payne.
Roosevelt meets again with General Wood, lunches with Frederick Holls and H. S. New, and hosts a White House reception.
Roosevelt dines with Mrs. Hobson, Mrs. Wolcott, General Young and J. R. Procter, and approves amendments to the civil service rules.

Roosevelt hears Senator Burrows, beet sugar men and their lawyers on Cuban reciprocity, then confers with Speaker Henderson and Representatives Payne and Dalzell on pending bills. He writes Douglas Robinson about a buildings superintendent.

Roosevelt receives naval officers and senators, reviews the city's police and fire parade, and lunches with George Kennan. He writes Will Cowles about William Sims's reports on poor Navy marksmanship and tells Senator Mitchell he never promised him the Alaska collectorship.
Germany informs Roosevelt that it plans to use force against Venezuela over unpaid debts. He holds a Cabinet meeting and confers with Mark Hanna.
Roosevelt confers with Lodge, Hanna, Spooner and Ambassador Choate.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.

The Senate ratifies the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, with Britain yielding to America's wish to build an isthmian canal. Roosevelt also receives the court of inquiry's report on the Sampson-Schley dispute over credit for the 1898 victory at Santiago, which leans toward Sampson. He refuses Lyman Abbott's plea to bring the Filipino leader Aguinaldo to America
Readying the Navy near Puerto Rico

Roosevelt orders the Navy to prepare an operating base off Puerto Rico against the chance of sudden war. He names Henry C. Payne Postmaster General, while General Nelson Miles publicly sides with Admiral Schley. Letters go to Edward Everett Hale, Andrew White and Charles Gleed.
Roosevelt meets a delegation of the American Asiatic Society and lunches with Andrew Carnegie, Root, J. R. Sheffield and W. N. Cohen.
Roosevelt meets Hay, Beveridge, Foraker and other lawmakers as Congress adjourns for the holidays, and writes William Rainsford about appointments.
After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt confers with Treasury Secretary Gage and Senators Hanna and Penrose.
Roosevelt faces General Nelson Miles over his public comments on the Schley case, and he and Secretary Root reprimand him. He writes Robert Patterson about the episode.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.

Roosevelt confers with Lodge, Hanna, Senator Warren and Joy, and lunches with Irish reformer Sir Horace Plunkett. He writes Charles R. Miller defending his choice of Henry Payne as Postmaster General.

Bob Ferguson is a White House guest and Chief Justice Fuller calls. Leslie Shaw is named Treasury Secretary. That evening Roosevelt and Edith go to a party at Bamie's and hang the children's stockings on the library mantel.
Twenty-six people sit down to Christmas dinner, then everyone dances in the East Room, Bob Ferguson among them. Roosevelt writes John Hay with sympathy on the death of their friend Clarence King.
The children sail on the Dolphin
Edith takes the children down the Potomac for three days on the presidential yacht Dolphin. Roosevelt dines with Root, Admiral Robley Evans and others, and thanks Mark Hanna for a note.

After lunch with Hay, Root and Knox, Roosevelt thanks Lieutenant William Sims for his counsel and urges him to keep challenging Navy orthodoxy. He also writes Admiral Henry Taylor about better gunnery.
Wayne MacVeagh, Charles Francis Adams, Clarence Bowen and Senators Cullom and Mason call. Roosevelt tells John Hay he is dining alone with editor Joseph Bucklin Bishop and invites Hay to come.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.
Roosevelt meets with Senators Lodge and Spooner.

Roosevelt agrees to serve as a trustee of the new Carnegie Institution. He writes Brander Matthews candidly about the Sampson-Schley-Miles-Alger feud, and tells William Allen White that Platt, angry over White's article, asked him to bar White from the White House, and that he refused.

Roosevelt and Edith come down the grand staircase to Marine Band music and greet diplomats and the public in the Blue Room for the New Year's reception. Edith carries flowers so she can graciously skip the handshakes.

A packed day of callers ends with Edith hosting her first Cabinet dinner: fifty guests who follow their hosts through the parlors to dinner. Roosevelt quits the copyright league, writes Foulke on civil service posts, and thanks Joseph Bishop for his help on the Philippines.

Alice's debut ball fills the Blue Room at 10 p.m., with dancing in the East Room until 2 a.m. Beforehand Alice grumbles about the plans and wants to use the $500 the Lees give her to alter them, but Edith says no.

Roosevelt confers with Hanna and Admiral Dewey and lunches with Leslie Shaw, three Rough Riders and others. He tells Endicott Peabody that Ted is second in his Groton class but worries that rough football, a smashed tooth and a broken collarbone may keep him off the field in college.
Hugh Whitney and Constance Gardner join Roosevelt for lunch.
Roosevelt confers with Admiral Schley and a string of senators, sees August Belmont at six, and dines with the Cowleses, Dr. Presley Rixey and the Redfield Proctors.
Roosevelt studies the Sampson-Schley dispute, lunches with Robert Patterson, and hosts the diplomatic reception that evening.

Roosevelt meets Platt, Admiral Walker, and Edouard Lampré, secretary general of the French Panama company, attends the Foraker wedding at noon, lunches with Foulke and James R. Garfield, and hosts a Cabinet dinner honoring Secretary Gage.

Henry Payne succeeds Charles Emory Smith as Postmaster General. Roosevelt lunches with Knox and railroad labor leaders including Frank Sargent and E. E. Clark, hosts the diplomatic dinner, and tells Secretary Long he wants Army engineers, not naval officers, manning coastal forts.
Dinner with Hay and Brooks Adams
Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting, sees Senators Burrows, O. H. Platt and Wetmore, Commissioner MacFarland and Major Llewellyn, and ends the day dining with Brooks Adams and John Hay.

Roosevelt receives senators and Speaker Henderson, meets the Chinese Exclusion Commission and Samuel Gompers, and dines at the Roots'. He tells Adolph Ochs that Oscar Straus is being named to The Hague tribunal.
After a midday visit with Regis Post, Roosevelt dines with Henry Adams, the Lodges, Mrs. Selmes and John Hay. Adams later wrote a cutting account of the evening.
Roosevelt confers with Gage, Crane and Choate, lunches with Horatio King, Moody and Smalley, and he and Edith are guests at a dinner given by Postmaster General Charles Emory Smith.
A morning of callers, including Senator Charles Fairbanks and Governor Winfield Durbin of Indiana, gives way to the judicial reception that night.
Corcoran visit and a conservation huddle

Roosevelt meets Chief Justice Fuller, Francis Leupp and Platt, visits the Corcoran Gallery with Edith, and spends the evening with Congressman John Lacey, C. Hart Merriam, Dr. Palmer and Gifford Pinchot.

Roosevelt sees Senator Pettus, Walter Emerson and Governor Bradley, and hosts the Supreme Court dinner. He tells Bellamy Storer that Stanton Sickles's posting to Madrid was a bad appointment and writes Andrew White about the Kaiser and Speck von Sternberg.
Roosevelt's morning caller is former Missouri Governor David R. Francis.

On Bamie's 47th birthday, Roosevelt hears Michigan beet sugar men opposed to Cuban reciprocity and receives the Walker Commission's revised report, now judging Panama the cheaper route. He and Edith dine with the Knoxes, and he jokes to Hay about Alice's words at the Kaiser's yacht christening.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.
The Isthmian Canal Commission's report goes to Congress, and Roosevelt meets Admiral Robley Evans that evening.

Grover Cleveland publicly supports Roosevelt on Cuban reciprocity. After a Cabinet meeting and visits from Senators Clay, Allison, Spooner and Foraker, Roosevelt dines in honor of Senator and Mrs. Depew. He writes Hanna on appointments and the District commissioners about smoke pollution.
Planning a stag dinner for Prince Henry
Roosevelt receives Senator Clapp and others and, in two letters, warns Douglas Robinson against any stake in buying government property and talks over plans for a men's dinner for Prince Henry.
Roosevelt lunches with John Hay, hosts the congressional reception, and asks George Carter to advise him on Hawaii's tangled politics.
After a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Solomon Bethea and others, Edith holds an afternoon tea and the Roosevelts give a dinner for Governor George McLean of Connecticut.
