Roosevelt confers with Platt, lunches with AP chief Melville Stone, and goes to the Gridiron Club dinner. Hay concludes a pact with Denmark covering the Danish West Indies, and Roosevelt tells Secretary Hitchcock that forest rangers must be real working rangers.
Roosevelt dines with the Lodges, Henry Adams, and Mr. and Mrs. Austin Wadsworth.
Roosevelt attends a Boone and Crockett Club dinner. Edith writes Cecil Spring-Rice a fond sketch of each of the six children, from pretty, level-headed Alice to clever little Quentin.
German Ambassador Theodor von Holleben calls in the morning; the evening brings dinner and a musicale. Roosevelt writes George Carter about Hawaii's governorship.
Roosevelt lunches with Paul Morton, sees Gifford Pinchot, and dines at John Hay's with Abram Hewitt, William Howard Taft, Andrew Carnegie, Elihu Root and the Carnegie fund trustees.

A photographer takes Roosevelt's picture in the morning. He confers with Governor Taft and Senators Quay and Penrose, hosts the Army-Navy reception, and writes Secretary Hitchcock about leases of Indian land in South Dakota.

Roosevelt issues an executive order barring federal officeholders from lobbying on legislation. He holds a Cabinet meeting on Cuban reciprocity, sees Quay and Penrose and Generals MacArthur and Barry, and welcomes Fanny and Jim Parsons. Prince Henry's goodwill tour of America gets under way.

Leslie Shaw succeeds Lyman Gage at the Treasury. Roosevelt receives Speaker Henderson, Francis Leupp and a string of other visitors, lunches with Johnstone, and he and Edith are dinner guests of Interior Secretary Hitchcock and his wife.

The ransom for missionary Ellen Stone is handed over to her kidnappers in Macedonia. Roosevelt writes Ted that a month of problems large and small has nearly worn him out, describes afternoon rides with Edith, Lodge and Root, and reports Kermit and Archie pelting passersby in the snow.
Naval officers on the Schley case

Roosevelt hears naval officers Wainwright, Evans, Taylor and Clark on the Schley case, meets General Miles and Commissioner Foulke, and lunches with four captains. He asks Seth Low to put Douglas Robinson on Prince Henry's welcome committee and writes Choate about the coming coronation of Edward VII.

Roosevelt confers on Cuban reciprocity and on the Schley case, holds a Cabinet meeting, and receives the National Industrial Association while Edith hosts an afternoon card reception. He writes Butler about Georgia patronage and race, and invites Senator Wolcott to the Prince Henry dinner.

Roosevelt lunches with Elihu Root and war correspondent Richard Harding Davis, receives Senators Platt, Clay and McLaurin and Representative Foss, and tells Philip Stewart he has raised the appointments question with Senator Wolcott.
A wedding and a dinner for Taft

Roosevelt attends the wedding of Helen Hay and Payne Whitney, confers with Hanna, Gallinger, Lodge and Gifford Pinchot, and hosts a dinner for William Howard Taft, governor of the Philippines. Richard Harding Davis stays the night.

Roosevelt lunches with the Whitelaw Reids, George W. Perkins, Secretary Shaw and the Evanses, meets his Cabinet about how federal jobs are classified, and writes Benjamin Tracy about the Santiago dispute.

Roosevelt meets Representative Hemenway, lunches with Wynne, Coolidge, West and Barry, and leaves for Groton, Massachusetts. A dinner Agriculture Secretary Wilson had planned for the Roosevelts is put off.
Roosevelt is in Groton, Massachusetts, as a guest of the W. H. Gardiner household.
Roosevelt remains in Groton. He had meant to travel to Charleston, South Carolina, around this time but dropped the trip.
Roosevelt is in Groton, Massachusetts; no other activities are noted.
On Alice's 18th birthday, Roosevelt, still in Groton, visits with the Reverend Charles H. Parkhurst.
Roosevelt leaves Groton and returns to Washington.
Roosevelt confers with Representatives Joy and Bartholdt and meets his Cabinet.
Who escorts whom at the state dinner?

After breakfast with Hanna and Postmaster General Payne and talks with Senate leaders and the Speaker, Roosevelt signs the urgent deficiency appropriation. As Prince Henry sails from Germany, he asks John Hay, half in jest, how to seat everyone without bruising German pride.
German Ambassador Theodor von Holleben calls on Roosevelt early in the afternoon.

Roosevelt meets General Miles, talks the Schley case with Shaw and Representative Foss and railroad rules with Senator Elkins, and lunches with editor Paul Dana, whose son joins them. He praises Frank Bullen's whaling book and tells Seth Low he wishes he could host Prince Henry his own way, not by protocol.

Roosevelt upholds the inquiry's verdict that Admiral Sampson, as overall commander, deserves credit for Santiago though Schley directed the fighting. He warns Root that Miles is angling for the Philippine command, threatening to expose Army abuses, and notes Miles led at Wounded Knee, where the treatment of Native Americans was far worse.

Roosevelt has Attorney General Knox announce a federal suit to break up the Northern Securities Company, the railroad holding company that Morgan and Kuhn, Loeb money built out of the Harriman and Hill lines; it will be filed at St. Paul in March. The Schley report is published. Ted falls ill with pneumonia at Groton and Edith hurries north to nurse him.
The trust suit hits the papers

Morning newspapers carry the Northern Securities suit. Roosevelt's callers include Attorney General Knox, railroad man James J. Hill himself, Board of Trade delegates, John Hay and Peru's vice president. He dines with David Starr Jordan.
After a Cabinet meeting Roosevelt talks railroad combinations with George W. Perkins of the Morgan firm, then lunches with publisher George Haven Putnam and Secretary Root.

J. P. Morgan, William Rockefeller and Pennsylvania Railroad chief A. J. Cassatt are among Roosevelt's callers. He talks Cuban tariff cuts with House members. Ted is better and Edith comes home. Roosevelt refuses a marshal's post to Ben Daniels, once jailed for murder, and writes Long about Sampson at Santiago.

Roosevelt calls at Secretary Root's home in the afternoon. In Macedonia, brigands release Ellen Stone, Mrs. Tsilka, and the baby Ellena, born to Mrs. Tsilka while they were held and given Miss Stone's name.
Beer steins for the Kaiser's brother

Prince Henry of Prussia, brother of Kaiser Wilhelm II, arrives at the White House. That evening Roosevelt gives him a stag dinner in the East Room, with beer served in steins, one bearing a joke inscription Roosevelt had added. In Cuba, electors choose Tomás Estrada Palma as president. At midnight the family leaves for New Jersey.

At Shooter's Island off Jersey City, Roosevelt and Edith watch Alice launch the Meteor, the Kaiser's new yacht. Prince Henry presents her with a diamond bracelet from his brother, newspapers giddily pair her with the prince, and the nickname Princess Alice is born. Everyone lunches aboard the Hohenzollern before the Roosevelts head home.

Booker T. Washington, Postmaster General Payne and Secretary Long are among Roosevelt's callers. He answers Herschel Jones's complaint about the surprise Northern Securities suit by saying no advance notice was required.
Roosevelt joins Prince Henry for a small, private dinner at the German Embassy.

Roosevelt attends Congress's memorial service for McKinley, lunches with Hanna, Fairbanks and others, and dines with Taft, while Edith receives 300 delegates of the Congress of Mothers. Amid press grumbling about American royalty, he tells Whitelaw Reid Alice should skip the coronation; instead she sails for Cuba with Harriet Blaine Beale to stay with the Woods.
Wisconsin lumbermen and a full day

In a crowded day, Roosevelt sees Commissioner Foulke, W. J. Calhoun, John Hay, William Rockhill and thirty Wisconsin lumbermen. He writes Hay about Alfred Moe's post in Honduras and Thomas Nast's in Guayaquil.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded for the day.
A ride in the rain with the prince

Roosevelt meets a delegation from the Charleston Exposition. He tells Whitelaw Reid he enjoyed Prince Henry's visit, above all a long horseback outing through the rain, and promises former Rough Rider Micah Jenkins a sword at Charleston.
The Cabinet takes up Cuba and a bill for a permanent Census Bureau, and Roosevelt lunches with Attorney General Knox.

Roosevelt confers with Speaker Henderson and Representatives Payne and Cannon about the Cuban reciprocity bill, and lunches with Irving Scott. He backs Root's refusal to give General Miles command in the Philippines.

After consulting Knox, Merriam, Foulke and Senator Proctor, Roosevelt signs the act creating a permanent Census Bureau. He hears California and Michigan lawmakers on tariff cuts, meets Root, and drafts a never-sent letter to Speck von Sternberg on Cuba, polo and Prince Henry.

After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt discusses Brooklyn patronage with Platt, lunches with Judge Day and Witherbee, and sees Foulke and Senator Hoar. He tells Root that Miles had once floated a 1900 challenge to McKinley, with Roosevelt on his ticket.

Roosevelt signs the Philippine Tariff Bill after meeting Speaker Henderson and Payne, sees Hanna and Colombia's minister, who presents his recall, and lunches with Eugene Philbin. Edith goes to see Quality Street. A short note tells Speck von Sternberg that Berlin has given no sign of sending him.
Roosevelt's Sunday is booked: Senator Hoar at one, Senator O. H. Platt, Representative Moody, dinner with Governor Odell, and reformer Josephine Shaw Lowell at nine.

Roosevelt talks Cuba with Payne and Grosvenor and gives a dinner for Governor Odell. He accepts Navy Secretary John D. Long's resignation with regret, and sends an Albany Sunday school teacher a favorite verse from Romans.
Roosevelt sends the Senate his first veto, rejecting a bill to clear a Civil War sailor's record of desertion. Two Boer envoys and a Mr. White call, and he lunches with C. C. Shayne.
Roosevelt meets Moody, lunches with John G. Milburn, sees Representative Hepburn and Senator Penrose, and hosts a late musicale.
Roosevelt confers with Secretary Shaw, Payne, Commander Evans, and Illinois Governor Richard Yates and his wife.
Cuban tariff and the Kershner case
After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt discusses the Cuban tariff with Payne and Dalzell and the Kershner case with Representative Butler, lunches with John Davis, and dines with editor Albert Shaw.

Roosevelt lunches with Senator Beveridge, Edward Everett Hale and Knox, and meets Russian Ambassador Arthur Cassini. In two letters to Root he asks whether three officers can attend German army maneuvers, and says Army surgeons in the Philippines must keep their prostitution reports out of print.
William Dinwiddie and Israel Putnam call on Roosevelt early in the afternoon.
Colombian Minister José Vicente Concha presents his credentials. Roosevelt lunches with Payne, Root, Leupp and several others.

Roosevelt goes walking with Count von Arnim, dines with the Storers and General Frederick Funston, and has Douglas and Corinne Robinson as overnight guests. He writes Jacob Riis about the Powderly-McSweeney inquiry and the Danish islands governorship.

A Mr. White photographs Roosevelt in the morning. He meets Senator O. H. Platt on Indian Territory, lunches with Judge Hornblower, and tells Root that Miles has leaked his side of the dispute to the newspapers.
Roosevelt breakfasts with James R. Sheffield, lunches with Jacob Gould Schurman and Belford, meets Root, and explains his philosophy of appointments to Lyman Gage.
The Cabinet weighs removing General Miles. Lawmakers including Foraker and Dalzell call, and Roosevelt lunches with Crimmins, Judge O'Brien and Dr. Dabney.

Roosevelt confers with Wood and Root on pulling U.S. troops out of Cuba and on Missouri patronage with Quay, Joy and Bartholdt, then goes to the Fencers' Club. Letters urge peace among Missouri factions, say he wants Miles gone, and tell President Eliot he will be in Cambridge to accept his honorary degree.
Roosevelt confers with Payne and Root about Cuba.

Roosevelt meets Root, Leonard Wood, Cuba's president-elect Estrada Palma and House members on reciprocity, and lunches with McIlvane. To Hermann Kohlsaat he vents that Miles has hurt the Army for eight years.
Roosevelt meets Estrada Palma and holds a Cabinet meeting on Cuba. He writes Senator George Hoar that he wishes he could attend the celebration of Edward Everett Hale's 80th birthday.
Late meeting with Platt and Aldrich
Roosevelt confers late in the evening with Senators Platt and Aldrich, and praises Donald Dickinson's note about Abram Hewitt.

Roosevelt sends 800 cavalry troopers to the Alaska-Canada border to hold key towns and ground should arbitration of the boundary dispute collapse. He talks with labor's Frank Morrison about a shorter-workday bill and keeping out Chinese laborers, and again endorses keeping Miles out of the Philippine command.

The Cabinet discusses taking U.S. forces out of Cuba. Roosevelt sees Ridder and Hanna, lunches with Williams, Holls and Torrance, and receives Commander Evans and Colonel Kitson of the British Embassy. He tells Horace White that Lodge and Butler urged him to keep Powderly.
Roosevelt meets western congressmen about the irrigation bill and writes his old political mentor Joe Murray that he wants him at the New York Custom House.
Roosevelt asks Joe Murray to send any evidence from past investigations or charges, so his record is spotless before the nomination.

The Deer Family comes out, the first book published by a sitting president. Roosevelt lunches with Dr. William Everett, receives Michigan teachers and others, and dines with his cousin James W. Roosevelt. The artist Cecilia Beaux paints Edith and Ethel together in the Red Parlor, though he dislikes the result.
A letter on Cecil Rhodes's passing

After a Cabinet meeting and talks with Hay, Beveridge and Knox, Roosevelt lunches with Wilkins, and he and Edith dine at the Hays'. He writes St. Clair McKelway on the Philippine friars and Albert Grey about Cecil Rhodes, who has just died.

Roosevelt breakfasts with Joe Murray, meets the Irrigation Commission and Boston schoolteachers, and gives a dinner for Stranahan with New York legislators. He tells Agriculture Secretary Wilson to check with him before saying anything publicly about the borax dispute with Germany.

Roosevelt lunches with banker Jacob Schiff. After dinner, Ignacy Jan Paderewski plays Chopin at a late musicale for the Roosevelts, sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens, the Lodges, Mrs. West Roosevelt and Senator Proctor.
Roosevelt breakfasts with George W. Perkins and visits with Senator Hanna.
Roosevelt breakfasts with Williams, lunches with Harry New, Sylvane Ferris of his Dakota days and others, confers with Senators Quay and Penrose, and dines with Joseph Bucklin Bishop.
After morning meetings with Sylvane Ferris and Speaker Henderson, Roosevelt leaves in the afternoon for the Charleston Exposition, stopping at Charlottesville, Virginia.
In Charleston, Roosevelt tours the harbor aboard the Algonquin and attends a reception.
Roosevelt rides in a parade and speaks in Charleston, then moves on to Summerville. At home, Archie turns eight.
Roosevelt heads back to Washington from Summerville, with stops at Branchville and Chester, South Carolina, and Charlotte, North Carolina.
Back at work, Roosevelt meets his Cabinet, sees Senator Burton, and dines with Associated Press chief Melville Stone.

Roosevelt signs the repeal of the Spanish-American War revenue taxes. Callers include Senator Quarles, General Sickles and Mooswa author W. A. Fraser. He dines with Cassatt, Spooner and Knox, and tells George von Lengerke Meyer that King Edward will not read The Winning of the West, though he was given a copy.
Hawaii's Governor Sanford Dole and George Carter call on Roosevelt in the evening.

Helen Keller and Alexander Graham Bell are among Roosevelt's callers. He lunches with Root, Villard, Leupp and Colonel Mills, talks Iowa patronage with Allison and Dolliver, and dines with John A. McCall. Historian James Ford Rhodes is an overnight guest.

Word reaches Washington that General Jacob Smith ordered troops in the Philippines to kill and burn. General Chaffee is told to investigate the atrocity reports and Roosevelt orders a court of inquiry. The Cabinet also takes up Indian Territory posts, and he writes Hitchcock about a forest reserve in Alaska.
Roosevelt has a full calendar of appointments and has Jacob Riis and the Attorney General to lunch.
Roosevelt confers with five senators: Hoar, Hale, Platt, McComas and Allison. Jacob Riis, Samuel Gompers and Francis Leupp call, and he dines with Marvin Hughitt and Payne.
After a Cabinet meeting and visits from the Sons of the Revolution, University of Michigan students and Senator Kean, Roosevelt leaves with Edith for New York City.

In New York, Roosevelt breakfasts with Nicholas Murray Butler, sees the Robinsons, cousin Emlen Roosevelt and architect Charles McKim, and with Edith attends Butler's installation as president of Columbia University, followed by a dinner at Sherry's. Then it is back to Washington.
Angry at a leaked dinner talk

Roosevelt meets W. C. Sanger and tells him he is reluctant to launch a campaign against the Moros. He writes George Eggleston in anger that his White House dinner remarks appeared in the New York Herald as an interview.
Senators and congressmen including Beveridge, Warren and Aldrich call. Roosevelt lunches with McKim, the Newbolds and Mr. Knott, and dines with Taft.

After a Cabinet meeting and talks with Littauer and Senator Foraker, Roosevelt lunches with Constance Lodge. He writes Admiral Henry Taylor about poor Navy gunnery as shown in William Sims's letters, and E. I. Bonner about Indian agents.
Roosevelt discusses a circuit judgeship with Platt and the customs service with Stranahan, lunches with Roche, Stranahan and George Peck, and thanks Joseph Bishop for an editorial.
Roosevelt meets Platt, lunches with railroad man Charles S. Mellen, and he and Edith are dinner guests of Navy Secretary Long and his wife. Edith writes her sister Emily that she is pregnant again.

The Cabinet weighs Colombian against Nicaraguan canal routes. General Corbin and Sanger call, and Roosevelt lunches with Taft, John Hay, Burlingame and Cecil Spring-Rice. He asks Stranahan to talk with Braun of the Hungarian Republican Club on New York's East Side.
Representative Joseph Cannon calls. Roosevelt lunches with Charleston Mayor J. Adger Smyth, John C. Rose and Captain Crozier, and sees Senators Quarles and Spooner at nine.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded for the day.

Roosevelt signs the Legislative Appropriation Act, lunches with editor Richard Watson Gilder, and he and Edith dine with Agriculture Secretary Wilson and his wife. He asks Trumbull Cary about buying a second horse, The Philosopher, and tells Hanna that Bob liked the cartoon.

On Corinne's 20th wedding anniversary, the Senate confirms William H. Moody as Navy Secretary. The Cabinet discusses illegal fencing of public land, and Roosevelt signs the Chinese Exclusion bill. He tells Moody that Subic Bay is too sprawling for the Navy to hold as a base.
Money to remake the White House

Congress votes over half a million dollars to renovate the White House under architect Charles McKim: a new office wing, guest rooms upstairs, a larger State Dining Room, Arthur's Tiffany screen gone, the greenhouses down. Roosevelt also meets Hanna and Payne, lunches with Root, and his article on blacktail deer appears in Outing.

William H. Moody succeeds John D. Long as Navy Secretary. Roosevelt breakfasts with Curtis, talks with Hitchcock and Land Commissioner Binger Hermann about monopolies on public land, and confers with Allison, Littauer and Fairbanks.

Roosevelt hands out diplomas and speaks at the Naval Academy commencement in Annapolis, telling the graduates that if war ever comes the country must win and the Navy will decide it, so every patriotic American should want the fleet built up. He returns to Washington.
A photo on a jumping horse

The Cabinet meets on illegal fencing of public land, and at noon Roosevelt is photographed on a jumping horse. He lunches with Smalley and Waller, meets the French ambassador, and dines with Henry Clay Frick and Knox. He assures Josephine Shaw Lowell he will work as hard as anyone to end cruelties in the Philippines.
Evening with the Roots and Taft
Secretary Root, Mrs. Root, their daughter and Judge Taft visit Roosevelt in the evening.

Cuba's Congress opens and Cuban flags fly for the first time. On a busy day, Roosevelt names labor leader Frank Sargent to head the immigration service, sits for photographer Strohmeyer, and lunches with Curtis Guild. He warns James Clarkson about civil service law and writes Hamlin Garland on homesteading and fenced western land.

After a Cabinet meeting and visits from Payne, Speaker Henderson and western lawmakers, Roosevelt lunches with naturalists George Bird Grinnell and C. Hart Merriam, then rides with General Young. He introduces London Times correspondent Smalley to Knox.

Roosevelt meets Gifford Pinchot and lunches with Root and Taft. He tells Secretary Hitchcock to keep sheep out of Yellowstone while letting cattle and horses graze, and argues with William Austin Wadsworth about Philippine atrocities.
Roosevelt receives a Maryland congressional delegation and Commander Evans, then dines with Lodge, James R. Garfield, Senator Kean, Secretary Moody and Ware.

Roosevelt attends Admiral William Sampson's funeral and lunches with Governor Taft. Overnight Edith suffers another miscarriage and is confined to bed for twelve days. In letters he answers Massachusetts church protests over Philippine atrocities, asks Wood to show Bryan courtesy in Havana, and asks Root about an investigating commission.
Beef trust suit and a deadline for McKim

Attorney General Knox opens the government's case against the beef trust. Roosevelt talks over the Rathbone case with Senator Hanna, receives a visiting English textile commission, and has Owen Wister and John Hay to lunch. He tells architect Charles McKim that speed comes first: the new offices and the family's rooms must be ready by October 1. Word is spreading of the eruption of Mount Pelée, which wiped out Saint-Pierre on Martinique two days earlier.
Roosevelt has an appointment with Colonel Sawyer.

Some 140,000 anthracite miners in eastern Pennsylvania walk out; John Mitchell's union seeks recognition, while George Baer of the Reading railroad speaks for the owners. Roosevelt asks Congress for aid to Martinique, meets Root and the Speaker, and dines at the Lodges'. He notes that captions in The Deer Family got switched.
Roosevelt confers with Platt and lunches with Bishop James Thoburn, while Edith passes a few hours on the presidential yacht Sylph. He writes supporter John Shafter about politics.
Senators Platt, Hanna, Penrose and Foraker call. In the afternoon Roosevelt travels to Tenleytown to lay the cornerstone of the McKinley Memorial Ohio College of Government.

Roosevelt watches the high school cadets' annual drill and receives Charles Francis Adams. He writes Leonard Wood upholding Estes Rathbone's Cuban conviction despite Rathbone's friendship with Hanna, and tells Henry White that John Singer Sargent is the artist to paint a president.
Roosevelt lunches with Charles Francis Adams and Commissioner Foulke and in the afternoon meets Ellen Stone, recently freed by her Macedonian captors. He dines with Senator Allison.
Roosevelt goes to Arlington Cemetery to speak at the reburial of Civil War General William Rosecrans, then lunches with Charles Bonaparte, the Civil Service Commissioners and Knox.
Roosevelt is in Washington; no activities are recorded.
Roosevelt writes John Hay a humorous letter about an appointment at Fort Erie.

After a Cabinet meeting Roosevelt takes the Pennsylvania Railroad to New York and speaks about Cuba at Carnegie Hall during a Central Presbyterian Church celebration of home missions, then returns to Washington.

Roosevelt sees a string of senators, discusses a Court of Claims vacancy with Littauer, and lunches with Henry Chapman. At Arlington he speaks as a new monument to the war with Spain is unveiled and dines with Dana, Root, Knox, Lodge and Spooner. Edith is up and feeling much better.
Crater Lake becomes a national park

Crater Lake National Park is established. A treaty with Mexico sets up a five-member panel, with members drawn from both nations and The Hague list, to settle the Pious Fund claims of California's Catholic Church. Roosevelt meets lawmakers on Indian appropriations and attends a dinner honoring Count Rochambeau.
Roosevelt spends the day at Annapolis aboard the French cruiser Gaulois, lunching on board, then dines at the French Embassy in Washington with Secretary Moody and Admiral Dewey.
Rochambeau statue; a dog that won't vote Democratic

Roosevelt watches the new Rochambeau statue unveiled across from the White House, with Alice standing in as hostess while Edith recovers. He tells Hermann Kohlsaat about Bozzie, a Milwaukee collie who barked Kermit's age, counted the crowd and made clear she would sooner die than vote for a Democrat.
Roosevelt attends Trinity Church's 100th anniversary observance.
On a busy day Roosevelt lunches with R. W. Patterson, reviews Washington's Knights Templars from the White House North Portico, and dines with Senator Allison. Whitelaw Reid stays the night.
Roosevelt meets Senators Aldrich, Scott and Beveridge, and writes Nicholas Murray Butler a defense of his course on reciprocity, tariffs and the Philippines.
Leonard Wood calls. At noon Roosevelt attends the funeral of British Ambassador Lord Pauncefote. His old friend Sir Michael Herbert, whom he called Mungo, is named the new ambassador.
Senator Platt calls, and Roosevelt writes Eugene Hale on the Navy personnel bill and John C. Rose about lowering tariffs.

On Memorial Day at Arlington, Roosevelt addresses Philippine policy, promising to root out every act of brutality by American troops. He also condemns lynching of Black Americans in the South, angering many Southerners as the Washington dinner had.

Roosevelt meets Senators Aldrich, Dolliver and Allison. Congress funds protection of the American bison, and a government herd is started in Yellowstone. The White House menagerie now counts a terrier, a Chesapeake Bay dog, the macaw Eli Yale, a spotted rat named Jonathan, two kangaroo rats, a flying squirrel and Archie's pony Algonquin.
Roosevelt spends Sunday evening at the White House talking with four senators: Stewart, Clapp, Millard and Dietrich.
Roosevelt gathers a large group of Republican leaders from both houses at night to push for a trade deal with Cuba, and writes Root to introduce Bishop Bienk of Puerto Rico.

The Cabinet takes up planned naval exercises and the needs of the consular service. Roosevelt lunches with Senator Aldrich and dines with Leonard Wood and Lodge, then answers critics in a run of letters, including one standing by his Memorial Day comparison of Southern lynchings with abuses in the Philippines.

Governor Van Sant of Minnesota is among the day's callers. Roosevelt writes Groton headmaster Endicott Peabody that Kermit will enter the school, with master Walter Hinchman coaching him at Sagamore Hill over the summer.
Roosevelt receives a delegation of railroad engineers in the morning and addresses the convention of the nation's military surgeons.
Public buildings on the Cabinet agenda

The Cabinet discusses the Public Buildings Bill, C. S. Francis calls, and Roosevelt writes his old Rough Rider Alexander Brodie, now governor of Arizona Territory, about Treasury business and patronage.
A Kipling portrait comes to the White House
Roosevelt goes over Army appointments with Secretary Root, lunches with Commander Ware and Leonard Wood, and in the afternoon views a portrait of Rudyard Kipling delivered to the White House.
Jasmine and honeysuckle on the South Portico

Roosevelt confers with Wright about the anthracite coal strike. After dark he and Edith sit out on the South Portico, looking toward the Washington Monument with the scent of jasmine and honeysuckle in the air.

Work starts on rebuilding the White House. Edith takes Ethel, Kermit, Archie and Quentin aboard the Dolphin down the Potomac, bound for Sagamore Hill, while Roosevelt moves into a temporary home on Jackson Place and hosts senators and Leonard Wood for dinner. He tells Joel Chandler Harris the children have heard every one of his stories.
Cabinet, dinner, then off to West Point

After a Cabinet meeting and dinner with Knox, Payne, Moody and Hanna, Roosevelt heads for West Point. His letters say General Miles should have been removed long before, discuss an embassy for Bellamy Storer, push Cuban reciprocity with Spooner, and ask Root for capable Army chaplains.
Speaking at West Point as Sagamore opens

Roosevelt gives a speech at West Point. On Long Island, Edith notes in the guest book that she has opened Sagamore Hill for the season; the season's first visitors are Mrs. Clifford Richardson and John R. Procter.
Back to Washington from West Point
Roosevelt returns to the capital in the afternoon and takes up with Senator Platt the charge that Leonard Wood spent Cuban money to circulate pro-reciprocity literature.

Roosevelt sends Congress a special message urging a trade bill for Cuba right away. He talks with Hepburn about a new Department of Commerce, dines with George Perkins, and asks Joe Cannon not to fight the irrigation bill in the House.
Breakfast at Hanna's, dinner with McKim

Roosevelt breakfasts at Senator Hanna's with Root and Payne, meets again with Hepburn, and dines with architect Charles McKim, Root and Littauer. He writes Dewey that the admiral will lead the fleet exercises in the fall.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record notes nothing more for the day.

A court of inquiry has found General Jacob Smith guilty over his conduct in the Philippines, and Roosevelt orders him retired. He meets Booker T. Washington at noon about appointments in the South, receives Cuban Minister Quesada, and cheers Woodrow Wilson's election as Princeton's president in a letter to Cleveland Dodge.

Roosevelt signs the Newlands Act, which puts money from public land sales in 16 Western states into a fund for irrigating the dry West. He dines with Lodge, Root and Colonel Johnson, and writes Grover Cleveland in praise of Woodrow Wilson.
Visits from the French ambassador and Butler
Leonard Wood is staying with Roosevelt. He sees the French ambassador in the morning and has Nicholas Murray Butler, John Hay and Hill to dinner; Butler stays overnight.
Senate picks Panama for the canal

The Senate votes for a Panama route and authorizes buying the canal rights from Colombia, which then held the isthmus. Roosevelt sits for photographer Prince in the morning, lunches with architect McKim, and has Moody, Hale, Lodge, Spooner and Knox to dinner.
Over breakfast with William Williams and in two letters to Joe Bishop, Roosevelt takes stock: senators are fighting Cuban reciprocity hard, and if it fails now he will bring it back next session.
Roosevelt goes over canal business with Congressman Hepburn and receives the Swiss minister. His Dakota friend Bob Ferguson signs the guest book.
Lunch with Hay, canal talk with Morgan
Roosevelt lunches with Secretary of State John Hay and spends the evening talking canal matters with Senator John T. Morgan.

Roosevelt hears Representative Mudd on Republican quarrels in Maryland, talks canal legislation again with Morgan, and dines with Navy Secretary Moody. Letters go to Hitchcock about rations being cut off on Indian reservations and to Governor Odell about the concessionaires removed from Ellis Island.
Senators call, then north to Harvard
After a Cabinet meeting and visits from seven senators, among them Platt, Beveridge and Spooner, Roosevelt leaves late in the afternoon for Boston and Cambridge.

Harvard gives Roosevelt an honorary Doctor of Laws at Commencement. At the alumni dinner he tells graduates a college education confers no special rank, only a heavier duty to live well, and he credits Leonard Wood, Root and Taft. He then leaves for New London.
Roosevelt takes in the Harvard-Yale boat race at New London, then heads back to Washington.
The Cabinet takes up the lands held by religious orders in the Philippines, and Roosevelt dines with the Lodges. Miss Alice Harder signs the guest book.
Spooner Act signed for a Panama canal

Roosevelt meets Admiral Walker and signs the Spooner Act, letting him buy canal rights across Panama from the French company and Colombia for no more than $40 million. He tells Senator Platt the coming Caribbean fleet maneuvers, the Navy's first, were his own idea.
Roosevelt breakfasts and dines at Senator Hanna's house, attends the late-morning unveiling of a memorial tablet to McKinley, and lunches with Senator Beveridge and Philip Stewart.
A full day as the canal news breaks

Roosevelt meets Admiral Walker while newspapers report his signing of the canal bill, then has Knox, Garfield, Lodge and Spooner to dinner. In Oyster Bay, Kermit's tutor Walter Hinchman settles in for the summer.
Congress adjourns with a flurry of signatures

Roosevelt signs a stack of bills, among them the Philippine Civil Government Act and the naval budget, as Congress goes home. He lays a church cornerstone in the afternoon and writes Hay that the canal will be the greatest achievement of his presidency.
Sulphur Springs becomes a national monument

Roosevelt proclaims Sulphur Springs in Indian Territory, today's Oklahoma, a national monument. He works on a Philippine amnesty with Root, lunches with a group of cabinet members and senators, and tells Hitchcock the irrigation program is of the first importance.
After lunch with Root, Butler, Spooner and McLaurin, Roosevelt leaves for Pittsburgh with Attorney General Knox. Bob Ferguson is again in the guest book.
Roosevelt gives an Independence Day speech in Schenley Park, lunches with Henry Clay Frick, joins a dinner in Knox's honor at the Schenley Hotel, and boards a train for Oyster Bay.
Home to Oyster Bay for the summer
Roosevelt's train pulls into Oyster Bay in the rain. Waiting are his secretaries Loeb and Cortelyou, Ted on horseback, and three more children, Ethel, Kermit and Archie, riding in the surrey.
Oyster Bay turns into the Summer White House

Reporters pour into Oyster Bay as Sagamore Hill takes on its role as the Summer White House, complete with a telephone, number 67, that Edith did not want. The family goes to Christ Church with Aunt Emily and Bob Ferguson. Archie's Boston bull pup Bozzie dies and is laid to rest in the family pet graveyard; his brother is sent for from Chicago.
A morning on the bumpy home tennis court

Cortelyou and Loeb set up the executive office in two rooms over the Oyster Bay Bank. Roosevelt plays tennis with the children all morning on the bumpy dirt court in the hollow below the house, where burrowing animals and low branches call for house rules. The Secret Service turns away its first crank, and fireworks light up the evening.

Roosevelt lunches with Montague White and writes Governor Odell about a Brooklyn Navy Yard job, adding that he would like a meeting with E. H. Harriman. He also complains to Payne about newspaper falsehoods.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Holding firm on the Alaska boundary

Roosevelt writes Hay that Canada's bid to send the Alaska boundary dispute to The Hague comes close to blackmail, that Britain must be held firmly to account, and that the United States will give up no territory.
Stranahan, W. B. Parsons and Senator McLaurin call at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt discusses the Philippine friars' estates with Father Malone.
Root and Father Donovan on church lands

Root visits Sagamore Hill to discuss the friars' lands with Father Donovan, and Dr. Alexander Lambert is a guest. Roosevelt tells Root he wants turned-down collars, not stand-up ones, on Army field uniforms.
Canal and church lands with Root and Spooner
Roosevelt continues the friars' lands talks with Root and reviews the canal plans with Root and Spooner.

Roosevelt looks over the presidential yacht Mayflower, one of three government vessels at his disposal, with Root and Dr. Lambert. Architect Charles McKim, who is directing the White House rebuilding, comes for lunch.
Roosevelt dines with Brooklyn Eagle editor St. Clair McKelway, who is entered in the guest book.

Robert Munn stays overnight at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Hay about posting soldiers to towns along the Alaska border for police work, and writes Eugene Philbin about Catholic representation on the Philippine Commission and the church lands.
Urging Hay to take a real rest

Roosevelt lunches with Hawley, Colonel Bingham, Charles Carroll, Regis Post and Caspar Whitney, and talks Cuban reciprocity with Hawley. Nellie Tyler and Lucius Littauer sign the guest book. He tells John Hay, for heaven's sake, to get some genuine rest.
The Roosevelts go on a picnic together. Edith's secretary, Belle Hagner, is a guest.
Lunch with Seth Low and New Yorkers

Roosevelt has New York Mayor Seth Low to lunch along with Crimmins, Elsberg, Kean and more. He writes Baron Speck von Sternberg about the Indian army, the Philippines and General Smith, and thanks Wilbur Wakeman for backing reciprocity.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Bamie and Will Cowles come to stay

Roosevelt talks with Hepburn about the canal and about who should replace Tichenor as general appraiser in New York, and sees H. S. Bliss late that evening. His sister Bamie and her husband Will Cowles arrive, along with Miss Helen Roosevelt.

Roosevelt meets Frederick Gibbs about state elections over lunch, and Mrs. Clifford Richardson visits again. He writes Simon Wolf about Jews in Romania and Russia, and tells Hay he has been reading the Lincoln biography Hay wrote with John Nicolay and admires it.

Nicholas Murray Butler and G. E. Graham call. Roosevelt goes over trusts and island tariff rates with Jacob Gould Schurman, lunches with Captain Goddard, Schurman, Graham and Butler, and dines with Leonard Wood and Butler.
Speaking at the Sea Girt encampment
Roosevelt travels to Sea Girt, New Jersey, to address the 2nd Regiment at its camp, is received by Governor Murphy, and spends time on Senator Kean's yacht.
Holmes chosen for the Supreme Court

Justice Gray has resigned, and Roosevelt writes Senator Hoar that he will name Oliver Wendell Holmes of Massachusetts in his place. Visitors include Meyer and Albert Shaw; Dr. Lambert, Treasury Secretary Shaw, painter Cecilia Beaux and Grace Potter are guests. He tells Speaker Reed he can only pass through Maine, not stay.
A day of New York callers

Roosevelt lunches with Knox, Spooner, William Byrne and New York's attorney general, Davies, dines with Eugene Philbin, Father Belford and F. C. Travis, and at nine sees Commodore Swan and Colonel Vrooman.
Navy Secretary Moody calls and is listed as a guest; Roosevelt has Mr. Perkins and Cushing Stetson to lunch.
Roosevelt lunches on the Mayflower and sees Colonel Hood at nine that evening.
Roosevelt spends the whole day with Edith on a long row and picnic down Long Island Sound and back. Sheffield, Garfield, Butler and Dr. Alderman come to dinner and stay the night.

Roosevelt discusses New York State politics with Senator Platt and Colonel George Dunn while his overnight guests are still in the house. He writes Hoar again about Holmes and complains to Paul Dana that the Sun's man at Oyster Bay is making up stories about the family.

Roosevelt lunches with Governor William Hunt of Puerto Rico, Adolph Ochs, Postmaster General Payne and others; Winthrop Chanler visits. He warns Taft that Catholic critics are stirring trouble over his mission to Rome and reports that the boys fill their days with rifle practice, tennis, riding, rowing and swimming. When Russian Grand Duke Boris visits, Edith arranges a lunch elsewhere to avoid receiving a man of notorious reputation.
Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill on tariff revision.
Roosevelt's lunch guests include editor George Harvey, Silas McBee, Edward Kent, Wakeman, a Mr. Cowles, Charles Nugel and Bishop Duducy.
Joseph Bucklin Bishop is a guest, and D. Leroy Dresser calls at nine in the evening.
Archbishop Ryan and Pinchot to lunch

Roosevelt talks with Archbishop Ryan about the friars' lands, then lunches with the Whitelaw Reids, the Elbridge Gerrys, the Archbishop and Gifford Pinchot, discussing Pinchot's planned trip to the Philippines. He urges Moody to give prizes for good gunnery on big naval guns.
Off on the Sylph with Edith

Late in the afternoon Roosevelt and Edith leave on the Sylph for Gardiner's Bay. He accepts Andrew White's resignation as ambassador, tells Hay that Charlemagne Tower will go to Berlin, and writes Philip Stewart about Colorado posts and his dislike of Senator Teller.
On Edith's 41st birthday, she and Roosevelt watch Navy gunnery practice from the Mayflower in Gardiner's Bay.

Back home, Roosevelt receives Senator O. H. Platt and a group of congressmen and talks over Western cattle ranges with Philip Stewart. Architect Grant La Farge arrives that afternoon. He tells Hay he had promised Berlin to Storer but now wants Tower, and asks Albert Gleaves to sharpen the Mayflower's gunnery.
Knox and the Pacific cable contract
Roosevelt reviews the Pacific cable firm's government contract with Attorney General Knox, then lunches with Knox, his cousin Christine Roosevelt, McCullough and Lieutenant Dick.
Letters on New York and an Army promotion
Roosevelt writes Senator Platt about a New York political quarrel, and tells Senator Quay that promoting Hugh Scott all the way to general from captain is too much.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing further is recorded.
Holmes named to the Supreme Court

Roosevelt puts Oliver Wendell Holmes on the nation's highest court and writes Senator Hoar that he will announce it. Charles McKim calls to see Edith about the White House work, and Roosevelt lunches with China's Prince Tsai Chen and Senator Burrows.
Thanks to Butler on the friar question
Roosevelt lunches with William R. Grace; Bob Ferguson and Joseph Wilmer are guests. He thanks Nicholas Murray Butler for his help with the friars and writes him about the tariff.

It is Ethel's 11th birthday. Roosevelt confers in the morning with J. M. Bliss and Albert Washburn about the New York appraiser post, and in the afternoon Gifford Pinchot and Grant La Farge arrive to spend the night.
Odell to lunch; Fuller approves of Holmes

Roosevelt confers and lunches with Governor Odell while Grant La Farge and Pinchot are still guests. He defends his trust policy, along with Knox and Root, in a letter to Frederick Goddard, and writes Chief Justice Fuller, who likes the Holmes choice.
Generals, a governor and Jacob Riis

Generals Corbin and Young, Governor Francis, Jacob Riis and several others come for lunch, and Albert Shaw stays for dinner. Roosevelt asks Hay whether it is true that Vienna would balk at a Catholic ambassador such as Bellamy Storer.
Bishop Thomas O'Gorman dines at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt confers with Dr. Presley Rixey, the White House physician, who visits with his wife.

Roosevelt has Major John Crane and F. C. Travers to lunch, then confers and dines with Congressmen Hull, Babcock and Overstreet on the state campaigns. He writes Senator Foraker, no friend of Storer, about the Berlin post.

Roosevelt tells Oliver Wendell Holmes he expects not one vote against him in the Senate. He also writes Governor Odell about Harriman and the trusts, and Massachusetts Governor Crane about campaign money.
Setting the record straight on irrigation
Albert Shaw and Frederick Holls call and stay for lunch with Lyon, and Grant La Farge is a guest. Roosevelt again tells Charles Lummis that Newlands had no part in getting the irrigation bill passed.
Can Washington act on the coal strike?

Roosevelt talks with Senator Pritchard about a vacancy on the Court of Claims and lunches with him and others. He asks Attorney General Knox whether the government can move against the coal operators to end the strike. Edith writes McKim proposing a gallery of First Ladies' portraits in the White House ground floor corridor.
New England tour opens on the trusts

Roosevelt takes the Sylph across to New Haven and starts a speaking swing to explain his case against the trusts. At Hartford he speaks on island policy and rides in a parade by automobile, which the record says made him the first president to ride in one. At Providence he gives a major speech on trusts, then speaks at three Connecticut towns and spends the night with the Winthrop Chanlers in Newport.
Roosevelt's train carries him from Newport up to Boston, pausing at Myricks, Taunton and Fall River, and spends the night at Lodge's home in Nahant.
Roosevelt speaks at the Nahant library and Lynn City Hall, then takes on the trusts in a speech at Boston's Symphony Hall. He dines with Governor Crane, Lodge, Senator Hoar and others.

Roosevelt praises former Puerto Rico governor Charles Allen at Lowell, speaks on the Philippines at Lawrence and on the Navy at Haverhill, then talks at Dover, New Hampshire, and at Old Orchard, Portland and Augusta in Maine, where he stays with Governor Hill.
Governor's Day at the Maine State Fair
Roosevelt speaks in Bangor on Governor's Day at the state fair, then at Ellsworth, and travels on to Waterville.
New Hampshire stops end at the Hays'
Roosevelt speaks at Nashua, Manchester, Concord, a soldiers' reunion at The Weirs, and Newbury, New Hampshire, where he spends the night at John Hay's summer home.
A boar hunt in New Hampshire
Near Newport, New Hampshire, Roosevelt goes boar hunting with Senator Proctor and Corbin.
With novelist Winston Churchill to Vermont
Roosevelt rides to Windsor, Vermont, in the company of novelist Winston Churchill, and passes the evening near Burlington, by Lake Champlain, at the home of L. M. Shaw.
Near Burlington, Roosevelt dines at Dr. Webb's. Kermit begins his first term at Groton School.

Roosevelt stops at eight Vermont towns from Vergennes to Brattleboro and spends the evening with Navy Secretary Moody at Northfield, Massachusetts. He arranges to meet Senator Aldrich at Sagamore Hill on September 16.
Alice waves from a passing train

Roosevelt's train winds through the Berkshires. By chance Alice passes on a train heading the other way and waves wildly, but her father, mid-speech, never sees her. He speaks on trusts at Fitchburg and stops at Miller's Falls, Athol, Springfield, Worcester and Dalton.

In Pittsfield an electric streetcar slams into the open landau carrying Roosevelt, Governor Murray Crane and George Cortelyou. Secret Service agent William Craig is killed, and a horse dies. Roosevelt is hurled about 30 feet, hurting his left leg and bruising his face; Cortelyou suffers a deep scalp wound. Half an hour later Roosevelt goes on to speak at Lenox, and 30,000 people greet him at Bridgeport before he sails home.
Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt has Joe Bishop as a guest.
Roosevelt sets out from Sagamore Hill for Chattanooga, Tennessee.
Wheeling speech; thanks to the King
Roosevelt speaks on the trusts at Wheeling, West Virginia. He thanks King Edward VII for asking after him, saying his injuries were minor, and compliments Martha Dunn on her article about Browning.
In Chattanooga Roosevelt reviews the 7th Cavalry and tours the Civil War battlefield.
Roosevelt addresses the locomotive firemen's union at its Chattanooga convention, then leaves for Knoxville.
Roosevelt speaks at Asheville and Greensboro, North Carolina.
Roosevelt returns home to Oyster Bay.
Lucius B. Swift visits and stays to lunch. Roosevelt writes James Garfield about civil service matters, including voluntary political donations from federal workers.

Roosevelt lunches with J. S. Clarkson and J. T. McDonough, who stays on for dinner. The record also notes a statement by Navy Secretary Moody pledging that the United States will keep the isthmus neutral and transit across it open.
Ted turns fifteen; an essay on trusts

It is Ted's 15th birthday. Albert Shaw, Arthur Lee and Postmaster General Payne call and stay for lunch. Roosevelt writes an Outlook article, "Big Corporations Commonly Called Trusts." The piece also touches on citizenship.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

The Roosevelts open Sagamore Hill to their Nassau County neighbors for an afternoon garden party. Thousands come, 60 New York City police stand guard, and guests take home 3,000 crystal punch cups engraved with the President's name and the year. He asks E. H. Harriman to talk tariff and trusts.
Party leaders gather at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt brings Lodge, Spooner, Allison, Aldrich and Hanna to Oyster Bay to set strategy on the congressional campaign, tariff revision and the trusts.
General Joseph Wheeler, Roosevelt's old commander from Cuba, visits and stays for lunch.
Trusts with Jenks; a writing table Edith dislikes

Lyman Abbott and Henry White call, and Roosevelt discusses trusts with economist J. W. Jenks before all three stay to lunch. Joe Bishop comes for dinner and the night. Roosevelt writes Hay about the Cuban treaty, while Edith tells McKim the new White House writing table is ugly and awkward to use.
Starting west as the coal strike drags on

Roosevelt leaves for a Western trip while Edith takes the Sylph into Manhattan, landing at East 23rd Street. He writes Senator Quay that John Mitchell refuses to call off the anthracite strike, which has run since May, and insists on a compromise.
Cincinnati speech on tariff and trusts
In Cincinnati Roosevelt speaks on the tariff and the trusts. The record also notes that the United States is guarding and guaranteeing passage across Panama.
Lunch with General Alger in Detroit
In Detroit Roosevelt lunches with General Russell Alger, McKinley's former Secretary of War.
Detroit speech on Cuba and the Philippines
Roosevelt speaks in Detroit on reciprocity with Cuba and on the Philippines.
Surgery in Indianapolis ends the tour

At Logansport Roosevelt tells Spanish-American War veterans he favors a tariff commission. In Indianapolis his leg, still swollen weeks after the Pittsfield crash, is found to hold an abscess; at St. Vincent's doctors numb it and draw off about two ounces of fluid. That evening he reads aboard his special train, leg propped up, headed for Washington.
Ordered to rest on Jackson Place
With the White House still under renovation, Roosevelt is carried to the house at 22 Jackson Place, where doctors insist on rest and quiet. Edith hurries down from New York to be with him.
In a wheelchair, still receiving callers

Roosevelt is in a wheelchair, his face still swollen three weeks after the crash, but he sees Japanese minister Takahira, Moody, Shaw, Wilson and Hitchcock. He congratulates Frank Higgins on his nomination for lieutenant governor and explains in a letter that the abscess forced him to give up the Western trip.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.
A second operation and moves on the coal strike

On Corinne's 41st birthday, Roosevelt sees Shaw and Wilson and explains to Hanna that his injury and the coal strike keep him from Ohio. When rest brings no relief, a doctor opens the abscess again and scrapes the shin bone; Alice helps care for him. Soon after, he twice gathers his advisers on what Washington can do in the strike and writes Lodge a key letter that sets up the talks.
Summoning both sides of the coal strike

Roosevelt wires John Mitchell asking to see him on October 3 about the failing coal supply, and invites railroad chief Alexander Cassatt and Senator Quay into the effort. He also sends condolences to Isabella Craig, whose son William, a Secret Service agent, died in the Pittsfield crash. Edith gets her first look at the rebuilt White House and plans an upstairs office for herself.
Smaller spurs and a mending leg
Roosevelt asks Root for smaller spurs for the cavalry, tells Senator O. H. Platt the rest has done him good and the doctors are done cutting, and writes Oswald Villard on the strike and the trusts.
Operators and miners meet the President

Still in a wheelchair, Roosevelt brings mine owners and union leaders face to face at his temporary home on Jackson Place, with Mitchell, Baer, Truesdale, Wilcox, Carroll Wright and Cortelyou among those present. He reports on the meeting to Hanna and Seth Low. In Panama, trains run under American protection.
Strike talks with Knox and Wright
Root calls in the morning, and Roosevelt confers with Knox and Carroll Wright on the strike.

Roosevelt spends Sunday on the strike with Wright and four Cabinet members. He writes Grover Cleveland that the operators' language toward Mitchell seemed designed to make the miners refuse everything.
Criticized from both sides; books from the Library

Roosevelt confers with Frank Sargent on the strike and tells William Allen White that one camp calls him too friendly to the miners, the other too friendly to the companies. He asks Librarian of Congress Herbert Putnam for histories of the Mediterranean peoples and of Poland.
Proposing an investigation of the strike
Roosevelt publicly proposes an inquiry into the coal strike and meets Albert Shaw and Lyman Abbott. To Robert Bacon he likens his position to Lincoln's; to Lodge he describes his strike troubles.

Roosevelt confers with Root and Knox and reviews the parade of Union veterans of the Grand Army of the Republic. He thanks Herbert Putnam for books that let him set aside everything useful for a while.

Roosevelt holds more strike meetings with Root and Knox and sees Wilkins of the Washington Post. He writes Villard on whether sending soldiers to work the mines would be possible or lawful, and praises Silas McBee's strike column.
Kermit's birthday; a commission takes shape

On Kermit's 13th birthday, the Cabinet meets on the strike and Roosevelt receives the U.S. minister to Belgium. He tells Grover Cleveland his leg keeps him from Woodrow Wilson's Princeton installation and asks him to sit on a strike inquiry board, and writes Hanna about his plan for a settlement commission.
A Siamese prince and more strike talks

Roosevelt keeps up the strike meetings with his Cabinet, Wright and Sargent, sees Noyes of the Washington Star, and receives a prince of Siam. It is his niece Eleanor's 18th birthday. He praises Governor Odell's stand and answers John Kernan's request to serve on the commission.

Strike meetings go on, with Root and Quay among the callers and Jenks at six. Cleveland agrees to serve on the commission. Roosevelt writes that he can now move about on crutches, and that while he is supposed to be minding Ethel, she will likely end up minding him.
Morgan brings a plan to Jackson Place

Roosevelt asks General Schofield about having the Army run the mines and receives the Chief Justice and the Supreme Court. That evening J. P. Morgan and Robert Bacon, fresh from talks with Root aboard Morgan's yacht Corsair, call on the President at his temporary quarters on Jackson Place. They agree to push the operators to accept a commission of Roosevelt's choosing, with the threat of Army control of the mines in the background.

Roosevelt confers with Wright and Wellman. He tells John Kernan the earlier commission plan must be dropped and writes Bishop that the strike is closer to ending. Back on Long Island, Sagamore Hill has Mrs. Clifford Richardson as a guest.

Roosevelt meets Mitchell, Wright and Sargent late in the morning, dines at John Hay's, and sees Bacon and George Perkins at night. He drafts but does not send a letter to Morgan saying he must pick the commission freely, because Mitchell is trusting him.
Naming the Anthracite Coal Strike Commission

Roosevelt names a seven-man commission to settle the coal strike: retired Army engineer General John M. Wilson; Labor Commissioner Carroll Wright; federal Judge George Gray of Delaware; E. E. Clark, head of the railway conductors' union, seated under the label of "eminent sociologist"; mining engineer Edward Parker; coal man Thomas Watkins; and Bishop John Spalding. He thanks Morgan and Hanna, explains to Cleveland that the operators would not accept him, and sends Mitchell the names.
Getting a bishop onto the commission
Roosevelt meets Wright, General Wilson and Parker of the new commission and lunches with Hay and Root. He tells Lodge how he got Bishop Spalding named and why Clark went on as a sociologist.

An executive order reminds federal officeholders to obey the laws on political donations. Roosevelt lunches with Regis Post; it is Bamie's son Sheffield's fourth birthday. He writes Bessie Van Vorst about wives, mothers and women's outlook.

Roosevelt writes J. H. Woodard about the strike's end. At Sagamore Hill to gather the children, Edith writes her sister Emily that unpacking the baby clothes saddened her, and that she means to hold on to them in hope of another child.

Root, Hitchcock, Knox and Japanese minister Takahira call; Roosevelt lunches with Judge Gray and dines at Hay's. He tells Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward he is nursing two tiny guinea pigs for Ethel, and tells Finley Peter Dunne the last strike conferences were funnier than anything Dunne ever wrote.

The anthracite strike is formally over. Roosevelt has John Kernan and M. E. Egan to lunch, and writes Taft that his Rome mission has failed and resentment of the Catholic church is growing in the Philippines.

Roosevelt receives the Dutch minister and sends Massachusetts Governor Crane a long account of the strike from start to finish. He tells Payne he will hold off on Colorado appointments until after the election.

The anthracite miners return to the pits. Roosevelt lunches with Root, dines at Payne's, and formally charges the new commission to study the strike's causes and recommend remedies. Finley Peter Dunne writes that he found nothing funny about the strike.
Commission meets; Yellowstone's bison and elk

Roosevelt meets the strike commission, which chooses Judge Gray as chairman, and speaks briefly. He sees Booker T. Washington at noon and asks Yellowstone superintendent John Pitcher how the park protects its bison and elk, and how many rangers it has.
Wilson installed at Princeton without him

Roosevelt misses Woodrow Wilson's inauguration at Princeton. In the Philippines, the new Independent Philippine Church is proclaimed and claims Catholic properties. Roosevelt confers with Knox on the Panama title and purchase and with two rear admirals, Bowles and Taylor, writes Mahan on ship size versus firepower, and tells Taft he would like to put him on the Supreme Court.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.

On Roosevelt's 44th birthday, a delegation from New York's Hungarian Club calls with good wishes. He writes Cuban President Tomás Estrada Palma, tells Quay the naval maneuvers will go ahead despite the strike, and asks to see Joe Bishop.
Roosevelt confers with Dudley Wooten on Alaska and takes no appointments after eleven. He writes Hay that Colombia has protested American meddling in its internal quarrel over the canal.

Roosevelt sees Benjamin Ide Wheeler in the morning and labor leader Samuel Gompers at noon, then dines with Father Doyle. He writes that the Kaiser likes Seth Low as mayor, that Taft is to remain in Manila, and replies to a bishop who wants him to condemn violence in the coal fields.

Roosevelt's essay "The Presidency" appears in Youth's Companion. The record adds a guest's sketch of a typical White House lunch that fall: bouillon, chicken and rice, salt fish and baked beans, with the President taking seconds of beans and fish, no cigar for him, and an American flag on his bread plate.
Roosevelt is at Manassas, Virginia; no details are recorded.
From Manassas Roosevelt visits the Civil War battlefield at Cedar Mountain, then returns to Washington.
Roosevelt takes an afternoon train north to Oyster Bay by way of New York.
Election Day walk with six dogs
On Election Day in Oyster Bay, Roosevelt and Edith go for a walk with all six of their dogs.
Moving into the rebuilt White House

After a speech in Philadelphia, Roosevelt and Edith settle back into the rebuilt White House. The ground floor is unfinished, but the enlarged State Dining Room now holds 107 diners rather than 60. Edith places an order for a new presidential china service and begins hunting for old sets, the start of the White House china collection. The Navy's Caribbean squadron reaches Culebra.
Election results and Tom Quartz the kitten

Roosevelt meets Procter, Foulke and Garfield on civil service and sees Senator Beveridge at six. He writes cousin Emlen that the elections went well for Republicans, though Odell hears that New York went poorly. To Kermit he describes Archie carrying the kitten Tom Quartz on the train and Quentin falling asleep.
Cabinet turns to the annual message
Regular Cabinet meetings resume with a session on the annual message. Roosevelt discusses talks with Colombia with Hay and twice sees a Herald correspondent, Mr. Brown.
Hay, Knox, Babcock and Lorimer call. Roosevelt congratulates Mark Hanna on the Republican win in Ohio.
Roosevelt works on his annual message and sees Representative Babcock at three.
The Isle of Pines and a rumor answered

Roosevelt confers with Senator Cullom and others on the Isle of Pines and sees Leonard Wood, Garfield, J. M. McCormick and E. F. Ware before leaving that evening for New York. He firmly answers Robert Rhett about a rumor that his appointees include Black men of bad character.
Chamber of Commerce and a call for preparedness

In New York Roosevelt meets Nicholas Murray Butler for breakfast at the University Club, speaks at the dedication of the Chamber of Commerce building, and argues for military preparedness at a dinner at the Waldorf-Astoria. At midnight he leaves on a hunting trip.

Roosevelt's train crosses Ohio, stopping along the way, bound for Smedes, Mississippi. He writes Jacob Riis about the dedication of Riis's new book and Root about keeping Army officers and men physically fit.
After a stop in Memphis, Roosevelt reaches Smedes, Mississippi.
Bear hunting in the Mississippi canebrakes
Near Smedes, Roosevelt goes after bear. In Washington, Edith writes her sister Emily that Dr. Rixey does not think her wish for another child is reasonable.
The bear hunt continues near Smedes.

The hunt goes on near Smedes. Newspapers have picked up a story that Roosevelt refused to shoot a bear, a cub in some tellings and an old bear in others. Clifford Berryman's Washington Post cartoon "Drawing the Line in Mississippi" appears, toy makers soon turn out stuffed bears, and the teddy bear is born.
Roosevelt is in Mississippi; no further detail is given.
In Memphis Roosevelt speaks on the Philippines and joins a reception honoring General Luke Wright, then leaves for Washington that evening. It is Quentin's 5th birthday.
Whistle stops on the way home
On the way back to Washington, Roosevelt's train stops at Knoxville and Asheville.
Cuba, the canal and the Pacific cable

The Cabinet takes up Cuba, the Panama canal and the Pacific cable. Roosevelt lunches with Lodge, goes over tariff changes with Senators Scott, Burrows and Lodge, and sees Francis Leupp in the afternoon. The North Atlantic battle squadron reaches Culebra.
Founder's Day at the Union League

In Philadelphia Roosevelt gives the Union League's Founder's Day address, promising to tackle the problem of trusts and business combinations. He dedicates a school, lunches with C. E. Smith, and attends a reception at E. T. Stotesbury's home.
Back in Washington, Roosevelt confers with Spooner and sees Baron Speck von Sternberg at 9 p.m. and Attorney General Knox half an hour later.

A long line of congressional leaders calls, including Speaker Henderson, Hanna, Cannon and Lodge. British editor John St. Loe Strachey is staying at the White House and rides with Roosevelt and Root, talking over Venezuela and the Alaska boundary. Sternberg comes to dinner.
Germany and Britain move on Venezuela

Germany and Britain formally announce they will force Venezuela to pay its debts. The Cabinet works on the annual message, and Roosevelt discusses the Philippines with Luke Wright, New York politics with George Dunn, and receives Senator Hale, the Italian ambassador and Chief Justice Fuller. It is Bamie's seventh wedding anniversary.
Bringing Taft home for the Court

On a crowded day, callers range from Clarence Darrow to Hay, Moody, Knox and several lawmakers. Roosevelt writes Taft that after a month of trying to arrange things his way, he will have to bring him home and seat him on the Supreme Court.

For Thanksgiving the family rides for three hours: Roosevelt on Renown, Ted on an Army horse, Edith on Jocko Root, Ethel on Yagenka and Archie on Algonquin, joined by Lodge, Douglas Robinson, cousin John Elliott, Bob Ferguson and Leonard Wood. Dinner follows in the enlarged State Dining Room with the riders, Corinne and her children and Brooks Adams, then a dance.
Quentin gives the kitten a bath

Senators T. C. Platt, Cullom and others call along with Leonard Wood; there is a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Judge Clarke. Roosevelt tells Kermit that Quentin gave the kitten Tom Quartz some special attention by setting him in the tub and turning on the tap.
The fleet gathers in the Caribbean

With the South Atlantic and European squadrons now at Trinidad, nearly the whole U.S. Navy is in the Caribbean. Roosevelt discusses the Venezuelan debt claims with Hanna, banker Isaac Seligman and Admiral Dewey, receives Salvador's new minister Rafael Lopez, meets congressional leaders, rides with Leonard Wood and dines with Root. He tells David Hill he will not commit himself on Venezuela before seeing Hay.

The new executive office wing is finished, with a staff of 38, and visitors stream through the new Cabinet Room from morning to early afternoon. A new tennis court sits just outside, on ground where the Oval Office was later built under Taft. Roosevelt confers with General Greene that night. The record also begins to describe his desk, made from a ship's oak timbers and presented to President Hayes.
Roosevelt confers with Lucius Littauer on trust bills and sees Quay, Millard, Beveridge, Gamble and Burke. H. H. Kohlsaat calls at ten and stays for lunch with New.
Second annual message: 'Not a cloud on the horizon'

Roosevelt sends his annual message to Congress, laying out his stand on the trusts. He meets congressmen on St. Louis vote fraud and naval bills, lunches with Jane Addams, George Kennan, Monsignor Kennedy and Eugene Philbin, and dines with Hanna, O. H. Platt and Payne. It is his and Edith's 16th anniversary. He asks Dean LeBaron Briggs when Ted should leave Groton for Harvard.

Roosevelt receives the Persian minister, lunches with Lyman Abbott, Luke Wright and Albert Shaw, and sees Senator Beveridge and Chaplain Vattmann in the evening. He writes William Brawley about naming Dr. William Crum, a Black physician, to a federal post in South Carolina over local objections.

On a busy day Roosevelt talks Cuban reciprocity with Senator Elkins and writes Quay about whether New Mexico and Arizona should become states. He tells Kermit that he and Leonard Wood often fence with padded wooden sticks, landing blows on each other.
Ordering Knox to take a holiday

The Cabinet meets on Cuban reciprocity and postal appointments, and Edith welcomes 150 members of a national Jewish women's organization. Roosevelt writes Butler about a Western trip next spring and orders Knox to take four weeks off.
Roosevelt meets Senators Carter and Thurston about the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, sees Addicks, and lunches with Von Briesen and Wilcox. He praises Woodrow Wilson's article on American ideals.
Canadian Prime Minister Sir Wilfrid Laurier visits Roosevelt. Word comes that Thomas Nast, the cartoonist serving as U.S. consul general in Ecuador, has died there of yellow fever.
Dewey takes the Caribbean fleet; praise for Edith

Germany and Britain break relations with Venezuela, and Admiral Dewey, aboard the Mayflower, takes command of the fleet in the Caribbean. Roosevelt meets senators and German Ambassador Holleben. Writing Maria Storer, he calls Edith the best of wives and mothers and the ideal mistress of the White House.
After a Cabinet meeting and talks with Senators Dryden and McCumber, Roosevelt speaks at an evening dinner for Justice John Marshall Harlan. He writes John Wilson about big business and labor.
A delegation from the Merchants' Association of New York meets with Roosevelt.
Venezuela talks and a plea for Turkey

Roosevelt discusses Venezuela with Hay and Senator Cullom, sees Finley Peter Dunne, and has Regis Post, Evarts and Sprague to lunch. In the afternoon Morris Jesup leads a delegation seeking aid for Turkey. Edith hosts a hundred women from the National Indian Association, and Don Dickinson comes to dinner.

The Cabinet meets on Venezuela. Roosevelt confers with Representative Lacey about public lands and with Congressman Dick and others about statehood for the Southwest territories, and writes General Young about Army uniforms.

German and British ships blockade five Venezuelan ports and shell Puerto Cabello. Roosevelt had approved the Anglo-German-Italian blockade over Venezuela's unpaid bonds, though with serious doubts. He sees Senators Platt, Cullom, Frye and Spooner, Lieutenant Commander William Sims and the Russian ambassador, and hosts a large dinner. He tells Clement Griscom his son Lloyd will go to Japan as minister.
Treasury Secretary Shaw calls in the morning and Senator Spooner in the evening.
Mr. Ingersoll photographs Roosevelt in the morning. He confers with Hay and Cullom, goes over the Cuba treaty with Root, lunches with Sheffield, Boardman and Devereaux, and has a dinner at eight.

After a Cabinet session on Cuba and Venezuela, Roosevelt decides to send American warships from Culebra into the blockade zone and hands reporters battle maps of the area. He works on the Militia Bill with Root, Proctor, Hull and Dick, and dines with a large party of congressional leaders.

On a busy day Hanna, Dillingham, Tawney, Martin and Clarkson call, and Roosevelt has Joseph Barnes, Stranahan and Clarkson to lunch. He tells James Tracey he wants him on the Philippine Supreme Court.

Britain agrees the Venezuela dispute should be arbitrated and asks Roosevelt to serve as arbiter. Roosevelt later said he warned Germany of war if it refused arbitration. The Pacific fleet begins maneuvers, alarming German envoy Holleben. The day ends with the annual Cabinet dinner.
Germany agrees to arbitration over Venezuela. The Cabinet meets on the crisis, and Roosevelt discusses currency with Lyman Gage and J. H. Rhoades.
Mrs. Grant's funeral; off to the Rapidan
Roosevelt breakfasts with Jacob Riis. Congress adjourns, Julia Dent Grant is buried, and after a meeting with Hay Roosevelt leaves for Rapidan, Virginia.
At Rapidan, Virginia, Roosevelt stays with Joseph Wilmer.
Back in Washington, Roosevelt meets Hay and writes Henry Higginson about duties on coal.
After a Cabinet meeting on Venezuela and lunch with George Perkins, Roosevelt writes Senator Hoar about Apolinario Mabini, the insurgent leader held by the United States in the Philippines.
Christmas Eve with Hay and the Sun
Roosevelt confers with Hay on Venezuela, sees a Sun newspaperman named Matthews, and asks William Allen White whether Leonard Wood can stay at his club.

The children are banging on the bedroom door by 6:45, and soon they are piled on the bed opening stockings; Archie has hidden a small gift-laden tree in a closet. After breakfast Archie gets a rifle and riding boots and Quentin an electric train. Roosevelt rides for three hours, lunches at Bamie's, fences single-stick with Wood and Ferguson, and ends with dinner and dancing in the East Room.

After a Cabinet meeting, the government announces the Venezuela dispute will go to the Hague Tribunal. Roosevelt sends a Christmas letter to young James A. Garfield, and writes Shaw, Taft and Cleveland about upholding the Monroe Doctrine, Agassiz on the Philippines and Schurz on the arbitration.
Roosevelt receives the Austrian ambassador in the morning and writes Root and the Rev. William Rainsford, the latter on the trusts.
Wayne MacVeagh is among Sunday's callers.
Got what he wanted on Venezuela

Wilson and Foulke call, Roosevelt lunches with psychologist Hugo Münsterberg, and Justice White visits in the evening. He writes George Hinman that he knew his aims in the Venezuela settlement and achieved them.
The Cabinet meets on General Land Office affairs. Roosevelt meets a Picayune editor, Mr. Robertson, and confers with Generals Young and Wood.
Roosevelt dines with the Rev. Billings on the last day of 1902.
New Year's reception in a renovated White House
The freshly remodeled White House is formally unveiled, and Roosevelt greets the public at the New Year's reception from late morning into the early afternoon.
Roller skates on the new East Room floor

Roosevelt discovers his children and their friends have turned the East Room's new parquet into a skating rink. The Cabinet takes up the shuttered post office at Indianola, Mississippi, and he confers with Postmaster General Payne.
German ambassador and a dinner at the Hays'

Roosevelt opens the day with German Ambassador Holleben, talks Cuban reciprocity with H. T. Oxnard, and sees a string of senators and officials. He lunches with Holls, and that evening he and Edith dine with Secretary and Mrs. Hay.
On a Sunday, Roosevelt meets the House Naval Affairs Committee to work over the Navy's spending bill.
Loomis named to the State Department

Roosevelt makes F. B. Loomis an Assistant Secretary of State, lunches with Clarkson and others, and sees Mark Hanna late in the evening. He warns Postmaster General Payne he may release the papers on a Delaware postmastership. Admiral Dewey's squadron leaves the Caribbean.
A call for trust laws, and a letter home

Roosevelt urges Congress to pass antitrust laws without delay, and the Cabinet weighs Venezuela and the Cuban treaty. Writing Kermit at Groton, he says the house feels empty without the boys and reports that Tom Quartz the kitten pounced on Joe Cannon.
Carnegie calls; a new public library opens

Roosevelt sends the Philippine Commission's yearly report to Congress and fills his morning with appointments, from cartoonist Clifford Berryman to Andrew Carnegie and his wife. After lunch with Knox and Moody, he speaks at the dedication of Washington's public library.
Diplomats, writers and a swollen wrist

Roosevelt sits for photographer Tucker, then hosts the diplomatic reception, where guests include Richard Harding Davis, Finley Peter Dunne, Howard Pyle and Owen Wister. He tells Ted his wrist is puffed up from singlestick bouts with Frank McCoy and that Alice keeps very late hours.
Wind Cave becomes a national park

Wind Cave in South Dakota is made a national park. Roosevelt receives a delegation from the Pope and meets C. D. Wright, and the Cabinet again discusses Indianola. Papers report Holleben's quiet recall from Berlin and the choice of Roosevelt's friend Speck von Sternberg to replace him.
Civil service talks and a Treasury dinner
Roosevelt meets E. H. Goodwin and others about civil service reform and lunches with George W. Perkins. In the evening Secretary of the Treasury Shaw and his wife give a dinner for him and Edith.
Late Sunday talk with Aldrich and Henderson
Roosevelt holds a late-night Sunday meeting with Senator Aldrich and House Speaker Henderson.
Government papers for the Library of Congress

Roosevelt talks with D. J. Hill and Librarian Herbert Putnam about moving government records into the Library of Congress. He writes Henry Taft about his brother and the Court vacancy, consoles Nicholas Murray Butler on his wife's death, and answers Senator Hoar on Mabini.

Roosevelt meets the Littlefield subcommittee on trusts, holds Cabinet, and confers with a long list of congressmen and others. Theodore Noyes and Lawrence Abbott join him for lunch, and protests to Mayor Seth Low that New York is taxing Elihu Root far too heavily.
Senators call; a note on Alaska
Hanna, Hepburn, Quay and Foraker stop by, and Roosevelt lunches with Knox, Moody and three House members. He writes Secretary Hay about the disputed Alaska boundary.
Romping with the boys, then a state dinner

After meetings with Quay, Shaw and Hay, Roosevelt wrestles with Archie and Quentin before dinner and rumples his evening clothes. The Diplomatic Corps dinner follows, with Whitelaw Reid, Douglas Robinson and young Roosevelt cousins among the guests.
Roosevelt huddles with Senators Aldrich, Lodge and Spooner over the Cuban reciprocity treaty, holds Cabinet, lunches with Guy Waring, and ends with a small dinner and music.
Chopping trees with Garfield and Pinchot

Luquillo National Forest is set aside in Puerto Rico, while German warships shell Fort San Carlos in Venezuela. Roosevelt confers on the Cuban treaty, trusts and statehood, has Joe Bishop to lunch, and tells Kermit he spent the afternoon felling trees with Garfield and Pinchot.
It is the 48th birthday of Roosevelt's sister Bamie. That night he meets Attorney General Knox with Senators Spooner and Aldrich.
A wireless greeting across the Atlantic

Roosevelt sends King Edward VII the first wireless telegram to cross the ocean. George Bird Grinnell brings Blackfoot visitors at noon, and that night Roosevelt speaks at a YMCA dinner. He presses Senator Fairbanks to back Knox's trust program and writes Henry Taft again about his brother's future.

After Cabinet and visits from senators, Roosevelt receives delegates of a German society from New York. He tells Ted singlestick has left him with a broken wrist and a battered arm, so he walks daily with General Wood instead, and says Archie and Quentin insist he make up stories rather than read them.

Roosevelt approves the Militia Bill and receives callers from the Japanese Legation, Congress and the Cabinet. Letters go to Edward Wolcott on Colorado politics, to Hay with thanks, and to General Francis V. Greene about New York's police commissioner.

Colombia's envoy Tomás Herrán signs the Hay-Herrán treaty, leasing the United States a six-mile strip across Panama for a century at $10 million down plus $250,000 a year. Roosevelt lunches with the Woods and hosts the judicial reception; the Grant La Farges begin a four-day stay.
Queen Liliuokalani at the White House

Roosevelt and Edith receive Hawaii's former queen, Liliuokalani. Lunch brings in the Steinways, Tiffany and the painter Dewing. He tells Hanna the new department should leave 'Labor' out of its name and writes William Williams about Jewish complaints over Ellis Island.
A portrait painter and a full calendar

On a crowded day, Roosevelt sees Delaware's Addicks and Allee and economist J. W. Jenks on trusts, and meets portrait painter Théobald Chartran. He lunches with Hay, Bowen and Wood, and the Knoxes host him and Edith for dinner.

Hanna, Foulke and Overstreet call in the evening. Roosevelt tells Kermit the singlestick injury has him greeting people with his left hand, that snow has turned his rides with Edith into walks, and that Grant La Farge is staying with them.
Lunch with Lady Minto, then a train to Canton
