Roosevelt lunches with Lady Minto, Hay, Root and the Lodges, then boards a night train for Canton, Ohio. Edith writes Aunt Lizzie that McKim's renovation finally lets her make guests comfortable.

In Canton, Roosevelt lunches at Judge William R. Day's home and marks McKinley Day, the late President's birthday, with a speech. Back in Washington, Alice confides to her diary that she believes her father cares far less for her than for the other children.
Roosevelt travels from Canton back to Washington.
Silver coinage and a Supreme Court dinner

Roosevelt asks Congress to back Mexico and China in seeking a common coinage standard for silver-using nations. He lunches with Lord Charles Beresford, Admiral Dewey and other officers, hosts the Supreme Court dinner, and tells Taft he will stay in the Philippines while General Wood heads there soon.

Roosevelt meets Cannon and Speaker Henderson, holds Cabinet, sees Root and Quay, and dines with Lord Beresford before a musicale. He refuses Senator Platt's pick for a military attaché post for the Germans.

Roosevelt meets Ambassador Speck von Sternberg and confers on the canal treaty, then dines with Secretary and Mrs. Moody. Alice heads off with Edith Root to Mardi Gras and on to Puerto Rico until April. Roosevelt covers the caterer's bills for official banquets from his own pocket.
The Army gets a General Staff

Congress passes the Army bill creating a General Staff. Roosevelt writes Kermit that a new dog, Bozzie, lives in the kitchen and Chartran is painting him, and tells Ted that Speck von Sternberg has turned up as Germany's ambassador.
Mayor Low at the White House
Roosevelt lunches with Postmaster General Payne and sees New York Mayor Seth Low in the early evening. He writes Philip Stewart again about Colorado.

Congress passes Roosevelt's three-part answer to the trusts: the Elkins Act, a Department of Commerce and Labor, and the Expedition Act. He also sees senators, the British envoy, Justice White and Arthur Street, editor of Collier's. Bill Sewall, his old Maine guide, arrives to stay.
Thanking Fairbanks for a fast vote
Roosevelt confers with Allison, George W. Perkins and Lodge, and thanks Senator Fairbanks for steering the bill to speed antitrust cases through the Senate.

Roosevelt's lunch table mixes General Booth, his old friend Bill Sewall with a party of seven, and Cabinet regulars. That night he hosts the congressional reception and asks Representative Hepburn to amend a bill before it passes.
Clergy and a general at lunch
Representative Vreeland calls at noon, and Roosevelt has Bishop Lawrence, Sheffield, Moody, General Duke and Rev. Peterson to lunch before seeing Leupp.

France's new ambassador, Jules Jusserand, presents his credentials, the start of a close friendship. On a packed day Roosevelt also sees three senators, lunches with Philip Stewart, and dines with the Paynes. He defends his Indianola stand to Richard Watson Gilder and praises Alice French's story about lynching.

Roosevelt writes Kermit about books and about meeting Jusserand, a diplomat he actually enjoyed talking with. Bill Sewall and his family have visited, and Edith walked to the Capitol with the dogs while Ethel skated and Archie biked along.

Roosevelt confers with Beveridge and a bloc of House leaders and opens a hall for the canning industries. He tells Ted that he too was sick on Sunday and that Alice has behaved well lately, and refuses Grant La Farge's plea to drop Byrne's Delaware appointment.
Roosevelt meets Littlefield, Spooner and Aldrich to push the antitrust bills along.
Odell at lunch; a fan letter on Shakespeare
New York Governor Benjamin Odell lunches with Roosevelt to talk state politics. Roosevelt writes Thomas Lounsbury that he loved his book on Shakespeare and Voltaire and wants him to meet Jusserand.
Alice turns 19; Chief Joseph at the reception

On Alice's 19th birthday, Roosevelt meets Platt, Odell and Littauer, rides with Edith, and hosts the Army and Navy reception, where the Nez Perce leader Chief Joseph and fellow chiefs appear. He tells Senator Knute Nelson that Cortelyou will lead the brand-new commerce and labor department.
Commerce and Labor Department signed into law

Roosevelt signs the law that creates a Cabinet department for commerce and labor, and sits for photographer Rockwood. Letters ask whether hounds may chase mountain lions in Yellowstone, salute a family of twelve, and sound out Taft about becoming Secretary of War in a year.

Roosevelt confers with Hay and Senators O. H. Platt, Hanna and Aldrich, twice with Aldrich. He tells Ted that he is back at singlestick, rode with Austin Wadsworth, and is sitting for a portrait by John Singer Sargent.
Cortelyou takes the new Cabinet seat
Roosevelt names George B. Cortelyou the first Secretary of Commerce and Labor. He meets Beveridge, Cullom, Garfield and Cannon, and writes Root on Philippine currency and the tariff.
Roosevelt meets Speaker Henderson and Senators Perkins and Spooner and lunches with three guests. He writes Joe Bishop about corruption at Ellis Island and the antitrust fight.

Roosevelt meets Senators Platt and Fairbanks, lunches with Saturday Evening Post editor George Horace Lorimer, and sees Ambassador Sternberg. He tells Major John Pitcher he hopes to go after cougars in the Yellowstone country, outside the park where hunting is barred.
Pressing the Senate on Panama and Cuba

Roosevelt publicly calls on the Senate to approve both the Cuban reciprocity pact and the Panama canal treaty at once. He greets Spanish-American War veterans, rides with Speck von Sternberg in good spirits over Venezuela, and sees William Allen White that evening.

Roosevelt signs the Elkins Act, aimed at the railroads' long practice of secret rebates. He talks Iowa politics with Albert Cummins, holds a Cabinet session on the Navy, has the William Allen Whites to lunch, and hears the Washington Symphony under Reginald De Koven.
Laying the Army War College cornerstone

Roosevelt speaks as the cornerstone of the Army War College is set in place. He confers with Root, Beveridge, Judge Van Devanter and others, lunches with Philip Stewart and Admiral Evans, and dines with the Hitchcocks. A playful letter to Root pokes fun at the appointment game.
Roosevelt sees Leupp and Crumpacker in the evening and fires off an angry reply to Senator Platt, who had protested one of his appointments.
Roosevelt meets Treasury Secretary Shaw, R. B. Armstrong and Representative Boutell about a standard for coinage.

Roosevelt approves the agreement giving the U.S. Navy coaling stations in Cuba. He dines with the Aldriches, Pattersons, O. H. Platts and Jusserands and hosts a German singing society concert. Letters urge Lodge to hurry the Philippine tariff cut and explain his Southern appointments to editor Clark Howell.
Feuding with Platt over New York jobs

Callers include Cummins, Luke Wright and Foraker, and Roosevelt lunches with Sargent and others. He writes Platt over a disagreement on New York posts, and Aldrich and Cannon on the Philippine tariff and Cuban reciprocity.
A Wesley bicentennial at Carnegie Hall

After morning meetings, Roosevelt dashes to New York City to speak at Carnegie Hall on the 200th anniversary of John Wesley's birth, then returns to Washington. He asks Speaker Henderson whether the House can pass a resolution letting the amended Cuban treaty take effect once the Senate approves it.
A thousand Daughters of the Revolution
Roosevelt urges Congress to pass the Philippine tariff bill and holds Cabinet. In the afternoon his sister Bamie arrives with the Griscoms, and he receives a delegation of 1,000 women from the D.A.R.

Roosevelt hosts a lively dinner with Harriet Blaine Beale presiding because Edith is ill; guests include Root, Justice Holmes, Seth Bullock, Eugene Ware and William Allen White. He tells Platt he will name his judge despite Platt's objections. Chartran's painting of Edith becomes her official portrait.
Roosevelt lunches with Root, Lodge and Turner and dines with C. S. Mellen and the Woodruffs. He writes Ted all about the previous night's dinner party.
Roosevelt confers with William Allen White, Leupp, Shaw and Cannon. He writes John Pitcher that he wants five dogs for his Yellowstone trip.
Roosevelt meets Francis Leupp and Senator Julius Burrows.

The 57th Congress closes and the 58th opens with Republican majorities of 57 to 33 in the Senate and 208 to 178 in the House. Roosevelt spends the morning at the Capitol and dines with the Hays. He writes Hay on Romania's Jews, thanks Speaker Henderson, and tells Booker T. Washington he will resubmit Crum's name.

Congress meets in special session, and Roosevelt asks it to ratify the Panama and Cuban treaties. Mrs. Taft and Seymour Edwards join him for lunch and receives the Argentine minister. He writes lumberman Frederick Weyerhaeuser hoping to talk forestry.
Chief Joseph, and captains to sea

Senators Hanna, Platt, Hale, Cullom and Lodge call, and Roosevelt discusses the Nez Perce leader Chief Joseph with Colonel Scott. He tells Navy Secretary Moody to send Captains Bradford and O'Neil to sea right away. Baseball's two big leagues agree on a joint rulebook.
Howells takes aim; Burroughs invited west

In Harper's Weekly, William Dean Howells criticizes Roosevelt's praise of big families. Roosevelt writes John Burroughs that he liked his piece on real and sham natural history, talks over the errors in animal stories, and invites him along to Yellowstone.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record notes nothing else for the day.

Roosevelt meets Representatives Calderhead and Hill about coming finance bills and sees Hanna. He writes Charles Walcott about a broad plan to explore the Philippines and approves a new bankers' committee.
Post Office scandal: Tyner asked to quit

After Cabinet and lunch with Cannon, Roosevelt writes about the Post Office corruption probe, noting that Tyner has been told to resign. He also tells labor leader John Mitchell whom he has put in charge of the new commerce department and the Bureau of Corporations.
Among the day's callers is General Frederick Funston.
J. P. Morgan, and sweating over treaties

Roosevelt names a committee under C. D. Walcott to study the executive departments and meets J. P. Morgan in the afternoon. He hosts a senators' dinner, and writes Hay that he is straining every nerve to get the Cuba and Panama treaties confirmed.

A commission led by Charles D. Walcott is named to look at the government's scientific work. Roosevelt sees Speck von Sternberg and sends Taft his sizing-up of Republican leaders in Congress. He tells Root there will be no compromise on principle over Alaska, and Hay that Americans will never let a European power control an American republic.
Pelican Island: the first bird refuge

Roosevelt sets aside Pelican Island in Florida as a federal bird reservation, the first of its kind, and five irrigation projects take shape in Montana, Arizona, Nevada, Nebraska, Wyoming and Colorado. He lunches with George Ward and Curtis Guild and is glad Burroughs will join him in Yellowstone.
Roosevelt confers with Senators Spooner, Thomas Platt and Beveridge. He asks Root for information on the coastlines of the Caribbean nations.

Roosevelt lunches with Major Scott, and Secretary Shaw comes to dinner and stays the night. He tells Thomas Stewart his favorite hymn is 'How Firm a Foundation' and that he greatly admires 'The Battle Hymn of the Republic,' and asks Beveridge to talk trusts and tariff.

The Senate approves the Hay-Herrán treaty without amendment, opening the way for a canal across Panama. Roosevelt chooses Root, Lodge and George Turner as the American members of the Alaska boundary tribunal and writes each of them about his stance.
Dinner for the coal strike commission

Roosevelt confers with Hopkins and O. H. Platt and gives a dinner for the members of the coal strike commission. He writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler that he enjoyed his critique of Herodotus on the Battle of Salamis.

The special session of Congress ends. Joe Bishop and Grant La Farge come to dinner and stay over, and Roosevelt meets five senators late at night. He writes Taft about the Philippine friars and repeats that he wants him at the War Department when Root leaves.

Roosevelt has George C. Lee Jr. and George Holls to breakfast and lunches with Lyman Abbott. At dinner his niece Eleanor joins the Winthrop Chanlers, the British ambassador and Lady Herbert, Lieutenant McCoy and Major Howze. He sends Ted family news.

The coal strike commission's report is published: miners win a 10 percent pay increase, but the United Mine Workers are not recognized. Roosevelt meets Archbishop Ireland and General Wood, and in the evening talks Indian policy with Commissioner Jones. Edith writes that she feels herself again and may ride.

Roosevelt sees Stranahan and lunches with Haskell and Woodbury Kane. He drafts two letters to Governor Odell on the Odell-Platt fight over New York patronage, sending only one, tells David Thompson no one has asked him to seek an American cardinal, and defends the Byrne appointment to George Kennan.
Admirals to inspect the canal route

Roosevelt lunches with General and Mrs. Wood and Charles Francis. He names Admiral John Walker and two others to survey the Canal Zone in Panama, and thanks Judge George Gray for the coal strike commission's work.
Roosevelt talks with J. M. Thurston about the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, then he and Edith go to the riding hall at Fort Myer.
Speaking to the foresters at Pinchot's

Roosevelt meets Hay and Root, Justice White and G. Minot Weld, then speaks that evening to the Society of American Foresters at Gifford Pinchot's home. He commends the National Economic League to Clarkson and urges William Crum, his Black appointee in Charleston, to run his office beyond reproach.
Roosevelt lunches with Amory Gardner and Cushing. Admiral Dewey tells the New York Herald that the recent Venezuela episode taught the Kaiser a lesson.

Roosevelt summons Admiral Dewey and reprimands him for his remarks about the Kaiser, and warns Admiral Taylor that such talk could harm the country. He tells Joe Bishop he means to stay clear of the quarrel between Platt and Odell, and writes John Clarke about Clarkson's plan for Republican clubs.
In the evening Secretary Cortelyou and Gifford Pinchot bring several lumbermen to see Roosevelt, followed by O. P. Austin and Frederick Holls.
Too big a people to be careless
Roosevelt lunches with James Barnes, Root, the Lodges, Harriet Blaine Beale, and the Holmeses. He writes Admiral Dewey that the nation cannot afford loose talk.

John Burroughs comes to stay the night before the western trip. Sargent and Chartran finish their portraits of Roosevelt, who prefers Sargent's. He asks C. Hart Merriam about reports on western Indian tribes and writes Villard on the Philippine atrocity inquiry. Edith and three children set off on the Mayflower.

Roosevelt sets out at 9 a.m. on his long swing through the West, speaking in Baltimore and Harrisburg and stopping at Altoona. Leaving the White House, he writes Corinne that it feels odd without the children and hopes her hand is mending.
Chicago: honorary degrees and the Monroe Doctrine

In Chicago Roosevelt is made a Doctor of Laws by the University of Chicago and also honored at Northwestern. That evening he argues for a bigger navy and defends the Monroe Doctrine, crediting Germany and Britain for keeping their word in Venezuela.
Roosevelt addresses the Wisconsin legislature in Madison and speaks at a merchants' dinner in Milwaukee.
Farmers and hired hands at trackside
Roosevelt speaks at La Crosse and St. Paul, talking from the train to crowds he describes to Hay as sinewy farmers, townsfolk, veterans and children.
In Sioux Falls, Roosevelt worships at a modest German Lutheran church and also attends a Dutch Reformed service. Afterward he covers 20 miles in the company of Dr. Rixey and Seth Bullock.

Roosevelt crisscrosses South Dakota, speaking at Sioux Falls, Yankton, Mitchell and Aberdeen, often from the back of the train. Local bands greeted him with 'Hail to the Chief' as if it were a fresh idea.

At Fargo Roosevelt talks about the Army and the Philippine islands, and in Bismarck he attends a barbecue of a whole roasted ox. At Mandan, Sylvane and Joe Ferris climb aboard, and at Dickinson and Medora old neighbors remember the young 'four-eyed dude' of ranching days.
Roosevelt finishes his Dakota visit and reaches Yellowstone National Park.
Elk everywhere; a win in Northern Securities

Entering the park from Gardiner, Montana, Roosevelt begins his camping trip and sees great numbers of elk. It is Archie's ninth birthday. In St. Paul, the federal circuit court rules for the government in the Northern Securities case.
Still camping in Yellowstone, Roosevelt sets off by himself on an 18-mile hike.
The camping party shifts to a second camp at Cottonwood Creek. Edith writes Aunt Lizzie that the West is the sole corner of his domain where her husband can get away from reporters.

On Easter Sunday the party moves camp to Tower Falls and sees a herd of some 3,000 elk. Edith writes her sister Emily that Alice has named her skinny green garter snake 'Emily Spinach' and carries it to fashionable parties.
Algonquin rides the White House elevator

Roosevelt is still camping in Yellowstone. In Washington Edith presides over the Easter Egg Roll, a custom she dislikes for what it does to the lawn. Archie is down with whooping cough and measles at once, and Quentin, with an usher's help, brings the pony Algonquin upstairs in the elevator to cheer him.

In camp, Roosevelt and John Burroughs spot a pygmy owl, and the party watches mountain sheep while Roosevelt still has shaving lather on his face. The group naps on the rocks near Tower Falls canyon; others fish while he walks alone.
Roosevelt has spent a week studying Yellowstone's elk. In a single day he counted 3,000 to 4,000 of the roughly 15,000 he estimates live in the park, where cougars are their only predator.

At Fort Yellowstone, Roosevelt writes Merriam that game is more abundant than on his visit twelve years before. He tells Ethel how tame the wild animals are, describing a dozen deer that wander onto the parade ground at the evening bugle.
Roosevelt tours Yellowstone's geyser country; Burroughs later described him there.
Roosevelt and Burroughs stop at the Norris hotel, then ride on to the Fountain Hotel.
Roosevelt fishes in the afternoon and skins a mouse he trapped, saving it for naturalist C. Hart Merriam.
From the Canyon Hotel, Roosevelt and Burroughs head out on skis across the snow.
Tall tales with Hell Roaring Bill Jones
Roosevelt trades stories with 'Hell Roaring' Bill Jones. Burroughs later recorded much of the President's campfire talk.

Back at Fort Yellowstone near Cinnabar, Roosevelt catches up on mail: praise for Taft and regret over the sugar beet bill, a note to Cleveland Dodge on trusts, more park observations for Merriam with a nudge to produce the standard work on the continent's mammals, and word to Hay on the Danish islands talks.
Roosevelt is at Cinnabar, Montana, as Assistant Attorney General Tyner is dismissed amid the Post Office inquiry.

At Gardiner, Roosevelt lays the cornerstone for a gateway to Yellowstone, then leaves for Livingston. He writes George Bird Grinnell about a Forest and Stream piece by 'Hermit' that attacked Burroughs's essay on fake nature stories.

Roosevelt stops at towns in South Dakota and Wyoming and speaks across Nebraska. He writes Thomas Carter that grouse are declining and he likes the idea of bringing in pheasants, and tells Charles McKim the White House dining room fireplace must be fixed this summer because it will not draw.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at Grand Island, Nebraska.

Roosevelt speaks his way across Nebraska, from Hastings to Lincoln, and gives an evening address on good citizenship in Omaha. He writes Butler unhappily about the Odell-Platt feud, Bishop on the tariff, and Payne about the Post Office probe and how the press is covering it.
Iowa, and a win on the franchise tax

Traveling with Albert Cummins and Treasury Secretary Shaw, Roosevelt gives speeches in Des Moines, Ottumwa and other Iowa towns. He writes Knox that he is delighted the Supreme Court upheld New York's franchise tax, a law he forced through as governor.
Roosevelt speaks in Hannibal, to a good-roads gathering in St. Louis, and in Quincy, Illinois. It is Corinne's 21st wedding anniversary.

Before 40,000 people in St. Louis, Roosevelt dedicates the Louisiana Purchase Exposition buildings, then leaves for Kansas City with Root and Butler. Gunton's Magazine comes out against his plan to lower tariffs.
Through the two Kansas Citys to Topeka
Roosevelt stops in Kansas City on both the Missouri and Kansas sides and in Lawrence, then speaks in Topeka that evening.
Roosevelt speaks in Abilene, Salina, Ellsworth and other Kansas towns, and telegraphs Hay about the American fleet in French waters.

At a packed church in tiny Sharon Springs, Kansas, a little girl offers Roosevelt a badger freshly trapped by her brother Josiah. His companions include Burton, Long, Butler, Warren and Foulke. In Washington, Edith dines at Henry Adams's farewell party before he sails for Europe.
Supper off a chuck wagon in a top hat

Roosevelt speaks in Denver and heads for Colorado Springs. Cowboys from a roundup ride in with their chuck wagon, and he sits on its tailboard eating range food in top hat and tails. He writes Hay about whether Grover Cleveland might seek a third term in 1904.
Santa Fe and a Rough Rider reunion
Roosevelt speaks in Santa Fe, which he calls a strange old desert civilization, and in Albuquerque, where old Rough Rider comrades, Captain William Llewellyn among them, climb aboard.

Roosevelt sees the Grand Canyon and is overwhelmed, calling it beautiful, terrible and unearthly. He speaks, visits a miners' camp with Alexander Brodie, Butler and Dr. Rixey, then leaves for California.
Crossing the Mojave Desert, Roosevelt stops at Barstow, speaks in Redlands about irrigation and forests, pauses at San Bernardino, and spends the night in Riverside.
Roosevelt speaks at Claremont and Pasadena and spends the night in Los Angeles, where flowers are everywhere he looks.
Roosevelt speaks in Ventura and Santa Barbara.
A beach ride at Del Monte

At Del Monte, Roosevelt visits with Secretary Moody and Benjamin Ide Wheeler. He tells Ethel about a gallop along the beach among seals and seabirds, notes that western women ride astride, and writes Kermit about Josiah the badger, Archie about Bill the lizard, and Quentin about the trip.

Roosevelt stops at Pajaro and Watsonville, speaks in Santa Cruz, and heads for San Jose. He writes Pinchot that California's George Maxwell opposes the irrigation plans, and Payne about the postal inquiry.
Forests at Stanford, a parade in San Francisco

At Palo Alto, Roosevelt visits Stanford's president David Starr Jordan and speaks there on saving the forests. He lunches with H. T. Scott, rides in a San Francisco parade, and attends a citizens' committee dinner.
Breaking ground for McKinley in Golden Gate Park

In San Francisco, Roosevelt attends a reception and a military review and breaks ground in Golden Gate Park for a monument to McKinley, then speaks that evening. He writes Hay about trouble in Manchuria and Cuba, and Moody about Navy marksmanship awards.
Roosevelt speaks in San Francisco, receives an honorary Doctor of Laws from the University of California, and speaks in Berkeley and Oakland.
Camping with John Muir among the sequoias
Roosevelt rides by way of Raymond, Berenda and Grub Gulch to meet John Muir at the Mariposa Grove in Yosemite, and the two camp beneath the giant sequoias.
In Yosemite, Roosevelt and Muir are caught in a snowstorm high among silver firs near the cliff edge.
Roosevelt sleeps out at Bridalveil Fall in Yosemite Valley, facing El Capitan with waterfalls roaring on both sides.

Roosevelt heads out through Wawona, Raymond and Berenda. The Government Printing Office drops William Miller from his post as assistant foreman. Roosevelt asks Hanna to meet him around the June 6 wedding of Hanna's daughter Ruth.

Roosevelt speaks in Carson City and Reno. He thanks John Muir for their days in Yosemite, asks Hitchcock to enlarge California's forest reserves, writes Allison about speaking on the tariff, and Root about wartime troop-transport blunders.
Roosevelt speaks at stops across northern California on his way to Oregon.
Lewis and Clark cornerstone in Portland

Roosevelt arrives in Portland and lays the cornerstone of the Lewis and Clark monument. He asks Hay to check with Root and Cortelyou about whether he should give $100 toward relief for Russia's Jews, and writes William Richards about Oregon's forest reserves.

Roosevelt speaks in Olympia and Tacoma. He fumes to Hay about Russia's refusal to open Manchurian ports and says he might accept a German state in Brazil. He sends a farewell note to departing ambassador Holleben and writes Taft about money matters behind his choices.

In Seattle, Roosevelt cruises Puget Sound and inspects the Bremerton Navy Yard. Hanna wires that he has stopped Ohio Republicans from endorsing Roosevelt early for 1904. Roosevelt appoints William Byrne U.S. Attorney for Delaware and writes Payne about the postal probe and Hanna's move.
Roosevelt predicts Seattle will one day be a city of a million people, and leaves that evening.

Heading east, Roosevelt speaks at Walla Walla, Wallula, Pasco, North Yakima, Ellensburg and Cle Elum. He replies to Hanna that he has asked no one for support, and invites Joe Cannon to join him through Illinois.
Roosevelt speaks at Spokane and at Harrison and Wallace, Idaho, and stops at Starbuck. Federal prosecutors win the Beef Trust suit.

Roosevelt speaks in Helena and Butte. He tells Clarkson the criminal rich are no better than the criminal poor, sends Bishop and Lodge copies of his telegrams with Hanna, and praises Alice for real service to the country on her Cuba visit.
Roosevelt speaks at Pocatello, Shoshone, Glenns Ferry and Mountain Home, and spends the evening in Boise, whose trees, library and homes impress him.

Roosevelt visits Ogden and Salt Lake City with a Rough Rider escort and heads for Laramie, swapping ranching tales with Seth Bullock along the way. He writes Hanna explaining the telegrams and how Hanna's apparent coolness struck him.
Roosevelt speaks at the University of Wyoming, then rides horseback 65 miles from Laramie to Cheyenne, stopping at the Van Tassell ranch and changing horses five times.
On Decoration Day in Wyoming, Roosevelt reviews U.S. Army troops.

At the Cheyenne fairgrounds Roosevelt watches top-notch steer roping and bronc riding, then heads for Iowa, speaking from the train at Osceola. He thanks Senator Hoar for kind words in Hoar's autobiography.
Speaking about the flood at Denison
At Denison, Iowa, Roosevelt speaks about the recent flood. Senators Allison and Dolliver and Treasury Secretary Shaw join his party.
Roosevelt gives nine speeches across Illinois, among them Freeport, Aurora, Joliet, Lexington and Bloomington.
Roosevelt speaks in Lincoln, at Lincoln's tomb in Springfield, and in Decatur and Danville, then leaves for Indianapolis.

The western tour ends with stops at Pittsburgh and Altoona. Roosevelt brings Josiah the badger home for Archie, is greeted at Washington's station, visits John Hay, and is back in the White House by 9 p.m.

Back at his desk, Roosevelt holds Cabinet and goes over the postal investigation with Root and Payne, then sees the British ambassador and Leupp. He tells Lodge the children have given the young badger a wild welcome.
Roosevelt speaks at the dedication of Grace Reformed Church, at the corner of 15th and O, then lunches with Ambassador Joseph H. Choate.
Roosevelt lunches with Root, Henry Taft and Wayne MacVeagh, and the talk turns to the Philippines.
Taft agrees to run the War Department

Roosevelt leaves at 3 p.m. for Cleveland with Alice, the Cowleses and Loeb, stopping at Harrisburg and York. He writes Taft, who has agreed to succeed Root as Secretary of War, that he wants to live simply as President and will gladly return to plain living afterward.

Roosevelt reaches Cleveland for the wedding of Ruth Hanna and Medill McCormick, then returns to Washington. In Morenci, Arizona, miners strike, and the territorial governor asks the President for help.

Roosevelt orders Regulars stationed in Colorado down to Arizona to keep order at the Morenci strike. He tells Henry Taft he wants Will in the Cabinet rather than as Vice President, writes Root about Taft's acceptance, and tells Burroughs that nature writer Rev. William J. Long is ridiculous.

Roosevelt meets Russian Ambassador Cassini about the Kishinev massacre of Jews and talks trusts with Judge Grosscup. He and Edith are dinner guests of the Hays, and he orders Payne to investigate New York Postmaster Van Cott.

On a crowded day, Roosevelt breakfasts with Curtis Guild, lunches with Senator Platt on New York politics and a new county chairman, and talks Panama with William Nelson Cromwell. He tells Lowell he will be friendly toward Canada and writes Higginson on currency. Speaker-to-be Joe Cannon opposes his program.
Navy Secretary Moody and Senator Eugene Hale visit the White House on Sunday.
B'nai B'rith on Kishinev; song in Baltimore

Roosevelt and Hay meet B'nai B'rith's executive council about the Kishinev massacre. After lunch with German and American guests and receptions for three ambassadors, he goes to the Baltimore Sängerfest with Speck von Sternberg and speaks about German immigrants. He writes Coubertin on physical education.
Commencement at the University of Virginia

At Charlottesville Roosevelt speaks at the University of Virginia's commencement on citizenship and a strong Navy, and visits Monticello before returning to Washington. He tells Leonard Wood the Senate is balking at his promotion to major general.

Roosevelt publicly endorses agreements between coal miners and mine owners. He lunches with Goddard, Moody, Governor Hunt and Captain Davis, dines with George Sheldon, and writes Root about General Wilson's speech attacking Wood and McKinley.
Speeding up the postal fraud cases
Roosevelt issues an executive order to hurry the postal fraud prosecutions. He meets Booker T. Washington at noon, sees Cecil Lyon, and lunches with Shaffer, Tracy and Ware.

After Cabinet and a midday meal with Hamilton Fish and Stranahan, Roosevelt has Byrnes and Mellen to dinner. Letters ask George Gray to speak for him on the Fourth in Wilkes-Barre, defend his policies to tariff leader Charles Moore, stand up for Payne, and tell John Wanamaker the postal corruption predates his administration.
Roosevelt hears from French and Chinese delegations and sees Payne.
Attorney General Knox calls in the evening. Roosevelt thanks George W. Perkins for his help in the Ohio endorsement affair, which Mellen had told him about.

Roosevelt tells Knox the Post Office wrongdoers must be prosecuted and takes responsibility for Payne's actions amid heavy press criticism. He writes Lyman Abbott about peonage of Black workers in Georgia and Russia's stance in Manchuria, where Russia refuses to open the ports.
No presidential name for a Jerusalem model

Roosevelt lunches with Speyer and Knox and has John McCall to dinner and overnight, with Cortelyou joining them. He writes John Proctor about irregularities at the Washington post office and wires Joseph Burton that he refuses to endorse a for-profit model of Jerusalem planned for the 1904 fair.

Roosevelt lunches with Melville Stone and Ware and dines with Benjamin Ide Wheeler, the Hays, the Jusserands and Wayne MacVeagh; Wheeler stays the night. He asks Francis Leupp to serve as an impartial investigator of the Oklahoma Indian reservations.

Roosevelt lunches with Crane, Cooley, Proctor and Major Carson, then dines at Great Falls, Virginia, with Pinchot, Garfield and Proctor. Letters touch the postal probe, Ray Stannard Baker's articles, the press, and a false coal-strike story. Hanna will not give up the national chairmanship.

Roosevelt hosts a lunch for yachtsman Sir Thomas Lipton with Moody, Andrew D. White, General Corbin, Hanna and others, and hears Perkins on Wall Street's view of his finance bills. He gives Perkins the pen that signed the Commerce and Labor act and spends the evening at Hay's with Douglas Robinson.
Roosevelt travels to Oyster Bay and dedicates a cannon on the village green.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Lyman Abbott comes to lunch and Joe Bishop stays the night. Roosevelt tells Hay the Alaska boundary must be settled without delay, and writes Platt on New York appointments.
Kermit off to hunt with Bullock
Wilson Bissell, Governor Hunt and Senator Long come to lunch. Kermit leaves for the Black Hills to hunt with Seth Bullock.
Angry at Russia over the Kishinev petition

Sagamore Hill fills with guests, among them niece Eleanor, Gifford Pinchot and Beekman Winthrop, and Beveridge comes to dinner. Roosevelt writes Francis Loomis about a petition to Russia protesting the Kishinev massacre, and tells Hay he is angered by Russia's impertinence.
General Joseph Wheeler is among the callers. Roosevelt asks Loomis how the government should now proceed with the Kishinev petition.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

On the Fourth of July Roosevelt speaks at Huntington, Long Island, to celebrate the newly completed cable across the Pacific, and sends a message across it to Governor Taft in Manila. He defends his irrigation policy to Ray Stannard Baker and tells George Holls he will act in the national interest whatever foreign powers think.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes John Burroughs, setting a Friday meeting and musing on Josiah the badger, animal instinct, and writers who falsify nature.

Secretary Hay, Winthrop Chanler and Grant La Farge are guests. Over lunch with Hanna, Fairbanks and others, Roosevelt and Hay take up Alaska, Manchuria and the petition to the Czar on behalf of Russia's Jews. He tells Seth Bullock that Ted and his cousin George will reach Deadwood on August 20 to hunt.
Winthrop Chanler, Grant La Farge and Massachusetts Governor Murray Crane are guests. Roosevelt urges Pension Commissioner Eugene Ware to take a vacation instead of resigning.
Up the Hudson on the Sylph
After dinner Roosevelt and Edith board the Sylph for a cruise up the Hudson. He thanks Rollo Ogden for the Evening Post's position on Black Americans and his Southern policy.
From the Hudson, Roosevelt calls on John Burroughs at his cabin, Slabsides, in West Park, New York, then returns to Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt receives Hiscock, Hendricks, Philbin, Dryden and Kean at Sagamore Hill.
Secretary of War Root is a guest. He and Roosevelt discuss Army promotions, the Kishinev petition and the Alaska boundary.
No union shop at the Printing Office

Roosevelt lunches with Root, Archbishop Farley, Jacob Riis and others, and appoints Robert Shaw Oliver Assistant Secretary of War. In two letters to Cortelyou he refuses to let the Government Printing Office become a closed union shop.

Roosevelt meets Leo Levi, Simon Wolf and Oscar Straus about the Kishinev petition, sees Albert Shaw, and dines with Judge Sherman. He tells Cortelyou that W. A. Miller must be reinstated at the Printing Office even though he is not a union member, and sends Hay a cable for Russia.
A family day aboard the Sylph

Roosevelt spends the day on the Sylph with his family, Treasury Secretary Shaw and Jacob Riis, and sees Bonaparte, Ray Stannard Baker and Herman Kohlsaat. Bamie, Will and little Sheffield Cowles are guests. He tells Holls that Cassini never officially refused the petition.

Lodge visits to discuss finance bills and Alaska, and Douglas and Corinne Robinson are guests. Roosevelt asks Hay to cable St. Petersburg, orders Payne to look into the letter carriers' convention, and warns Clarkson that Printing Office strikers would never work for the government again while he is President.
Roosevelt releases a statement on currency reform legislation. Nicholas Murray Butler calls, and Roosevelt forwards to Root some praise Taft wrote about him.

Seth Low, George Meyer and W. L. Ward call, and Butler and the Clifford Richardsons are guests. Roosevelt tells Hay he does not mind the Russians knowing how irritated he is over Manchuria, and writes Charles Emory Smith about his clash with Proctor.
Congratulating Hamlin Garland on a baby
Dr. Alexander Lambert and Nicholas Murray Butler visit and stay for lunch. Roosevelt congratulates Hamlin Garland on his new baby and lays out his belief in large families.
Roosevelt lunches with Whitelaw Reid and his wife. He informs Colonel Thomas Barry that he now outranks more senior colonels as a newly made brigadier general.
Bracing for a fight over Wood

Titus Sheard calls. Roosevelt writes Ebenezer Hill on finance, warns Root that Wood's promotion may bring an ugly fight, and complains to Joe Bishop about Boston Herald falsehoods on the McSweeney case.
Platt, Frick and a crowd of visitors

A stream of visitors reaches Sagamore Hill, among them Senator Platt, Henry Clay Frick, Gifford Pinchot and Charlemagne Tower, and Roosevelt goes over finance bills with Cannon. He tells a congressman he listens to party bosses only selectively, and writes on Indian affairs and money matters.
At 2 in the morning Roosevelt sets out on horseback for Sayville, Long Island, to stay with his uncle, Robert B. Roosevelt, and lunches there with J. E. Roosevelt.

Roosevelt returns to Oyster Bay and talks Navy growth with Secretary Moody. He replies to Emanuel Bloomingdale's letter on the persecution of Russian Jews and writes Whitelaw Reid on the Monroe Doctrine and Knox on lynching.

Roosevelt discusses Puerto Rico with Samuel Lindsay. He tells Justice Holmes there will be no arbitration of the Alaska boundary, asks William Round not to publish an 18-year-old letter of his about Indians, and tells Oswald Villard he was advised against promoting Captain John J. Pershing.
Miss Helen Buchanan is a guest, and Bishop McFaul and Father Belford come to lunch.
John Barrett calls at 10 a.m. Roosevelt writes S. Weir Mitchell about a West Point appointment for Mitchell's son.
Roosevelt asks Augustus Saint-Gaudens to see that western sculptor Edward Kemeys has work shown at the 1904 fair in St. Louis.

Roosevelt talks finance with W. D. Washburn and lunches with Frank Higgins. He writes about friar land sales in the Philippines and tells Hay that Root will be missed, but that Hay is one man he could not do without.

Roosevelt and Payne go over the postal fraud cases, and John R. Proctor is a guest. Letters cover the Port of New York, Father Hendrick's appointment as a bishop in the Philippines, the Panama Canal Commission, an article by Andrew D. White, and family life.

J. R. Proctor and Agriculture Secretary Wilson call; Roosevelt lunches with Woodbury Kane and reviews the Government Printing Office investigation with Proctor. Wilson stays the night, and nephew Stewart Douglas Robinson is a guest. He writes Archbishop Ireland about agitation for the friars in the Philippines.
Night camping trip with the boys by rowboat

Roosevelt heads out after dark to camp with Kermit, Archie and their cousins Philip, Oliver and Nicholas, the party filling two rowboats. His letters that day touch the Government Printing Office row, Leonard Wood's contested promotion and Seth Low's mayoral bid.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill; the guest book records Bob Ferguson.
Roosevelt writes Augustus Saint-Gaudens to admire his new equestrian statue of General Sherman, newly unveiled in Manhattan.
Bareback ride leaves the President raw

After a run of callers, among them Hamilton Fish and Melville Stone, Roosevelt and Ted ride bareback for an hour and a half, Ted on Renown and his father on Bleistein. The President comes home with the skin rubbed off the insides of his legs.
Root confers on gloves and the General Staff
Elihu Root comes out to talk over the new General Staff law and the Littauer-Lyon glove contract affair. Kermit and Philip set off to camp overnight but bad weather drives them home.
Edith's birthday with cake and haybarn games

Edith turns 42, and the appointment book is marked to keep visitors away. Ethel hemstitched handkerchiefs and wrapped the gifts, opened at breakfast; Kermit and Ethel carried in a cake at lunch, and the whole family spent the afternoon tumbling in the haybarn. Root also confers on the Alaska boundary.
Roosevelt receives Speck von Sternberg, who formally presents his papers as Germany's ambassador. Senator Heyburn, Millard, Howland and Regis Post also call, and Dr. Alexander Lambert is a guest.
Miles retires as Alaska warning reaches London

General Nelson Miles leaves the Army. In London, Colonial Secretary Chamberlain tells Prime Minister Balfour that Justice Holmes delivered a private letter from Roosevelt: the President agreed to arbitrate the Alaska boundary only to keep peace with Britain, and would occupy the American claim himself if the result fell short.
Long letter to Hay recounting the Western tour
Roosevelt sits down and writes John Hay a full account of his 1903 Western trip, stocked with stories from the road.
Letters on the Cuban treaty session
Roosevelt writes Senator Fairbanks about calling Congress back to act on the Cuban treaty, and Senator Hanna about the Outlook's Howland. Meanwhile his friend Jacob Riis is at work on a biography.
Knox briefs him on glove and postal cases
Attorney General Knox comes to discuss the glove contract case and the Post Office frauds. Bishop O'Gorman calls, and at three Howland arrives with a photographer.
Colombia's senate rejects the canal treaty

Roosevelt sees Jacob Riis, then spends the whole night with Senators Allison, Spooner, O. H. Platt and Aldrich hammering out a currency bill. Far away, Colombia's congress turns down the Hay-Herran Treaty, which would have paid $10 million in gold plus $250,000 a year for a canal zone in Panama.
Ethel turns eleven; canal outlook murky

Ethel's eleventh birthday. Roosevelt admits to Senator Morgan that he cannot see how the isthmus question will end, and presses Joe Cannon for congressional action on Cuban reciprocity. The Wall Street scare is easing.

Treasury Secretary Shaw, Senator Cullom, Interior Secretary Hitchcock, John G. Carlisle, Lauterbach and Bishop Rooker all call. At noon a Mr. Hewitt photographs Ted, and Joseph Bucklin Bishop stays for dinner and the night.

Captain Cowles settles in for the weekend and Monday's naval review. Roosevelt lunches with Robert Shaw Oliver, receives the Mayflower's officers at six, and hosts Captain Brownson overnight. From Bogota the American minister warns Hay that Panama's delegates now lean toward independence.
"American Manhood" speech to Holy Name men

Roosevelt speaks on American manhood to Holy Name Society members from Manhattan, Brooklyn and Long Island. Writing Emily Carow, he recounts a family ride and picnic at Jane's Hill with Speck von Sternberg and the children's backyard play, with Ted as George Washington and Quentin as Cupid. Everyone visits the battleship Kearsarge.
Reviewing the fleet off Lloyd's Neck

From the deck of the Kearsarge, Roosevelt reviews the North Atlantic Squadron's Caribbean ships off Lloyd's Neck with Sir Thomas Lipton, Navy Secretary Moody and Admirals Dewey and Taylor, then lunches aboard the Mayflower.
A blank day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
After callers Kearns and J. H. Sleicher, Roosevelt tells Hay to hold off on the canal for now, but floats building at Panama under the 1846 treaty and scorns the Bogota government as jack rabbits.
Wilcox visits; no youth memoir, please

Ansley Wilcox dines and spends the night. Roosevelt answers criticism for sending no commendation to the retiring General Miles, writes Senator Frye on the special session, and asks Richard Watson Gilder not to publish the story of his boyhood.
Currency talks and a happy childhood

Roosevelt talks currency legislation with Representatives Hill and Babcock, lunches with Governor Odell and dines with Babcock; Cortelyou stays the night. To Gilder he credits his parents for a happy childhood.

Roosevelt sees G. W. Dunn and lunches with Carter. He writes Hanna that his offer of the War Department to Taft is now public, Platt about the Printing Office inquiry, and banker James Stillman with financial ideas.
Roosevelt rows Edith to the tip of Lloyd's Neck, where they picnic and read, explore a bit, and pull home under an odd, glimmering sunset.
Taft says yes; Root steps down

Roosevelt tells Bamie that Taft has taken the War Department, and accepts Elihu Root's resignation with warm praise. He lunches with Hermann Kohlsaat, sees Senator Aldrich, and swipes at the Sun and the Journal.

Roosevelt writes Ted, away hunting, that Kermit has his hands full with the horse Wyoming and off limits to Edith; he rides Bleistein and she Yagenka. Senator Fulton hears about Oregon patronage and a fired Land Office man.
Defending Wood and the currency system

F. C. Travers drops by, as does Thomas Woodlock, a Wall Street Journal man. In letters he tells Bamie the nation's money system is sound overall, warns Cannon about pressure for inflation, and promises Leonard Wood he will keep fighting for his promotion.
Fusionists call; false alarm from Beirut

Roosevelt breakfasts with Jacob Riis, receives New York Fusion leaders and others, and lunches with Ansley Wilcox. The Mediterranean squadron sails for Beirut on reports, later proven false, that the American vice consul has been murdered. He offers Beekman Winthrop a Philippine commission seat.

John Hay confers with Roosevelt over lunch, and Treasury Secretary Shaw stays the night. Letters go to Bamie, to Joe Bishop on Taft and money, and to James Clarkson about next year's campaign and Herbert Parsons.
Mrs. Alexander Russell and Mrs. Ballington Booth visit. Roosevelt writes Nicholas Murray Butler about what he means to say on Labor Day.
Nothing is recorded for the day beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.
Alice off with the Newport set

After callers including McMackin, Roosevelt confirms Beekman Winthrop's Philippine appointment, tells Shaw he stands behind him and Hanna in Ohio, and writes Jacob Schurman on currency and Canadian trade. Alice is rarely home, spending her days with Newport society.
Roosevelt writes Theodore Brentano about condolences on Pope Leo XIII's passing, and tells Paul d'Estournelles de Constant his views on war and peace with Turkey and Beirut in mind.
Senator Albert Beveridge, John H. Finley and Major Llewellyn come to lunch.
Hunting tales for the little boys

Roosevelt thanks Agriculture Secretary Wilson for advising silence on currency, writes Taft about the War Department and Miles, and tells Lodge about the Printing Office fight. He is reading hunting stories aloud to Archie and Quentin and calls Ethel a perfect little housewife.
Cortelyou and Loomis call, and Roosevelt writes Albert Shaw about sending warships toward Beirut and the dispute with Turkey.
Six steps on labor and capital

Roosevelt writes Payne about a Delaware postmistress pushed out by the Addicks machine, congratulates John Finley on the NYU presidency, and sends Lyman Abbott a long letter on trusts, Indian agencies and the coal strike, listing six things he has done on labor and capital.
After lunch with James R. Garfield, Roosevelt leaves in the evening for Syracuse with Jacob Riis and William Loeb. He tells Florence LaFarge he read Aristophanes and Euripides side by side.
Labor Day at the State Fair
At the state fair in Syracuse, Roosevelt reviews the Labor Day parade at 10:30, gives his Labor Day address, reviews the letter carriers at five, and dines as the guest of F. H. Hiscock.
Back to Oyster Bay; senators bristle

Roosevelt returns to Oyster Bay, speaking at Richmond Hill on the way, and sees Cooley and a Sound Money League group. He writes Harvey Scott about senators angry that he has meddled in appointments they treated as their own.
Archbishop of Manila and two writers
Paul Morton and Francis Leupp call; Gordon Johnston and Will Cowles come to lunch. At three Archbishop Harty of Manila and H. M. Hoyt arrive, and in the evening Grant LaFarge and Owen Wister.
Wary of stirring revolt in Panama
LaFarge, Wister and Hamlin Garland are houseguests. Roosevelt again writes Payne about Miss Todd's removal and tells Jacob Schurman why he cannot say what he thinks about Panama.
Roosevelt writes Alford Cooley about how the merit rules apply to fourth-class postmasters and explains to Hay why the Beirut squadron had to go and must stay.
Miss Todd's case may be lost
Roosevelt tells Payne the Delaware postmistress's removal may now be impossible to reverse, and writes Wood about charges meant to sink his promotion.
Ted's sixteenth birthday at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no activity is noted.

The Storers and Willis Ogden call, and Roosevelt dines with John Bassett Moore, LaFarge, Wister and Albert Bushnell Hart. He tells Hay to do nothing about Colombia for now and writes Taft that the coming winter may bring a start on Nicaragua or a move at Panama.
Inspecting Ellis Island aboard the Sylph
Roosevelt takes the Sylph out to the immigration station, touring it with Commissioner William Williams, to look over the station, meets Senator Platt, and leaves that evening for Antietam.
Honoring New Jersey's dead at Antietam
At Antietam, Roosevelt speaks at the dedication of New Jersey's monument to its soldiers, dines with Governor Franklin Murphy, and heads back to Oyster Bay.
Seawanhaka dinner; at wits' end over the city race

Roosevelt dines at the Seawanhaka Yacht Club at eight. He tells Alford Cooley that fourth-class postmasters fall under the new civil service rules and confides to Seth Low his puzzlement over the New York City election.
Literary lunch with Matthews and White

Roosevelt lunches with Brander Matthews, Stewart Edward White, Captain W. C. Brown and Nicholas Murray Butler, who stays over. He writes LeGrand Cannon about the tariff league's campaign against the Cuba treaty.
Nicholas Murray Butler remains a guest at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt talks over the special session with Harvey Scott and Senator Redfield Proctor and federal patronage with Representative Curtis. He warns Hay that the Alaska tribunal is under pressure against the United States and writes Clarke Davis about Miller and labor unions.
Roosevelt writes Governor Taft about filling a seat on the Philippine Commission.
An emptier house, and Archie's overalls

With Ted and Kermit back at Groton, Roosevelt writes Kermit that home feels empty though hardly quiet, thanks to Archie in his faded blue overalls and Quentin. Edith is shutting the house for winter. He also writes Bill Sewall about the burdens of the presidency, and LaFarge and Wister arrive for the night.
Three-hour ride; a Panama plot at the Waldorf

Roosevelt rides three hours with LaFarge and Wister, lunches with Lyman Abbott, chops wood in the afternoon, and hosts Parsons overnight. In New York, Philippe Bunau-Varilla and Dr. Manuel Amador meet at the Waldorf-Astoria hotel and lay plans for a Panamanian revolution.
Riding with Edith, talking game with Grinnell
Roosevelt and Edith ride for four hours. At lunch George Bird Grinnell and Sears discuss Indian reservations and the zoology of big game, and Roosevelt plays tennis in the afternoon.
All day on the water with Edith
Roosevelt and Edith spend the day in a rowboat, picnicking at the big marsh off Lloyd's Neck before a hard pull home into wind and tide. He also writes Henry White about the Alaska boundary.
Roosevelt leaves for Washington. Writing Corinne, he looks back on a lovely summer, praises her son Stewart, and wryly notes that Alice spent it mostly at Newport among the Four Hundred.
Labor leaders at the White House

Back at work, Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, receives the American Federation of Labor's executive council, and lunches with mine leader John Mitchell. He also takes up the postal inquiry with Payne and the Printing Office probe with Sargent and Garfield.

Roosevelt visits Dr. Harban at eleven and lunches with Bonaparte and Conrad. To Lodge he reports he is reading Lincoln and Plutarch and covers the Printing Office, postal scandals and the Platt-Odell feud. British Ambassador Sir Michael Herbert has died in Switzerland, and London picks Sir Mortimer Durand as his successor.
Delaware attorney talks; first World Series opens

Roosevelt and Delaware's two senators, Allee and Ball, discuss a new district attorney for that state; sees R. P. Skinner and Senator Stewart, lunches with Secretary Wilson, and at three receives Ambassador and Mrs. Charlemagne Tower. In Boston the first World Series begins at the Huntington Avenue Grounds.

After a Cabinet meeting and talks on Alaska and postal indictments, Roosevelt writes his family: Quentin has started at the Force School, and Kermit should study more and play less. He adds that he enjoys the presidency and is reading about Lincoln.
Drafting the annual message; jumping Bleistein
Roosevelt works on his annual message, lunches with Moody, Shaw and Cortelyou, and receives Justices McKenna and Harlan and a string of officials. Then he rides out to Chevy Chase to jump Bleistein.
Roosevelt writes Ted, now on Groton's second football squad, with some misgivings, and tells headmaster Endicott Peabody he will let the boy play even at some risk of injury.

Roosevelt names J. P. Nields Delaware's U.S. attorney as a grand jury charges Tyner and Barrett over postal fraud. He sits for three photographers, receives Venezuela's minister, and tells Hanna that Colombia must be warned his patience has limits; to Lodge he says Britain has no case on Alaska.
After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt attends a noon memorial for the late Sir Michael Herbert at St. John's Episcopal Church, then sees a druggists' committee and lunches with George Becker.
Langley's aircraft falls into the Potomac

Roosevelt confers with Cromwell on the canal, Knox on judgeships and Payne at the Post Office, and goes to St. Thomas Church for the marriage of General Young's daughter. On the Potomac, Charles Manly tries to fly Samuel Langley's Smithsonian aircraft and fails.

Roosevelt meets Payne, Moody and C. E. Smith on the postal investigations, Representative Theodore Burton on rivers and harbors, and Joseph Folk on extradition with Canada and Mexico. He asks J. P. Morgan to talk finance.
Cabinet day and lunch with McClure
Roosevelt meets his Cabinet and lunches with magazine publisher S. S. McClure.

At 11:30 Roosevelt and Assistant Secretary Loomis meet Philippe Bunau-Varilla of Paris. He talks Ohio with Senator Foraker, lunches with Will Cowles and visiting English traffic commissioners, and sees Lincoln Steffens. To Albert Shaw he writes that an independent Panama would delight him. It is Kermit's fourteenth birthday.
Evening tea with Hay and reformers
At 7:30 Roosevelt takes tea with Arthur von Briesen, John Hay and William Dudley Foulke. He writes Ted that he belongs on Groton's third football team, not the second. His niece Eleanor turns 19.
Praise for Uncle Remus, a quarrel with Long

Atha Cunningham photographs Roosevelt at nine. He meets Moody and Congressmen Grosvenor, Dalzell and Olmsted, receives the Supreme Court, and lunches with Lloyd Lowndes. He praises Joel Chandler Harris and protests John D. Long's Outlook article suggesting he wanted Spanish ships sunk before war began in 1898.

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt shares lunch with the Corbins, Clarke Davis and a visiting English lord and lady. He tells Taft he needs him home by late January for help on labor and trusts, and suggests to Roger Baldwin that Yosemite's forest rangers double as game wardens.
Boston wins the first World Series

Roosevelt confers with Knox and receives Henry Clay Frick, Regis Post, Simon Wolf and Senator McComas, then has Generals Bell and Crozier to dinner. Boston beats Pittsburgh in game eight to take the first World Series, and Amador and Bunau-Varilla meet again at the Waldorf.
Sherman statue speech; word of a Panama revolt

Roosevelt speaks at 2:30 at the unveiling of General Sherman's statue in Washington. Navy Commander John Hubbard tells him a rising in Panama is coming. Postal investigators confer with him, General Dodge and the Thorndikes stay overnight, and he orders Payne to look into Perry Heath.
Army officers predict a Panama uprising

After the Cabinet meets and he talks with Representatives Payne and Dalzell about a special session, two Army officers tell Roosevelt that Panama is close to rising against Colombia. Arthur Sage and Albert Shaw stay the night.

The Alaska boundary tribunal decides in favor of the United States. Roosevelt sees Hay and Senators Scott and Hansbrough, lunches with Generals Oliver and Brooke, John Logan and John C. Black, meets A. Maurice Low, and has Joe Bishop to dinner and overnight.

Roosevelt meets Hay and, at 2:30, Ambassador von Sternberg, and enjoys Washington's autumn color. Once he is home, the two youngest boys, Archie and Quentin, ambush him with pillows, and once they are bathed he reads aloud from Uncle Remus. Nephew Sheffield Cowles turns five.

Roosevelt sends the Boston to Nicaragua and the Atlanta to Guantanamo. He discusses land laws with Senator Hansbrough, has Paul Morton and General Black to lunch, and tells Kermit that a car spooked Renown on a family ride.

Roosevelt summons Congress to meet November 9 on the Cuban treaty. The Alaska tribunal's ruling, with Lord Alverstone siding with the Americans, gives Canada nothing; the two Canadians refuse to sign. He writes Ted about his own fast rise, and writes Holmes on the boundary.
Claiming credit for the Alaska win

Roosevelt meets a group of senators including Quay, Clark, Mitchell and Fulton, lunches with Wayne MacVeagh and Bishop William Lawrence, and hosts Henry Lee Higginson overnight. He tells Ted his warnings over Alaska were decisive and praises Ray Stannard Baker's article on union bosses.

Roosevelt sets up the Public Lands Commission to study how the nation's land laws work. He reviews the postal prosecutions with Bonaparte, Conrad and Knox, lunches with James R. Garfield, and writes Shaw about a Boston business meeting.

After the Cabinet and callers including Senator Cullom and Charles Walcott of the Geological Survey, Roosevelt comes down with Cuban fever. He spends the afternoon still on the sofa while Edith knits beside him in a rocker.

Several hundred Universalist convention delegates call. Roosevelt cheers Ted's grades but confesses he is slipping physically, stiff with what may be rheumatism or gout. He tells Kermit that Quentin fell off the pony unhurt and the family has gone to Dr. Rixey's farm, while he works on his annual message.
Bishops and a talk at Mount St. Alban
Roosevelt receives a delegation of American bishops and speaks at Mount St. Alban on Christian virtues.
Inquiry into the New York Post Office

A probe of the post office in New York City gets under way. Roosevelt sees Senator Scott, meets Secretary Moody and the West Indies archbishop, and entertains the Satterlees, the Rixeys and Chief Justice Fuller.
Forty-five, with greetings from Hungarian Republicans

Roosevelt turns 45. A Hungarian-American Republican club from New York stops by that morning with good wishes; he also meets the Cabinet, talks the glove contract case with Littauer, and sees Baldwin and Burgess.
Glove case talks and a crowded lunch table
Roosevelt meets Littauer and John G. Milburn, sees Senators Cullom and Cockrell and Representative Dixon, and lunches with Silas McBee, General Joseph Wheeler, Bishop Talbot, the Dudleys and others.

Roosevelt confers with Interior Secretary Hitchcock on public lands and lunches with Dean Worcester and Alexander Agassiz. He tells Lincoln Steffens he likes Joseph Conrad's work and writes Lyman Abbott about the Caribbean islands and about his policies toward Black Americans.
The Cabinet works over the annual message, and Roosevelt confers with Long and Darling. The gunboat Nashville is sent to Colon on the isthmus.
Roosevelt appoints George R. Carter territorial governor of Hawaii, receives the Portuguese minister, sees Mr. Emerson of the New York Herald, and writes Hanna about Ohio patronage.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt talks with Representatives Cannon and Mondell, greets the sailors of the Sylph and Mayflower, lunches with John W. Foster, and leaves that night for Oyster Bay. The Panama rising planned for this day is held back until U.S. warships take station; the Nashville reaches Colon by 5:30.

Roosevelt votes at Oyster Bay on Election Day, sees Jacob Riis, and heads back to Washington that evening. In Panama City, Colombian troops are bought off with $50 apiece in gold, railroad workers and firemen seize the city, U.S. ships keep Colombian forces from landing, and Panama proclaims independence with Dr. Amador as president.

American Marines come ashore at Colon. Roosevelt writes Nicholas Murray Butler about the elections, including a lengthy rundown of his reading since 1900, and writes Hanna on the canal and Gilder on the coal strike.
War council on the Panama rising

Roosevelt meets Hay, Moody, Loomis and Admirals Taylor and Walker on events in Panama, sees the immigration commissioners, and has Senator and Mrs. George Turner overnight. He writes General Francis Greene on the elections and Lyman Abbott about Hanna's place in the presidential picture.
America recognizes the Republic of Panama

The United States recognizes Panama, and the Cabinet agrees to open canal treaty talks with the new republic at once. Roosevelt sees Congressmen Grosvenor and Hepburn, dines with Governor Franklin Murphy, and insists to Albert Shaw there was no conspiracy with the rebels.
Senate leaders and the Cuba treaty

On a crowded day Roosevelt meets Senators Spooner, Aldrich, Cullom, Allison, Hale and Orville Platt about changes to the Cuban treaty, lunches with John Sleicher, and dines with General Francis Greene. He writes Hay on Congress's role in foreign affairs.
Late-night talks with Root and Aldrich
Roosevelt meets Elihu Root at nine about Panama and Senator Aldrich at ten about finance.

Congress gathers in extra session to act on Cuban reciprocity. Roosevelt discusses the Republican National Committee chairmanship with Hanna, dines with Lodge, and spends the evening with a roomful of party leaders over his Cuba message. He presses for Spring-Rice's posting to Washington.
Cuba message goes to Congress; Booker T. Washington calls

Roosevelt sends Congress his special message on Cuban reciprocity after a Cabinet session on Panama. He meets a joint committee including Hanna, Lodge and Cannon at 10:30, lunches with Baroness von Sternberg, sees Booker T. Washington at 2:30, and dines with House leaders.

Roosevelt breakfasts with Senator Beveridge and holds an evening dinner conference on Panama with Hay, Wilson and a group of senators. He assures Jacob Schurman and Lawrence Abbott that he and Hay had no advance knowledge of the Panama revolution.

At 9:30 Roosevelt receives Philippe Bunau-Varilla as Panama's minister. After Cabinet and talks with Senators Fairbanks, Hoar, Allison and McComas, he lunches with Knox and dines with Lodge and Hay. To James Wilson he recalls urging McKinley in 1898 to treat Spanish torpedo boats' sailing as an act of war.

After meeting Hanna and Puerto Rican delegates, Roosevelt leads Ethel, Archie, Quentin and three Garfield boys on a scramble through Rock Creek Park. That evening he dines with members of the Ellis Island investigating commission.

Roosevelt has dinner with Lodge and his sister Bamie and her husband. With Edith away nine days, he tells Kermit he spends 45 minutes every evening reading aloud to the two little boys, from Algonquin legends and Scott to Macaulay, Jim Bludso and the Bible. Ted has broken his nose at football.
Speech on Lincoln at New York Avenue church

At Congressman Hitt's request, the House receives the Panama documents. Roosevelt sees Beveridge, Fairbanks, Moody, Cortelyou, Cannon and Governor Durbin, lunches with Hughitt, Hendricks and Low, and at 7:45 gives an address on Lincoln at New York Avenue Presbyterian Church. He sends Harvard's football team a rousing letter.
Senators to dinner as the treaty takes shape

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with Governor Durbin, Justice Harlan and others while Bunau-Varilla and Hay draft a canal treaty. He dines with Lodge, Root, Knox and a table of senators, and writes on labor unions and the canal.

At 6:40 in the evening John Hay and Philippe Bunau-Varilla sign the canal treaty between the United States and Panama, on the same $10 million terms Colombia had refused. Earlier Roosevelt sees Simon Wolf and lunches with Moody, Ream and Wayne MacVeagh.
Quentin's birthday cake in the nursery

Quentin turns six, nursing a cold; his birthday cake is brought up to the nursery, where Edith, Aunt Emily, Ethel, Archie, his father, Mame and Georgette join him. The House passes the Cuban reciprocity bill, Roosevelt addresses Washington's German societies, and he wires Alice forbidding her to pour tea at a charity show.

Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and at 2:30 the Panama commission with Bunau-Varilla. In New York, Alice ignores his wishes and serves tea at $5 a cup at the Charity Portrait Show with Ethel Barrymore and Maude Adams.

Roosevelt lunches with W. D. Murphy, goes over the Bristow report with Payne and Bristow, sees Tawney and, at 2:30, the Russian ambassador, and dines with Joe Bishop. In New York, Enrico Caruso makes his Metropolitan Opera debut in Rigoletto.
Roosevelt is in Washington; no activity is noted.
Opening the German-American fair by button

Roosevelt lunches with Senator Platt and G. W. Dunn, sees Foraker and Fairbanks, and at seven touches an electric button that starts the German-American fair at Convention Hall before meeting Hanna at 8:30. He writes Philip Stewart about Colorado politics and bear hunting.

After the Cabinet takes up Panama, Roosevelt brings Governor Odell, Senator Platt and Dunn together to settle their New York feud. He lunches with Montana labor leaders, Cortelyou, MacVeagh and Carroll Wright, meets the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and keeps Odell overnight.
Bamie marks eight years of marriage. On a packed day Roosevelt lunches with Slicer and Shaw and meets Austria's ambassador.
Thanksgiving, then north for Uncle Jimmie

On Thanksgiving evening Roosevelt leaves for New York after the death of his uncle James K. Gracie and stays at Corinne's, where Eleanor is also a guest; everyone but Eleanor goes out to play. He answers Packard's charge that he is anti-labor and tells G. H. Putnam of a Collier's deal for his collected works.
Roosevelt attends the funeral of his uncle James K. Gracie in New York and returns to Washington.

Roosevelt sees S. Fred Nixon at ten, meets Ball, Quay and Fairbanks, and lunches with Eugene Philbin. He tells Kermit that 500 police ringed the church at Uncle Jimmie's funeral, yet a crank slipped in with a petition about curing the Kaiser's cancer. Ted has sprained an ankle and is urged to read Trevelyan's American Revolution.
His Bristow report comments go public
Roosevelt's comments on the Bristow report on postal frauds are published.

Roosevelt receives Cannon with an Illinois delegation and dines with Senators Spooner and Orville Platt. To Otto Gresham he explains why Panama's break from Colombia is no parallel to Southern secession: the Panamanians have right on their side.

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with Captain John J. Pershing, Monsignor O'Connell and Major and Mrs. Howze, confers with Senator Penrose, and writes Joe Bishop about press guesswork over his talk with Platt and Odell.

As he and Edith mark 17 years of marriage, Panama's government ratifies the Hay-Bunau-Varilla treaty. Roosevelt talks Panama and Illinois with Cullom, lunches with John R. Proctor and Garfield, sees Foraker, Fairbanks and the British ambassador, and writes Arthur von Briesen on immigration tests.
Roosevelt confers with Root, Moody and Hay, lunches with Ray Stannard Baker, and sends Congress a message on the Alaska boundary award.
Hanna at night on canal and Wood

Roosevelt sees Hill of the Tribune at ten, meets the Cabinet, takes up New York appointments with Senator Platt and confers with Hay. At 9:15 p.m. he and Hanna go over canal legislation, the Wood case and the national committee chairmanship.
Roosevelt breakfasts with Putnam and writes Hanna about rumors swirling around his meeting with Platt and Odell.
Roosevelt confers in the evening with Joseph Bristow and Francis Leupp.
Annual message: building the canal is a duty

Congress opens its regular session and hears Roosevelt's annual message, which calls building the Panama canal a national duty. He confers with Senator Warren on Alaska and lunches with Gordon and Peck. To Arthur Lee he praises the Alaska settlement and teases that Britain did well to face such reasonable jurors.

Charles Manly makes a second try at flying Professor Langley's aircraft off the Potomac, and fails again. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, lunches with Andrew Carnegie, Henry Pritchett, Moody and others, and dines at Root's at eight.

Roosevelt confers with Representative Foss on the Navy, visits Root in the evening and sees Senator Aldrich at 8:30. He tells Charles Osborn that Panama concerns him more than anything else right now.
Roosevelt meets Republican National Committee members, takes Commander Winslow on as an aide, has Hugh Bond and Congressman Dayton to lunch, and sees H. H. Kohlsaat at 9:30.
After the Cabinet, Roosevelt lunches with Root, Mott, Stewart and Brooke, receives Ambassador von Sternberg at 2:30, and meets the Republican National Committee.

Roosevelt names W. I. Buchanan U.S. minister to Panama, discusses Oklahoma statehood with Bird McGuire, and meets National Republican League leaders. He tells George Otto Trevelyan his book is the best history of the Revolution, defends Wood to Root, and answers Abbott on the postal frauds.
Roosevelt sees Elihu Root in the afternoon and, at nine that night, Gifford Pinchot and James B. Reynolds.

Roosevelt talks statehood with Delegate Wilson, sees Root, Moody, Proctor, Cockrell and Foraker, and meets Shaw and von Sternberg about exports to Germany. Jacob Riis is his guest. He writes Austin Wadsworth about New York business jitters over his financial course.
Funeral for a civil service commissioner

At 10:30 Roosevelt attends the funeral of Civil Service Commissioner John R. Proctor, then lunches with Shaw and Speaker Cannon and discusses German export duties. Beveridge calls at nine and Riis stays over. He names John Black to Proctor's seat.

The Senate passes the Cuban reciprocity bill. Roosevelt breakfasts with Albert Shaw, meets the Cabinet, reviews with Bonaparte and Conrad the report upholding Tulloch's postal fraud charges, and lunches with G. H. Putnam.
Signs Cuban reciprocity as the Wrights fly

Roosevelt signs the Cuban reciprocity bill, lunches with Root, Cortelyou, Lodge and Massachusetts Governor Crane, gives a Cabinet dinner at eight, and hosts Governor Odell overnight. At Kitty Hawk, Orville and Wilbur Wright make the first powered flights; the longest, Wilbur's fourth, lasts 59 seconds over 852 feet.

After a Cabinet session on Panama, Roosevelt discusses New York politics with Governor Odell and has Kennedy, Jones, Crane, Root, Cortelyou and Lodge to lunch. He writes Daniel Coit Gilman in support of Robert Peary's North Pole expedition.
Western land frauds and a jab at Bryce

Roosevelt calls in Knox, Lodge, Root, Moody, Hitchcock and Cortelyou to deal with land frauds in the West, lunches with Judge Grosscup, and dines with Joe Bishop, Professor Lounsbury and Nicholas Murray Butler, who stays over. He objects to James Bryce's portrait of Godkin and lays out his Panama policy for critic George Harvey.
At 9:15 in the morning Mrs. Trescott arrives to photograph the President and Edith.
Roosevelt calls on John Hay and orders Navy Secretary Moody to keep forces in Panama from shooting unless fired on.

After the Cabinet, Roosevelt lunches with Spring, Moore, Garrison and MacVeagh. He writes Hay about negotiations with Colombia's General Reyes and David Thompson about comparisons between Panama and the Civil War.
Friars' lands and a question about Yaviza

Roosevelt breakfasts with Paul Morton, takes up the Philippine friars' lands with Root and Shaw, lunches with Pennsylvania Governor Pennypacker, and sees H. G. Squiers. He telephones Senator Warren about Wood instead of sending a letter, rebukes George Carter for airing MacArthur's slurs on German-Americans, and asks Admiral Walker whether the Navy should take Yaviza.

Roosevelt meets the Spanish minister and Root, attends Miss Locke's funeral at St. Paul's at two, and visits Bamie that evening. He writes Shaw twice on Philippine bonds, urges Governor Hunt to hire Puerto Ricans, and tells Carl Schurz why he would not abet stripping Black Southerners of their basic rights.

At seven on Christmas morning the children pile onto Roosevelt's bed to open their stockings, while Allan, Kermit's terrier, sits in the thick of it and Bob Ferguson and Aunt Emily looking on. After breakfast the bigger gifts wait in the library on separate tables. The Lodges, the Cowleses, Brooks Adams and Ferguson come to dinner.
A Christmas like the old days
Senator Elkins calls at 9:45 and Secretary Shaw at three. Roosevelt tells Corinne the family's Christmas recalled the ones their parents gave them decades before.
Roosevelt writes Bellamy Storer about his indiscreet remarks on getting Archbishop Ireland a cardinal's hat and on removing an American diplomat named Hurst in Vienna.
Roosevelt lunches with the Irish poet William Butler Yeats, Maurice Francis Egan and William Dudley Foulke, then confers at three with Moody, Root and Quay.

At four the Cabinet takes up Colombia. Roosevelt sees Simon Wolf, and the Hays give a dinner for him and Edith. He writes John Byrne about New York bankers and honest money, and Samuel Small on Southern opposition to the canal.

Roosevelt receives the Spanish Treaty Claims Commission, Simon Wolf and Congressmen Dixon and Loomis. He rebukes Bellamy Storer over Archbishop Ireland and Hurst, and writes about the postal frauds and three letter carriers fired without cause.
Year-end conferences; Santo Domingo seeks protection
Roosevelt ends the year meeting Root, Garfield, Knapp, Cortelyou and Librarian of Congress Herbert Putnam. Santo Domingo asks the United States to make it a protectorate to keep European powers out.
Roosevelt confers with Secretary Shaw, then greets the public at the White House New Year's reception from eleven to 1:30.
Roosevelt lunches with Senator John Spooner.
Roosevelt is in Washington; no activity is noted.

As Congress returns, Roosevelt sends the Senate a special message asking it to approve the canal treaty with Panama. He sees Senator Hansbrough and Whitelaw Reid and lunches with David Starr Jordan, Moody, George Kennan, Merriam and Higgins. He tells Charles Lummis he may not have gone far enough with Colombia.

Russian troops move into Korea, and the Cabinet discusses the Far East. Roosevelt takes a long-distance call from Governor Odell, meets Senator Platt at 12:30, lunches with Baldwin, sees Booker T. Washington at 2:30, and with Edith dines at Secretary Root's.

Roosevelt asks Senator Quarles how the public is taking his canal policy and receives a stream of callers, among them Smoot, Beveridge, Burrows, Ball, Burton, Humphrey and Baldwin of the Outlook. At noon he attends Isabel McKenna's wedding to Mr. Duffield. He thanks John Bigelow and John Bassett Moore for help and praise on his canal message and writes Lodge, who is leading the Senate fight.
Henry Adams frowns at the court

Roosevelt confers with Quay and sees Allison, Hopkins, Boutell and Mondell. At the evening diplomatic reception Henry Adams is struck by what he considers royal trappings and imperial airs, and judges the presidency changed for the worse. Roosevelt writes Douglas Robinson on family money and Burlingame a comic verse about Panama.
Senators all day, music at night

Roosevelt confers with Representative Hinshaw and Senators Foraker, Aldrich, Fairbanks and Orville Platt, then with John Sleicher and Maurice Low, before a White House dinner and a ten o'clock musicale.

Roosevelt meets Arthur von Briesen's Ellis Island commission at nine, confers with Congressmen Bartholdt and Burton, Senators Allison and Dolliver, and at 2:30 Ambassador von Sternberg. He tells Jacob Riis his biography is so kind it embarrasses him.
Two evening callers, Captain Charles H. Scott and John Winfield Scott, see the President.
Steering Ted away from West Point

Roosevelt is photographed at nine, confers with Kearns and Aldrich, sees Governor Durbin and others, and lunches with Root, Knox, Beveridge and MacVeagh. He writes Ted weighing military against civilian careers and hoping he will skip West Point and Annapolis.
Persian minister and a Knox dinner
After the Cabinet, Roosevelt meets Senator Elkins, sees Representative Champ Clark, receives Ambassador von Sternberg at 12:30 and the Persian minister at 2:30, and dines with Edith at the Knoxes'.
Roosevelt confers with Lucius Littauer and sees Penrose, Governor Murray Crane, and Moody, who comes to review Naval Academy appointments.
Snowy ride; Hanna told who the nominee is

After a day of callers, the Roosevelts take their horses through deep snow along Rock Creek, and the White House holds its diplomatic dinner at eight. He writes Hanna, after press talk of a Hanna candidacy, leaving no doubt that he himself will be the nominee.

Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, talks New York politics with Woodruff and confers with Beveridge, sees Senator Long at ten and Sternberg at 12:30, lunches with Norman and Alderman, and receives Ida Tarbell at three. He and Edith ride again through the snow before a 10 p.m. musicale.
Among a crowd of callers are Quay, Governor Hill and Senator Beveridge. Roosevelt confers with Hay and Representative Hitt.
Roosevelt writes John Morley about his life of Gladstone; Morley plans to visit Washington in December.

On Bamie's 49th birthday Roosevelt receives a Michigan Republican delegation led by Senators Alger and Burrows, sees Rockhill and Amos Pinchot among others, and sits for Hewitt at 2:30. He tells Kermit the family went to see Kellar the magician, and Ted that he relaxes with riding and broadsword bouts.

Hewitt photographs the President at nine and Edith at 2:30. The Cabinet takes up the canal treaty, and Roosevelt confers with Senators Cullom and Allison about it. He and Edith dine at the Paynes', and he tells Joe Bishop he doubts Hanna will contest the nomination.

Hewitt photographs the President again at nine. Roosevelt confers with Aldrich on the canal treaty while the House debates the Hepburn pure food bill. Spring-Rice writes Edith from St. Petersburg that he is to marry Florence Lascelles, whom he has known eight years.
Senators Cullom, Frye and Hopkins and the Board of Indian Commissioners call. Roosevelt receives French Ambassador Jusserand at 2:30 and hosts the judicial reception that evening.
