After the Cabinet, Roosevelt discusses Ohio with Foraker, sees former Governor Merriam and Millard, lunches with Knox and Gates, and hosts a 10 p.m. musicale. Japanese troops land in Korea. He praises Alfred Henry Lewis's The Boss and tells George Harvey that General Miles resembles the early republic's James Wilkinson.

Roosevelt talks canal treaty with Fairbanks, sees Cannon, Grosvenor, Chief Justice Fuller and Justice Harlan, confers with Root, and lunches with Caspar Whitney and Lodge. At eight he goes to the Metropolitan Club to dine with his fellow Boone and Crockett members. He tells Kermit that Ethel is wonderful with the little boys and reports on Loretta the parrot.
Roosevelt is in Washington; no activity is recorded.

Roosevelt confers with Heyburn, Shaw and Beveridge and sees Dalzell and Lodge. He writes Trevelyan about the craft of history and asks Cortelyou to let Quan Yick Nam, a merchant from China, enter the country.

After a Cabinet session on Panama, Roosevelt meets St. Louis's good roads committee, sees Delaware's two senators and Representative Smith, and dines at Moody's. He sends Cullom State Department papers on Panama and Root and Moody memos on Wood and on Army and Navy actions on the isthmus.

Heyburn, George Perkins and Metcalf call, and Sternberg comes at 2:30. From nine to midnight Roosevelt attends a reception for Elihu Root at Russell Alger's home. He tells Hay he opposes the Philippine inter-island shipping bills.

Roosevelt talks Nebraska politics with Millard, lunches with Root, Taft and Bonaparte, confers with Chauncey Depew, sees the Spanish Treaty Claims Commission, and at eight gives the Supreme Court dinner.
"I doubt if they can prevent my nomination"

After the Cabinet and callers including Aldrich and Beveridge, Roosevelt lunches with Governor Crane, joins a reception for William Howard Taft, and closes with a White House dinner and musicale. He tells Ted that Hanna and Wall Street worry him a little but cannot likely stop him.

Roosevelt confers with Crane and Kohlsaat and on Ohio with Foraker, lunches with Alice French, Mrs. Oliver Wendell Holmes, Pinchot and Taft, and goes to the Gridiron Club's dinner; Butler is his overnight guest. He thanks Albert Shaw for friendly editorials and says his nomination is now certain.
Root, Taft, Moody and Archbishop Ireland

After a dinner for Elihu Root, Roosevelt sees Governor Taft at nine, Secretary Moody at 9:30 and Archbishop Ireland at ten. Critics are attacking the Roosevelts' style of living and what they call an imperial presidency.
Root steps down as Secretary of War

Roosevelt learns that Elihu Root, a frequent sparring partner on policy, is leaving the War Department for private practice. Word also comes that rebels at Santo Domingo have shot at the U.S. cruiser Yankee. Senators and Taft fill the day's call list.

William Howard Taft takes charge of the War Department as Root's term ends. Roosevelt holds a Cabinet session, talks over the Panama treaty with Cullom and railroad regulation with Elkins, then dines at Secretary Hitchcock's home.
Canal money talks with Platt and Shaw

Roosevelt works through the financing of the Panama canal with Senator Orville Platt and Treasury Secretary Shaw, and reviews upcoming bills with Allison. In the evening he hosts a dinner that includes Chapin, Saltonstall, Winsor and Robert Bacon.

After meetings with Senators Depew, Hopkins and Scott and a noon visit from the German ambassador, Roosevelt hosts the evening reception for members of Congress. His uncle Robert Roosevelt stays over. He writes to novelist Alice Hegan Rice about his love of books.
Filling Taft's seat on the Philippine Commission

The Cabinet takes up who should replace Taft on the Philippine Commission. Roosevelt sees George Perkins, Moody and others and goes to visit Senator Mark Hanna, while reports arrive that rebels near Santo Domingo City are menacing American property.
The Kaiser's letter and Dominican affairs

Roosevelt meets Moody, Loomis and Ambassador Speck von Sternberg, who hands him a letter from Kaiser Wilhelm, to talk over the Dominican crisis. Illinois politicians come in about their state, and Justice Holmes is among the dinner guests. He writes Ted that he regrets losing Root.
Russia and Japan break off diplomatic relations, bringing war in the Far East close. That Sunday evening Roosevelt sees Treasury Secretary Shaw.
Ready to send troops to Santo Domingo

Roosevelt resolves that American troops will go to Santo Domingo to restore order if it comes to that. At noon he goes to St. John's Church to see Justice Brewer's daughter married. He thanks Ambassador Jusserand for sending him the medieval Song of Roland.

That evening Japanese torpedo boats strike Russia's ships at Port Arthur and the Russo-Japanese War begins. Roosevelt's Cabinet meets on the Far East. He tells Oscar Straus that Japan turned down his offer to mediate, and writes about help for fire-ravaged Baltimore.

Russia formally declares war. Roosevelt goes over canal financing again with Secretary Shaw, and the Shoshone reclamation project in Wyoming is established. He tells Ted that winter has left him with little exercise beyond walking.

With Japan now formally at war with Russia, Roosevelt issues a proclamation of American neutrality. He talks pensions with Cannon, lunches with Taft and hosts the White House reception for the Army and Navy.

It is Alice's 20th birthday, and the family marks it with a dinner at the White House. Earlier Roosevelt meets his Cabinet, calls on the ailing Senator Hanna and receives Uruguay's new minister. He tells Maryland's governor he will not send troops to Baltimore.
Jamieson told to mind his oath

On a crowded Saturday Roosevelt calls on Mark Hanna and lunches with Harvey, General Greene, Seth Low and Taft. He warns T. N. Jamieson, his embattled pick for Chicago's port, to be scrupulous, and suggests to Moody that the Cabinet consider more ships for Asia.

Senator Mark Hanna, the Ohio power broker, dies of typhoid fever. Roosevelt's callers that day range from Governor Herrick and Ambassador Sternberg to Buffalo Bill Cody and a group of cotton mill owners, and Ambassador Jusserand comes at midday.

Roosevelt sees H. M. Hanna and talks with Speaker Cannon, then has Lincoln Steffens in that night. He thanks Root for a Union League Club speech that is winning him Wall Street support, and pays warm tribute to Hanna.
Roosevelt attends the Senate's funeral service for Mark Hanna. To Henry White he writes candidly that resistance to his nomination had already crumbled before Hanna fell ill.
Roosevelt confers with Senator Kean, Taft and Beveridge and receives Senator Millard and others. At lunch he entertains the German ambassador and his wife along with Captain Fournier and the Folgers.

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt confers with Representative Landis and Senator Thomas Platt and in the afternoon receives Francis Hendricks with a group from Syracuse. He writes Ted about Hanna's death and Buffalo Bill's recent lunch visit.
Dewey sent to look into Santo Domingo

Roosevelt meets a run of senators, including Lodge and Thomas Platt, and lunches with Hendricks and Hiscock. He picks Admiral Dewey, joined by Loomis and Admiral Taylor, to look into the troubles in Santo Domingo.
A quiet Sunday note to Corinne
Roosevelt sends his sister Corinne a brief thank-you. In the evening Admiral Walker and Loomis come to the White House.

Roosevelt confers with Senators Perkins and Bard about the canal commission and with railroad man A. J. Cassatt, Thomas Platt and Admiral Walker. In Chicago that day Elihu Root tells the Union League Club that the President's course on Panama was right.

The Senate approves the canal treaty with Panama. Roosevelt's Cabinet meets on Dominican affairs, and his dinner table holds Gifford and Amos Pinchot, Leupp, Moody and the Rev. Rainsford, who stays over. He tells Bishop he has no wish to meddle in Santo Domingo.
Canal Zone health on his mind

Roosevelt talks New York politics with Depew and lunches with Kohlsaat. Benjamin Ide Wheeler spends the night after dinner with the Garfields, Cooley and Librarian of Congress Putnam. Roosevelt writes Admiral Walker about sanitation on the isthmus.

Roosevelt gives his own approval to the Panama Canal Treaty. He lunches with the Jusserands, Walter Berry, Benjamin Wheeler, and the young poet George Cabot Lodge with his wife, and dines that night with Senator Lodge. He writes Bonaparte about support for Indian mission schools.

Roosevelt formally proclaims the treaty with the Republic of Panama that clears the way for an American-built canal. Earlier he hears from Dr. Rixey on health conditions on the isthmus and the Cabinet takes up the Philippine Commission. He tells William Hale he hopes to keep involvement in Santo Domingo small.

Panama's minister Philippe Bunau-Varilla calls in the afternoon. Roosevelt writes Kermit a lively family bulletin: Quentin and his nurse Mame are both laid up, Edith is home from three days in New York, and Ethel has been a big help with the younger boys.
Sunday evening with Knox and Bacon
Roosevelt spends Sunday evening with two callers: Attorney General Knox at 8:30 and his old friend Robert Bacon an hour later.
Leap-day essay on the party's mission
The Critic prints a Roosevelt essay on what the Republican Party is for. He sees Knox and Lodge during the day and has Speaker Cannon and Senator Allison in that night.

The Cabinet works on the Panama canal contract. Roosevelt then confers with a long line of lawmakers and officials, among them Fairbanks, Aldrich, Beveridge and Thomas Platt, and lunches with Navy Secretary Moody.

Roosevelt confers with Lodge and shares lunch with Taft, Jessup and Truman Newberry. He tells Senator Thomas Platt that Isaac Stoddard, nephew of a Platt friend, has pulled out of the running for Secretary of Arizona Territory.
Roosevelt and Edith are Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes's dinner guests. During the day he talks New York politics with Littauer, receives Japan's minister Takahira and lunches with Stranahan.

The Cabinet discusses a proposed cable across the Pacific. Roosevelt confers with Admiral Walker, Foraker and Thomas Platt, visits with Japanese minister Takahira and lunches with Bonaparte and Hitchcock.

Admiral Dewey's commission reaches Santo Domingo. Roosevelt fills a big dinner table with Cabinet members, senators, Pinchot, Lodge and Holmes; Admiral Frothingham and historian A. B. Hart stay over. He tells Kermit he wrestles two Japanese wrestlers three times a week and has a sore throat from being choked.
Bible Society centennial at St. John's
Roosevelt and Edith go to St. John's Church in the afternoon for the hundredth anniversary of the Bible Society. Secretary Shaw calls that evening.

Roosevelt gets the first findings of his commission on public lands, and the Bonaparte-Woodruff findings on Indian Territory go to Congress. He lunches with Governor Crane, works on canal talks with Knox and Walker, sees Lincoln Steffens among his callers and dines at Secretary Moody's.

The Cabinet meets on canal negotiations without the ailing Agriculture Secretary Wilson. Roosevelt charges the new Isthmian Canal Commission and tells Interior Secretary Hitchcock that the government must pay for Chief Joseph's trip home from Washington.

Roosevelt rides out to Arlington, Virginia, in the afternoon to see the ailing Postmaster General Payne. Henry Adams dines at the White House and afterward writes that the President now talks of nothing but the election.
Roosevelt talks with Hay about enforcing neutrality, and with Cannon, Overstreet and Bristow about Payne's report on the Post Office scandals.
Albert Shaw and LaFarge stay over

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt discusses civil service pensions with Sulloway and Gibson. Editor Albert Shaw and architect Grant LaFarge come to dinner with Taft and Chandler, and both stay the night.

Photographer Handy comes at 9 a.m. to take Roosevelt's picture. He lunches with Harvey, Moody, Taft, Knox and MacKay, and Joseph Bishop stays the night. He tells Charles Mellen he cannot predict how the Northern Securities case will end.
Roosevelt spends Sunday evening at supper with his sister Bamie.

By a 5-4 vote the Supreme Court rules that the Northern Securities Company broke the Sherman Antitrust Act and must be dissolved, a landmark win for Roosevelt's trust policy. He shares lunch with Cardinal Gibbons, Secretary Hay, Moody and his sister Bamie and defends his White House spending to Lawrence Abbott.
The Cabinet discusses the Northern Securities decision. Roosevelt sees Senator Hopkins and congratulates Andrew Draper on becoming New York's first state Commissioner of Education.
Lunch with Mrs. Lodge and Taft
Roosevelt confers with Senator Foraker and has Taft, Bowers and three ladies, Mrs. Lodge among them, to lunch. He writes James Roche about American neutrality in the war in Asia.

Roosevelt lunches with AP chief Melville Stone and John Wise. He tells Illinois Governor Richard Yates he will not stand in the way of his renomination and sends editor St. Clair McKelway a detailed account of White House spending.
A quieter day: Roosevelt receives Allison, Foraker, Beveridge, Kean, Millard and Leupp, and lunches with Bliss.

Roosevelt lunches with illustrator Howard Pyle and sees Booker T. Washington in the afternoon. He tells Leonard Wood the Senate has unexpectedly confirmed him as major general, and assures Spring-Rice that he means to keep America neutral in the Russo-Japanese War.

Roosevelt breakfasts with James Sheffield. That day Elihu Root sits down with Depew, Thomas Platt, Governor Odell and Dunn and makes peace in New York's Republican ranks: Odell will chair the state party while Platt stays its leader.

Roosevelt sends warm notes to Thomas Platt, Governor Odell and Root on the New York peace settlement. He receives the Isthmian Canal Commission, lunches with Sheffield, Knox and Adams, and hosts a dinner that includes Justice Day, the Aldriches, Forakers and Mrs. Leonard Wood.
After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with the Canal Commission and Secretary Taft, talks Alaska with Kearns and sees Hendricks in the afternoon.
Roosevelt goes over Ohio politics with Senator Dick and Missouri politics with Representative Bartholdt, receives Elkins and Redfield Proctor, and lunches with Noyes and James.
Platt and Odell as Jungle Book wolves

Roosevelt talks Illinois politics with Representative Rodenberg and receives Depew, Penrose and Hill of the Tribune. Writing to Root, he says the two New York chieftains remind him of Kipling's Jungle Book wolves, and sends Knox two letters on labor planks for the convention.
No canal job for his friend Bishop

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt sees Admiral Walker about the Canal Commission. He explains to Joseph Bishop, who hopes to become the commission's secretary, that their close friendship makes the appointment awkward.
Telling the public about the Beef Trust

Roosevelt plans for the Republican convention with Senator Scott and meets the Canal Commission. Among his callers are Japan's envoy Kaneko, Richard Olney and Lodge. He urges Knox to publicize what has been done against the Beef Trust.
Roosevelt's cousin Emlen Roosevelt visits him on Sunday morning.

Senator Joseph Burton of Kansas is found guilty in a postal fraud case. Roosevelt goes over money bills with Aldrich and Cannon, lunches with the Chinese-born physician Dr. Yamei Kin, and writes Knox about the verdict.
The Cabinet meets, and Roosevelt goes over canal finances with Knox and lunches with Father Vattman. He compliments Yale scholar Thomas Lounsbury on an article about language.
At 9 a.m. tailor Rock arrives to fit Roosevelt for new clothes. He goes over spending bills with Hemenway and tells Senator Foraker that the island possessions should be run by the Secretary of War.
Canal money, campaign plans, dinner with Holmes

Roosevelt goes over canal finances with Attorney General Knox and the coming Republican campaign with Senator Quay, then dines with Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes. Across the Atlantic, Britain and France are closing in on the Entente Cordiale, trading a free French hand in Morocco for British control in Egypt.

The Cabinet takes up canal finances. Roosevelt writes Moody about Lieutenant Sims's push for better naval gunnery and new gun sights, and writes his brother-in-law Will Cowles about the inquiry into the collision of Cowles's Missouri with the Illinois.
Dinner with the Roots and Lodges
Roosevelt lunches with Elihu Root, receives the Countess Cassini in the afternoon, and at 8 p.m. dines with the Roots, the Lodges, the Wadsworths and Taft.
Correcting the press on the Cowles inquiry
On Sunday Roosevelt writes Navy Secretary Moody about the findings of the Cowles inquiry and the made-up newspaper accounts of them.

Roosevelt sees Moody and a group of steel executives from Pittsburgh and dines with Mr. and Mrs. Parsons. He drafts but holds back a letter to Harvard's Charles Eliot arguing that the Philippines are not yet ready for independence.
Root says no to the national chairmanship

The Cabinet discusses a strike on the Panama Railroad. Roosevelt dines with the Leupps, Garfields, Foulkes, Egans and Wares, and tells Charles Emory Smith that Root cannot chair the Republican National Committee and asks him to draft the platform.
On a packed day Roosevelt discusses the convention chairmanship with Depew and Thomas Platt and New York politics with J. A. Stewart. He lunches with Knox, Grey and Dodge.

Roosevelt addresses the Periodical Publishers Association dinner. Earlier he sees Knox, receives his Dakota friend Seth Bullock among other callers and lunches with L. Clarke Davis. Jacob Riis stays the night.

The Cabinet discusses Chinese exclusion. Roosevelt's lunch table holds Jacob Riis, Seth Bullock, William Allen White, Moody, editor Norman Hapgood and publisher Robert Collier. At home he has to spank young Quentin for stealing.

It is Archie's tenth birthday: he gets a cake and a tool chest. Roosevelt lunches aboard the Mayflower and dines with Bamie, Bob Ferguson and David Gray. He tells Ted his Japanese wrestling has left him bruised but taught him three new throws, and tells Kermit, down with mumps, about press lies.
Roosevelt has Sunday lunch with Gifford Pinchot, James Garfield and William Dudley Foulke.
Roosevelt lunches with Bishop Spalding, George Meyer and Rawle.

The Cabinet meets on the Chinese exclusion laws. Roosevelt confers with Fulton, receives tariff advocates from the American Protective Tariff League and others, and he and Edith dine with Secretary and Mrs. Shaw.

An explosion during target practice aboard the battleship Missouri kills 33 men. Roosevelt confers on a proposed Senate probe of the Post Office Department and on Canal Zone bills, and sees George Perkins at night.

Roosevelt continues talks on the Post Office investigation with Penrose, Aldrich and Spooner and greets members of the Knights of Columbus at a reception. He asks Representative Hepburn to get the canal bill through.
Roosevelt confers with Spooner, receives Warren, Fairbanks and Quarles, and holds another Cabinet session on the Chinese exclusion laws.

On a busy Saturday Roosevelt discusses Chinese exclusion with Knox, sees a delegation from Alaska and several senators, and tells Senator Aldrich that Congress must confirm William Crum. He sets up a meeting with Cornelius Bliss about the national chairmanship.
Roosevelt breakfasts at the Shaws' with novelist Owen Wister. Former Senator William Chandler calls late in the evening.

Roosevelt discusses Indian affairs with Penrose, Fulton and Philip Stewart and West Virginia's party squabbles with Senator Scott, lunches with Taft and attends a benefit show at the Lafayette Theater.
Wister and Stewart Edward White as houseguests
The Cabinet discusses wireless telegraphy. Roosevelt confers with Senator Orville Platt, and writers Owen Wister and Stewart Edward White are overnight guests.

On a heavy day Roosevelt confers with former Puerto Rico Governor Hunt and Knox, receives Spooner, Beveridge, Akins and a party of Union veterans from the Grand Army, and lunches with Ambassador Sternberg.

Roosevelt signs a bill allowing rations for children at Indian mission schools. He writes George Bowers about California's golden trout and Moody about naval marksmanship, among a full day of conferences and letters.
After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt confers with Harvard psychologist Hugo Münsterberg, with Wadsworth, and with Lacey about public land bills.

Roosevelt appoints Beekman Winthrop governor of Puerto Rico, and the Minidoka reclamation project in Idaho is established. He dines with Nicholas Murray Butler and Joseph Bishop and writes his Harvard-era friend Kentaro Kaneko praising the Japanese people.
Roosevelt dines on Sunday with Cameron.
Odell comes to talk New York

Governor Odell confers with Roosevelt on New York politics and stays for lunch with Littauer, Warren and Sherman. A musicale is held at four, and Roosevelt writes a memorandum on Senator Proctor's talk with him about appointments.
Lunch at Hay's, dinner at Cortelyou's
The Cabinet meets on canal affairs. Roosevelt and Edith lunch at Secretary Hay's and dine at Secretary Cortelyou's. He tells Cardinal Gibbons that Dominic Murphy will join the Canal Commission staff.
Sullys Hill National Park in North Dakota is established. Roosevelt discusses the homestead laws with Representatives Dietrich and Kinkaid and lunches with Governor Murray Crane.
Congress creates the Canal Zone government

An act of Congress provides for governing the Panama Canal Zone, and Congress adjourns. Roosevelt names Thomas Dawson minister to Santo Domingo and writes Nicholas Murray Butler about the ICC and the coal walkout.
Richard Strauss at the White House

On Corinne's 22nd wedding anniversary, Roosevelt talks Kansas politics with Senator Long and the state's governor, Willis Bailey and lunches with Civil War General Osterhaus and others. Composer Richard Strauss is among his callers. He tells Butler why Bishop did not get the canal post.
The St. Louis World's Fair opens

The Louisiana Purchase Exposition opens in St. Louis. Roosevelt hosts a large lunch for visiting royalty with Bamie, Lodge, Hay, Whitelaw Reid and the German ambassador, then watches a drill at Fort Myer with Edith. His article on the merit system appears in Cosmopolitan.
On Sunday evening Roosevelt gathers the Republican leadership, including Aldrich, Allison, Spooner, Lodge, Cannon and Cortelyou, to shape the party's campaign platform.
Choosing a chairman and a running mate

After breakfast with Von Briesen, Roosevelt and senior senators weigh who should run the national committee and who should share the ticket. He also talks New York politics with Thomas Platt and tells Senator Proctor that letters clear Secretary Shaw of Proctor's charges.

Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, Postmaster General Payne and Admiral Walker. In her diary Alice writes of her rivalry with Marguerite Cassini, the Russian ambassador's daughter, over Ohio congressman Nicholas Longworth, who had proposed to Marguerite and been refused.
Platform work and a conservation lunch
Roosevelt works on the Republican platform with Cortelyou and Senators Spooner, Cullom and Allison, then lunches with Cornelius Bliss, Gifford Pinchot and James Garfield.
Roosevelt's visitors include Lodge, Burrows, Fulton, Ball and Senator Redfield Proctor.
Asking Bliss to run the campaign

The Cabinet discusses the canal, and Roosevelt talks with Representative Adams about a proposed immigration bill before lunching with Taft. He writes Cornelius Bliss that he wants him as Republican national chairman.
Roosevelt confers with Admiral Walker on the canal and receives a delegation from the Baltimore branch of the American Federation of Labor.
Roosevelt receives Hamilton Fish at nine on Sunday evening and Ambassador Speck von Sternberg half an hour later.
A charter for the Canal Zone

Formal instructions go out to the Isthmian Canal Commission, and Roosevelt sends Taft an official letter laying out the treaty terms, including a six-mile-wide zone, that serve as the Canal Zone's founding charter. He also talks with mine union leader John Mitchell about the Colorado strike.

The Yuma, Belle Fourche and Lower Yellowstone reclamation projects are created, the last reaching into North Dakota. The Cabinet takes up canal finances, and Roosevelt asks Payne whether a Black delegate should second his nomination at the convention.
Roosevelt confers with Taft and sees Hitt and Dr. Rixey. He writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler about a French study of the Phoenicians and the Odyssey, and Lodge about the protective tariff in the platform.
Roosevelt writes Root about politics and learns that Cornelius Bliss will not take the national chairmanship. He tells Bliss he will likely press for George Cortelyou instead.

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt receives the Spanish minister. Robb's findings about the post office in New York are published. He asks Senator Beveridge whether Fairbanks will accept the vice-presidential slot, since Fairbanks keeps telling reporters he will not.
Saving the old elm in Lafayette Park

Roosevelt receives Archbishop Riordan and the German ambassador and attends Miss Young's musicale. He tells Ted about scrambles in Rock Creek Park and his preference for Robert Hitt over Fairbanks as running mate, and forbids the felling of an old elm in Lafayette Park.
The record for this Sunday in Washington is empty.

Photographer Oscar Marshall takes Roosevelt's picture in the morning. He confers with labor statistician Carroll D. Wright, dines with Herbert Smith and Richard Watson Gilder, and has Jacob Riis and his wife as overnight guests.
George Cortelyou is picked to lead the Republican campaign as national chairman. Elihu Root comes to stay, and Roosevelt writes Butler about politicians who fight party machines.
Drafting the platform with Root and Lodge

Mr. Prince photographs Roosevelt in the morning. After dinner with the Lodges he goes over the proposed party platform line by line with Root, Lodge and Black. Whitridge and Hunt are overnight guests.

From Tangier, Consul General Gummere wires that Ion Perdicaris, an American, and his English stepson Cromwell Varley have been seized by the bandit chief Raisuli. Roosevelt orders four warships of the South Atlantic Squadron to Morocco. At home he works on campaign plans with Elmer Dover.

At a dinner marking two years of Cuban independence, Root reads a Roosevelt letter that lays out the policy later called the Roosevelt Corollary. Roosevelt also confers with William Cromwell on the canal and dines with the Lodges and Moody.

The White River National Forest in Colorado is established. Roosevelt hosts the Republican National Editorial Association at lunch and tells Root he has picked Frank Black to place his name in nomination.

Roosevelt sees Judge Blanchard on Sunday evening. In Morocco, a go-between, the Sherif of Wazan, delivers Raisuli's terms: troops withdrawn, the Bashaw of Tangier dismissed, his partisans freed, a $70,000 payment, and governorship of two districts.

Roosevelt sees Admiral Evans, Secretary Shaw and others, has Hale, Bacon, Dalzell and Elkins to lunch, and leaves at 5:35 p.m. for Groton, Massachusetts. Admiral Chadwick's squadron steams toward Morocco, with the European Squadron sent to back it up.
Feet on the ground at Groton
Roosevelt speaks to the boys of Groton School, urging them to pair high ideals with practical sense, then heads back to Washington that evening. He offers his good offices to Japan and Russia.

Back in Washington, Roosevelt receives Shaw, Hale and Alger, lunches with Monsignor O'Connell, Roberto Centaro and his kinsman Captain Harry Roosevelt, and dines with railroad magnate E. H. Harriman. He explains to Senator Orville Platt why he chose Cortelyou.

Landscape gardener Scott Brown calls first thing. Roosevelt confers with Taft, Spooner and others, including Harper's Weekly art editor H. T. Clinton, lunches with the Jusserands and Russian ambassador Cassini, and sees labor leader Samuel Gompers at night.

Roosevelt rides up Rock Creek after a day of Cabinet and diplomatic business. At home, the children's pet Peter Rabbit dies and gets a funeral: Archie pulls the little coffin in a wagon and Edith is chief mourner. Quentin and Archie, playing in the sandbox, can't wait to get back to Sagamore Hill.

Senator Matthew Quay of Pennsylvania dies. Roosevelt describes his White House routine to Ted: breakfast with Edith on the South Portico, a garden stroll, work until late afternoon, official guests at lunch, then a ride, walk or tennis. He tells Kermit about a Mount Vernon outing with the children.
Word arrives that Raisuli will kill Perdicaris and Varley unless his demands are met within two days. Roosevelt sees Elliott Woods that night and leaves at 10:30 for Gettysburg.

Roosevelt gives a Memorial Day address at Gettysburg and returns to Washington. At Tangier, the Brooklyn and Admiral Chadwick's squadron drop anchor at dawn, and Moroccan Foreign Minister Mohammed Torres comes aboard but refuses Raisuli's terms.
Roosevelt receives a delegation of Wisconsin Republicans loyal to Robert La Follette, and Mr. Prince photographs him in the East Room. Alice is off seeing the St. Louis fair.

A North Carolina man, A. H. Slocomb, privately tells the State Department that Perdicaris is a Greek citizen, not an American, and Roosevelt huddles with Hay, Moody and Admiral Evans over it. He and Edith have a late-afternoon lunch at the Library of Congress as guests of Librarian Herbert Putnam.
A record for Root's convention speech

Roosevelt sees Senator Foraker and talks Alaska with Knox. For Root's convention speech he sends a list of his administration's achievements, and he confides to Lodge that he is unsure how the election will turn out.

Roosevelt has General Crozier and two admirals, Evans and Taylor, to lunch, then takes Crozier on a three-hour cross-country scramble. He sends Butler a very long letter on falsehoods in Collier's and other magazines.
Praise for Wood among the Moros

Washington asks its envoy in Greece to verify whether Perdicaris is a Greek national. Roosevelt lunches with Warner Miller and Paul Morton, and writes Leonard Wood praising his work with the Moros and noting Wood has been hurt at singlestick.

On Sunday Roosevelt writes Ted that the horse Renown has died, that the family is puzzling over Kermit's going to St. Louis, and that once home he will lead a point-to-point hike through the pond and marsh. He and Edith have just ridden on the Virginia side.
Talking peace with Takahira and Kaneko

Roosevelt lunches with Japan's Takahira and Kaneko, Pinchot and Bromwell, a talk he later recounts at length to Spring-Rice. He discusses a board for the planned Great Lakes naval training school with Moody and hosts a reception for Ambassador Jusserand.
Perdicaris turns out to be Greek

Word comes from Athens that Perdicaris became a Greek citizen in 1862. Seven American warships now lie off Tangier, a British warship arrives and France asks what America intends in Morocco. Roosevelt writes Root about the outcry over his Monroe Doctrine letter.

Violence breaks out in the Cripple Creek mining district of Colorado, beginning a long strike. Roosevelt confers with Taft and Hitt and holds a public reception. He explains to Leonard Wood why he will not be named governor general of the Philippines.
Knox to take Quay's Senate seat

Word comes that Attorney General Knox will succeed the late Matthew Quay in the Senate. Roosevelt confers with Hay, Taft, Shaw and Hitchcock, lunches with Speaker Cannon and others, and he and Edith dine with the Hays.

The Cabinet discusses Cortelyou's tour inspecting immigration in the U.S. and Canada. Roosevelt entertains the commissioners from the Philippines at a luncheon and reception and dines with Taft, Moody, Cortelyou and Lyman Abbott.

Roosevelt watches a monument to Richard Rush unveiled at the Naval Museum, lunches with Hawaii's Governor Carter and Beekman Winthrop, and has Lyman Abbott and Joseph Bishop as guests. He writes Quentin a bird-picture note about feeding a young elk at the zoo, and tells Archie an owl came in the mail.

Roosevelt talks New York politics with Littauer and Philippine affairs with Taft. Nicholas Murray Butler comes to dinner and stays the night. He writes Spring-Rice a full account of his June 6 talk with Takahira and Kaneko about the war.

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt talks West Virginia politics with Representatives Dayton and Hughes and lunches with George Gould and Butler. He sends Root two letters praising his speech and discussing Cabinet changes. Edith writes Kermit about her own struggles learning languages as a girl.

The excursion steamer General Slocum catches fire in New York's East River, killing many women and children. Raisuli raises his demands, and Roosevelt tells Hay the government has gone as far as it can for Perdicaris, while exploring joint action with Britain and France if the captive is harmed.

Roosevelt orders an investigation into the General Slocum disaster. He receives Paul Morton and Lincoln Steffens, lunches with Benjamin Ide Wheeler and Frank Travers, and names Victor Metcalf Secretary of Commerce and Labor.

After a Cabinet session on naval and judicial business, Roosevelt leaves for Hyde Park. He wires that he will tolerate no opposition to Cortelyou as party chairman, telling Cortelyou that disloyalty to him is disloyalty to the party.
A family wedding at Hyde Park
At Hyde Park, Roosevelt sees his nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson married to Helen Rebecca Roosevelt, whose father is James "Rosy" Roosevelt, then heads to Philadelphia.

Roosevelt spends Sunday at Attorney General Knox's home at Valley Forge and gives an impromptu talk in a church there. Gummere cables that Raisuli's demands have all been met and Perdicaris should go free on June 21. Roosevelt leaves for Washington that evening.

Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou about the Slocum investigation and sees Ambassadors Cassini and Jusserand. Raisuli calls off the release; Gummere and Chadwick believe Moroccan officials are plotting against him.

Republicans gather in Chicago for their national convention while Roosevelt stays in Washington for Cabinet talks on the Slocum disaster. Gummere warns that America's position in Morocco is becoming humiliating and urges landing Marines. Roosevelt sends letters, some with pictures, to his children at Sagamore Hill.

As the convention continues, Hay sends his blunt cable to Morocco demanding Perdicaris be saved or his captor killed, while forbidding a Marine landing. Unknown to Washington, Raisuli is already escorting Perdicaris and Varley to Tangier, and they are freed that evening.

The Republican convention in Chicago nominates Roosevelt for President, with Senator Charles Fairbanks of Indiana as his running mate. Just after lunch, as he and Edith sit on the White House's South Portico, his secretary William Loeb arrives with word of the vote.

Japan loses some 1,200 men in a battle with Russia. The Cabinet discusses tariffs for the Canal Zone, and the coming Cabinet shuffle is announced. Edith leaves for the summer at Oyster Bay, and Seth Low dines and stays the night. Roosevelt congratulates Fairbanks.

Roosevelt sees Admiral Dewey, Shaw and General Chaffee among others, lunches with S. M. Ferris and the Tafts, and welcomes Panama's minister De Obaldía. He charges Paul Morton, his new Navy Secretary, to carry on Moody's good work.
Nothing is recorded for this Sunday in Washington.

Roosevelt receives Cortelyou, Elmer Dover and Boutell, confers with Payne, and lunches with Hay, Ambassador Sternberg, Simpson, who stays over, and Captain Rutgers. He dines with General Oliver and the Cortelyous.

Roosevelt breakfasts with editor Albert Shaw and sees Hitchcock and Colonel Bingham. He tells Lodge that the Cripple Creek miners' strike tops his worries, and comments on the platform and Taft's Harvard speech.
Roosevelt sees Civil Service Commissioner Black and others, lunches with Senator Proctor and Yerkes, and writes Richard Harding Davis that his sympathies lie with Japan in its war with Russia.
Roosevelt drops in on Cortelyou at his Commerce and Labor offices on his final day as secretary. L. F. Payn visits, and Paul Morton stays the night.
A reshuffled Cabinet takes its seats

The Cabinet meets with its new lineup: Moody moves from the Navy to Attorney General in place of Knox, now Pennsylvania's senator; Paul Morton takes the Navy; and Victor Metcalf succeeds Cortelyou, who is running the campaign. Roosevelt talks Panama with John Barrett, and Metcalf stays the night.
Fourth of July picnic by rowboat

Roosevelt breakfasts with Lieutenant Moore and leaves for Oyster Bay. At Sagamore Hill, where William Hunt's Puerto Rico report reaches him, Independence Day guests include his niece Eleanor, Bob Ferguson and Alvord Cooley. He, Edith and Gifford Pinchot spend the whole day picnicking from a rowboat.
Senator Albert Beveridge visits Sagamore Hill and stays for lunch with W. N. Cohen. Gifford Pinchot is a house guest.
Writing to Taft from Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt says he cannot predict the fall election, but a Republican loss would harm the country unless the winners adopted every one of his policies.
Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill working on his speech accepting the nomination.

Governor Odell and William Barnes come to Sagamore Hill to plan the campaign and choose who should run for governor; they settle on Elihu Root. They stay for lunch, and Joseph Bishop dines and spends the night.

The Democrats choose New York judge Alton B. Parker as their presidential candidate with West Virginia's Henry G. Davis as his running mate. Roosevelt lunches with cartoonist Homer Davenport, tells Odell he is pleased with the July 8 meeting, and praises Hay's July 6 speech.
His running mate, Charles W. Fairbanks, comes to Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt works over campaign issues with Fairbanks, Bliss and Cortelyou. He refuses Colonel J. F. Smith's resignation in the Philippines, tells Hay the Democrats will skip a currency plank, and vents to Taft about Mrs. Bellamy Storer.

Pach and Strohmeyer photograph Roosevelt and Fairbanks on the lawn outside his study. The two confer with Cortelyou, and Roosevelt lunches with Governor Hunt. In Chicago, the meat packers' butchers walk out.

After a day on his acceptance speech, Roosevelt takes Kermit, Archie and two friends camping, rowing two boats some eight or ten miles along the Sound and frying steak, chicken and potatoes over a fire. He tells Garfield about a clothes-on point-to-point hike with six boys.

Roosevelt lunches with James Sheffield and receives Justin McCarthy. He tells Bliss that Oscar Straus and other Cleveland Democrats back him, hopes Joel Chandler Harris might help his standing in the South, and worries to Lodge about the strikes in Chicago and Colorado.

Senator Thomas Platt and Cortelyou confer with Roosevelt about New York politics, and Platt stays for lunch. Roosevelt warns Payne there must be no charge of postal workers meddling in Wisconsin's factional fights.
Nicholas Murray Butler is a guest. Roosevelt writes Pinchot about filling an Agriculture Department post and answers Governor Odell on electors and his advice for the acceptance speech.
Nicholas Murray Butler spends time with Roosevelt, and Howard Gould and E. D. Winslow drop in around midday.

Roosevelt receives musicians' union leaders and confers with Knox and Root. Bamie, her son Sheffield Cowles and Bob Ferguson are guests. He mails Cortelyou the completed acceptance address for a final review.
Roosevelt confers with Root and receives a Colorado labor delegation led by John B. Walsh, plus the Rev. John Chidwick of New York. He keeps at his acceptance speech.
Gifford Pinchot calls. Roosevelt tells William Hunt he has gone over his report on conditions in Puerto Rico and thanks Herman Kohlsaat for advice on revising the speech.

Roosevelt receives Richard Murphy and Father Pitass of Buffalo's Polish church. He tells Admiral Evans he has read his report on naval wireless, and tells ornithologist Edward Forbush he has seen no decline of birds around Oyster Bay or Washington.

Roosevelt confers with W. L. Ward and receives conservationist George Bird Grinnell, Mrs. Doubleday, C. F. Francis and J. A. Sleicher. Social secretary Belle Hagner is a guest. He tells Lodge, who is suffering with his teeth, that Republicans cannot break with La Follette in Wisconsin.
Root says no to the governorship
Roosevelt confers with Leslie Shaw and gives a speech at College Point on Long Island. Elihu Root asks not to be considered for governor of New York. Mr. and Mrs. Clifford Richardson are guests.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill
Nothing is recorded for this Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt lunches with Silas McBee and General Grenville Dodge, then meets with them and publisher M. H. de Young, Millard and Edward Brown. Former Governor Murray Crane dines and stays overnight. He writes Jacob Schurman about propaganda against him.

Senator Kean, Grant LaFarge, brother-in-law Douglas Robinson and Cortelyou are guests. Roosevelt tells Lyman Abbott about press falsehoods and the lily-white southern delegates, and tells Hay he expects Japan to win and that America may help keep it from being cheated of its victory.

At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt receives the notification committee led by Speaker Cannon and delivers his speech accepting the Republican nomination. Russia seizes the ship Arabia, flying a German flag, calling her flour cargo contraband.

Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Washington. He writes Root about his speech poking at the age of Henry Davis, the Democratic vice-presidential nominee, who was born during James Monroe's presidency.

The Cabinet takes up national finances. Roosevelt confers with Senator Proctor, then leads Admiral Converse and Secretary Metcalf on a scramble down Rock Creek. He tells Hay he feels none too kindly toward Russia and asks Captain Pillsbury whether the Russian fleet could be bottled up at Vladivostok.

Roosevelt meets Cabinet members and congressional leaders on the Chicago butchers' strike. He tells Bamie he enjoyed her visit and that by next March he will have nearly seven years of public work since joining the Rough Riders, and asks the Canal Commission about a coal bid to an English firm.
Roosevelt and Edith ride out to Burnt Mills. He asks Charles Mellen whether the attacks on Lodge in Massachusetts can be stopped.
Naval base talk and a pile of letters

Roosevelt confers with Agriculture Secretary Wilson and labor statistician Carroll Wright, lunches with the big-game hunter St. George Littledale and Moody, and fires off letters on a Philippine naval base, religious tolerance, the press, and who should fill the open Agriculture post.
Pressing Root to run for governor

After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt urges Elihu Root to seek the New York governorship, thanks editor Ervin Wardman for his paper's backing, sends Justice Holmes a lighthearted note, and writes Booker T. Washington about rallying Black Republicans.

Roosevelt meets Taft and Postmaster General Payne, talks over the beef strike with Moody, and writes Speaker Cannon a defense against the charges flying at him, among them that his Benton biography slighted Quakers and that he has trampled the Constitution.

Roosevelt maps out the campaign with party chairman George Cortelyou and sees labor leader Samuel Gompers among other callers. He sends Carroll Wright his thoughts on the Colorado miners' strike report and thanks allies stumping for him.

The Cabinet takes up Turkey, which has broken its treaty promise of equal treatment by mistreating American missionaries and teachers. Roosevelt also talks West Virginia politics, tells Carroll Wright he will not send troops to Colorado's mines, and dines with Hay, Taft and others.

On Edith's 43rd birthday, Admiral Jewell takes a strong U.S. squadron toward Smyrna while a second force at Gibraltar is told to stand ready. Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou and Moody, and warns Butler that Standard Oil is pouring money into Parker's campaign.
No activities are recorded for this Sunday; Roosevelt is in Washington.

Roosevelt meets Hay, receives Speaker Cannon and others, and refuses to spare John W. Burley from execution. To Daniel Sickles he explains the Smyrna deployment, insisting he has no power to start a war and no wish to.
Steffens and Speck von Sternberg visit

After a Cabinet meeting on Turkey, Roosevelt sees Garfield and Senator Foraker. Lincoln Steffens and German Ambassador Speck von Sternberg come for dinner and stay the night, and Roosevelt tells Moody federal judgeships must never be party rewards.
A railroad president stays the night

Roosevelt lunches with Patrick Egan, Treasury Secretary Shaw and Payne, then confers and dines with Hay, Moody, Morton, Loeb and railroad man Charles S. Mellen, who sleeps at the White House. At Sagamore Hill, the guest book lists George Martin plus Helen and Mallory Church.
Proud of the Northern Securities case

Roosevelt mocks Parker's promise of no change in a letter to Bamie, tells Lodge the Democrat's speech was poor, and reminds Cortelyou that the Northern Securities suit is among his proudest achievements, proof that the most powerful men answer to the law.
The Sun endorses him; Turkey backs down

Roosevelt picks up the endorsement of the New York Sun. Once the Cabinet has discussed Turkey and East Asia, he wires Minister Leishman that Turkey's statement satisfies the U.S. and the fleet will withdraw for now, and writes John Burroughs about Yellowstone bears with tin cans stuck on their paws.

On Ethel's birthday, Roosevelt receives Loomis and Shaw. He writes Carroll Wright again about Colorado's strike and labor relations, and tells Cortelyou the news from New York is good, though he frets over how Methodists will vote.

Roosevelt dines with Switzerland's minister and John Hay. Writing to his ailing sister Corinne, he says Edith has come back to Washington to spend a week with him, a real honeymoon, and confesses his worry about Corinne's health.

Roosevelt talks campaign with Shaw and receives Japanese Minister Takahira. In a busy round of letters he suggests a Puerto Rico governor, tells Speck von Sternberg he distrusts British aims in Manchuria, and thanks Emperor Franz Joseph for books.
Roosevelt discusses the Panama Railroad contract with Governor Davis of the Canal Zone, sits through a Cabinet meeting, and lunches with John McCook.
Roosevelt confers with Taft, sees Metcalf, Long and Jay, and has Taft and Garfield to dinner.

Roosevelt goes over his letter accepting the nomination with Hay and Taft, sees Takahira, and hears from Robb about the Paper Trust inquiry. Silas McBee and Medill McCormick join him for lunch, and writes Moody about suing International Paper.
Japan seizes a Russian ship at Shanghai

Roosevelt has editor Albert Shaw for breakfast and lunch. The Cabinet weighs the Panama Railroad contract and Japan's capture of a Russian vessel at Shanghai, which endangers China's neutrality. He tells Moody the paper trust facts are not yet ready for action.
Roosevelt leaves Washington for Oyster Bay.

Home at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Bamie a long letter about his election worries, adds a thank-you to her husband for a cheese scoop, and reports that Quentin now walks to Aunt Lizzie's on his own, has a toy sailboat, and swims quite well.

The family heads out on a picnic and Lodge arrives to spend the night. Roosevelt writes on tariffs, possible governors, Colorado's militia at Cripple Creek, and China's neutrality, and warns the State Department not to suggest the Navy will intervene.

Roosevelt and Lodge talk over Canadian reciprocity and the acceptance letter, and he lunches with Hinckley and Lucius Swift. He tells the State Department the U.S. won't guarantee China's neutrality and writes Endicott Peabody that Ted, now teaching Sunday school, will enter Harvard a year from this fall.
Hunting for a New York governor

Woodruff, Root, Cortelyou and Schurman gather at Sagamore Hill to sort out the New York governorship. Roosevelt writes Moody on antitrust suits, Morton on an admiral's promotion, and Hay that the U.S. won't step in if Japan hits Russian ships sheltering in a Chinese harbor.

Joe Bishop is a guest and Congressman McCleary calls. Roosevelt presses Nicholas Murray Butler to seek New York's governorship, though Butler would rather stay at Columbia, and asks Moody to look into the Colorado strike while doubting Washington can intervene.
Fairbanks is saying the right things

Congressman Lucius Littauer and Mrs. Clifford Richardson visit Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Schurman on Philippine independence as a campaign issue, praises running mate Charles Fairbanks's speeches, thanks Root, and promises to help Bluford Wilson's son into the cavalry.

Representative Landis stays for lunch and a German Roosevelt League delegation calls. Roosevelt writes journalist Ray Stannard Baker that his labor record must be weighed alongside his dealings with capital, both summed up in his favorite formula: a square deal for everyone.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

Roosevelt agrees with Butler's decision to stay out of the governor's race, chides a government employee over a letter, and tells Hay he expects Japan to beat Russia soundly, adding that a victorious Russia would be unbearable.

Roosevelt puts the finishing touches on his letter accepting the Republican nomination. He tells Hay that Venezuela's President Castro is seizing American property, but any U.S. response will wait until after the election.
Judge Hansbrouck stays to lunch, and two Brooklyn Eagle men, Justin McCarthy and Robert Evans, stop by along with Edward Riggs. Nicholas Murray Butler signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt tells Robert Grant that a restful visit is out of the question this year. He also writes, plainly angry, about a letter he received from a man who opposes marriage.

Roosevelt confers and lunches with Senator Albert Beveridge. He instructs acting Secretary of State Adee that foreign diplomats should address him as "Mr. President," not "Your Excellency," and writes Hay about Panama's complaints over Canal Zone tariffs and postage.
Percy Chilton and F. C. Travers call at Sagamore Hill at six in the evening.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Cortelyou comes to confer and stays overnight, John Hay visits, and Francis Leupp briefs Roosevelt on Indian affairs. Over lunch with George Bird Grinnell and the Doubledays, he tells John Morley he never plays bridge, has hunted only once as President, and now rides sedately.
Attorney General Moody comes to Sagamore Hill to talk about the campaigns in Vermont and Maine and stays for lunch with George Smith. John Gaffney calls in the afternoon.

Roosevelt sees Francis Loomis, lunches with Governor Odell and Captain Cuppers, and has Cortelyou as a guest. He tells Fairbanks the outlook is brightening and that Democrats want Parker out on the stump, and writes Charles Tweed of his dissatisfaction with Venezuela.
The Chicago meatpacking strike falls apart as most skilled workers return to their jobs. Roosevelt writes Edward Butler that victory is theirs unless Republicans throw it away.
Count Albert Apponyi and the Austro-Hungarian Ambassador Hengelmüller call on Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

A crowd of callers arrives at six, and Mrs. Clifford Richardson is a guest. Roosevelt writes Taft about the Philippine display at the St. Louis world's fair, muses to Eugene Philbin that a Catholic may one day be President, and tells Carroll Wright his letter on Chicago unions was very interesting.
Roosevelt's letter accepting the Republican nomination is published. Late that night he confers with running mate Fairbanks, and Clifford Richardson and Alvord Cooley sign the guest book.

Roosevelt confers with Senator McCumber, and Senator Fairbanks and Dr. Alexander Lambert are guests. His formal acceptance of the nomination, addressed to Speaker Cannon, lays out at length what his administration has done and what it means to do.
Ted's birthday and the Russian ship Lena

On Ted's 17th birthday, Roosevelt meets Platt and Governor Odell. When the Russian ship Lena limps into San Francisco and Japan demands action, he orders it dismantled; it stays in U.S. hands until the war ends. He also asks Cortelyou to send Fairbanks to Wisconsin.

Bellamy Storer and Joe Bishop are guests and the Baroness von Münchhausen calls. The New York Republican convention names Frank W. Higgins for governor, the man Roosevelt and Odell finally settled on after Root and others said no.

Father Power and Father Rosa call in the afternoon. Roosevelt writes Hay about Democratic charges that he has broken the Constitution, charges that have even spawned a 'Constitution Club', and about the state Republican convention.
Roosevelt sends news to the British editor John St. Loe Strachey and tells Whitelaw Reid that E. H. Harriman might make a large gift to the campaign.
George Ade and the Stimsons at lunch
Roosevelt's lunch table includes humorist George Ade, Delavan Smith, Taber, and Henry L. Stimson and his wife. He writes Ervin Wardman about Republican chances in New York and New Jersey.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt receives several callers, including Nevada Stranahan. He tells Hay that, unlike most observers, he does not think Russia will win, and answers George Harvey about his past statements on Jefferson Davis, standing by his blunt verdict.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the state of the race and the quarrel between Cuban and American cigar makers.
Reading his letter between the preserves

Frank Higgins, the new nominee for governor, and Jacob Riis come to lunch. Roosevelt sends a warm note to Mrs. C. H. Brown, whose letter Edith read aloud to him, picturing her reading his acceptance letter while putting up preserves.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for the capital. He writes Governor Odell about the fight against Democratic gubernatorial nominee D. Cady Herrick, a judge thought by Republicans to be corrupt.
A short story and its heroine

Back at work after a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt sees Garfield, Knox and Senator Proctor. He brushes off E. H. Harriman's offer to meet, and tells his young friend Martha Selmes he liked her short story but not how its heroine behaved.

Roosevelt speaks to delegates of the Interparliamentary Union and gives a dinner honoring Canterbury's archbishop. He writes Hay about U.S. demands concerning Russian Jews and heaps praise on Lieutenant Commander William Sims and his gunnery ideas.
Sunday with Apponyi and the Tafts
Count Apponyi and Bishop Charles Brent join Roosevelt for lunch, Ambassador Speck von Sternberg calls in the afternoon, and the President dines with William H. Taft and his brother Henry.

A crowded day: Roosevelt confers with Hemenway and Eugene Ware, hosts a big lunch that includes Benjamin Ide Wheeler and the Tafts, and receives Italy's ambassador along with the Marquis di San Giuliano. French pastor Charles Wagner dines and spends the night.

On his sister Corinne's 43rd birthday, Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting, plots the campaign with Cortelyou, and lunches with Taft, Moody and others. In the East Room, Professors Newcomb and Münsterberg present 75 members of the International Congress of Arts and Sciences.

Roosevelt sees Taft, Moody, General Corbin and others, and Albert Pulitzer calls in the evening. He writes Oscar Straus urging a Hague conference about Armenia, and answers charges that import stamps help sell Cuban cigars.

Roosevelt meets Admiral H. A. Taylor and receives Gompers among other callers. Tired of playing defense, he tells Cortelyou in two letters to change the campaign's focus and go after Parker, and orders Taft to make no defensive speeches.
James Bryce at the White House

Senator George Frisbie Hoar dies. After a Cabinet meeting Roosevelt calls on the ailing Postmaster General Payne, then hosts British scholar James Bryce, who is staying at the White House, at a dinner with the Rockhills, the Italian Ambassador, and Justice and Mrs. Brown.

Roosevelt backs Frank Higgins for governor in letters to Platt and Bishop, complains to Moody that the Panama Canal Commission is inefficient, and writes Cortelyou about Democratic claims he is squeezing corporations for cash. Edith confides to Emily Carow that her nerves grow as the election nears.

Roosevelt is slated for morning service at Mt. Pleasant Congregational Church, then goes to see Postmaster General Payne. He dines with William Dudley Foulke and writes Lodge that Payne is near death, and that Samuel McCall's Atlantic article has upset him.

Mr. Ives photographs Roosevelt at nine in the morning. He meets Agriculture Secretary Wilson, has Lord Hamilton, Crozier, Forwood and Greene to lunch, goes to the theater in the evening, and answers rumors of a votes-for-a-Senator bargain with the Mormons.
Breton Island becomes a bird refuge

Roosevelt creates the Breton Island Reservation in Louisiana for birds. He also discusses Alaska with W. A. Day, replies to accusations that he is hostile to Catholics, and learns that Postmaster General Henry Clay Payne has died.
Who will run the Post Office?

Roosevelt asks Cortelyou whether to fill the Post Office temporarily through Election Day or have Cortelyou quit the party chairmanship and take the job now. He also writes Bishop about Representative Heflin's remark that a bomb killing the President would be no loss.

Roosevelt confers with Senators Foraker and McComas and lunches with Julius Meyer. He writes Cortelyou about Wisconsin and the La Follette faction, recommends standard guns for the battleship New Hampshire, and tells Leonard Wood the dull campaign is finally getting lively.

Roosevelt attends the funeral of Postmaster General Henry C. Payne, holds a campaign session with Cortelyou and Woodruff, and lunches with publisher Frank Munsey and others. He thanks Lyman Abbott for an editorial defending Cortelyou.

Roosevelt sees Gifford Pinchot and others and lunches with Henry Clay Frick and John Hay. He proudly tells writer Stewart Edward White that Ted, hunting in Canada with Dr. Lambert, killed a moose at night with 56-inch antlers, and names White a special inspector of California forest reserves.
Ambassador Speck von Sternberg calls at 8:30 in the evening. Roosevelt writes Nathan Scott about the speeches Scott has been giving for the Republican ticket.
Wynne takes over the Post Office

Kermit turns 15, and Robert J. Wynne succeeds the late Henry Payne as Postmaster General. Roosevelt lunches with Egan, Sheffield Cowles and Wynne, writes Taft about Andrew Rowan of 'Message to Garcia' fame, and invites E. H. Harriman to Washington.
Eleanor gets a ring; Taft offers to quit

On his niece Eleanor's 20th birthday, Franklin Roosevelt gives her an engagement ring. Roosevelt dines with Root, Hay and Morton, and assures Taft, who offered to resign after their public split on the tariff, that no such step is needed.

After a hectic morning, Roosevelt meets Navy Secretary Morton and Admirals Dewey, Converse and Evans about new warships and receives the Isthmian Canal Commission. He removes three New York steamboat inspectors over the General Slocum disaster.
Roosevelt confers with Senator Boies Penrose at ten, sees Secretary Taft, and lunches with Barrett and Springer.
Potomac scramble and a night at the theater

As Russia's Baltic Fleet sets out on its 18,000-mile voyage to fight Japan, Roosevelt takes the afternoon off for a rough scramble near the Potomac with Ted and tutor Matthew Hale, then brings Edith, Ted and Ethel to see The Yankee Consul, which he found very funny.

Roosevelt and Edith ride the train to Valley Forge to see Senator Knox's daughter married, returning that night. En route he dictates a letter to Kermit with news of Ted studying with tutor Matthew Hale, the governess Mademoiselle, and Archie staying at Dr. Rixey's.

Roosevelt, Edith and Ethel take a Sunday drive out to Burnt Mills. The official report on the General Slocum disaster is made public, and in the evening Rev. Vattmann, Secretary Taft, Maurice Egan and James Jeffrey Roche call.

Roosevelt receives Moody, Morton, Ambassador Jusserand and others, and lunches with John Hay. At nine that night he goes over Panama business with the canal lawyer William Nelson Cromwell, then reports on the talks to Taft.
Sending Taft to inspect the Canal Zone

On nephew Sheffield Cowles's sixth birthday, the Cabinet takes up Panama and Roosevelt orders Taft to go see the Canal Zone himself. He tells Bamie he breakfasts daily with Edith, Archie and Quentin, and tells Corinne the election looks rather favorable.

After a busy morning of meetings with Metcalf and Moody, Roosevelt hosts a dinner for Taft, Storer, Garfield, Morton and Ambassador Jusserand. He writes Harvard President Charles W. Eliot to thank him for backing his reelection.

Roosevelt has Gifford Pinchot, Woodruff and Charles Dawes to lunch and meets immigration chief Frank Sargent. He writes Benjamin Trueblood, the Quaker who heads the American Peace Society, about the Hague conferences.
The Cabinet discusses the campaign and the proposed Hague Conference. Roosevelt writes Cortelyou, thanks writer Thomas Lawson for his support, and sends Justice Holmes some thoughts on history.

Wireless pioneer Guglielmo Marconi, Viscountess Falmouth and her son, Hay, Moody and McCormick join Roosevelt for lunch. He writes Lodge on Panama and the race, and tells Robert Collier he is staying out of Missouri's governor fight between Folk and Walbridge.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.
Among Roosevelt's visitors are Ulysses Grant and H. T. Scott.
A mind steeled for the outcome

Roosevelt confers with Hay, holds a Cabinet meeting, and lunches with Knox and Sheffield Cowles. He tells brother-in-law Douglas Robinson that things look favorable but he is braced for any result, and asks John Morley to be his houseguest in November.

Roosevelt orders Cortelyou to give back the $100,000 Standard Oil donated to the campaign. He sends Kermit $5 to celebrate a win or soothe a loss, declaring that his record is what he must "stand or fall" by.
A 46th birthday, and no third term

Roosevelt turns 46 with a celebration and good wishes from New York's Hungarian Republican Club. He writes a memo on the Standard Oil money, twice more tells Cortelyou to give it back, and declares to Arthur von Briesen that he will not seek a third term.

After a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Moody, Roosevelt has Joe Bishop to dinner and to stay over. He writes Boies Penrose about the Jacob Bunn civil service case and Augustus Gardner about postmaster appointments.
British steelmen at the White House

Roosevelt welcomes a visiting party from Britain's Iron and Steel Institute and lunches with John Hay. He writes Collier about rumors of his support in Missouri and twice more presses Cortelyou on returning Standard Oil's $100,000, a request Cortelyou is thought to have ignored.
Elihu Root calls on Roosevelt at nine on Sunday evening.

Roosevelt breakfasts with Albert Shaw and writes Collier again about Missouri, where Democrat Folk is widely said to have his quiet favor. He confides to Lodge that a week ago his horse put a foot through a rotten bridge plank and somersaulted, landing him on his head.

The United States and France sign an arbitration treaty. Roosevelt has the Sternbergs to lunch, writes Lodge about Moody and Admiral Davis, confesses to publisher Frank Doubleday that he wishes the election were behind him, and thanks Rudyard Kipling for a book.
Roosevelt lunches with Navy Secretary Morton, the Earl and Countess of Dartmouth, and international lawyer John Bassett Moore. He writes Cortelyou about a statement he intends to give the press.

Roosevelt receives Cuban minister Quesada and Ambassador Sternberg and thanks illustrator Howard Pyle for his support. To Kermit he praises a volume of Edwin Arlington Robinson's poems and lists his reading: Macaulay's essays, Martin Chuzzlewit, Bleak House and Arlo Bates on literature.

After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt answers in the newspapers Parker's charge that his campaign has squeezed money out of corporations. His forceful rebuttal and Parker's feeble response are thought to have swayed the race. He also wires Root thanks for a stirring New York speech.
Roosevelt writes William Loeb a campaign note that he never finishes; Edith sends news to her sister Emily.

Roosevelt confers with Hay, sees Morton and Dalzell, and leaves that evening for Oyster Bay to cast his vote. He writes about a New York City postmaster, newspapers, and thanks Don Dickinson for praising his November 4 statement.

Election Day. Roosevelt votes at Oyster Bay, hears early returns with only Francis Leupp for company, and heads back to Washington. He and Fairbanks sweep the country but for the Deep South, carrying 336 electoral votes and the largest popular majority yet, and he pledges never again to seek or accept a nomination.
The day after the election, Roosevelt lunches with Taft and Fortescue.
Victory letters and a dinner for Morley

Roosevelt hosts a dinner for English writer John Morley, who stays the night with Joe Bishop. A flood of victory letters goes out: he tells Kermit no candidate has ever won such majorities, admits to Anna Lodge he cannot explain the scale of it, and promises Tawney he will visit the St. Louis fair.

The Cabinet takes up Philippine tariff revision and Roosevelt discusses Panama with Representatives Hepburn and Mann. He tells Corinne he has received eight to ten thousand messages of congratulation, and writes John Goff that he'd like to hunt bear out West, though the party should claim to be after mountain lion.

After a hectic morning, Roosevelt invites Douglas and Corinne Robinson to the St. Louis fair with him and asks Vice President-elect Fairbanks to open talks on a reciprocity treaty with Canada. He also writes about Southern sectionalism and the Newfoundland treaty.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt spends a busy morning receiving visitors, among them naturalist George Bird Grinnell, Admiral Davis, Charles E. Smith and Keep, and has Taft, Philbin and Wynne at his table.
Prince Fushimi and new boxing gloves

Roosevelt receives Japan's Prince Fushimi, returns the call at the Arlington Hotel, and gives a dinner in his honor. He asks his old sparring partner Michael Donovan of the New York Athletic Club to ship him boxing gloves and to suggest opponents in Washington.

Roosevelt talks New York politics with Governor Odell and tariff revision with Representative McCleary. Oscar Straus and Lyman Abbott and his son dine and stay the night. He offers Senator Cockrell a seat on the Interstate Commerce Commission and, against Lodge's wishes, chooses Robley Evans over Harry Davis for top naval command.
Can Kermit come to the Inauguration?

Roosevelt works with Taft on his annual message to Congress and lunches with Crane and Metcalf. He consoles John Hay on his brother's death, writes Tawney about a special session on the tariff, and asks Endicott Peabody to let Kermit leave Groton for the March 4 Inauguration.

After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt lunches with Root and writer Alfred Henry Lewis, then dines with the Sternbergs and visiting German officers. He tells Richard Watson Gilder that people don't realize how little he enjoys posing for photographs.

On Quentin's seventh birthday, Roosevelt attends the unveiling of the War College's new statue of Prussia's Frederick the Great. Butler and Treasury Secretary Shaw dine and spend the night, Archbishop Ireland and Booker T. Washington call late, and he writes sculptor Frederick MacMonnies about a Rough Rider statue of himself.
Speaking at a parish school dedication

Roosevelt sees Governors Van Sant and Cummins, then speaks at St. Patrick's Catholic Church as Father Stafford's new school is dedicated. He has supper with Robert Bacon and, at nine, talks over the New York City postmastership with Governor Odell.
Roosevelt confers on tariff revision with Governor Cummins, Senators Foraker and McCumber, and Representative Gillett. Lodge spends the night.

The U.S. and Germany sign an arbitration pact. Roosevelt addresses the YMCA, lunches with Archbishop Ireland, Congressman Littauer and Ward, and heads to the Lafayette Opera House for a talk by Pastor Charles Wagner. He warns Senator Orville Platt he may call Congress back to revise the tariff.
Whitelaw Reid to London; praise for Mr. Dooley

Roosevelt lunches with Stranahan, Rosewater, Lauterbach and others. He tells Joe Bishop he has named Whitelaw Reid ambassador to Britain to succeed Choate, and writes humorist Finley Peter Dunne that his philosophy truly influences the country, having taken a Dooley piece on England and ancestry to heart.
Thanksgiving, and a train to St. Louis

On Thanksgiving Roosevelt sprains a leg when his horse Rusty takes a jump. At midnight he boards a train for St. Louis with Edith and Alice, Douglas and Corinne Robinson, the Loebs and Dr. Rixey. He writes George Otto Trevelyan a lengthy letter about the vote, Parker and third terms, likening Martin Chuzzlewit characters to modern politicians.
On the way to St. Louis, Roosevelt's train stops at Richmond, Indiana, where he gives a speech. It is also the ninth wedding anniversary of his sister Bamie.
A whirlwind day at the World's Fair

Roosevelt tours the Louisiana Purchase Exposition at a near run and gives a dinner speech there. He later recalls the day as a perfect whirl, with Edith keeping right up behind him, and thought the fair beautiful, above all when the buildings lit up at night.
Still in St. Louis, Roosevelt attends a dinner hosted by David R. Francis, president of the exposition.
Roosevelt leaves St. Louis for Washington.

Back at 7 a.m., Roosevelt goes straight to a Cabinet meeting and tariff talk with Lodge. He tells historian James Ford Rhodes he is half Southern and proud of his mother's Confederate kin, though their cause was wrong, and warmly congratulates Franklin Roosevelt on his engagement to Eleanor.
A tariff plan for the Speaker

Roosevelt receives Senators Hale, Cockrell and McComas and lunches with British journalist Valentine Chirol and others. He lays out a tariff revision plan for Speaker Cannon, writes Harriman on rail rates, and asks Populist Tom Watson to talk over Georgia politics.
A place for Black Americans at Jamestown

On a busy day, Roosevelt lunches with the Pattersons and Cohen. He thanks Sterling Edmunds for his St. Louis Chronicle's campaign support and tells Fitzhugh Lee that Black Americans should have an exhibit at the Jamestown Exposition.
Tariff reform without splitting the party

On his 18th wedding anniversary with Edith, Roosevelt works over the New York City postmastership with Platt and Littauer. He tells Butler he will push for tariff changes but will not split the party over them, and urges Charles Dawes toward a stronger Interstate Commerce Commission.
Musicale night; Big Jim White again

Roosevelt confers on tariff revision with Senator Smoot and Representative Dixon and lunches with Charles Bonaparte, Frank Polk, Fox and Harvey. The White House holds a musicale, and he tells Kermit he has seen Big Jim White again.
Architect Charles McKim calls in the afternoon, followed in the evening by Chauncey Depew, Senator Aldrich and Vice President-elect Fairbanks.

Congress convenes. Roosevelt meets Senator Kean and Representative Burton and sees Ambassador Sternberg. He writes Justice Holmes about Harvard President Eliot's new book, about history, and about Shelley's poem 'Ozymandias'.
Annual Message: give the ICC teeth

Roosevelt's annual message reaches Congress. He wants the Interstate Commerce Commission empowered to set reasonable railroad rates, presses for the Santo Domingo treaty and an employers' liability law for federal workers, and backs admitting Arizona, New Mexico and Oklahoma as states, plus two new battleships.

Roosevelt meets the House Interstate Commerce Committee and Senator Dietrich, and novelist Owen Wister is his houseguest. He writes Philip Stewart on Colorado politics and Beveridge on the liquor ban in Oklahoma's Indian Territory.
Pershing, Dunne and Holmes at dinner

Roosevelt meets Representative Watson on the tariff and the House Military Affairs Committee, and lunches with publisher G. H. Putnam and Hay. His dinner table holds Justice Holmes, Thomas Nelson Page, Brander Matthews, Finley Peter Dunne, Brooks Adams and Captain John J. Pershing, followed by a musicale.

A parade of senators calls after the Cabinet meeting, and Roosevelt lunches with Frick, Gilder, Dunne and others. He accepts the resignation of labor commissioner Carroll Wright with praise for twenty years of service, and writes Butler about congressional resistance to his tariff aims.

Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou and Speaker Cannon and lunches with Morton, Greene, Bacon and Ripley. Angered by a false Boston Herald story that his children ran after a turkey through the mansion on the holiday, he cuts the paper and its reporter off from official news until it retracts.
J. P. Morgan on a Sunday night
Roosevelt holds evening meetings with Treasury Secretary Shaw, J. P. Morgan, and then Senators Allison, Cockrell and Cullom with Commissioner Cooley.

Roosevelt confers with Judge Grosscup and cabinet members, sees J. P. Morgan again, meets Samuel Gompers in the evening and dines with Root. He tells Bamie to let Eleanor know he can attend her wedding to Franklin if it is before March 17, and writes Sheffield about New York's Senate seat.
A sparring blow to the eye

Roosevelt confers on Arizona statehood and Canadian reciprocity and lunches with Seth Low and Pinchot. He tells boxing coach Mike Donovan that sparring with Ted's friends and young officers wrenched his thigh and broke a blood vessel in one eye. The injury was worse than he knew: by 1908 the left eye was blind.

The United States signs an arbitration treaty with Italy. Roosevelt receives Sereno Payne and Fairbanks, sees George W. Perkins late at night, declines Gompers's invitation to a National Civic Federation dinner, and writes MIT's Henry Pritchett about the moral egotist in politics and about Black Americans in public life.

Roosevelt confers with Taft, with Beveridge on statehood, and with Representative Cooper on the Cooper-Quarles rail bill. He lunches with Andrew D. White and Bamie, speaks that evening at Grace Reformed Church, and writes James Ford Rhodes about Southern anger at his appointments of Black officials.
After a Cabinet meeting, a long line of senators and representatives calls, along with Pennsylvania Railroad president A. J. Cassatt. Roosevelt lunches with Roche and Rose.
Reading The Deerslayer to the boys

Roosevelt confers with Admiral Walker and Representatives Humphrey and Jones on the canal and lunches with novelist Booth Tarkington and others. He tells Kermit of a cold, snowy week, rides at dusk and after dark, reading Cooper's Leatherstocking tales to Archie and Quentin, and Ethel singing on stage.
Senator John C. Spooner calls on Roosevelt at nine in the evening.

Roosevelt receives Depew, Fairbanks and other senators, and lunches with Commander Takeshita and Japan's Baron Kentaro Kaneko. He writes Knox, who opposes him on railroad rates, about investigating the Interstate Commerce Commission, and Edith asks the Robinsons to come for the March Inauguration.
After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt lunches with Western writer Charles Lummis and receives Puerto Rico's Governor Winthrop, Cortelyou, Garfield and Senator Knox.

Roosevelt confers with Moody, Morton and shipper E. P. Bacon about controlling railroad rates, and with Speaker Cannon. Congress adjourns for the holidays. He recommends William Hall Harris to Senator McComas as Baltimore's postmaster.
Roosevelt and Gifford Pinchot plan the upcoming forestry congress. F. N. Goddard, Morton and Taft call, and he lunches with George Cortelyou and his wife. He writes Platt about New York appointments.
Pershing at lunch; the Newfoundland treaty

Roosevelt confers with Garfield on antitrust laws and with Cannon, and lunches with Captain Pershing, General Crozier and other officers. That night Lodge, Hale and Moody talk over the Newfoundland treaty and Joe Bishop stays over. He presses Cannon to lower duties on Philippine goods.
A Viking saga from John Hay

John Hay gives Roosevelt a Viking saga for Christmas. He confers with Hepburn on the ICC, presses Sereno Payne on cutting the Philippine tariff, and accepts the resignation of Joseph Choate, his longtime ambassador in London.
Roosevelt's old Badlands friend Bob Ferguson spends Christmas at the White House. The Dawes Commission's report on the Indian Territory is published.

Roosevelt confers with Hay and Loomis on foreign affairs. He writes George von Lengerke Meyer, ambassador to Italy, that he wants to avoid bluster yet act firmly when American interests are threatened, and that he hopes to move Meyer to St. Petersburg.

Roosevelt talks freight rates with Moody. He tells Cecil Spring Rice he warned Germany away early in the Russo-Japanese War and urges 'Springy' to come over from St. Petersburg, asks Shaw for handsomer coins, plans a hunting trip with Philip Stewart, and names Henry White ambassador to Italy.

Roosevelt confers with Foraker on federal judgeships and attends an evening talk given by a Mr. Walstein in the East Room. He writes Knox about antitrust suits against anthracite coal, tobacco and International Harvester, while Edith offers to hold Eleanor's wedding at the White House.
Roosevelt confers with Taft on reducing the Philippine tariff, lunches with Lodge and others, and sees Gifford Pinchot at nine that evening.
After the Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt confers with Hay and Cooley; few other appointments are on the books.

Senator John H. Mitchell and Congressman Binger Hermann are indicted in the Oregon land fraud cases. Roosevelt confers with Moody, Wilson, Morton and Hay, and writes Senator Gallinger about William Crum, the Black customs collector at Charleston whose confirmation Senator Tillman and others have stalled.
Mrs. Paul Thorndike calls at nine on New Year's evening.
New Year's reception; Port Arthur falls
Roosevelt greets the public at the White House New Year's reception from late morning into the afternoon. Far away, Russia surrenders Port Arthur to Japan.

Roosevelt announces he is willing to mediate between Russia and Japan. The Cabinet weighs a special session on tariff cuts, and he sees Beveridge, Platt and George Perkins. He writes Richard Harding Davis about good and bad ambassadors, the bad ones being 'pink tea men'.
Climbing Rock Creek with the boys

Congress returns. Roosevelt sees Pinchot, Garfield, Fairbanks and others. He tells Emlen Roosevelt and his wife of a recent clamber along Rock Creek with Ted, Kermit, Archie and Archie's friends, writes Taft about Army weapons, and refuses to carve land out of Yosemite National Park.
Speaking to the American Forest Congress

Roosevelt speaks to the American Forest Congress, meeting at the National Theatre. He talks freight rates with Senator Elkins, meets Senator Dick, and hosts a Cabinet dinner; illustrator Howard Pyle, the Whitridges and their wives stay the night.
Arbitration treaties go to the Senate
