Seven general arbitration treaties, with Spain, Italy, Portugal, Switzerland, Germany, France and Britain, go to the Senate. Roosevelt hosts a dinner on Southern questions and complains to Spooner that senators want to curb presidential power by calling every agreement a treaty.
Senate leaders on arbitration and tariff

Roosevelt meets congressional leaders including Aldrich, Spooner, Cannon and Payne on the arbitration treaties, tariff bills and a possible special session. The Senate tacks a special-agreement amendment onto the treaties. He lunches with Munro Ferguson and dines with Dr. Lambert.
Judge Thomas Jones calls at midday, and Roosevelt dines with New York's Governor Frank Higgins and Nevada Stranahan.

Roosevelt confers on railroad rates, naval appropriations and more, then attends a dinner given by Fairbanks. He tells Taft that canal sanitation chief Dr. Gorgas should be paid $10,000 a year, rebuffs Maria Storer's lobbying, and notes the Beef Trust case has reached the Supreme Court.
No halt in building the Navy

Roosevelt issues a statement calling for immediate tariff revision, holds a Cabinet meeting, and dines at John Hay's. He tells Representative George Foss he earnestly hopes naval building will not pause, and writes Sternberg about German policy in China.

Roosevelt publicly urges the Senate to ratify the arbitration treaties without amendment. He hosts a big dinner with Bob Ferguson, Justices Harlan and Brewer, Pinchot and others, drops in on the architects' dinner at the Arlington, and tells Lyman Abbott he treats the tariff as a matter of expediency.
Henry James at the White House

Roosevelt's lunch table gathers Henry Adams, painter John La Farge, sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens and novelist Henry James, who stays the night after the diplomatic reception. Roosevelt also confers with Cullom on the treaties and writes Hay and Sternberg about China.

The Isthmian Canal Commission's report goes to Congress. Roosevelt confers on the treaties, discusses making Joseph Bristow a special Panama Railroad commissioner, sees Owen Wister and goes to the National Theatre. He flatly refuses Representative Foss's idea of pausing naval building for a year.
Talking railroads with James J. Hill

Roosevelt goes over railroad rate changes with Hepburn and Taft and with Morton and railroad magnate James J. Hill. Oscar Straus and Jusserand are among his callers, and he writes Dr. William Sturgis Bigelow about a letter the Japanese envoy's son sent Archie.

Roosevelt confers with Senators Daniel, Foster and McCreary about the arbitration pacts at nine, then sees W. W. Rockhill. Edith writes Emily that she liked Henry James, and that her husband changed his mind and liked him too.

Roosevelt lunches with Costello, Nelson and Page. He directs Hay to write both Japan and Russia urging them not to violate China's neutrality, and tells Treasury Secretary Shaw he wants Augustus Saint-Gaudens to design new American coins.

After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt discusses the steamboat inspection probe with George Uhler and naval appropriations with Morton and Taft. Treasury Secretary Shaw gives a dinner, and Roosevelt writes Robert Underwood Johnson about Yosemite and Yellowstone.

On his sister Bamie's 50th birthday, Roosevelt goes over the Beef Trust investigation with Moody and Solomon Bethea. He tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler he wants a strong ICC and wires Sternberg that Britain, Italy, Germany and the U.S. stand behind China's territorial integrity.
Diplomatic dinner and a houseful of girls
Roosevelt confers with Knox and hosts a diplomatic dinner at the White House. Three young guests, Eleanor Whitridge, Isabella Selmes and Lorraine Roosevelt, stay the night.

Roosevelt confers with Representative Dayton on naval spending and lunches with Bishop William Lawrence and a crowd that includes his old ranch partner Frank Merrifield, Pinchot, Leupp, Philip Stewart and the Swiss Minister. He dines with J. S. Elliott.
A new room for Sagamore Hill

Roosevelt receives William Jennings Bryan and lunches with Charles Emory Smith. He hires architect Grant La Farge to add a large north room to Sagamore Hill for $16,000, nearly what the whole house cost in 1884, with work to run from March to June.
Roosevelt has supper with J. S. Elliott.

Roosevelt writes Kermit about presidential electors in town, among them Frank Merrifield from Montana. He and Ted keep boxing with Grant, a wrestler and so-so boxer; young Corinne and her friends visited for the diplomats' dinner; Archie and Quentin have the grippe; and he has finished reading The Deerslayer to them.

A new law creates the Wichita Game Preserve. Roosevelt attends a Peabody trustees' meeting at the Arlington Hotel, lunches with Shaw, Governor Francis and Saint-Gaudens, receives the Japanese and British envoys, and he and Edith dine with the Tafts.
Roosevelt confers with Speaker Cannon and lunches with Bamie, Perkins, Berry and Hasbrouck. He tells Moody that the District of Columbia's laws governing corporations fall short.

Roosevelt attends Mrs. Warren's wedding at noon, addresses a church conference on marriage and divorce, and hosts the judiciary dinner. He tells Elbert Baldwin he wants authority to act on his Caribbean policy and writes Hay about running Santo Domingo's customshouses.
Cutting corners on the North Room?

After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt sees Senators Aldrich, Bard and Dietrich and Representative Crumpacker, and lunches with Joe Bishop. He asks Grant La Farge whether Sagamore Hill's new North Room could be built for less by using cheaper woods.

Artist Ellen Day Hale sketches Roosevelt at nine in the morning. A packed day follows: treaty and Alaska talks, lunch with journalist Ray Stannard Baker, calls from Booker T. Washington and Bishop Satterlee, and the Gridiron Club dinner. He vents to Lyman Abbott about the stalled treaties.

Cecil Spring Rice arrives quietly in Washington, sent by the British government to talk with Roosevelt, who does not get on with Ambassador Durand. Staying with Henry Adams and dining with the President, he warns of Russia's sweeping Asian ambitions and harsh crackdown at home. The press never learns of the visit.
Annapolis graduation and a Philadelphia speech

Roosevelt addresses the graduating class at the Naval Academy in Annapolis, then speaks that evening at a Union League Club banquet in Philadelphia, calling for a stronger Interstate Commerce Commission able to enforce fair railroad rates. He also sends Congress a message about corporations operating in the capital.

Roosevelt urges the Senate to ratify the arbitration treaties at once. The Beef Trust ruling is affirmed by the Supreme Court, and over congressional objections the U.S., at the Dominican government's invitation, takes charge of its customshouses. That evening he and Edith dine with Attorney General Moody.

The nation's forest reserves pass from Interior to Agriculture, where Gifford Pinchot's Forest Service takes charge. Roosevelt confers with senators on Alaska, arbitration and forests, lunches with General Young and dines with Cecil Spring-Rice.
Justices dine at the White House

Roosevelt talks with James Garfield about the Supreme Court ruling against the Beef Trust, lunches with General Chaffee and Colonel Schuyler, and hosts the justices for dinner that evening. C. Grant LaFarge and Robert Grant sleep over.
Railroad rates and the Santa Fe charges

The Cabinet takes up railroad rates and Alaska. Roosevelt meets Paul Morton and William Moody about Interstate Commerce Commission charges against the Santa Fe line, sees Senator Cullom on arbitration, lunches with the Robert Grants and receives the German ambassador.

After meetings with Paul Morton and Treasury Secretary Leslie Shaw and lunch with railroad chief A. J. Cassatt, Roosevelt joins the Boone and Crockett Club for dinner at the New Willard, where Dr. William Smith lectures. He writes Taft about Senate stalling on the Canal Commission.
On Sunday evening Roosevelt confers with his friend Cecil Spring-Rice and British Ambassador Mortimer Durand, and also sees Secretary of War Taft.

Roosevelt meets Taft, Morton, Depew and Lodge, then writes a stack of letters: civil service exams for Agriculture hires, Senate trouble over the arbitration treaties, Russia and Japan, and Andrew Carnegie's acceptance of the Senate amendments.
A scientific survey for the Philippines

Roosevelt asks Congress for a scientific survey of the Philippines. He also holds Cabinet, meets Senators Allison and O. H. Platt, talks Indiana politics with Charles Fairbanks, and dines with Edith at Postmaster General Wynne's. He writes Taft about floating mines.

After lunch with editor Albert Shaw, Roosevelt tells Andrew Carnegie he opposes the Senate's treaty amendments and writes Congressman John Sharp Williams that a new President and new Congress ought to start work in January, not March.

A packed day of talks on statehood, railroad rates and the Russo-Japanese War ends with the House passing the Esch-Townsend rate bill and the Congressional dinner at the White House. Booker T. Washington calls, and Roosevelt asks Taft to study Japanese labor in Hawaii on his trip east.
Following Cabinet, Roosevelt meets Booker T. Washington, French Ambassador Jusserand and the Japanese minister, and writes Senator Cullom that he wants the arbitration treaties left unamended.

The Senate ratifies seven arbitration treaties, but with the amendment Roosevelt opposed. Gifford Pinchot hands in the Public Lands Commission report, and in the afternoon Roosevelt takes in an afternoon Keller show at the Lafayette Opera House.
Alice celebrates her twenty-first birthday. Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about Indian mission schools and charges that federal money for them was mishandled; the letter later runs in The Outlook.
Lincoln Day speech in New York

Roosevelt heads to New York, speaks briefly at a Press Club dinner at the Hotel Astor, and addresses the Republican Club's Lincoln Day dinner on the South and the shortage of federal posts for Black Americans. He declines to put the weakened arbitration treaties into effect.
University Club lunch in New York

At 422 Madison Avenue Roosevelt receives Seth Low, Oscar Straus and George Perkins, then joins Root, Taft, Joseph Bishop, Nicholas Murray Butler and others for lunch at the University Club. He speaks to the Hungarian Republican Club and takes a midnight train south.
Dominican treaty goes to the Senate

Roosevelt sends the Dominican treaty to the Senate with a message applying the Monroe Doctrine to Santo Domingo. He also meets Moody and Representative Charles Curtis about the Osage Indian bill, lunches with a group of guests, and dines with Edith at Secretary Morton's.

Roosevelt confers on the rate bill, sees Senator Platt and the German ambassador, and hosts the Army and Navy dinner. In letters he blasts the Senate's treaty amendments and tells Charlemagne Tower he doubts Britain wants a share of China.
After a Cabinet session on appointments, Roosevelt works over the naval appropriation bill with Cannon, Allison, Wadsworth and Tawney, then talks Alaska legislation with Senator Beveridge.
Planning for a second Hague conference

Roosevelt discusses the naval bill with Morton and Rep. Dayton, talks with Richard Bartholdt about a second Hague peace conference, receives the Chinese minister and writes Moody on railroad legislation.
Alvord Cooley and Ambassador Jusserand call on Roosevelt Sunday evening.
Looking into Standard Oil in Kansas

Roosevelt meets Garfield and Rep. Campbell about investigating Standard Oil's Kansas operations and confers with the authors of the rate bill. Letters go to historian James Ford Rhodes, Colombian President Rafael Reyes and Navy Secretary Morton.
Indian land leases before the Cabinet
The Cabinet takes up leasing of Indian lands. Roosevelt sees James B. Reynolds, lunches with John Hay and journalist Maurice Low, and dines with Edith at Interior Secretary Hitchcock's.
On Washington's Birthday Roosevelt travels to Philadelphia, gives a talk at the University of Pennsylvania, which awards him an honorary Doctor of Laws, then lunches with the First City Troop.

Roosevelt meets Hitchcock, Moody and prosecutor Francis Heney on the land-fraud cases and calls the Senate into special session for March 4. At five, he and General Mills watch his sparring partner Grant wrestle his jiu-jitsu teacher Professor Yamashita, who wins.

After Cabinet and talks on the Santa Fe rebate inquiry, Roosevelt tells Kermit his grades might rise if he pined less for home. He also boxes with Grant, the national middleweight wrestling champion, and urges Senator Spooner to move on the Dominican protocol after a plot against that country's president.
Former Confederate raider John Mosby calls in the morning, and Japan's Baron Kaneko comes in the evening.
Indian Affairs Commissioner Francis Leupp calls on Roosevelt Sunday evening.
A royal letter about the Kaiser

Roosevelt receives Taft, Rep. Hepburn, General Francis Greene and others. He writes John Hay about a letter from King Edward VII concerning the Kaiser, and Cecil Spring-Rice about the naval fighting between Russia and Japan.
Canal contracts and a farewell dinner

The Cabinet discusses Panama Canal contracts. Roosevelt sees Congressmen Sulzer and Grosvenor and Senator McComas, lunches with Archbishop Ireland, Pinchot, Taft and others, meets Herbert Knox Smith, and is honored at a dinner given by Agriculture Secretary James Wilson at the New Willard.

The Philippine Tariff Bill clears the Senate. Roosevelt talks Alaska with Senator O. H. Platt and lunches with old friend Seth Bullock and his wife, General Otis, Moody and Metcalf. He tells Alice Gitterman which bills are stuck and writes about schools in the capital.

A delegation of his old Rough Riders calls on Roosevelt ahead of the inauguration, along with Senator O. H. Platt. Late in the evening he takes up consular appointments with Francis Loomis, and he writes about the Panama Canal Commission.

On the eve of the inauguration John Hay gives Roosevelt a ring holding a lock of Abraham Lincoln's hair, and Roosevelt thanks him for three years of counsel. Garfield's meat-industry report goes to Congress, governors and their staffs arrive, a Columbus glee club sings in the East Room and neighbors from Oyster Bay call.
Inaugurated President in his own right

Roosevelt takes the oath before a record crowd of about half a million, with his whole family looking on, and tells the nation, "Much has been given us, and much will rightfully be expected from us." Cowboys, miners and Rough Riders march in a parade of three and a half hours, and that night he talks it all over with Corinne and Douglas in his room.
Edith writes home about the big day
A quiet Sunday after the inauguration. Edith sends her sister Emily the news of the ceremonies.

Speck von Sternberg brings Roosevelt a message from the Kaiser, who suspects France and Spain of lining up against Germany in Morocco. Roosevelt sends Congress a second message on Santo Domingo, goes to the Columbia Theatre, and thanks Uncle Rob for standing in for his late father at the inauguration.
Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou and Robert Wynne, and he and Edith dine at the home of Commerce and Labor Secretary Victor Metcalf.
The Supreme Court pays a call

The justices of the Supreme Court call on the newly inaugurated President. Roosevelt lunches with the Danas and Lafayette Young, sees the German ambassador, and in the evening welcomes Seth Bullock and some two dozen companions.

Roosevelt creates the Stump Lake bird reservation in North Dakota. In a long letter to George Otto Trevelyan he reflects on Lincoln and the plain people, on reining in big corporations without crippling business, and on the Monroe Doctrine's obligations. He also praises Booth Tarkington's stories and writes King Edward VII.

Roosevelt confers with Speaker Cannon and Illinois Senators Hopkins and Cullom over federal judgeships in their state, holds Cabinet on appointments, and writes Taft about the Bates survey report, which recommends a canal with locks at Panama.
Vice President Fairbanks, Senator Elkins and Representatives Hepburn, Bartholdt and Townsend are among Roosevelt's callers.
Roosevelt goes to a meeting of the American Tract Society held at the Presbyterian church.
Speaking to the Congress of Mothers

Roosevelt addresses the National Congress of Mothers, worrying aloud about the falling birthrate and calling for the same divorce laws in every state. He lunches with Alfred Thayer Mahan and General Crozier and writes Taft twice about the canal and the Army. Spring-Rice opens a private correspondence with him by way of Edith.

An Italian cruiser appears off Santo Domingo to press money claims. Roosevelt breakfasts with Albert Shaw, holds Cabinet, and in letters tells Robert Grant he firmly opposes easy divorce and explains how honest American collectors would run the Dominican customs houses.
Roosevelt works over the Santo Domingo treaty with John Hay and Taft and receives Ambassador Jusserand in the afternoon.

Roosevelt calls on his ailing Secretary of State, John Hay. He also meets senators, lunches with Governor Crane, and writes about saving Civil War flags, Japan and the Philippines, and a possible wolf hunt.

Roosevelt spends St. Patrick's Day in New York, addressing a Friendly Sons of St. Patrick gathering, reviewing the parade and speaking at a Sons of the American Revolution dinner. In the afternoon he gives his niece Eleanor in marriage to Franklin D. Roosevelt, with Alice as a bridesmaid, and the guests trail him to the dining room.
Coal miners' delegation with John Mitchell

The Senate adjourns its special session. Roosevelt receives anthracite coal miners led by union chief John Mitchell, along with Lyman Gage and others, lunches with Judge and Mrs. Francis Lowell, Moody and Senator Crane, and sees both the German and British ambassadors.
Boys in the White House trees
Archie and Quentin have friends over and the boys spend the day climbing trees on the White House grounds. Frank Travers dies. Senator Beveridge calls in the evening.
Riding with Edith, tennis with Ted

Roosevelt sits for a photograph by Mr. Prince, sees senators and lunches with Baron Kaneko. Writing Kermit, he reports John Hay ill and describes a ride with Edith and tennis with Ted and Matt. He also writes Taft about Dr. Charles Reed's article on health in Panama.
A false treaty with Santo Domingo

The Cabinet discusses canal business. Roosevelt lunches with the Lodges and with Admirals Evans and Davis, and writes Robert Bridges about a bogus Dominican treaty and about a stenographer who helped with The Rough Riders.
Roosevelt meets Generals Crozier and Oliver on Army funding, lunches with Senator Knox, Buxton, Hollander and Generals Crozier and Butt, and sees Taft in the evening.

Roosevelt talks Virginia politics with John S. Wise and Dominican affairs with Admiral Dewey and three senators, then sees Booker T. Washington at night. To Joseph Bishop he confides a worry that stubborn financiers will push moderates into radical railroad measures, and touches on his pledge not to seek a third term.
The Cabinet weighs Venezuela, Santo Domingo and a reorganized Isthmian Canal Commission. Roosevelt sees Baron Kaneko at midday and lunches with Taft, Curtis Guild Jr. and a Mr. Neland.

Congressman Nicholas Longworth stops by in the morning. With White House physician Dr. Rixey, Roosevelt hands out diplomas at the Naval Medical School's graduation at the National Museum, then talks with Depew about the Dominican treaty and sees Senator Foraker at night.
Senator John Spooner calls on Roosevelt Sunday evening.
A fan letter to a struggling poet

The Boise reclamation project in Idaho and Oregon gets under way. Roosevelt sees Taft, Senator Dick and Philippe Bunau-Varilla, and writes the little-known poet Edwin Arlington Robinson to praise The Children of the Night and ask how he is getting by.
Holding the line in Santo Domingo

After Cabinet and talks with Senators Spooner and Foraker, Roosevelt orders Minister Dawson to keep things as they are in Santo Domingo until the treaty is ratified. He attends the Mexican ambassador's funeral and writes Alvey Adee on the stopgap modus vivendi for running Dominican customs.
Morning walks with Edith and Jack

Roosevelt meets Moody, sees Dalzell and Fairbanks, and lunches with Taft, Bunau-Varilla and others. He sends a picture letter to his little nephew Sheffield Cowles, who is ill. Each morning after breakfast he and Edith stroll the garden with their dog Jack.
Russia and Japan look toward peace

Roosevelt receives Senators Kean and Lodge, Vespasian Warner and the German and British ambassadors. Writing to the ailing John Hay, he reports that Dominican President Morales has asked the U.S. to run the customs houses and that both Russia and Japan want to begin peace talks.

Kaiser Wilhelm visits Tangier and backs the Sultan of Morocco against France and Britain, alarming Europe. In Washington Roosevelt sees Jane Addams among other callers and writes about Edwin Arlington Robinson and Russo-Japanese peace talks, while Edith takes the children, minus Quentin, cruising on the Sylph in Florida.

Roosevelt's reorganized Panama Canal Commission takes over, with Theodore Shonts as chairman, Charles Magoon governing the Canal Zone and John Findley Wallace as chief engineer. He also talks Nebraska patronage with Rep. Hinshaw and lunches with Shonts and journalists.
Wrapping up before a long trip

On the eve of a six-week trip west, Roosevelt meets Francis Loomis, sees Clement Griscom and the Spanish ambassador, dines at Lodge's, and sends John Hay a survey of affairs at home and abroad, defending action in Santo Domingo.
Off to hunt in the Southwest
At nine in the morning Roosevelt leaves Washington to hunt in the Southwest, leaving Taft in charge at home. He writes Theodore Shonts about sanitation in Panama.
Roosevelt's train heads west, with a speech in Louisville and stops in five states from Kentucky to Missouri.

Roosevelt speaks at Parsons, Kansas, and at Muskogee, South McAlester and Durant in Indian Territory, then arrives in Dallas in the evening for another speech. Sternberg writes that Germany wants French ambitions in North Africa checked.

Roosevelt stops at Taylor, addresses the Texas Legislature in Austin and reaches San Antonio. His diary jots notes on the men he will hunt with, including wolf catcher Abernathy, who lifts a coyote by the jaw on horseback, and Burk Burnett.
Rough Riders reunion in San Antonio

Roosevelt joins a reunion of his Rough Riders in San Antonio, where the regiment had trained in 1898, and says how much he admires Texans. His diary sketches Abernathy, who takes wolves with his bare hands, Texas Ranger Captain McDonald, and the cattlemen of the Four Sixes brand.

After speeches in Fort Worth and Wichita, Roosevelt reaches Frederick, Oklahoma, and starts hunting at Cecil Lyon's ranch. Dogs catch the first coyote in a creek, and Alec Lambert rides well. He tells Taft he is handling Russia, Japan, Santo Domingo and Morocco just right.

On Archie's eleventh birthday Roosevelt rides hard after coyotes from a camp in a bend of the Red River, on a Kiowa pony in the morning and a cow pony later. His hosts are old-style Texas cattlemen including Burk Burnett and Cecil Lyon. He writes Bamie about little Sheffield's ear trouble.

Out with greyhounds and staghounds, Roosevelt's party takes a coyote after a three-mile run. In the afternoon comes an extraordinary ten-mile chase, and Abernathy captures the coyote alive with his hands, with Roosevelt one of the few riders there at the finish.
Camped on Deep Red Creek, Roosevelt is up before dawn for a morning hunt after bobcats that turns up nothing, and he rests in the afternoon.

With the chuck wagon along, the party rides southwest toward the Red River and kills six coyotes, losing only one after a seven-mile chase. A cowpuncher with nothing but a rope chases that one back for miles.
Last day of the coyote hunt

Roosevelt is in at the death of two more coyotes, then rides back to Frederick, where he speaks before leaving for Colorado. His diary tallies the party's total. Sternberg reports that the Kaiser is pressing for an international meeting on Morocco.
Colorado speeches, and tales of Abernathy

Roosevelt speaks at Trinidad, Pueblo and Colorado Springs and spends the night at Newcastle. He tells Kermit the hunting party took 47 wolves plus raccoons and rattlesnakes, and describes how Abernathy takes wolves alive. He also writes Garfield about the probes into Standard Oil and the Beef Trust.

Roosevelt rides about 20 miles from Newcastle with Philip Stewart, Dr. Alexander Lambert and guides John Goff and Jake Borah to Camp Roosevelt on East Divide Creek, with three horses, a Springfield rifle and some thirty hounds and terriers. Snow lies in drifts.

Roosevelt spends eleven hours in the saddle over rough ground. The dogs tree a bobcat, the bull terrier Shorty climbs nearly to it, and when it jumps the pack seizes it. A big glossy black bear is spotted.

With 26 hounds and four terriers Roosevelt follows a black bear through snowy canyons for nearly two hours. The bear refuses to tree and fights off the dogs, killing a terrier; Roosevelt breaks its hips at 60 yards and finishes it at 30. It weighs 330 pounds.
Skip and Shorty, the fighting dogs

Six hours in the snowdrifts turn up nothing. Roosevelt's diary praises the little terrier Skip, who loves to ride on horseback, and Shorty, the bull terrier mauled by the bear, who staggers back wagging his tail. He notes cranes, eagles, ravens and the first songbirds.
Secretary William Loeb spends the night in camp. Roosevelt rides all day in the high mountains without seeing game, and records local talk about wolves, cougars and a trapper who took dozens.

Snow keeps the party in camp, and Roosevelt fills his diary with birds and small mammals. In letters he tells Ted about his guides, tells Taft the government should stay out of Morocco, wires Loomis that the U.S. will remain friendly with both France and Germany, and writes Lodge on Newfoundland fisheries.

More than ten hours in the saddle and on foot through belly-deep drifts end with the hounds treeing a bobcat. Stewart photographs it, Lambert shoots it with a revolver, and the little terrier Skip climbs thirty feet up the tree to bite its tail.
Fever and a move to West Divide
Roosevelt feels his old Cuban fever. The party moves camp to where Clear Creek meets West Divide, though the late cold season may have kept the bears denned up.
Roosevelt stays in camp and records guide Jake Borah's story of a 115-pound wolf his pack once held at bay before he shot it.
A she-bear shot through the heart

In an eleven-hour, forty-mile ride, four of them bucking snow, the pack jumps a yearling and its glossy dark mother. Lambert shoots the yearling in an aspen; Roosevelt drops the she-bear from a spruce with a shot through the heart.

After twelve hours and more than thirty miles, Lambert shoots two yearlings with his revolver and the hounds tree their mother high in a spruce, where Roosevelt kills her. He notes what the bears had eaten. Sternberg writes that the Kaiser wants Roosevelt to nudge Britain toward harmony with Germany over Morocco.

A touch of fever keeps Roosevelt in camp while some twenty hard-riding ranchmen turn out hoping to see the President kill a bear. He writes Ethel about prairie girls and admits he is homesick for the family.
Cutting the trip short for peace

Still feverish, Roosevelt stays in camp while Lambert has a big day of bear hunting. Sensing that Russia and Japan may reach an honorable settlement, he wires Taft that he will end his trip a week early.
Another feverish day in camp. Roosevelt describes a tame bee martin that stays near the buildings with a plaintive note, and a big field mouse in the ranch house.
Roosevelt spends another day in camp with fever. It is his sister Corinne's 23rd wedding anniversary.
Church in a schoolhouse; Edith finds Pine Knot

Roosevelt goes to church in a little blue schoolhouse and wires Taft that he backs Japan's call for direct peace talks with Russia. In Virginia, Edith buys a small timbered house and five acres in Albemarle County for $195, calling it Pine Knot, a hideaway for the two of them.
Hunting along Divide Creek, Roosevelt rides for eight hours without seeing anything. His secretary William Loeb stays over in camp.
Storms roll through camp and Philip Stewart rides out to join the party. Roosevelt tells Kermit he has taken ten bears and three bobcats, and has been fighting his Cuban fever for a week.
A heavy, wet snowstorm hits the camp on Divide Creek.
Through snow Roosevelt rides six hours without seeing game, but notes an owl on its nest, a great owl and a very tame lark, and adds to his running list of birds.
Another snowy six-hour ride ends with a bobcat taken. Roosevelt keeps up his bird list.
Out of the mountains to Glenwood Springs

Roosevelt rides down to Glenwood Springs and speaks there. He writes John Hay, glad to hear he is better and urging a summer of rest, and tells George Kennan about California's push to segregate schools amid fear of a yellow peril.
Roosevelt spends the day at Glenwood Springs, still noting the birds he sees.

Heading east, Roosevelt stops at Pueblo and Colorado Springs and in Denver argues for federal control of corporations. His diary ends with house finches singing in Denver and spring wildflowers, though he misses the blue columbine, Colorado's state flower.
Roosevelt's train crosses Nebraska stopping at Fremont, Grand Island and North Platte, and he speaks in Omaha and in Council Bluffs, Iowa.

After speeches in Cedar Rapids and Clinton, Iowa, Roosevelt lunches and speaks at Chicago's Merchants Club. A labor delegation objects to any plan to send federal soldiers into the teamsters' strike, and he ends the day at the Iroquois Club banquet.
Roosevelt speaks at Alliance and Canton, Ohio, and in Pittsburgh, then reaches Washington at midnight.

Roosevelt is back at work, having cut his trip short over Morocco and the chance of Russo-Japanese talks. He has brought home Skip, the little hunting dog who attached himself to him in Colorado. Cabinet meets, and he confers with Fairbanks, Taft and Cortelyou.
The Kaiser presses for a conference

Sternberg hands Roosevelt the Kaiser's memo demanding a general conference on Morocco and blaming Britain for blocking it. Roosevelt and Herbert Knox Smith win at tennis, and he writes a batch of letters, telling Spring-Rice how he handles the Kaiser and Root about his three bears.
Taft and Moody call in the evening. Roosevelt tells Kermit that work piled up while he was away, that he went riding with Edith, and that Kermit's Groton marks delight him.
Idaho forests and Chicago labor trouble

Roosevelt talks over Chicago's labor troubles with Foraker, Grosvenor and Herbert Bowen and goes over Idaho's forest reserves with Gifford Pinchot. He lunches with the new canal leadership and tells Lodge the crowds in Texas and Kentucky were wildly enthusiastic.

The press reports that the Isthmian Canal Commission will buy construction supplies in foreign markets wherever they are cheapest, and Roosevelt takes full responsibility for the policy. He also holds Cabinet, sees Senator Elkins and receives Baron Kaneko.

Roosevelt tells Interior Secretary Hitchcock that the nation's forest reserves will be consolidated under Pinchot's Forest Service. He discusses tariffs and rebates with Rep. Davis and Santo Domingo with Jacob Hollander, and informs the Japanese minister that the Kaiser denies calling Japan the yellow peril.

Roosevelt discusses reciprocity with Speaker Cannon, Hemenway, Dolliver and Rep. Foss, and twice receives Baron Kaneko. He writes William Rockhill about China and Japan, and writes the Indian chief No Shirt about reservation land and relations between whites and Indians.

Having put tariff adjustment before Congress, Roosevelt has Taft cancel the May 16 order to buy canal supplies abroad. He meets Cortelyou and Morton after Cabinet, lunches with Cannon, Bonaparte and others, and praises Bishop Charles Brent's defense of American missionaries in the Philippines.
Nicholas Murray Butler comes to stay
Roosevelt lunches with Oscar Straus, Senator Warner and a Mr. Cowan, and dines with the Jusserands. Columbia's Nicholas Murray Butler arrives for a two-night White House visit.
Word comes that Connecticut Senator Orville H. Platt has died. Sportswriter Caspar Whitney calls at one, and Interior Secretary Hitchcock in the evening.
Hopeless to reconcile England and Germany

Roosevelt lunches with Taft, the Duke of Sutherland and naturalist George Bird Grinnell. He tells Ambassador Meyer he has given up trying to improve relations between England and Germany, and warns Senator Thomas Platt he will remove an appointee regardless.
After Cabinet, Roosevelt and Taft take up the feud between diplomats Francis Loomis and Herbert Bowen. He lunches with Lyman Abbott, Moody, Taft and Richard Harding Davis.

Roosevelt sees senators, the Brazilian ambassador, Sternberg, and in the evening Garfield and Pinchot. To Lodge he argues that killing the railroad rate bill would only feed the drive for government ownership of the railroads. He lets Hay know the Kaiser hopes to meet him, and admits he has no liking for Bowen.
A government job for a poet

Roosevelt confers with Joseph Bristow about the Panama Railroad and lunches with psychologist Hugo Münsterberg and others. He tells Kermit that Edwin Arlington Robinson, Kermit's favorite poet, is now at work in New York in the government post Roosevelt arranged for him.

After Cabinet, Roosevelt sees Senators Dolliver, Cullom and Dillingham, and dines with Justice Edward White and his wife. Joseph Bishop stays the night. He writes Spring-Rice about the Kaiser, the war and reports of a Russian-German alliance aimed at England and Japan.
Japan sinks the Russian fleet at Tsushima

Admiral Togo's Japanese fleet destroys the Russian fleet of Admiral Rozhestvensky in the Tsushima Strait. In Washington Roosevelt discusses a possible extra session of Congress with Senators Cullom and Elkins, sees Baron Kaneko, and asks Senator Thomas Platt to have management give a little in the Chicago strike.
The record for this Sunday in Washington is empty.

Roosevelt sees naturalist C. Hart Merriam early, then Puerto Rico's Tulio Larrinaga and others, and lunches with the Sternbergs, the Mortons and Father Zahm. He writes John Burroughs about Rev. William Long's attacks and about protective coloration in animals, gets a new Morocco memo from the Kaiser, and leaves for Brooklyn at midnight.
In Brooklyn Roosevelt breakfasts at the Union League Club, reviews the Memorial Day parade and speaks at the unveiling of a monument to General Henry W. Slocum, then heads back to Washington.
The Kaiser threatens war over Morocco

A new message from the Kaiser, sent through Sternberg, warns that Germany may fight France over Morocco. Roosevelt confers on the Russo-Japanese War, congratulates Baron Kaneko on Japan's naval victory, and asks Taft to stress Subic Bay as a naval base on his Philippine trip. Around this time the Trophy Room is added at Sagamore Hill.
Opening the Lewis and Clark Exposition

At four o'clock Roosevelt presses a button that lights and opens the Lewis and Clark Exposition in Portland, Oregon. He sees the British, German and Japanese envoys during the day and tells Andrew White he will test whether an offer to mediate between Japan and Russia can work.

Roosevelt names a Commission on Departmental Methods, led by Charles Keep with Frank Hitchcock, Lawrence Murray, James Garfield and Gifford Pinchot, to root out waste and modernize executive departments. The Wichita Forest game preserve is set up in Oklahoma, and he meets Russia's Ambassador Cassini.
Roosevelt meets Moody, Morton and Taft about Russian warships moving off the Philippines, lunches with Ambassador Jusserand, and sees Japan's minister Takahira at night.
Sternberg brings Roosevelt a note in which the Kaiser says the President should mediate between Russia and Japan. Dr. Merriam also calls in the evening.

Roosevelt wires Ambassador Meyer to seek an audience with the Czar, and briefs Lodge on his steps to end the war. Japanese admirals from Port Arthur visit, he lunches with the Bonapartes and Deweys, and Ted and a friend beat him and Alvord Cooley at tennis, four sets to three. He thanks Frederick MacMonnies for a statuette of him at San Juan.
British fleet to visit New York

Roosevelt confers with the British and French ambassadors on the war, sees Rep. Sulzer, and lunches with the Keep Commission members and others. He writes Arthur Lee on friendship among English-speaking peoples as Prince Louis of Battenberg's British squadron prepares to call at New York.

Roosevelt confers with the envoys of Russia, Germany, France and Britain, along with Hugh O'Beirne, as peace efforts gather pace. Thomas Dawson, Dr. Rixey and the Italian ambassador call, and he lunches with Baron Kaneko.
Proposing peace talks to Russia and Japan

Roosevelt sends formal notes to Russia and Japan proposing a peace conference, after a run of afternoon and evening meetings with Durand, Kaneko, Takahira and Sternberg. Edith goes ahead to Pine Knot to ready it for his first visit.

After seeing Francis Loomis, Roosevelt takes the train to Rapidan, Virginia, and goes on to Pine Knot, the little cabin Edith has just bought. He visits Joseph Wilmer and they dine at Plain Dealing. Edith is thrilled with the place.
Alone at Pine Knot; both sides agree to talk

Roosevelt and Edith have Pine Knot to themselves. He cooks breakfast and chops firewood while she rests in a hammock, and they fry chickens for supper with biscuits, cornbread, cherries and wild strawberries. Word comes that Japan accepts his call for peace talks; Russia will follow two days later.
Beefsteak, church and the train home

Roosevelt fries beefsteak for Edith's breakfast, they go to church together, and he takes the train back to Washington for talks with Taft and Loeb. He writes Kermit that Russia and Japan have agreed to meet. Another Kaiser memo on Morocco arrives.

Roosevelt sees Cassini and Takahira, decides not to prosecute Santa Fe railroad officers individually in the rebate case, and clears Paul Morton, who has left the Cabinet for Equitable Life. He urges Clara Hay to make John rest, and tells Clark Howell his 1885 retort to Jefferson Davis no longer seems clever.
After Cabinet, Roosevelt discusses Chinese exclusion with Commerce Secretary Metcalf, lunches with Root, Robert Bridges and Baroness von Sternberg, and writes Senator Heyburn about forest reserves.
Roosevelt receives Jusserand in the morning and Cassini before lunch, lunches with Shaw and Speyer, sees John Barrett and Edwin Denby, and meets Baron Kaneko in the afternoon.

Roosevelt talks over the Panama Railroad with Shonts and Maxwell Evarts and receives Cassini, Takahira and Durand in turn. He tells Oscar Straus he hopes to bring the two warring powers to The Hague and writes Cassini about his talk with Takahira.

Roosevelt meets Booker T. Washington and Jusserand, then writes a flurry of letters on the war. To Spring-Rice in St. Petersburg he sketches a peace in which Russia gives up Sakhalin and pays an indemnity but keeps most of its East Asian holdings, and he sends Lodge a long, important letter on the negotiations.

Roosevelt takes up the Santa Fe rebate case with Moody and Morton and Army appointments with Taft, and Cardinal Gibbons calls. He writes former President Cleveland asking him to chair the Jamestown Exposition committee and touches on the Equitable Life scandal.
German Ambassador Speck von Sternberg praises Roosevelt for his work in easing the Morocco crisis.

Roosevelt talks with Moody about the Santa Fe case, lunches with Rep. Augustus Peabody Gardner, and dines with John and Clara Hay. He writes about Chinese labor, Russia, and prejudice against the Japanese.
The Cabinet takes up the Loomis-Bowen case and Roosevelt goes over postal appointments with Cortelyou. At nine that night he leaves for Worcester, Massachusetts.

Roosevelt gives the Clark University commencement address in Worcester and leaves for Williamstown. He sends Taft a long letter on the Bowen-Loomis affair and directs Francis Loomis to go to France and bring home the remains of naval hero John Paul Jones.
Roosevelt speaks at the Williams College commencement in Williamstown and heads back to Washington.
France agrees to a Morocco conference

Roosevelt tells Speck von Sternberg that France has quietly dropped its objection to an international conference on Morocco, calling it a diplomatic triumph. The Cabinet discusses Chinese exclusion, and he sees Jusserand and Takahira.
A mission to Japan for Calhoun

Roosevelt confers with Penfield and Metcalf about Chinese exclusion and dines with the Jusserands. He asks William Calhoun to travel to Japan and report back, and responds to Lincoln Steffens's McClure's article on Ohio politics, McKinley and Hanna.
The Jusserands come at midday and Sternberg in the evening, and Roosevelt writes the German ambassador about smoothing matters between France and Germany.

Roosevelt talks railroad rebates with Moody and sees Takahira, Durand and Jusserand before leaving for Cambridge at 5:30. He sends Russia a note about mediation. Edith goes ahead to open Sagamore Hill, getting her first look at the newly built North Room.
Roosevelt attends the 25th reunion of his Harvard class of 1880 at the Hotel Somerset, staying with George B. Lee Jr. and Bishop William Lawrence.

Roosevelt attends Harvard's commencement and speaks at the Harvard Union and the alumni dinner. Sternberg writes to Sagamore Hill that the Kaiser is delighted with his work toward a Morocco conference.
By the Sylph to Oyster Bay

Roosevelt speaks in Bridgeport, Connecticut, and takes the Sylph home across the Sound to Oyster Bay, where Sagamore Hill opens for the summer with Bob Ferguson as a guest. Puck runs a color cartoon, "Peace," showing a battleship fleet with Roosevelt's face on the lead ship.
Nearly mad over Russia and Japan

At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt sees immigration official Marcus Braun and Judge William Calhoun, who stays to dinner. He vents to Whitelaw Reid about Russia's muddle, asks Alice to join Taft's goodwill trip to Japan as his representative, and names John Stevens to replace John Wallace as chief canal engineer. Bob Ferguson marries Isabella Selmes.

Secretary of State John Hay dies at his New Hampshire home. Roosevelt writes his widow Clara of the Sunday hours after church he spent with them. Charles Bonaparte succeeds Paul Morton as Navy Secretary, and Dan Moore and James Tracey of Albany visit Sagamore Hill.

Word goes out that Russian and Japanese envoys will meet on August 5, with Oyster Bay named as the place. Roosevelt tells Taft he will make Elihu Root Secretary of State, adding that he had done most of the State Department's work himself. Alice and the Taft party reach Chicago on their way to Japan.
Guests at Sagamore Hill include brother-in-law Douglas Robinson, Bob Ferguson, Elliott Cowdin and E. C. Hammer Jr. Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about John Hay's death.

Sternberg visits and stays for lunch, and that afternoon Roosevelt sets out for Cleveland with members of the Cabinet to bury John Hay. Out west, Alice sets off fireworks and shoots a revolver off the back of the Taft party's train, the men take in the Hart-Root prizefight at Reno, and the group reaches San Francisco.
Roosevelt attends John Hay's funeral in Cleveland and returns to Oyster Bay.

Roosevelt names Elihu Root to succeed John Hay at the State Department. Winthrop Chanler comes to dinner and stays over, with the E. D. Morgans also at the table. He sends Taft word of Root's acceptance and his love to Alice.
Speech to the teachers at Ocean Grove

Roosevelt travels to Ocean Grove, New Jersey, to address the National Education Association and returns home, where Teresa and Clifford Richardson and Baron Kaneko are guests. He tells Senator Spooner the Dominican treaty needs no amendment.

After meeting Baron Kaneko, Roosevelt lunches with Robert Bridges, Alvord Cooley and the poet Edwin Arlington Robinson, while Douglas and Monroe Robinson, Senator Knox and others fill the guest book. Alice sails from San Francisco on the Manchuria with Taft's party of 80. He praises Augustus Saint-Gaudens's inaugural medals.

In Paris, Germany and France sign an agreement on Morocco, a settlement Roosevelt helped broker and one that likely headed off war. At Sagamore Hill he lunches with Bishop Knight and the Washburns and has James Garfield and Gifford Pinchot to tea in the evening.
The record for this day at Sagamore Hill is empty.
Robert Bacon to the State Department

Senator Philander Knox spends the night at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Lodge about Hay's death, Hay's deep dislike of the Kaiser and the choice of Root, tells Root that Robert Bacon will be his first assistant, and sends Jusserand a letter on the Mongol campaigns of the 1200s.

John Mitchell, James Duncan and Samuel Gompers, who lead the American Federation of Labor, meet Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill. William Calhoun leaves on a special mission to Venezuela, and Roosevelt tells Moody that an Agriculture statistician, Edwin Holmes, was fired for using government data for private gain.
Russia's new ambassador comes to lunch
Baron Roman Rosen, Russia's new ambassador, lunches at Sagamore Hill and presents his credentials. Jacob Riis is a guest. Alice and Taft's group land in Honolulu.
Ted wants to work on railroads

Roosevelt and Japan's minister Takahira discuss Count Witte's naming as a Russian envoy to the coming peace talks. He lunches with Harriman, Takahira, Shonts, John Stevens and Hynes, and Root and others sign the guest book. To Harvard's Byron Hurlbut he explains that Ted hopes for a railroad career and a scientific school.

An explosion of the gunboat Bennington's boilers kills more than 50 men. Roosevelt confers with Takahira, has Bamie among his guests, and tells Ambassador Lloyd Griscom to assure Japan that Americans reject the anti-Japanese agitation on the Pacific coast and that there will be no discrimination while he is President.
The record for this Sunday at Sagamore Hill is empty.
Rowing around Lloyd Neck with Edith

Roosevelt and Edith row fifteen miles around Lloyd Neck with a picnic lunch and a few books, carrying the boat overland at one point. He writes London editor John St. Loe Strachey that he has no great hopes for the peace conference, and tells John Sleicher he doubts Congress will cut spending.

Roosevelt takes the boys out by rowboat to sleep under the stars, frying chicken or steak in bacon fat that the youngsters swear tastes like nothing else. He asks animal trainer Frank Bostock to compare the big cats, writes Morgan about a Chinese railroad concession, and tells Lodge that Ted passed his Harvard entrance exams with points to spare.

Elihu Root takes office as Secretary of State. Roosevelt rows home from his overnight camp with the boys and writes Henry Needham a modest self-portrait: no athlete, not good at games, but a decent walker, rider and rifle shot.
The record for this day at Sagamore Hill is empty.

Roosevelt confers with Secretary Root, and Dr. Alexander Lambert and Lyman Abbott visit. He sends Alice, far off in Asia, one of his cartoon-filled picture letters, assuring her it is no posterity letter.
Roosevelt confers again with Root, and Paul Morton and Dr. Lambert spend the evening at Sagamore Hill.
Dr. Alexander Lambert is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Across the Pacific, Alice and Taft's group reach Tokyo, where she stays at the American embassy with the Griscoms.

Roosevelt lunches with Hawaii's George R. Carter. He tells Spring-Rice that the Monroe Doctrine cannot stand still while the nation grows, urges Shonts to improve living conditions for canal workers, and writes Governor Higgins about the Equitable Life troubles.
Roosevelt writes Ambassador Jusserand about France, Germany and Morocco.
Roosevelt confers with Takahira about the peace talks and writes author Myra Kelly that he enjoyed her book Little Citizens.

Roosevelt meets Japan's chief envoy Baron Komura, with Kaneko and Takahira, aboard the presidential yacht Mayflower. He writes Commander William Sims that Japan's eight-inch guns badly mauled the Russian ships at Tsushima.
To Coney Island with Jacob Riis
Senator Murray Crane is a guest at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt goes with his old friend Jacob Riis to see the Coney Island hospital.

Roosevelt wires the Kaiser his thanks for help in settling where the Russo-Japanese peace talks will meet, and writes Taft, Whitelaw Reid and Baron Kaneko on Santo Domingo, Panama, Root and the preliminaries to peace.
The record for this Sunday at Sagamore Hill is empty.

Roosevelt wires Taft confirming the agreement he has reached in Japan, under which Washington accepts Japan's stake in Korea while Tokyo accepts America's position in the Philippines. He also lunches with Baron Rosen, Secretary Wilson and others, and discusses the Agriculture Department investigation with Wilson.
Moody's overnight visit to Sagamore Hill

Roosevelt talks with William Moody about the probe into the Department of Agriculture, and Moody stays for dinner and the night. In a letter, TR admits that after two car rides as President, the fuss in the papers over his safety has kept him out of automobiles.
The White House physician, Dr. Presley Rixey, calls on Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.
Lunch with diplomats and a Western maxim

Roosevelt hosts a crowded lunch table that includes British Ambassador Sir Henry Durand and Commander William Sims. Writing to Whitelaw Reid, he sums up his approach to power with a frontier rule about never drawing a gun without intent to fire.
Count Witte comes to Sagamore Hill

Russia's chief peace envoy, Count Sergei Witte, visits Roosevelt along with Ambassador Roman Rosen. TR also edits Treasury Secretary Shaw's tariff speech with a blue pencil and writes about yellow fever in New Orleans.
Russian and Japanese envoys meet aboard the Mayflower

On the presidential yacht Mayflower in Oyster Bay, Roosevelt formally greets the delegations of Russia and Japan and raises a glass to a fair and durable peace. The envoys then head for Portsmouth, New Hampshire. Edith takes the children on a picnic to Cooper's Bluff.
Edith celebrates her 44th birthday at Sagamore Hill, with William Wilmer on hand as a guest.
Morgan and a Chinese railroad deal

Roosevelt meets Treasury Secretary Shaw, then sits down to lunch with Judge Ingram and the financier J. P. Morgan over the Hankow railroad concession in China. In the afternoon Japan's Baron Kaneko comes to talk.
Roosevelt has lunch with Assistant Secretary of State Francis Loomis and Jacob Hollander, then holds a separate talk with Hollander.

Russian and Japanese negotiators sit down at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, while Roosevelt follows from Sagamore Hill. Ambassador Jusserand passes along French thanks for TR's work toward calm over Morocco.
Speaking to the coal miners at Wilkes-Barre
Roosevelt leaves Oyster Bay for Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, to address the United Mine Workers convention. Cameras catch him there alongside Cardinal Gibbons.
At Chautauqua, New York, Roosevelt speaks on the Monroe Doctrine and U.S. policy toward Santo Domingo and Venezuela, then heads back to Sagamore Hill.

The Outlook runs Roosevelt's review of Edwin Arlington Robinson's The Children of the Night, singling out the young poet as a rare bright spot in American verse. Senator Lodge is staying at Sagamore Hill.
Baron Kaneko is among the day's visitors. Roosevelt writes Interior Secretary Hitchcock about naming a federal district judge for Oregon.

Writing to canal chief Theodore Shonts, Roosevelt takes up Shonts's criticism of conditions in Panama and Dr. William Gorgas's then-mocked idea that mosquitoes carry yellow fever. TR takes Gorgas seriously.
Insurance oversight and a nod to Kermit

Roosevelt confers with Charles Keep about his inquiry into the Government Printing Office and with James Beck and Representative John Dryden about federal oversight of insurance companies. He credits Kermit, in a letter, with first steering him to Robinson's poetry.
No special session on the tariff
George Cortelyou joins Roosevelt for lunch. TR tells journalist Walter Wellman he won't call Congress back early to take up the tariff, and writes Morgan about the Chinese railroad question.
Roosevelt meets Kaneko as the Portsmouth talks freeze on Japan's demand that Russia pay an indemnity. Dr. Alexander Lambert arrives for a stay through August 21.
Siding with Canada on the fisheries

After meeting Ambassador Rosen, Roosevelt writes Lodge that in the Newfoundland fisheries quarrel the Gloucester fishermen have the weaker case and Canada has the better case. He refuses Massachusetts calls to send warships.
No events are recorded; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
A message to the Czar through Berlin

After a morning session with Kaneko and dinner with Shonts, Roosevelt cables Ambassador Speck von Sternberg to relay word on the peace talks to the Czar by way of Germany. He also briefs Jusserand on how negotiations stand.
Roosevelt warns Baron Kaneko that the world will not look kindly on Japan if it drags out the war just to win an indemnity. Philip Stewart visits and stays the night.

With Portsmouth still deadlocked, Roosevelt floats a compromise: Russia gives Japan half of Sakhalin Island, Japan gains Port Arthur, the Kwantung Peninsula, Manchuria and Korea, and no indemnity is paid. He sends a flurry of letters and cables to push it.
Edith reads The Lances of Lynwood aloud to Archie and Quentin, and their father wrestles boisterously with the boys. At Portsmouth, Sakhalin and the indemnity still block a deal.
Fifty minutes under Oyster Bay in a submarine

Roosevelt climbs into the submarine Plunger and spends 50 minutes beneath Oyster Bay, even taking the controls for a stretch; no President had done anything like it. That evening he reads poems to Archie and Quentin after prayers and tosses them around on the bed.

Roosevelt writes Kermit about his 50-minute plunge beneath Oyster Bay the day before. He also passes along a family joke: asked by a reporter about his father, young Quentin claimed to see him now and then but to know nothing of his home life.

The Portsmouth negotiations come close to breaking apart. Roosevelt sees Melville Stone of the Associated Press in the evening, dines with Shonts, and cables the Kaiser a proposed formula built around Sakhalin and no indemnity.
Bishop named to the Canal Commission
Roosevelt lunches with J. P. Morgan over China's Hankow railroad rights and puts Joseph Bishop on the Panama Canal Commission. He tells the Civil Service Commission its rules can't work in Panama.
Russia and Japan agree to peace
Word comes from Portsmouth that Witte and Komura have settled terms to end the Russo-Japanese War. Roosevelt wires his delight to Herbert Peirce.
Roosevelt hosts Senator Nelson Aldrich, Arthur von Briesen and Elbert Baldwin for lunch.
Congratulating the Czar; Ted heads to Harvard

Roosevelt wires Czar Nicholas II his congratulations on the peace and tells Douglas Robinson he is pleased. Far away, riots erupt in Japan over the treaty, China boycotts American goods over exclusion, Alice's party with Taft turns for home, and Ted begins at Harvard.

Russia and Japan sign an armistice. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt meets Francis Loomis and Senator Henry Burnham, and John St. Loe Strachey introduces the Evening Post's London man, Dibblee. TR tells Bamie the British squadron will skip New York.
Rainy-day house party and a tired President

The children play in the old barn on a wet afternoon during a house party for Ted and Ethel. Roosevelt writes Alice in China that Portsmouth made the peace possible, invites Kaneko to collect a bearskin, and confides to Lodge that the summer has worn him out.

With J. W. Wadsworth as a house guest, Roosevelt sees Cortelyou, Beveridge and Penfield and talks Panama civil service with Cooley. He tells Bonaparte he will keep Santo Domingo as it is until the Senate acts on the treaty, and will put down any revolt.

The Treaty of Portsmouth is signed, formally ending the Russo-Japanese War. Roosevelt names Robert Bacon Assistant Secretary of State and explains to General Francis Greene that he got peace by going around old-style diplomacy and dealing directly with heads of state.

Roosevelt writes Czar Nicholas II and Japan's Emperor Mutsuhito about the new peace. He tells Lodge he plans to oust Public Printer Frank Palmer and sends Speck von Sternberg a mixed letter touching on an old Roman fort and submarines.
Nothing is recorded for the day beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.
Vice President Charles Fairbanks and his wife come for lunch, and Philippe Bunau-Varilla and his wife for dinner. Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz at Lake George making the case against disarmament.
Lunch with Komura, dinner with Witte

Roosevelt hosts Japan's negotiators Komura and Takahira at lunch and Russia's Witte and Rosen at dinner, with cousin Emlen Roosevelt and his wife at the table. He also writes China's Guangxu Emperor about the peace.

Baron Kaneko lunches at Sagamore Hill. Edith writes Spring-Rice that the times feel so exciting she can barely wait for what comes next, and TR assures Rockhill that China will respect the treaty's terms.

Roosevelt lunches with the Panama Canal's board of consulting engineers. He credits the Kaiser, in a letter to Whitelaw Reid, for his help as a go-between, and writes Senator Fulton about an Oregon judgeship.

In a long letter to George Otto Trevelyan, Roosevelt reviews the peace conference, gives an unflattering portrait of Count Witte, mentions Tolstoy, and says he is reading William Morris. He hopes to visit England someday as a private citizen.
Ted celebrates his 18th birthday. Baron Rosen lunches with Roosevelt, who writes Ray Stannard Baker about his McClure's series on the railroads.
Roosevelt tells Root that Rosen brought word the Czar wants to revive the Hague Conference. Although the idea was originally TR's, he is content to let the world think it came from the Czar.
Roosevelt writes Shaw and Senators Aldrich and Allison about the tariff deal under discussion with Germany.
A forest reserve in the White Mountains
Roosevelt writes William Harvey about possibly buying White Mountains land for a forest reserve. He also accepts Archibald Sampson's resignation as Minister to Ecuador and writes Shaw and Reid.
Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt meets members of the Chinese legation about China's boycott of American goods. Charles and Ellen Bonaparte dine, and Nicholas Murray Butler stays overnight.
Roosevelt tells Whitelaw Reid he sees little he can do to warm relations between England and Germany. He writes William Riordon that he enjoyed Plunkitt of Tammany Hall.
Root, Lodge and Choate stay over
Clarence Mackay and his wife call in the afternoon with the Duchess of Marlborough. Root, Lodge and Choate come to confer and stay for dinner and the night.
A newsy letter to Arthur Lee
Roosevelt sends his English friend Arthur Lee a letter of news from Sagamore Hill.
Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt writes Wayne MacVeagh about the uproar over big corporations' gifts to the 1904 Republican campaign. To Edith's sister Emily Carow he explains why Ted quit Groton one year ahead of schedule to be tutored for Harvard, and he praises Archie warmly.
Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt tells Lincoln Steffens he is annoyed by the idea of handing back every campaign gift from big money. He recommends Alexander Sutherland's book on the moral instinct to Florence LaFarge, touching on the U.S. birth rate, and writes Richard Bartholdt about the Navy's size.
Groton headmaster Endicott Peabody, General Horace Porter, canal chief Theodore Shonts and Cleveland Dodge are among the day's visitors.
Taking aim at a nature faker

On Corinne's 44th birthday, Roosevelt writes George Locke objecting to the animal myths in the Rev. William J. Long's Northern Trails. He tells Senator Allison the Germans want tariff talks held in Berlin.
A fitter from Brooks Brothers comes to Sagamore Hill in the evening.
Roosevelt writes Harvard President Charles Eliot of his worry over newspapermen hounding Ted, who has just started his freshman year. Reporters and photographers trail the boy around Harvard Yard.
Roosevelt and Edith leave Sagamore Hill in the morning and return to Washington. Senator Thomas Platt calls at 9 that night.
Back in Washington, Roosevelt dines with French Ambassador Jules Jusserand.

Roosevelt confers on the Keep Commission's work, railroad rebates and rate legislation. He writes Ted about coping with reporters, admits Pinchot beat him at tennis three sets to one, and describes Archie hauling a long garden hose toward the sandbox.
Cabinet takes up the boycott and the Beef Trust

The Cabinet discusses China's boycott and the Beef Trust case. Roosevelt also confers on postal jobs, rate legislation and coal with John Mitchell, and shares lunch with muckraker Lincoln Steffens, Robert Bacon and William Moody.
A word to McClure on muckraking
Roosevelt spends the day on rate legislation, consular posts, naval bills and the Ohio campaign. He writes Samuel McClure about the exposé articles his magazine favors.

Roosevelt meets Townsend on rates and confers with Moody and Taft, then shares lunch with Japan's Minister Takahira and two doctors, Rixey and Stokes. He writes Taft about Vatican displeasure that Alice reportedly made much of an out-of-favor archbishop during the Far East trip.
Calling a summit on football injuries

The Cabinet works through Chinese exclusion, meatpacking, a second Hague Conference and canal administration. Roosevelt invites George Gray to a White House meeting on college football injuries set for October 9.

Roosevelt talks with Bartholdt about the coming Interparliamentary gathering in Brussels and with Virginia's Representative Slemp about his state's politics, and dines with Bacon and Garfield. He writes Taft about the Taft-Katsura agreement and Trevelyan about the ancient Greeks.

Roosevelt asks Root whether Charles Evans Hughes might be talked into running for mayor of New York; Hughes later says no. He tells MacVeagh the clamor over returning corporate campaign money is mostly hysteria with a little dishonesty.

Roosevelt and Root meet with representatives of Yale, Harvard and Princeton about making college football less brutal. That evening the justices of the Supreme Court are honored at a White House reception.

On Kermit's 16th birthday, Roosevelt creates bird reservations at the Siskiwit and Huron Islands in Michigan and Passage Key in Florida. The Cabinet debates members campaigning locally, and he confers on tariffs, rates and Venezuela.

Niece Eleanor Roosevelt turns 21. Roosevelt confers on the Philippines, receives a lumbermen's delegation, and writes Frederic Delano on why railroad legislation matters. Edith writes Kermit praising his growth and tells Aunt Lizzie that Quentin is scaling the trees outside her window.
Roosevelt works with Metcalf and Garfield on his Annual Message, confers on rates and the Philippines, and lunches with Knox and Root. Senator Proctor calls.
The Cabinet takes up Venezuela, and Boutell, Cooley and Jusserand call. Across the Pacific, Alice boards the Siberia at Yokohama to come home.

Roosevelt directs the Keep Commission to look into Interior Secretary Hitchcock's statements about his own employees. He also meets Root, Bacon and Taft and writes Lyman Abbott about an Outlook piece alleging misuse of government privilege.
Roosevelt writes George Kennan a long letter correcting a misleading article about the Portsmouth peace, rich with background on how the settlement came about.
Roosevelt meets Grosvenor on finance bills and sees callers including Baron Rosen and John McIlhenny, who will join the coming Southern tour. Oscar Straus and Root come to lunch.

An executive order lets Cabinet department heads remove employees. Roosevelt talks Philippines business with Sereno Payne and writes William Murphy that he wants no part of the so-called Roosevelt Home Club.

Roosevelt sets out with Edith, Dr. Rixey, J. C. Greenaway, Maurice Latta and others on a speaking swing through the South. He speaks at Fredericksburg, Ashland and Richmond, Virginia, then rolls on overnight toward Raleigh. Nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 7.
Railroads and forests in North Carolina

At Raleigh, Roosevelt speaks on railroad regulation and forestry, then stops at Greensboro, Durham, Salisbury and High Point. In Charlotte, Edith is welcomed by local women, among them Stonewall Jackson's widow.

Roosevelt and Edith visit Bulloch Hall in Roswell, Georgia, where his mother Mittie grew up. He meets Mam Grace and Daddy William, once enslaved on the plantation, and finds the house familiar from Mittie's stories though he had never seen it. He speaks in Atlanta; Edith heads back to Washington.

In Jacksonville, Roosevelt speaks about the Panama Canal. That evening in St. Augustine he sits through a banquet with a string of six short speeches he found tiresome. Edith writes Kermit about her part of the trip.
A swim in the Florida surf

After church and a drive around St. Augustine with the mayor, Roosevelt takes a launch out to the island with Dr. Rixey, William Loeb and two Rough Riders and swims in the surf. He writes Ethel about the day and leaves that evening for Mobile.
Telling Harriman to slow Alice's train

Roosevelt is in Mobile. Alice lands in San Francisco from Yokohama and boards a special train east that E. H. Harriman hopes will set a coast-to-coast record. TR wires Harriman to ease off; the train breaks the record anyway.
Roosevelt addresses Tuskegee Institute on citizenship, then speaks in Montgomery and Birmingham.
In Little Rock, Arkansas, Roosevelt gives a speech condemning lynching.
New Orleans, then home by sea
Roosevelt speaks and holds a reception in New Orleans, then boards the cruiser West Virginia that afternoon for the voyage back to Washington.

Roosevelt marks his 47th birthday aboard the West Virginia. Alice gets back to Washington from four months in Asia, 20 pounds lighter, with the homeward leg from Yokohama done in a record 13 days. In New York, his birthplace on East 20th Street opens as a private museum.
Roosevelt is still at sea on the West Virginia, bound for Washington.
The West Virginia continues north with Roosevelt aboard.
Roosevelt is still aboard the West Virginia. In Washington, Edith tells Kermit that Alice seems careworn and worried but won't say why.
Alice is engaged to Nick Longworth

Roosevelt lands back in Washington and confers with Jusserand. Scribner's runs his "Wolf Hunt in Oklahoma." Around this time Alice finally tells Edith she is engaged to Congressman Nicholas Longworth, breaking the news while Edith brushes her teeth, as Nick asks TR for her hand downstairs. Both parents are delighted.
Back from the South, catching up

Roosevelt meets Root, Minister Takahira and Representative Tawney, then lunches with Jusserand and Joseph Bishop. He tells Kermit he enjoyed the Southern trip, has heard Alice's travel tales, rides and walks with Edith and the dog Skip, and admires the boys' pumpkin giant.

Roosevelt talks rate legislation with Senators Cullom and Dolliver. Hungarian-American Republicans from New York stop by with late birthday greetings, and the poet Madison Cawein is among his lunch guests.
After a Cabinet meeting and a rates conference with Vice President Fairbanks, Roosevelt receives Britain's Prince Louis of Battenberg. He lunches with Speck von Sternberg and Root.

Roosevelt sees Admiral Dewey and Senator Depew, lunches with Speck von Sternberg, and gives a formal state dinner in honor of Prince Louis of Battenberg. He thanks William Ripley for articles including one on his railway policy in The Atlantic Monthly.
At 9 p.m., Roosevelt confers with Paul Morton about the investigation of the Equitable Life Assurance Society.
Greek-style coins and a trip to vote

Roosevelt discusses Cuban sanitation with Cullom and the atrocities in Russia with Oscar Straus and Root, and lunches with Prince Louis of Battenberg. He sends Augustus Saint-Gaudens ideas for the new U.S. coins and leaves at midnight for Oyster Bay to vote.
Roosevelt casts his vote in Oyster Bay and heads back to Washington.
Roosevelt writes Lodge and Senator Beveridge of his pleasure at Republican wins, and sends George Otto Trevelyan three books he admires. He also takes up Oklahoma statehood and Panama conditions.
Roosevelt confers on Delaware politics with Senator Allee and lunches with Nevada Stranahan and Root. He writes Senator Allison about revising the tariff.

Roosevelt talks Southern politics with John McLaurin and Judge Emory Speer. Writing to Nicholas Murray Butler about the New York district attorney's office, he makes clear he dislikes William Travers Jerome.

Booker T. Washington calls on Roosevelt at midday. TR tells editor Robert Bridges how much he enjoyed Ellen Velvin's new book about wild animals, and writes Paul Morton about Shonts and the Canal Zone.
The famed African hunter Frederick Selous dines with Roosevelt and spends the night. TR writes Ted about playing football and about social life at Harvard.
Scrambling through the woods with Selous

Roosevelt takes Selous on one of his cross-country scrambles joined by Pinchot, Garfield, Bob Bacon and Ambassador Meyer. The hunter entertains Ethel, Archie and Quentin with lion and hyena stories and stays for dinner, while Edith is away in New York.
After a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Shonts, Roosevelt dines at Secretary Root's. He writes Augustus Saint-Gaudens again, urging that the new coins look like those of ancient Greece.

Susan B. Anthony visits Roosevelt late in the morning. He also confers with Senator Platt and William Barnes on New York patronage and hears Massachusetts shoe manufacturers on the tariff. Philip Stewart and his family settle in at the White House.

In a packed day, Roosevelt confers on railroads with Charles Mellen, on pure food legislation with Senator McCumber, and on the life insurance inquiry with John Dryden. Historian James Ford Rhodes dines with Root and Taft and stays on, as do the Stewarts.

After Cabinet and talks on the tariff and railroads, Roosevelt hosts a White House dinner and musicale with Baron Rosen, Commander Sims and Justice Brewer. He tells Nevada Stranahan that Benjamin Odell should lose his post as New York Republican leader.

Representatives Hepburn and Hopkins, Senator Cullom and Speaker Cannon call. Roosevelt writes Paul Morton about Shonts, John Allison about economic manipulation, and Henry Whitney to say he was misquoted on reciprocity.

Quentin turns 8 and is given a live pig by Oscar Straus. Roosevelt writes Kermit about racing and playing hide-and-seek with Archie's football team, his frequent tennis with Jusserand, and Nicholas Nickleby. He congratulates Ted on his first Harvard game and hopes his grades rise.

Roosevelt gathers Cabinet officers Root, Knox and Moody with Cullom, Hepburn, Mann and Prouty to plan railroad rate legislation, then talks Pennsylvania and New York politics, the latter over dinner with Governor Frank Higgins. He writes Baker on the rate bill and Senator Fulton on Oregon land frauds.

At noon Roosevelt attends the wedding of Lieutenant Commander William Sims and Anne Hitchcock. He names Charles Wolverton a district judge in Oregon and sends Brander Matthews a playful letter about his review of Edwin Arlington Robinson.
What the rate bill must do

Roosevelt sets out for Ray Stannard Baker his views on rail rate regulation and the goals the coming bill must meet. He confers with Senator Heyburn on Idaho appointments and lunches with Henry Taft and Moody.

Roosevelt confers with Frantz and Commissioner Leupp on Osage Indian affairs. He writes T. C. Friedlander about the exclusion of Chinese immigrants and bias against them, Secretary Shaw on German tariff changes, and Senator Platt about Olcott.
Ted breaks his nose against Yale

Roosevelt assures Yale coach Walter Camp that Ted came through the Yale game without serious harm, though Ted in fact broke his nose. The day also brings a Cabinet meeting, a diplomatic reception, and letters on coinage, insurance law and the Republican chairmanship.
Letting the Dominicans fight it out

Roosevelt has the Navy told not to stop arms moving by sea between Dominican ports; he will let the factions fight as long as foreign lives and property are left alone. He writes Platt on picking a fair New York chairman and Root on Japan's protectorate over Korea. It is Bamie's 10th wedding anniversary.
Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence in Washington.

Mark Twain joins Roosevelt at lunch with Speck von Sternberg, Moody and Bonaparte. TR works New York party politics with Root and Olcott, writes Pinchot on the open-range grazing problem, and holds a late conference. Edith tells Aunt Lizzie that Alice is truly in love.

After a Cabinet meeting and a talk with Senator Dolliver on railroad legislation, Roosevelt writes Ray Stannard Baker that he despises demagogues as much as the corrupt and wants a rate law that will stand up in court.
Senators Beveridge and Foraker, Representative Lacey, Root and Bonaparte call. Roosevelt lunches with Beveridge, his old Buffalo friend Ansley Wilcox, and a Mr. Winsor.

Roosevelt leaves in the morning for Albemarle County, Virginia, to spend Thanksgiving with the family at Pine Knot, near Plain Dealing. Unable to attend Mark Twain's 70th birthday dinner at Delmonico's, he sends regrets. He asks Root to find a capable Black candidate for the Freetown, Sierra Leone post.
After the Thanksgiving holiday at Pine Knot in Albemarle County, Virginia, Roosevelt heads back to Washington in the evening.
Army-Navy game and three water projects

On his and Edith's 19th wedding anniversary, Roosevelt watches Army play Navy at Princeton. The same day brings three new federal reclamation projects: Rio Grande and Carlsbad in New Mexico and Okanogan in Washington.
At 9 p.m. Roosevelt receives Robert Bacon, William Willcox, Elbert Baldwin, Mrs. John Van Voorst and a Mr. Quellenec.

The 59th Congress gathers. Roosevelt talks New York politics with Olcott and that evening sees Chief Justice Fuller, Justice Holmes and Alexander Graham Bell. The Umatilla project in Oregon is approved, and TR tells Moody wood pulp should carry no tariff.

Roosevelt sends Congress his fifth Annual Message, a more forceful document pressing for railroad rate regulation and pure food laws. He also holds Cabinet, lunches with Brooks Adams, and sees Minister Takahira at night; Nicholas Murray Butler is a White House guest.

Roosevelt thanks Paul d'Estournelles de Constant for an early printing of the Duke of Sully's memoirs, a gift from the French government in gratitude for his help keeping peace with Germany. He also confers on Brooklyn patronage and on health in the Philippines with Dr. Gorgas, and dines with Lodge, Nick Longworth and others.

Roosevelt writes David Starr Jordan about the golden trout named for him, a fish he had worked to protect. He tells Selous how much the family enjoyed his visit and demands that Charles McClelland account for his insurance dealings.
A marshal's badge for a Rough Rider
After Cabinet and a tariff talk, Roosevelt writes Senator Clarence Clark about naming Ben Daniels, a former Rough Rider and Western lawman, as a U.S. marshal. A musicale fills the evening.

Roosevelt confers with Beveridge on statehood, then sits down to lunch with two old Western friends, Seth Bullock and William Llewellyn, plus General Thomas and Nick Longworth. Booker T. Washington calls at 9 p.m., followed by Moody, Brownlow and Hale.
Sunday evening callers at the White House include New York Republican William Barnes.

In separate letters to Bellamy and Maria Storer, Roosevelt ends their meddling in Vatican affairs: they must stop writing Rome on Catholic matters and misrepresenting U.S. policy, or Bellamy loses his post as ambassador in Vienna. TR also meets labor leaders Mitchell and Gompers on Chinese exclusion.

The Yakima reclamation project in Washington is approved. After Cabinet, Roosevelt discusses insurance legislation with Representative Landis and meets William Sulzer and immigration inspector Marcus Braun; Andrew Carnegie is among his callers.

Roosevelt discusses irrigation with Senators Smoot and Sutherland and canal business with Joseph Bishop. Nick's mother, Mrs. Longworth, comes to lunch, and art collector Charles Freer dines with the Lodges, the Holmeses and Mrs. Gardner.

The White House announces that Alice will marry Congressman Nicholas Longworth of Cincinnati on February 17, 1906. Roosevelt also writes Lyman Abbott about how party politics is tangling both the rate bill and the Dominican treaty, and Jacob Schiff about Russian Jews.
A customs post for Bill Sewall

Roosevelt proposes his old Maine guide Bill Sewall for a customs collectorship, thanks the Provençal poet Frédéric Mistral for a copy of Mirèio, and writes Moody denying any shielding of Paul Morton in the Equitable affair. The Strawberry Valley project in Utah is approved.
Snowball fights behind the White House

Snow falls, and Archie, Quentin, cousin Sheffield Cowles and Helen Elliott go sledding and pelt each other with snowballs behind the White House. Roosevelt's article "Federal Social Legislation" appears in Charities and the Commons, and he confers on Santo Domingo and the canal.
At 7:30 Roosevelt sups with Major W. A. Wadsworth, and later sees Senators Allison and Hale, Theodore Shonts and Joseph Bishop.

Roosevelt meets Senator Kittredge, Shonts, Moody and Taft about pay for canal workers, and lunches with editor Richard Watson Gilder. He urges Frederick Selous to put his big-game knowledge into a book.
A gift for his childhood nurse

Roosevelt sends a $20 check, by way of Corinne, to Dora "Dolly" Watkins, his nurse as a boy. Joseph Bishop is named to the Canal Commission, and TR writes a stack of letters, thanking Admiral Togo for a revolver and denying he called Argentines superior to other South Americans.

Roosevelt tells Herbert Parsons that Wadsworth has been picked over Merritt for New York Assembly Speaker, a setback for Odell. He asks Bonaparte to circulate an article on the Russo-Japanese naval fighting so it can shape U.S. ship design.

Congress breaks for the holidays, and Roosevelt hosts a Cabinet dinner; Eliot Gregory and Paul Morton stay the night. He tells Shonts a Mr. Sullivan is wrong to think William Cromwell ever had his confidence, and writes Secretary Wilson on saving Western grazing lands.

Roosevelt and the children chase one another through the mansion in a game of hide-and-seek. He talks Wyoming forest reserves with Senator Warren, sees Whitelaw Reid, and goes with Edith to a dinner in their honor given by Vice President Fairbanks.

Roosevelt confers on Brooklyn patronage and canal business, lunches with the Fairbankses and two Japanese visitors, Commander Takeshita and Mr. Kitagaki, and dines with James Whitcomb Riley and the Vice President.
