On Christmas Eve, Roosevelt discusses New York politics with James Wadsworth Jr. and Commissioner Cooley, then sees Ambassador Jusserand and later Francis Leupp.
The Roosevelts spend Christmas Day in Washington.

Roosevelt meets Root, Taft and Bonaparte in the afternoon. He tells Indiana reformer Lucius Swift that he will name Rothschild, Senator Beveridge's choice, surveyor of customs despite Swift's objections.
Off to Pine Knot for the holidays
Roosevelt receives Peru's new minister at 10 a.m., then leaves with the family for Pine Knot, their cabin in Albemarle County, Virginia.
The Roosevelts are at Pine Knot in the Virginia countryside; nothing else is recorded.
The family remains at Pine Knot; no events are noted.
While Roosevelt is at Pine Knot, Harry Orchard, a Western Federation of Miners man, kills former Idaho Governor Frank Steunenberg.
Roosevelt returns to Washington and sees Senator Eugene Hale at 10 p.m.

Roosevelt greets the public at the White House New Year's reception from late morning into early afternoon, and sees British Ambassador Durand that night. He praises Charles Larned's article on the Army, which called for better pay.

Roosevelt wires Herbert Parsons to stand firm for James Wadsworth against Hamilton Fish's man, Wainwright. Wadsworth becomes Speaker of the New York Assembly, a clear victory for TR. The day also brings Cabinet and a stream of senators.

Roosevelt talks statehood with Beveridge and confers with Grosvenor, then attends a Cabinet dinner at Secretary Root's. He sends counsel to James Wadsworth on his new job and writes Governor Higgins about Odell.
The Hepburn rate bill goes in

Congress returns, and Representative Hepburn's railroad rate bill is put before the House. Roosevelt's lunch table includes Herbert Parsons, Lloyd Griscom, Butler, Reid and Speck von Sternberg, and hosts the diplomatic reception that night.
Humorist Finley Peter Dunne joins Roosevelt for lunch with Taft, Root, Jusserand and others. That evening TR takes up the Naval Personnel Bill with four Cabinet members; Butler stays over.
The coinage is his pet project

Roosevelt tells Augustus Saint-Gaudens that the new coinage is a project close to his heart and that he dislikes the Mint's objections to the designs. He also discusses canal labor with Shonts and J. B. Harris, Black appointments with Charles Anderson, and sees Alexander Graham Bell.
Roosevelt writes Senator Platt that he wants Henry L. Stimson named district attorney to prosecute the American Sugar Refining Company and the New York Central Railroad under the Elkins Act.
A special message on the canal

Roosevelt sends Congress a special message on the Panama Canal and receives the American Bar Association's commission. He writes Leonard Wood with concern over a head wound, asks John Pitcher whether John Goff was mauled by a lion, and tells Luke Wright he wants him as Minister to Japan.

Roosevelt gives Lincoln Steffens free rein to investigate the executive branch. Writing Jeter Pritchard, he denies any shift toward a whites-only Republican policy in the South and flatly rules out a third term.
A Medal of Honor at the White House

Roosevelt pins the Medal of Honor on James Robb Church, the first such award handed out at the White House under the formal ceremony TR had ordered. He also makes Henry Stimson the federal prosecutor in Manhattan and addresses the American Medical Association.

Roosevelt hears Dominican property holders on the Santo Domingo treaty and discusses the Philippine tariff bill with E. J. Hill. The White House hosts a diplomatic dinner, and he writes Root on Venezuela and Taft on Army camps and the Chinese boycott.
After Cabinet and a talk with Watson about tariffs on Philippine goods, Roosevelt writes Butler again about Jacob Schiff's January 4 speech attacking U.S. finance policy, which he thinks did harm.
A lock canal, and gifts for Alice

Roosevelt writes Kermit that he favors a lock canal over a sea-level one at Panama, that he often rides and walks with Edith, and that wedding gifts for Alice are starting to come in. He sends along a pin given him by Oklahoma ranchmen.
Roosevelt confers with William Willcox, postmaster of New York.
Jane Addams and Steffens drop in
Roosevelt discusses New York politics with Herbert Parsons and the canal inquiry with Senator Kittredge. Among a crowd of visitors are reformers Jane Addams and Lincoln Steffens.

The Algeciras Conference on the Franco-German quarrel over Morocco opens in Spain, a meeting Roosevelt helped arrange, with Henry White there to guide it. That afternoon Ion Perdicaris, the kidnap victim of 1904, calls with his wife. The House passes the Philippine tariff bill.
Roosevelt establishes the Sevier National Forest in Utah. In a packed day he confers on Alaska, railroad rates and the Hague Conference and lunches with Taft and Herbert Parsons.
Arizona and New Mexico as one

On Bamie's 51st birthday, Roosevelt tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler he hopes to bring the Arizona and New Mexico territories in together as a single state, since separate admission would take years. He meets Spooner on the Dominican treaty and a Puerto Rico delegation, and hosts the judiciary reception.
Roosevelt appoints Luke E. Wright U.S. ambassador to Japan after a Cabinet meeting. His brother-in-law Douglas Robinson is staying at the White House.
Roosevelt confers with Senator Elkins on rate legislation, and separately with Admiral Dewey, Senators Frye and Spooner and Representative McCall. Root, Hitchcock and Alger also call.
On a Sunday, Roosevelt talks Brooklyn appointments with Timothy Woodruff, and Lincoln Steffens stops by.

Roosevelt asks the Army's General Staff whether a war plan against Venezuela should be drafted and urges Leonard Wood to think about fortifying Hawaii given Japan's ambitions. To Trevelyan he writes that liking every sort of book is a great comfort and that reading rests him from work.

After Cabinet and a meeting with Speaker Cannon and Representative Humphrey, Roosevelt writes Whitelaw Reid that he opposes bringing Chinese coolie labor into the United States. Attorney General Moody gives a dinner for TR and Edith.

Roosevelt receives China's imperial commissioners and talks Far Eastern matters with Paul Morton. He tells Jane Addams he admires her kind of reformer, writes Leupp about coal lands on Choctaw and Chickasaw reservations, and defends the Hague Conference to Ian Hamilton.
Roosevelt works the statehood bill with a number of congressmen, lunches with Bowdoin president William DeWitt Hyde, and gives the justices of the Supreme Court an evening dinner.
Bribes in the Beef Trust case

Roosevelt writes Moody about bribes the meatpackers used to try to influence the government's Beef Trust prosecution and Senator Aldrich about tribal funds going to church-run Indian schools. He meets on trade with Asia and hosts a 32-guest dinner; Hugo Münsterberg calls.
Roosevelt lunches with Dryden and Governor Stokes, sees C. E. Smith and Overstreet, and goes to the Gridiron Club's dinner at the Willard Hotel. He tells Ted he is glad his Harvard work has improved.
Explaining the muck-rake speech to Steffens

With canal money, the Hepburn rate bill, the Philippine tariff, the Dominican treaty and joint statehood all pending in Congress, Roosevelt sees Senator La Follette at 9:30 p.m. and then Lincoln Steffens, to whom he explains the thinking behind his Gridiron remarks.
Roosevelt goes to General Joseph Wheeler's funeral, confers with Representative Keifer, and hosts an evening musicale.

Roosevelt confers with Governor Charles Magoon on Panama and sees Lincoln Steffens again. Jacob Riis is a White House guest, and Secretary Cortelyou gives a dinner for TR and Edith. He tells French Chadwick a new President and Congress ought to take office together at New Year's.

Gifts pour in for Alice and Nick: a Gobelin tapestry from France's president, embroidered gold cloth from Japan's emperor, a $25,000 pearl necklace from Cuba, a Saint-Gaudens bronze, an Italian mosaic table and a hogshead of popcorn. Alice turns nothing down. The Senate begins to move on the Hepburn bill.

Roosevelt tells Representative George Foss he is letting Midshipman John Paul Miller return to the Naval Academy, though hazing ordinarily meant automatic dismissal. He also writes Meyer about French jitters over German demands at Algeciras and confers on rate legislation and Wisconsin patronage.
Roosevelt and Edith go riding. He discusses Government Printing Office business with Representative Landis, and Douglas and Corinne Robinson stay at the White House for a dinner and musicale.

Roosevelt hosts a dinner for his Harvard Class of 1880. Ted arrives from college and rides with his father, who writes Kermit about David Copperfield and his fondness for Thackeray. He presses the Storers for answers to his December letters.
Edith writes Kermit that Alice wears the amber beads he sent as a wedding present constantly; he had paid $50 for them at Fisher's.
A report on the Pennsylvania Railroad
The Interstate Commerce Commission's report on alleged antitrust violations by the Pennsylvania Railroad goes to the House. Taft, Speaker Cannon and three senators call on Roosevelt.

Roosevelt lunches with naturalists John Burroughs and C. Hart Merriam and Major John Pitcher. A letter of his to Congress on Annapolis hazing is made public, and he complains to Steffens that the Senate killed the Santo Domingo treaty along party lines.

Roosevelt lunches with Dr. Alexander Lambert and Secretary Metcalf and dines with Robert Wynne. He writes Senator Knox backing better training for coast and field artillery and urging that the rate bill become law.
The House passes the Hepburn bill

The House of Representatives approves the Hepburn railroad rate bill, a key piece of Roosevelt's program. He also meets House naval committee members about hazing at Annapolis, hosts the Army-Navy reception, and writes Francis Heney about corruption in San Francisco.

Roosevelt sees journalist Ray Stannard Baker at 12:45, confers with Senators Depew and Platt and editor Edward Butler on Buffalo jobs and on rates with Elkins, and gives a dinner for the Republican National Executive Committee.

Roosevelt creates the Indian Key bird reservation in Florida. He meets a National Businessmen's League delegation, sees Jusserand, and warns Bonaparte and Taft that ammunition stocks would fall short in a war.
Senators John Spooner and George Nixon call on Roosevelt at 9 p.m.
Alice turns 22; Bill Sewall at lunch

On Alice's 22nd birthday, Roosevelt lunches with his old Maine guide Bill Sewall, Guy Murchie and Taft, and the White House throws a dinner and musicale in her honor. In a lengthy letter to John St. Loe Strachey he covers presidential power and free trade and describes Nick as a fine fellow and Harvard's best violinist.

Roosevelt calls on Americans to help the people of Japan, then suffering a famine. He spends part of the day lunching and walking with John Burroughs, and tells Dr. Lambert he cannot write Wadsworth and Higgins about legislation.
A treaty to protect Niagara Falls

Roosevelt writes Root about a treaty with Canada to preserve Niagara Falls. He meets Bonaparte, receives members of the Dawes Commission among many callers, and writes Nevada Stranahan about Higgins and Odell.
Two days before the wedding, the White House gives a dinner for Nick Longworth. Booker T. Washington is among the day's visitors, and Roosevelt lunches with Moody and Crane.

On the eve of Alice's wedding, Roosevelt warns Bonaparte that the Army and Navy lack enough smokeless powder and writes John Hull about funding military training. He hears a Massachusetts group on pure food legislation and dines with Endicott and Fannie Peabody.

At noon on a clear, mild day, Alice Roosevelt, 22, marries Congressman Nicholas Longworth, 36, in the East Room before roughly 700 guests, with no bridesmaids. Her Lee grandparents are there, as are Sara Delano Roosevelt and young Franklin. Afterward Alice hugs Edith, and the couple leave to honeymoon in Cuba.
The day after the wedding, Roosevelt confers in the evening with Charles Stillings and Gifford Pinchot. Douglas and Corinne Robinson are staying at the White House.
A lock canal, not sea level

Roosevelt tells Congress he favors building a lock canal at Panama rather than a sea-level one. He meets railroad men and regulators on the rate bill, writes Speaker Cannon on the Knapp amendments, and Root sends Germany TR's specific proposals for Algeciras.

After Cabinet and a railroad session with Knox and Spooner, Roosevelt and Edith go to a dinner in their honor given by Agriculture Secretary James Wilson at the Willard. He writes William Ripley and Representative Edmund Hinshaw about the rate bill.
Admiral Togo's words for U.S. sailors

Roosevelt has the speech Admiral Togo gave his Japanese sailors reprinted for American sailors to read. He holds a string of rate-bill meetings, lunches with Bishop William Doane and Mrs. Doane, and writes Archbishop John Ireland about the Storers' indiscretions.
Hold the Hepburn bill as written

Roosevelt sees Lincoln Steffens in the morning and Speck von Sternberg at 6, and dines with Lodge. He tells Pennsylvania Railroad president Alexander Cassatt he wants the Hepburn bill passed unamended, and presses for stricter medical screening of immigrants arriving at Ellis Island. In Chicago, Taft argues for a standing army.

Roosevelt learns Ted has been put on academic probation at Harvard and writes him to buckle down, confident he can do it. He also defends Lodge to Lyman Abbott after The Outlook branded the senator a Massachusetts boss.

Roosevelt names Ralph Easley, Jeremiah Jenks and James Reynolds to investigate the immigration bureau, and asks Francis Robbins to help prevent a coal strike. He also works on the German tariff and a ship subsidy bill.
Roosevelt writes John Sleicher that the Hepburn bill has moved to the Senate and that the New York Times is mocking him over it.

The Sun River reclamation project in Montana is created. Roosevelt meets Senator Elkins about rail regulation and with Lodge on the Philippine tariff and statehood. He also tears into Carl Schurz's ideas in a letter to Oscar Straus on Morocco and Germany.

Roosevelt writes King Edward VII to thank him for his gift to Alice, adding words about Nick and the Russo-Japanese War. He asks Speaker Cannon for a new canal commission law and meets a long list of callers, among them England's Count Gleichen.
The Ladies' Home Journal prints a Roosevelt article on factory laws protecting working women and children.
Rail bill talks and a dinner for diplomats

Roosevelt opens the day with Senator Clapp, then huddles with Crane and Spooner over the railroad rate bill and sees Ambassador Jusserand. That night he dines with Choate, Porter, Root, Bacon and Captain Sperry, and writes Whitelaw Reid that France and Germany are deadlocked at Algeciras.
Roosevelt confers with Senator Spooner, receives Flint, Fulton and Warner, and in the afternoon meets Interstate Commerce chairman Knapp and James Garfield.
A christening for the Loeb baby

After a morning of meetings with Lodge, Allison, Cannon, Taft and others, Roosevelt and his wife Edith go to Bishop Satterlee's home for the christening of William Loeb's son. His essay holding up Washington as a model city appears in Charities and the Commons.

Roosevelt releases the Bureau of Corporations' findings on Standard Oil and sees Secretary Taft in the morning. Edith writes Kermit that Ted's slipping grades at Harvard have come at a bad time for his father.

Roosevelt formally asks Bellamy Storer to step down as ambassador in Vienna after Storer leaves his letters unanswered. He also asks Congress for more Army and Navy ammunition, sits for artist Helen Todd Hammond with Edith, and spends the evening at the Belasco Theatre.
Lunch talk on the Chinese indemnity
After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with Root, Taft, Elkins, Lawrence Abbott and the missionary Arthur Smith, among others.

Roosevelt goes to St. John's Church for General John Schofield's funeral after a busy morning on Puerto Rico and the railroad bill. In letters he weighs Harvard football and talk that he might one day lead the university, and admits he does not care for Mahan's latest history of the 1812 conflict.

Roosevelt addresses a delegation of the National Lumber Dealers Association, receives the justices of the Supreme Court and sees Jusserand. In the evening he and Loeb take up the Tillman-Gillespie resolution, and Root and Archbold call late.
Archie stands by a hurt classmate

At school Archie stays to help a boy struck in the eye by a baseball after the others flee. Roosevelt meets his Cabinet, Knox and Hopkins on the canal, and writes Edward Bacon about changes to the Hepburn bill. In Idaho, Haywood, Moyer and Pettibone are indicted in the Steunenberg murder.
A short telegram to Gordon Johnson
Roosevelt goes over Panama Canal progress with Senators Dryden and Ankeny and talks statehood with Beveridge. He wires Gordon Johnson, wounded in the Philippines, a short question.
Letters about the boys in the sandbox

Gordon Johnson wires back that he is well. Roosevelt sends Nannie Lodge a playful note about dinner talk and writes Kermit about how unlike Quentin and Archie are, the baseball episode, and the hours both boys spend in the sandbox.

Roosevelt talks over a Supreme Court appointment with Root and Taft, takes up statehood with Cannon and Watson, and receives the Chinese minister. He writes Agriculture Secretary Wilson about investigating the meatpackers in the wake of Upton Sinclair's The Jungle.

After the Cabinet meeting and a talk with Spooner about the Tillman-Gillespie measure, Roosevelt and Edith go to the National Theatre to hear the visiting Boston orchestra. He backs New Mexico governor Hagerman for ousting dishonest officials.
Talking consular reform at the White House

Roosevelt lunches with Alice and Nick Longworth and a table of diplomats and friends, then speaks at the White House to delegates of the Consular Reform Convention. He writes Baron Kaneko about the Portsmouth treaty and Count Witte's careless handling of documents.
A moral standard for the very rich

With Edith away at Groton for Kermit's confirmation, Roosevelt dines at the Longworths' and writes a flood of letters: to Taft on his choice between the Chief Justiceship and the presidency, to Root naming Charles Francis to replace Storer in Vienna, and to Upton Sinclair on Zola, Tolstoy and The Jungle.
Statehood and supper at the Lodges
Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, presses Speaker Cannon on statehood, and hosts a lunch that includes Will and Bamie Cowles. He takes dinner with the Lodges.
The muck-rake, first told at the Gridiron

Roosevelt meets Admiral Dewey, talks canal matters with Hepburn, and sees the German and French ambassadors. After dining with Speaker Cannon he goes on to the Gridiron Club's dinner at the New Willard, where he first compares a certain breed of journalist to the man with the muck-rake in Pilgrim's Progress. Dr. Rixey calls near midnight.
The record shows Roosevelt in Washington with no recorded activity.

Roosevelt meets Dryden, Elkins and Representative Garner on the canal and lunches with the Sternbergs and the Cowleses. He tells Kermit how the dogs Skip and Jack greeted Edith's return and that he has sent for Phineas Finn and De Quincey, and he fumes to Moody over a Debs article on the Haywood case.
After the Cabinet meeting and talks with Elkins and Jusserand, Roosevelt goes to Gifford Pinchot's home at night to meet the Keep Commission, then sees Ambassador Sternberg.
A gift from the King of Italy
The Italian chargé d'affaires delivers a present from King Victor Emmanuel, and Roosevelt then sits down with Samuel Gompers over labor bills. He dines with the Endicotts and Henry Adams.

Roosevelt meets Moody, Taft and Garfield, takes up Smithsonian business with Henderson, and goes to the opera. He thanks Charles Morrison for help on the meatpacking inquiry, tells Frank Morrison he will hold government contractors to the eight-hour day, and urges Moody to move on the alien contract labor question.
Oklahoma lands and evening with Bishop

After Cabinet and a railroad rate session, Roosevelt discusses Oklahoma public lands with Taft, Leupp and Lacey, lunches with Shiras and Holt, and sees both ambassadors. Joseph Bishop calls that night.

Roosevelt confers with Moody and prosecutor Francis Heney on the Bristol case, receives Olcott, Lacey, Campbell and A. W. Dunn of the Associated Press, and meets Moody, Metcalf and Garfield late in the evening.
Journalist Henry Needham and Postmaster General Cortelyou call on Roosevelt in the evening.
Federal troops and the Idaho trial

Roosevelt hears Charles Neill on breaches of the eight-hour law and writes Moody about using federal soldiers to keep the peace in Idaho during the Haywood trial. Other letters cover Kansas ranchers and the range laws, and charges over Cornelius Bliss's 1904 campaign fundraising.

Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, then gathers Taft, Moody, Knox and others to settle the Bristol appointment. He also discusses Puerto Rico with Representative Cooper and writes Bishop O'Gorman about Storer's removal.

Roosevelt receives Spooner, Bartholdt and Foss. He praises Lindsay Denison's Everybody's article on the canal, welcomes Andrew Carnegie's support on the rate bill, and writes Representative Foss about his bill for an enormous battleship.
Roosevelt hosts Root, Bacon, Governor Hoggatt and others at lunch, and has Senator Beveridge to dinner. He writes Thomas O'Brien about insurance bills.
The Cabinet meets on the threatened coal strike. Roosevelt talks railroad legislation with Dolliver, has Upton Sinclair to lunch along with Neill and Leupp, and dines with the Longworths.

Roosevelt holds a big railroad conference with senators and commissioners, takes up New York appointments with Wadsworth and the Five Civilized Tribes bill with La Follette. He writes Theodore Shonts about a coal commission and rebukes John Winder, a coal company president who opposed miners' raises and tried to undercut his conference.
Home alone with Skip and the kittens

With Edith and the younger children in Cuba, Roosevelt writes each of them: Kermit hears he is through volume one of Trollope's Phineas Finn and that the rate fight is heating up; Archie that Skip misses the family and Jack has run off; Quentin that the kittens will be ready to pet when he returns. He also names a new Washington postmaster over Senator Platt's friend.

Roosevelt confers with Elkins on the Hepburn bill amendment about judicial review and with Winthrop on Puerto Rico, then dines at Henry Adams's. He writes General Wood that he is pleased Wood is well and that no force will go to China.

Roosevelt hosts a dinner for Canada's Governor General, Earl Grey, who stays overnight at the White House with Lady Grey and their daughter. He also approves missionary Arthur Smith's idea of putting part of the Boxer indemnity toward scholarships for Chinese students in America.
Roosevelt works the rate bill with Hepburn and takes up Alaskan railroads with Burnham, Piles, Kinkaid, Ankeny and Tawney. He dines at the Lodges'.
Owen Wister arrives for a visit
Roosevelt receives a group of city mayors led by Chicago's Edward Dunne. In the evening his old friend Owen Wister arrives to stay through Saturday, and they dine with the Bacons and David Gray.

Roosevelt meets senators on the rate bill and lunches with Captain Seth Bullock among others. At dinner the table holds the Jusserands, the Longworths, Owen Wister and the Bay Lodges. He tells Lodge the Philippine tariff can wait until the railroad vote.
Roosevelt confers with Lacey on public lands, lunches with Moody, Spooner, Wister and others, and meets the Russian envoy Rosen. That night he joins the Boone and Crockett Club at the New Willard.
Sunday with the Danas and the Lodges
Roosevelt shares a midday meal with Richard Henry Dana and Mrs. Dana, sees Ambassador Sternberg, and dines with Dr. Bigelow and the Lodge and Gardner families.
Archie turns twelve; Bat Masterson at lunch

On Archie's twelfth birthday Roosevelt lunches with Taft, the Cowleses, Colonel Sanger and the old lawman Bat Masterson. He signs a bill easing hazing penalties at Annapolis, writes Ray Stannard Baker about his muckrake speech, and asks Gilder to set a date for H. G. Wells to come to lunch.

After the Cabinet meeting and a railroad session with Clapp, Nelson and Spooner, Roosevelt talks with Representative Burton about protecting Niagara Falls. He writes Oscar Straus about the plight of Russian Jews.

Roosevelt romps at "tickley" with Archie and Quentin and, with Captain Lee along, tries out his new horse Roswell for the first time. He reassures a jittery Upton Sinclair that the meatpacking abuses will not be swept under the rug.
A St. Bernard puppy for Archie

Roosevelt sees Taft, Cannon, Ambassador Sternberg and others. He writes Kermit about Archie's new St. Bernard puppy, just seven weeks old and the morning walks he and Edith take around the White House grounds.
After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt works the rate bill with Crane, Overman and Nelson and goes over Interior Department matters with Fulton. He writes John Kernan on the same railroad bill.

Roosevelt lays the cornerstone of the new House Office Building and repeats in public his warning against writers who see only the muck. He calls for federal oversight of interstate corporations, presses Congress to pass the Hepburn bill, and backs a progressive inheritance tax. He also talks Indiana politics with Hemenway and ship subsidies with Taft and Humphrey.
Roosevelt spends Easter Sunday in Washington; no other activity is recorded.
Easter Egg Roll for children only
The annual Easter Egg Roll fills the White House lawn until one o'clock, and Roosevelt keeps the adults out. He meets Moody and Taft, and his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson calls that night.
Roosevelt breakfasts with his cousin Emlen Roosevelt, meets the Cabinet, and takes up the rate bill with Spooner and Simmons. Francis Vinton Greene and James Garfield are among the afternoon callers.

A great earthquake strikes San Francisco before dawn, and fire follows, leveling hundreds of blocks and killing hundreds. In Washington Roosevelt carries on with rate bill meetings, sends Congress a special message on the beef packers' trial, wires California's governor about the disaster, and tells Taft he will send troops to Idaho.

Roosevelt calls on the nation to help San Francisco, sees a long list of senators and the German ambassador, and holds a reception for the DAR. On the Senate floor, newcomer Robert La Follette breaks custom by speaking on the Hepburn bill, and many senators walk out.
The Cabinet devotes its meeting to the San Francisco disaster. Roosevelt confers with Spooner and writes Edgar Wells about Ted at Harvard and Moody about the rate bill.

The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's muckrake address. He spends the morning on the rate bill with four senators, Allison among them, sees Jusserand in the afternoon, and receives Booker T. Washington that evening.
Apple blossoms and a healed eye

Edwin Emerson walks back from the Dutch Reformed Church with Roosevelt. He tells Kermit that Ted is over his eye surgery, the apple trees are in bloom, and Quentin is writing poetry, and writes Mabel Boardman about Red Cross relief for San Francisco.

Roosevelt declines to receive the Russian writer Maxim Gorky. He welcomes Admiral Campion and a party of French naval officers to a reception and dinner, and writes William Potter and Lyman Abbott about his proposed inheritance tax and taxes generally.
Honoring John Paul Jones at Annapolis
Roosevelt leaves Washington for the Naval Academy at Annapolis, where he speaks at the ceremonies for John Paul Jones.
Crediting Jusserand with keeping the peace

Roosevelt takes up San Francisco relief with Senator Flint and sees August Belmont. He writes Mayor Schmitz about the city's recovery, tells Jusserand he believes the ambassador kept France and Germany from war, and introduces F. W. Whitridge to King Edward VII ahead of the Spanish royal wedding.

Roosevelt meets the Interstate Commerce commissioners Knapp and Prouty on the rate bill, sees Archbishop Messmer and Jusserand, and answers two opposite complaints: one that he is too tough on labor, the other that he favors it and attacks great fortunes.

Roosevelt confers with Allison and Cullom and sits for a group photograph by Wiles with Root, Alger and two others. He writes Owen Wister a long letter on his new novel Lady Baltimore, which Edith loved and he found much to fault in, and on Black Americans and the Indianola post office.
Off down the Potomac on the Sylph

Roosevelt talks with Allison about court review in the Hepburn bill, then he and Edith set off for an afternoon cruise on the Sylph. He sends Whitelaw Reid a very long history of the road to the Algeciras conference, sharply doubting British ambassador Durand.
A lonely spot tied to Washington
Aboard the Sylph, Roosevelt and Edith visit a lonely spot linked to George Washington, then in ruins. At home it is his sister Corinne's 24th wedding anniversary.

Back in Washington, Roosevelt tells Kermit the White House flowers are blooming and Archie is drenching himself with a hose. He writes Lodge on Egypt, Wood, the anti-imperialists, Cuba and Santo Domingo, and thanks Henry White for his Algeciras work. Congress gives the War Secretary control of water diversion at Niagara Falls.
After the Cabinet meets, an act lets the Edison Electric company use certain southern California power sites for 40 years, paying rent each year. Roosevelt confers with Moody and Cannon.
Roosevelt sees Beveridge, Hopkins, Moody and the Associated Press man A. W. Dunn, then goes to Gallaudet College for its spring ceremonies. He dines with the Cowleses.
A step forward, not a leap

Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt's daughter Anna is born. Roosevelt receives Japan's new ambassador, Aoki, and writes Brooks Adams that the Hepburn bill moves reform ahead in measured steps that will disappoint the extremists.

Roosevelt decides to back the Allison amendment to the rate bill and, without fanfare, sends federal troops into Idaho ahead of the Haywood trial. Columbia's Nicholas Murray Butler and Dr. Bigelow are staying at the White House, and a bootmaker fits the President for new shoes.
Cape May warbler and Mount Vernon

Roosevelt publicly endorses the Hepburn bill with the Allison amendment, then takes Butler aboard the Sylph for a trip to Mount Vernon. He talks New York politics over dinner with Governor Higgins, and tells John Burroughs about a Cape May warbler he has just seen.
Roosevelt wires the Pennsylvania State Grange at Harrisburg explaining why he supports the Hepburn bill.

Roosevelt spends the day lobbying a long line of senators on the rate bill and lunches with Albert Shaw. In the evening he joins the crowd at the Arlington Hotel celebrating Uncle Joe Cannon's seventieth. He assures Hannah Schoff, who leads the national mothers' congress, that Mormons have given up polygamy.

The Cabinet discusses the California disaster and Secretary Metcalf's trip west. Roosevelt meets Kansas Attorney General Davidson on the Standard Oil cases, receives the old Confederate raider John Mosby, and lunches with James Speyer.
H. G. Wells comes to lunch

Roosevelt meets Upton Sinclair in the morning and lunches with H. G. Wells, then touring America for a newspaper series. The two disagree, but Roosevelt tells Wells that even if nations must decline, he chooses to live as if America will not, and that the effort is worth it.

Roosevelt talks New York politics and lunches with Taft. He tells Isaac MacVeagh he will follow his inheritance tax proposal with a graduated income tax, presses Allison on the Philippine tariff, and gives Quentin's teacher at the Force School leave to discipline him.

Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and goes over Indian policy with Hitchcock and Leupp. Meanwhile the Senate adopts four Allison amendments to the rate bill, and he grumbles to Senator McCumber about the flood of pension bills in Congress.

Roosevelt meets labor leaders Gompers and Frank Morrison about breaches of the eight-hour law and a bill to curb injunctions. He asks Commerce and Labor Secretary Metcalf to investigate the labor of women and children, and writes George Horace Lorimer at length about David Graham Phillips's novel The Plum Tree.
Evening call at a servicemen's club
Roosevelt dines with the Lodges, the Lowells and the Luces, confers with Root, Taft and Lodge, and looks in on a club for soldiers, sailors and Marines that evening.
Carl Schurz, the reformer and former senator, dies. Roosevelt works the rate bill with Allison, Moody and two other senators and writes Allison about Senator Tillman's opposition.
Civil service reformers at the White House
After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt welcomes delegates to the convention of the civil service reformers' league. Garfield and James Reynolds see him at night.
Naval affairs and a stream of senators
Roosevelt goes over naval matters with Representatives Sherman and Cocks, meets Moody and Cortelyou, and receives a run of senators and congressmen.
A wedding in the Harlan family
Roosevelt sees Justice Harlan's granddaughter married and urges the Interstate Commerce Commission to value railroad property, an idea not carried out until 1912.

The Senate passes the Hepburn Act, Roosevelt's hard-won railroad rate law, giving the Interstate Commerce Commission power to set railroad and express rates and reach over pipelines and sleeping cars. He meets the Cabinet and sends Gilder a note about a piece on old Irish sagas for The Century.

Roosevelt sees Cannon, Hepburn and others. He writes Lodge about the flap involving Chandler, Bailey and Tillman and the rate bill, Charles Keep on inefficiency at Interior and the printing office, and William Curtis on western irrigation.
Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie that the rate bill passed in fine shape and that Japan's new ambassador, Aoki, has given him a suit of old armor. He writes Ted about Dickens.

Senator Carter confers with Roosevelt on the Panama Canal among a run of callers. He has Egan, Hyde and Joseph Dunn to lunch and tells canal engineer John Stevens the Y.M.C.A. has sent A. Bruce Minear to Panama.
Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and receives Shonts, Cannon, Taft, General Wilson, the AP reporter A. W. Dunn and others.
Roosevelt confers with Senator Aldrich and a long list of callers, and writes Beveridge about press stories claiming the President inspired his speech on meat inspection.
Roosevelt confers on Delaware politics and the Chicago stockyards, lunches with his friend Philip Stewart, and gives a dinner for Japan's Ambassador Aoki with the Forakers, Hales, Lodges and Pellews.
Beveridge offers a meat inspection amendment
Senator Beveridge attaches a meat inspection amendment to the agriculture appropriations bill. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and confers with Allison, Knox and Hepburn on Panama and the railroads.
Rounding up votes for meat inspection

Roosevelt spends the day in meetings with Cannon, Cullom, Neill and others on the Beveridge plan to inspect meat, lunches with Root, Taft, Nick Longworth and Crane, and writes James Wadsworth about the amendment.

Moody and Hitchcock call in the evening. Roosevelt writes Hitchcock about charges against Oklahoma's governor Frantz and Commissioner Cade, and urges Speaker Cannon to pass the immigration bill, which did not pass.
Roosevelt keeps at the beef inspection fight with Beveridge, Neill and Carter. He writes Harry Rubens, once Schurz's secretary, of his sorrow at Carl Schurz's death.
Wichita forest and a trip to Norfolk

Oklahoma gains the new Wichita National Forest, with added land for its game preserve. Roosevelt sails for Norfolk on the Mayflower that afternoon after writing Sinclair, Beveridge, naturalist Henry Bigelow, and Hepburn, whom he wants to be sure the new act can reach Standard Oil and the coal-carrying railroads.
Monument in Portsmouth, speech at Hampton
On Memorial Day in Portsmouth, Virginia, Roosevelt speaks at the dedication of a veterans' monument, then addresses Hampton Institute on the education of Black Americans.

Back in Washington, Roosevelt meets Beveridge, Cannon and two others on beef inspection, lunches with the Sternbergs, and attends a dinner for Justice Henry Brown at the New Willard. He writes Garfield about Standard Oil and the railroad monopolies.

Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and works on the meat inspection amendment with Wadsworth, Crumpacker and Reynolds. That evening at the Congregational Church he addresses Howard University's graduating class.

Roosevelt receives the report of Charles Neill and James Reynolds on conditions in the Chicago stockyards. He sees congressmen and Moody, meets Dr. Egan and Father Zahm in the afternoon, and Senator Penrose at night.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded for the day.
Packinghouse message, and a sprained ankle

Roosevelt sends Congress a special message calling for federal meat inspection, with the Neill-Reynolds findings attached. He breakfasts with Albert Shaw, lunches with Dr. Egan and Father Zahm, and turns his ankle at tennis but keeps playing a couple more sets.

Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, receives the railway special agents' association, and dines with the Lodges. He writes Senator Perkins about enlarging Yosemite National Park and General Wood about Grover Cleveland's vote on the immigration bill.
Schoolgirls in the morning, cadets at night
Roosevelt speaks to the graduating girls of the National Cathedral School in the morning, and in the early evening watches Washington's High School Cadets drill at the American League ball grounds.
Roosevelt confers with Speaker Cannon, receives a Cooper Union delegation and a run of senators, and in the evening meets Reynolds and Neill again on the packinghouse findings.

The Antiquities Act passes, giving the President power to proclaim landmarks, ancient ruins and other places of historic or scientific value on federal land as national monuments. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and Neill on the beef trust, and the Agriculture Department's packinghouse report goes to Congress.
Opening the house at Sagamore Hill

Edith goes ahead to ready Sagamore Hill for summer. Roosevelt tells Kermit his ankle has gotten much worse since Monday's tennis, that Dr. Sturgis Bigelow is visiting amid days of rain, and that he is glad Kermit will stay another year at Groton.
Lodge, Gardner and Metcalf call on Roosevelt late in the evening.

All national forest land is opened to farm settlement. Roosevelt meets Knox on the canal and Cannon, Beveridge and others on meat inspection, hosts a large lunch with the Tafts, Fairbanks, Garfield and Pinchot, and writes Ethel that he already misses her mother and their Long Island home.

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt confers with a California delegation about rebuilding San Francisco and with Missourians about packinghouse conditions. He wires Treasury Secretary Shaw, annoyed by Shaw's protectionist speeches in Iowa.
Roosevelt takes up canal matters with Hepburn, sees several congressmen and Taft, and receives cartoonist Homer Davenport in the morning and Joseph Bishop in the afternoon.
Roosevelt discusses Delaware politics with Allee, meets members of the Immigration Protective League, and gives the morning commencement address at Georgetown University.
Beveridge does not speak for him

Roosevelt confers with Cannon, Hopkins and Reynolds and with three congressmen on the meat inspection bill. He writes Wadsworth on the bill and warns Beveridge that nothing he says should be taken as the administration's official view.

Roosevelt signs the Statehood Bill and spends the day on the canal, San Francisco's rebuilding and the Chicago stockyards. He praises Idaho Governor Gooding to Calvin Cobb for pursuing Steunenberg's killers, and explains to Minnie Kimberly why he missed his Uncle Robert's funeral.

Roosevelt writes Ethel about how they both love poking through attics and wonder about mental telepathy, and notes she will teach Sunday school this summer. He writes Tawney about a travel allowance for the President and Platt about a New York appointment he opposes, and confers with Cannon that evening.

Roosevelt meets Allison and Representative Humphrey on beef legislation and lunches with Grant La Farge. He writes Finley Peter Dunne about Mr. Dooley, wires Russell Alger about a lock canal, and writes Platt again on the New York appointment.
Roosevelt signs a joint resolution enlarging Yosemite National Park. He also talks the meat bill over with Beveridge and Judge Cowan and with Bonaparte on Maryland patronage.

Simon Wolf meets Roosevelt about massacres of Jews in Russia. He also takes up South Dakota appointments, Oklahoma politics, and a stream of callers, and warns a North Carolina revenue collector to keep honest or lose his job.

The Senate approves a lock canal for Panama. Roosevelt confers with Representative Boutell about a training ship for the Great Lakes, and writes George Carter on island sugar interests and Owen Wister a postscript on the Indianola post office.
The Cabinet takes up the Standard Oil prosecutions. Roosevelt receives senators and congressmen and tells Hitchcock what he thinks of La Follette's complaints about the Indian bill.
No fan of Wister's new book
Roosevelt discusses South Dakota patronage and Standard Oil proceedings, and at night meets Flint, Hitchcock, Pinchot and Walcott. He tells Winthrop Chanler he dislikes Owen Wister's new book.
Saving a kitten on the way to church

Walking to church, Roosevelt rescues a kitten from two dogs and hands it to a Black girl, he tells Ethel, who is looking after her two youngest brothers on Long Island while Edith stays with him. He signs himself the Tyrant, adds a sketch, and urges the newlywed Longworths to visit Budapest on their honeymoon to learn about Austria-Hungary.

Roosevelt meets Cannon and Hepburn, plans his Panama trip with Taft, and receives the British and French ambassadors among many callers. In New York, Harry Thaw shoots and kills the architect Stanford White in Madison Square Garden in a jealous rage over his wife, Evelyn Nesbit.
Put the date on the can

Roosevelt confers on Montana appointments and dines with Lodge. He tells Gilder that Taft is not the man to speak on the tariff, urges Cannon to require packing dates on canned meat, and complains to Senator Cullom that the Senate is stalling the Algeciras treaty.
A pile of letters on canal and treaty

Roosevelt takes up Indian appropriations, lunches with Robert Bacon and has Gardner, Scott and his brother-in-law Will Cowles to dinner. His letters range over German-American relations and Venezuela, the Algeciras treaty, the type of canal for Panama, Poultney Bigelow's charges against the canal commission, Arizona statehood and an immigration inquiry.
Roosevelt reviews the National Guard parade, receives senators and officials including F. B. Kellogg, and dines with Taft, Moody and Bacon. He writes Neill about the immigration investigation.
Hepburn Act signed; Mesa Verde created

A landmark day: Roosevelt signs the Hepburn railroad rate act. A Grand Canyon game preserve of nearly 1.5 million acres is authorized, and Platt and Mesa Verde national parks are created. He dines with Will Cowles, Root and Bacon.
Pure food and meat inspection become law

As Congress adjourns, Roosevelt signs the Pure Food and Drug Act and the agricultural appropriation that carries the new meat inspection law, and sends Beveridge the pen used on the meat bill. He also approves a law on shooting in the District that makes three-quarters of it a wildlife refuge, and leaves at midnight for Oyster Bay. Alice and Nick head to Cincinnati before sailing for Europe.

On his first day home at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about business combinations and organized labor out in the Rockies, setting his trust policy beside Cleveland's, which he finds close to his own, and Bryan's, which he sees as its opposite.
The New York World, usually hostile to Roosevelt, runs an editorial applauding him for enforcing the laws already on the books.
Thanks to the World's editorial writer
Roosevelt thanks Frank Cobb for his World editorial on law enforcement and writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler about the rate law and Taft. Guests at Sagamore Hill include Cecilia May and a Roosevelt cousin.
Fourth of July in Oyster Bay

Roosevelt gives the Independence Day address in Oyster Bay. Secretary of State Root sets off on a goodwill tour of South America that will last until late September, and Alice and Nick drop in at the American embassy in London.
Roosevelt writes Navy Secretary Bonaparte about Root's goodwill voyage to South America.
Sir Joseph Ward, premier of New Zealand, comes to Sagamore Hill for lunch.
Taft visits to discuss Army business. Roosevelt wires Whitelaw Reid about canned meat and tells Commander William Sims he is heartened by the Navy's improved gunnery.
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
John Heard Jr. signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
The record places Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill with no further detail.
Roosevelt's physician and friend Alexander Lambert visits, and Barclay Farr is a guest.
The record places Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill with no further detail.
Roosevelt wires Robert Bacon about the danger of war between Guatemala and El Salvador. E. Du Pont Irving and Elisha Gilbert are among the house guests.
The record places Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill with no further detail.

Roosevelt confers with Taft and Bacon on Latin American affairs and gathers them with Whitridge, Finley Peter Dunne, police commissioner Bingham and Dr. Lambert. Far off in Alaska, on St. Paul Island, seal poachers are fired on as trespassers; five die and two are wounded.
Roosevelt dines at the home of Mrs. J. West Roosevelt.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Guatemala and El Salvador settle their quarrel at a Central American conference held on the U.S. cruiser Marblehead.
Roosevelt writes Senator Knute Nelson about the Bureau of Corporations and Henry White about Archbishop Ireland, the Storers and Root's South American trip.
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Speaker Cannon, Senator Penrose and three other party men lunch at Sagamore Hill and talk strategy for the congressional elections.
The banker Mortimer Schiff visits Roosevelt in the evening.
Roosevelt writes James Watson about drafting the main Republican campaign statement for the 1906 elections himself.
Roosevelt writes Jacob Schiff about America as a haven for Jews fleeing Russia.
Lunch with Gordon Johnston, and thoughts on Bryan

Roosevelt confers with E. E. Clark on the Interstate Commerce Commission and lunches with Lieutenant and Mrs. Gordon Johnston, General Barry, Bacon and others. He writes Taft about Chinese labor on the canal, and praises Whitelaw Reid for defending American meat inspection in England and for handling the visiting Bryan, about whom he has strong feelings.
Charles Emory Smith lunches with Roosevelt to talk about Pennsylvania politics.
Roosevelt goes to services at the Oyster Bay Presbyterian Church, where the Rev. Charles Thompson of the Home Missions Board preaches. Thompson, the Washburns and the Russells join him for lunch.
Roosevelt tells Representative Edgar Crumpacker that revising the tariff is not possible in the near term.

Senator Dick and Elmer Dover lunch with Roosevelt to talk Ohio and Midwest politics, and Admiral Mahan and Grant La Farge are guests. He writes William Allen White about his book Stratagems and Spoils, Bryan, the meat law and the rate law. In Cuba, rebels rise against President Estrada Palma.
Roosevelt tells Yale president Arthur Hadley he liked his Harper's essay on how wealth and democracy play out on American campuses.
A new governor for the Philippines
Roosevelt writes Taft that Henry Ide will step down from the top post in Manila and that James Smith should succeed him, and comments on Taft's views on the islands and Panama.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Edith turns 45; a picnic in the boats

On Edith's 45th birthday Roosevelt hosts neighbors and Henry Stimson at lunch, meets Senator Penrose, and ends the day with a picnic out in the boats. He tells Lodge he is truly resting this summer, muses to Lyman Abbott about joining The Outlook after the presidency, and plans the September fleet review. Archie is off for a week's sail with Captain Joshua Slocum.
The Hague and the Spanish claims
Roosevelt writes Moody about the Spanish Treaty Claims Commission and tells Whitelaw Reid that English thinking on the Hague Conference matches America's.
Roosevelt and Kermit row Edith over to Lloyd's Neck, where they share a picnic supper with about twenty people, and they pull back home under the stars.

Roosevelt meets former Senator Jones and Barnsdall about the Standard Oil investigation. He praises Frederick Oliver's Alexander Hamilton and weighs Hamilton against Jefferson, and tells Lodge he is a bit more hopeful about the November congressional races but would not wager on them.
Worry over Japan and the seals
Roosevelt writes Bonaparte about the coming naval review and his concern that July's seal poaching killings could stir trouble with Japan.
Alice and Nick home from Europe

Alice and Nick come back from Europe and the whole family gathers at Sagamore Hill before the couple goes on to Rookwood, the Longworths' house in Ohio. Roosevelt writes John Sleicher on the tariff and William Allen White on Taft's chances for 1908.
Arthur Woods signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

On Ethel's 14th birthday Roosevelt talks congressional campaign strategy with Sherman and Nick Longworth and canal matters with Shonts and Joseph Bishop. Willard Straight, Henry Taft and Robert Bridges are guests.

At night in Brownsville, Texas, gunfire kills a white bartender and wounds two policemen; men of three Black Army companies at Fort Brown are blamed, and none will confess or name others. Roosevelt writes Henry White about the Kaiser and the 1902 Venezuela ultimatum, tells Robert Bridges of Ted's poem in Scribner's under a pen name, and writes Taft on Panama.
Keeping immigration out of the Watson letter
Roosevelt answers Speaker Cannon's objections to his tariff statement and tells Lodge he will leave immigration out of the campaign letter he is writing for James Watson.
Moody and Bacon confer with Roosevelt and stay the night. He writes Bonaparte about the possibility of scrapping the frigate Constitution.

James S. Harlan gets a seat on the ICC. Roosevelt has Cleveland Dodge and General John Wilson to lunch and writes Cortelyou on railroad rates for mail and Taft on Bigelow's attacks on the canal commission.

Roosevelt congratulates Root on his South American tour, and tells Kermit that Quentin is a pagan philosopher who swims and rides well while Archie dotes on his sailboat Why. He sums up his presidency for Trevelyan, fearing the pendulum may swing against him, sends James Watson his statement of Republican aims, and praises Winston Churchill's novel Coniston.
Teresa and Clifford Richardson and William Sheffield Cowles are guests at Sagamore Hill.

After lunch with Admiral Robley Evans, Roosevelt tells the public printer, Charles Stillings, that he favors spelling reform and wants government publications to use simplified spellings. He also forces Senator Spooner's brother out as superintendent of the Indian warehouse.

Father York and two other priests call at 11 a.m. Roosevelt tells Neill he has read his eight-hour law report and wires Stillings with concern over a threatened walkout by government printers seeking an eight-hour day.
Journalist Henry Beach Needham calls on Roosevelt.
Roosevelt talks campaign plans with Cortelyou, hears from General J. F. Bell about the Brownsville shooting, and confers with Gifford Pinchot.

Roosevelt writes Pinchot about reclaiming and irrigating western lands as an irrigation conference meets in Boise. He wires acting War Secretary Ainsworth to have the battalion bring the accused Brownsville soldiers to San Antonio and hold them under guard.
Robert Bacon and Dr. Hollander confer with Roosevelt about Chile.
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt directs the government printer to adopt simplified spelling in all public documents from now on, and adds a gleeful postscript to Taft calling it his first letter in the new style. He also chides Hitchcock about the Interior Department's poor treatment of Indians.
Spelling aims, and Moody may go
Roosevelt explains his goals for simplified spelling to Charles Scott of the Simplified Spelling Board and writes Moody, who is weighing leaving the Cabinet for private life.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Postmaster General Cortelyou meets Roosevelt in the morning.

Roosevelt pushes his simplified spelling plan, first urged on him by Brander Matthews of Columbia, which respells some 300 words like thru, tho and catalog. The government will not adopt it, but he keeps the spellings the rest of his life. He talks New York politics with Parsons, and riots erupt in Atlanta.
Wary of sending troops to Cuba

Roosevelt tells Army Chief of Staff Bell he is reluctant to send soldiers to put down the Cuban insurrection. He backs Charles Evans Hughes for New York governor in a letter to Jacob Schurman and tells Taft that Edith and Taft, not Loeb, will go with him to Panama. The Sternbergs and the La Farges are among the guests.
Ambassador Sternberg, Dr. and Mrs. Rixey, the writer James B. Connolly and Grant and Florence La Farge are staying at Sagamore Hill.
Reviewing the fleet from the Mayflower

From the deck of the Mayflower, Roosevelt reviews the ships of the North Atlantic Squadron with a party that includes the Dunnes, the Bacons, the Bonapartes, the La Farges and Commander Sims, and has the Dunnes and Bacons to dinner aboard.

Roosevelt writes Gardner on immigration limits, asks Vice President Fairbanks to speak in Chicago, sends Root a long letter on his tour, the naval review, the elections, Bryan and Hughes for governor, and writes Lodge about the Supreme Court choice.
An evening at the Masonic lodge

Roosevelt hears tariff reformers H. E. Miles and Lyman Bass, talks New York politics over lunch with Cortelyou and Littauer, and spends time at his Masonic lodge in town. He defends Joe Cannon to Edgar Clark and writes Florence La Farge about the Greek play Electra.
Alice and Nick are staying at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt lunches with W. H. H. Llewellyn and writes Andrew Carnegie about limits on battleship size and the Hague Conference.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie and her husband Will Cowles are guests, and he confers with A. R. Page.

Roosevelt speaks at Christ Church in Oyster Bay for its 200th anniversary and confers with Bacon and Reynolds. He wires Bonaparte to send two warships to Cuba to protect American interests, and tells James Bede that his Watson letter will be his only endorsement of Republican candidates.
Roosevelt writes Sir George Otto Trevelyan about Arthur Balfour and British distrust of him, and about unrest in Cuba and the Newfoundland dispute.
Roosevelt goes over state politics with Governor Higgins of New York and lunches with Homer Saint-Gaudens. He writes Admiral Converse about naval armament and Bacon about the Cuban insurrection.
Roosevelt writes Wilson on meatpacking and the elections, Treasury Secretary Shaw on the tariff and Augustus Saint-Gaudens's new coin designs, and Strachey that he liked his piece on spelling reform.
Roosevelt works on his Annual Message. He writes Samuel Harper about Aaron Burr, tells Lodge of his dislike of Winston Churchill, and wires Bacon, and Bonaparte, to send more ships to Havana.

On Ted's 19th birthday, Roosevelt learns that 125 Marines have gone ashore in Cuba without his authority and wires Bacon to pull them back to the ships. He writes Moody on the Washington ice trust, Standard Oil and spelling, and Harvard's President Eliot about honoring Walter Reed.
Ready to send troops to Cuba

Roosevelt meets Taft, Bacon and Bonaparte about the revolt in Cuba, lunches on the Mayflower and greets a yacht race delegation. He tells Bacon that if President Palma resigns he will send troops, and explains to Cuban Minister Quesada why that is necessary.
The Knoxes come to Sagamore Hill
Senator and Mrs. Knox are guests, and Woodruff, Sherman and Albert Shaw call. Roosevelt tells Pinchot he wants Taft to campaign in Idaho.
No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Cannon about the party's election preparations and Taft about readying the Army for possible intervention in Cuba, a lock canal, and the outlook in Colorado and Idaho.
Roosevelt writes Indian Commissioner Leupp about Flynn, Frantz and investigations in the Indian service.
Father Power calls in the morning. A proclamation opens Oklahoma land to homesteaders, and an order extends the eight-hour day to government work.

Roosevelt lunches with Jacob Riis, William Allen White and others, hosts Senator and Mrs. Knox overnight, and dines with Archbishop Ireland and Bishop O'Gorman. He wires Taft asking whether Americans are financing the Cuban revolutionists and demands an honest count in Arizona's statehood vote.
Taft and Bacon sent to Havana
Roosevelt wires Taft about landing troops in Havana, concluding that Washington cannot keep President Palma in power, and sends Taft and Assistant Secretary of State Bacon to Cuba.

Roosevelt presses Senator Knox to campaign, tells Harvard's Eliot that few Americans have funded the Cuban rebels and that Leonard Wood is needed in Cuba again, and wires Taft twice approving his moves to restore order.

Roosevelt writes Kermit that he and Edith are off for a row, that he plays tennis daily and is cutting trees to keep the view open. Quentin hopes to join his friend Mike Landon at the Fay School, which pains Edith; Archie is sailing with Emlen; and the family went to church, where Ethel met them after Sunday school.
Devils Tower, the first national monument
Roosevelt proclaims Devils Tower in Wyoming the first national monument under the new Antiquities Act.

With Taft in Cuba, Roosevelt wires that President Palma should resign and that U.S. troops will go in if needed; he wants order restored without a drawn-out guerrilla war. He also writes Whitelaw Reid about Bryan.
Ralph Peters calls at noon among other visitors, and Roosevelt wires Taft three times about the rebels in Cuba.
Corinne's birthday; big guns for battleships

On his sister Corinne's 45th birthday, Roosevelt vents to Lodge about congressional critics of his Cuba moves, especially Foraker, and praises Commander Sims's answer to Mahan: both favor battleships armed only with big guns.
Off to Provincetown; land the troops

Roosevelt sails on the Mayflower for Provincetown and a review of the Atlantic fleet, with Grant La Farge along. He explains his Cuba policy to Senator Foraker and wires Taft three times, agreeing to a provisional government and telling him to land troops.

Roosevelt boards the battleship Missouri in Buzzards Bay for target practice and lunch, then heads back to Oyster Bay on the Mayflower. Wireless telegrams relayed to Taft order the Marines ashore at once.
Roosevelt wires Taft that 6,000 American soldiers are bound for Cuba. Secretary Root finishes his South American tour, reporting a remarkable journey and an enthusiastic welcome across the continent.

The Roosevelts shut up Sagamore Hill for the season and Roosevelt heads south, talking New York politics with Charles Evans Hughes aboard the train. That evening he meets Moody and Root in Washington.

The Cabinet meets on the crisis in Cuba, and a stream of callers follows, Knox and Foraker among them. Roosevelt wires Secretary Taft on how the Army should keep order on the island and writes Hughes about his odds in the governor's race.
Roosevelt puts Charles E. Magoon in charge of Cuba as its interim governor, then has dinner with both the Magoon and Root families. He tells Root he is unhappy with the American minister in Havana.

Roosevelt makes a day trip into Pennsylvania with Knox, Penrose and Dr. Rixey, speaking at the dedication of the new capitol in Harrisburg and then at the York fair before heading home. He writes Hughes about Catholic voters as Hughes trails William Randolph Hearst.

After a Cabinet session, Roosevelt names C. H. Robb an associate justice of the District's Court of Appeals. He sends Hughes more encouragement and answers Senator Beveridge about congressional pushback on his Cuba policy.

Roosevelt confers on Cuba with Magoon and General Bell and later sees Ambassador Speck von Sternberg. To Interior Secretary Hitchcock he writes about findings that Senator Warren took part in fencing off public land, findings Roosevelt set aside, opening a rift that ended with Hitchcock's resignation.

Roosevelt spends Sunday on politics with James S. Sherman and Senator Penrose, then has Sherman to dinner. He wires Taft about the so-called horse order, which let Cuban rebels keep the horses they had seized.
Canal talk and a court reception

Roosevelt works through New York and Indiana politics with Sherman and Overstreet, discusses the canal with Theodore Shonts, and hosts a White House reception for the Supreme Court. He tells Lodge that E. H. Harriman will give nothing to Hughes because of the administration's stand on corporations.
Antitrust plans with Root and Bonaparte

Between a Cabinet meeting and talks on Illinois politics with Hopkins and with Tawney, Roosevelt sits down with Root and Bonaparte on antitrust law. He asks Oscar Straus to help swing Jewish voters to Hughes.
Kermit's seventeenth birthday. Roosevelt receives Cabinet members, Father A. P. Doyle, Major J. M. Burke and others, holds a reception for Spanish War veterans, and wires Taft on Cuba.

San Francisco's school board orders Japanese children out of the city's regular schools, and that afternoon Roosevelt sees Japanese Ambassador Aoki. Earlier he talks Cuba with Spooner and New York politics with W. J. Youngs; Arthur Lee arrives to stay at the White House. It is also his niece Eleanor's 22nd birthday.
Lunch with Arthur Lee; a night at the theater

Roosevelt talks New York politics with Ward and Wainwright, shares lunch with Admiral Cowles, Paul Morton and Arthur Lee, and takes Edith to the theater. He tells James S. Sherman that Cortelyou and Bliss oppose Hyde for an ambassadorship.

Charles E. Magoon replaces Taft as Cuba's provisional governor. Roosevelt discusses Cuban annexation and his annual message with Beveridge, sits for photographer Mrs. DeWentworth, and in the evening speaks to about 45 members of the Aztec Club.
Wishing an old Assembly friend well

Roosevelt meets Cannon and Watson at dinnertime. He sends good wishes to William O'Neil, a friend from his Albany Assembly days now running for the state senate, and writes Woodruff again on the New York races.
Thanking Arthur Lee for crossing the Atlantic

Roosevelt goes over Delaware politics with Allee, DuPont and Ball and Ohio politics with Grosvenor. He thanks Arthur Lee for coming from England at his request to talk over Anglo-American problems, a sign of his low regard for British Ambassador Durand.
Called a Socialist on the stump

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt confers with Root and Cortelyou and lunches with Governor Montague, McBee and Allison. He writes Lodge about the New York contest and about charges that he is a dangerous radical and a Socialist.
Dentist at noon, Indian agents at night

Roosevelt helps Root shape a campaign speech for Hughes, sees Cortelyou, and visits the dentist at noon. He lunches with Knox over Pennsylvania politics and that night meets the government's Indian agents.

Nephew Sheffield Cowles turns eight. Roosevelt reviews the annual message with Knox, sees Colonel McCook, and dines with Robert Bacon, the Tafts, General Greene and Kohlsaat; Kohlsaat stays the night.
A Cabinet meeting, then a session with Attorney General Moody about prosecuting the trusts.

Roosevelt meets Justices Harlan, White and Day about the coming Supreme Court vacancy, then goes over bids for canal work with Ropes, Bishop, Root and Taft. He explains to Lodge why he will not write Gussie Gardner a personal endorsement.
Treasury Secretary Shaw comes by at night to discuss federal finances. Roosevelt asks Woodruff to keep his planned Cabinet shuffle quiet until October 23.

A photographer named Dunn catches Roosevelt signing the Thanksgiving proclamation. He confers on canal contracts, on the campaign trips of Taft and Root, and on the Standard Oil case, and writes Sir Edward Grey on the Hague Conference and disarmament.

Roosevelt announces the Cabinet that will serve from March 4, 1907: Root at State, Cortelyou at Treasury, Taft at War, Bonaparte as Attorney General, Meyer as Postmaster General, Metcalf at Navy, Garfield at Interior, Wilson at Agriculture and Straus at Commerce and Labor. He writes Kermit about Archie racing the dog Skip.
Roosevelt and Metcalf review conditions at Ellis Island. Cabinet members, Henry Lee Higginson and Herman Ridder come by, and he urges Republicans to stand together in the elections.

Roosevelt confers with Secretary Wilson, shares lunch with Cowles, Taft, Root and Jusserand, and takes up Cuban finances with J. D. Terrill. To John St. Loe Strachey he writes about Hearst, Bryan and Hughes.
Taking the school fight to court

Roosevelt names A. W. Cooley an assistant attorney general and goes riding with Speck von Sternberg while Edith, Ethel and Archie head down the Potomac by boat. He assures Baron Kaneko that the Justice Department is moving against San Francisco's segregation of Japanese pupils.

Roosevelt turns 48. A New York club of Hungarian-American Republicans stops by to wish him well, and he spends much of the day on California's treatment of Japanese schoolchildren, conferring with Metcalf and writing Senator Hale. Hugo Munsterberg joins Root and Metcalf for lunch.
Edith, Ethel and Archie come home from their river trip. In the afternoon Roosevelt and Quentin attend an open-air service on Cathedral Heights led by the old Rough Rider chaplain.
Troops ready to protect the Japanese

With his Panama trip ahead, Roosevelt gives Root authority to call out federal forces to shield Japanese residents if needed. He also asks Moody to look into a Wisconsin court order against the iron molders' union.
Another round on New York politics with Root and Cortelyou, then lunch with Admiral Cowles and a Mr. Kitigaki. Booker T. Washington calls at nine that evening.
Off to Pine Knot with Edith
Roosevelt hears from Hawaii's acting governor, Atkinson, about labor conditions in the islands, then leaves in the afternoon with Edith for their Virginia retreat, Pine Knot.
Roosevelt is at Pine Knot. In New York, Elihu Root gives a forceful speech at Utica on behalf of Charles Evans Hughes.
Roosevelt is at Pine Knot. The source records nothing more.
The source places Roosevelt in Richmond, Virginia, with no further detail.
Roosevelt leaves Pine Knot for Washington and writes Kermit that he and Edith had a fine stay, with some turkey hunting for him.

Roosevelt orders the soldiers of three Black infantry companies tied to the Brownsville, Texas, shooting dismissed from the Army, a decision that will dog him for years. He lunches with Arthur Lee and leaves at midnight for Oyster Bay to vote.
Election day: Hughes wins New York

Roosevelt casts his ballot at Oyster Bay and returns to Washington. Hughes wins the New York governorship, Nick Longworth keeps his House seat, and Gooding is chosen governor of Idaho. Lolo National Forest in Montana is created.
Labor leaders on the anti-injunction bill

Samuel Gompers and other labor men press Roosevelt about the anti-injunction measure sponsored by Pearre. He congratulates Hughes on his win and tells Alice he admired the campaign she and Nick ran in Ohio.

Roosevelt and Edith take the yacht Mayflower down the river to Chesapeake Bay and transfer to the new 16,000-ton battleship Louisiana to start their voyage to Panama. Before leaving he thanks Taft for a speech that helped the party in Idaho.
Aboard the Louisiana, the presidential party passes Cape Hatteras.
The Louisiana runs south along the coast, off Savannah, Georgia.
Big guns named Tedd and the Big Stick

Off Jacksonville, Roosevelt writes Quentin about the pets on board and tells Archie that the Tennessee and Washington are escorting them and that two of the ship's guns carry the nicknames Tedd and The Big Stick. Meanwhile Edith watches the crew's inspection and writes Aunt Lizzie that she has studied canal maps closely.
Cuba and Haiti on the horizon
With both Cuba and Haiti in view, Roosevelt and Edith talk over the islands' past. He writes Navy Secretary Bonaparte full of praise for the Louisiana and her men, with a few suggestions.
Reading Milton and Tacitus at sea

Nearing Colón, Roosevelt admits to Kermit he is "a little bored" while Edith is loving the voyage. He passes time with Milton, Tacitus and the German novel Jörn Uhl, walks the deck, inspects the ship, and recalls the troopships that carried him to Cuba eight years before.

The Louisiana drops anchor at Colón. After a big reception on board, Roosevelt and Edith sleep on the ship. He writes Ted that the clean, well-run battleship shows America at its best and muses on Panama's history as the coast comes into view.

In a steady downpour, Roosevelt and Edith ride the railroad from Colón across to Panama City with Theodore Shonts, John Stevens and President Amador. Film records the trip, and they stay over at the Hotel Tivoli.
At the controls of a steam shovel

Roosevelt spends eighteen hours in the field, from before six in the morning until nearly midnight, looking at workers and their living conditions. At Culebra he gives a speech, watches steam shovels bite into the cut and takes the controls of one, a moment caught on film. Heavy rain has turned the villages to mud.

Roosevelt views the future Gatun Dam site and wishes he could linger to collect specimens. He speaks at Colón, dines with General Manager Biers at Cristobal, attends a reception and ball, and sails that night for Puerto Rico.
The Louisiana heads for Puerto Rico. Edith writes Kermit of Panamanian children who waved American flags and sang "America" for the visitors.
At sea on the way to Puerto Rico. Back home, it is Quentin's ninth birthday.

Off Ponce, Roosevelt writes Kermit about his hectic days on the isthmus and tells Ted about the stiff trade winds and how the jungle's flowers and animals captivated him. Edith, he reports, enjoyed every minute.

Roosevelt and Edith come ashore at Ponce, where Governor Winthrop greets them and Roosevelt speaks at City Hall. They motor some 80 miles over the mountains to San Juan, stopping at Cayey and Río Piedras, then dine, attend the governor's reception and sleep in the old Spanish governors' palace. Mr. Grahame turns up in his kilt.

The Roosevelts drive back to Ponce by another route, through Arecibo, and stop for an outdoor meal of chicken and eggs with bread and wine. Back on the Louisiana that afternoon, the crew puts on skits and three boxing bouts for them.

Heading north, Roosevelt writes Kermit a full account of Puerto Rico and describes both islands to George Otto Trevelyan. He is reading Milton and Samuel Dill's study of Rome in the age of Nero and Marcus Aurelius.
The Louisiana rounds Cape Hatteras on the way home.
Last day at sea; Nobel news

Roosevelt's last day aboard the Louisiana falls on Bamie's eleventh wedding anniversary. The source also logs here that he has won the Nobel Peace Prize, formally awarded December 10, and lists Quentin's "White House Gang" of boyhood friends.
Back at the desk: railroads, child labor, Peary

Home from the tropics, Roosevelt goes straight to work: interstate commerce law with Hepburn, a child labor bill with Beveridge, and the Army budget with Warren and Hull. Robert E. Peary is among the day's many visitors, and Joseph Bucklin Bishop comes by at nine that night.

Roosevelt and Edith reach their twentieth wedding anniversary and let it pass without fuss, though the Washington Post salutes them as ideal keepers of the White House's social traditions. E. H. Harriman calls at one o'clock.

Congress opens its new session and members stream into Roosevelt's office. At lunch he hosts a naturalists' table: William T. Hornaday, C. Hart Merriam and John Phillips, with Robert Collier and others.
A bold annual message, in simplified spelling

Roosevelt's annual message is read to Congress. It argues that big business, being interstate, belongs under federal oversight, rattling Wall Street, and draws more comment for being printed in simplified spelling. He receives Mabel Boardman and about 100 Red Cross delegates and later hears the Boston Symphony with Edith.
Canal labor and the I stories

Roosevelt hears from Moffett and Neill about labor on the Canal Zone and sees Ambassador Aoki. He writes Kermit about the first-person hunting tales, his "I" stories, that he tells Archie and Quentin, and about winning the Nobel Prize.
A long line of senators, congressmen and politicians files through, including La Follette, Spooner and New York's William Barnes Jr., along with Russia's Baron Rosen. Hemenway comes at 2:30.
Rivers and harbors speech; Ted joins Porcellian

Roosevelt addresses delegates to the Rivers and Harbors Congress and dines at Lodge's. He presses Senator Hale for more battleships, praises Treasury Secretary Shaw's record, and learns that Ted has been taken into Harvard's Porcellian Club.
Mark Twain to lunch; three new monuments

Roosevelt proclaims El Morro, Montezuma Castle and Petrified Forest as national monuments. Mark Twain, John Philip Sousa and Admiral Dewey are among the day's callers, and Twain stays for lunch. Harriman calls at six, and Roosevelt finishes the night at the Gridiron Dinner.
Bellamy and Maria Storer publish their private correspondence with Roosevelt.

In Christiania, Norway, Roosevelt is formally awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for ending the Russo-Japanese War, the first American so honored. He wires thanks to the Nobel committee, pledging the prize money to a permanent body for industrial peace. That night he and Edith go to the Columbia Theater.

Roosevelt talks New York politics with Governor-elect Hughes and sees Mark Twain once more among the callers. He lunches with Cleveland Dodge and hosts the Republican campaign committee for dinner with Hughes, Taft, Lodge, Cannon and others.

A full lunch table includes Pinchot, Garfield, Taft, Bacon, Stevens and Kellogg. Roosevelt writes Senator Matthew Butler about his growing quarrel with Senator Foraker, who has become a sharp critic of the Brownsville discharges.

Under heavy pressure, Roosevelt withdraws his order telling the Public Printer to use simplified spelling. Two houseguests, Beekman Winthrop and Paul Morton, are staying at the White House, and the Cabinet comes to dinner. He writes Hitchcock about illegal fences on public land and federal coal lands.
Inviting Uncle Joe to Lincoln Day
After the Cabinet meets and senators call, Roosevelt lunches with Ambassador and Mrs. Jusserand. He asks Speaker Cannon to give a speech at New York's Lincoln Day dinner in February.
Buffalo Bill and a medal for Peary

Buffalo Bill Cody talks western irrigation with Roosevelt, and Representative Townsend raises the shortage of freight cars. After dinner at Vice President Fairbanks's, Roosevelt goes to the National Geographic Society banquet at the New Willard and gives Commander Robert Peary a medal. His brother-in-law Douglas Robinson is a houseguest.
Root calls on Sunday evening. Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews he could not have saved the reformed spelling by fighting for it, and thanks Moody for his years in the Cabinet.
Moody to the Supreme Court; a Cabinet shuffle

Roosevelt puts Moody on the Supreme Court, moves Bonaparte from Navy to Attorney General, shifts Metcalf to Navy and names Oscar Straus to Commerce and Labor. He sends Congress special messages on naval personnel and public land laws, and one on the canal illustrated with Canal Zone photographs.

Roosevelt sends Congress a message on the Japanese immigration question. He takes up government pay, the freight car shortage, Indian affairs and a proposed loan to the Jamestown Exposition, and dines with Horace Plunkett. To Sir Edward Grey he urges tact over the Newfoundland fisheries.

Iowa's Governor Cummins and senators from the northern plains meet Roosevelt about the shortage of freight cars. Hamilton Fish is among a long list of visitors, and Roosevelt writes Representative Foss about battleships.

Roosevelt meets Walcott, Newell and Flint on the breach of the Colorado River and wires Harriman about who should pay to fix it. He discusses child labor law with Neill, writes Seth Low about turning his Nobel money into a peace commission, and dines at the Roots'. Nicholas Murray Butler stays the night.
After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt shares lunch with Whitelaw Reid, the Durands and other guests. To John St. Loe Strachey he writes about the Storer letters, Japan and William Jennings Bryan.

Roosevelt lunches with Belmont and Foulke, sees Speck von Sternberg, and attends Justice and Mrs. Harlan's fiftieth-anniversary reception. He offers Philip B. Stewart a Land Office job; Stewart will say no.
Secretary Taft and a Mr. Barrow call at nine in the evening.
Christmas Eve at work; radio's first voice

Roosevelt spends Christmas Eve on immigration with Sargent, the canal with Taft, and Brownsville with Senators Warren, Long and Cullom, then lunches with canal engineer John Stevens. Near Plymouth, Massachusetts, Reginald Fessenden makes the first radio broadcast of a human voice.
At six in the morning the children's footsteps in the hall wake Roosevelt and Edith, and the family launches into one of its traditional Roosevelt Christmases.

After talks with Taft and Walcott and lunch with Bacon, Speyer and Root, Roosevelt and Edith leave for Pine Knot. He writes Corinne that Ted no longer gets as worked up about Christmas as he did as a boy.
Turkeys and a life of Morton
At Pine Knot, Roosevelt hunts turkey and reads William Dudley Foulke's biography of Indiana's Civil War governor, Oliver P. Morton.
Roosevelt is at Pine Knot. The source records nothing more.
Another quiet day at the Virginia retreat; no details recorded.
The Roosevelts remain at Pine Knot; the source adds nothing else.
Roosevelt and Edith return to Washington from Pine Knot to close out the year.

Roosevelt opens 1907 by meeting sociologist Edward A. Ross, then comes down to trumpets for the New Year's reception: diplomats first, then the public, 8,150 hands in all, a record that stood for decades. Afterward he washes up, takes the family for a country drive and goes to Bamie's N Street house for chocolate, whipped cream and champagne. He ends the day reading Gissing on Dickens and Lowes Dickinson's The Greek View of Life.
