He writes a long letter to Cecil Spring-Rice touching on his friend's frustration with diplomatic life, Australia, population and the panic, and tells Thomas Watson why printing greenbacks is no cure.

On Sunday evening Postmaster General Meyer and Secretary Root call. Roosevelt writes Arizona's Governor Kibbey about maneuvering ahead of the Republican convention, where Taft's backers are battling Foraker's.
A grandnephew is born to Franklin and Eleanor

James Roosevelt, son of Franklin and Eleanor, is born. Roosevelt sits for photographer Frederick Hyde, discusses Pacific Coast defenses with Flint and Humphrey, and lunches with Leo Rowe and Kitagaki. He tells Charles Magoon the pitcher and basin Magoon sent will be Edith's Christmas present, and asks Bonaparte about stopping union boycotts.
Christmas tree at the German Embassy

On Christmas Eve Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, talks finance with Senator Hansbrough, and stops by the German Embassy to admire its Christmas tree before tennis with Pinchot and Jusserand. He tells Root that Panama has no say at all over the waters approaching the Canal Zone.

At seven in the morning the children, Alice and Nick included, pile onto the bed to open stockings, then everyone heads to the library for presents. Roosevelt rides three hours with Root, Lodge, Fitz Lee, Ted, Kermit and Ethel, admires Archie's tree, and plays an hour and a half of tennis, while Quentin's three friends roughhouse all evening.
Off to Pine Knot for the holidays

Roosevelt heads for the family's Virginia cabin, Pine Knot, stopping in Charlottesville. He protests a New York Tribune editorial claiming Admiral Brownson quit over the order putting naval doctors in command of hospital ships, and tells Arthur Lee why he won't run again and about Philip de László's wish to paint him.
Roosevelt is at Pine Knot, the family's retreat in the Virginia woods. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

From Pine Knot Roosevelt wires Governor Sparks that Nevada's legislature must be summoned at once. Keeping order is the state's job, he says, and if the call does not go out within five days the federal troops will leave.
Roosevelt remains at Pine Knot as Treasury Secretary Cortelyou turns in his account of the autumn's financial panic.
Back to Washington from Pine Knot
Roosevelt leaves Pine Knot in the afternoon and has appointments that evening in Washington. He writes Alabama judge John C. Anderson to praise him for enjoining state railroad regulation laws.
Year ends as the panic eases

Roosevelt closes 1907 with tennis and letters: to Taft on Ohio politics and Foraker, to Leo Rowe on ties with South America, and to Owen Wister on scholarship in America. With the economy recovering, the panic is over. Scribner's publishes his "In the Louisiana Canebrakes."
Six thousand at the New Year's reception

Roosevelt opens 1908 with breakfast with Captain Greenaway, then greets some 6,000 people at the New Year's reception. That afternoon he takes a hard two-hour ride with his children and their cousins and friends, and writes Trevelyan about the inscribed loving cup and the Revolution.

Roosevelt names J. E. Pillsbury to head the Bureau of Navigation, tours the Corcoran early, and lunches with Taft, illustrator Howard Pyle and Eugene Philbin. He writes Archie at Groton about Edith's fondness for the little dog Scamp, and congratulates Bonaparte on a Chicago speech on the misdeeds of the rich.
After the Cabinet meeting and a few callers, Roosevelt plays tennis and hosts Goethals, Rockhill, Whitelaw Reid and Beveridge at dinner, followed by music.

Roosevelt hears from Charles Neill on labor conditions in Nevada and from Representative Humphrey on Puget Sound defenses, and sees Jacob Riis and Seth Bullock. He orders that medical officers will now command Navy hospital ships, and grumbles to Senator Warren about how badly many Army officers ride.
Roosevelt's old Dakota friend Seth Bullock and his wife spend Sunday night at the White House.

As Congress returns, Roosevelt widens the authority of Colonel Goethals as chairman of the Isthmian Canal Commission. He poses for Mr. Hyde on the South Portico, plays tennis, and writes Taft about removing federal officeholders.
Aldrich offers an emergency currency bill

Senator Aldrich introduces a bill allowing $500 million in emergency currency when credit tightens. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, lunches with Taft, Longworth and Seth Bullock, walks, and he and Edith dine with Vice President Fairbanks.
Roosevelt confers with Payne and Dalzell, the House's tariff men, and lunches with humorist George Ade, Robert Porter and Sloan Simpson, who stays the night. After a ride he dines with Captain Lee.

Roosevelt proclaims Muir Woods in California a national monument, protecting its redwoods. Taft and La Follette are among the day's callers, he rides at three, and that night hosts the diplomatic reception. He sends George Meredith congratulations on the novelist's 80th birthday.

Roosevelt sorts out Nebraska postal jobs with Senators Burkett and Brown and later hosts a dinner and musicale honoring Speaker Joe Cannon. In New York, Taft speaks at Cooper Union on the origins of property. Roosevelt thanks his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson for managing his money.
Grand Canyon becomes a national monument

Roosevelt proclaims the Grand Canyon a national monument. He discusses fortifying Pearl Harbor, the tariff and an employers' liability bill, lunches and walks with Jusserand, and writes about saving Appalachian forests, better language teaching at West Point, and his record for working people.
Senators Warner and Warren call in the afternoon, and Roosevelt writes Cortelyou about the currency bill.

Roosevelt goes over land fraud prosecutions with Garfield and Ballinger and sees Bonaparte and Nebraska's Senator Burkett. Tennis is called off, so there is no exercise; he and Edith spend the evening at the National Theater. Letters go to Taft on returning Cuba to self-rule and to George Lee, his first wife's brother, on corporations.
Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, goes over the Standard Oil prosecutions with District Attorney Sims, plays tennis, sees Louis Payn at six, and he and Edith dine at Secretary Root's.
A growling teddy bear from the Black Forest

Roosevelt hosts a late reception for both houses of Congress. To Archie he reports that Ted hopes to finish college in three years and earn his own way, that Quentin is playing with the Turkish minister's son, and that a walking, growling black teddy bear has made Ethel jealous.
Pinnacles protected; a pure food inquiry

Roosevelt sets aside the Pinnacles in California as a national monument. After tennis he hosts the diplomatic corps at dinner, and asks Johns Hopkins president Ira Remsen to lead a board looking into how the pure food law is being abused.
An unsent rebuke to The Outlook

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt sees Senators Smoot and Brown and the Mexican ambassador, then rides. He drafts a protest to Lyman Abbott over an Outlook editorial on Admiral Brownson's resignation but holds it back, and writes about Pearl Harbor's defenses and a counterfeiter he has kept behind bars.
It is his sister Bamie's 53rd birthday. Roosevelt meets again with Nebraska Senators Burkett and Brown, sees C. H. Treat, and rides.
Roosevelt spends Sunday writing to William Dudley Foulke about patronage and Taft's nomination.

Roosevelt lunches with C. A. Congdon and Herbert Smith, plays tennis, and takes Edith to the National Theater. He tells Archie about a letter from Mrs. Peabody at Groton and about Quentin, the family "philosopher," who is making regular use of the YMCA gym and pool.
After the Cabinet meeting and a lunch with Kellogg, Fox and Witherbee, Roosevelt rides, sees Booker T. Washington at six, and dines with Edith at Secretary Cortelyou's.

Roosevelt meets Representatives Bennet and Fassett about the push to nominate New York's Governor Charles Evans Hughes for President. Morris K. Jesup dies. Tennis fills the afternoon and Senator Beveridge calls late in the evening.
Roosevelt talks Army business with Senator McLaurin, rides in the afternoon, and hosts the annual reception for the judiciary that evening.
Platt calls; a crowded lunch table

Senator Thomas Platt calls at ten, and the Cabinet takes up postal appointments. Roosevelt's lunch guests include the Jusserands, the Strauses, the Meyers and the Cooleys, and after a walk he gives a dinner for lawmakers including Chauncey Depew, followed by music.

Roosevelt discusses New York politics with Herbert Parsons and lunches with steel man Elbert Gary and Mackenzie King, Canada's deputy labor minister. Aldrich calls in the afternoon, and that evening Roosevelt goes to the Gridiron Club dinner.
Journalist John Callan O'Laughlin calls on Roosevelt Sunday evening.

Roosevelt greets a group of newspaper editors from around the country and lunches with historian Brooks Adams and William Phillips. He writes Kermit that Taft's campaign is moving along and that Hughes, he thinks, envies him, and tells Archie about Scamp and the kitchen cat.
Low and Gompers on trust law

Roosevelt meets Seth Low and labor leader Samuel Gompers on trust legislation and talks with Representative Campbell about Taft's candidacy. After a ride, he and Edith dine with Attorney General Bonaparte. He writes Henry Thompson on illuminated manuscripts.

Roosevelt sorts through Kentucky appointments with a delegation led by Representative Langley and receives senators and congressmen before riding. In Cleveland, Taft argues against American isolationism.
Roosevelt sees Governor Floyd, Senator Dolliver and others, rides at half past three, and hosts the Supreme Court justices at dinner.
The most radical message of his presidency

Roosevelt sends Congress a special message unlike any before it: he calls for a new employers' liability law, limits on injunctions in labor disputes, federal control of stock gambling, and tighter rules for railroads and big combinations. He blames Standard Oil, the railroad combines and the panic on the trusts, and faults the courts for siding with big business. That afternoon he plays tennis on a frozen court.
Snow, and a letter to Laurier

Snow falls on Washington. Roosevelt discusses the Government Printing Office with Representatives Landis and Overstreet, lunches with Bryce, Foulke and Mackenzie King, and walks. He writes Canadian Prime Minister Wilfrid Laurier about relations between the two countries, Japanese immigration and the deliberate overissue of passports.
Three hours over the frozen snow

From 4:30 to 7:30 Roosevelt tramps with Meyer and Winthrop over crusted snow to Chevy Chase and home by way of Rock Creek. He writes Arthur Lee about Maurice Low's attacks on him in the English papers and the de László portrait Lee suggested, and sends Kermit his thoughts on the January 31 message.
Arctic explorer Robert Peary is among Roosevelt's callers, along with Vice President Fairbanks and Senator La Follette. After a walk he discusses New York politics with Woodruff and Barnes.

After the Cabinet meets, Silas McBee joins him for lunch, and following a walk Roosevelt and Edith dine at Postmaster General Meyer's. He wires Governor Sparks that the troops must leave Nevada no later than February 15, and writes William Jennings Bryan about his message and court rulings hostile to labor.

Public Printer Stillings is suspended, and Roosevelt writes Representative Landis about the inquiry into his office. He meets Taft and General Bell, hears manufacturers argue for a permanent tariff commission, and lunches with William Barnes. There is no time for exercise.

Roosevelt meets the House Naval Affairs Committee, lunches with Taft, and has supper with his old friend Jacob Riis, an overnight guest, before the congressional reception. He writes Nicholas Murray Butler, who has criticized his messages, and Seth Low about the Hughes boom.

Roosevelt creates Jewel Cave National Monument in South Dakota. He reviews Cuban affairs with Taft, Root and Magoon, sets March 7 for pulling troops out of Nevada, and stops Hawaii's governor from discussing more Japanese laborers with Japan. Groton's Endicott Peabody and Jacob Riis are house guests.

The children play the banjo for Roosevelt in the afternoon, and that evening he visits the YMCA. He turns down Richard Watson Gilder's ideas of a memoir and world travels after the presidency, and writes Thomas Coolidge about backing Taft.
Roosevelt and Edith attend a funeral at St. John's Church in the afternoon.

Roosevelt hears Representative Hull on balloon experiments and talks Ohio politics with son-in-law Nick Longworth; there is no outdoor exercise. Taft speaks to young Republicans in Kansas City. A memo records how Roosevelt sees his ties to Lodge and George Lyman and Lyman's requests for jobs.

After the Cabinet meeting and lunch with Cecil Lyon, Roosevelt walks, then dines with Edith at Secretary Metcalf's. He writes Metcalf about naval bases and defenses at Pearl Harbor and in the Philippines, and praises Senator Knox for his Columbia speeches on big business.

It is Alice's 24th birthday. Roosevelt confers with Aldrich and rides. He writes Charlemagne Tower about Japanese advisers in Mexico and South America, and tells King Edward VII about the battle fleet's cruise and its planned stops in Australia.
No patience for Jane Addams's book

Roosevelt talks with Frank Hitchcock about Taft's campaign in the South and with Bonaparte about a miners' strike in Alaska, then rides. To Florence La Farge he pans Jane Addams's Newer Ideals of Peace, likening it to Tolstoy, whom he does not admire.

Roosevelt lunches with William Allen White and Lyman Abbott, rides, and attends an evening reception given by a fine arts society. He congratulates Ted on his midyear grades and tells Thornton Simmons he was never Harvard's lightweight boxing champion.

After lunch with Coolidge and a walk, Roosevelt tells Root he suspects the battleships England is building for Brazil may really be meant for Japan; they were in fact for Brazil. He writes Philip Stewart that he cannot think Ethan Hitchcock a bad man, though he had lost faith in his judgment.
William Allen White in the evening
Roosevelt meets census expert W. S. Rossiter, and Kansas editor William Allen White calls at half past nine.

On Alice and Nick's second anniversary, Roosevelt dines with Ambassador Whitelaw Reid, and Douglas and Corinne Robinson come to stay. He writes Root about China and Japan, and tells young cousin Philip J. Roosevelt at St. Mark's how much he enjoyed Philip's poem about the Badlands.
Against wage cuts on the railroads

The Cabinet takes up immigration. Roosevelt rides and dines at Garfield's with Lodge, Jusserand, Justice Day and others. He writes the Interstate Commerce Commission objecting to railroad rebates and wage cuts, and urges the government to mediate.

Roosevelt discusses the antitrust laws with Sherman and Knox and postal jobs with Meyer, sees Ambassador von Sternberg, and gives a dinner for Lodge, Governor Fort, Bourke Cockran, Nicholas Murray Butler and others, capped by a recitation. He writes about railroad pay cuts and a laborer disabled on the Panama works.

Roosevelt talks battleship funding with Representative Hobson and meets financier James Speyer and Senator Smoot. Taft and Goethals come in at 2:30, Japanese Ambassador Aoki at 2:45, and that night he hosts the Army and Navy reception.

A day of meetings: Judge Wilfley's possible impeachment, an industrial school bill, finances with Aldrich, and Panama labor with Taft and Goethals. After a ride Roosevelt dines at Lodge's. He presses Vice President Fairbanks, and Speaker Cannon in a similar letter, for quick action to fortify the Pacific.

On Washington's Birthday Roosevelt fields congressmen on a Southern Pacific claim for Colorado River repairs, the military budget, Massachusetts politics and an alleged submarine lobby. He lunches with Judge Lowell and cousin Emlen Roosevelt, rides, and dines with the Jusserands and Justice Moody.
Roosevelt dines with his sister Bamie. He writes Kermit his views on Dickens, Bunyan and Thackeray, and writes Senator Bourne about the Standard Oil case.

Roosevelt hears from Senator McCumber and Representative Gronna about La Follette's campaign, goes over the canal with Goethals, and lunches with Taft, Root, Garfield and others. A National Educational Association delegation calls, Mackenzie King comes at three, and he dines with the Longworths.
Opening the Hudson tubes by telegraph

From Washington Roosevelt presses a button that starts the first trains running through the Hudson tunnels between Hoboken and Sixth Avenue at 19th Street in New York. He goes to Bishop Satterlee's funeral, rides, and he and Edith dine with Agriculture Secretary James Wilson and his wife.

The Inland Waterways Commission's report goes to Congress, and Roosevelt sends a message opposing bills that would free power companies from federal control and fees. He sees senators, walks, and gives a dinner for Japanese Ambassador Takahira.
Indian commissioners at the White House

Roosevelt meets the Board of Indian Commissioners, confers with Taft, and talks with Representative Langley about naming a new Public Printer. Judge Wilfley calls, and after a ride Roosevelt writes Grafton Cushing about the country and the French Revolution of 1789.
Trying on riding clothes for a portrait

Painter Gari Melchers and Taft come to lunch; Melchers is to paint Roosevelt in riding clothes for Charles Freer. Afterward Roosevelt models several outfits for Edith and Alice until they approve one. The Cabinet discusses the Wilfley case, and in the evening he and Edith go to the Columbia Theater.

Philip de László finishes a portrait of Roosevelt in riding clothes and a pastel of Edith, which both admire, and Gari Melchers completes his portrait too. Roosevelt writes Kermit a scathing verdict on Dickens after reading Martin Chuzzlewit, and urges Cannon to back a stronger navy. At Harvard, Ted lands on probation again for skipping lectures.

Representative Denby calls at one and there are meetings in the evening. Roosevelt writes Taft about appointments made out of sympathy, hoping Taft will make fewer of them as President than he himself has.
Roosevelt meets Hepburn and Crane and rides, then he and Edith dine with Henry Adams. He tells G. H. Davis he backs child labor and employers' liability laws whatever big business thinks.
After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt lunches with Kohlsaat, Seth Low, Senator Brandegee, zoologist William Hornaday and others, rides, and dines with Edith at Secretary Straus's.

Senator Redfield Proctor of Vermont dies. Roosevelt rides and meets Kohlsaat in the evening. He sends Kermit a passage of Dickens against pacifism, and tells Taft the Army's tests for chaplains are too hard, though they ought to include math.

Roosevelt meets Senator Burkett and Representative Hinshaw and rides. He writes Arthur Balfour about his essay on decadence, weighing examples from history and biology, and writes Charles Knoblauch about Wall Street bills stuck in committee.
Dewey on warships; Beveridge for chairman

The Cabinet takes up mail agreements with Italy and France, and Admiral Dewey talks warship building with Roosevelt. Lodge and Aldrich call. He suggests to Republican chairman Harry New that Senator Beveridge preside over the convention.
Quentin's ball team on the White House lawn

Quentin's ball club from the Force School holds practice on the White House grounds. New York Republicans endorse Governor Hughes for President. Roosevelt discusses the tariff commission bill with Beveridge, rides, and writes Arthur Lee on Balfour and Japan, Corinne about a sorrow in her daughter's life, and James Creelman in praise of his article on Mexico's President Díaz.
Admiral Will Cowles calls at lunchtime. Roosevelt tells Archie that Ethel has a new white bull terrier named Mike, and passes on to Kermit the Kaiser's view of the American navy.

After naval talks with Representatives Hobson and Foss, Roosevelt visits his dentist, Dr. Bryant, walks, and dines with Edith at Miss Tuckerman's. He writes Henry Adams that, like John Quincy Adams in his diary, he finds parts of the presidency tedious.
Speaking to the Congress of Mothers
Roosevelt addresses and receives the National Congress of Mothers, meets the Cabinet and Aldrich, sits for painter Philip de László at three, and rides.

In a special message Roosevelt endorses the Brownsville findings of most of the Senate's military committee. He talks Taft's campaign with Senator Long, hears Montanans on the Northern Pacific's allegedly illegal land holdings, and in the evening discusses restitution for the Colorado River break with Garfield and Maxwell Evarts.
No signature for the Foraker bill

Roosevelt discusses Oklahoma politics with Governor Frantz, lunches with railroad man Stuyvesant Fish, Leslie Shaw and Alexander, rides, and takes Edith to the Columbia Theater. He tells Ernest Abbott he will not sign Foraker's Brownsville bill.

After the Cabinet meeting and talks with Parsons and Langley, Roosevelt plays tennis with Bacon, Cooley and Jusserand. He compliments Lawrence Abbott on his Outlook piece about Taft and writes Eugene Philbin about Bishop Hendrick in the Philippines.

Roosevelt tells reporters the battle fleet, already at sea, will go all the way around the world. On the White House grounds Quentin's Force School team trounces the P Street School 22 to 5. He also confers on Taft's campaign, the third-term question and Brownsville, and warns Metcalf that Japanese ships outclass American ones.

Edith and Emily Carow leave for New York, Emily soon to sail back to Italy, and Roosevelt dines at Bamie's. He tells Archie that Mike attacked Ethel's horse and must be given away, asks C. Hart Merriam about an air gun to shoot English sparrows at Sagamore Hill without hurting other birds, and complains to Kermit that Ted has cut 38 lectures since New Year's.

Roosevelt goes over legislation with Aldrich, discusses Tennessee politics with Representative Hale, sees muckraker Lincoln Steffens at one, and plays tennis with Garfield, Pinchot and Jusserand. Taft speaks on the rights of Black Americans at Plymouth Church in Brooklyn.

Roosevelt meets and lunches with Andrew Carnegie after the Cabinet meeting, sees Cullom and Representative McKinley, and rides. He urges James Miller that Washington help pay to fix the broken Colorado River dam, a plea Congress ignored; the Southern Pacific paid instead.

Roosevelt confers on a Tennessee judgeship, the ship subsidy bill and Aldrich's currency bill, then lunches with Nick Longworth and William Barnes, plays tennis, and dines with the Longworths. He sends Senator Frye a statement on federal water rights and writes Spokane publisher William Cowles about railroad pay cuts.
Roosevelt discusses the Philippines with Taft and Eugene Philbin, receives Representative Cockran and a group of Spanish War veterans, rides, and sees Booker T. Washington at six.
First letters about an African safari

Roosevelt starts planning life after the White House: he asks hunter Frederick Selous when and where to go in Africa, and puts the same question to John Patterson. He also tries to stop La Questione Sociale, an anarchist paper out of Paterson, N.J., or failing that to bar it from the mails, and talks tariff revision with Western businessmen.
Careful with shore leave in Japan

Roosevelt meets Aldrich, Payne and Dalzell on legislation and Crane and Beveridge on the tariff, lunches with Leigh Hunt, and rides. He warns Admiral Charles Sperry to be cautious about sailors' shore leave when the fleet reaches Japan. Lincoln Steffens calls in the evening.
Japanese Ambassador Aoki calls at 9:30 Sunday night, followed by Representative Hepburn and Seth Low.

Roosevelt talks New York politics with Woodruff, lunches with Low, Merriam and the British ambassador, and walks. He accepts Admiral Robley Evans's resignation with regret and presses Speaker Cannon to authorize four new battleships and fortify Hawaii, mentioning the tariff along the way.
The Cabinet weighs a raise for postal workers. Roosevelt talks battleship funding with Hobson, Brownsville with Senator Borah, and the fleet's cruise with Senator Flint, then rides.

Roosevelt sends Congress a special message on antitrust, interstate commerce, finance and child labor laws. He meets Nebraska cattlemen on federal land grants and the Pure Food advisory board, and asks every cabinet officer to avoid Sunday work in their departments wherever possible.

Roosevelt discusses antitrust law with Hepburn, sees Beveridge, Purdy and others, and rides. He tells Bonaparte there will be no reindictment of Senator Borah, and writes Albert Key on improving the Navy.
The Cabinet discusses strikes in Alaska and the quarrel with Venezuela. Roosevelt meets Senator Frazier and Tennesseans about a judgeship, plays tennis at 4:30, and spends the evening at Lodge's.

Roosevelt weighs rival employers' liability bills with Senators Borah and Knox and currency with Representative Weeks, plays tennis, and dines with the Boone and Crockett Club at the Metropolitan Club. He writes Root about how many Japanese laborers are being let in.
Roosevelt lunches with Taft, Yale's Arthur Hadley and Silas McBee and dines with Bamie. He writes Root that Venezuela's President Castro will not accept arbitration.

Roosevelt discusses Venezuela with Root and a yellow fever quarantine in Cuba with Taft, lunches with Alice, and meets Interstate Commerce Commissioners. After tennis he spends the evening with the German ambassador, Bacon and Root, and writes Whitelaw Reid about Japan and the fleet.

Roosevelt nominates David Jayne Hill as ambassador to Germany and picks S. F. Eddy to represent the country in Argentina, and sends the Senate the diplomatic papers on Venezuela. Former Treasury Secretary John G. Carlisle calls. He dines with the Austro-Hungarian ambassador, the Meyers, Alice and Nick, and Mrs. Beale, and writes Beveridge about curbing child labor in the capital.

Roosevelt confers on the Massachusetts primaries, Indian affairs and battleships, sees Speaker Cannon, and hosts a big lunch for Alice, Bamie and her husband, and G. C. Ward. After a ride he sees von Sternberg and then Henry Adams. He writes Seth Low on executive control of corporations.

Roosevelt writes Booker T. Washington about equality for Black Americans and instructs the Justice Department that train accommodations for Black passengers must equal those for whites. He tells Cecil Lyon he will turn down the party's nomination, and dines at Ambassador von Sternberg's.

Roosevelt meets mine workers' leader John Mitchell about an inquiry into labor conditions on the isthmus, sees Senator Curtis, and watches troops drill at Fort Myer before tennis with Winthrop. He drafts, but does not send, a letter to Charlemagne Tower about opposition to Hill's appointment in Berlin.
Dinner with the Holmeses and Henry Adams

Roosevelt names J. S. Leech Public Printer, talks Indiana politics with Beveridge and battleships with Hobson, and sees editor Henry Watterson. After tennis he dines with the Roots, the Lodges, Henry Adams, and Justice Holmes and his wife. He writes the Kaiser about Hill and the fleet, and Magoon on Cuba's government after the American withdrawal.
Ambassador von Sternberg calls at 12:30, Herbert Smith at 2:30, and Speaker Cannon at 9:30 that night.
Bird refuge in the Dry Tortugas
Roosevelt creates the Tortugas Keys Bird Reservation in Florida. He meets Representatives Hill and Weeks, sees von Sternberg, and rides.
After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt hears Herman Ridder on the paper trust, sees Senator Heyburn, receives Booker T. Washington at three, and rides.
A waterway from Boston to Key West

Roosevelt talks with Heyburn about a Snake River irrigation dam and with a group of congressmen about an inland waterway from Boston to Key West, then walks with Captain Fournier and William Phillips. He tells Arthur Lee he enjoyed sitting for de László, and writes Edward Curtis about Custer's final fight.

On Archie's 14th birthday Roosevelt asks Congress for laws against anarchism, discusses New York politics with Fassett and Cocks, and tosses the medicine ball with Pinchot, Garfield and Jusserand. He writes Metcalf about the very high desertion rate among Navy engine-room crews.

On a rainy day Quentin and three friends decorate the White House hallway portraits with spitballs. Roosevelt defends his Brownsville decision to Herbert Parsons and objects to New York Republican resolutions on Southern representation and on Brownsville. He rejects Albert Key's plan to reorganize Navy command and wants a Pacific drydock in two or three years, not five or six.
Mad at Quentin over the spitballs

Roosevelt meets Senator Cullom and Puerto Rico's Larrinaga, rides, and dines with the Bacons, Longworths, Cowleses, novelist Mrs. Humphry Ward and her husband, and others. He tells Archie that Ethel has a bulldog pup on trial and that he is angry with Quentin over the spitballs, and writes Kermit about books, politics and next year's African hunt.
Roosevelt rides, and he and Edith dine with Henry Adams. Gardner, Pinchot and Jusserand call in the evening.

Roosevelt confers on New York politics and with Garfield on Alaska's coal lands, plays tennis, and he and Edith dine at Justice Moody's. He tells Representative Humphrey he wants a Pacific drydock built in two years.
Foraker speaks for the Brownsville soldiers

On the Senate floor Joseph Foraker speaks in defense of the Brownsville troops. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, talks currency with Representative Vreeland, plays tennis, and discusses adjournment with James Watson in the evening.
A strong call for four battleships

On a very full day Roosevelt has Ambassador James Bryce to lunch (he once called Bryce, fondly, a prodigious memory with hair on it) and sends Congress a forceful message asking for four new battleships. He rides at 4:45.
Natural Bridges and a new national forest

Roosevelt proclaims Natural Bridge National Monument in Utah and Manzano National Forest in New Mexico. He meets bankers on currency, the National Gallery's advisory committee, and Taft, and plays tennis. Ted arrives home from college nursing a sore throat.

After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt discusses Japanese immigration with Representative McKinley and plays tennis with Hallowell, Winthrop and Phillips. He writes Root about Japan and the chance of war, and Bonaparte about an employers' liability bill.

Roosevelt and Edith ride in the late afternoon, and he notices the season's wildflowers along Rock Creek. He hears Ralph Easley on amending the Sherman Act, and writes Kermit and Senator Warren about his fight for four battleships, Frank Munsey with thanks for his articles, and Pearl Wight about sending a Black Louisianan to the convention.
Roosevelt suggests to Treasury Secretary Cortelyou that the gold reserve be moved inland from San Francisco to Denver should war come.

Roosevelt talks currency with Representative Hill and Alaska game preserves with writer Emerson Hough and C. Hart Merriam, and plays tennis with Ted, Cooley and Hallowell. In New York, Taft addresses a laymen's missionary gathering at Carnegie Hall.
After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt discusses a Minnesota judgeship with Senator Clapp, lunches with Bonaparte, Kellogg and others, rides, and dines with Winthrop, Phillips and the Longworths.

The Outlook runs Roosevelt's article on how Grover Cleveland handled the coal strike. He meets West Coast senators about the battleships, rides, and plays tennis. He thanks Senator Piles for leading the Senate fight for four battleships and asks Lodge to stand strong, or at least appear to, for them.
Roosevelt sees Cooley, Charles Pepper and Senator Overman, plays tennis, and dines with the Lodges. He presses Senator Frank Flint to hold out for all four battleships.
Roosevelt signs the employers' liability bill covering government workers. He also writes Senator William Smith, restating his conviction that Black soldiers carried out the Brownsville shooting.
Roosevelt talks with Representative Gaines about a Tennessee judgeship and plays tennis with Meyer and Winthrop.
Edith wary of the Africa plan
Senators Clay, Overman and Dixon call late Sunday evening. Edith writes Kermit that she dislikes the idea of Roosevelt's planned hunting trip to Africa.

Roosevelt works senators on the battleship issue and sends Congress a special message on injunctions and national control of corporations. He rides with Ambassador von Sternberg and writes Henry White that he likes Asquith, Britain's new prime minister. Congress agrees to two new battleships.
A short record: the Cabinet meets, and Roosevelt plays tennis at 4:30 with Jusserand, Garfield and Cooley.

On Corinne's 26th wedding anniversary Roosevelt discusses Indian land claims with Senators Ankeny and Piles, receives a long list of callers, and rides. He writes Speaker Cannon about the civil bill, lifting wage limits in Panama, and the child labor bill.

Roosevelt talks Western politics with Representative Hull and the Snake River dam with Piles and Jones, and meets four congressmen on money to enforce the Hepburn Act. After tennis, Edith goes to a lecture. He writes Cannon about the ICC section of the sundry civil bill.
After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt sees Parsons, Piles and Long and rides. Edith invites some of Ethel's friends to dinner.
General Wood to watch European maneuvers

Senators Elkins and Rayner call, then von Sternberg, and Roosevelt plays tennis. Grant La Farge and his wife and Miss C. Roosevelt arrive as house guests. He writes General Bell about Leonard Wood attending German and French army maneuvers, and Charles Littlefield about injunctions.
The La Farges and Miss C. Roosevelt remain at the White House.

Roosevelt talks Taft's campaign with Frank Hitchcock and currency with two congressmen, plays tennis with Grant La Farge and others, and takes Edith to the National Theater. He warns Root that more than 1,000 Japanese arrived in April and an exclusion law may follow, and writes Emerson Hough on socialism and Marx.

Roosevelt discusses a postal savings bank bill with Senator Carter, Brownsville with Borah, and pending legislation with Speaker Cannon, then rides. The La Farges and Miss C. Roosevelt are still visiting.
Cardinal Gibbons to lunch; Burroughs arrives

Roosevelt confers on a Tennessee judgeship, Oklahoma patronage, an Alaska game preserve bill and Utah forest reserves, and lunches with Cardinal Gibbons. John Burroughs joins the house guests. He writes the Kaiser hoping for an arbitration treaty with Germany, and C. Hart Merriam about Mendel's law.
Off to Pine Knot with Edith

Roosevelt and Edith leave late in the morning for Pine Knot. He writes Senator John Stewart about discharging the Brownsville soldiers, remarking that he is often accused of breaking the Constitution.
Archie Butt joins the White House

While Roosevelt is at Pine Knot, Captain Archibald Willingham Butt takes up duties as a military aide at the White House in place of Charlie McCauley. By September Butt will be chief aide, succeeding Frank McCoy.
A brisk bird walk with Burroughs

John Burroughs comes out to Pine Knot, and Roosevelt marches him four quick miles to the cabin while the two name the birds they pass. Edith scolds her husband for the punishing pace he set for the old naturalist. She tells Kermit her husband is now pretending the African trip holds no appeal for him.
Squirrels evicted, then let back in

Roosevelt swats a mosquito so hard Burroughs likens it to a lion-killing blow, and says he needn't fear assassins because he carries a gun; he doesn't know Edith has two plainclothesmen in the woods at night. After a bird walk they head back to Washington. He tells Archie that Burroughs evicted some squirrels from the cabin and the Roosevelts moved them back.
Cornerstone for the Pan American building

Roosevelt lunches with Kerens, Root, Archbishop Ireland and Andrew Carnegie, then helps lay the cornerstone of the Bureau of American Republics building. He proclaims Lewis and Clark National Monument in Montana and loses at tennis to Pinchot. By telegram he agrees to Taft's request for U.S. oversight of Panama's elections.

Governors from across the states and territories, Supreme Court justices, the Cabinet, scientists and public figures including William Jennings Bryan come in Washington for the conservation conference. Roosevelt hosts a dinner for seventy. He writes Ted about Rabelais and other writers, Quentin learning baseball from the butler James, and Archie losing his head and steering into the other boat at Groton.

The Governors' Conference on conserving the nation's resources opens in the East Room, and Roosevelt sits in from 10:30 to 2:30 before turning to appointments. Archie Butt attends his first White House luncheon, with Yale's President Hadley, the Cowleses and the Lodges. Roosevelt asks Speaker Cannon to pass a bill making the Inland Waterways Commission permanent; it fails.

Roosevelt again spends 10:30 to 2:30 at the conservation conference, then discusses the anti-injunction bill and a Norfolk Navy Yard contract. After tennis with Winthrop, Cooley and Meyer, he thanks the Kaiser for a letter and gift and tells him about the fleet. Edith goes to the National Theater.

The Governors' Conference closes with a declaration in favor of conservation; 38 states go on to form conservation commissions, and the meeting gives rise to the annual governors' conferences. Pinchot will call it the first national gathering anywhere to treat resource protection as a single problem. Roosevelt creates Kansas National Forest, lunches with historian James Ford Rhodes, and holds a reception; rain turns the planned garden party into a White House tea.

Roosevelt discusses the Rainy River dam bill, sees John Mitchell, Borah and others, and talks with Robert Peary about his coming Arctic expedition. He speaks at the Methodist gathering at American University near Tenleytown, opens a St. Louis charity bazaar by pressing a button, and plays tennis.

Archie Butt is called to the White House because Roosevelt's horse Roswell has been kicked, and finds the President calmer than he expected. Timothy Woodruff comes in the evening to talk New York politics. Roosevelt tells Archie that Quentin is wrapped up in baseball and the grounds are in full bloom.

Roosevelt discusses Kentucky patronage, plays tennis, dines with the Cowleses and the Italian ambassador, and meets Taft late on canal business. He writes Captain Cone of the torpedo flotilla traveling with the fleet about what the cruise has done so far.

The Cabinet discusses election fraud in Panama. Roosevelt meets congressmen on the Inland Waterways bill, sees Newberry and Pinchot, and dines with Metcalf. Miss Potter and Mr. and Mrs. Harvier are house guests.
Ship subsidies and the Sherman Act

Roosevelt meets Speaker Cannon at ten, then discusses anti-injunction legislation, Sherman Act amendments and the ship subsidy in the postal bill. After tennis with Garfield and Jusserand he dines with Bacon. David Gray and Miss Potter are staying.

Roosevelt discusses Venezuela with Cullom and the Rainy River dam with Bede, Hepburn, Garfield and Stevens, and hears a delegation pushing battleship work at the Norfolk yard. He lunches with Root, General Young and his wife, and others, rides, and at ten that night receives Clarence Darrow and Lincoln Steffens.

After the Cabinet meeting, Admiral Robley Evans, Senator Sutherland and Representative Langley call. Roosevelt discusses New York politics with Wadsworth, plays tennis, and writes Albert Shaw about the coming convention.
A range for the bison; the little bear leaves

A new law creates the National Bison Range in Montana, starting with 18,000 acres and 80 bison, and Roosevelt declares the Minnesota National Forest. He writes Edward Buxton about planning next year's African trip, and tells Ted, who is deciding what to do in the fall, that it pains him to see "the little bear" heading out into the world.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists nothing for this Sunday.

Roosevelt meets Senators Beveridge and Kean, grants Austrian Ambassador Hengelmüller a private audience, and with Root receives three envoys from Liberia. After tennis he discusses Indian Territory with Garfield. He tells Whitelaw Reid he dislikes the custom of presentation at court. Archie Butt escorts Edith to the theater.
A noon wedding on N Street

Roosevelt goes to a noon wedding at 1753 N Street, where Francis R. Stevens marries Elizabeth Oliver. Between conferences with his cabinet, he talks with Depew about the government liability bill and with Fassett about James S. Sherman for Vice President, lunches with Colonel Hugh Scott, and rides.
Senator Bourne calls in the morning and Walter Hale, representing veterans of the war with Spain, at 11:30. Roosevelt confers with Taft and Root in the afternoon and plays tennis at 4:30.
The New Haven merger will stand

Father Doyle brings twelve student priests to call, along with the District commissioners, and Roosevelt rides at five. He writes Alston Dayton about West Virginia delegates for Taft, John Hull on revising Army promotions, and Lodge that the New Haven railroad combination will not be broken up.

Roosevelt plays seven sets of tennis with Archie Butt, Garfield and Captain McCoy, after which they all have mint juleps, joined by the Longworths, Pinchot and others. He gives Fitzhugh Lee a pistol. He tells Alston Dayton he will not let his name go on the ballot, and Lyman Abbott that he will not be renominated.

The Aldrich-Vreeland currency bill passes and Congress adjourns; Roosevelt signs the last bills at the Capitol that evening. He rides with Archie Butt, lunches with Ranger Bill McDonald and Admiral Cowles, and plays tennis. To Kermit he describes summery evenings under the apple tree with Edith and La Follette's filibuster; to Archie, Quentin's new beehive and a foul tip to the eye.

Roosevelt calls on J. J. Gaff at 1520 20th Street to see a painting of a farmer, and dines with the Jusserands. "The Successful Mother" by Roosevelt appears in the Ladies' Home Journal, and Ted finishes at Harvard. Archie Butt has become Edith's regular escort on solo outings, long walks and antique hunts. On June 18 the Republicans will nominate Taft.

Roosevelt talks labor and paper-trust legislation with House members, plays tennis in the afternoon, and spends the evening plotting the fall campaign with Taft and party leaders. He also tells the Republican chairman flatly that he will not seek a third term.
Cabinet day and a stream of callers
After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt receives a busy line of senators, congressmen and the journalist James Creelman, then gets out for a ride. He writes to Elmer Youngman about the currency bill.
Writing Ray Stannard Baker on race

Roosevelt sees Taft, Cortelyou and Jacob Schiff among other callers and plays afternoon tennis with Ambassador Jusserand. In letters he discusses New York politics with Chauncey Depew and responds to Ray Stannard Baker's magazine series on Black Americans in the South.

Roosevelt confers with Senator Cullom on what the Republican platform should say about the tariff, talks campaign matters with Senator Long, and meets Agriculture Secretary Wilson with food-safety chemist Dr. Harvey Wiley. Ambassador Bryce calls, and Roosevelt rides.
Waterways letters and a note to Steffens

Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting, discusses an executive order on hiring extra federal workers, and plays tennis. He writes about the Inland Waterways Commission and sends Lincoln Steffens a lengthy defense of his battle against corruption.

Roosevelt goes over Canal Zone business with Taft, rides, and holds an evening campaign meeting with Taft, Root and Burkett. Looking ahead to Africa, he tells Kermit that big-game hunters must cover for one another.
Thrown into a brook on a ride
A Sunday ride ends with Roosevelt's horse spilling him into a stream. He also meets with Taft and writes to ornithologist Frank Chapman about bird photography.

Roosevelt names the National Conservation Commission, chaired by Gifford Pinchot, to take stock of America's natural resources. Between naval talks and tennis, he dines that night with Edith at the home of Alice and Nick Longworth.

Roosevelt beats his military aide Archie Butt at tennis on a day of Cabinet business, currency talks with Cortelyou, and lunch with Massachusetts Governor Curtis Guild Jr. He weighs a new Army Chief of Engineers and wires about rival Louisiana delegations.
Liberian delegation and Booker T. Washington

Roosevelt receives a delegation from Liberia late in the evening, accompanied by Booker T. Washington. Earlier he sees Taft, Root and others, plays tennis, and dines with Postmaster General Meyer, and he assures his brother-in-law Will Cowles about his future.
Praise for a corporate annual report

Roosevelt talks with Francis Loomis about the planned Tokyo exposition and receives several callers before riding. He writes George W. Perkins about International Harvester's annual report, an early experiment in a company courting public goodwill.
A senator declines the Conservation Commission

Roosevelt plays tennis, meets the Spanish Treaty Claims Commission and the Japanese ambassador, and sees George Perkins and Ray Stannard Baker that night. John Sharp Williams wires that he is refusing his seat on the new commission, arguing only Congress can create such bodies.
Talk of a national anthem on horseback

Out on his new mount Georgia, joined by Fitzhugh Lee and Archie Butt, Roosevelt muses about a national anthem; both he and Butt favor Julia Ward Howe's Civil War battle hymn. That afternoon the 150 voices of the Arion Chorus sing at the White House for about fifty guests.
Roosevelt takes his new horse Georgia out for a second ride.

Roosevelt meets Taft, discusses prison reform with Commissioner Macfarland, and plays tennis with Archie Butt. He writes Joel Chandler Harris about Uncle Remus and patriotic songs, and wires Lodge about planks in the Republican platform.

As the Republican National Convention gets under way in Chicago with Alice in attendance, Roosevelt fires off telegrams opposing a proposed plank on court injunctions and again turning down a third term. At home he plays tennis in the rain and greets delegates bound for a scientific congress in Chile.

With the Chicago convention still in session, Roosevelt rides and writes letters. To Lyman Abbott he takes on Christian Socialists, Eugene Debs and Big Bill Haywood, and condemns Tolstoy's Kreutzer Sonata as the work of "a sexual degenerate."
Taft nominated after a Roosevelt stampede

The convention erupts in a 45-minute demonstration for Roosevelt before Lodge heads off any move to draft him, and Taft wins the nomination on the first ballot. Progressives balk at the adopted platform. In Washington Roosevelt confers with Root and Taft, plays tennis with Bacon, and wires Lodge his thanks.
Quentin dreads leaving the White House

New York's James S. Sherman takes the vice presidential nomination in Chicago. Roosevelt holds Cabinet, meets Taft and Ambassador Aoki, and writes Nannie Lodge praising her husband and passing along Quentin's lament about leaving home.

Roosevelt leaves Washington for Oyster Bay, and the guest book notes that Sagamore Hill has been opened for the season. He writes Charles Walcott about plans and routes for his coming African expedition.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

Writing to his sister Bamie, Roosevelt says his mind has already left politics for Africa and that Ted has finished Harvard and begun working. He tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler he would have preferred Dolliver or Cummins to Sherman.
A snake expert visits; Grand Canyon preserve set aside

Harris Dickson of Vicksburg comes to lunch, invited to bring a specimen of a so-called stinging snake. That day a game preserve is established at the Grand Canyon. Roosevelt tells his sister Corinne he is delighted with the convention and calls Lodge's management of it masterly.

Former President Grover Cleveland dies at Princeton, New Jersey. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Lodge about the convention, Taft's chances and the African trip, and answers charges that immigration laws are going unenforced.
Selous on Africa, and no sun helmets
Roosevelt writes to the famed hunter Frederick Selous about plans for his African hunting trip, adding that he does not care for sun helmets.

Roosevelt travels to Princeton, New Jersey, to attend the funeral of former President Grover Cleveland. Along the Texas border, Mexican rebels raid Las Vacas in a short-lived uprising. He writes Corinne explaining why he is giving up the presidency.
Taft, Stimson and Steffens to lunch

Roosevelt goes over War Department business with Taft and Luke Wright and talks politics with Frank Kellogg and W. L. Ward. Robert Bridges and Lincoln Steffens also come, and the whole group, Henry Stimson included, stays for lunch.
Quentin comes in with legs badly burned by the sun and jokes that they resemble one of Turner's sunsets, then adds a line from Poe.

Senator Bourne and Standard Oil's John D. Archbold come to Sagamore Hill hoping to settle the government's case out of court. Roosevelt also plans the African trip with Caspar Whitney, entertains a Mexican senator at lunch, and wires about the border incident.
Taft steps down from the War Department

Taft's resignation as Secretary of War takes effect so he can run his campaign full time, and four troops of cavalry head for the Mexican border. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt sits for the sculptor Victor D. Brenner and writes Navy Secretary Metcalf about flaws in American ship design. Half a world away, an enormous blast flattens the forest near the Tunguska River in Siberia.

Ninety-four National Forests are established on this day. Luke E. Wright, once ambassador to Japan, succeeds Taft as Secretary of War. Roosevelt hosts S. S. McClure and Caspar Whitney for lunch and writes about San Juan Hill, warships and an unhappy H. C. Frick.
An honor for Edith from the Sultan

With calm returning along the Mexican frontier, Roosevelt writes Meyer again about Frick's discontent and asks Root about an award the Sultan of Turkey wishes to give Edith. He also tells Taft about Hitchcock as party chairman and discusses African trip articles with Robert Bridges.
Joel Chandler Harris, the Uncle Remus author Roosevelt admired, dies. Roosevelt writes Truman Newberry about warship building and Senator Bourne about Standard Oil.
The Sagamore Hill guest book fills with Fourth of July visitors, among them Beatrice Flagg, nephew Monroe Douglas Robinson and Elizabeth Hoyt.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Condolences to Joel Chandler Harris's son

Roosevelt sends two letters of sympathy to Julian Harris on the death of his father, Joel Chandler Harris. He also agrees to speak at the Naval War College on July 22 and writes Meyer about Post Office removals.
Peary sails the Roosevelt into Oyster Bay

Robert Peary brings his ship, named the Roosevelt, into Oyster Bay on the way north to try for the Pole, and he and his wife come to lunch. Roosevelt tells the explorer he believes in him and in his success. He also meets Robert Bridges about Africa and the Public Printer about the Government Printing Office.

Lyman Abbott comes to lunch, and Fortescue, Needham and Sullivan call. Roosevelt writes Admiral Chadwick about Spain and history's great navies, and tells Senator Bourne he wants a federal incorporation law passed next session.
Dr. Lambert arrives for a long weekend

Dr. Alexander Lambert, Roosevelt's physician and friend, comes to Sagamore Hill to stay through Monday. Roosevelt writes Robert Collier about his African articles and assures Richmond Hobson he never called war with Japan likely.
Weighing a return to his frontier history

Dr. H. H. Washburn calls. Roosevelt writes Taft about a friendly New York Times editorial, asks George Putnam about completing The Winning of the West, and writes Harvard's President Eliot about two students disciplined for stealing books.
Speech at the John Underhill monument

Roosevelt speaks at Matinecock, Long Island, as a monument to the colonial captain John Underhill is unveiled. Dr. Lambert is staying at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Taft about campaign money and Harry Johnston about a planned book on Black Americans.
Root and family at Sunday lunch
Elihu Root, Dr. Lambert, Arthur Woods, and Douglas and Corinne Robinson with their son Monroe are among the Sunday guests, and Roosevelt lunches with Root and Bacon.

Roosevelt writes Frances Cleveland proposing that the San Jacinto National Forest be renamed for her late husband. Father York calls at noon, and Roosevelt advises Taft on how to take on Bryan and the Democrats.

The Deschutes and Fremont National Forests in Oregon are created. Roosevelt writes Medill McCormick about the Democratic platform's call to drop tariffs on lumber, timber and pulp, which Republicans firmly resist.
A lunch table of writers and publishers
Henry Fairfield Osborn, the painter F. D. Millet, publisher Charles Scribner and George W. Perkins are among Roosevelt's lunch guests. He writes Frank Hitchcock about labor leaders and party funds.
No to Prohibition, thanks to a riding mentor
Roosevelt thanks David Gray for helping Kermit become a better horseman and tells Taft he objects to any national prohibition law.
Henry Fairfield and Josephine Osborn, Frederic Burnham and the Munns sign the guest book. Roosevelt writes Taft about campaign issues, including a postal savings bank.

Roosevelt meets Attorney General Bonaparte and talks Central American affairs with Robert Bacon. He tells Senator Culberson that the Abilene postmaster, Mrs. Morrow, a descendant of Sam Houston, has already been given two chances.

In a letter to Lodge, Roosevelt says he has no wish to cling to power and lays out his belief that the presidency should be a mighty office held by a forceful man. Guests at lunch are Creel, Buchanan, and an assistant attorney general named Bacon with his wife.
Roosevelt writes Secretary of State Root about affairs in Cuba.
Off to Newport on the Mayflower

Roosevelt boards the presidential yacht Mayflower in the evening, bound for Newport. He tells George Putnam he cannot commit to finishing his frontier history now, writes Spring-Rice about soft living among English-speaking peoples, and wires Taft a critique of his acceptance speech.
A big-navy speech at the War College
Speaking to the Navy's War College gathering in Newport, Roosevelt makes his case once more for a powerful fleet, warning that the Monroe Doctrine means little without warships behind it.

Roosevelt brings the Mayflower back to Oyster Bay. Taft stays the whole day and overnight, and Root is also a guest. Letters go to Perkins on railroad rates and Bonaparte on the Indiana Standard Oil case.
Archie Butt arrives for a Sagamore stay

Military aide Archie Butt and Beekman Winthrop arrive at Sagamore Hill, swim, and sit down at eight to fried chicken in white gravy and corn on the cob. Butt records Edith's remark that the house has no rules at all. Earlier Roosevelt meets Taft and the sculptor Brenner.
Swimming in the rain, and a cut toe

William Phillips arrives in time for a breakfast of peaches and cream, liver, bacon and grits. Despite rain the household swims and plays tennis; when Archie Butt gashes himself while swimming, Roosevelt teases Phillips about his toenails. Over lunch he talks at length about Africa, and Butt senses Edith's worry.

Archie Butt goes to church with the family; Roosevelt keeps Sundays free of work and games. Afterward they visit the West Roosevelts, where Roosevelt spins stories after dinner and talks about Africa.
Roosevelt and Archie Butt play tennis and talk over William Jennings Bryan's campaign.
In Cincinnati, William Howard Taft formally accepts the Republican nomination for president.
A placeholder entry with forward notes
The record for this date holds only forward-looking notes: Ambassador Speck von Sternberg's death and the creation of the Country Life Commission, both of which belong to later August dates.

After breakfast with Bacon, Roosevelt takes up West Point dismissals with Luke Wright and canal business with Joseph Bishop. In the afternoon he visits the Squadron C camp at Huntington, and he tells naturalist Edgar Mearns the African passage is booked for March 23, 1909.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day passes without other recorded activity.

His sister Bamie and her son Sheffield Cowles come to Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Taft that Hitchcock needs reining in, asks Root to chair the New York Republican convention, and writes Bryce about Tibet and India and Jusserand about books and leaving office.
Lunch with Collier's editors and Cortelyou
Roosevelt's lunch guests include publisher Robert Collier, journalist Mark Sullivan, Norman Hapgood and Treasury Secretary Cortelyou.

News arrives that Iowa's Senator William B. Allison died the day before. Architect C. Grant LaFarge stays the night, and Roosevelt asks Henry Fairfield Osborn for a standard natural history reference so he can study up on African wildlife.
Edith celebrates her 47th birthday, and Jacob Riis comes to dinner. Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about the 1902 coal strike and his offer to place Grover Cleveland on the arbitration board.

Roosevelt plans the campaign with Frank Hitchcock and takes up the cadet dismissals again with Secretary Wright. Henry Lee Higginson and Frank Chapman call. He thanks his English friend Arthur Lee for the gift of a painting and discusses Quebec's tercentenary.
Bird refuges at Key West and Klamath Lake

Federal bird reservations are established at Florida's Key West and at Klamath Lake on the Oregon-California line. Roosevelt tells John Hammond the Brownsville decision was his alone, not Taft's, and writes Lodge that Edith is pleased his African trophies will go to a museum.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing further is noted.

Worried that farm life is fading as cities grow, Roosevelt creates the Country Life Commission and asks Cornell's Liberty Hyde Bailey to lead it. He also tells Truman Newberry a naval lieutenant should not be dismissed and writes William Allen White about Ohio's Senate seat.
A quiet Tuesday at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no activity is recorded.
A report on the Kaiser from Oscar King Davis

Times correspondent William Bayard Hale calls, and Oscar King Davis brings Roosevelt an account of the Kaiser, later describing the visit in his memoir. Roosevelt writes Taft about disclosing campaign donations and praises James B. Reynolds's Panama report.

Ethel turns 16. The Clifford Richardsons and William Appleton visit, and Roosevelt lunches with New York Republicans William Barnes, Francis Hendricks and Herbert Parsons along with Gifford Pinchot. He writes Commander Sims about a commission to reorganize the Navy.

John Donovan and Representative Barchfeld call. Roosevelt asks Robert Bridges to keep publicity about the African trip to a minimum, and advises Taft to back Governor Hughes privately without issuing a statement.

Roosevelt tells Robert Thompson he will not pardon Curtis and Morse, the two indicted top officers of a New York bank. He also asks Newberry for the Newport conference's battleship findings and writes Bonaparte about rising railroad rates.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

Roosevelt lunches with Cortelyou, Fassett, the Filipino leader Manuel Quezon, Escamillo and Olin. Former New York police chief John McCullagh and Lindsay Denison call, and Charles Sheldon and Truman Newberry stay for dinner and the night.
Invited to give Oxford's Romanes Lecture

Roosevelt accepts Lord Curzon's invitation to deliver the Romanes Lecture at Oxford, which he will give in 1910. Malheur Lake in Oregon becomes a bird reservation. He tells Taft that Bryan is attacking his Unitarian faith, and sends Lodge a clipping about a Texas statue of himself that amuses him.

Roosevelt goes through Selous's list of supplies for Africa, keeping tinned beans, peaches and tomatoes, cutting back the liquor, dropping pepper and mustard, and swapping cocoa for coffee. Secretary Meyer comes to dinner and stays the night.
Hughes renomination talks; a colonel's uniform for Europe

Roosevelt huddles with Sherman, Hitchcock, Bacon and New York party men over renominating Governor Hughes. He writes Whitelaw Reid about African game licenses and royal visits, saying he wants to wear his cavalry colonel's uniform at European courts.

Roosevelt writes William Barnes Jr. that Governor Hughes ought to be renominated, shortcomings and all, and discusses the race with Lyman Abbott. He also sends thanks to the authors of the Panama report.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

Roosevelt's old friend Baron Speck von Sternberg, the German ambassador, dies of cancer in Germany, and Roosevelt wires his sorrow. Alice and Nick Longworth visit, and he writes William Barnes Jr. about Hughes and New York politics.

After lunch with Governor Charles Magoon of Cuba, Roosevelt leaves in the evening for Jordanville, New York, to visit Corinne and Douglas Robinson. He asks Hitchcock to have an expert review Taft's labor rulings for the campaign.
In Jordanville, Roosevelt dedicates the public library his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson has given to the town. Clifford and Teresa Richardson sign the guest book.
Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt lunches with Cornelius Vanderbilt and sends Herbert Parsons his thoughts on the governor's race.
Chase Lake refuge in North Dakota

A bird reservation is set aside at Chase Lake, North Dakota. Roosevelt thanks Douglas and Corinne for their hospitality, concedes to Newberry on the Newport battleship plans, and cites history in defending Taft against attacks on his religion.
Baron Takahira and Dr. Iglehart call. Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about missionaries in China and Taft about bank deposits and postal savings.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Olympians at Sagamore; the children scatter

Roosevelt welcomes members of the American Olympic team. The children head off to new chapters: Ted starts at a Connecticut carpet mill for $7 a week, Kermit begins college at Harvard, Archie returns to Groton, and Quentin enrolls at Episcopal High School across the Potomac in Alexandria.
Telling Taft to go on offense

Roosevelt meets Cortelyou and W. L. Ward and lunches with publisher George Haven Putnam, Francis Leupp, Colonel Brodie and William Travers Jerome. The architect Grant LaFarge and his wife Florence arrive for a stay. His advice to Taft is blunt: don't reply to Bryan, go after him.

Roosevelt issues a press statement backing Charles Evans Hughes for another term as New York governor, then spends the evening at Matinecock Lodge. He tells Arthur Lee that the gift painting hangs in the North Room for lack of a better place.
Fisheries and Africa in a letter to Reid
The LaFarges are still Sagamore Hill guests. Roosevelt writes Whitelaw Reid about the Newfoundland fisheries dispute and his coming African trip.
Bishop Brent and the press at lunch

Immigration commissioner Frank P. Sargent dies. John Sleicher and Henry Wise call, and Roosevelt's lunch table includes Bishop Charles Brent, correspondent Richard Oulahan and Hamilton Fish; Major Wadsworth stays overnight.

With Major Wadsworth still at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt warns Taft that Bryan is using DuPont's role to paint Republicans as the party of trusts. He also writes Sherman about labor and Root about the campaigns and extraditing Russian Jews.
Roosevelt attends the Presbyterian church to hear a sermon by Dr. Fox.
The Dalai Lama and the fleet in Australia

Frank Kellogg comes to lunch. Roosevelt tells Ambassador Bryce about Tibet and the splendid welcome the American fleet received in Australia, and writes William Rockhill about his meeting with the Dalai Lama.
Roosevelt receives a string of local and political visitors and writes Charles Welles about improving housing in Washington's overlooked neighborhoods.
Taft and he share the same views

In a letter meant for the record, Roosevelt tells Conrad Kohrs that Taft and he see eye to eye on the national interest. He also lists his accomplishments for William B. McKinley, discusses Jack London and animal intelligence with Mark Sullivan, and writes Lodge about canal supply ships.

After a big lunch whose guests include William Loeb, Paul Morton, Bonaparte and Medill McCormick, Roosevelt tells gunmaker A. H. Fox he will bring a 12-bore to Africa. Other letters touch on farm schools, Speck von Sternberg's death and lies told about Grover Cleveland.
Roosevelt urges Taft to go after Bryan's record and keep smiling while he does it. He also writes Henry Needham about endorsing Republican congressmen for reelection.

A Pall Mall Gazette writer named Dawbarn calls. Roosevelt tells Selous he hopes to see him on safari, and writes General Samuel Young about a string of stagecoach robberies in Yellowstone; he will later propose civilian park rangers.
Ted reaches his 21st birthday. Working as a mill hand in Connecticut and eager to make money quickly before entering politics, he had declined to join the African trip. His father gives him $1,000.

Roosevelt meets Root and Cocks and wires Root at the Saratoga convention as he works to quiet resistance to Hughes. He tells Kermit the Winchester rifles have come and he will try them tomorrow, and describes Ted's birthday picnic on Jayne's Hill.

Tumacacori National Monument in Arizona is proclaimed and Florida's Pine Island becomes a bird reservation, while New York Republicans renominate Governor Hughes. Roosevelt writes Metcalf about battleships carrying 14-inch guns and tells General Young that Yellowstone needs civilian rangers.
Silas McBee pays a call at Sagamore Hill.
Oyster Bay neighbors and German singers

Roosevelt hosts his Oyster Bay neighbors at a reception, hears a German singing society from Hicksville, and lunches with Collier's editors Mark Sullivan and Norman Hapgood. He teases Spring-Rice for fretting about his safety in Africa, admits he would have liked to stay President, and praises Root's work at Saratoga.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt's essay on Taft's candidacy appears in The Outlook. He lunches with Lord Bryce and Mrs. Brown, and wires Taft twice after Hearst publishes letters showing Standard Oil payments to Senator Foraker, which ended Foraker's career.
After two months of European leave, Archie Butt is back in Washington.

Roosevelt meets Woodruff and Congressman Augustus Gardner, cuts Foraker loose, and confides to Bamie that he wishes Taft would smash into Bryan. He insists campaign money must not come from the trusts and compliments Nick Longworth on a speech.
Back to Washington for the season
Roosevelt reaches Washington at 6 p.m., ending his summer at Sagamore Hill. He writes Lyman and Lawrence Abbott about Foraker.

Roosevelt has no time for Archie Butt while he drafts a reply to a Bryan telegram published in the newspapers, tying Governor Haskell and Foraker to shady money. He demands DuPont's resignation from the campaign, sees Ballinger, Bonaparte and others, and receives the International Fisheries Congress.
An old trolley injury still aches

Roosevelt talks West Virginia and Ohio politics and sees Archie Butt at five, mentioning that his leg still hurts from the 1902 trolley crash. He and Edith go to the National Theater. A letter from Quentin reveals he is being hazed at boarding school.

Coleman du Pont resigns from the campaign. Roosevelt holds Cabinet, discusses Illinois politics, and welcomes Gifford Pinchot and the members of the farm-life commission. He asks Selous to make sure only he and Kermit will be shooting on the expedition.
New coins and two Florida bird refuges

Roosevelt talks New York politics, immigration and the design of new coins, and sees Admiral Dewey. Matlacha Pass and Palma Sola in Florida become bird reservations. He wires Lawrence Abbott to come to Washington about evidence against Oklahoma Governor Haskell, while Edith fixes up Quentin's school room in Alexandria.

On Corinne's 47th birthday, Lawrence Abbott meets Roosevelt in the morning; Abbott later wrote of how Roosevelt composed his Bryan letter and talked of Cabinet choices. Roosevelt sends Bryan his published answer.
Quentin comes home from boarding school

Quentin, hazed without mercy at boarding school, is sent home sick. Roosevelt talks tariff with Senator Burrows and impresses Archie Butt with his deft handling of Ambassador Aoki. His public exchange with Bryan comes to an end.

The Cabinet takes up the Standard Oil cases. Roosevelt sits for a photograph by Ward, dines with Mrs. Taft, Bacon, and the Corbins, and goes with Edith to the Columbia Theater. Quentin writes Archie that the older boys forced cigarettes on him and made him box a much bigger boy.

Callers include John Hays Hammond, Fletcher Maddox and the portrait painter C. A. Whipple. Roosevelt writes Sherman about grumbling from state committees and tells Fitzhugh Lee how much the family misses him, with news of the four boys.

The surviving fragment for this date covers the campaign's issues: Democrats want federally guaranteed bank deposits, caps on corporate size and Philippine independence. Roosevelt calls the size limits unworkable and independence premature.

After his rough start as a boarder, Quentin returns to Episcopal High School as a day student and happily lives at the White House. Roosevelt confers with Ray Stannard Baker on race and Goethals on the canal, wins three sets of tennis, and has Alice to tea. Ted starts at the carpet company.

Roosevelt addresses the International Congress on Tuberculosis and talks labor with railroad union leaders Patrick Morrissey and Warren Stone. He writes Kermit about his Harvard courses and reading Greek.
Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.
An evening at The Melting Pot

Roosevelt and Edith see Israel Zangwill's play The Melting Pot. Earlier he meets Bonaparte and Governor Comer about railroad injunctions, and in letters he discusses Taft's candidacy, a poorly run government sanitarium, early popular Senate elections, and socialism in Denmark.
Refusing to send Pouren to Russia

Roosevelt tells Root he wants the extradition of Jan Pouren to Russia denied, and writes Lawrence Abbott about Black appointments and Taft's attitude. After Cabinet and lunch with George Sheldon, he spends the evening with Root, Cortelyou and others mapping the New York fight.
A heated lunch with Israel Zangwill

Roosevelt hosts a White House luncheon for Israel Zangwill, author of The Melting Pot, and the two argue long and hard. Later he meets the Austro-Hungarian ambassador, Prince Hatzfeldt and Dr. Koch, plays tennis, takes tea with the Jusserands and dines at the Straus home.
Tea-table talk of Alice in Wonderland

Roosevelt invites himself to lunch at Archie Butt's next Tuesday. George Hamlin sings at the White House. On the court, Jusserand and Meyer beat Roosevelt and Phillips, and over tea the group talks about Alice in Wonderland.
The labor vote and the fleet

The Cabinet discusses the fleet's voyage and Army appointments, and James B. Reynolds briefs Roosevelt on the labor vote. He lunches with Silas McBee and John Mott. In Newfoundland, voters reject British policy on the fisheries.

On Kermit's birthday Roosevelt takes Archie Butt on a hard afternoon scramble in Rock Creek Park, tumbling into the creek along the way. They swim, climb and talk of George Washington, and Roosevelt names Poe the best American writer. He writes Sherman about religious bigotry aimed at Taft.
It is the 24th birthday of Roosevelt's niece Eleanor. Nothing else is recorded.
A message to Russia's young men

Roosevelt sees his tailor, receives the Supreme Court, and dines with Bacon; Justice Moody and Dr. Lambert are overnight guests. He sends John Mott a message for young Russian men and praises Taft while condemning anti-Catholic attacks on him.

Roosevelt pays Archie Butt the rare compliment of lunching at his home, with Edith, Belle Hagner, McCoy, Cheney and Phillips, while detectives ring the house. The meal runs from cantaloupe to peach ice cream, and Phillips finds spurs in his soup with a mock knighthood. Roosevelt stays past three and has a fine time.
Lord and Lady Northcliffe join a large lunch at the White House. Roosevelt goes over the New York race with Mark Sullivan and writes Governor Hughes praising his campaign.
Zangwill trims the lines he disliked

Roosevelt thanks Israel Zangwill for cutting the divorce lines in The Melting Pot that had offended him. He confers with Garfield, Pinchot and Straus, lunches with Lord Northcliffe and rides. Edith tells Archie Butt she is uneasy about his attending the open-air play on the White House grounds.
Players on the White House lawn

Edith's children's playground charity opens the White House grounds to the Ben Greet Players, and Roosevelt watches part of the open-air show. Garfield, Spreckels and Greet join him for lunch. He lashes Governor Haskell in a letter and accepts General Young's resignation as Yellowstone superintendent.
Welcoming the players on a hot day

In unseasonable heat the Ben Greet company performs "Pandora's Box" and "Midas" on the White House grounds, and Roosevelt gives a short welcome. He writes Kermit that Quentin has sold one of his pigs to an animal dealer, and discusses the Kaiser's insulting remarks about England with Henry White and Arthur Lee.

Taft returns from a Southern campaign swing unsure of the region's vote, and spends the day with Roosevelt over breakfast, lunch and a working dinner. Root, Knox, Moody and Loeb join the lunch, and Roosevelt goes to All Souls' Church. It is nephew Sheffield Cowles's 10th birthday.
Dutch nursery rhymes for a diplomat

On a hot day Roosevelt receives the Dutch and Honduran envoys, singing the Dutch envoy nursery rhymes he learned as a child. He also greets survivors of a Vermont Civil War regiment, plays tennis, and goes to the National Theater with Edith.

While Joseph DeCamp paints his portrait, Roosevelt dictates his Oxford Romanes Lecture at the same sitting. He hosts a Cabinet dinner with the Meyers, Lord and Lady Rodd, Root and the Bacons, and tells Kermit about a quiet campaign against Taft's Unitarian faith.
Morning walk in the garden with Edith

After his 8 a.m. breakfast Roosevelt strolls the garden with Edith until a quarter to ten, then talks safari preparations with Archie Butt. Charles Freer and Root are among the lunch guests. He writes Senator Knox, in a letter soon published, comparing Taft's and Bryan's records on labor.
Roosevelt discusses Indiana politics with Lieutenant Governor Miller, lunches with R. P. Perkins and rides. He tells Kenneth Grahame he will enjoy his book.
Cheering the fleet's welcome in Australia

The Cabinet takes up Ohio politics, and a new Florida bird reservation is created. Roosevelt congratulates Admiral John Pillsbury on how well the fleet's cruise is going and on its Australian welcome.

Roosevelt plans the African trip with J. C. Hartsell and C. Hart Merriam, and his Outlook article on American attitudes toward the Philippines appears. He tells Kermit the campaign is improving and assures Taft that victory is certain.
Roosevelt spends the day with his friend Winthrop Chanler.
Army machine guns and a Wyoming refuge

Roosevelt discusses New Jersey politics with Representative Parker and the Army's machine gun service with General Bell. Evangelist Gipsy Smith and Ambassador Aoki call. Loch Katrine in Wyoming becomes a bird reservation.
Roosevelt marks his 50th birthday by riding his horse Roswell over every jump in Rock Creek Park. The Hungarian Republican Club calls with birthday wishes, and he urges Taft to speak out on labor.
The Great White Fleet reaches Japan. Roosevelt walks for exercise, tells Frederic Remington he has no plans to slow down at 50, and thanks Alice for her birthday wishes.

Roosevelt attends memorial services for his late friend, Ambassador Speck von Sternberg. Earlier he discusses Ohio politics with Meyer and meets with Bonaparte, Representative Dwight and the painter DeCamp, among others.

After Cabinet and a meeting with Jusserand, Roosevelt assures John Pringle he expects Taft to win. He writes William Dudley Foulke about newspaper falsehoods claiming he took tainted money in 1904 and abetted corruption in Panama.
Art store, oil cases, and talks with Japan

Roosevelt stops at Fisher's art store after breakfast and goes over the Standard Oil prosecutions with Frank Kellogg. Talks go on toward what becomes the Root-Takahira Agreement, under which the United States and Japan pledge to respect each other's Pacific holdings.
Frank Kellogg calls. Archie Butt is back in the capital, having buried his mother. Roosevelt declines Charles Bodkin's offer of a Catholic Encyclopedia subscription.

Roosevelt works on his Annual Message and plays tennis with Jusserand, while Edith and Archie Butt cruise the Potomac on the Sylph and take a launch to Pohick Church. At 10:30 that night he and Edith board a train for Oyster Bay to vote.
Taft wins: beaten to a frazzle

Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay as Taft defeats Bryan, 321 electoral votes to 162, to become the 27th President. Back at the White House by six, he lets an election-night party run until 12:30 while he reads upstairs. Alice and Nick spend the evening at Taft's side in Cincinnati.
A medal for the Cuban occupation

Roosevelt authorizes a campaign medal for service in the occupation of Cuba. Luke Wright calls. He writes Taft about Catholic missionaries to Native Americans, backs a pension for Frances Cleveland, and sends J. C. Martin a letter on religious tolerance.
Archie Butt finds Roosevelt glowing over Taft's win. After talking trusts with Bonaparte, he rides with Butt, Roosevelt on Audrey and Butt on Georgia, then plays tennis at 3:30.
No President has enjoyed it more

Roosevelt tells E. S. Martin that no President has had a better time in office, though he will miss the levers of power a little. He compares British and American elections with Bryce, sees Aldrich on the tariff and Goethals on the canal, and talks Africa that evening with Sir Harry Johnston, his overnight guest.

It is announced that Roosevelt will join The Outlook as a contributing editor from March 5, 1909. He confers with Payne on the tariff and Cameron Forbes on the Philippines, walks in Rock Creek Park, and watches Archie Butt stumble through the introductions at a diplomatic tea.
A purposeful tumble into Rock Creek

Ambassador Bryce calls, and Liberty Hyde Bailey, Gifford Pinchot, Beekman Winthrop and John Graham Brooks come to dinner. Roosevelt writes Archie that Quentin is thriving at school and recounts a spill into Rock Creek during a climb; Butt believed the fall was deliberate, to make the out-of-shape officers follow.
Arizona returns and a farm-life letter

Roosevelt's callers range from Representatives Dalzell and Hull to former Interior Secretary Ethan Hitchcock and the Cuban minister Quesada. After afternoon tennis he writes about Arizona's election, Grover Cleveland, and the Country Life Commission.
