Roosevelt writes Taft his congratulations, along with thoughts on the House revolt against Speaker Cannon and Thomas Platt's exit from the Senate. He also writes Harriet Taylor Upton on votes for women, talks tariff with Senator Cullom, and sees Wanamaker and Bourke Cockran.
Howard Pyle sketches the lunch table

At a big White House luncheon with the incoming Vice President, James Sherman, plus the Bryces, Seth Low and others, the illustrator Howard Pyle draws the guests and gives the sketches to Alice. Mrs. Bryce takes Roosevelt to task over his religious tolerance letter. He writes Kermit comparing the American and Japanese navies.
Roosevelt discusses the tariff with Representative Weeks and receives Justice McKenna, diplomat Henry White, editor Albert Shaw and other callers before riding.
Writing on race and the Indianola affair

After Cabinet, Admiral Evans calls and Roosevelt plays tennis. He writes John Brooks about the rights of Black Southerners, appointments and the Indianola post office case, and John O'Laughlin about relations with Japan.

Roosevelt speaks at Episcopal High School in Alexandria, Quentin's school, and later hosts a big dinner with Major Edgar Mearns and Percy Madeira to discuss Africa. Truman Newberry is named Secretary of the Navy as of December 1, and Taft spends the night.
Roosevelt meets and lunches with Root while Taft remains a White House guest. He takes a walk and writes Alvin Sanders about revising the tariff.

William Randolph Hearst and Chauncey Depew call, and word arrives that China's Emperor and Empress Dowager have died; Roosevelt sends condolences. Preoccupied with Congress, he plays tennis in silence. Letters defend Black appointments, praise Cleveland and discuss H. G. Wells.

Roosevelt hosts a dinner for labor leaders including Terence Powderly, P. H. Morrissey and Warren Stone, joined by Justice Holmes, Straus, Pinchot, General Wood and the Abbotts. He also discusses the tariff with Senator McCumber and rides.

Roosevelt lunches with the Abbotts and Robert Bridges of The Outlook, which he will join under contract next March. Ethel appears in grown-up dress and Archie Butt finds her charming. Roosevelt discusses postal savings with Senator Carter and spends the evening on safari plans with Cecil Lyon.

On Quentin's 11th birthday, Roosevelt jokes with Root and Archie Butt about special yellow Army underwear as a jab at timid leadership in the Army's upper ranks. He and Edith laugh over the Reichstag's rebuke of the Kaiser. He writes Gilder proposing Howe's battle hymn as national anthem.
Carl Akeley on Africa; Leech asked to resign

Roosevelt plans the safari with naturalist Carl Akeley, talks Ellis Island with Straus, and takes Edith to hear a concert at the National. He asks Public Printer John Leech to resign and writes Ted about the Kaiser and women's suffrage.

As Edith oversees a top-to-bottom cleaning of the White House, serious damage turns up on Gilbert Stuart's famous Washington portrait, and she sends it out for restoration. Roosevelt lunches with Akeley, Merriam and Pinchot, plays tennis, and confers with Lodge that evening.

Edith pins a rose in Roosevelt's buttonhole before their morning walk. He writes Archie that Quentin's leg is in a cast, and tells Kermit he has sought safari advice from Carl Akeley and Colonel Patterson and has written both his Romanes Lecture and a Sorbonne address the French government requested for 1910.

Roosevelt writes Harvard's Charles W. Eliot on his retirement after forty years as president. He discusses the tariff with Representative Tawney, sees Vice President Fairbanks and Lodge, plays tennis, and writes about Panama supply ships and civil service reform.
National Forests in Florida and North Dakota

The Ocala National Forest in Florida and the Dakota National Forest in North Dakota are created. Lincoln Steffens calls at 12:45. Roosevelt writes John Loomis about the books he wants to take to Africa.

Roosevelt lunches with sculptor Gutzon Borglum on the day Borglum's statue of General Sheridan is unveiled. Booker T. Washington calls, Speaker Cannon and Senator Aldrich stop in, and Roosevelt writes Bryce about charges of American misbehavior at the Olympics. It is Bamie's 13th wedding anniversary.
Thanksgiving: a 25-pound turkey and a new YMCA

With Archie Butt and William Loeb, Roosevelt helps dedicate a new YMCA building for young Black men. Quentin, out of his cast, roller-skates and plays football with friends, and the family sits down to a 25-pound turkey and roast pig with the Longworths and Willard Straight. Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis and Ambassador Bryce call.

Choctawhatchee National Forest is created in Florida, and Roosevelt holds the White House reception for the diplomatic corps. Between tariff talks and tennis, he writes Franklin K. Lane on railroad rates and Leonard Wood with praise for his work in Cuba.
The Awakening of China in The Outlook
Roosevelt's article on the awakening of China appears in The Outlook. He discusses with Lucius Littauer the New York Senate seat Platt is leaving, and sees Charles P. Taft and Senator Penrose.
Roosevelt spends Sunday on letters, writing Taft and Luke Wright about the two canal supply vessels and Chauncey Depew about Satterlee for Assistant Secretary of the Navy.

Out hunting with Dr. Rixey, Quentin brings down three rabbits. Roosevelt confers with Root and several senators, and his essay "Christmas Dinner on a Ranch" appears in Everybody's Magazine. Taft's plan to replace the White House ushers with liveried servants dismays Edith.
A Navy shake-up and an embassy from China

Roosevelt's Cabinet names Truman Newberry to lead the Navy in place of Victor Metcalf. Roosevelt attends a jubilee high mass for Austria's emperor at St. Patrick's, tours the Corcoran, shares lunch with Mark Sullivan and Minot Weld, then greets a special Chinese embassy, bristling once more at the title "excellency."

Roosevelt and Edith mark their 22nd wedding anniversary. He confers with Hepburn, Root and Woodruff, rides in the afternoon, and tells the Associated Press's Melville Stone he will have no reporters trailing him in Africa.
Wolf-catching film at the White House

Roosevelt screens kinetoscope film of Oklahoma marshal John Abernathy seizing a live wolf barehanded, a show Edith skips and disapproves of. The Chinese ambassador gives Alice jade bracelets from the Empress, and Roosevelt hears from Bryce and from his lawyers on the Anaconda Copper case.
Congressional dinner with family at the table

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with Caspar Whitney and rides. About 80 sit down to a congressional dinner, Bamie and Corinne among them, where one hostile congressman is heard wishing the African lions luck.
Hashing out the Anaconda smelter dispute

Roosevelt gathers Hoyt, Pinchot, Lodge and Montana men to sort out the Anaconda Copper quarrel, then receives Lord Northcote, Bryce and a string of senators. In letters he forgives William Garrott Brown and asks Admiral Sperry about keeping the fleet in battle gray.
Roosevelt's one recorded appointment is a 6 p.m. visit from New York Republican leader William Barnes Jr.
Congress returns and the President is cross

As the 60th Congress opens its second session, Roosevelt is out of sorts, sees Dr. Lambert, and fumes at the press, the New York Sun above all. He confers on Oklahoma land frauds, proclaims Wheeler National Monument in Colorado, and ends the night at the Saint-Gaudens show.

Roosevelt's final annual message lands on Capitol Hill, restating his ignored proposals more sharply and scolding Congress for curbing the Secret Service, a blow that ends what goodwill was left. He addresses a conservation meeting, is stung by a New York World editorial on Panama, and hosts a dinner capped by the wolf pictures.
Deciding to sue Pulitzer for libel

Roosevelt tells Henry Stimson he will take the New York World and its owner, Joseph Pulitzer, to court for libel. He and Taft attend the governors' meeting at the Belasco, and he gets in a tennis match with Meyer, Winthrop and Jusserand, while Archie Butt persuades the Tafts to keep Edith's favorite ushers.
A quiet lunch for the President-elect
Roosevelt confers on the canal with H. W. Farnham and on appointments with Scott and Elkins, then gives Taft a small informal luncheon. He sends Taft his views on who deserves federal posts.
After the Cabinet session and a walk, Roosevelt dines with the Earl of Warwick, takes Edith to the opera at the Belasco, and talks with Taft late in the evening.
Eye exam, then two club dinners

Roosevelt works through appointments with a parade of senators and lunches with Taft and Root. Dr. Rixey checks his eyes, and that night he goes to the Gridiron Club's dinner as well as the Boone and Crockett Club's.
Sending Taft to inspect the Gatun Dam

Roosevelt receives the Chinese ambassador and stops by the Corcoran. He writes Colonel Goethals that Taft and a team of engineers will go to Panama to inspect the Gatun Dam and answer the canal's critics.
Congress receives the Brownsville report. Roosevelt spends the afternoon on the tennis court with Garfield, Pinchot and his son Ted.
Answering the Panama critics, then tennis

Roosevelt sends Congress a message rebutting newspaper lies about the Panama Canal contracts. He and Meyer beat Jusserand and Archie Butt three sets of four, Taft barges into tea with whisky distillers, and he speaks that night at the Saint-Gaudens memorial meeting.

Roosevelt talks over the African expedition with the Smithsonian's Charles D. Walcott, goes over patronage with three congressmen, and rides. He writes Ted advising him against joining the governor's staff.
A state dinner he would rather skip

Roosevelt sends Congress a message on governing the District of Columbia and talks with Wright about Foraker's push to investigate the Secret Service. He lunches with both Taft brothers, walks, and endures a Cabinet dinner, the kind of formal state affair he heartily disliked.
Bison, not lions, for the mantel

The Cabinet takes up the Foraker resolution, and Roosevelt lunches with illustrator Howard Pyle and Pinchot. His essay "Lessons From China" appears in Science, and he asks architect William Kendall to swap the State Dining Room's lion heads for American bison carved in stone.

Roosevelt gets in tennis with Pinchot, Garfield and Jusserand and dines with the Vice President and his wife. He writes Cass Gilbert asking that the newly restored White House be guarded against change.
On a Sunday, Roosevelt meets newsman Oscar King Davis and writes his friend Arthur Lee that he has largely accomplished what he set out to do in office.

Roosevelt receives Irish farm reformer Sir Horace Plunkett, plus China's envoy and Representative Bates. He thanks Henry Fairfield Osborn for his review of the Oxford Romanes Lecture, and asks Taft to meet Plunkett and to send biographical notes for a sketch TR is writing for the inaugural book.
Roosevelt shares lunch with Sir Horace Plunkett and Gifford Pinchot, and sits down with Senator Lodge at 9 p.m.

The Country Life Commission convenes at the White House, and Roosevelt confers with Knox and sees Heney. At lunch are his sister Bamie with her husband Will, Whitelaw Reid, Newberry, Bacon and the Harringtons.

On Christmas Eve Roosevelt goes over the African expedition with Army surgeon and naturalist Edgar Mearns. At lunch are Knox, Joseph Alsop, and the Heney, Garfield and Cowles couples, and he invites Canada's Wilfrid Laurier to the coming conservation conference.

Photographers Harris and Ewing pose the Roosevelts on the South Portico, and more than 50 relatives and friends, Lodges and Longworths included, gather for Roosevelt's final Christmas dinner as President. Afterward everyone heads downstairs to the tree in the crypt to swap presents.

Roosevelt confers on Indian land frauds and immigration work and greets a run of callers. He cheers the news that hunter Frederick Selous will go to East Africa, sends the Kaiser New Year greetings, and asks Root to vet his speech on British rule in India.
The chronology lists Roosevelt in Washington with no events noted for the day.
Ethel's debut in the White House

Ethel makes her debut before 440 guests on the White House ground floor. Earlier Roosevelt confers on Alaska with Governor Hoggatt and greets New York musicians. Alice, back from Boston, mourns the coming end of the Roosevelt years, and Ted meets Eleanor Alexander socially for a second time.

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with Ambassador Bryce, Justice Holmes and Lodge, then rides. His letters range from a government job for his secretary William Loeb to naval gun sizes, battleship design and the rights of American Indians.

Count von Bernstorff presents his credentials as Germany's new ambassador. Roosevelt confers on the savings bank bill, sees Underwood and Jusserand, stops in at the Navy Department, and dines with humorist Finley Peter Dunne.

Roosevelt spends the last morning of 1908 trying out rifles for the safari, then heads out to his physician Rixey's farm by Cherrydale in Virginia. He writes Taft that Taft never wrote the Serbian women the press claims he did.
Shaking 6,665 hands on New Year's Day

Roosevelt greets 6,665 people at his final New Year's reception, and the receiving line runs so long that he, Edith, Archie Butt and Bromwell miss lunch until 3 p.m. He writes Taft about his maneuvering to send Burton, not Foraker, to the Senate from Ohio.

Roosevelt gathers Cabinet officers and congressmen to arrange American relief after the Messina earthquake. Major Mearns and a stream of officials call, and he writes the Kaiser on Speck von Sternberg, a possible Berlin speech, the fleet and China.
The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes no events.
Messages on the Secret Service and Italian relief

Roosevelt sends Congress a special message defending the Secret Service and another seeking aid for earthquake-stricken Italy, then receives a long line of lawmakers. Taft agrees to put William Loeb in charge of the New York customs house as collector.
A luncheon full of Ethel's friends

After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt hosts some 30 at lunch, among them Owen Wister and his family and a daughter of J. P. Morgan, most of them Ethel's society friends. That evening he and Edith dine at the Roots'.
Praising Churchill's book, not the man

Roosevelt sends Congress a message on the Tennessee Coal and Iron Company. China's ambassador, now out of favor at home, dines with him alongside Mrs. Beale and the Lodges, and Roosevelt writes Winston Churchill to praise My African Journey, though he heartily disliked its author.
Franklin and Eleanor at the White House

Land fraud charges against Senator Tillman go public. Roosevelt holds a reception for 350, Bamie regales Archie Butt with stories of their mother Mittie and Georgia, and Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt are house guests.
Roosevelt works through a Cabinet meeting and visits from senators and Speaker Cannon. That night a ball is given for Ethel, and he and Edith take the floor, his dancing marked by lively little hops.
Roosevelt receives a string of visitors, Cabinet members Meyer and Straus, Senator Lodge, his old Buffalo friend Ansley Wilcox and reformer William Dudley Foulke among them.

Roosevelt writes Kermit about Ethel's ball and the safari rifles. To Archie he reports that Quentin came home with a cough after crashing through ice, slipping away from school and lying about it, and so got the first real whipping TR ever gave a child.

The National Conservation Commission hands Roosevelt its three-volume report, and he urges Congress to improve the capital's civic life. He attends a reception for senators at Fairbanks' home and writes Lyman Abbott on Governor Hughes's plan to change how candidates are nominated.

Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting and sees senators and congressmen, then is honored at a dinner given by Secretary Wright. He writes his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson, who will be a witness in the libel suits against the World and the Indianapolis News.

To prove his three-day, 90-mile riding test for officers is fair, Roosevelt leaves at 3 a.m. with his aide Butt, Dr. Rixey and naval surgeon Cary Grayson for Warrenton, Virginia, and back in one day. They push through sleet and reach Washington near 8 p.m., some 17 hours later; the distance was first put at 98 miles and later at 104.
Labor leaders at the White House

Roosevelt confers with Newberry on the Navy, meets the American Federation of Labor's executive council, and sees Senator Knox. After a diplomatic dinner he writes Kermit about his long ride and his battles with Congress.
Roosevelt hosts a working lunch on reorganizing the Navy Department with Admirals Mahan, Luce and Evans, Captain Sims and others. He also writes a letter of praise for Archie Butt's service record.

Roosevelt confers on the Navy with Senator Hale and receives a stream of callers. He fires off two telegrams to California Governor James Gillett, determined to stop anti-Japanese bills in the legislature, while Archie Butt quietly sorts out an awkward affair involving one diplomat's wife and another envoy.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the chronology lists no events for the day.

On Bamie's 54th birthday, Roosevelt addresses Methodist missionaries in the evening and commends Britain's rule in India. He tells painter Gari Melchers he loves the new portrait, which shows him dressed as he was for his long ride.
Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting, sees Congressman Davidson and W. H. Phipps, and attends a Cabinet dinner at Attorney General Bonaparte's.
A Council of Fine Arts and a Nevada forest
By executive order Roosevelt sets up a national arts council, and Humboldt National Forest in Nevada is established. Knox, Senator Curtis and Mark Sullivan are among his visitors.

Roosevelt confers with Senators Flint and Fulton on California's treatment of Japanese schoolchildren, and Moapa National Forest in Nevada is created. He hosts the judicial reception and hears from Bryce that his India speech was well received.

Roosevelt sends Congress the National Conservation Commission's report with a special message, as the House passes the Navy bill. He enlists Andrew Carnegie and William Kent against California's anti-Japanese bill, seeks backing for ballad collector John Lomax, and stays for the dance after a 30-plus dinner.

Roosevelt meets a California delegation on the Japanese school question, and his essay on national statesmen appears in The Outlook. He tells Kermit he is having his teeth seen to before the safari and asks Bay Lodge to critique his European address.
Roosevelt is in Washington; no events are noted for the day.
Edith rules out prize fights at dinner

Roosevelt sees Fairbanks, Root, Bonaparte and others, plus a group of state dairy and food officials, and takes up the care of orphans in Washington. When boxing comes up at a formal dinner, Edith shuts the topic down, which she thought unfit for the table.

Roosevelt accepts Elihu Root's resignation as Secretary of State, enlarges the Pelican Island bird reservation in Florida, and renames Cleveland National Forest. He sends Governor Gillett legal arguments against California's anti-Japanese bills and speaks at a dinner on the care of dependent children.

Robert Bacon replaces Elihu Root at the State Department; Root heads to the Senate in Platt's seat, and John Callan O'Laughlin becomes assistant secretary. Roosevelt names a commission to reorganize the Navy, Mahan among its members, and writes Taft denying he ever demanded the Cabinet be kept intact.

Government of Cuba returns to Cuban hands, and Pecos National Forest in New Mexico is created. Roosevelt lunches with the Meyers, Alice and Mrs. Frederick Vanderbilt, dines with the Supreme Court, and writes Lodge disputing much in the newly published Letters of John Hay.
Callers from La Follette to Hoggatt
After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt receives Senators La Follette and Borah, editor Albert Shaw and Alaska Governor Hoggatt, among others.

Roosevelt sees Woodruff, Cortelyou, Pinchot and others and lunches with family, the Douglas Robinsons and George Sheldon. He spends the evening at the Gridiron Club dinner while Archie Butt hosts Alice and 18 others for poker.

As the household packs and Roosevelt hands out souvenirs, he writes Ted that he has worked to avoid an outright break with Congress and wires the AP that no reporters go to Africa. His essay "A Tribute to Lincoln" appears in the Review of Reviews, and Edith drops her wish to keep a White House sofa after a leaked request stirs a press outcry.

Roosevelt sees Bacon, Pinchot, Beveridge and other callers, stops in at Holy Cross Academy, and Prescott National Forest in Arizona is created. He and Edith dine with the Lodges, and he writes Lawrence Abbott about Africa.
Roosevelt and Edith dine at Navy Secretary Newberry's. He writes Senator Aldrich on the Brownsville resolution and Albert Shaw about a postmastership in Fremont.

Roosevelt sets aside the Hawaiian Islands Bird Reservation, a vast refuge for seabirds. A crowd of senators, editors and officials call, and he is troubled by the Nevada legislature's stance on a measure the record leaves unnamed.
Up to his ears in work

Roosevelt tells Selous he is buried in the last of his presidential work, wires Governor Gillett that California's anti-Japanese school bill must fail, and informs cousin William Roosevelt that on March 4 he will ride public transit like any private citizen.
Roosevelt vetoes the census bill. Indian Commissioner Leupp, Pinchot and Representative Sulzer are among the day's visitors, and he later meets with Bacon, Cummins and others.
Alice slips off from Ethel's dance

At a White House dance, Alice sneaks away to Archie Butt's house and throws a dinner party of her own. Roosevelt defends his census veto, praises Governor Gillett's handling of the Japanese school fight while grumbling about Senator Perkins, and wires California's assembly speaker.
Selous gets a second white hunter

Roosevelt writes Selous that he has cabled R. J. Cunninghame, the safari's professional hunter, to engage a second man. Other letters go to Secretary Wright about the Brownsville bill and Arthur Lee on his closing weeks in office.

Roosevelt confers with Bacon, O'Laughlin, Franklin Lane and two California lawmakers on the Japanese school question, and Calaveras Bigtree National Forest is declared to protect California's giant sequoias. He lunches with Henry Adams and writes Knox, Taft's coming Secretary of State, on foreign policy.
Roosevelt sends Congress the Country Life Commission's report on rural America, sees Speaker Cannon, Pinchot and Lodge, and dines with Edith at Secretary Garfield's.
California backs down; four forests added

Roosevelt congratulates Governor Gillett after the California Assembly defeats its anti-Japanese bill. Tonto, Marquette, Nevada and Dixie National Forests are created, and he tells George Turner the fleet he built now ranks behind only Britain's.

After talking New Mexico statehood with Governor Curry and creating Michigan National Forest, Roosevelt leaves Washington at 11 a.m. for Kentucky with Edith, Ethel, Secretary Wright, Loeb and Dr. Rixey. He reads the whole way, with stops at Baltimore, Harrisburg and Altoona.

On the 100th anniversary of Abraham Lincoln's birth, Roosevelt speaks in Kentucky and sets the cornerstone for a memorial on the farm where Lincoln was born. Alice celebrates turning 25 far away in Grand Rapids, Michigan, where Nick is giving a speech.
Back to Washington; Edith a little sad

Roosevelt returns to Washington as Klamath and a Minnesota national forest are created. He writes Ted about the California school fight and his Lincoln speech, and Stimson about indicting Pulitzer, while Edith confides to Aunt Lizzie that she is a bit sad to leave the White House.
Roosevelt is in Washington; the chronology lists no events.

Roosevelt sees Bacon, Knox, Aldrich and others, and several national forests in New Mexico and the Dakotas are created, Black Hills among them. Edith has Archie Butt burn a portrait the family mocked as the "mewing cat" and smash all the chipped presidential china, and TR goes to a church reception at Grace Reformed.
Tafts back from Panama; lunch with the safari team

The Tafts return from Panama, and Roosevelt confers with the President-elect. He lunches with members of his African expedition, sees Justice Holmes and Hamlin Garland, an Alaska forest is created, and he praises Garfield and Pinchot for their conservation work in letters meant as a foreword to their book.
Taft's Panama report goes to Congress
On Alice and Nick's third wedding anniversary, Roosevelt meets Taft and sends Capitol Hill Taft's findings from his canal inspection. Colonel Goethals is among his callers.

Roosevelt addresses the North American Conservation Conference, gathered at the White House to weigh the continent's natural resources, with Pinchot, Bacon and Garfield as the U.S. commissioners. The evening brings a reception and the Army and Navy dinner, and General Wood stays the night.

As the conservation conference goes on, Secretary Bacon invites 45 nations to a world conservation meeting at The Hague, a plan that died after Roosevelt left office. TR thanks Corinne for the Pigskin Library, a set of his favorite books bound in tough pigskin for the safari, and trades thoughts on Jefferson and Hamilton with William Allen White.

With the conservation conference still meeting, Roosevelt begins reaching his desk at 9 a.m., an hour earlier than before, and drops his morning walk. Toiyabe National Forest in Nevada is created; he lunches with Wright and Newberry and ends the day at a reception at Senator Depew's.

Corinne's youngest boy, 21-year-old Stewart Robinson, falls to his death from a Harvard window, and Corinne is shattered. Roosevelt wires condolences to her and Douglas, then boards the Mayflower with Edith and Alice for Hampton Roads.
The Great White Fleet comes home

Sixteen months after it sailed, the Great White Fleet steams back into Hampton Roads, and Roosevelt reviews it from the Mayflower's deck as some 2,000 small boats look on. He later judged the voyage his greatest service to peace. In Washington the conservation conference closes with a call for an international meeting.

After the Cabinet meets, Datil and Chugach National Forests are created and Roosevelt leaves that evening for New York. He writes Lawrence Abbott about the Outlook editorship he takes up March 5, and Taft about a push to keep Fowler as port collector, a job Taft had promised Loeb.
In New York, Roosevelt, Edith, Ted and Kermit attend the funeral of Corinne's son Stewart Robinson, and TR heads back to Washington. He writes Pinchot in praise of Interior Secretary Garfield.
Seventeen bird refuges in one day

Roosevelt creates 17 bird reservations across the West, most of them on new irrigation reservoirs, plus Modoc, Ozark and California National Forests. The Naval Commission's report goes to Congress, and he writes Jusserand about John Lomax's cowboy ballads and denies the stories about his drinking.

Roosevelt sends Congress the North American Conservation Conference report. At a lunch for Admiral Sperry, inventor Hiram Percy Maxim shows off his new noiseless rifle. Edith writes Kermit that Corinne's grief is her own.

Seth Bullock, Garfield and Pinchot are among a crowd of callers. Roosevelt proclaims Arkansas National Forest, the Fire Island game preserve in Alaska and seven bird reservations from the Bering Sea to Puerto Rico, and asks Carl Akeley where to aim at an elephant's head.
Every Roosevelt belonging is now out of the White House, and Edith makes sure the rooms are spotless. Roosevelt makes plain he means to step aside fully, with no wish to cling to past power.
Farewell lunch for the Tennis Cabinet

Fortified by his usual eggs and rolls, with saccharin in the coffee, Roosevelt gives a farewell luncheon for 31 friends of his "tennis cabinet," some of them in tears, who present him with a bronze cougar by Alexander Phimister Proctor. He bids Congress goodbye, and he and Edith go on to teas and a dinner at Secretary Bacon's.
Final Cabinet meeting and a burst of forests

Roosevelt holds his last Cabinet meeting and greets Haiti's new minister at a full diplomatic reception. In a final sweep he proclaims Mount Olympus National Monument, thirteen national forests from Shasta to Sequoia, and the Bogoslof bird refuge in Alaska, then hosts 50 close friends and dines at the Strauses'.
Last night in the White House

The Tafts dine and stay overnight at the White House, a meal Taft later called "that funeral"; only Roosevelt seemed cheerful. He leaves Taft a parting warning never to split the battleship fleet between the oceans before the canal is done, and writes final notes of praise for Archie Butt, Garfield and Pinchot.
Taft sworn in; home to Sagamore Hill

A winter storm drives the inauguration indoors, and William Howard Taft takes the oath as the 27th President in the Senate Chamber. Skipping the customary ride back to the White House, Roosevelt and Edith head straight to Union Station with New York Republicans, bands playing "Auld Lang Syne," and return to Sagamore Hill. The National Bison Range is created.
His first full day as a private citizen, Roosevelt officially joins The Outlook as an editor, contracted for twelve articles a year at $1,000 each.
Roosevelt's essay explaining why he believes in the kind of journalism The Outlook stands for appears in the magazine.
Writing to Archie, Roosevelt guesses Washington was sorry to see the family leave. He does not miss the White House or the office.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about rumors that Taft may remove Henry White as ambassador in Paris, and about the African trip ahead. He and Edith enjoy walks together in the Sagamore woods.
Dictating by a roaring fire in the North Room with snow outside, Roosevelt tells Bamie his homecoming was a happy one and that Edith has recovered from readying the White House for the Tafts.
First day at the Outlook office

Roosevelt reports to The Outlook at 287 Fourth Avenue in New York, sets up his office, and at an editorial meeting proposes a piece on the government's case against the Sugar Trust. He writes Cecil Spring-Rice that he has had a great time as President.
Henry Adams writes Edith explaining why he could not bid her goodbye in person.
The people of Oyster Bay hold a reception for Roosevelt and Edith.

Roosevelt goes into New York for a breakfast Robert Collier gives in his honor. Robert La Follette praises him in his weekly magazine, and an Outlook piece by TR drawing on judicial experience appears.
The Sagamore Hill guest book records a visit from Von Steiner.
Carrie Louise Munn signs the guest book
Carrie Louise Munn is recorded as a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee that he looks forward to seeing him in England in 1910, and gives his forwarding addresses for the long trip: Nairobi until November, then Khartoum.
Roosevelt attends a meeting of Matinecock Lodge, his Masonic lodge in Oyster Bay.
Franklin and Eleanor's son Franklin Jr. is born. Roosevelt receives the Nassau County delegation that attended the inauguration and writes Charles Amidor about flaws in the courts.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.
Where he parts ways with socialists
Alice visits Sagamore Hill, and The Outlook prints Roosevelt's essay on the points where he cannot work with socialists.
The family gathers at Sagamore Hill for a reunion before Roosevelt leaves for Africa.

In New York, Roosevelt visits Mame Ledwith, his children's old nurse, and the Theodore Douglas Robinsons, then crosses to Hoboken to look over the S.S. Hamburg, the ship that will carry him to Europe.

At 11 a.m. Roosevelt and Kermit sail from Hoboken on the Hamburg amid a crush of well-wishers. He has signed with Scribner's for African articles at $50,000, thanks Taft for his farewell gift, and notes in his diary that he sailed. Edith, who thinks him too old for the venture, spends the rest of the day walking the Sagamore woods.
Roosevelt is aboard the Hamburg bound for Europe; nothing more is recorded.
On the crossing, Roosevelt spends time with fellow passengers Emily Putnam and Ruth Dana Draper.
Roosevelt thanks Corinne for the note she handed him at the pier, says he was touched by how many acquaintances came to see him off, and admits he is homesick for Edith.

The Outlook runs two Roosevelt essays, one on where he can work with socialists and one on his scientific expedition. He writes Bamie that he and Kermit are well apart from one queasy day, and that every American aboard has come to talk with him.
The Hamburg continues east; nothing else is recorded.
Another day on the Atlantic with no events noted.
The Hamburg stops at São Miguel in the Azores, and Roosevelt goes ashore at Ponta Delgada and Horta.

As Roosevelt steams on, the record details his safari: about $75,000 in costs borne mainly by the Smithsonian, with Carnegie and other friends contributing; naturalists Mearns, Heller and Loring; hunters Cunninghame and Tarlton; and his khaki kit, rifles and Pigskin Library. At home Edith writes Kermit that only the children give her strength to bear the separation.
Roosevelt is still aboard the Hamburg; no events recorded.
The ship puts in at Gibraltar, where Roosevelt calls on the governor, General Forestier-Walker.
The voyage continues; Cornelia Landon appears again in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Another day at sea; cousin Nicholas Roosevelt is recorded as a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Naples, and a new ship for Mombasa

Edith's sister Emily Carow and cousin's wife Laura Roosevelt greet Roosevelt in Naples, and he visits the Aosta ducal couple at the Capodimonte Palace. He and Kermit then board the S.S. Admiral for Mombasa.

At Messina, Roosevelt meets King Victor Emmanuel III aboard an Italian battleship and walks through the wreckage of the great earthquake, a scene he calls terrible beyond words. Far to the north, Robert Peary's party arrives at the Pole that same day.
Roosevelt is aboard the Admiral; Edith sends Kermit a newsy letter.
The Admiral steams on; Roberto Centaro is recorded in the Sagamore Hill guest book.
F. K. Watson greets Roosevelt at Port Said, and he dines with officials of the Suez Canal. Back home, Archie turns 15.
The Admiral passes through the Suez Canal while The Outlook prints Roosevelt's essay mocking political snake-oil remedies.

On Easter, with Roosevelt at sea, Alice, Belle Hagner and Archie Butt motor out to Quentin's school in Alexandria with presents from Edith. Alice slips him two dollars despite family rules against extra gifts.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that the Kaiser sent him flowers and that Frederick Selous is traveling on the same ship.

Roosevelt tells Corinne neither he nor Kermit enjoys sea voyages and that writer Francis Dawson will tag along. To Ethel he paints passengers straight out of Kipling and praises Kermit, who plays poker and bridge with young Englishmen and strums his mandolin.
The Admiral stops at Aden, which Roosevelt notes in his diary.
The voyage down the African coast continues; the Osborns and Evelyn Irving are recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is aboard the Admiral headed for Mombasa; no events recorded.
Roosevelt is aboard the Admiral headed for Mombasa; no events recorded.
Still at sea; Barclay H. Farr and Martha R. Phillips begin a stay at Sagamore Hill lasting through the 22nd.
Roosevelt is aboard the Admiral headed for Mombasa; no events recorded.
The Admiral reaches Mombasa, where Lieutenant Governor Frederick Jackson welcomes Roosevelt and Kermit to Government House. After dinner at the Mombasa Club, TR notes a downpour in his diary.

Roosevelt takes the train inland toward Kapiti Plains, riding with Selous on a seat rigged on the engine's cowcatcher. He takes in the tidy stations and the dress and ornament of the people along the line.

Riding the cowcatcher again through game country, Roosevelt and Selous see giraffes, waterbuck, hartebeest, zebras, impala and ostriches. At Kapiti Plains station the safari waits with its supplies and some 200 porters.

Roosevelt and Kermit move from Kapiti Plains to Sir Alfred Pease's ranch as guests, and TR hunts in the afternoon and lists his bag. The camp sits on a bare, dry plain where all water must be boiled and ticks are a nuisance.

Roosevelt rides to Pease Ranch and shoots a hartebeest bull, sketching each animal with the spot where his bullet struck. Riding out with Kermit, Sir Alfred and Hill, the party sets up camp and takes a Thomson's gazelle and three tick-covered wildebeest.

A 16-mile ride brings the party into the Kitanga hills, country that reminds Roosevelt of Montana and Wyoming. He marvels at herdsmen with filed teeth and finds the Boers he meets know a Dutch nursery song from his boyhood.
Roosevelt calls it a blank day for himself, but Kermit, after a ten-mile chase on horseback, rides down and shoots a hyena.
At Pease Ranch Roosevelt fills his diary with long descriptions and drawings of hartebeest and other game.
Twelve hours afield with the Peases
Roosevelt spends twelve hours out with Sir Alfred, Lady Pease and Miss Pease, and writes up a lion kill with drawings. At home it is Corinne's 27th wedding anniversary.
Lunch with the McMillans and Selous

The McMillans and Selous come to lunch at Pease Ranch, and Roosevelt spends time writing. In America a comic animated cartoon of his African arrival appears, and Alice's "night riders" are dropping in on Washington hosts at all hours demanding refreshments.
Lion country in the Mua Hills

Out after lions with Selous in the Mua Hills, Roosevelt drops a very old hartebeest bull for the camp pot but scolds himself for poor shooting, ten cartridges for four hits. He rides over to tea with Mrs. McMillan, and Sydney Brooks's essay on his record as President is published.
After a 13-hour hunt that ends in camp at Potha on the plain, Roosevelt records killing three lions, while Kermit shoots five cheetahs.
Roosevelt shifts camp in the afternoon to a small pond at Bondini, shooting a warthog sow on the way, and delights in the safari's march with chanting, horns, whistles and drums.
Roosevelt's hunt comes up empty; he watches the beaters knock over rabbits with throwing sticks and notes the wildlife.
On the march to Kilimakiu, Roosevelt misses a steenbok, an impala and a Grant's gazelle and calls it awful; Kermit does better, taking a hartebeest and a Grant's.

Riding all day with Captain Slatter, Roosevelt kills an eland cow after long shots, then walks up on a rhino bull, hits it at 35 yards with his .450 Holland, and drops it at 14 paces as it charges. He later goes out with Heller and porters to the carcasses.
Out with Clifford and Harold Hill, Roosevelt misses a galloping giraffe at long range but, after poor shooting, kills a good male Chanler's reedbuck.
Roosevelt misses a waterbuck bull and a wild dog, and records how a lion killed Captain Slatter's horse. His article on the Japanese question appears in The Outlook.
Roosevelt kills two giraffes, one a medium bull dropped by a spine shot at 350 yards, and Kermit takes another.
The day goes to skinning the giraffes for the museum collection.
The safari moves on toward Potha.

Roosevelt heads to Machakos and spends the night at Sir Alfred Pease's. He writes Robert Bridges at Scribner's with his first African article and a plan for the series, though the letter waits until May 23 to go out.
At Machakos, Roosevelt stops at the American mission, then rides to Juja Farm.
Roosevelt settles in at Juja Farm, William McMillan's home, and writes Quentin with safari news.

Roosevelt is out for hours before dawn; Kermit shoots a leopard that charges and mauls a gun bearer. TR's letter to Lodge covers the tariff fight, the Turkish uprising and the hunt so far, adding a note about the next day's rhino and Kermit's leopard.
Off by 5:30, Roosevelt is charged by a cow rhino and has to shoot her, and writes up a rhino story with a drawing of the kill.
Roosevelt records a waterbuck and another buck with weights and distances. He tells Ted he is proud of Kermit, the once-timid boy now cool and daring, and writes Root about the trip and the tariff.
Roosevelt shoots an impala buck at 300 yards and records a python and its weight.
Homesick, and a bad shooting day
Roosevelt misses everything while Kermit gets two waterbuck, and they see the Nairobi falls. He tells Bamie he misses Edith but the hunt is going well and the three naturalists are splendid.

Roosevelt, Kermit and taxidermist Heller move on to Kamiti Ranch, owned by Hill and Heatley, while Mearns and Loring head down the Nairobi River to collect specimens. Roosevelt shoots two wild pigs on the way.
While moving camp, Roosevelt kills two buffalo bulls, finishing one Kermit probably hit first, then gets a third bull in a swamp.
In an afternoon shoot Roosevelt kills two zebras and two hartebeest to feed the camp.

At Kamiti, Heatley's ranch and the largest dairy farm in East Africa, Roosevelt goes after buffalo in the morning without seeing any. His May 12 letter to Bridges finally goes out with the first two Scribner's articles.
Nearly charged by a buffalo herd
Roosevelt drops a buffalo and nearly has the entire herd come at him, in country laced with game trails, dusty and swampy by turns.
Roosevelt goes to Heatley's house and describes the farm and its plants and animals.
Roosevelt travels from Kamiti Ranch into Nairobi.
Willard Straight in the guest book
Roosevelt is at Kamiti Ranch; George Marcius and diplomat Willard Straight sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt moves to William McMillan's house in town.
Roosevelt tours the French Catholic Mission near Nairobi, seeing its plantations and school, works through the day, and spends the evening at "Nairobi Hollies."
Roosevelt attends the Episcopal church and visits a Catholic mission.
A new gun bearer, a memory trick
Roosevelt notes a visit involving Loring and Dawson. A man named Gouvimali replaces Mahomet as his gun bearer, and when TR keeps forgetting the name, Kermit suggests he think of "Gouverneur Morris."
Naturalists rejoin the party in Nairobi

Edgar Mearns and J. Alden Loring come back from a specimen-gathering trip, and the whole party stays with Lieutenant Governor Frederick Jackson. Roosevelt writes Andrew Carnegie for more expedition money and sends Scribner's four more articles, floating a title for the eventual book.
Roosevelt's diary for the day notes only an afternoon tea call at the governor's residence in Nairobi.
Roosevelt leaves Nairobi for Kijabe, the jumping-off point for the next leg of the safari.
At Kijabe, Roosevelt calls at the American mission station and stays for lunch.

With 196 porters and four ox wagons, the safari leaves Kijabe heading south toward the Sotik and the waterless stretch called the thirst. They reach it about midday, rest while the porters dance, water the animals and push on at dusk. The Outlook prints a Roosevelt piece on the South.
The march goes on. Once the sun is high the party halts to rest and sleep, then sets off again at noon through hilly brush country, moving again at 9 p.m. in rain.
A 3 a.m. start in the rain
Roosevelt is in the saddle by 3 a.m., and the rain keeps falling as the safari keeps moving.
A rest day in camp. The porters straggle in about 10:30, and the oxen get water for the first time in three days once the wagons arrive.
The safari moves on to the Nyarok, and Roosevelt jots notes about a python.
Reaching the Guaso Nyero, Roosevelt drops a wildebeest bull on the run at long range, and Kermit takes topi. That night Masai herders swap hunting stories at the fire.
Hunting the Sotik, reading by the tent

In the Sotik, Roosevelt hunts with two gunbearers and a dozen porters, taking a Thomson's gazelle and two bull elands, and records weights, ranges and sketches. Later he settles at his tent door with a book from his Pigskin Library.

Kermit kills a pair of cheetahs, and Roosevelt logs other kills with sketches. At home, the record notes friction over Nick Longworth turning up at the White House in casual dress, and warmth toward President Taft.
Roosevelt goes out by himself for impala and Roberts' gazelle and brings in two impala and a Grant's gazelle.
Hunting lion with Leslie Tarlton, Roosevelt kills a lioness near sundown, a pregnant animal topping 300 pounds that porters haul back to camp. Archie Butt calls on Edith at Sagamore Hill.
Five days' tally, then camp moves
The party breaks camp. Roosevelt's bag from five days of shooting includes a hyena, a warthog boar, two zebra, two eland, topi, two impala and gazelles.

Riding out under cool, cloudy skies to find rhino and giraffe for the museum, Roosevelt shoots giraffes while Kermit photographs. Edith writes Kermit of Butt's visit, Mrs. Taft's stroke and the President's wavering.
Kermit takes a Roberts' gazelle and three topi; Roosevelt gets a topi bull and a wildebeest, adding notes and sketches.
Roosevelt's diary records a rhino taken at a gallop and a wildebeest bull.
Kermit rides an eland to a standstill while Roosevelt hunts on his own and brings back a Grant's buck, a hartebeest and a Thomson's gazelle. The Outlook carries his essay on names.
Roosevelt and Kermit go shooting together and come upon a rhino cow with her calf.

A lion turns up close to camp in the morning. Writing to Bamie, Roosevelt says he has stayed clear of the news, frets that Kermit takes risks, praises his shooting and likens him to Bob Ferguson. He tells Corinne he is busy on his Scribner's pieces.
Roosevelt shoots a Roberts' buck, zebra and an old wildebeest bull. Archie Butt writes Edith with good wishes for her coming trip to Europe.
Roosevelt's terse diary line records a lion shot at just eight and four yards.
Camp moves to a pool near a Masai settlement under a line of tall hills. Roosevelt gets a Thomson's buck; Kermit kills a lioness and an impala.
Roosevelt stops a maned lion in mid-charge with a shot to the chest at a hundred yards.
Edith and the children sail for Europe
Roosevelt shifts camp and shoots a zebra. Across the Atlantic, Edith boards the S.S. Crete with Ethel, Archie and Quentin, carrying $10,000 for five months of travel in Europe.
Roosevelt drops two topi at 350 and 400 yards, plus a Thomson's gazelle, a boar and an impala.
A full day's bag: a rhino at 60 yards, zebra on the run, a steinbuck and two kinds of bustard.
Roosevelt shoots an impala doe. In Virginia, Alice is in the crowd at Fort Myer for the Wright brothers' test flights.
A mail delivery catches up with the safari in the Sotik.
Roosevelt shoots a dik-dik buck as it runs at fifty yards.
Camp moves to a salt marsh
The safari packs up and moves camp to a salt marsh.
A big Grant's buck and a rhino
On the Fourth of July Roosevelt takes a large Grant's gazelle buck and a rhino, measuring its two horns.
Roosevelt drops a wildebeest buck on the run, along with a sow and a Thomson's gazelle.
Back to the Guaso Nyero camp
The party returns to its earlier campsite on the Guaso Nyero.
Roosevelt spends the day at his writing.
The safari marches to the Nyarok; Roosevelt shoots a Thomson's gazelle at 230 yards.
The party reaches the camp it used after crossing the thirst on the way south.
Roosevelt parts from the ox wagons and heads for Lake Naivasha, making camp after dark at the base of the Mau.
The marchers find water by mid-morning and make Naivasha by nightfall.
Edith settles on the Italian Riviera

Roosevelt moves to Attenborough's place at Naivasha. Congress sends the income tax amendment to the states. In Italy, Edith and the children are met at Genoa and settle into the little Villa Magna Quies near Porto Maurizio, with a Secret Service man on guard; the children take up bicycles and lessons with Franciscan friars.
Out on the lake in a launch, Kermit shoots a hippopotamus.
Roosevelt works the lakeside marsh from a rowboat. In Washington, Alice is late to a Bastille Day dinner, and Butt records Taft's mixed view of her: disapproving, yet charmed by her quick tongue.
A hippopotamus charges Roosevelt on Lake Naivasha.
Roosevelt keeps writing despite a bout of fever, and sends Oscar Straus congratulations on his appointment as ambassador to Turkey.
Still feverish, Roosevelt writes on. He tells Robert Bridges that Kermit's photos are good and will run with the Scribner's pieces, and The Outlook prints his essay on poverty and riches.
Roosevelt notes that the fever is lifting.
While Roosevelt stays by Lake Naivasha, the Hudson tubes open under the river linking Manhattan with Jersey City.
Roosevelt records five hippos in his diary, with sketches.

Roosevelt works in camp and writes Henry White, whom Taft has replaced as ambassador in Paris despite assurances; he calls it a tragedy. Edith tells Kermit of walks on donkey paths and a pebbly Italian beach.
Roosevelt rides to Naivasha and shoots two ibis, one in flight. Archie Butt dines with the Longworths, where Alice mentions keeping a diary through her first two White House years.

Heading back toward Nairobi, Roosevelt shoots a pelican from a boat. He tells Charles Walcott of the Smithsonian that $70,000 is now in the bank for the expedition, and reports on specimens collected.
Back in Nairobi for race week
After a long trek the party is back in Nairobi, staying again with the McMillans. Roosevelt sees Selous, and Kermit rides in the race week events.
Roosevelt goes to church from the McMillans' Juja Farm.
Roosevelt dines with Edwards. He writes Lodge, missing their contact, about Root, Platt, White's ouster, the tariff, his specimens and a charging hippo, and thanks Carnegie for the money.

Roosevelt dines at the Wards'. He tells Bamie he is refitting at the McMillans' and has eight Scribner's articles done, and writes Corinne about Carnegie's generosity and his happy distance from American politics.
Roosevelt is a dinner guest of C. W. Hobley.
Turf Club dinner at the Norfolk
Roosevelt attends the races and an 8 p.m. Turf Club dinner at the Norfolk Hotel in Nairobi.
Roosevelt's diary notes Governor Frederick Jackson for the day.
Roosevelt sees an aviator and the races. In France, Ethel and Archie tour Provence with Ambassador Lloyd Griscom and his wife.
Roosevelt worships at the Scotch Presbyterian church.
A dance at the Nairobi Club
Roosevelt goes to a dance at the Nairobi Club. A letter from Edith says she is glad of the extra room with Ethel and Archie off traveling.
In Nairobi, Roosevelt gives an address on education in Africa, then goes out to dinner.
Cornerstone at Kijabe, springhaas by lantern
Roosevelt lays the cornerstone for a new building at the Kijabe mission and travels on to Naivasha. That night Mearns and Loring take him hunting springhaas, dazzling them with a lantern.
A wet morning at Lake Naivasha gives way to an afternoon of hunting. Edith and Quentin, with a Swiss maid, head for Avignon.

Edith turns 48. She and Quentin see the Papal Palace in Avignon and a play in the Roman theater at Orange, then rejoin Archie and Ethel at Lyon. Taft puts his name to the Payne-Aldrich tariff and a Philippine free-trade bill.
Roosevelt grumbles about his misses but notes a fine shot at a stork at 180 yards.
Roosevelt and Kermit leave Nairobi for the Mount Kenya country, starting toward the Aberdare Range. Edith writes her Aunt Lizzie that she is growing more sure of managing on her own.
At the base of the Aberdares
The safari reaches the foot of the Aberdare Range.
Roosevelt crosses the top of the Aberdares and finds it bitterly cold.
Edith in Paris with old friends
The safari pushes on toward Nyeri. In Paris, Edith and the children take an apartment on the Avenue Gabriel, share lunch with the Jusserands and Sturgis Bigelow, and dine with Henry Adams.
At Nyeri Roosevelt watches a Kikuyu dance, and the day is captured on film.
Kermit and Leslie Tarlton strike off northward on their own. In France it is Ethel's birthday.
Fever on the road to Kenya
Roosevelt moves toward Mount Kenya with a fever.
Camped in the Kenya foothills, Roosevelt reports he is improving.
Roosevelt stays in camp with a mild return of fever. At Beverly, Massachusetts, where he is vacationing with Taft, Archie Butt gets a Roosevelt letter written June 27.
A rainy day on the mountain. Butt writes Roosevelt about life under Taft, Alice and Nick, the tariff battle, Mrs. Taft's poor health and the public's endless fascination with TR.
Roosevelt sets out on an elephant hunt with light Whymper tents.
Roosevelt kills a bull elephant on the slopes of Mount Kenya.
Roosevelt hikes back to the main camp, leaving Cunninghame and Heller behind with the elephant.
Roosevelt writes in camp near Mount Kenya.
Roosevelt prepares a new safari with Maxwell and Kikuyu porters. Writing Ethel, he admits he is homesick, talks of money and her mother's thrift, and says Kermit sometimes worries him.
In the afternoon the safari marches and pitches camp in a glade in the forest.
Roosevelt covers 18 miles and shoots a steinbuck along the way.
After a ten-mile march to camp, a heavy thunderstorm rolls in during the afternoon. Film shot around Roosevelt's camp this month survives.
Roosevelt hunts from morning to evening, with heavy rain after midday, and takes a steinbuck.
Roosevelt shoots a bull eland at 280 yards.
Roosevelt brings down a cow oryx at long range and a marabou stork.
Roosevelt misses a waterbuck and wounds an oryx that gets away. Alice has surgery to remove bone from her troublesome jaw. At home, Interior Secretary Ballinger and Gifford Pinchot start their feud.
Roosevelt wounds an oryx and shoots a crane. From the Shetland Islands, Frederick Cook wires the world's newspapers that he stood at the North Pole in April 1908.
Roosevelt kills a handsome oryx at 125 yards.
R. J. Cunninghame and Edmund Heller rejoin Roosevelt in the afternoon.
Marching along the equator, the party wakes to frost after a cold night.
Peary nails the flag to the Pole

Roosevelt reaches Meru Boma on Mount Kenya's northeast slopes and finds Kermit and Tarlton there. The press receives Robert Peary's telegram announcing he stood at the Pole on April 6, launching his long quarrel with Cook.
At 11 a.m. three elephants are spotted three miles off in rough jungle. One charges, and Roosevelt brings down a bull at 50 yards; the specimen later goes to the University of California.

Cunninghame and Heller come in and another bull elephant falls. Roosevelt writes Lawrence Abbott, the Lodges and George Otto Trevelyan: he is reading Shakespeare with real pleasure for once in his life, faults Eliot's reading list, and favors an inheritance tax over an income tax.

Roosevelt kills a bull elephant at 70 yards; his sketch shows ten hits. Archie and Quentin sail home with an adult escort to start at Groton, Quentin's first year there, while Edith and Ethel remain in Europe.
A quiet day by Roosevelt's diary. He writes William Foran about three cables concerning the rival Cook and Peary claims.
Roosevelt shoots a cow elephant. Ted marks his 22nd birthday, still at work for the Hartford Carpet Company in Connecticut.
The safari moves on to Lake Ingunga.
Roosevelt and Kermit kill a rhino and an elephant.
Roosevelt leaves his diary blank for the day.
Roosevelt spends the day organizing the safari for the next leg.

Kermit and Tarlton head southwest for Lake Hannington while Roosevelt and Cunninghame make for the Guaso Nyero. An ailing Heller takes skins to Nairobi by donkey. Roosevelt shoots a crane in flight, and camp sits by a palm-lined brook full of monkeys.

Roosevelt and Cunninghame reach a branch of the Guaso Nyero and settle in for several days of hunting on the plains. He shoots a big oryx and writes Herbert Bridgman to pass his congratulations to Peary.
Roosevelt flubs a shot at an ostrich and spends a beltful of cartridges on one distant oryx, plus two gazelles.
Roosevelt gets a hen ostrich, a bull oryx and a big zebra, and writes notes on the ostrich.
Roosevelt misses a cock ostrich a second time, but takes an oryx and a zebra and runs down another zebra on horseback.
Roosevelt finally gets his cock ostrich, and a giraffe after a gallop.
The bag includes two guinea fowl, an impala buck and a bull oryx, at the cost of another beltful of cartridges.
The party moves to the Guaso Nyero close to the empty boma of Nyama Yango; Roosevelt shoots a waterbuck bull in the evening.
Roosevelt shoots a serumik at 90 yards.
African Game Trails goes to press
Roosevelt kills another serumik and a buffalo cow, while Kermit hunts sable antelope alone. Roosevelt's African Game Trails begins appearing in serial form.
Roosevelt comes back empty-handed from a hunt and spends time writing.
The safari travels along the river, and Roosevelt shoots a young impala ram.
Moving farther up the river, Roosevelt drops a waterbuck at 120 yards.
Roosevelt scolds himself for losing a wounded buffalo bull, but takes two gazelle bucks.
The party pushes upriver to Mamba camp, and Roosevelt shoots two kongoni.
"An elderly man," he tells Arthur Lee

Roosevelt shoots five zebra to feed the porters. He writes Arthur Lee that the African settlers recall America's Western pioneers and that he has ideas on colonial rule to share, and tells Cecil Spring-Rice he hopes to see him in May.
Roosevelt's bag runs to two gazelle, an oryx and a giraffe bull.
Edith witnesses a deed in Italy

Roosevelt writes in camp. Edith and Ethel come back to Porto Maurizio from a tour of Switzerland and northern Italy and serve as official witnesses when Edith's sister Emily Carow signs the deeds to her villa.
After lions in the morning, camp moves three hours farther up the Guaso Nyero; Roosevelt notes a monkey.
Roosevelt marches to a waterhole in a gorge and shoots a bull oryx. Kermit, hunting antelope on his own elsewhere, celebrates his 20th birthday.
Roosevelt takes a big gazelle buck, then hits a running oryx too far back, and notes a crescent moon hanging over the sunrise. In America, Eleanor Roosevelt turns 25.
Among the day's game are a waterbuck and an eland, which Roosevelt sketches in his diary.
A long trek over high rolling downs brings the party back to the marsh where Roosevelt killed an eland in August. Cutting an eland from the herd puts him in mind of his ranching days.
Reaching Nyeri on the way to Nairobi, Roosevelt mails Robert Bridges chapters nine and ten of African Game Trails and discusses plans for the series and the book.

At Nyeri, Roosevelt tells Charles Walcott that Carnegie has sent $20,000 more, thanks Carnegie and weighs his idea of getting the Kaiser into a world peace council, and writes to console Corinne, traveling the world with Douglas after their son Stewart's death.

At the foot of the Aberdares, with a month's mail just in and his ink and paper used up, Roosevelt writes Bamie. He is stunned by the death of Lodge's son Bay, yet holds that death should not be mourned, and weighs in on the polar dispute.
The safari reaches the middle of the plateau. Back home, Sheffield Cowles turns 11.
The party camps an hour past the bottom of the Aberdare escarpment.
The safari arrives at Lake Naivasha.
The whole expedition, Kermit included, regroups in Nairobi. Roosevelt writes Lawrence Abbott about Eliot's list of best books, Russia, and Tolstoy, whom he condemns.
Roosevelt dines with the Hobleys in Nairobi.
Roosevelt is a dinner guest at Nanderman's.
Lunch with Loran, dinner with Jackson
Roosevelt lunches with Loran and dines with Frederick Jackson.
Roosevelt, Tarlton, Kermit and Heller leave the Londiani railhead, aiming for the Nzoia River on the Uasin Gishu plateau.
The safari makes camp five miles beyond Londiani.
Roosevelt turns 51 marching hard across rolling hills, with no time to hunt. The party crosses the equator again into cold nights, and he likens the country to Oregon and northern California.
Camp is twelve miles beyond the ravine.
Roosevelt hunts and gets a young Defassa waterbuck bull at 125 yards.
Roosevelt marches ten hours and shoots a duiker. Edith and Ethel travel on to Florence, Siena and Rome, and another installment of African Game Trails comes out.

After a seven-hour march Roosevelt shoots two Jackson's hartebeest bulls but runs short of ammunition while after oribi. In the United States, Franklin and Eleanor's infant son Franklin Jr. dies at seven months.
As Americans vote, Roosevelt hunts all day and brings in three oribi and a reedbuck.
The party reaches Sergoi Lake, where Roosevelt records notes on animals.
Camp moves again, and Roosevelt shoots a hyena on the run at 70 yards.
Kermit gets a bull giraffe and Roosevelt a kongoni at 150 yards.
Roosevelt drops a running oribi but misses kongoni after kongoni. In Rome a false report spreads that he has been killed; friends in Nairobi cable a denial, but Edith is shaken.
A day's hunting yields two hartebeest, an oribi and a hyena.
The safari marches to a spring in a swamp, and Roosevelt shoots a running warthog.
Reaching the Nzoia River, Roosevelt shoots two kob.
Roosevelt brings in a waterbuck bull, a big hartebeest bull and a young kob.
Roosevelt shoots two kob in very high grass.

Roosevelt shoots two bushbuck and Kermit a leopard, as Edith and Ethel sail for New York. He sends Christmas letters to Loeb, boasting that Kermit now outshoots him, and to Ethel and the boys, and writes Edith of a dream.
The safari halts so the men can eat well, and Roosevelt shoots a dozen antelope for them.
Camped beside the swamps, the party is joined by naturalist Carl Akeley.
Out with Akeley, Roosevelt kills three elephants, and Kermit one more.
The hunters return to the swamp camp; Roosevelt writes up the animals.
Camp moves to a valley, and all hands shoot meat for the safari: topi, kongoni and oribi.
The safari goes back to Sergoi Lake.
Roosevelt joins Nandi warriors on a lion hunt that comes up empty. Quentin turns 12 at school in Groton.
The Nandi warriors kill a lion.
The safari marches to Impey's place.
Roosevelt reaches a government post in Nandi country and writes Oscar Straus hoping to meet near Turkey or Greece in March. In Washington, Alice turns up to watch a house fire on H Street.
Roosevelt and the porters beat a swamp; he misses a lion but gets a hyena and reedbuck. Edith and Ethel land in New York, and Archie Butt sends Edith a White House bloom.
A second drive through the swamp turns up nothing but meat for the porters.
Roosevelt moves camp and shoots a reedbuck on Thanksgiving, which is also Bamie's 14th wedding anniversary.
The party returns to its former camp on the Londiani road, on the fringe of the juniper forest.
Roosevelt marches to a stream in the juniper belt, now heading for Lord Delamere's ranch.

Roosevelt reaches Little Lake and shoots three roan antelope. Edith writes Kermit that America is wild about his father, that Taft is having a hard time, and that New York newspapermen have formed a club toasting TR's return.
The safari slogs through rain to Kongoni camp.
Roosevelt reaches Londiani and goes on to Delamere's, bidding the safari goodbye. Another African Game Trails installment appears.
Roosevelt settles in with Lord Delamere at his Soysambu ranch, farmland where the Mau escarpment begins, and camps in the forested foothills.
Roosevelt and Edith's 23rd wedding anniversary passes with a bongo hunt that finds nothing and an evening of stories. He writes Lawrence Abbott about the dispute over his role at San Juan Hill.

Roosevelt shoots two colobus monkeys. He reports on Smithsonian specimens to Charles Walcott, and tells Ethel he is sorry Edith heard the death rumors and that Kermit is after bongo with Lady Delamere's brother.
Roosevelt shoots two more colobus. At home his niece Corinne Robinson weds Joseph Alsop; the couple will farm tobacco in the Connecticut Valley and raise sons who become columnists.
Roosevelt camps in the forest. Edith writes Kermit that Quentin is a handful, always busy and on first-name terms with every tough in town.
Another fruitless hunt. At home, Sagamore Hill's guest book records the house opened up again.
Roosevelt shoots a colobus. William Phillips signs the Sagamore Hill guest book, and railroad magnate E. H. Harriman dies.
Praise for William Allen White's novel
Roosevelt returns to Delamere's and writes William Allen White that he enjoyed his first novel.

Back in Nairobi, the naturalists, Cunninghame and Tarlton ready the Uganda leg and start shipping specimens home. New books arrive for the Pigskin Library. Warrington Dawson and Eleanor Alexander, Ted's future wife, visit Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt dines with the governor. Worried that Edith is fretting over him, he tells Ethel he will reach Khartoum, and Edith, earlier, by March 15.
Roosevelt dines with Watts in Nairobi.
Roosevelt dines with Milne. He writes Carnegie again about a peace league with the Kaiser's help, and tells Henry Beach Needham his thoughts on returning home and on Taft's presidency.
Lunch with Sanderson, dinner with Tarlton
Roosevelt lunches with Sanderson and dines with Leslie Tarlton.
Roosevelt's diary notes a lunch with Badelu.

A farewell lunch and dinner close Roosevelt's time in Nairobi. He writes Bamie about the Alsop wedding and his longing to see everyone, and Bridges about a photo of a hyena inside an elephant and Helen Sanderson's African stories.
Roosevelt sets off for Lake Victoria and Uganda, and members of Nairobi's American mission come to the station to see the party off.
From Port Florence in Kavirondo country, the party boards a lake steamer for Entebbe, recrossing the equator. Sagamore Hill's guest book fills with visitors including Hamilton Fish Jr.
After a day on the water the party lands at Entebbe, near an outbreak of sleeping sickness. They stay with Acting Governor Boyle, and Roosevelt tours missions.
Meeting the boy king of Buganda
In Kampala Roosevelt stays with District Commissioner Knowles, is welcomed by Bishop Alfred Tucker at the Anglican mission, calls on King Daudi Chwa and visits King Mutesa's grave.
On a sitatunga hunt near Kampala, Kermit gets one.
Roosevelt hunts leopard as the safari moves out, and writes Ethel that he misses home, above all her and her mother.
Roosevelt overtakes the safari on the trail into Uganda. At Sagamore Hill, his November letters arrive, and Helen Leigh Hunt and Alice and Nick Longworth sign the guest book.
Roosevelt spends Christmas Day marching with the safari and sends Helen Sanderson holiday greetings and news of the trip.
Roosevelt marches on and shoots a bushbuck. In the United States, artist Frederic Remington dies after his appendix ruptures.
Another day's march, with three reedbuck among the animals Roosevelt shoots.
Rain delays the start, but the party makes a long march and camps by mid-afternoon. Afterward Roosevelt and Kermit bring down a huge bull elephant standing 10 feet 9 inches.
The tusks are cut from the elephant, and Roosevelt writes in camp.
On the march, Roosevelt kills a Uganda hartebeest bull at 80 yards.
Guinea fowl to close the year
Roosevelt ends 1909 marching and shooting two guinea fowl. Isabella Hagner is a guest at Sagamore Hill, and African Game Trails continues as a serial.
Nineteen miles on New Year's Day
Roosevelt opens 1910 with a 19-mile march through Uganda.
Roosevelt stays at Hoima. Barclay H. Farr signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
At Hoima, Roosevelt receives the king of Bunyoro before the safari moves on.
By midday the party is at Butiaba on Lake Albert, about 160 miles from Lake Victoria, and pitches camp on the sand. From here boats run down toward the Nile.
Roosevelt spends the day at Butiaba. Warrington Dawson is again a guest at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt travels by boat to Koba. In Washington, President Taft dismisses Gifford Pinchot, and Edith writes Kermit that the Ballinger-Pinchot inquiry leaves Taft in a hard spot and that she pities him.
The boat carries Roosevelt past Wadelai. Five visitors sign the Sagamore Hill guest book, among them Evelyn Irving and Helene Coster.
The party makes camp in the Lado Enclave.
Roosevelt shoots a white rhino cow and calf at 60 yards, sketching where each bullet struck.
Roosevelt shoots two oribi, then helps battle a fire in the evening.
Women smoke at the White House
Rhino skins are carried into camp. In Washington, women light up at a public White House event for the first time, and Archie Butt shares stories about Alice.
Kermit kills a bull rhino and Roosevelt a waterbuck bull.
Roosevelt shoots two kob at 90 and 180 yards.
A hunt turns up nothing. Woodrow Creen, David Paton and Cornelia Landon visit Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt shoots a white rhino bull and cow, and a hippo nearly blunders into camp.

A runner brings word that Gifford Pinchot has been removed, and Roosevelt writes him in disbelief, praising his public service. He tells Lodge about the hunt, evening mosquitoes and Kermit's skill, hoping the Pinchot news is false.
Roosevelt shoots oribi, hartebeest, kob and a guinea hen. Bamie marks her 55th birthday, and Warrington Dawson visits Sagamore Hill again.
Kermit kills a cow rhino. Teresa Richardson is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt's bag includes a crocodile, a kob, a hartebeest, a bustard and a bushbuck ram. Binks signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt shoots two oribi. He writes Bamie that the United Press reports Pinchot's dismissal, which he still can't credit, and tells Corinne the expedition has been everything he hoped.
Roosevelt writes, notes that the local bushbuck differ from East African ones, and approves of rhino meat.
The party marches to Sukuni village in the scorching January noon, two to three degrees from the equator.
At a camp beside a lily pond, Roosevelt shoots two waterbuck.
Roosevelt sees nine rhinos and shoots a duiker. In New York, panic hits Wall Street.
The party returns to the village.
Roosevelt shoots a buffalo bull at 80 yards.
Camp moves to the river, and Roosevelt shoots a cow rhino. Ethel arrives in Washington to stay with the McLeans.
Roosevelt goes out in a boat with J. Alden Loring.
Roosevelt spends the day writing while African Game Trails continues in serial form.
A young bushbuck from the boat
Roosevelt hunts from a boat in the Lado Enclave and brings down a young bushbuck at about sixty yards, sketching the shot in his diary.
A full day of shooting in the Lado Enclave: Roosevelt logs a bushbuck ram, several hartebeest and a kob, with the range of each shot and sketches beside them.
Roosevelt's party begins the trip to Nimule. Back home in Washington, Archie Butt gives a luncheon at the house of Roosevelt's daughter Alice.
The safari reaches Nimule on the upper Nile.
Halted at Nimule, Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge, admiring the late poetry of Lodge's son Bay, reporting illness among the men, and worrying over Justice William Moody's health.
The overland march to Gondokoro begins. That night the party camps beside a shallow, palm-lined river.
Walking rather than riding, Roosevelt marches on and camps beneath two leafy trees by an anthill, with water a mile away among the bamboos.
Another day's march ends in camp beneath three big trees, close to the remains of a native blacksmith's forge.
The whistle sounds before three in the morning. After the march the party camps past a dry riverbed, near a pool.
The safari stops early, pitching camp beside a creek among trees.
Rest day hunt on the march
The column halts for a day and Roosevelt hunts, taking an oribi, a reedbuck and a red baboon. At home, his daughter Alice turns 26.
An early start, and camp that night beneath one large tree.
The party marches early and camps near a village and a rocky hill. Roosevelt shoots an oribi at 100 yards.
A brutal eighteen-mile march in shade temperatures of 112 degrees leaves the porters spent. Roosevelt kills a hartebeest at 80 yards.
Roosevelt expects elephant, but none turn up.
The march ends at Gondokoro. At home, Alice and Nick Longworth mark four years of marriage.

From Gondokoro the party heads for Redjaf, moving at night and in the early hours and shooting game to eat in the dry country. Roosevelt writes Andrew Carnegie about Europe, the Kaiser, and his longing for Edith and Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt and Kermit go from Redjaf on an eight-day side trip into the Congo after giant eland, heading for the Kabo River.
The eland hunters camp about two hours short of the Koda River, near a hill.
Roosevelt spends fourteen hours out hunting and takes one hartebeest.
Another thirteen-hour day. Roosevelt finds roan antelope and records one shot the day before.
The giant eland bull at last
After eleven hours out, Roosevelt brings down a bull giant eland at 120 yards, the trophy he came for, and records its measurements.
The day goes to preparing the skins. Roosevelt also shoots an oribi at 60 yards.
The hunters turn back, covering seventeen miles toward Redjaf with an afternoon march along the dry Kabo River.
Roosevelt passes through Redjaf and returns to Gondokoro.

At Gondokoro, Roosevelt meets the steamer that General Reginald Wingate has sent to carry the party down the Nile to Khartoum, and writes Archie about it. A Scottish engineer, Captain Middleton, commands.
The party boards the steamer Dal and starts down the Nile. Roosevelt notices the swift current and the walls of reeds, marsh grass and papyrus, passing Lado and Mongalla.

A tally of the African year: Roosevelt has taken 296 animals and Kermit more than 200, including nine lions and eight elephants for Roosevelt. He was ill only five days. Ted is now engaged to Eleanor Alexander, and Americans are starting to look ahead to Roosevelt's homecoming.
Steaming down the Nile to Bor, Roosevelt writes Gifford Pinchot of his shock at Pinchot's dismissal, and tells Lodge about it along with his European plans and the giant eland hunt.
Dinner at Mongalla, then the Sudd
The steamer stops at Lado, and at Mongalla the party has dinner with Colonel Owen, who runs the southern Sudan, before pushing into the great Sudd swamps toward Lake No.
A tramp on the shores of Lake No

While the boat creeps along Lake No, Roosevelt walks five hours with Cuninghame and spots kob. He tells Lodge he will stay silent on politics at home, and touches on Bay Lodge and Taft's renomination.
Near the mouth of the Bahr el Ghazal, Roosevelt shoots a white-eared kob and takes in the vast marshes and their crowds of water birds.
The steamer travels the Bahr el Ghazal.
A shoebill on the White Nile
From the Bahr el Ghazal and Lake No the boat moves on toward the Bahr el Zeraf and the White Nile. Roosevelt shoots a shoebill stork and more kob.
On the Bahr el Zeraf, Roosevelt shoots three kob at long range, between 230 and 280 yards.
Meat for the mission at Taufikia
The boat reaches a mission where the Sobat joins the Nile, near Taufikia, where Roosevelt shoots a waterbuck cow to feed the local people.

Passing Kodok, Roosevelt catches up on mail: praise for William Loeb's customs work, a blessing on the match of Joe Alsop and his niece Corinne, the Standard Oil breakup case for Frank Kellogg, and English plans for Arthur Lee.
Newspapermen have hired boats to meet Roosevelt upstream, and he gives his first press interview in a year. He talks freely about the expedition but refuses every question on politics at home.

At Khartoum, Slatin Pasha greets the party and Governor General Wingate hosts them. Edith and Ethel are waiting for Roosevelt and Kermit after a year apart. Lawrence Abbott arrives too and offers to serve as secretary in Europe.
Roosevelt drafts the foreword and appendices for African Game Trails, tours the old battlefield at Kerreri, speaks at Gordon Memorial College, and dines at the Sirdar's palace.

The family tours Khartoum and Omdurman. Roosevelt speaks at the Government School and then at the American mission, where he talks about fairness and order under Sudanese rule, before dinner at the Sudan Club.

After lunch at the palace, a mission visit, a hotel reception and a talk to Egyptian officers, the family boards the night train north. Roosevelt welcomes Eleanor Alexander into the family in a warm letter.
Boarding the Ibis at Wadi Halfa
The train reaches Wadi Halfa at nine at night, and the party transfers to the steamer Ibis for the Nile run toward Cairo. Roosevelt and Edith send Corinne the news.
The party stops to see Rameses II's temples at Abu Simbel. Swamped with mail despite two volunteer secretaries, Roosevelt writes Bamie, who is ill, and William Loeb about his New York homecoming.
From Shellal the party explores ruined Philae, inspects the Aswan Dam, and visits the hillside tombs at Mount Grenfell.

Leaving Aswan, the party reaches Luxor for a welcome at the Winter Palace Hotel and an evening at Karnak. Roosevelt writes Ted a glowing letter about Eleanor. At home, Alice's grandfather George Cabot Lee dies.
Roosevelt tours the temples and tombs of Thebes, speaks at the American Mission, and lunches with Weigall.
A day among the ancient temples at Luxor and Karnak, with a call at the United Presbyterian mission.

Arriving in Cairo, Roosevelt is greeted by Major Stack and the U.S. consul-general and exchanges calls with the Khedive. That night he sleeps out by the pyramids at the Mena House. He insists by letter that Edith be with him in Berlin.
No strings on a papal audience

After touring the tombs at Sakkara, Roosevelt catches up with Oscar Straus, who has traveled from Constantinople to see him. He cables Ambassador Leishman that he will accept no conditions on whom he visits in Rome, after the Vatican objected to his planned Methodist call.
Roosevelt visits Al-Azhar University and that evening dines at the American Agency, where a reception follows. He writes Selous to arrange a visit in London.
On Easter Sunday Roosevelt receives a delegation of Coptic, Muslim and Egyptian journalists, and dines with Wingate.

Roosevelt addresses Cairo's National University on keeping order under the law in Egypt, and students march against what he said. He also receives Syrian visitors, calls at the American mission, and promises Lodge to stay apart from politics when he returns.
Students protest again. Roosevelt lunches with Hatzfeldt and cables Leishman that, given the Vatican's condition that he skip the Methodists, an audience with the Pope is now out of the question.
The Roosevelts leave Cairo for Alexandria and sail for Naples aboard the Prinz Heinrich, a ship they find dirty and uncomfortable.
At sea. The European tour party is Roosevelt, Edith, Kermit and Ethel, with a valet and a maid, plus three secretaries, Frank Harper, Lawrence Abbott and John Callan O'Laughlin.
A quiet day aboard ship on the way to Naples.
Roosevelt lands at Naples to a reception so huge it embarrasses him. The family spends the evening at the opera, and he writes Henry White about British rule in Egypt.

Roosevelt arrives in Rome and dines at the embassy, and Edith's sister Emily Carow joins the family. He writes Lyman Abbott a letter, later printed in The Outlook, explaining his stand with the Vatican and denying any hostility to Catholics.
Received by the King of Italy

King Victor Emmanuel III receives Roosevelt. He sees the Pantheon, lunches with Ambassador Leishman, receives the Methodist B. M. Tipple among other callers, and attends a state dinner at the Quirinal.
The day meant for the Pope

Roosevelt's diary still marks the papal audience that was canceled. Instead he rides out with the King to see the Royal Bodyguard of Cuirassiers, goes sightseeing, and dines with Edith at the British Embassy while the young people visit Pisa.
