After calls on Professor Boni and lunch with Ferrero, and a city dinner at the Capitoline, Roosevelt and Edith slip away toward Spezia by carriage, just as they traveled on their honeymoon 23 years earlier. He writes Lodge about the papal muddle.
Roosevelt and Edith take a carriage over the mountains from Spezia to Sestri Levante, lodging in an old hotel where they lie listening to the sea against the walls below.
Town officials call, and a band plays for the couple, badly. Then they drive on to Chiavari past crowds lining the road.

Roosevelt sees Chiavari and meets Catholic students, then he and Edith meet up with the rest of the family in Genoa. Archie turns 16 at Groton. The Outlook prints Roosevelt's statement on the papal audience.

Porto Maurizio makes Roosevelt an honorary citizen, names a boulevard for him, and pelts his carriage with flowers. He and Edith settle into a house near Emily's and lunch with the novelist Fogazzaro.

Gifford Pinchot spends nearly the whole day with Roosevelt, recounting his fight with Ballinger and his firing by Taft and showing a stack of anti-Taft letters. Roosevelt writes Lodge that the Taft leadership has misread the country.
Roosevelt stays on at Porto Maurizio.
After meeting with Phelan, Roosevelt leaves Genoa with Kermit for a fast swing through Vienna and Budapest, while Edith and Ethel head to Paris to stay with Ambassador Robert Bacon.
Roosevelt and Kermit see the sights of Venice and take an evening train for Vienna.

Roosevelt arrives in Vienna, calls on Henry White, Count Aehrenthal and Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and is received by Emperor Franz Joseph. He tours the famous riding school and the Hussar barracks and dines with Aehrenthal.
Roosevelt and Kermit visit Count Wilczek at Kreuzenstein Castle. Roosevelt receives the papal nuncio and attends an official dinner at Schönbrunn. The Outlook runs his Sudan speech.
Bound for Budapest, Roosevelt stops to visit Count Apponyi at Eberhart.

In Budapest Roosevelt pays a call at the Royal Palace, gets a formal welcome at Parliament, visits Kossuth, lunches with Archduke Joseph, and dines with Baron Hengelmüller. In Paris, Edith tells Corinne she dislikes the political picture at home more each day.
Roosevelt tours the government stud farm at Bábolna and attends a Foreign Office dinner and reception before a midnight train out of Budapest.
Roosevelt and Kermit board the train in Budapest at one in the morning and travel to Paris.
Arriving at 7:30 a.m., Roosevelt and Kermit rejoin Edith and Ethel. He calls on President Fallières and former President Loubet, and the family goes to the Comédie-Française.
Roosevelt visits Napoleon's tomb with French generals, Ambassador Bacon and Jusserand, lunches with Baron de Coubertin, and dines with the family at the Élysée as President Fallières's guest.

At the Sorbonne, Roosevelt gives his address on citizenship in a republic, urging character over cleverness or wealth and taking aim at the Socialists. Earlier he takes part in a meeting of the moral and political sciences academy of the Institut. Film catches him leaving.
Roosevelt visits the château at Saint-Germain and lunches with Jusserand, who crossed to France to greet him. A film camera records the day.
Paris City Hall and Edith Wharton

The city of Paris welcomes Roosevelt at the Hôtel de Ville. He calls on Edith Wharton and has dinner with Rochambeau Mission officers at the Military Club. At home, Taft picks Governor Charles Evans Hughes for a Supreme Court seat.
More sightseeing. Roosevelt receives two delegations, one from France's Interparliamentary Union and one a Franco-American committee, then dines with Ambassador and Mrs. Bacon.
A full day: the Vincennes garrison, the Salon, Rodin's studio and Versailles, then dinner at the Foreign Ministry. Roosevelt asks Root for his view of Taft and writes Lodge about his future.

Leaving Paris for Brussels, the Roosevelts lunch at the American legation, are welcomed at the town hall, and dine with the King and Queen of the Belgians at Laeken, where the family spends the night.
An unloved queen at Het Loo

The family lunches with Queen Wilhelmina at Het Loo, and neither Roosevelt nor Edith warms to her. In Amsterdam the burgomaster welcomes them, Roosevelt attends a meeting at the Free Church, and the city gives a dinner. Corinne's wedding anniversary falls today.
Delft and the House in the Woods

In Holland, Roosevelt visits the royal House in the Woods, is received by Queen Mother Emma, tours Delft, and attends an embassy dinner. The Outlook prints his Sorbonne speech and "The Pigskin Library." Halley's Comet is in the sky.

The Roosevelts leave The Hague for the national tulip show and art gallery at Haarlem. In Amsterdam the burgomaster greets them at the Rijksmuseum, and with their luggage astray they turn up in travel clothes.

The family reaches Copenhagen in the afternoon and stays at the palace of Denmark's crown prince and princess, Christian and Alexandrine, with a palace dinner and a legation reception. Roosevelt tells Whitelaw Reid he would rather be home at Sagamore Hill.

The family tours Elsinore Castle, caught on film, before a city dinner in Copenhagen. Roosevelt confesses himself puzzled by the crowds that greet him everywhere. That evening they set out for Norway.
King Haakon and Queen Maud welcome the Roosevelts to Christiania and put them up at the Royal Palace, where Roosevelt plays happily with little Prince Olav before the state dinner.

Roosevelt finally gives his Nobel address on international peace, proposing that peace-minded powers band together in a league ready to stop others from breaking the peace, by force if need be. Nansen calls. He tells Lodge the party held power only because he kept it moving forward.
A cowboy, not a statue of me

The University in Christiania awards Roosevelt an honorary doctorate, and word comes that Britain's King Edward VII has died. Roosevelt asks Louis Hanna to make North Dakota's planned statue an ordinary cowboy rather than himself, then leaves for Stockholm.
In Stockholm the Roosevelts stay with Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf and Crown Princess Margaret, see the city, and attend a dinner given by its citizens. The Outlook prints the Nobel address.
Roosevelt lunches with Ambassador Graves and the explorer Sven Hedin, receives the crown prince and a delegation of Swedish parliamentarians, and leaves Stockholm in the afternoon.
The Roosevelts travel south and reach Berlin in the afternoon.
Lunch with the Kaiser at Sanssouci

Staying with the American ambassador, the Roosevelts go to Potsdam for a midday meal with Wilhelm II and the Empress at Sanssouci, where Wilhelm shows Edith the paintings. Roosevelt writes Reid about the King's funeral.

Though down with bronchitis, Roosevelt rides out with Wilhelm II to review the German army in mock battle at Döberitz. The Kaiser later sends him photos with joking captions his ministers wish he had not. Glacier National Park is created back home.
Lecturing at the University of Berlin

Roosevelt delivers "The World Movement" at the University of Berlin with the Kaiser and Kaiserin in the audience, and accepts an honorary doctorate. He dines with Bethmann-Hollweg. In America, an animated cartoon spoofs his European welcome.
Lunch at the American Embassy, a visit from the German Interparliamentary Union, and dinner at the French Embassy.
The zoo and a cool German welcome
The Roosevelts visit the Berlin zoo, and the wildlife writer Schillings calls. Roosevelt later judged that the Germans liked neither him nor America. The Outlook publishes his Berlin lecture.

Leaving Berlin early, Roosevelt writes Lodge on the trip about the progressive-conservative split in the Republican party, Taft's alliance with the conservatives, Cannon's loss of power, and the public's appetite for real reform.

The Roosevelts reach London and stay with Ambassador Whitelaw Reid. the new King, George V, and his queen receive them, and they pay respects at Edward VII's bier. Visiting royals call, and Alice arrives from America.
Roosevelt's diary notes a question mark beside a trip to Oxford.
Roosevelt has audiences with the Kings of Denmark, Norway and Greece. His old Dakota friend Seth Bullock comes calling.
Roosevelt lunches with Lewis Harcourt, calls on the Kaiser, and sits down at a Buckingham Palace state banquet with eight kings. He found the mourning there brief before the merriment resumed.
America's envoy at the King's funeral

As special ambassador of the United States, Roosevelt attends Edward VII's funeral at St. George's Chapel, Windsor, on a gray, heavy day, amused by the squabbles over precedence and livery. He lunches at Windsor Castle and drives back for an embassy dinner.
The family goes to Wrest Park in Bedfordshire to stay with Whitelaw Reid and his wife.
A family gathering with the Reids at Wrest Park.
Back in London with Arthur Lee

The Roosevelts return to London and settle in at Arthur Lee's Chesterfield Street house. Roosevelt lunches with Lord Lansdowne and sees Andrew Carnegie, and writes Robert Bridges about his book chapters and a bogus safari book.

Roosevelt calls on the widowed Queen Alexandra and her sister Marie, Russia's dowager empress; Edith has her own audience. At lunch he joins Owen Seaman, Maxse and Arthur Conan Doyle, and writes Lodge about Calhoun and Manchuria.
Breakfast with Grey, a call from Kipling

Roosevelt breakfasts with Foreign Secretary Sir Edward Grey, tours the zoo with his safari friend Leslie Tarlton and Seth Bullock, and receives Rudyard Kipling and the British Interparliamentary Union.

Speaking to Cambridge undergraduates, Roosevelt defines success as an honest life that leaves others better off, while students dangle a teddy bear above him. He takes an honorary degree, tours the colleges, and goes on to Arthur Lee's Chequers with Balfour and Lord Roberts among the guests.
At Chequers, Roosevelt and Arthur Balfour hit it off at once and spend the day in lively conversation.
Lord Kitchener joins the Chequers party for lunch. Neither Roosevelt nor Edith cares for him, finding him overbearing and forever striking a strongman's pose.
The Roosevelts return from Chequers to London, where Buxton calls. Alice slips over to France and wins enough at the races to pay for the trip.

Called to the American Embassy, Roosevelt sees Elihu Root, who carries word from President Taft and advises him to say nothing political for sixty days or more after he gets home. He lunches with the Royal Geographical Society and dines with Lord Beresford.
Telling Britain to govern Egypt or leave

Given the freedom of the City of London, Roosevelt uses his Guildhall speech to tell Britain bluntly that it must keep order in Egypt or get out. Spring-Rice and Arthur Lee had looked over the text beforehand. He lunches with the Lord Mayor.
Roosevelt tours the National Gallery and lunches with Irish Nationalist members of Parliament, then the family goes down to Worplesdon in Surrey to stay with his hunting friend Frederick Selous.
The Roosevelts come back to London from Worplesdon, and Roosevelt dines with the editor John St. Loe Strachey.
Calling on the Duke of Connaught
Roosevelt pays a visit to the Duke of Connaught and lunches with W. N. McMillan, his host in East Africa. The day ends at Chequers.

The family stays with the historian George Otto Trevelyan at Stratford-upon-Avon. Roosevelt tells Lodge he has met every leading Briton except Winston Churchill, whom he chose to avoid. The Outlook runs his piece on Black Americans.

The Roosevelts visit the house where Shakespeare was born. Alice, back from the Derby, spends time at the John Wards' country place. Roosevelt wires Owen Seaman a joking reply to a Punch story about his Latin outburst at Frith's "Derby Day."
Back in London, the Roosevelts are the King and Queen's lunch guests. Roosevelt tells Spring-Rice how much he enjoyed seeing him and his wife.

In the Sheldonian Theatre Roosevelt delivers the Romanes lecture, "Biological Analogies in History," and is made an honorary Doctor of Civil Law. The Archbishop of York grades the talk a B-minus and the speaker an A-plus. The family sees Magdalen and spends the night at Lewis Harcourt's Nuneham Park.

After a reception at Dorchester House and a farewell dinner, Roosevelt writes President Taft that he is troubled by some of what he hears but has chosen to keep silent. He carries the letter home himself and gives it to Archie Butt.
Birding the Itchen with Edward Grey

Roosevelt and Foreign Secretary Grey meet at Waterloo Station and spend the day walking the Itchen valley and the edge of the New Forest, listening for birds. Reaching Brockenhurst around sundown, they tally 41 species heard in song and 23 more seen.
The family, with Alice along, sails from Southampton for New York on the Kaiserin Auguste Victoria.
At sea. The Outlook publishes his Oxford lecture.
A day at sea on the voyage home.
The ship steams west toward New York.
Roosevelt writes Governor Hughes asking to talk over the primary fight, and Robert Bridges about a book appendix in which he takes apart theories of protective coloration in animals.
An invitation from the White House
A letter from President Taft, carried by Archie Butt, waits for Roosevelt: a warm welcome back and a request that he visit the White House, with a matching note from Helen Taft to Edith.
While the ship is at sea, Archie Butt calls on Roosevelt's sister Corinne and finds her deep in grief.
A hero's welcome in New York

Roosevelt sails into New York to a roaring reception. After a short speech at the Battery he rides in a huge parade up Broadway and Fifth Avenue with 500 Rough Riders, then heads home to Sagamore Hill. A press boat teases his spelling reform with a "Pres Bot" sign.

From his piazza rocker and then on a walk, Roosevelt counts 42 bird species at Sagamore Hill, one more than on his English walk. In the evening the family goes into the city to stay at Corinne's, where he talks politics with Nick Longworth, Meyer and Lodge.

On a sweltering day, Ted and Eleanor Butler Alexander are married in Fifth Avenue's Presbyterian church, with a Baptist and a Methodist minister reading the Episcopal service. Roosevelt writes Taft that a trip to Washington must wait, and that being invited would not be proper.
The Cowleses and General Wright come by, and the Bishops and LaFarges are guests. The newlyweds set out for San Francisco, where Ted will work for the Hartford Carpet Company.

A big crowd gathers on Fifth Avenue while Roosevelt meets Scribner's about African Game Trails, and the crush unsettles him. He addresses the Camp Fire Club over lunch, sees visitors including Booker T. Washington at the Outlook office, and dines with Robert Collier.
Garfield and Pinchot visit Sagamore Hill. In the New York Times, Roosevelt says any New Yorker against direct primaries qualifies for his Ananias Club of liars.
Roosevelt confers with Garfield and Pinchot and then takes them on at tennis. McCormick calls, and the Heneys, Tarlton, Tritton and Greenaway sign the guest book.
Roosevelt's lunch guests are the naturalist C. Hart Merriam, Henry Stimson and Archbishop Spalding.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt confers with Senator La Follette. He tells Governor Hughes he cannot openly side with him against the bosses Barnes and Wadsworth on primaries, and turns down a trade group presidency offered by C. W. Post.
Roosevelt goes to Cambridge to speak to Harvard Law School alumni. He writes Pinchot that Taft is a man shaped by those around him, who did well under Roosevelt.
Back in the fight for primaries

At Harvard Commencement, Roosevelt and Governor Hughes are so deep in talk they miss the start of the procession. Hughes asks for help with his direct primary bill; Roosevelt agrees, introduces him at lunch, and wires Lloyd Griscom his support, his first public political stand since leaving office. He spends the night with Lodge at Nahant.
A scotch and soda with Taft

Roosevelt and Lodge call on President Taft at his summer place in Beverly. Over a scotch and soda Roosevelt talks about Europe and New York politics, and afterward tells reporters the visit was friendly. He signs on as an Outlook editor at $12,000 a year.
In Boston, Roosevelt visits his ailing friend William Moody, then heads home to Sagamore Hill. In Albany, the direct primary bill goes down to defeat.
Roosevelt meets with Griscom and the insurgent congressmen Bristow, Murdock and Madison. Three of his pieces run in The Outlook, including one on Hughes and primary reform.
No events recorded at Sagamore Hill.
A full house for the Fourth
Independence Day brings a crowd of guests to Sagamore Hill, among them John Burroughs, the publisher Henry Holt, Lucius Swift and William Dudley Foulke.
Roosevelt meets Representative Miles Poindexter of Washington, and newspapers report he has promised to help fight Ballinger. Bacon and Gardner also call.
At The Outlook Roosevelt sees William Loeb and other visitors. Back at Sagamore Hill he talks with John Burroughs, Lucius Swift and William Dudley Foulke.
A stream of visitors: Senator Beveridge, Carter, Churchill, the Bass brothers of New Hampshire, Fish, Sheffield, Bacon and Burroughs.

Roosevelt denies that he and Miles Poindexter see eye to eye on everything, a claim that had embarrassed Taft. He explains the meeting to Lodge and tells William Barnes Jr. that a New York World interview was fake.
At Reno, Jack Johnson beats Jim Jeffries to keep boxing's heavyweight crown. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Five guests sign the Sagamore Hill book, among them Hamilton Fish Jr. and F. W. Whitridge.
Roosevelt writes his son-in-law Nick Longworth about the Payne-Aldrich tariff, Taft, and the political picture. Marion Oliver is a guest.

At The Outlook Roosevelt sees Pinchot, Wadsworth, Stimson and others and shares lunch with Reverend Cranston, the Kansas City editor W. R. Nelson and his nephew Douglas Robinson. That evening Governor Hughes confers with him at Sagamore Hill.
Jacob Riis, Charles N. Fowler and others call at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt's nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson is a guest.
Nothing is recorded for the day at Sagamore Hill.
Back at the Natural History Museum
Roosevelt confers with Herbert Parsons and Wainwright at The Outlook, sees other callers, and stops in at the natural history museum on Central Park West.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's piece on the Johnson-Jeffries prize fight.
A Sunday at home. Edith sends Kermit the family news.
Wood becomes Army chief of staff
Leonard Wood takes up his post as Chief of Staff of the United States Army, a job he will hold until April 1914.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the trouble of standing behind a split Republican party, and tells Arthur Lee how he feels about Taft.
Roosevelt's physician and friend Dr. Alexander Lambert is a guest.
Roosevelt writes Sir Percy Girouard about African affairs. Three guests sign in, including James L. Breese Jr.
Roosevelt agrees to speak in Indiana for Senator Beveridge's campaign and writes Nick Longworth about Ohio politics. Joseph Burden and Eliot Cross are guests.
The Outlook carries Roosevelt's account of English songbirds.
Bamie's husband, Admiral William S. Cowles, is among three guests.
Edmund Heller and Edgar Mearns, naturalists from the African expedition, visit along with the Lamberts and Constance Leupp.
Roosevelt lunches with Neill and Kellogg, and sees Beveridge, Joseph Bishop and others at his Outlook office.
The Outlook prints Roosevelt's article on his old friend Leonard Wood.
Archie, thrown out of Groton for a letter mocking the headmaster, is briefly home before being sent to school in Arizona. Richard C. Paine is a guest.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for the Lackawanna Valley in Pennsylvania's anthracite region.
Touring mine towns with John Mitchell
With mine union leader John Mitchell, Roosevelt visits coal villages in the Lackawanna Valley, then travels to Scranton in Bishop Hoban's company and to Wilkes-Barre in Father Curran's.
Roosevelt's coal-country tour continues through the mining towns of the Wyoming Valley.
Roosevelt returns to Oyster Bay. Eliot Cross and Joseph Burden are guests.
In the city, Roosevelt lunches with his former Navy Secretary Truman Newberry and sees Youngs, Betts and Morrisey.

On Edith's birthday, The Outlook prints Roosevelt's article on selfish legislation. He writes Edward Vreeland on state politics and currency, and tells Nick about the coal towns and his coming tour, joking his throat may not hold out.
Alice and Nick reach Beverly, Massachusetts, to stay with the Bryce Allens, while Alice takes heavy criticism for smoking cigarettes in public.

Roosevelt tells Alice he admires how Nick is carrying himself, and writes William Allen White about John Brown and his upcoming Osawatomie speech. Senator Bourne calls at The Outlook; William Loeb stays at Sagamore.

Roosevelt confers with Garfield and Pinchot. He complains to Bamie that his correspondence is crushing and says young Franklin should enter politics on his own terms, and writes Ted about quietly backing Hiram Johnson in California. Most afternoons he rides with Edith.
Roosevelt inspects a pair of experimental farms on Long Island, one at Medford and one at Wading River.
Roosevelt lunches with Lloyd Griscom, leader of the fight against boss William Barnes Jr., and sees Pinchot and others at The Outlook. Bishop Charles Brent is a guest.
Ethel turns 19. Roosevelt confers with Pinchot.
Gifford Pinchot is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt meets with Griscom, Ward and Barnes. As he expected, the Republican State Committee, with Taft's blessing, backs Vice President Sherman as temporary chairman of the state convention. He calls himself a genuine radical in a letter to Arthur Lee and writes Archie, who is in the Badlands.
Roosevelt tells Lodge the Republican break is as deep as it could be, and that Taft can neither mend it nor let anyone else try. He also writes Pinchot about the Osawatomie speech.
Roosevelt confers with Loeb, Griscom and Cocks, and writes the San Francisco editor Fremont Older about California politics.

Roosevelt lays the cornerstone for Doubleday, Page and Company's new building in Garden City, then speaks to the Negro Business Men's League in New York. He apologizes to Vice President Sherman over a letter that went astray.
Nick Longworth calls at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt announces he will seek the temporary chairmanship of the state Republican convention, a direct challenge to the Old Guard. He assures William Allen White he has no wish to head a faction in the state.

Roosevelt sets out on a sixteen-state speaking trip to Kansas in a private car lent by The Outlook. He writes Ted that Taft is helpless as a leader and that the old Oyster Bay summers of the children's youth are over.
Ten thousand at a Grange picnic
At Utica, Roosevelt talks about farming and country life to a Grange picnic crowd of about 10,000.

Roosevelt talks railroads at Dunkirk, speaks to 250 Buffalo businessmen at breakfast about cleaning up the lake waters, and gives speeches in Ohio towns from Conneaut to Toledo before a Press Club talk in Chicago.
Twins in Iowa, Archie in Omaha

Crossing Iowa, Roosevelt is shown a pair of twins at Ogden and speaks about children, then speaks at Carroll and Council Bluffs, where Walter Smith drives him around town. At Omaha, Archie and James Garfield join him.
In Cheyenne, Roosevelt speaks on conservation, is entertained by Governor Brooks, and watches a pony race and rodeo.
Roosevelt rides 30 miles on a bronco with Senator Francis Warren to Warren's ranch, eats dinner there, and returns to Cheyenne.
Taking on the Supreme Court in Colorado

In Colorado, Roosevelt reviews a parade in his honor, eats a chuck wagon lunch, and tells the state livestock association that democracy must be progressive, criticizing recent Supreme Court rulings. He also addresses the legislature and Spanish-American War veterans. Edith is at Corinne's Henderson House.
Roosevelt speaks in Colorado Springs and Pueblo, conferring with Pinchot and Garfield as they travel, and meets General Bell's four-year-old daughter.

At the dedication of a John Brown memorial in Osawatomie, Kansas, Roosevelt delivers "The New Nationalism," the most important speech of his post-presidency. He calls for a living wage, decent hours, and conservation that uses resources without robbing future generations, laying out the program he will carry to 1912.
Roosevelt speaks on both sides of the state line, in the Kansas City of Missouri and the Kansas City of Kansas. Edith comes home to Sagamore Hill from Herkimer County.
After a stop in Sioux City, Roosevelt tells a Sioux Falls crowd that his years on a Dakota ranch were the most important part of his education. The Outlook prints two of his articles.
Roosevelt gives a Sunday sermon at Willmar, Minnesota, and travels through parts of Minnesota and the Dakotas.
Roosevelt spends the day in Fargo, North Dakota, giving speeches and setting the cornerstone for Fargo College's new Carnegie-funded library.
Roosevelt gives speeches in St. Paul, Minnesota.
In Milwaukee Roosevelt tells his audience that in a democracy the quality of leaders depends on the quality of ordinary citizens.
Roosevelt speaks at Freeport, Illinois, then addresses Chicago's Hamilton Club, having agreed to come only once Senator William Lorimer, who had bought his Senate seat, was out of the club.
Roosevelt addresses the crowds at Cincinnati's Ohio Valley Exposition, then visits the Columbus scene of recent rioting in a streetcar strike and calls for justice from both companies and workers.
Roosevelt makes speeches in Pittsburgh. The Outlook runs his article on the pioneer spirit, and James Derby signs the Sagamore guest book.
The tour over, Roosevelt comes back through New York City to Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt confers with Griscom and sees Parsons and Prendergast; Alice is a guest. He writes Lodge that his labor-over-capital line was borrowed from Lincoln, admits his remarks on courts have alarmed people, and discusses Lodge's reelection and Dolliver.
Ted marks his 23rd birthday in San Francisco.
Nothing is recorded at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt speaks at the county fair in Riverhead. He writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler about the Earl lectures he will give at Berkeley next spring, and Lodge about New England and the bosses.
Sizing up Taft for Arthur Lee

Roosevelt dines with the New York Press Club. To Arthur Lee he opposes Butler's advice that Britain slow its navy, and predicts Taft will win renomination yet lose the 1912 election, weighing his own strengths and failings too.
At the state fair in Syracuse, Roosevelt links the New Nationalism to old-fashioned morality. The Outlook prints his case that the tariff is a moral question.
Roosevelt writes Arthur Baker on behalf of a fired employee named LaForce, father of seven, and Baker gives the man another chance.
Speedboat to New Haven to see Taft

Roosevelt races across Long Island Sound in Dodge's motorboat at 40 miles an hour, nearly swamping, then drives from Stamford to New Haven. At Henry White's house he meets President Taft, with Griscom, Bannard, Norton and Yale's President Hadley present.
Who called the New Haven meeting?
Papers report Roosevelt's denial that he arranged the New Haven meeting, which annoys Taft by making it look like the President's idea. Quentin heads back to Groton for his second year.

Roosevelt confers with John Dwight and Cocks and writes Governor Hadley, Ted and Lodge about politics ahead of the Saratoga convention. Ethel and Evelyn Irving play tennis, and Edith, sad at Quentin's leaving, goes with Archie to Aunt Lizzie's.
Roosevelt meets Griscom, Bannard, Parsons and Prendergast, and asks George Cortelyou for facts on E. H. Harriman's 1904 campaign contributions.

Roosevelt confers with progressive Republicans and sees a long list of callers, among them General Baden-Powell and Ernest Thompson Seton. Franklin and Eleanor's son Elliott is born. In Cincinnati, Taft dines at the Longworth house with Alice and Nick.
Roosevelt's Outlook article on criticism of the courts explains the New Nationalism. Willcox and Wainwright call, and he writes Lodge about Taft and the Saratoga convention.
The state Republican convention opens at Saratoga. Roosevelt huddles with Griscom, Hapgood, Bannard, Parsons and other allies.
Beating the Old Guard at Saratoga
Delegates defy the state committee's choice of Vice President Sherman and elect Roosevelt temporary chairman, 568 to 443. In his keynote he praises President Taft. It is also Corinne's 49th birthday.
Roosevelt speaks again, and the convention nominates his close friend Henry L. Stimson for governor of New York.
Roosevelt speaks at the fair in Poughkeepsie and returns to Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt meets progressive Republicans, sees Griscom and Longworth at The Outlook, and speaks to the state's league of Republican clubs. Alice and Nick are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt hosts the Nassau County delegation to the state Republican convention for lunch at Sagamore Hill. He writes Lodge about speaking in New England and admits his voice is wearing thin.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill, where the guest book records Richard Derby, Nick Longworth and Willard Straight.
Strategy talks with Stimson and Longworth
Roosevelt meets at home with Henry Stimson, the Republican pick for governor, and his son-in-law Nick Longworth. Novelist Stewart Edward White and his wife Elizabeth are among the guests.
Roosevelt travels to Freeport, Long Island, to address the state's volunteer firemen, and lunches with Kansas City editor William Rockhill Nelson and journalist Ray Stannard Baker.
In Manhattan, Roosevelt confers with Lloyd Griscom, the county Republican chairman, and sees Senator Albert Cummins at The Outlook before heading to Brooklyn to talk about citizenship.
Busy office day, then off south

A steady stream of visitors reaches Roosevelt at The Outlook, labor leader John Mitchell and canal builder George Goethals among them. After lunch with Herbert Croly, he boards a train for a southern speaking tour with Harper and the Howlands.

Roosevelt speaks his way across East Tennessee, from Bristol to Knoxville. In a letter to Lucius Swift he defends his role at the state convention despite its tariff plank, noting the West stands firmly against the tariff.
In Georgia, Roosevelt tours the Berry School at Rome, gives speeches in Atlanta, and goes to Roswell to see Bulloch Hall, where his mother Mittie grew up.
The southern tour rolls on with talks across Tennessee, Alabama and Mississippi.
Hot Springs, and a gift for Kermit
Roosevelt speaks in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Back east, Kermit turns 21 and carries on at Harvard; his father marks the day with a $500 gift.

In St. Louis, Roosevelt climbs into a plane with aviator Arch Hoxsey and rides about four minutes at some 50 feet. Landing, he tells reporters it was the best thing he ever did. He also addresses audiences in Clayton and St. Louis. Niece Eleanor turns 26.
Illinois stops at Springfield and Peoria
Roosevelt addresses crowds in Springfield and Peoria, and makes a plea for religious tolerance in Africa.
Roosevelt crosses Indiana, from Covington to Indianapolis, campaigning for Senator Albert Beveridge's re-election. Beveridge is a firm opponent of President Taft.
Back in his home state, Roosevelt speaks at six stops along New York's southern tier, from Dunkirk to Elmira.
In Manhattan, Roosevelt meets with Griscom and the state Republican committee. The Outlook runs his article on clean government and popular rule.
Henry Stimson comes to Sagamore Hill for lunch.
Roosevelt works up the Hudson and Mohawk valleys with speeches from Yonkers to Hudson. He writes Sydney Brooks a frank letter about American politics, prompted by Brooks's article on the subject.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the 12th birthday of his nephew Sheffield Cowles.

On a foggy day at home, Roosevelt writes Ted about his California political friends and reports that James is giving Scamp and Ace, the dogs, a bath in his own tub. He also writes Senator Bourne and thanks poet Edwin Arlington Robinson for a dedication.
Roosevelt speaks in New York City and writes Annie Bissell to rebut false claims that he skipped paying his 1898 taxes.
Boston rally for Lodge and Draper
Roosevelt goes to Boston to speak for Senator Lodge and Governor Eben Draper. He tells Elihu Root he will not return to Ohio before the election, despite their wishes and Taft's.
Roosevelt campaigns in Concord, Manchester and Nashua for Robert Bass, New Hampshire's progressive candidate for governor.
Roosevelt travels from Boston to New York City.
The upstate campaign continues with stops at Binghamton, Ithaca and Oswego.
Roosevelt speaks through the Finger Lakes country, from Penn Yan and Canandaigua to Auburn and Syracuse.
Roosevelt's train carries him north from Phoenix and Fulton through Oswego and Watertown to Ogdensburg on the St. Lawrence, with speeches at each.
Roosevelt spends his 52nd birthday campaigning through the Mohawk Valley, from Fonda to Utica.
More upstate speeches, this time in Rome, Lyons and Rochester.
Roosevelt addresses audiences at Kingston, at Bronxville and in New York City. The Outlook carries his piece on the late Iowa Senator Jonathan Dolliver.

Edith writes Kermit that she is glad winter will keep his father safely at Sagamore, and wishes Kermit will grow more like him over the years. Roosevelt speaks in New York City and dines with Henry Stimson.
African Game Trails hits the shelves
Scribner's publishes African Game Trails, Roosevelt's account of his safari, and it becomes a bestseller at once. Putnam's brings out his African and European Addresses the same day.
Buffalo to Manhattan in a day
Roosevelt speaks at Buffalo, Lockport and Albion, then in New York City, and dines with Buffalo publisher Edward H. Butler.

Roosevelt speaks in Baltimore. He writes Simeon Baldwin, Connecticut's Democratic nominee for governor, about remarks he made against him and about the courts. To Wall Street broker Alfred Borden he defends his record, including leaving the tariff alone as President.
A long day on the rails brings talks across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois.
In Iowa, Roosevelt speaks at four Iowa stops, Davenport to Des Moines, on behalf of Grilk, Carroll and Senator Albert Cummins.
Roosevelt speaks in Toledo and Cleveland. The Outlook publishes his tribute to William H. Moody, his former Attorney General and Supreme Court appointee.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill.
On the last night of the campaign, Roosevelt speaks in New York City and dines with the Hungarian Republican Club.

Roosevelt casts his vote in Oyster Bay and watches the Republicans take a beating. Stimson, his choice for governor, loses. Democrats win the House for the first time since Cleveland, 26 governorships including Woodrow Wilson's, and ten Senate seats, among them Beveridge's. Franklin Roosevelt wins a state senate seat.
Beaten, but enlisted for the duration
The day after the defeat, Roosevelt writes General Francis Greene that he means to see the fight through.
Roosevelt writes John Jacob Astor about the untruths he finds in Thomas Platt's autobiography.

Roosevelt sends a stack of post-election letters. He jokes to his sister Bamie about cats and dogs, tells Ted his hopes for 1912 and plans for California, and admits to Arthur Lee that the defeat was heavy, hoping he won't be a candidate in 1912 and judging Taft harshly.
Roosevelt rides on horseback to call on Henry Stimson, the defeated candidate for governor.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt tells Seth Low that leaning harder or softer toward Taft would only have made the loss worse. He forwards Low's view of the situation to Henry Stimson and writes George Tait about the wallpaper trust and his tariff position.

In the city, Roosevelt confers with Lodge and receives callers at The Outlook, including Wisconsin's Charles Van Hise and Henry Pritchett. He tells William Allen White that New Yorkers found him too radical.
In Washington, Roosevelt is received at the National Press Club and lectures the National Geographic Society on people and animals of Africa.

With Taft away in Panama, Roosevelt revisits the White House, tours the staff quarters, inspects the new oval office and takes his old seat at the President's desk. Ike Hoover, the chief usher, weeps. He sees callers, dines with the Smithsonian, and speaks there to an overflow crowd. Quentin turns 13 at Groton.
Five Sunday guests, among them Richard Derby and Josephine Osborn, visit Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt tells Joseph Bucklin Bishop he is glad not to face choosing whether to accept the 1912 nomination. In a long letter to Benjamin Ide Wheeler he concedes he erred in letting himself be drawn into the fight and dissects what went wrong.
Roosevelt is based at Sagamore Hill these weeks but often goes into Manhattan to his Outlook office on Fourth Avenue. Cornelia Landon is a guest.

Roosevelt tells Henry Pritchett where he went wrong in the campaign, chiefly by giving too many speeches, and has words for crooked politicians. He thanks author Gouverneur Morris, a descendant of the founder whose biography he wrote, for three books.
Roosevelt spends Thanksgiving Day at Sagamore Hill.
At Sagamore Hill on the 15th wedding anniversary of his sister Bamie and William Sheffield Cowles.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt writes Congressman William Kent about Pinchot and Ballinger, Taft, and the Japanese in California. He tells President Taft he cannot come to the White House or the Gridiron Dinner, and passes on Kent's warning of new anti-Japanese bills in California.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

The Outlook Company publishes The New Nationalism. The family is scattered: Alice in Washington with Nick, Ted selling carpets in San Francisco, Kermit a Harvard sophomore, Archie at school in Arizona, and Quentin suddenly thriving at Groton. Only Ethel is home.
Roosevelt is home with frequent trips to the city. Guests include his old Maine guide and Elkhorn foreman Bill Sewall, Oscar Straus and his wife, editor Albert Shaw and his wife, and Alice and Nick.
Roosevelt and Edith mark their 24th wedding anniversary at Sagamore Hill.
James L. Derby, Cornelia Landon and the Chadwicks sign the guest book.
A long ride, then a blizzard
Roosevelt and Edith ride together for three hours. That evening they settle by the fire in the North Room as snow outside builds into a blizzard.

Roosevelt writes Ted about a warm note from Johnston, pokes fun at a know-it-all letter from William Kent, and discusses Taft, the Japanese question and the California trip. Ethel is back from Geneseo and Kermit heading there. He feels no itch to be elsewhere.
Roosevelt sends a short note to Ernest Harvier and writes Taft about Panama, thanks him for his kind words, and discusses the Japanese situation in California. He plans to see Secretary Knox.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt sends Taft his comments on the President's annual message to Congress, along with thoughts on Japan and immigration.
Roosevelt thanks Indiana State Geologist Willis Blatchley for sending his book on beetles.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt explains to William Allen White why he should not run again, describing a happy life at home with Edith and only Ethel still under their roof. He backs the initiative, referendum and direct primaries and lays out his political creed, though many think him too radical.
Roosevelt speaks to New Haven's business leaders; Governor-elect Simeon Baldwin declines to come. He sends Ernest Harvier a brief note about an interesting comparison.
At Harvard, Roosevelt delivers the Noble Lecture on applied ethics, touching on conservation.
In Boston, Roosevelt pays a call on Governor Eben Draper.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Visitors include Roosevelt's nephew Monroe Douglas Robinson, along with Alice and Nick.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt writes Louis Lang, who helped Thomas Platt with his autobiography, listing what he disputes: Platt's story of the 1900 vice-presidential nomination, his claimed backing for the Navy post, and money in the 1898 governor's race.
Roosevelt writes Oregon Congressman Abraham Lafferty about farm and forest lands, national forests in Oregon, and federal versus state control of forests.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Japan, Manchuria and the open door

In a very long letter, Roosevelt reports to Taft on his talk with Knox and the Japanese question. He will not urge steps against Japanese moves in Manchuria, though Knox favors them, and discusses the open door.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's account of his August visit to Pennsylvania coal country.
Roosevelt and Edith share Christmas dinner with Alice, Nick, Kermit, Ethel and Quentin; Ted is in California and Archie in Arizona. The children fill their parents' stockings with joke gifts.
Dorothy Whitney comes to Sagamore with Robert Bacon Jr. Roosevelt thanks Ted and Eleanor for a book he treasures and notes Kermit has not yet made the Porcellian Club.
Barclay H. Farr and Grafton H. Pyne sign the guest book.
On John Brown and Homer Lea
Roosevelt gives Lyman Draper his view of John Brown. He also writes General Ian Hamilton about Homer Lea's book imagining a Japanese invasion of the West Coast, which he dislikes.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt turns down membership in the new progressive Republican league organized by Senators Robert LaFollette and Jonathan Bourne. Its platform calls for direct election of senators, direct primaries, recall, initiative, referendum and laws against corrupt practices.
A settee from the White House
President Taft sends Edith, as a New Year's gift, the settee she loved in the White House. The Outlook runs Roosevelt's Christmas in Mid-Africa. Isabella Hagner visits.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Lloyd Griscom lunches at Sagamore, seeming less buoyant than before. Roosevelt sends Ted a zebra skin and offers a rhinoceros-foot inkstand, calls LaFollette and Bourne extremists, and writes Robert Bacon's family that Quentin has stunned Groton by ranking high in his class.

Roosevelt writes Lodge about bribery charges against Vardaman and Senator William Lorimer, sends him a zebra skin, and mentions a book on superstitions he is reading. He also writes LaFollette about the new progressive league.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt writes General Ian Hamilton about conscription in the British Army and about his own soldiering at Santiago with the Rough Riders.
Splitting the day between home and the city, Roosevelt tells Ernest Harvier he will write him about Mitchell.
Staying out of the Lorimer fight
Roosevelt writes Taft that Beveridge is moving to expel Senator Lorimer and that both of them will keep out of the fight. He thanks Taft for the settee sent to Edith.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Richard Derby, Evelyn Irving and a couple named Grey are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Between Sagamore Hill and the city
Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan.
In Cambridge, Roosevelt sits with the Harvard Board of Overseers and dines with the Alumni Association's directors.

Roosevelt writes Lodge about his re-election speech and the Lorimer case. He tells Taft that Knox's trade reciprocity pact with Canada is excellent and will help the party in the long run, and notes Lodge is cool on Beveridge's resolution.
Roosevelt addresses the National Civic Federation in New York.
Ted and Eleanor share news that a baby is due in August, and Roosevelt answers with delight. The Outlook carries his article on international neighborliness.
Lloyd Griscom and his wife come to Sagamore Hill. They later tell Archie Butt that Roosevelt and Edith seemed low in spirits.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt writes Cleveland Dodge about New Jersey progressives, answers Gifford Pinchot's complaint that he called Taft upright, tells Thomas Gill he favors Irish Home Rule but won't say so publicly, and writes Lodge about campaign lies and two Panama supply ships.

Roosevelt speaks to the governing council of the Reform synagogue union. It is his sister Bamie's 56th birthday. He writes Edwin Van Valkenburg about the employers' liability law and the 1912 nomination.

Roosevelt writes Maurice Egan about Catholic missions and socialism. Told he has been elected a vice president of the American Historical Association, he tells John Jameson he doubts he would serve well and wants to decline. He writes John O'Laughlin on Lorimer.
Whitelaw and Elizabeth Reid and Josephine Osborn are guests at Sagamore Hill.

LaFollette and Bourne launch the National Progressive Republican League to liberalize the party, with the unspoken aim of blocking Taft in 1912. Roosevelt holds back from formal support but praises it in The Outlook, where he also writes on popular rule. He attends Paul Morton's funeral.

Roosevelt writes Ted that he and Edith think four, or five at most, is a fine number of children, and that grandchildren are the one thing their happiness lacked. He also discusses the California trip.
J. Alden Loring, the naturalist from the African safari, and Elizabeth S. Hoyt sign the guest book.

Roosevelt tells William Allen White he will support the progressive league without joining, and that a 1912 nomination would be a mistake. To LaFollette he offers help through The Outlook but wants distance, recalling complaints about his political meddling in 1910.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt goes between home and the city; five guests sign the Sagamore Hill book.
The Outlook publishes two Roosevelt pieces: an open letter to Judge Simeon Baldwin and an essay on nationalism and special privilege.
Roosevelt sends a warm note to his cousin, State Senator Franklin D. Roosevelt, who heads a revolt of reform Democrats in Albany against Tammany.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt endorses the Consumers' League of New York, where Frances Perkins is executive secretary, in its fight against sweatshops, child labor and overlong workdays. He also writes Lodge about Platt's autobiography, Canadian reciprocity and Lorimer.
Roosevelt is based at Sagamore Hill, often heading into Manhattan to his Outlook office. Former Massachusetts governor Curtis Guild Jr. is among the guests.

Roosevelt writes zoologist Charles Kofoid about a paper by Henry Chester Tracy on white markings in perching birds. He argues that protective coloration does not explain every case and rejects Abbott Thayer's theories.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt writes Isaac Russell to refute a Pearson's Magazine charge that he traded leniency on plural marriage for Mormon electoral votes in the West. The Outlook runs his essay on nationalism and the working man. Cousins and safari naturalist Edmund Heller visit.
Roosevelt spends time with Edmund Heller, the naturalist from his African safari.
Roosevelt tells Smithsonian Secretary Charles Walcott that Heller should complete mounting the Roosevelt expedition's specimens before setting off on another trip.

Roosevelt writes John O'Laughlin about Senator Lorimer and says voters, not legislatures, should choose senators. He also writes historian William Roscoe Thayer about his article on great Italians and about the Catholic Church.
Roosevelt writes British author Frederick Oliver about a plan to reform the House of Lords, and compares Jefferson and Hamilton to today's progressives.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt sends regrets to Boy Scout leader James West but voices strong belief in Scouting. He wishes Heller well as he joins Paul Rainey's African expedition, and writes Eben Martin about trusts and Will Cowles about reciprocity, Admiral Sperry's death and Lodge's stand on senators.
Roosevelt gives the Lincoln Day address in Grand Rapids, Michigan. The Outlook publishes his essay on nationalism and working women.
Roosevelt attends the Republican Club's Lincoln dinner in New York and speaks. It is Alice's 27th birthday. In Illinois, President Taft privately compares Roosevelt and Lincoln.
Roosevelt tours poor neighborhoods of Brooklyn and has lunch with his old friend Jacob Riis.
Hungarian statesman Count Albert Apponyi visits, along with General Francis Greene and E. Reeve Merritt.
Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
On Alice and Nick's fifth anniversary, Roosevelt presses Cleveland Dodge to let Catholics serve as YMCA directors; he later learns they may. He also welcomes Congressman Edmund Madison's support.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's essay on Greeley, Sumner and Morton and his article on a higher-education project.
Roosevelt writes his daughter-in-law Eleanor, expecting her first child, that she and Ted fill his and Edith's thoughts.
Roosevelt boards the Lake Shore Limited at Grand Central at 5:30 p.m., bound for Chicago. He writes Michigan's progressive governor Chase Osborn about electing senators by popular vote.
In Chicago, Roosevelt addresses the Harvard Club's dinner.
Roosevelt speaks in Chicago, including at a Union League Club dinner on Washington's Birthday.
Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan.
In Gramercy Park, Roosevelt comes to the aid of a little boy who has lost his way.
Clifford and Teresa Richardson are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Three guests, among them James L. Breese Jr., sign the Sagamore Hill book.
Roosevelt writes Syracuse English professor Joseph Pennypacker about Amherst's curriculum plan, and Paul Collins about Canadian reciprocity and postal rates for periodicals.
Alice is among the guests at Sagamore Hill. The Outlook carries Roosevelt's piece on nationalism and the courts.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Roosevelt tells Quentin he can't find a Springfield rifle for Quentin's friend James White, but bursts with pride over the boy's class standing and reports that the family car is worn from a hard winter.
Roosevelt tells Elisha Garrison he opposes Senator Aldrich's banking reform plan, and writes Lodge about the pension bill both men oppose.
The Outlook runs Roosevelt's account of the battle of San Juan along with his judiciary essay. Alice, Richard Derby and Dorothy Whitney are among the Sagamore guests.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

Taft accepts Interior Secretary Ballinger's resignation. Roosevelt writes General Greene about Washington, Frederick the Great and the 1905 Portsmouth peace, Frank Tracy about Francis Lowell's death, and anti-suffragist Mary Swift that he leans toward votes for women, though only mildly.
Roosevelt sets out with Edith and Ethel on a speaking tour that will last 34 days, stopping first in Washington. He writes Lucius Swift about reciprocity and Indiana opinion.
In Atlanta, Roosevelt addresses the Southern Commercial Congress.
Roosevelt speaks to the National Child Labor Conference in Birmingham, Alabama.
Roosevelt speaks in Jackson and McComb, Mississippi, and in New Orleans. The Outlook carries his judiciary essay and a piece on the Third Avenue railway and its workers.
The tour reaches Texas with speeches in Houston and Beaumont.
Roosevelt speaks his way through San Antonio, Austin, Waco, Fort Worth and Dallas, and visits the Army post at Fort Sam Houston.

With Mexico's Díaz government collapsing, Taft quietly sends troops to Texas for so-called maneuvers. From Dallas, Roosevelt writes Taft about the danger of war and says he would want to raise a regiment if serious fighting came.
Roosevelt speaks in El Paso and Albuquerque. Edith joins him in Albuquerque after visiting their old friend Bob Ferguson, who is ill with tuberculosis, in Silver City.
After talks at Flagstaff and then Williams, Archie meets his parents, healthy but lean.

With Governor Richard Sloan, Roosevelt and his son Archie descend into the Grand Canyon on horseback while Edith rests at the rim. Later that day the party heads to Phoenix and drive out toward Roosevelt Dam, which he has been asked to dedicate.
Roosevelt speaks at the opening of the great reclamation dam on the Salt River that bears his name, then returns to Phoenix. The Outlook again runs his judiciary essay.
The Roosevelts drive from Phoenix to Mesa to see Archie's school.
Roosevelt speaks in Phoenix, lunches with Rough Rider veterans, and visits the Territorial Normal School at Tempe.
In Los Angeles, Roosevelt lunches with Earl and Francis Heney and gives a speech, then speaks at Throop Polytechnic Institute in Pasadena.
Roosevelt speaks to the City Club and at Occidental College in Los Angeles.

After a speech in San Francisco, Roosevelt gives the University of California's Charter Day address at Berkeley, with his famous line about taking the Isthmus and letting Congress debate him while the canal got built.
Roosevelt opens his Earl Lecture series at Berkeley with a talk on realizable ideals and speaks at a student rally.
Home and child; fire in New York

Roosevelt's Earl Lecture at Berkeley is about home life and children. Back east in Manhattan, fire sweeps the Triangle Shirtwaist factory near Washington Square, killing 146 workers, mostly young women, trapped by poor safety measures and too few exits. The Outlook runs his essay on nationalism and democracy.
Roosevelt's Earl Lecture at Berkeley takes up the Bible and everyday life.
Public servants and the Eighth Commandment
In another Earl Lecture, Roosevelt discusses honesty in public life and the moral duties of both employers and workers.

Roosevelt's last Earl Lecture concerns the press and the Ninth Commandment; he then speaks in San Francisco. Quentin meets the family there, and the three of them lodge at Ted and Eleanor's home while Ethel lodges with friends.
Roosevelt remains in San Francisco with his family; no specific activity is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in San Francisco with his family; no specific activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is in San Francisco. His Earl Lectures, which included a talk on money and wealthy men, were given without a text, taken down by stenographers, and later published as Realizable Ideals.
His last speaking tour, he says

From San Francisco, Roosevelt tells Taft this will be his final speaking tour and thanks him for explaining the Mexican situation. He had been asked to mediate in Mexico but thought it improper. The Outlook runs his essay on international relations.
Roosevelt is in San Francisco; no specific activity is recorded.
In Reno, Nevada, Roosevelt speaks out against the city's reputation as a haven for quick divorces.
Roosevelt addresses the California Legislature in Sacramento. In Washington, Congress meets in special session to take up Canadian reciprocity.

Roosevelt speaks in Eugene, Albany and Portland, Oregon. Edith writes Cecil Spring-Rice that the welcome he receives everywhere is moving and funny, and that she is proud of both the country and its people.
Roosevelt speaks in Tacoma and Seattle.
Roosevelt is in Spokane; no specific activity is recorded.
In Spokane. The Outlook publishes two Roosevelt essays, one on old and new education and one on falling birthrates among English-speaking peoples.
Roosevelt speaks in Moscow and Sandpoint, Idaho, on Archie's 17th birthday.
Roosevelt is in Spokane; no specific activity is recorded.
Missoula, and a portrait of Quentin

Roosevelt speaks in Missoula. Edith writes Spring-Rice that Quentin is a warm-hearted, oversized puppy of a boy, wrapped up in his wireless and anything mechanical, and now first in his class at Groton.
Roosevelt is in Helena; no specific activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is in Helena; no specific activity is recorded.
Roosevelt leaves Helena, Montana, heading for Madison, Wisconsin.

After speeches in Madison, Roosevelt, Edith and Ethel turn back toward New York. The Outlook runs his piece on ethics in journalism, and Collier's prints his February letter rebutting the Mormon polygamy charges.
The Roosevelts arrive back at Oyster Bay and Sagamore Hill after five weeks on the road.
Roosevelt is home again, with regular trips into the city. At Douglas, Arizona, Mexican rebels and federal troops fight, and several Americans are wounded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Janetta Alexander and J. T. Coolidge visit Sagamore Hill.
Arnold Hunewell signs the guest book.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's account of a tenement visit. The Richardsons and Cornelia Landon are guests.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
R. May signs the guest book.
Roosevelt speaks to the Berry School Association in New York and sends Annie Nathan Meyer his thoughts on her play The Dominant Sex.

New Hampshire Governor Robert Bass visits, and the two discuss initiative, referendum and recall. In Manhattan, Taft and Archie Butt attend an exposition for the blind at the Metropolitan Opera House, where Roosevelt's sister Corinne and her husband Douglas turn up too.
Ambassador James Bryce and Mrs. Bryce come to Sagamore Hill, along with F. L. Derby.

Roosevelt lunches with Charles Walcott. He writes James Garfield about Ballinger's exit, Scouting and Taft's handling of Mexico; tries, unsuccessfully, to persuade Emma Kennedy to endow a Smithsonian publication fund; complains to Ida Tarbell about a magazine piece on James Gordon Bennett; and sends Charles Willard a long letter on direct democracy.
It is the 29th wedding anniversary of Roosevelt's sister Corinne. Old friends Winthrop and Margaret Chanler are among the Sagamore guests.
Archie comes home, his long arms poking out of his sleeves. Ethel is torn: Dr. Richard Derby, a 30-year-old surgeon, has proposed.
Roosevelt is settled at Sagamore Hill again, often going in to his Manhattan office.
Veteran diplomat Henry White and Florence Lafarge visit. Roosevelt writes Oscar Hallam about a historical point in his essay on the judiciary.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Cornelia Landon is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt writes Groton headmaster Endicott Peabody about his essay on falling birthrates, Constantine Howard about the Bayne Law he helped pass to protect small game, Ted about the warm reception in Wisconsin, and William F. Knox that he will not accept the 1912 nomination.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's piece on the dynamite case. He tells Ida Tarbell what he thinks of the Herald, discusses The Outlook's format, and touches on free trade.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Senator Lodge and General Ian Hamilton are guests. Roosevelt tells Henry Fairfield Osborn he is at work on an article about protective coloration in animals.
Roosevelt writes Senator William Borah about Central American treaties and direct election of senators, and urges Senator Joseph Dixon to pass the constitutional amendment providing for it.
Fighting across the Mexican border near El Paso, Texas, kills four Americans. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Henry Stimson and his wife spend the night at Sagamore Hill. Taft has named Stimson Secretary of War, and he talks the appointment over with Roosevelt.

Roosevelt addresses students at DeWitt Clinton High School in Manhattan. He tells John Greenaway he dislikes Taft's handling of the border fighting, and suggests to W. H. Wilmarth taxing unmarried and childless people to reverse a falling birthrate.
The Outlook carries Roosevelt's article on workmen's compensation. Clifford and Teresa Richardson visit.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
In New York, Roosevelt speaks to a gathering of ministers from the church federation.
F. W. DeLaw signs the guest book.
Roosevelt's old Dakota friend Seth Bullock, the Deadwood sheriff and marshal, is among the day's callers.

In Brooklyn, Roosevelt speaks to immigrants seeking citizenship. He writes British envoy James Bryce about the arbitration pacts Taft proposes, Judge Ben Lindsey on the great money interests, and William Knox that he will not be the 1912 nominee.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's case against Taft's proposed arbitration treaties with Britain, France and Germany.
Four guests sign the Sagamore Hill book.
Conservation allies Gifford Pinchot and James Garfield visit Sagamore Hill, with Evelyn Irving.
Statehood for Arizona and New Mexico
Roosevelt tells Owen Wister he enjoyed Members of the Family, and urges Lodge to back statehood for New Mexico and Arizona. The bill will pass, only for Taft to veto it.
Roosevelt writes Harvey Simmons that he is troubled to hear Fisk University, the historically Black school in Nashville, needs money.

The Outlook runs Roosevelt's article on the great moneyed interests. He writes Labor World editor Leon Sutton, upset that New York's highest court has voided the workmen's compensation law, and lays out his views on labor.
Child labor and the Alaska boundary
Roosevelt writes Judge Ben Lindsey about child labor laws. To John W. Foster, who has called his arbitration views inconsistent, he sends a rebuttal that also takes up the Alaska boundary dispute.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's essays on the Bible in everyday life and on Wisconsin as a model for the nation, praising that state's progressive government.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

In Newark, Roosevelt speaks as a new statue of Lincoln is unveiled. At Grant's Tomb that Decoration Day, he criticizes Taft's policies and answers wealthy critics who claim his ideas invite revolution, saying true revolutionaries fear him most.

Roosevelt tells Oscar King Davis he has no intention of running in 1912 and notes Stimson's appointment as Secretary of War. He writes Lodge about the arbitration treaty and Lodge's Outlook article on American folk myths. Archie is home studying for Harvard exams, with Edith teaching him French and his father history and civics.
Roosevelt spends June based at his Oyster Bay home, heading into Manhattan often for work.
Writing about House probes and arbitration
Roosevelt warns William Loeb that the new Democratic House means to use investigations of Panama, sugar and steel to embarrass Republicans, and writes James Bryce about warmer ties with Britain.
Outlook essay on the Standard Oil ruling

The Outlook carries Roosevelt's response to the Supreme Court's Standard Oil decision, laying out his updated thinking on how to regulate trusts. Douglas and Corinne Robinson are among the day's visitors.
Roosevelt spends a quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.
An angry letter to John W. Foster
Roosevelt sends John W. Foster a scorching reply to an article he wrote, objecting to several untruths in it, among them words Foster put in John Hay's mouth.

In Baltimore for Cardinal Gibbons's jubilee, Roosevelt speaks and meets President Taft along with Root, Lodge, Penrose, Sherman and Cannon. Archie Butt later recalled TR trading wisecracks with Taft while others spoke. He also writes Richard Knott on breaking up trusts.

Roosevelt gives a speech in White River Junction, Vermont. He also answers Samuel Gompers, who had replied to TR's article condemning the 1910 dynamiting at the Los Angeles Times, and writes Ralph Easley on trusts.
Henry and Margaret White visit Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Alfred Thayer Mahan, whose New York Times letter backed TR's position on arbitration, and touches on the Alaska boundary fight.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt welcomes James F. Curtis to Sagamore Hill.
A Sunday at Sagamore Hill with nothing on record.
A batch of letters on arbitration

Roosevelt fills the day with correspondence: to Hiram Collier on pacifists, to novelist Cora Older on her book and Jefferson, to Senator Coe Crawford on pending treaties, and to Lodge on arbitration and Mahan's Panama article.
Calling John W. Foster a liar
Roosevelt writes John W. Foster again, flatly denying that John Hay ever gave Foster a mocking nickname. He also writes historian John Bury about his Romanes Lecture.
Roosevelt writes editor Edwin Van Valkenburg about an Associated Press report, issued June 7 and denied by TR the next day, claiming he had backed Taft for 1912.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record is silent on the day's doings.
Answering Gompers and Otis in print

The Outlook runs Roosevelt's piece on the dynamite charges, taking on both Samuel Gompers and General Harrison Gray Otis. The same day Senator Robert La Follette formally enters the race for the 1912 Republican nomination.
Roosevelt passes Sunday at home; no events are noted.
Ready to testify on Tennessee Coal

Roosevelt writes James Drain on pacifism, Thomas Warren on his poetry address, John Jackson on garbled reports of his Decoration Day speech, Lodge on Taft and the treaties, and Nick Longworth to say he will testify on Tennessee Coal and Iron if summoned.

As Ted and Eleanor mark a year of marriage, Roosevelt writes Ted that he likes La Follette but expects Taft to win the nomination, and reports on Archie's Harvard exams. Other letters go to Charles Willard, Gilson Gardner, Hiram Collier and Charles Walcott.
A group of visitors comes to Sagamore Hill, including E. H. Madison, Harold Howland and Boston merchant Edward Filene.
Grace Potter visits, and Roosevelt sends Thomas Marvin his views on the tariff.
The Bishops come to Oyster Bay
Joseph Bucklin Bishop and his wife Harriet are among the guests at Sagamore Hill, along with R. Perkins, George Marvin and James Breese.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's article on Arizona and the recall of judges.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill for a quiet Sunday.
Archie Butt's prank at Alice's party

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. In Washington, Archie Butt writes of an evening at Alice's home where she sat reading the Bible amid the guests, and he livened things up by pouring mineral water from a White Rock bottle down a diplomat's collar before fleeing home to brace for revenge.
A long family letter to Arthur Lee

With Alice among the day's guests, Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee a wide-ranging letter about the children, Sagamore Hill, animal camouflage and British politics. He also writes Ben Lindsey on child labor, Mahan, James Drain, Henry Wallace and War Secretary Henry Stimson.
Roosevelt writes Maurice Egan, the American minister in Copenhagen, about Denmark and Russia.

Roosevelt tells his sister Bamie he supports votes for women, a view she does not share. He also writes Melville Post about a letter printed without his consent and Frank Chapman about Abbott Thayer's angry defense of his camouflage theories.
Last day of June at home
Roosevelt closes out June at Sagamore Hill with no recorded events.
July finds Roosevelt at Oyster Bay, making regular trips to his Fourth Avenue office in Manhattan. The Outlook prints his article on the novelist H. Rider Haggard and the work of the Salvation Army.
Arnold Hunnewell, E. Dick Jr. and Francis Gray visit Sagamore Hill.
Hamilton Coolidge visits, and Roosevelt courteously declines Stephen Pierson's invitation to speak to a historical group in Morristown, New Jersey.
Independence Day at Sagamore Hill is scorchingly hot.
Ogden and Helen Rogers Reid visit. Roosevelt urges New York City Comptroller William Prendergast to buy land for an oceanfront park; Rockaway Beach was later acquired.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt tells John Queeny that years of using saccharin, which he took in large daily amounts, seem to have done his health no harm.
Roosevelt's Outlook article on running the Panama Canal answers a critical piece by Hayden Talbot printed in the same issue.
Roosevelt spends a quiet Sunday at home.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill with nothing on record.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Will Cowles visits; decency essay runs
Roosevelt's brother-in-law Will Cowles is a guest, and The Outlook publishes TR's essay on decency.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is at home; the record notes nothing more.
Roosevelt commends Samuel Dobbs for his work to make advertising truthful.

Josephine Osborn visits. Roosevelt writes John Rose a reflective letter about his record and why he took the Outlook job, noting he must provide for his sons. To James West he praises the Boy Scouts as training for citizenship.
Clifford and Teresa Richardson visit. Roosevelt writes Joseph Bucklin Bishop about Hayden Talbot's Outlook article on the canal.
Two Roosevelt pieces run in The Outlook. In the one on Alaska he stands by his own administration's record and faults Taft's.
Alice and Nick come to visit
Alice and Nick Longworth are at Sagamore Hill, along with Austrian visitor Hans Gregor Wilczek.
Struggling with a long letter to Trevelyan

Hans Gregor Wilczek stays on. Roosevelt tells George Otto Trevelyan he is dictating an account of his 1910 trip from Khartoum to London but finds it hard to finish, worrying it sounds too self-centered. The letter finally went out October 1.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as President Taft sends Congress a message standing behind his Alaska policies.
Roosevelt suggests that Harry Judson publish Captain Charles Young's study of military morale. Young was then the only Black officer on active duty in the Army.

Roosevelt thanks Will Cowles for peaches and sends Bamie a chatty letter: Edith wants a new paved road to the house, Teresa Richardson is visiting, Archie is cramming for Harvard and Quentin plays ball with the butler. He also writes Ernest Harvier, George Wickersham and Charles Bonaparte.
Edward Kent visits. The Outlook prints Roosevelt's articles on the initiative and referendum and on Oxford and Kansas, plus his review of a much-discussed book by Houston Stewart Chamberlain.
Roosevelt writes his daughter-in-law Eleanor about Ted's infancy.
A paved road; Kermit heads west
Workers lay a hard-surfaced road at Sagamore Hill. Kermit goes to visit the Fergusons in Silver City and hunts in the Mexican desert, Ethel is with friends in Maine, and Archie and Quentin are home.
Roosevelt tells Judge Edgar Aldrich he cannot speak in New Hampshire, and comments on the Post Office Department and the supposed attack on the courts.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Arbitration treaty goes to the Senate
Secretary of State Philander Knox signs the general arbitration treaty, which is then sent to the Senate for approval. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

Roosevelt goes into New York City to testify before the congressional committee probing U.S. Steel. The Outlook carries his article on labor unions and class feeling, along with an editorial critical of Taft's Alaska course.
For Edith's 50th birthday Roosevelt gives her a set of Punch drawings she had picked and a surprise thermos pitcher. In the afternoon the two row across to the Mathisons' on Lloyd's Neck.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

Roosevelt writes Richard Knott on price fixing, Albert Walker on his steel testimony, Bamie on Archie's studying and Quentin's new beehive, and General William Wotherspoon with questions about German and Japanese air power.
Roosevelt writes Ted about Edith's birthday and his U.S. Steel testimony, saying he thought it improper to have been called. He also writes Outlook writer William Hulbert about corruption in Alaska.
While Roosevelt stays at Sagamore Hill, Kermit is in Wellton, Arizona, with Win and Ike Proebstel, where the thermometer reads 140 degrees.

Kermit crosses the desert to Tinajas Altas hunting bighorn. At home, Roosevelt writes Congressman Edmond Madison, who with Asher Hinds had mocked George Earle's sugar trust charges, and Arthur Farquhar on breaking up Standard Oil.
The Outlook prints Roosevelt's second editorial on Alaska, again critical of Taft.
On Ethel's 20th birthday, Roosevelt lunches with Japan's Admiral Togo, who presents him with small-scale samurai armor and cleans TR's samurai swords.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he likes Lodge's proposed amendments to the British arbitration treaty and is surprised the insurgents are dragging out the special session.
Roosevelt writes William F. Knox in dismay at the opening of Alaska public lands to railroads tied to big corporations, a point on which he firmly opposes Taft.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
In San Francisco, Ted's wife Eleanor delivers a daughter, Grace, the first grandchild of Theodore and Edith. Edith plants pines at Sagamore Hill as a small grove for the baby to play in.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
In The Outlook Roosevelt sums up his U.S. Steel testimony about the 1907 panic and the takeover of Tennessee Coal and Iron, granting the steel men may have had mixed motives.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt praises a poem by his sister Corinne and asks Mahan to write The Outlook about the arbitration treaties, which Mahan never does.
Sizing up Taft, Wilson and Pinchot

As Congress's special session ends, Roosevelt writes Rider Haggard, Lodge, Arthur Lee, Spring-Rice and Ted. He confides disappointment in Taft, hopes to retire at 60, calls Pinchot a fanatic, and predicts Wilson could beat Taft.
The American Museum of Natural History's Bulletin publishes Roosevelt's paper on concealing and revealing coloration in birds and mammals, a critique of Abbott H. Thayer's theories.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing on record.
The Outlook runs Roosevelt's essay arguing that Dante wrote about the gritty everyday life of Florence with a frankness no 19th-century author brought to his own hometown.
Dr. Alexander Lambert and his wife Ellen, editor Robert Bridges and Norman Hapgood spend the day at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt applauds George Viereck for turning his German-language paper into an English one, and writes William Hulbert about Alaska and public ownership of railroads and coal.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Alice and Nick head for Panama
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as Alice and Nick Longworth set out for Panama.
September opens with Roosevelt dividing his time between Oyster Bay and Manhattan. He tells Frank Knox he is open to the government working Alaska's coal fields itself.
Edward Kent visits, and The Outlook prints a Roosevelt article on how not to pursue self-government.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
Isabella Hagner visits, and Roosevelt shares a midday meal with Abbot Charles H. Mohr of St. Leo Abbey in Florida, who teaches theology and commercial law.

Roosevelt writes Ernest Harvier in favor of nonpartisan city government, William Hulbert criticizing Taft's pick of Walter E. Clark as Alaska's governor, and Maurice Egan about notes on Russia and Father John Zahm.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day goes unrecorded.
Bryan calls; treaty attack in print
At The Outlook office, Roosevelt's callers include William Jennings Bryan. His criticism of the arbitration treaty runs in the morning papers, and he writes James Bryce about Dante.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's article laying out his position on the arbitration treaty with Britain.
Ellen Rogers, Chalmers Wood and Evelyn Irving visit Sagamore Hill.
A long ride with Stimson and Wood

Roosevelt lunches and takes a long ride with Henry Stimson and General Leonard Wood, both of whom share his views on the arbitration treaty. He also urges Frederick Selous, nearly 60, to go on safari again.

Roosevelt tells Lodge his Outlook colleagues want the arbitration treaty adopted at once while he and Lodge want better wording. He discusses German moves in Morocco and the Congo, possible German marches through Belgium or Switzerland, and the need for a strong French army.
Ted celebrates his 24th birthday in San Francisco while his father is at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
A visit to the Children's Court
Roosevelt goes into New York City and visits the Children's Court.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's piece on hunting and natural history across two continents.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt writes Congressman William Kent, a fierce Taft opponent who wants a La Follette and Pinchot ticket, and invites him to Sagamore Hill to discuss politics.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.

Roosevelt tells Ernest Harvier that Progressives try to do too much, writes Lodge on the treaty and Canada, and urges Ted not to back Wilson over Taft. Archie has finished another round of Harvard exams, and Quentin heads to Groton with a cheeky reply to his mother.
The Outlook prints Roosevelt's article on West Coast Americans.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
Teresa Richardson visits. Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about Canadian trade and the treaty, mentioning that he is suffering from rheumatism.
