At The Outlook in New York, Roosevelt's callers include a party of 100 Pennsylvania Grange members.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 50th birthday.
Belle Willard, later Kermit's wife, and Gertrude Evans are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Ernest Harvier about open primaries and tells Senator Robert La Follette he likes the autobiography running in the American Magazine.
Edith badly hurt in a riding fall

Riding at a gallop with Roosevelt and Archie, Edith is thrown from Pine Knot onto the paved road by Cove School and knocked unconscious. TR flags down a delivery wagon whose driver, Benny Vorhis, was an old schoolmate of Ted's, to carry her home; she lies insensible for 36 hours. The Outlook runs his review of Arthur Weigall's book on ancient Egypt.

Roosevelt finally sends George Otto Trevelyan his marathon letter: why he sent the battle fleet around the world, impressions of the Kaiser and Germany, and a country-by-country tour of his 1910 trip from Khartoum through Rome, Vienna, Paris and Scandinavia to London.
Roosevelt writes Ted about Edith's riding accident; she is in severe pain from a headache.
Dr. Rixey comes to treat Edith
Dr. Presley Rixey arrives to care for Edith. Roosevelt writes Lodge about her accident, the Honduras and Nicaragua treaties and the Alaska committee.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

Roosevelt writes Herbert Parsons on Assembly nominations and Corinne in anger at the Barnes-run state party's treatment of her son Teddy. To David Gray he sends a comic sequel to his Trevelyan letter about royals feuding over rank at King Edward's funeral.
Dr. Alexander Lambert comes to Sagamore Hill, staying through October 8 to care for Edith.
How the canal rights were won
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's account of how the United States gained the right to build the Panama Canal.
Roosevelt attends a meeting of the local society working to improve Oyster Bay village.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

As Kermit turns 22 at Harvard, Edith is gaining ground but recalls nothing of her fall and has lost taste and smell; her headaches are agonizing. Roosevelt brings in a neurologist and a pair of nurses for round-the-clock care. Her ability to smell would never return.
Roosevelt's niece Eleanor Roosevelt marks her 27th birthday.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt stays at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.
Two Roosevelt articles run in The Outlook. One deals with the Chicago Vice Commission and the post office; the other urges arbitration rather than tearing up the U.S. treaty with Russia.
Roosevelt spends a quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as the National Progressive Conference calls for direct primaries and endorses Robert La Follette for president in 1912.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Bamie's son Sheffield Cowles celebrates his 13th birthday.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Carnegie Hall speech on women and children

Roosevelt speaks at Carnegie Hall on protecting women and children. He thanks Bob Ferguson for career advice to Kermit and writes Lodge about Russia's exclusion of Jews and the treaty, reporting Edith is finally better.
In an Outlook article on commercialism and hysteria, Roosevelt urges Americans to take part in sports rather than merely watch them.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt writes William Allen White about the novel White is working on, says he is steering clear of nomination talk, and sizes up La Follette.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
The Justice Department sues U.S. Steel, implying that Elbert Gary and Henry Frick misled Roosevelt in 1907 when the company bought Tennessee Coal and Iron. Roosevelt is furious.

On his 53rd birthday Roosevelt tells Marshall Stimson he won't accept the 1912 nomination, yet confides to California's Governor Hiram Johnson that he may be the best one to lead a lost cause. He also writes Charles McCarthy, Ray Stannard Baker and Will Cowles.
Kermit is elected to Harvard's Porcellian Club, adding to his memberships in Hasty Pudding, DKE, the Sphinx and the Institute of 1770. Roosevelt writes Ernest Harvier and Charles Willard.
Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt tells Ted that Kermit made the Porcellian after one classmate stopped blackballing him, that Edith is better but still frail and headachy, and that the new road cost a lot. He also writes Everett Wheeler about the U.S. Steel suit.

Roosevelt tells James R. Garfield he believes Taft is using the U.S. Steel suit for political advantage. The Republican Party is now divided between conservative Standpatters and progressive Insurgents.
November between Oyster Bay and Manhattan
Through November Roosevelt lives at Sagamore Hill and travels often to his New York City office.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing on record.
Naturalist Carl Akeley is among Roosevelt's visitors. The Outlook prints TR's piece contrasting real and sham arbitration, and he writes Henry Stimson about labor and how it is managed in government.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay on Election Day. His nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson, Corinne's son, wins a State Assembly seat representing Herkimer County.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

Roosevelt tells Ted his letters have cheered Edith, who is walking a little but still cannot taste or smell. He celebrates nephew Teddy Robinson's win over the party bosses and discusses Woodrow Wilson. He also denies to Edwin Van Valkenburg that he endorsed Rudolph Blankenburg for mayor of Philadelphia.
Roosevelt writes Harvard president A. Lawrence Lowell about Owen Johnson's articles on college life.
Kermit comes down from Harvard for a visit.
Kermit spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill while Ethel is away.
Roosevelt writes Ted that Edith keeps getting better, that Kermit is on Harvard's cross-country team, and about his forthcoming Outlook article on the trusts.

Roosevelt tells Ernest Harvier he will always resist mixing religion with politics. He also writes William Llewellyn on New Mexico and Senate graft, and William Hulbert on Interior Secretary Walter Fisher's plans for Alaska.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt writes Edith Wharton that Edith is recovering. His wife read Ethan Frome first and passed it to him; he found it powerful.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
In The Outlook Roosevelt answers the U.S. Steel suit and attacks the Taft administration's whole approach to trusts, arguing that some combinations are good and others bad.
Quentin celebrates his 14th birthday at Groton.
Olivia Cutting and the Richardsons visit. Roosevelt writes William Jennings Bryan about electing senators by popular vote and Abbot Charles Mohr about Catholic appointments and prejudice.
Roosevelt sets out his trust policy for Brooks Adams and writes New York state Senator T. Harvey Ferris about water power.
Roosevelt explains his thinking on recalling judicial decisions to Judge Learned Hand.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt tells James R. Garfield he is uncomfortable that Toledo's Garfield Republican Club has endorsed him for the nomination.
On lynching and the tobacco trust
On Bamie's 16th wedding anniversary, The Outlook prints Roosevelt articles on the tobacco trust ruling and on lynching. He tells Alexander Moore he still does not want to run.
Irish playwright Lady Augusta Gregory and Mary Cadwalader Jones are Sunday guests.
Correcting a history of the Cabinet
Roosevelt writes Thomas Lounsbury about his essays, Browning and Kermit's writing, and sends Mary Hinsdale corrections for her Cabinet history, insisting Lodge was never his Senate mouthpiece.
In New York Roosevelt attends Synge's Playboy of the Western World as Lady Gregory's guest. He tells John Yeiser he won't speak but says nothing about withdrawing from Nebraska's primary.
Roosevelt addresses Groton's students and spends time with Quentin. Alice and the Richardsons are with him.
Roosevelt speaks to the boys of St. Mark's School in Southborough, Massachusetts.
December, and no to the nomination
Roosevelt starts December at home in Oyster Bay, often going in to his Manhattan office, and tells James R. Garfield he does not want the nomination.

Theodore and Edith mark 25 years of marriage. The Outlook runs his essay on reverent inquiry, discussing books by Thomas Dwight and Émile Boutroux, and he writes George Sheldon, Dan Hanna and James Kennedy about 1904 donations, muckrakers and the nomination.
Telling Sheffield to stick with school
Roosevelt urges his nephew Sheffield Cowles not to quit school.
Janetta Alexander visits as Congress reconvenes. In Washington, Alice passes Archie Butt a spoken message from Roosevelt: leave his White House post for his own sake, since the strain is showing.
Roosevelt turns down Millard Bloomes's December 30 banquet and discusses treaties. He tells Ben Lindsey a 1912 nomination would be a disaster for him personally, though he would accept it.
Defending a third term in principle
Roosevelt tells Herbert Parsons he doesn't seek the nomination but insists he could rightly serve again after a gap.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Roosevelt dashes off a short note to Ernest Harvier.
The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's piece on the American hunter-naturalist.
Priscilla and J. Howland Auchincloss and Cornelia Landon visit Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Charles Willard about California politics, Taft, the Progressives, his possible nomination, and the McNamara brothers' trial for the Los Angeles Times bombing.

In Boston Roosevelt attends a Travelers Club meeting. He tells Ray Stannard Baker, a La Follette man, he doesn't want the nomination, and warns Pinchot that George Record's extreme plans drive people away.

Still in Boston, Roosevelt attends a Harvard Overseers meeting and confers with Progressive Republicans, assuring Baker and Gilson Gardner he won't take the nomination from La Follette. He writes Lodge about his speech against direct democracy and Bishop about avoiding the nomination.
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Young guests and Labrador missionary Wilfred Grenfell and his wife Anna visit. The Outlook prints Roosevelt's 'Murder is Murder' piece on the dynamite case.
In New York Roosevelt preaches a lay sermon on applied Christianity at the Labor Temple.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
Julian Kerns visits. Roosevelt sends a playful letter to William Allen White about not wanting the nomination, repeats the point to Garfield, and writes George Sheldon about 1904 campaign money.

Otto Bannard informs President Taft in Washington that Roosevelt would enter the race should Taft stand aside. TR writes Herbert Croly about his 1900 vice-presidential nomination for Croly's book on Mark Hanna.

Roosevelt writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler on treaties, trusts, the nomination and the field; introduces Medill McCormick to Cecil Lyon; writes Franklin K. Lane; and sends his picture to young Kermit Roosevelt Nothstein, a boy named for his son.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

The Outlook prints Roosevelt's Carnegie Hall speech on women and children. He writes Archie that Quentin has come home half an inch taller than his father, and tells William Howland he is not a candidate, though he'd accept a draft. Other letters go to Watts, Lodge, Hulbert and Archibald Gracie.
Roosevelt is at home on Christmas Eve; no events are recorded.
Christmas with chopping and a long walk

Kermit, Archie, Quentin, Alice and Nick, and Laura Roosevelt with her children Oliver and Nick spend Christmas at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt and Nick Longworth chop wood in the morning, and TR takes a walk of three or four hours in the afternoon.
Roosevelt writes Ted that Christmas loses some edge when the youngest is taller than his father. He hopes to give Kermit advice and to talk politics with Ted.
Nick and Alice Longworth visit. Roosevelt tells William F. Knox he would accept the nomination only if public demand were overwhelming.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Francis C. Gray visits. Roosevelt writes Japanese diplomat Kogoro Takahira on Jutaro Komura's death, the Portsmouth peace and China.

The Outlook carries Roosevelt's attack on abrogating the treaty with Russia, which was dropped because Russia barred Jewish Americans from travel, and his denial concerning Republican campaign contributions.
Year's end; Ted takes a banking job

Roosevelt ends the year at Sagamore Hill. Around this time Ted joins the New York investment bank Bertron Griscom & Co. and moves with Eleanor and Grace to East 74th Street, and Kermit's article on desert sheep appears in Scribner's.
Roosevelt begins 1912 at Oyster Bay, making regular trips to his Manhattan office.

Roosevelt tells George Norris he won't ask to be removed from Nebraska's primary, rebuts stories to Thomas Robins that he was pandering to labor, and writes Jacob Schiff about a remark on Oscar Straus and a 'Jew in the Cabinet' falsely pinned on him.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.
Lawrence Abbott on TR and Taft
Lawrence Abbott publishes an article in a Cornwall, New York, paper about the relationship between Roosevelt and Taft.
At The Outlook, Roosevelt's callers include James R. Garfield and his old boxing teacher Mike Donovan. He writes Lodge about the arbitration treaties.

New Mexico enters the Union as the 47th state. The Outlook runs Roosevelt's piece on judges, drawn from his Carnegie Hall speech, and he writes Bernardo San Severino about possible U.S. arbitration between Italy and Turkey, then at war.
Roosevelt meets with Henry L. Stimson at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

Roosevelt speaks at an Aldine Club dinner in New York. He writes Florence Kelley that he could become a fierce suffragist if convinced women would fight sexual vice, and trades notes with William Ward, Herbert Parsons, a Taft man, and Henry Needham about the nomination.
In the city, Roosevelt lunches with George McAneny and William Prendergast, and urges Senator William Borah to oppose the arbitration treaties unless amended.
Roosevelt suggests David Goodrich leave Wall Street for state government in New Mexico.

At The Outlook Roosevelt sees callers including Frankfurter. He tells Bamie he expects Taft to win renomination, ice covers the roads, and Edith, sick with erysipelas, is recovering in the sunny old nursery. He also writes Charles Brown recalling a long-ago Maine trip with Sewall and Dow.
A Roosevelt committee forms in Chicago

Alice and Cornelia Landon visit, and The Outlook prints four Roosevelt pieces. In Chicago, Tribune editor James Keeley, William Ward, Frank Knox and John C. O'Laughlin set up a Roosevelt National Committee against his wishes.
Butt and Corinne talk of the feud
At a luncheon at the Longworths' in Washington, Archie Butt and Corinne discuss the bitterness between Taft and Roosevelt.
Roosevelt praises Francis Herrick's pamphlet on how birds build nests, and discusses Darwin and his theories.
Won't seek it, would accept it

With Roosevelt headquarters now open in Chicago, he tells Frank Munsey he will not chase the nomination but would take it if offered, and recalls how Lincoln weathered press attacks. He writes Senator Elihu Root on the treaties.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

On Bamie's 57th birthday, Roosevelt works with Michigan's Governor Chase Osborn to arrange a joint letter from seven Progressive governors urging him to run; his planned reply: he won't go after it, but he would serve if chosen.
Roosevelt writes former Senator Joseph Foraker about who authored the Sherman Antitrust Act, and Henry Stimson about the U.S. Steel case.
Horace White and Everett Colby call at The Outlook, which runs Roosevelt's article on the George Junior Republic. He writes the Progressive governors that he would run if nominated.
Eliot Cross, Joseph Burden and Cornelia Landon visit Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt dines in the city with social reformers Homer Folks and Edward Devine. He tells Chase Osborn the moment may have arrived to declare himself publicly and writes Will Cowles and William Allen White.
Roosevelt confers with the brother of New Hampshire's Governor Bass, a war correspondent, and writes Governors Hadley, Stubbs, Johnson and Bass about the nomination.
Roosevelt sends a short note to Ernest Harvier and tells Franklin Shotwell his name will stay on Nebraska's primary ballot.
Roosevelt writes Kentucky's Governor Augustus Willson that Governor Bass agrees with Willson: the moment has come for TR to declare himself.

Roosevelt lunches in town with Governor Glasscock and Crothers; Norman Hudson and Arthur Hill are guests. He writes White that Governors Hadley and Aldrich advise silence, Perkins on the Palisades and Wilson, Root urging a federal children's bureau, and former Governor John Fort on the nomination.
Roosevelt lunches with Kansas Governor Walter Stubbs, Judge Nortoni and John C. O'Laughlin. The Outlook runs his article on the church and the people.

Archie Butt visits Sagamore Hill, joining a houseful that includes Ambassador Jusserand, Ethel, Ted and Eleanor, and little Grace. Roosevelt has been felling trees that fell across the telephone lines to the house.

At The Outlook Roosevelt sees Governor Carey, Jacob Riis and Reynolds, then tours a Brooklyn factory with William Redfield. He tells Joseph Bucklin Bishop he doubts he could be elected again, and discusses the canal investigations.
Roosevelt sends Governor Chase Osborn two letters as they consult about the nomination.
Edith leases Laura Roosevelt's house on East 31st Street in Manhattan so she can enjoy plays, the opera and friends, and above all escape the political commotion at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt opens February at Sagamore Hill, running into New York City often as talk of a 1912 candidacy builds.

A worn-out Senator Robert La Follette gives a rambling talk to publishers in Philadelphia that sinks his own presidential hopes, and many of his backers drift toward Roosevelt. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes to Robert Schauffler about race and stereotypes.
Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further for the day.
Talks with Pinchot and a leaked letter
Roosevelt meets Gifford Pinchot and fires off letters, including an angry note to Hermann Kohlsaat after his January letter to Frank Munsey about the nomination turned up in print.
At The Outlook offices Roosevelt receives Colonel George Goethals, builder of the Panama Canal, and Mrs. Goethals, and asks William Allen White to come see him about the nomination.

Roosevelt tells Missouri Governor Herbert Hadley he will wait before declaring for the nomination, writes son-in-law Nick Longworth about his backing of Taft, and hears from Michigan Governor Chase Osborn about direct primaries.
A premature report of his candidacy
A Lincoln Steffens piece in the Washington Star wrongly says Roosevelt has entered the race. Roosevelt writes about his old 1904 pledge against a third term and about La Follette's collapse.
Roosevelt sees a caller named Hull at The Outlook before heading back to Sagamore Hill.
Seven governors ask him to run
Meeting in Chicago, seven progressive Republican governors, from West Virginia to Wyoming, sign a petition urging Roosevelt to declare for president. He writes William Sulzer about trust legislation.
Roosevelt speaks at a New York Historical Society meeting. Edith writes Kermit that his father now feels he must join the fight since La Follette's collapse, and that politics fill her with dread.
On Alice's 28th birthday, President Taft publicly attacks Roosevelt in New York. Roosevelt writes John O'Laughlin about the race and the bogus report of his candidacy.
Old Dakota friend Seth Bullock and D. C. Collier visit The Outlook. Roosevelt tells Nick Longworth he has to speak out and declare, and notes that Loeb, now a Taft appointee, cannot help him.
A war council at The Outlook
Roosevelt huddles with Pinchot, Bullock, Oscar Straus, California Governor Hiram Johnson and others. Arizona becomes the 48th state. He answers Elihu Root's case against running with his own.
Amos Pinchot and his brother find Roosevelt's planned Columbus speech too mild; Roosevelt writes back that the Pinchots run a bit too radical. Senator Moses Clapp calls at The Outlook.
William Rockhill Nelson of the Kansas City Star calls on Roosevelt at The Outlook.
An Outlook essay on industrial justice
Alice and Nick mark six years of marriage, and Roosevelt's article "A Phase of Industrial Justice" runs in The Outlook.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing else recorded.
Roosevelt shuttles between Oyster Bay and Manhattan; no details survive.
Roosevelt heads west to Columbus, Ohio. In letters he denies abandoning La Follette and tells Truman Newberry he is in it for principle, though he privately expects Taft to win the nomination.

Before the Ohio Legislature Roosevelt delivers "A Charter of Democracy," backing popular recall of judicial decisions, a stand that alarms conservatives and business. Chatting with reporters along the way, he lets it be known that his hat is in the ring. His formal answer to the governors who urged him to run comes three days later.
Roosevelt returns to New York and writes Edwin Earl to knock down claims that he drinks to excess.
Roosevelt sees Ward and Halpin at The Outlook and lunches with Prendergast, O'Meara and Curry, then writes Senator Joseph Dixon about organizing the campaign.

Roosevelt answers the seven governors that he will accept the nomination if it is offered, then dines at Harvard's Porcellian Club. Edith and Ethel set off for South America, and two of his essays appear in The Outlook.
Judge Grant's house at the center

In Boston Roosevelt stays with Judge Robert Grant, whose home suddenly becomes the focus of national attention as the reply to the governors is released. Dinner brings in William Allen White, Arthur Hill and William Thayer.
Roosevelt tells the Massachusetts legislature he supports direct nominations and primaries, then shifts his lodging to J. D. Cushing's house. New Hampshire Governor Robert Bass drops by.
Roosevelt confers with Robert Bass and Matthew Hale, dines with Harvard President A. Lawrence Lowell, and stays with W. S. Bigelow.
Roosevelt sits in on a Harvard Board of Overseers meeting in Cambridge, lunches with Arthur Hill, and returns to New York.

Roosevelt's campaign team forms: Senator Joseph Dixon runs the New York office, Truman Newberry the Chicago money operation, and John O'Laughlin Washington. He writes Hadley that he is officially in, and tells Will Cowles judicial recall has split him from Lodge.
Roosevelt assures Henry Cabot Lodge that their split over the campaign will not cool his affection, and hosts William Allen White, Regis Post, Judge Hand and others for dinner at Sagamore Hill.
Torn in loyalty between Taft and Roosevelt, both of whom he served as aide, Major Archie Butt leaves for a rest in Italy. Roosevelt's "The Court of the Children" runs in The Outlook.
Senator Albert Beveridge and C. B. Landis call at Sagamore Hill, and the guest book records his sister Corinne, her husband Douglas Robinson, Benjamin Ide Wheeler and Frances Theodora Parsons.
Even mid-campaign, Roosevelt reports for jury service at Mineola. He asks Ormsby McHarg to assure him no Southern votes have been bought.
Grief for Corinne, fire for the fight

Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne in sorrow after her infant grandchild dies of whooping cough. He also tells Andrew Carnegie he has "not changed" and owes a duty to the people, and complains to Matthew Hale that party bosses oppose him.
Alice stops by during jury week
George Perkins calls at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt serves another day on the Mineola jury, and daughter Alice signs the guest book.
Roosevelt again sits as a juror at Mineola.
Roosevelt writes Senator Joseph Dixon that the progressive fight is about putting the people's will into effect, not prizes for individuals. Six states hold their first direct primaries this year.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is noted.
Juvenile-court reformer Judge Ben Lindsey and McCormick dine at Sagamore Hill.

After another day of jury service, Roosevelt writes Congressman Charles Lindbergh, the aviator's father, about North Dakota, and tells Governor Bass that officeholders, bosses, newspapers and money are stacked against them.
Between jury sessions Roosevelt lunches with Stoddard and Duell, and writes about the North Dakota primary and about taking a stand against loans for international wars.
Roosevelt confers with a man named Ward at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt declines an offer from former Rough Rider John Rhoades to act as his bodyguard, and complains to Senator Moses Clapp that Massachusetts lacks seasoned leaders. William Draper Lewis and George Rublee visit.
A full house at The Outlook
A stream of supporters, including Amos Pinchot, Beveridge, Perkins, Frank Munsey and Governors Hadley and Glasscock, crowds into The Outlook to see Roosevelt.

Expecting to lose North Dakota, Roosevelt tells Dixon to call a La Follette win a progressive triumph since it rebukes the administration. He bristles at Hermann Kohlsaat's plea to quit and notes Taft men purging his federal supporters.
Dr. Harvey Wiley and Richmond Pearson visit Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt lunches with Father York in Huntington and confides to Joseph Bucklin Bishop that he sees no chance of taking the nomination.

Edith and Ethel return from Panama, Tobago and Costa Rica. In North Dakota's primary La Follette wins 34,123 votes to Roosevelt's 23,669, with Taft far behind at 1,876. A delegation of Black New Yorkers from Harlem visits The Outlook.
Carnegie Hall case for popular rule
At Carnegie Hall Roosevelt makes the case for popular government, calling for leaders who dream greatly, and clarifies that recall would never apply to judges or the Supreme Court.
Owen Wister signs the guest book. Roosevelt thanks North Dakota's campaign manager and writes Arthur Lee in England that he feels isolated, rates his chances very low, and is moved by Lee's loyalty.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Portland, Maine.
In Portland Roosevelt meets with Robert Bass, McCormick, F. Hale and Frank Dingley, then gives a speech.
After meetings in Portland Roosevelt returns to New York, where he and Edith see Cabot and Nannie Lodge; the two men keep their friendship intact despite their split.
Roosevelt gives speeches on Manhattan's Lower East Side.
Crushed in the New York primary

In a deliberately confusing New York primary with a ballot 14 feet long, Taft routs Roosevelt, who wins just 13 delegates. Roosevelt sets out on a Western speaking tour and thanks John St. Loe Strachey for defending him in the British press.
Roosevelt speaks in Fort Wayne, Indiana, and in Chicago.
In St. Louis Roosevelt gives speeches and meets with his Missouri backers.
Roosevelt speaks at ten stops in a single day, from Cedar Rapids and Waterloo in Iowa to the Twin Cities of Minnesota.
The tour crosses Michigan with six speeches, ending in Detroit, then pushes on to Milwaukee.
Roosevelt returns to New York and Oyster Bay. Aunt Lizzie dies, and his old friend Henry Adams is disabled by a stroke.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill between campaign swings; nothing else is recorded.
After seeing Duell and George Henry Payne at The Outlook, Roosevelt leaves on a speaking swing through the South.
Roosevelt works his way by rail through southern West Virginia, from Ronceverte to Huntington, then across Kentucky, ending the day in Louisville.
More rear-platform speeches carry Roosevelt from Point Pleasant and Parkersburg in West Virginia to Covington, Augusta and Maysville in Kentucky.
Roosevelt speaks in Martinsburg, West Virginia, and boards a train for Chicago.
Ten Illinois towns in a day
Roosevelt barnstorms Illinois from Rockford to Springfield. Back east, Collier's Weekly prints Kermit's hunting story "After Moose in New Brunswick."
On Easter Sunday in Springfield, Roosevelt lunches with Illinois Governor Charles Deneen and visits Abraham Lincoln's grave.
Roosevelt speaks in Danville, Decatur, Mattoon, Urbana and other Illinois towns, then in Peru and Fort Wayne, Indiana.

Roosevelt carries the Illinois primary two to one over Taft, his first victory, taking 56 of 58 delegates. New York's Republican convention goes for Taft. It is also Archie's 18th birthday, and Roosevelt speaks in Pittsburgh.

Roosevelt speaks his way east across Pennsylvania from Jeannette to Philadelphia. He wires Medill McCormick that Illinois was a win over bosses and money, and laments delegates lost in Michigan, Kentucky and Indiana conventions.
Roosevelt speaks in Easton, Reading and Allentown before returning to New York and Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt leaves Oyster Bay for New England and speaks in Springfield, Massachusetts.

Roosevelt wins the Pennsylvania primary, taking 55 of 64 delegates, while he campaigns through Worcester and other Massachusetts towns and on to Nashua, Concord and Manchester in New Hampshire. Alice signs the guest book.
The Titanic goes down with Archie Butt

As Roosevelt returns home, the liner Titanic, bound for New York, collides with an iceberg and goes down in the North Atlantic. Among the dead is Major Archie Butt, his former military aide, coming home from his rest in Europe.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill on another Western speaking trip.

Speaking across western Illinois and southern Iowa, Roosevelt writes Michigan Governor Chase Osborn that a third party is possible should party bosses steal the nomination, and blasts the Taft managers' tactics.
Roosevelt takes his campaign into Nebraska with speeches in Hastings and Omaha.

Roosevelt crisscrosses southeastern Nebraska with ten speeches. By telegram he refuses Congressman Augustus Gardner's challenge to debate, and answers Gardner's claims that he went easy on Morgan-backed trusts.

Roosevelt wins all 16 Nebraska delegates, polling 46,795 votes to La Follette's 16,785 and Taft's 13,341, and takes most of Kansas. Edith tells Arthur Lee his hair is curling hard, which she jokingly credits to psychic electricity.

Roosevelt speaks in Oklahoma and in three Arkansas towns, including Little Rock, then wires Oscar King Davis that his voice is failing and the rear-platform speeches must stop. "On Natural Resources" appears in The Outlook.
Roosevelt spends Sunday traveling to North Carolina.
Roosevelt campaigns in North Carolina with speeches in Greensboro and Salisbury.
Roosevelt heads home as Taft wins New Hampshire's primary by about two votes to one.
Roosevelt writes Lodge wondering why Lodge's son-in-law, Congressman Augustus Gardner, has attacked him personally, and discusses Lodge's letters about Senators Lorimer and Crane.

In Boston President Taft finally answers Roosevelt, charging him with breaking his no-third-term pledge, flip-flopping on Canadian reciprocity, and pushing recall; offstage Taft breaks down in tears. Roosevelt has already been calling Taft a "fathead" on the stump.
Roosevelt leaves for Massachusetts and, in Worcester, tosses aside his prepared text to tell a roaring crowd that Taft has deliberately twisted his record.
Roosevelt speaks in six towns between Brockton and Fall River, finishing the day in Boston.

Roosevelt plans strategy with Baxter, Arthur Hill and Matthew Hale and stays with W. S. Bigelow. Edith writes Kermit that his reserved manner, like her own when young, can be mistaken for indifference.
On Corinne's 30th wedding anniversary, Roosevelt speaks in Lowell, Lawrence, North Adams and Pittsfield, then returns to New York and Oyster Bay.

Taft narrowly edges Roosevelt in the Massachusetts primary, 86,722 votes to 83,099, though eight at-large delegates pledge to Roosevelt. Roosevelt sweeps Oregon's 10 delegates, and Washington State's results are in dispute.

Roosevelt says he will honor the Massachusetts preference vote and tells his at-large delegates to back Taft, though they later stay with him at the convention. Pennsylvania's state convention hands him all 12 at-large delegates on top of his 55 from the primary.
After callers Matthew Hale and C. H. Thompson, Roosevelt leaves for Maryland. He explains to Lodge why he held off criticizing Senator Crane before the Massachusetts vote.
Roosevelt campaigns in Salisbury and Havre de Grace and in Baltimore.
While Roosevelt works western Maryland from Westminster to Cumberland, Taft tells a Hyattsville crowd that though he is a man of peace, he will hit hard when cornered.
Roosevelt travels back to New York and Sagamore Hill.
At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt meets Walter F. Brown and James Garfield, both key to his Ohio effort.
Four callers, Amos Pinchot among them, visit The Outlook. Roosevelt writes Paul Murphy about his meager backing in New York State.
Ward calls, and James and Helen Garfield and Grace Alexander are guests; the Roosevelts dine with the Garfields.
Roosevelt writes Nick Longworth about Ohio and instructs Walter Brown that nothing in the campaign should set him against his son-in-law.
Roosevelt sends William Sturgis Bigelow his thoughts on Bigelow's Buddhism book.

Roosevelt refuses to be filmed with Boy Scouts, calling it cheap, and tells George Payne he drinks no whisky and no wine on the road. He bars his committee from buying liquor that critics could use against him.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no further activity is recorded.
As Roosevelt leaves for Ohio, Taft brands him an egotist and a demagogue. Roosevelt writes Elon Hooker about the crooked New York primary of March 26.

Roosevelt barnstorms a dozen eastern Ohio towns from Bellaire to Canton and wins California's primary and all 26 delegates, though Taft claims two from San Francisco. He tells Arthur Lee that Taft is "a good bit of a blackguard."
Roosevelt speaks in fourteen Ohio towns from Kenton to Dayton. In Chicago, real estate man R. M. Patterson tells the newspapers Roosevelt is insane.
Roosevelt speaks in Greenville, Piqua, Lima and Defiance before ending in Toledo.
From Ironton on the Ohio River, Roosevelt campaigns north through Chillicothe, Athens and Lancaster to Columbus.
Roosevelt speaks in Marion, Delaware, Mansfield and Akron and closes the day in Cleveland.
Roosevelt rests at Mentor, Ohio, as a guest of James and Helen Garfield.
Roosevelt's final Ohio swing runs from Marietta through Zanesville and Newark to New Philadelphia.
Taft beaten in his home state

Roosevelt wins Taft's own Ohio, 165,809 votes to 118,362, with La Follette at 15,570, taking 34 of 42 delegates. Alice backs her father while the Longworth family stands with Taft, leaving Nick caught in the middle.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill between campaign trips.

Roosevelt speaks across northern New Jersey from Paterson to Jersey City. He writes about Little Missouri roundups, Denver elections, and convention plans, pushing Governor Hadley over Elihu Root for temporary chairman.
Roosevelt campaigns from Burlington through Egg Harbor City and Atlantic City to Camden and Trenton, and writes T. R. McAnally about the contested Washington primaries.
Roosevelt speaks in eleven central New Jersey towns from Trenton to Elizabeth and tells Senator Dixon he wants Wisconsin Governor Francis McGovern as the convention's permanent chairman.
At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt meets Senator Dixon and Medill McCormick, and writes Dixon that he welcomes industrialists like T. Coleman du Pont but will promise them nothing.
Northern New Jersey, and a weary Edith
Roosevelt campaigns from Hoboken and Bayonne west to Phillipsburg. At home, Edith apologizes in a note to Ethel for being stern, writing that she has much to bear.

Roosevelt wins the New Jersey primary. He urges Senator Clapp to fund more battleships, discusses Trevelyan's new book, declines to pick a running mate, and seeks a convention alliance with La Follette's delegates.
Roosevelt dines with Regis Post and Reynolds in New York, then leaves for Gettysburg.
Roosevelt gives a Memorial Day address on the Gettysburg battlefield and returns to New York.
Roosevelt has now won primaries in nine states, from Illinois to Oregon. He accuses Taft of stealing delegates and wires Arizona allies to meet on their own if unseated.
A delegation from Illinois visits Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill, along with McNinch, Revell, F. Hale and C. Dewey.
Ted and Eleanor visit Sagamore Hill along with Evelyn Irving, the Leigh Hunt family, Hapgood, Hand, Joseph Cutting and George Rublee.
Roosevelt confers with Perkins, Gifford Pinchot, Frank Kellogg, Senator Dixon and others. Arizona's Republican convention picks only Taft delegates, and Roosevelt's backers there meet on their own.
Roosevelt tells William Kent he will fight Elihu Root's selection as temporary convention chairman, and explains his views on recall to Sydney Brooks.
Roosevelt plans with Hapgood, Judge Hand, McCormick and Gifford Pinchot at Sagamore Hill.

The Republican National Committee opens its sessions in Chicago. Roosevelt talks with Pittsburgh boss William Flinn, editor Van Valkenburg and publisher Alexander Moore, and writes Lorenzo Lake about federal help after the Mississippi floods.
Roosevelt tells Oscar Straus that William Randolph Hearst will back him if the Democrats nominate Bryan or Wilson. Enrique Fernandez of Costa Rica signs the guest book.
Roosevelt urges Senator William Borah to put conservation, government railroads and harbors for Alaska in the Republican platform; the Progressives later adopt them.
Roosevelt meets with Richmond Pearson and Truxtun Beale at Sagamore Hill.
Masons on the lawn, a wire to Chicago

Some 400 Masons from three North Shore towns gather on the lawn while Perkins, Munsey and Walter Brown talk platform inside, and two telegraphers in the Gun Room keep a direct line to Chicago. Roosevelt tells Lyman Abbott how much he enjoys working at The Outlook.

Roosevelt writes that Kermit has taken a job with the Brazil Railroad Company, asks that a Black delegate second his nomination, and tells James B. Reynolds he no longer considers himself a Republican.
Roosevelt meets Judge Ben Lindsey; a caller named Fort also stops in.
Eleanor Greene signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Alarmed supporters summon Roosevelt after the National Committee hands Taft 238 of 254 contested seats, about a third of the convention. He and Edith leave for Chicago.
Arriving with Roman history in hand

Roosevelt and Edith reach Chicago with books of Roman history and a primary tally of 1,157,397 votes to Taft's 761,716. He speaks at the Congress Hotel and meets McCormick, Dixon, Pinchot, Garfield and Cecil Lyon.
Roosevelt is 70 delegates shy of nomination. His daughter Alice with Nick, Kermit, and Ted and Eleanor join him in Chicago as he confers with allies.

After meetings with the seven progressive governors, Perkins, Dixon and Pinchot, Roosevelt gives a speech Edith and Alice helped review to a progressive rally at the Coliseum, closing with a call to battle for the Lord.
The Republican National Convention opens, and Elihu Root, a Taft man, wins the temporary chairmanship and rules to seat the Taft delegates. Roosevelt keeps meeting with his allies.
The convention votes down, 564 to 510, Governor Hadley's motion to keep disputed delegates from voting on their own contests. Roosevelt confers with allies.
Perkins and Munsey pledge their money

As the Credentials Committee argues over seats, George Perkins and Frank Munsey meet Roosevelt late into the night and agree to fund an independent Progressive campaign. Perkins soon becomes his de facto manager. It is Ted and Eleanor's second anniversary.

With ruling after ruling going to Taft, Roosevelt delegates scrape sandpaper and toot like a steamroller. Allies including Senator Borah, Perkins, Straus and Governors Johnson and Stubbs call on Roosevelt.

The Republicans renominate Taft and Sherman; Taft gets 561 votes, Roosevelt 107, and 349 delegates sit out. Roosevelt brands the proceedings void, and his followers gather at the Chicago Opera House to call a new party convention.
Roosevelt sets up committees for the new campaign in Chicago, while Alice and Nick take the train back to Washington.
After a last round of talks with progressive leaders, Roosevelt and Edith leave Chicago for Oyster Bay.

Roosevelt shares lunch with editor Albert Shaw, Father John Zahm, Dean George Kirchwey and others, and writes about organizing the Progressive Party. Alice and Nick travel to watch the Democratic convention in Baltimore.
Roosevelt confers with William Prendergast; Delano Andrews and Teresa Richardson sign the guest book.
Roosevelt meets George Perkins and a group of Brooklyn Republicans who have broken with the party, and writes about the fraudulent convention.

As the Democratic convention deadlocks, Roosevelt hopes Champ Clark wins. He tells Rider Haggard the fight is worth making, discusses protective coloration with Frank Chapman, and writes Hadley that the Republican Party is finished as a tool for reform.
The Outlook publishes the speech Roosevelt gave at the Chicago Opera House on June 22.

Cameras record Roosevelt at home for the first time: riding his horse Sidar, romping with three dogs, and chopping down a tree with Archie's help. Kermit and Alice tour the African specimens at the Smithsonian, and Ted's wife Eleanor and their baby Grace are staying at Sagamore Hill.
R. S. McCormick calls, and Roosevelt warns William Dudley Foulke that a progressive Democratic nominee would likely carry the election.

On the 43rd ballot in Baltimore, the Democrats nominate New Jersey's reform governor Woodrow Wilson, with Alice and Kermit watching. Roosevelt lunches with Dixon, Munsey, Croly and Outlook editors and writes that Wilson's nomination makes his own path much harder.
Roosevelt meets Perkins, Munsey and Flinn and writes Herbert Knox Smith about his decision to run for president.
Roosevelt spends the Fourth at Sagamore Hill conferring with C. H. Thompson.
Roosevelt confers with McCormick, Dixon, Perkins and Stoddard, and writes Governor Chase Osborn, who has publicly backed Wilson, and Paul Ewart about false drinking stories.
Callers including Ransom, Heney and Merriam visit, and Roosevelt meets Perkins. His analysis of how Taft's convention majority was built runs in The Outlook.
The call for a Progressive Party
A general call goes out to form a Progressive Party. General Daniel Sickles, Curry and E. Colby visit Sagamore Hill.
A group of New York Progressives, with Chadbourne and W. M. Chandler, calls at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt lunches with Hotchkiss and writes Will Cowles and others on whether Progressives should run for lesser offices or only the top of the ticket. He warns Madison Peters that backing Wilson means backing the bosses.
Herbert Knox Smith visits. Roosevelt thanks poet William Watson for a sonnet, admitting his cause this year is a forlorn hope, and writes about weak Iowa support and wavering insurgents.
Former Senator Richard Pettigrew and M. Butler visit Sagamore Hill.
A Delaware Progressive delegation, Woodruff, A. P. Moore, Heard and Allee call. Roosevelt writes about the tariff and about presidential electors.
Roosevelt's article "Thou Shalt Not Steal" appears in The Outlook, and he writes Herbert Knox Smith about flaws in the Democratic platform.
Wisconsin's Charles Van Hise and Henry Cochems call, and Dr. Alexander Lambert, Helen Leigh Hunt and Henry Morgan are guests.
Roosevelt writes Governor Hadley that he regards Taft's nomination as fraudulent.

Roosevelt admits to W. F. Cochran his odds are small, refuses shared Taft-Roosevelt electors, and tells LaVerne Noyes a navigable channel from the Great Lakes to the Gulf would rival the Panama Canal in importance.
Roosevelt meets Dixon, Perkins and Oscar King Davis and writes Robert Bass about third-party tickets.

Roosevelt brings social reformers to Sagamore Hill to draft the Progressive platform, among them Homer Folks, Raymond Robins, Walter Weyl, Henry Moskowitz, the Kellogg brothers and Samuel McCune Lindsay.
Roosevelt writes Albert Nortoni about Governor Hadley's decision to remain with the Republicans.
Progressive leaders including Charles McCarthy, George Record and Herbert Knox Smith gather at Sagamore Hill for strategy. Roosevelt's "Men Who Live Softly" appears in The Outlook.
Cochems calls, and Henry Fairfield Osborn and his wife Josephine, along with Hamilton Fish Jr., sign the guest book.
Roosevelt meets William Flinn and writes Medill McCormick about Lithuanian support in Chicago.
Roosevelt meets 48 Progressive county chairmen from across New York State at the Metropolitan Tower, and writes about New England support and Governor Deneen's backing of Taft.
Alice visits. Roosevelt writes O. J. Moore about Cummins and boss rule in the Republican Party, and Rev. Bradley Gilman on equality for Black Americans.
Roosevelt meets Progressives from Minnesota and Oyster Bay and writes F. A. Johnson about third-party tickets.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt's first diary entry of the year notes Kermit sailing via England for a railroad job in Brazil. A Freeport delegation calls, and an Outlook article attacks the Democratic platform as insincere. Alice, kept from the convention, is home to see Kermit off.
Roosevelt talks politics with Dean George Kirchwey and Senator Dixon.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with no other details recorded.

A delegation of Black voters from three states, Virginia among them, visits The Outlook. Roosevelt writes on Black voters and Booker T. Washington's support of Taft, jokes that Croly could write his biography, and clarifies he has no contract with The Outlook.
A group of Vermont Progressives calls on Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt writes Julian Harris, whose father created Uncle Remus, about Black delegates to the coming Progressive convention, favoring the white Southern delegations. The stance leaves Southern delegations all white and alienates Black voters, many of whose leaders, including Booker T. Washington, back Taft.
Roosevelt writes Frank Munsey about the campaign.

At Chicago's Congress Hotel, the party's provisional committee gathers to settle whether Black Southern delegates will be seated. Roosevelt writes Horace Plunkett his analysis of Wilson and the Democratic platform.
Roosevelt and Edith board a train west for the new party's national convention in Chicago.

Just after 12:40 in the afternoon the new party's convention opens at the Coliseum before 10,000 people and 2,000 delegates from every state except South Carolina. Beveridge delivers the keynote. The committee votes not to seat the Black Southern delegates.

On Edith's 51st birthday Roosevelt gives a 52-minute "Confession of Faith" laying out the New Nationalism: direct election of senators, unemployment insurance, an end to child labor, a minimum wage, and initiative, referendum and recall.
Nominated by the Bull Moose party
The Progressives nominate Roosevelt for president and California Governor Hiram Johnson for vice president. Jane Addams seconds Roosevelt, the first woman to address a major party convention.

The convention adopts a platform calling for trust regulation, farm credit, direct primaries, woman suffrage, a tariff commission, safer factories, a minimum wage, an eight-hour workday and no child labor. Roosevelt thanks Jane Addams and heads home with Edith, who tells Kermit of red bandannas and the "Battle Hymn of the Republic."
Roosevelt travels home through Manhattan to Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt writes Cecil Spring-Rice that though he is probably losing, with the press and most cultivated opinion against him, he has never been more contented. Ted's wife Eleanor visits.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt wires Judge Ben Lindsey his thanks for a seconding speech at the convention.
On Ethel's 21st birthday Roosevelt meets Perkins, Dixon, Bird, Judge Lindsey and O. K. Davis. The family picnics on Jayne's Hill, and Roosevelt walks there with Archie and young Nicholas Roosevelt.

Roosevelt tells Arthur Lee that Wilson will win but he will outpoll Taft; he likes Wilson but doubts he is a true progressive. He also plays tennis with Ethel, joined by Archie, and talks late with Nicholas.
Roosevelt answers charges that his 1910 Vatican episode alienated Catholics, plans how to win over Taft-pledged Republican electors, and explains again why he is running.
After meeting Dixon, Perkins and Prendergast at The Outlook, Roosevelt travels to Providence and speaks at Infantry Hall.
Roosevelt addresses up to 10,000 people at the Point of Pines Hotel in Revere, speaks again to Progressives indoors, then draws 18,000 on Boston Common. It is granddaughter Grace's first birthday.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no more is recorded.
Ted signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Lindbergh, E. Colby and Heney call. Roosevelt asks Governor Robert Bass to urge Charles S. Bird, the governor's father-in-law, to seek the Massachusetts governorship.

Roosevelt leaves for Wilkes-Barre to honor Father Curran's fiftieth jubilee. He writes Hermann Hagedorn about a poem to the Progressives and asks Gifford Pinchot for material against the Democrats, including his conservation pamphlet.
Roosevelt formally opens his campaign with speeches in Wilkes-Barre. Edith asks Corinne to send him good books: history, science, or a novel where he can play the hero.
Roosevelt returns to New York and Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is home; no further activity is recorded.
George Fred Williams and William Loeb with his family call at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing else noted.
William Prendergast visits Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

Before leaving for Vermont, Roosevelt sends Senator Moses Clapp a long letter on Senate probes of 1904, 1908 and 1912 campaign gifts, including the Harriman money, Penrose's charges, and Perkins. He also praises a Catholic group fighting indecent plays and films.
With gubernatorial candidate Fraser Metzger beside him, Roosevelt speaks from Bennington north to Burlington.
Roosevelt speaks across northern Vermont, and at St. Johnsbury he backs votes for women and rebuts Senator Boies Penrose's attacks.
Roosevelt finishes in Vermont with speeches in Barre, Randolph, Windsor, Bellows Falls and Brattleboro. A caller named Churchill visits.
"Never was there a fight better worth making"
Back home before heading west, Roosevelt tells his sister Corinne the campaign is a draining but worthy fight, and he looks to election day as the end of a battle.
Roosevelt launches his long campaign tour with four Connecticut speeches, from Stamford to Hartford.
Roosevelt speaks in Mattoon, Illinois, Indianapolis, and St. Louis.
Starting at 7 a.m. in Keokuk, Roosevelt speaks across Iowa to Des Moines, where he meets Senator Albert Cummins.
Fifty thousand at the State Fair
Roosevelt draws some 50,000 at the Minnesota State Fair grounds in St. Paul and rides in a Minneapolis parade. In Syracuse, New York Progressives nominate Oscar Straus for governor.
Roosevelt campaigns in North Dakota, speaking at Grand Forks, Fargo and Jamestown.
Roosevelt speaks his way west through Miles City, Billings, Livingston and Bozeman to Helena, where he takes on Wilson.
Leaving Helena for Spokane, Roosevelt writes Oscar Straus that though he had wanted Prendergast for governor, Straus is the stronger candidate.
In Spokane, where women already vote, Roosevelt speaks and attends two women's rallies.
Roosevelt speaks in Seattle and Tacoma.
After more Oregon stops, Roosevelt speaks in Boise and confers with Senator William Borah.
On Ted's 25th birthday, Roosevelt speaks in Blackfoot and Pocatello, Idaho, and Ogden, Utah.
After stops in Reno, Sacramento and Oakland, Roosevelt delivers in San Francisco a full rebuttal of Wilson's "New Freedom," titled "Limitation of Governmental Powers."

In San Francisco Roosevelt lunches with Benjamin Ide Wheeler and meets Heney, Pinchot and Pardee. He writes Corinne that the trip is wearing but the fight is fine, and writes Loeb, who will testify to the Senate about the 1904 Harriman gift.
Crowds estimated at 200,000 line the Los Angeles streets, and Roosevelt speaks at the Shrine Auditorium before heading on.
Roosevelt speaks in Arizona, including Phoenix.
Roosevelt campaigns in New Mexico at Laguna and Albuquerque.
Taking on the trusts in Colorado
Roosevelt speaks from Trinidad through Pueblo and Colorado Springs to Denver, hammering the trusts.
Motion pictures capture Roosevelt speaking in Pueblo, Colorado. He then campaigns in Nebraska at Hastings, Lincoln, Minden and Omaha.
Roosevelt speaks in Ottawa and Topeka and confers with Senator Joseph Bristow, Victor Murdock, Governor Stubbs, W. R. Nelson and William Allen White.
Roosevelt spends the day in Kansas as the guest of editor William Allen White.
Roosevelt campaigns through southeastern Kansas towns such as Pittsburg, then crosses into Missouri for Lamar, Springfield, Aurora and Monett.
Roosevelt campaigns in Tulsa, Chandler, Oklahoma City and McAlester.
In Little Rock, Roosevelt speaks to a group promoting a Great Lakes-to-Gulf waterway.
Roosevelt speaks in Tennessee at Memphis and Jackson.
On Corinne's 51st birthday, Roosevelt parades through New Orleans's French Quarter and gives a speech.
Roosevelt speaks at Montgomery, Opelika and other Alabama towns and in Atlanta.
Hecklers badly disrupt Roosevelt's Atlanta speech. He visits Roswell and Bulloch Hall, his mother's girlhood home.
Roosevelt speaks at four East Tennessee stops, from Chattanooga to Knoxville. Funk publishes his collection "Conservation of Womanhood and Childhood."
Bull Moose campaign crosses North Carolina
Roosevelt carries the Progressive campaign through North Carolina, stopping at Raleigh, Durham, Burlington, Salisbury, Asheville and Hickory.
Roosevelt heads back to Sagamore Hill after the southern swing.
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt meets a stream of Progressive allies and advisers, among them Senator Joseph Dixon, Frank Munsey, Oscar King Davis and his cousin George Roosevelt.
Testifying on campaign money in Washington

Roosevelt appears before a Senate committee probing campaign contributions, then tours the National Museum. He spends time with General and Mrs. Albert L. Mills, Senator Moses Clapp, John Callan O'Laughlin and John McIlhenny.
Back to New York; thanks to Henry White
Roosevelt returns through New York City to Sagamore Hill. He writes diplomat Henry White to thank him for a gift to the campaign.

Roosevelt meets Oscar Straus, Governor Hiram Johnson, Frank Munsey, George Perkins and others at Sagamore Hill. He writes his sister Corinne admiring her first book of verse, The Call of Brotherhood, and admits the campaign has been costly to his friends.
Off on a Great Lakes speaking tour
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill to begin a campaign tour through the Great Lakes states.
The campaign train rolls through Michigan, with Roosevelt speaking at Detroit, Flint, Saginaw and Bay City.
Roosevelt keeps campaigning in Michigan, reaching Marquette, Cheboygan and Houghton.
The tour crosses into Minnesota, with Roosevelt speaking at Duluth. A family 23rd birthday falls on this day.
Roosevelt campaigns in Wisconsin, including a stop at Oshkosh. A Roosevelt family member turns 28.

After a parade, Roosevelt tears into Wilson and the New Freedom before more than 12,000 at the Chicago Coliseum, his voice worn ragged from weeks of speaking; Alice is in the hall. A Michigan paper, the Iron Ore, smears him as a liar, a curser and a drunk.
With his voice spent, Roosevelt calls off planned appearances in Wisconsin, Indiana and Illinois. He dines with Alice and with Medill and Ruth McCormick, and the talk turns to the campaign.
Shot in Milwaukee, he gives the speech anyway

Leaving the Gilpatrick Hotel for an evening speech, Roosevelt is shot in the chest by John Schrank. He begs the crowd to spare the gunman, then delivers all 50 pages of his address with the bullet in him, holding up his bloodied shirt. The folded manuscript and his glasses case slowed the bullet, which cracked a rib and stopped short of his lung.
Roosevelt lies in Chicago's Mercy Hospital on Prairie Avenue. Alice arrives from Cincinnati while Edith is still on her way, and Father Vattman and Albert Beveridge stop in.

Edith arrives in Chicago with Ethel, Ted and Dr. Alexander Lambert, met by Alice. Father Curran visits, and both Wilson and Taft halt their campaigns while Roosevelt is laid up. Edith writes Bamie that he is doing well but she fears infection.
From his hospital bed: keep fighting

Roosevelt issues a statement urging that the campaign go on without him. Jane Addams visits, and Beveridge carries a message from him to a Louisville audience. Edith tells her sister Emily the wound is no bigger than a dime and shows no infection.
Bacon and Johnson at the bedside
Robert Bacon and Governor Hiram Johnson call on Roosevelt at Mercy Hospital. His nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 14.
A hospital stay he calls a spree

Francis Heney reads reporters Roosevelt's answer to Wilson's charges. Visitors include Oscar King Davis and Governor Johnson. Roosevelt dictates a letter to Bamie from bed, saying the days with Edith and the children have been a treat; Edith adds that he tires easily.
A quiet Sunday in the hospital
Roosevelt spends the day mending at Mercy Hospital.
Roosevelt and Edith leave Chicago by train for Sagamore Hill. Edith writes Kermit in South America that his father is improving and reading magazines in his berth.
Home again, and a demand to Bryan
Roosevelt and Edith reach New York and go on to Sagamore Hill. He writes William Jennings Bryan insisting he retract printed misstatements of Roosevelt's views on trusts and monopoly.
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt receives George Perkins and Lyman Abbott. Cecil Lyon signs the guest book.
Mark Sullivan, Finley Peter Dunne, Robert Collier and Cecil Lyon visit Roosevelt. He thanks Senator William Flinn for writing after the shooting.
George Perkins, Frank Munsey and Frederick Hotchkiss call on Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.
On his feet too soon for Edith
Barely a week and a half after the shooting, Roosevelt is out of bed and moving around Sagamore Hill, much to Edith's dismay.
The family gathers at Sagamore Hill to celebrate Roosevelt turning 54. He writes Bamie that he loved her gift and feels strong, though the wound has not yet closed.
For the first time since he was shot, Roosevelt is permitted to see reporters. Frederick Davenport calls, and Roosevelt tells Henry Cabot and Nannie Lodge he is on the mend.
Accepting the risks of public life
Roosevelt answers a worried letter from the historian George Otto Trevelyan, saying a man in public life must reckon with the chance of being shot.
A 41-minute ovation at Madison Square Garden

Still weak, Roosevelt speaks to 16,000 about what the Progressive Party stands for packed into Madison Square Garden. The crowd cheers for 41 minutes until he pounds a table and calls for quiet. Corinne and Douglas have to slip past the guards; Edith watches from a box with Ethel, Ted, Eleanor and Quentin.
Senator Joseph Dixon and George Perkins call at Sagamore Hill in the last days of the race.

Roosevelt returns to Madison Square Garden to speak for Oscar Straus, the Progressive candidate for governor. He also writes Frederick Selous hoping he can bag a fine bull giant eland for the museum in Kensington.
Roosevelt lunches with Frances Kellor at Sagamore Hill. A message from him runs in Collier's, and he sends Ernest Harvier a note about the race.
Sunday lunch with Alice and Jacob Riis
Alice Longworth and the reformer Jacob Riis join Roosevelt for lunch at Sagamore Hill two days before the election.
On election eve Roosevelt speaks close to home in Oyster Bay and Mineola. He writes Beveridge, Straus and other Progressive candidates that the fight was worth making whatever the outcome.
Election Day: Wilson wins, Roosevelt runs second

Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay. Woodrow Wilson takes the presidency with 435 electoral votes; Roosevelt, carrying six states and 88 electoral votes, finishes ahead of President Taft. In New York, Straus loses the governor's race, Franklin Roosevelt keeps his state Senate seat, and Nick Longworth loses his House seat by 97 votes.

The day after the defeat, Roosevelt meets George Perkins, Frank Munsey, Senator Dixon, Governor Johnson and Amos and Gifford Pinchot at Sagamore Hill. Edith writes Kermit that the outcome was no surprise.
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt walks a visitor, his young cousin Nicholas Roosevelt, through the attempt on his life in Milwaukee in close detail.
We kept the faith, he tells Garfield

Roosevelt goes to The Outlook, where Hotchkiss, Bainbridge Colby and Senator Dixon call. He writes James Garfield that the Progressives have nothing to regret, and writes Andrew Rahn on Minnesota, a state he carried while the party lost locally.
A guest identified as S. Farr signs in at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more.
The Progressives are here to stay

Roosevelt tells the press the new party will endure. He answers Gifford Pinchot's ideas for its future, such as a Washington headquarters and a salary for Dixon, but rejects his doubts about William Flinn and George Perkins.
Cheers for Spring-Rice; Schrank in court

In Milwaukee, John Schrank is arraigned and plainly insane. Roosevelt congratulates his old friend Cecil Spring-Rice on becoming British ambassador to the United States, and writes Henry White, Henry Summers and Seth Bullock that the new party must keep its independence.
Roosevelt, dividing his time between Sagamore Hill and the city, again defends William Flinn and George Perkins, chairman of the party's executive committee, in a letter to Gifford Pinchot.

Mark and Marie Sullivan visit. Roosevelt writes Charles Willard about keeping the Progressives going, with more praise for Perkins, and tells New Hampshire's Governor Robert Bass that local organizations need building up.
Roosevelt writes Britain's Foreign Secretary, Sir Edward Grey, summing up the election and describing the shooting, including why he gave his speech before going to the hospital.
Ruth Draper visits; Quentin glad it's over

Ruth Draper, Bill Bird and Alice Longworth are guests at Sagamore Hill. From Groton, Quentin writes his mother that school is gloomy and he is relieved the election is done. Roosevelt tells Ben Lindsey he regrets nothing and Perkins deserves support.
Edith writes Kermit that Ted spends too much time at the Brook Club and that Eleanor may not see it.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.
Woman suffrage and a woman in the cabinet

Roosevelt speaks to a gathering of party leaders at the Holland House on Quentin's 15th birthday. He tells British suffragist Millicent Fawcett he favors equal footing for women and would have named Jane Addams to his cabinet, and writes on antitrust policy, judicial recall and party feuds.
Belle Willard is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler about the Progressives and the incoming Wilson administration.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Schrank ruled insane; a bird quarrel

A Milwaukee court formally finds John Schrank insane. Roosevelt writes Witmer Stone objecting to an article in The Auk that disputes his views on protective coloration, and sends two letters on Maine politics.
Roosevelt's article on the Balkans appears in The Outlook. He writes Charles Merriam agreeing with his thoughts on the party and the income tax, and touches on Perkins.
A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie marks 17 years of marriage.
Looking ahead to a party convention
Roosevelt sends Ernest Harvier a brief note and writes Governor Hiram Johnson about the coming Progressive convention.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt writes Richard Newton to thank him for standing with him.
In New York, Gifford Pinchot, William Draper Lewis and Roosevelt's nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson call on him at The Outlook.
Where the children are this fall

Cecil Spring-Rice reaches Washington as Britain's ambassador. Ted is selling bonds for a New York firm and often brings Eleanor and baby Grace to Sagamore Hill; Archie is a student at Andover's Phillips Academy, and Quentin, at Groton, has a nose broken by a hockey stick.
Edith writes Kermit that Alice looks sick and exhausted and has struggled with Nick, who cannot accept losing his seat in Congress.
Roosevelt and Edith mark their 26th wedding anniversary at Sagamore Hill.
Worried for Edith, writing to Kermit

Roosevelt meets William Prendergast and his nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson. He tells Kermit, traveling in South America, that Edith has not been well since a riding fall a year earlier. Other letters go to Selous, to Fanny Parsons about what a striving boy can achieve, and to two Maine correspondents.

Roosevelt writes Edna Ferber about his campaign remark that one of her characters ought to have married. He also advises Ruth Hanna McCormick that her husband Medill ought to keep his Springfield seat rather than run for the Senate, and writes Mark Sullivan and Walter Emerson on party matters.
A long letter to Amos Pinchot
Oliver W. Roosevelt is a guest. Roosevelt writes Amos Pinchot at length on Perkins, trusts and antitrust policy, the party platform, race, and Lincoln's stand on slavery.
Charles H. Duell signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Fairman Dick is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt sets out for a Progressive conference in Chicago aboard a train chartered by party members from New York and New England.
In Chicago, Roosevelt speaks to the state legislators who joined the Progressives.

Roosevelt opens the Progressive conference at the La Salle Hotel before some 1,500 delegates and speaks again at a crowded evening dinner. He writes his old friend Bob Ferguson about the Balkan war and the Pinchots' attacks on the party's moderates.

The Progressive National Committee debates moving headquarters to Washington and whether to keep George Perkins as chairman; Roosevelt has come to Chicago to block the push to remove him. He is a guest at a Progressive women's luncheon honoring Jane Addams and dines with her that night.
Roosevelt starts home for New York and Sagamore Hill.

Back in New York, Roosevelt writes James Pound, his Detroit lawyer in the libel case against editor George Newett of the Ishpeming Iron Ore, about witnesses to his sobriety. He also defends Perkins to Francis Heney and writes George Record on the Sherman Act plank.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded.
Whitelaw Reid, the American ambassador to Great Britain, dies; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
On the man who shot him
Writing to the British editor John St. Loe Strachey, Roosevelt argues that Schrank was less a madman than a man of criminal temperament who knew where to strike, and says he bears him no ill will.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events noted.
Few hopes for his own future
Mark and Marie Sullivan visit again. Roosevelt writes Sir Henry Lucy that he expects little from his own political prospects.
Lawrence Abbott of The Outlook signs the guest book.
Praise for a book of parodies
Roosevelt compliments Franklin P. Adams on his new collection of parodies, In Other Words, and writes E. C. Bowler about Maine politics.
Roosevelt meets with Joseph Alsop and Herbert Knox Smith, and lays out his position on Perkins to Gifford Pinchot. Both Pinchots object to Perkins as too wealthy and not radical enough.
Edwin Mead, Chalmers Wood Jr., and Philip and Katherine Weld sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt writes Senator Joseph Bristow about bills for an industrial commission and for electing postmasters; he favors the first and is cool toward the second.
A blizzard sweeps over Sagamore Hill.
Christmas stockings in Edith's drawing room

The family opens stockings and gifts in Edith's drawing room, with Ted, Eleanor, Archie, Quentin and Grace Alexander on hand. Roosevelt is sorry that little Gracie must stay away because of the storm.
Esther Rowland, Ted, Eleanor and Alice Longworth are recorded as guests.

In Boston, Roosevelt is elected president of the American Historical Association and delivers his address 'History as Literature.' He stays with William Sturgis Bigelow and tells Ben Lindsey the party team is pulling together.
Roosevelt addresses the Military Historical Society in Boston.
Jack Wiley and Clifford Rochman are guests. Edith writes Kermit that Ted chose lunch at the Ritz with business contacts over a trip to Sagamore Hill, and calls it his low point.
Nicholas Roosevelt is a guest. Roosevelt writes James Keeley about the 'Take me to Murphy at Mercy' rumor and claims that he drank heavily in Mercy Hospital.
A trade risk, he tells Spring-Rice

Roosevelt returns to Sagamore Hill and writes a stack of letters: telling Spring-Rice that being shot is simply a hazard of public life, discussing Panama Canal tolls, a white slavery bill and an industrial commission, and urging the defeat of Republican Edwin Burleigh for the Senate.
New Year between home and the city
Roosevelt begins 1913 at Sagamore Hill, making regular trips into New York City.
Roosevelt has started writing his memoirs. Lawrence Abbott of The Outlook is a guest.
Letters on electors and a mother's burden

Roosevelt writes four senators about Progressive electors barred from the 1912 ballot. A woman writes him that raising a big family has held her back, a letter he later cites in his autobiography. He also wires a protest after Progressive newspapermen are jailed in Boise.
A walk with Edith to Cooper's Bluff

Roosevelt and Edith take a stroll to Cooper's Bluff. He thanks her sister Emily for two books of simple Italian stories and reports that Edith is mending but weak, with Ethel handling the mail, checkbook and household.
Roosevelt meets Connecticut Progressives about whether to merge forces with the Republicans.
Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan; no details survive.
Roosevelt writes about Progressive electors, the Industrial Commission bill, and, to his friend Brander Matthews, about race problems in America.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Senator Joseph Bristow about Senate elections.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
A novel for a weary mother
Roosevelt answers the woman who wrote on January 3 about her large family, sending her Kathleen Norris's novel Mother. He also writes James Bryce with news and Dan Hanna about the party.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Resisting a merger with the Republicans
Martha Wadsworth visits. Roosevelt tells Charles Bonaparte he opposes any fusion of Progressives and Republicans, and writes Bishop Charles Brent that Wilson could turn out a good President.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Garment strikers and a full guest book
On Bamie's 58th birthday, Roosevelt talks with Miss Doty about striking garment workers. A crowd of guests, Father Zahm among them, signs in, and his Outlook article on white slavery appears.
Hester Chanler is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt goes into the city to see striking garment workers at St. Mark's Place and on Henry Street. The mother he wrote to sends her thanks, and he writes several letters about West Virginia politics.
Witness in the U.S. Steel case

At The Outlook, Roosevelt sees Henry Moskowitz, Bourke Cockran and John Purroy Mitchel. He testifies in a special examination in the government's U.S. Steel case, and lays out for Robert Vessey and other correspondents where he stands on the party.
Roosevelt writes R. G. Anderson about American prisons and sends greetings to Indiana Progressives through A. W. Tracy.

Roosevelt has lunch with leaders of the garment strike. He writes Michael Schaap, Progressive floor leader in the state Assembly, that he stands firmly with the union, and reports on his visit to the strikers.
Collier's publishes Roosevelt's 'Sara Knisley's Arm,' an argument for a workmen's compensation law.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Governor Robert Bass on New Hampshire's Senate race, Governor Hiram Johnson on hostile press coverage, the party and Wilson, and Henry White on Panama Canal tolls.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Walter Strong about George Perkins.
Ethel decides to marry Dr. Richard Derby. Chapters from Roosevelt's memoirs begin appearing in print.
A month of home and city
Roosevelt opens February at Sagamore Hill, going into New York City often.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Governor Robert Perkins Bass about politics in New Hampshire.
Recalling the moment he was shot

In a letter to his friend William Sturgis Bigelow, Roosevelt describes the Milwaukee shooting: stepping into the car from a bright hotel, telling the crowd not to hurt the gunman, and feeling almost no pain beyond his broken rib.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Maud Nathan about benefit concerts to raise money for the Progressive Party.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Joseph Bucklin Bishop about Wilson and a proposed amendment limiting presidents to a single six-year term.
Roosevelt writes Silas McBee, and Thomas Nelson Page in much the same vein, about having Democrats head the Progressive cause in the South.
At the Progressive Party's Lincoln Day dinner in New York, Roosevelt speaks on 'The Heirs of Abraham Lincoln.' His daughter Alice turns 29.
Roosevelt, in New York, writes George Wicker about New Hampshire politics.
Roosevelt speaks at a Rough Riders dinner in New York and writes Lucius Watkins about Michigan's April local elections.
Roosevelt writes John Callan O'Laughlin on improving how the Army and Navy deal with the press, and Frank Munsey on talk of merging Republicans and Progressives.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt, Edith and Ethel are staying at the Marquis Hotel on East 31st Street. After a 9 o'clock breakfast he walks down Madison Avenue to his Outlook office, works till 5:30, then returns for tea with Edith. He writes Charles Bonaparte about Munsey's push to merge the parties.
Evening train to Oyster Bay; coup in Mexico
Another day like the last, except Roosevelt leaves the office at 5 to catch the 5:30 home from Pennsylvania Station. In Mexico, Victoriano Huerta seizes power from Francisco Madero.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Two historians and Will Cowles visit
Historians Max Farrand and Archibald Cary Coolidge and Roosevelt's brother-in-law Will Cowles are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt holds a reception at Sagamore Hill for Progressives from Nassau County.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Teresa Richardson visits. Roosevelt writes Ernest Harvier that former Republicans in the new party are truly pursuing industrial reform, and sends Walter Clyde Jones his thoughts about the Senate.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Lodge likes the memoirs; African game book

Warrington Dawson visits. Roosevelt is pleased Lodge enjoyed his Outlook reminiscences, and mentions he is writing a natural history of Africa's big game together with Edmund Heller. He warns William Cochran and Beveridge that La Follette is luring Progressives back to the Republicans.
Another installment of Roosevelt's memoirs is published. Out in Ohio, Alice now lives in Cincinnati with Nick and his mother and must make big adjustments.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with frequent trips to the city. W. R. Cross and three others identified only by first names sign the guest book.
Ethel and a trip to Brazil
Edith writes Kermit that she will not stop Ethel from going to Brazil, though she needs her at home.
Frances Kellor and Lawrence Abbott are guests at Sagamore Hill.
At the Armory Show as Wilson takes office

While Woodrow Wilson is sworn in as the 28th President in Washington, Roosevelt tours the modern art exhibition now known as the Armory Show, plus a housing exhibit. He suggests enlisting South American nations to deal with Mexico's new regime and argues the flood-prone Mississippi must be managed by the government as one system.
A bullet like a pocket watch
Roosevelt writes Charles Washburn about how little real power kings hold, and says the bullet lodged in him troubles him no more than something in his vest pocket.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Charles and Edith Lindley and Ethel's fiance Richard Derby are guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt speaks at the Philadelphia Opera House about the Progressive Service.
Still in Philadelphia, Roosevelt speaks before the state's Electoral College Association.
Roosevelt returns through New York City to Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Franklin heads to the Navy Department
Roosevelt's cousin Franklin D. Roosevelt wins Senate confirmation as the Navy's assistant secretary.
Congratulations to Franklin and Wilson's cabinet

Roosevelt writes Franklin to wish him well at the Navy Department and sends congratulations to new ambassador James Gerard, Interior Secretary Franklin Lane and Attorney General James McReynolds. He also writes O'Laughlin on organizing Progressive congressmen.
