Roosevelt thanks George Otto Trevelyan for a portrait of Macaulay and writes William Cochran on Massachusetts local elections.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
James Breese, Chalmers Wood, Eleanor Greene, Cornelia Landon and H. Osborn Jr. sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Henry Cochems about the Aldrich Bill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

After meeting Congressman William Hinebaugh, Roosevelt goes to Albany to speak to New York Progressives and calls on Governor William Sulzer and Lieutenant Governor Martin Glynn, then leaves for Detroit. He writes Gifford Pinchot on politics and on charges about land reclamation.
Detroit, suffrage, and the Armory Show

In Detroit, Roosevelt meets Gifford Pinchot and Michigan Progressives and speaks in favor of votes for women. His Outlook piece on the Armory Show appears, waving off cubist canvases yet applauding the show's break with the conventional.
Roosevelt travels home to Oyster Bay.
A new installment of Roosevelt's autobiography is published.
Who to invite to Ethel's wedding

Roosevelt urges Winthrop Chanler to see that Lodge and George Meyer attend to Ethel's wedding, fearing election wounds might keep them away; he would rather Root, Taft and Nicholas Murray Butler stay away. He also writes Perkins about a memo for his autobiography and the tariff.
A rallying letter to Progressives in Congress
Roosevelt sends the Progressive members of Congress an encouraging letter declaring the party stands for the people's rights.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Ethel weds Dr. Richard Derby at Christ Church in Oyster Bay before 500 guests. Alice comes but Nick does not; Lodge and George Meyer attend. Roosevelt tells Bamie that Derby is the finest young man he knows.
Worn out, Edith stays in bed until lunch and spends the afternoon roaming the woods. Alice does not spend time with her.
Supper with Lillian Wald and a settlement play
Roosevelt dines with Lillian Wald and watches the Henry Street Settlement's drama club put on The Silver Box. Edith writes Emily, Bigelow and Ethel about the wedding.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Spring setbacks; Wilson goes to Congress

The Progressives fare poorly in spring elections in Michigan and Chicago. In Washington, Wilson addresses both houses of Congress in person, something no president had done since George Washington. Roosevelt writes J. M. Wall about the party.
Roosevelt's son Archie celebrates his 19th birthday.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Harold Ickes about the Progressives' poor showing in Illinois local races.
Roosevelt's English friends Arthur and Ruth Lee come to stay at Sagamore Hill through April 17.
Arthur and Ruth Lee are staying at Sagamore Hill.
Arthur and Ruth Lee are staying at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt visits schools on the Lower East Side, eating lunch at P.S. 95, then meets the Progressive Service's child welfare committee at The Outlook.
Gifford Pinchot is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Warning California on alien land law
With the California legislature set to bar non-citizens from owning land, a move stirring trouble with Japan, Roosevelt wires Governor Hiram Johnson urging that it not pass.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
William Rockhill Nelson and Dr. Alexander Lambert call at The Outlook. Roosevelt tells Henry Stoddard he favors John Purroy Mitchel for mayor of New York.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
George Perkins calls, and Roosevelt sends Governor Johnson another telegram about California's land bill.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne marks 31 years of marriage.
Wilson's essay and a new book of essays

Roosevelt wires Johnson again on California, and writes Herbert Drake about Wilson's World's Work article attacking his ideas on regulating corporations. Scribner's brings out a new collection of his essays, and another memoir installment appears.
Roosevelt writes Ethel, sending a picture letter and delighting in her happiness with Dick. He notes Kermit is struggling in South America and wishes he were better company for Edith in the evenings.
Suffrage speech; no run for mayor

Roosevelt speaks at a woman suffrage meeting. He tells Henry White that Wilson and Secretary of State Bryan have handled California badly and that he will not run for mayor, and backs Governor Sulzer's direct primary bill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
No single tax in the platform
Roosevelt tells George Record the Progressive platform will leave out the single tax because the public is not ready for it.
Roosevelt writes Dean George Kirchwey that, though he preferred the Progressive version, he heartily supports the direct primary bill Governor Sulzer is pushing.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Lunch with Carnegie; powerless on Japan

Roosevelt lunches with Andrew Carnegie, Joseph Choate, Judge Alton Parker and British delegates to a peace celebration. To Japan's Baron Kaneko he writes that he has done all he can on California but has no power.
Japan's government lodges a formal protest with Washington over California's proposed land law.
Roosevelt warns Franklin, now at the Navy Department, that trouble with Japan is unlikely but could come without warning, and the fleet must not be split.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt speaks in Plainfield, New Jersey, to a men's group supporting votes for women. In Albany lawmakers called back for a special session reject the primary bill, and Tammany boss Charles Murphy moves to impeach Governor Sulzer over campaign funds.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Governor Hiram Johnson signs California's anti-Japanese land bill, calling it the people's will; it breaks no federal law.
Roosevelt writes Senator Miles Poindexter of the Naval Affairs Committee against splitting the fleet.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Off to Michigan for the libel trial

Roosevelt leaves for Marquette, Michigan, to press his libel suit against editor George Newett. Edith writes Kermit that Nick's absence from the wedding mattered little to the family but deeply hurt Alice.
Roosevelt is on his way to Marquette.
Staying with George Shiras, Roosevelt takes the stand in his suit against George Newett, whose Ishpeming Iron Ore had branded him a liar, a curser and a drunk.
Roosevelt remains in Marquette as the libel trial goes on.
Roosevelt is still in Marquette for the libel case.

A parade of witnesses testifies to Roosevelt's character and sobriety, among them Gifford Pinchot, Leonard Wood, George Dewey, Jacob Riis, his doctors Alexander Lambert and Presley Rixey, and cousins Emlen and Philip Roosevelt.
Edith writes Cecil Spring-Rice that politics make a visit unwise just now, though the old friends long to see each other.

Newett gives up, and Roosevelt wins his libel case, taking just six cents in damages. He writes Bamie that the libeler caved. The 17th Amendment takes effect, moving the choice of senators from state legislatures to the voters.
Kermit's news from Brazil, sent from Michigan
From Marquette, Roosevelt writes his daughter Ethel that her brother Kermit has taken a job with the Anglo Brazil Iron Company in the south of Brazil.

Roosevelt gets back to New York and Sagamore Hill and writes diplomat Henry White about his autobiography chapter on the Portsmouth peace and the Japanese complaints it drew, along with present-day trouble with Japan.
Roosevelt and his wife Edith head out on a picnic. He also makes clear that Dick Derby, about to join the family through Ethel, will be counted as fully one of his own.
Roosevelt receives visitors at Sagamore Hill, among them Mitchel and Father York.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Cheering schoolboy athletes in Central Park
Roosevelt travels into the city to watch a field day in Central Park put on by boys of the Public Schools Athletic League.
Arthur Hill and Romulo Naon, Argentina's minister to the United States, spend time as Roosevelt's guests at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Commencement speech at the Hill School
Roosevelt goes to Pottstown, Pennsylvania, and speaks to the graduating class of the Hill School.
Stumping for direct primaries in Buffalo

In Buffalo, Roosevelt addresses the Progressive Club to push for direct primaries in New York, staying with C. J. Hamlin. His wife Edith sails for Europe to be near her sister Emily after emergency appendix surgery.
In Rochester, Roosevelt sits down to lunch with some five hundred Progressives, and speeches follow.
Roosevelt travels toward Andover, Massachusetts. Ted, his wife Eleanor and little Gracie sign in as guests.
Roosevelt watches his son Archie finish at Phillips Academy in Andover, speaks at the alumni luncheon, and then leaves for Hartford.
Roosevelt leaves Hartford, Connecticut, and makes for Oyster Bay.
A full house at Sagamore Hill
Ted and Eleanor bring baby Gracie to Sagamore Hill. Alice Longworth and Eleanor's mother, Mrs. Alexander, are staying too.
A Bunker Hill Day speech on the flag

For Bunker Hill Day, Roosevelt gives a rousing talk on the American flag at a Boston banquet of Charlestown's Hayes Square Outing Club. He dines with W. S. Bigelow, is received by the city's press club, and returns to New York.

Roosevelt lunches at the American Museum of Natural History with Frank Chapman and Father Zahm, a South America traveler, to start arranging his trip to Brazil. He also writes several men about the Underwood tariff.
Roosevelt meets with Whitman at Sagamore Hill. Alice and Nick are the house guests.

Herbert K. Smith and his wife visit Sagamore Hill as word comes from Europe: Ethel and Dick have joined Edith at Lausanne's Hotel Mirabeau, and Emily's surgery went well. Roosevelt writes Arthur Hill about his Charlestown speech attacking the red flag.
Ludwig Moorehead visits Sagamore Hill on the third wedding anniversary of Ted and Eleanor.
The boys come home from school
Quentin and Archie arrive back at Sagamore Hill for the summer.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

With his sister Corinne and her husband Douglas visiting, Roosevelt writes Kermit in Brazil, backing his work, sketching ideas for their coming South American journey, and reporting that Eleanor is keeping house while Edith is away.
Mrs. Leigh Hunt and Mrs. Kinsolving join Roosevelt for lunch, and Jose DeLima, secretary to Brazil's foreign minister Lauro Muller, calls. Roosevelt writes William Hotchkiss about the race for mayor.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt urges Donald Richberg to have Progressives in Congress press for a workmen's compensation law, and writes Walter Brown about Black voters in the North.
James B. Eustis and his wife visit Sagamore Hill, along with Ted and Eleanor.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Another installment of Roosevelt's "Chapters of a Possible Autobiography" appears. Alice and Nick set off for Panama, and the record notes the coming western journey with Archie, Quentin and cousin Nicholas Roosevelt to the Indian lands beyond the Grand Canyon's north side.
Roosevelt writes William Nelson again about the Underwood tariff bill.
At Newport, Roosevelt marks the Progressive Party's first birthday with a speech on the American Navy, then joins party leaders in an open discussion.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt writes his old friend Cecil Spring-Rice about friction between the United States and Japan, saying he wants to see him and never mind diplomacy. From Europe, his wife Edith complains to Kermit that Ted's in-laws have crowded into Sagamore Hill.
Off west with Archie and Quentin

Roosevelt sets out on a western trip with his sons Archie and Quentin. He writes Arthur Lee about his libel trial, a peace conference and the coming South American trip, glad to be beyond the Progressives' reach for a while, and admitting he disliked Edith's going abroad though she had to.
Roosevelt and the boys are on their way west.
No change on the Southern question
Still traveling west, Roosevelt writes Walter Brown that he will not change the Progressive Party's all-white policy in the South.
With Bob Ferguson in Silver City
Roosevelt and his sons arrive in Silver City, New Mexico, as guests of his old friend Bob Ferguson.
The Roosevelts remain at Silver City with Bob Ferguson.

From Albuquerque the Roosevelts head for the Grand Canyon, reaching Flagstaff at 9:45 at night, where cousin Nicholas Roosevelt joins them. They resolve to pack in to see Rainbow Natural Bridge while in Arizona, then ride the train on to Williams.
An old professor on the canyon rim

Roosevelt, Quentin and Nicholas reach the Grand Canyon at 8 a.m. and check into the near-empty El Tovar Hotel. After a day of planning and a walk along the rim, they run into Dr. Fisher, once Roosevelt's professor, who joins them for dinner and talk of canyon plants and animals.

Archie comes in from Flagstaff by train, bringing Jesse Cummings of Mesa to cook, pack and wrangle for the trip. Roosevelt and Quentin spend part of the day on horseback near El Tovar. Edith writes Kermit that the coming Brazil journey worries her.

After an early hotel breakfast, Roosevelt, Archie, Quentin, cousin Nicholas and Jesse Cummings ride mules down the Bright Angel Trail and finish the steepest pitch on foot. Rain turns to a thunderstorm as they ride a hand-pulled cable car over the Colorado. A Bar Z hand named Stevenson lends horses for the climb north, and supper by the river is bacon, flat pancakes and canned peas.
Night climb to the North Rim

Woken at 1:30 a.m. by Mansfield of the Bar Z, the party eats graham meal and canned chicken and sets off up the trail at 2:45 under clouds. By noon they top out on the North Rim and meet game warden "Uncle Jimmy" Owens, then ready the hunt as rain falls.

The Mormon guides who were supposed to bring horses down to the river on the 15th never came, so they are let go. Uncle Jimmy Owens and prospector Joe Wilson will guide the hunt instead, and the party meets Forest Supervisor Pelton and his rangers.
In a drizzle, the party persuades Joe Wilson to come along on the hunt.
The Roosevelts spend the day preparing for the hunt on the canyon's north side.

After a night of sour beans and rain in Uncle Jim's tent, the party gets moving at 9. The hounds tree a cougar near the canyon rim and Nicholas brings it down. Lunch comes in a thunderstorm at Kanabownits Canyon; later a cold trail, a new camp and more rain.

On a clear, cold morning the hunters ride southeast along the rim toward Point Sublime looking for cougars, but find none. Back at camp, a Mormon visitor is waiting for Roosevelt and leaves soon after.
Writing a speech for Brazil in camp

With the horses strayed and a hound's leg broken, Roosevelt sits in the tent drafting the speech he will give in Brazil and tells the boys stories of earlier Roosevelt childhoods. Next morning, after burnt biscuits, he hunts near Cliff Spring without luck and explores ruined pueblos and cliff dwellings.
Two cougars and a supper of cougar meat

Roosevelt and Archie each kill a cougar, as does Uncle Jimmy, and Roosevelt eats the meat with gusto. Over the next days the party washes up at the ranger station, rides Wooley's Trail to camp under a ledge facing the San Francisco Peaks, hears his ghost stories, and returns to see Supervisor Pelton.
After a morning at the ranger station, the party rides to the Bar Z Ranch, where Roosevelt questions Al Doyle about the route to Rainbow Natural Bridge. Nicholas finds Doyle a bit of a talker.
The month closes with another installment of Roosevelt's "Chapters of a Possible Autobiography" in print.

Leaving the Bar Z before dawn, the party stops at Kane, where Mansfield lets them keep his horses free of charge, then drops down off the Kaibab into House Rock Valley beside the Vermilion Cliffs. A fierce sandstorm drives them into a stone cabin; Roosevelt beheads a rattler he has caught, and all sleep on the ground.

Up at first light, the party rides through hot desert country that impresses Roosevelt, to Lees Ferry, where Tom Caffell gives them a chicken lunch. Archie and Nicholas go over to the far bank to meet the men J. L. Hubbell has sent: the Navajo cook Loko, Navajo policeman Choke and Sneeze, and guide Francisco Marquez.

At Roosevelt's suggestion the party shifts its gear and camp to the river's south bank. Joe Wilson and Uncle Jimmy Owens turn back for the Grand Canyon. From Europe, his wife Edith writes Kermit that she had wanted this trip so father and Quentin would come to understand one another.
With two wagons, the party reaches Tanner's Well, 25 miles out, by noon, covers 15 more after lunch, and camps on a ridge. Roosevelt has been watching the Navajo people along the way.

On a cool, fast day the party lunches and bathes at Willow Springs, then rides into Tuba City to the Preston trading post. They visit with Mr. Sullivan, who serves as both Indian agent and head of the school; Roosevelt and Quentin sleep in his house, Archie and Nicholas outside.
Hearing out Hopi and Navajo leaders

Mr. Sullivan drives the party to a Hopi village, where the chiefs lay their complaints against the government before Roosevelt; later he hears Navajo chiefs do the same. Quentin and Nicholas ride in Preston's automobile, one of three in town, and dinner is at Preston's. In Italy, Edith turns 52.
Through deep sand toward Marsh Pass
After breakfast the group sets off for Marsh Pass across 25 miles of deep sand, an 8-hour ride, pausing an hour at Red Lake Trading Post and reaching Halfway House at 9 p.m. for the night.
Camp under a half moon at Marsh Pass
The riders cross grassland past Black Mesa, see many pueblo ruins, and camp in lovely Marsh Pass under a bright half moon.
At the Wetherills' post in Kayenta

After 40 miles in the saddle, the party reaches the Kayenta trading post of John and Louisa Wetherill before noon, meets Mr. Colville and Mrs. Peabody, and is shown Navajo sand paintings by Mrs. Wetherill.

The Roosevelts leave Kayenta for Rainbow Natural Bridge, seen by whites only four years before. Guiding them are John Wetherill, Jesse Cummings and a Navajo called Glad Hand, soon joined by Nasja Begay, the Paiute who first led whites there. Traveling light without tents, they pass a cave pueblo and camp by Bubbling Spring.

After a slow start up Paiute Canyon and a night below Navajo Mountain, the party strips down to essentials, rides rough slickrock, squeezes through a crack in the rock, and walks in for a grand first look at Rainbow Bridge. They wash in a pool and sleep under the arch as a full moon rises.
Back to Navajo Mountain; Sulzer impeached
Making good time on the way back, the party reaches its old camp below Navajo Mountain by evening. It is Ethel's 22nd birthday, and in Albany the legislature votes to impeach Governor William Sulzer.
The party lunches in Paiute Canyon and spends the night at Bubbling Spring.
A five-hour ride brings the party back to Kayenta in time for lunch.
Resting at Kayenta, the party reads cheap novels and listens to Mrs. Wetherill on Navajo ways.

With a fresh pack outfit and John Wetherill, Dave Miller and two Navajo men, Snake Dance and Hound, the party rides eight hours straight, eating only an evening meal. Back east, granddaughter Gracie turns two.
Another long day crossing Black Mesa brings the party to the Hopi reservation. The two Navajo guides shoot, roast and eat a few prairie dogs.
A short ride brings the party to Walpi, where Lorenzo Hubbell meets them amid a tangle of tourists and film crews who have come to see Roosevelt.

Lorenzo Hubbell takes Roosevelt into a kiva for a quarter hour, introduces him to the Hopi chiefs, and wins permission for the family to see the next day's snake washing. They watch an antelope dance and meet Indian Service officials and Natalie Curtis. Edith, Ethel and Dick reach home from Europe.

Roosevelt watches a Hopi footrace, joins about 20 men in a kiva for the 40-minute snake washing, and at 5 p.m. sees the snake dance before some 800 whites, most there to see him. Seated with Governor Hunt before Hunt's cameramen, he then motors with Hubbell through the desert night to Ganado.

The Roosevelts pull in at Hubbell's place at one in the morning. Hubbell's daughter, Mrs. Goodman, welcomes them after breakfast, and they spend the day bargaining for horses with Hubbell and enjoying his yarns.
Mud, baths and the Chicago train

Roused at 4 a.m., the Roosevelts drive toward Gallup, pushing a stuck car out of the mud near St. Michaels. In Gallup the Cotton and Manning families lend their tubs, and at noon the party boards the California Limited for Chicago before a big crowd. Roosevelt writes George Perkins about the Progressive pledge.
Roosevelt, Archie, Quentin and Nicholas are aboard the train from Gallup, crossing the plains toward Chicago.

Burned red by the desert sun, Roosevelt is met in Chicago by a reception committee and a crowd of photographers. He lunches and speaks at the Progressive Club, talks with party leaders, and within a couple of hours boards the Pennsylvania Limited for home.

The train pulls into New York in the morning. Roosevelt heads straight to the Outlook office to confer with Progressive leaders, meets George McAneny and the fusion candidates at the Harvard Club, and then goes home to Sagamore Hill. He writes Hiram Johnson about California's Progressives, admitting little faith in Wilson, and Frank Dingley about the party in Maine.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Edith writes Kermit that Quentin seems more grown-up since coming home from the Southwest.
A further chapter of Roosevelt's "Chapters of a Possible Autobiography" comes out.
Sagamore Hill, with trips to the city
Roosevelt is based at Sagamore Hill this month and goes into New York often.

Roosevelt praises Albert Beveridge's Saturday Evening Post article, tells Governor Sulzer he believes him innocent, disagrees with George Record on the single tax, tells Arthur Lee about his trip through the West, and admits to O. K. Davis that the South's whites-only approach may need to be dropped.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Alice Longworth comes to stay until late September. Roosevelt writes Beveridge denying talk of a Progressive-Republican merger or of Progressives aiding Tammany, and writes Lodge criticizing Wilson and Bryan, above all on Mexico.
A blind eye and bad tennis

Roosevelt invites Robert Perkins to Sagamore Hill in hopes of drawing him into Progressive politics, says Ted acts like a boy again at home, and admits his left eye is now blind and his tennis worse than ever.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt goes into the city to meet with Prendergast.
Edith writes Kermit that Alice is being spiteful with everyone.
Roosevelt writes William Cadmus about the Progressive Party and R. M. Meroney about equal rights for Black Americans.
Roosevelt writes Matthew Hale about the Progressives.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Rochester, New York.
In Rochester, Roosevelt is a luncheon guest of the Chamber of Commerce and addresses the Progressive State Committee before heading back to Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes William Allen White on whether he would accept a Republican presidential nomination in 1916.

Privately, Roosevelt tells Victor Murdock he will not run in 1916 under either party. A Century Magazine article lays out the Progressive aims, arguing neither old party serves ordinary people. In Albany, Governor Sulzer is removed after his impeachment trial.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
A Progressive send-off in New York

New York Progressives throw Roosevelt a farewell dinner at a city roof garden. Albert Beveridge speaks, and Roosevelt follows with an attack on two party bosses, Republican William Barnes Jr. and Tammany's Charles Murphy.

At 1 p.m. Roosevelt, in a gray suit and hat, sails from Brooklyn on the Vandyck with Edith, cousin Margaret Roosevelt, naturalist George Cherrie, Anthony Fiala and his secretary Frank Harper. Crowds pack the ship, pier and streets; the Progressives send a band, and envoys of three South American republics see him off.
Roosevelt's party is at sea aboard the Vandyck, bound for South America.
Roosevelt's party is at sea aboard the Vandyck, bound for South America.
Writing for Boys' Life at sea
Aboard ship, Roosevelt writes an article for Boys' Life that will run in December.
From the ship, Roosevelt writes William Allen White that he will give no flat yes or no about the 1916 nomination.
Roosevelt's party is at sea aboard the Vandyck, bound for South America.
At Bridgetown, Barbados, Roosevelt gives a short speech, tours the town and lunches with the governor. Naturalist Leo Miller joins the expedition. In Brazil, Kermit turns 24.
The party is at sea. Back home, his niece Eleanor Roosevelt turns 29.
While Roosevelt is at sea, Timothy Woodruff dies in the United States. He had been Roosevelt's lieutenant governor and a Bull Moose backer in 1912.
Roosevelt's party is at sea aboard the Vandyck, bound for South America.
Roosevelt's party is at sea aboard the Vandyck, bound for South America.
At sea, Edith writes Bamie that her husband seems freed of the Progressive Party, like Christian in Pilgrim's Progress shedding his bundle.
Roosevelt's party is at sea aboard the Vandyck, bound for South America.

Officials greet Roosevelt at Bahia, where Governor Seabra and Mayor Brandao receive him. After breakfast he meets the city council at City Hall, gives a speech and tours the city. Kermit, building bridges for the Anglo-Brazilian Iron Company, joins the party.
Back at sea, Roosevelt and Kermit are caught on film aboard the Vandyck. It is the 15th birthday of his nephew Sheffield Cowles.
Roosevelt's party is at sea aboard the Vandyck, bound for South America.
Roosevelt's party is at sea aboard the Vandyck, bound for South America.
Officials greet Roosevelt in Rio, a great public reception fills the Naval Arsenal, and he calls on President Hermes da Fonseca and Foreign Minister Lauro Muller.
Roosevelt breakfasts with President da Fonseca, tours the Supreme Court and Military College, speaks to the YMCA, and spends the evening at the Russian ballet.
Roosevelt tours Rio's Bacteriological Institute and is guest of honor at a reception hosted by the American ambassador, Edwin Morgan.
The party goes up Tijuca Peak and attends the president's garden party in the Botanical Gardens. At the national university, Roosevelt lectures on "American Internationalism."
On a cruise around the bay, Roosevelt listens to the birds. He visits the Naval School and receives a group of teachers and advanced students. Edith writes a friend that she finds Brazil lovely.
The party visits the mountain town of Petropolis and then leaves for Sao Paulo.
On his 55th birthday, Roosevelt is received by President Alves of Sao Paulo, sees the city and lectures at the university on "Character and Civilization."
Roosevelt inspects local industry, including the Anglo-Brazilian Iron Company where Kermit works.
Roosevelt leaves Sao Paulo, bound for Montevideo.
In Parana, the travelers pause at Morungava to see a ranch run by Brazil Land, Cattle and Packing Company.
The party is in Parana. At home, another installment of Roosevelt's "Chapters of a Possible Autobiography" appears.
The party crosses the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina. In New York, The Outlook prints Roosevelt's "American Internationalism."
Rolling across Rio Grande do Sul
Crossing Rio Grande do Sul, the train pauses at Cruz Alta and again at Santa Maria.
Passing through Porto Alegre, Roosevelt is met at the frontier by officials from Uruguay.

In Montevideo, Roosevelt lunches with President Batlle y Ordonez and attends a state dinner before leaving for Buenos Aires. Back home it is election day. He writes Frank Chapman about the trip and a cougar skull from the West.

U.S. Minister John Garrett and Argentine officials greet the party in Buenos Aires. The American community holds a reception, the Roosevelts are guests of President Saenz Pena, and Roosevelt calls on acting President de la Plaza.
Roosevelt is in Buenos Aires; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt sits in on a session of the Argentine Congress, is received by Foreign Minister Bosch, and speaks at the Colon Theater to the Museo Social Argentino on "Democratic Ideals."
Roosevelt visits schoolchildren in Buenos Aires. "Character and Civilization" is published in The Outlook.
The party spends the day at the racecourse known as the Hippodrome and at the farm exposition.
An honorary degree and "Truths and Half Truths"
The University of Buenos Aires gives Roosevelt an honorary doctor of laws, and he lectures at the Colon Theater on "Truths and Half Truths."
From Buenos Aires, Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie about the journey.
Roosevelt reviews troops at Campo de Mayo, stops at the Military Club, and speaks on "American Ideals" at a Museo Social Argentino banquet.
A telegram reaches Kermit in Buenos Aires: Belle Willard has agreed to marry him.
Edith writes Ethel that she feels a little low, unable to help her husband and no longer needed by Kermit.
Roosevelt sets off into Santa Fe province, stopping at Rosario. "Democratic Ideals" appears in The Outlook, and he sends Sir Edward Grey a look back at the 1912 campaign.
In Tucuman, Roosevelt visits the library and the industrial schools.
Roosevelt tours sugar plantations around Tucuman.
Traveling through Cordoba, San Luis and Mendoza, Roosevelt stops at the provincial capitals.
Roosevelt is in Mendoza province. At Groton, Quentin turns 16.
Roosevelt visits the agricultural college and wineries of Mendoza.
Chilean officials welcome Roosevelt to Santiago.
Lecture at the University of Chile
Roosevelt calls on President Barros Luco and lectures to the University of Chile on democracy as a movement within a republic.
Roosevelt is in Santiago; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is in Santiago; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is in Santiago. At home, his sister Bamie marks 18 years of marriage.
At Valparaiso, Edith and Margaret leave Roosevelt and Kermit and board a ship for Panama. Roosevelt visits the Navy Club.
Roosevelt sees the sights of Valparaiso, then attends a reception by the American community in Santiago.
Roosevelt tours the naval base at Talcahuano, then turns back toward Argentina.
Setting out from Puerto Varas, Roosevelt and Kermit travel by boat over Lake Llanquihue and Lake Esmeralda to Peulla.
Over the Andes; the Autobiography appears

Roosevelt and Kermit ride over the Andes to Lake Frias, then go by oxcart to Lake Nahuel Huapi and Bariloche. Back home, Scribner's publishes his Autobiography, and Boys' Life prints his "To All Boys."
Roosevelt and Kermit drive across the barren Patagonian plains.
Roosevelt and Kermit reach Neuquen. It is the 27th wedding anniversary of Roosevelt and Edith.
Heading back toward Buenos Aires, Roosevelt stops to see the naval base at Bahia Blanca.
Back in Buenos Aires, the city's equestrian society hosts Roosevelt at the Club Hipico, and he visits the flower festival.
Roosevelt leaves Buenos Aires for Asuncion.
The journey north passes through the provinces of Entre Rios and Corrientes.
In Asuncion, Roosevelt and Kermit stay with a former president of Paraguay.
Roosevelt visits Villa Hayes with President Eduardo Schaerer.

In the afternoon Roosevelt starts up the Paraguay River aboard President Schaerer's yacht, with Tex Rickard along. His book Through the Brazilian Wilderness, and his 1913 diary, both pick up the story here.
Roosevelt and Kermit catch a piranha and reach Concepcion just before midnight. He writes Ted's wife Eleanor, glad she is expecting again, with news of Kermit, Archie and Quentin.

In Concepcion, Roosevelt and Kermit stroll the streets, attend a reception, inspect army barracks, and Roosevelt speaks at City Hall. Back on the river he shoots two crocodilians. Edith and Margaret sail from Panama for home.

Steaming north through tropical country, the yacht reaches Brazil's border at the Apa River at noon, where Colonel Candido Rondon and the Brazilian members join. They take on wood at Porto Murtinho. Roosevelt writes Lodge that the Monroe Doctrine should rest on shared agreement.
Under gray skies, Father Zahm baptizes two children in a river town, and Roosevelt shoots caymans, which he likens to crocodiles.
Rain falls over marshy plains to the east as the boat, flying the American flag, passes Coimbra. Roosevelt later describes the river's golden sunsets in his book.
At Corumba the town council hosts a reception and official dinner. Roosevelt and Kermit rejoin Cherrie and Miller, who have gathered about 800 bird and mammal specimens.
The expedition sorts and packs gear while Colonel Rondon checks supplies. Roosevelt hears plenty of animal tales, many about piranhas.
Up the Taquari after an anteater
Aboard the shallow river steamer Nyoac, the party heads up the Taquari toward Senhor de Barros's ranch, Las Palmeiras. Roosevelt shoots a giant anteater and many caymans, and they camp on shore.
Riding to the fazenda; Margaret ill
The party rides 20 miles over five or six hours to the de Barros ranch, with baggage hauled by oxcart. In New York, Edith and Margaret arrive home, Margaret gravely ill.
Roosevelt and Kermit ride and hunt all day through the Pantanal swamp, and Kermit shoots a giant anteater.
Kermit brings down two large marsh deer, and Roosevelt kills a jaguar and fires at a cayman.
Kermit gets a jaguar and Roosevelt a capybara. They push their horses through a stream full of piranhas, and Roosevelt marvels at the birdlife.
The party rides overland back to the Taquari. Roosevelt drops a wood ibis in flight.
Downriver; the Federal Reserve becomes law
Roosevelt and Kermit ride to the boat and steam downstream, towing a small craft for a peon. In Washington, the Federal Reserve Act is signed into law.
The River of Doubt party assembles

Back at Corumba, Roosevelt and Kermit rejoin the rest aboard the Nyoac. The party includes Harper, Father Zahm and his aide Jacob Sigg, Cherrie, Miller, Fiala, Colonel Rondon, Captain Magalhaes, Lieutenants Lyra and Filho, geologist Oliveira and taxidermist Reinisch. Roosevelt writes Edith.
On Christmas the Nyoac pushes upstream against a strong current, the expedition on deck and Kermit busy preparing skins.
Flies and heat on the Sao Lourenco
The Nyoac turns up the narrower Sao Lourenco, with biting flies everywhere and the thermometer at 100 degrees.
Steaming up the Cuiaba in heavy rain, the boat pulls in at a ranch to take on milk and beef.
The party reaches Sao Joao, the ranch of Brazil's agriculture secretary, Senhor da Costa Marques, for a big reception. Afternoon rain, 97 degrees.
Father and son da Costa Marques take the party out after jaguars on an overcast day. Roosevelt kills a wild boar with a spear before heavy rain sets in.
In soaking rain the party heads back down the Cuiaba to the Sao Lourenco and anchors by the bank for the night.

In steady rain the hunters cut through dense jungle, beset by mosquitoes and fire ants. Roosevelt shoots a monkey, the party bags coatis and bush deer, and when the sun breaks through around 2 he gets a capybara. Packed for the trip: Gibbon, Sophocles, More's Utopia, Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus.
A hard, empty New Year's hunt
Up at 5, the party eats hardtack, ham, sardines and coffee, then tramps all day through jungle and marsh in the heat and comes back with nothing.
The expedition runs down the Sao Lourenco to the Paraguay and begins working upstream.
Parakeets on the river; Margaret dies
Steaming up the Paraguay, Roosevelt watches parakeets build nests. At home, Margaret Roosevelt, who sailed south with the party, dies of typhoid fever.
Going up the Paraguay, the party watches wildlife by day and enjoys calm nights on deck.
Leaving the marshes behind, the party reaches Sao Luis de Caceres late in the day, and Roosevelt stays with Lieutenant Lyra. In the United States, Margaret Roosevelt is buried.
The expedition heads up the Sepotuba, known as the River of Tapirs, and pitches camp at Porto Campo. Baggage goes ahead to a staging point, and the flag is raised each day.
At Porto Campo the party observes wildlife and hunts.
The expedition stays in camp at Porto Campo.
With four canoes, three dugouts and one Canadian, the party hunts tapir. Hunting on foot with Fiala, Roosevelt takes a bush deer and later shoots a tapir as it swims.
A hunt for white-lipped peccaries comes up empty, and the bugs make it miserable: ticks, wasps, mosquitoes and fire ants.
Roosevelt and Colonel Rondon try again for peccaries and get five, plus a small bush deer.
The supply boat comes back to camp at Porto Campo.
The party strikes camp, packs a launch and houseboat, and starts up the Paraguay for Tapirapoan with 30 men and five dogs, in rain.
Reading Gibbon at a mile and a half an hour

The boat crawls upriver while the men cook on deck over a makeshift hearth. Roosevelt's reading includes Gibbon, Scott's Quentin Durward and the Song of Roland. At home, Alice's grandmother Lee dies, leaving her an annual income from a trust.
A man who went missing is found, lunch is on an island, and the party reaches Tapirapoan. Ants chew through their tents at night.

At Tapirapoan, Roosevelt readies for the unexplored country with Kermit, Colonel Rondon, Cherrie, Miller, Fiala, two Brazilians and the paddlers. He writes Quentin about the trip and Kermit, and reports early results to Frank Chapman.
At Tapirapoan, Roosevelt studies vampire bats.
Seventy pack oxen leave Tapirapoan ahead of the party. In the United States, Bamie turns 59.
At Tapirapoan, Kermit goes out hunting.
The expedition is at Tapirapoan; nothing else is recorded.
Mule train to the Sepotuba falls
The party sets out on riding mules and covers 15 miles to the Sepotuba waterfall.
Turning west away from the river, the riders cut their way through dense forest with machetes and make camp in rain.
A steep climb brings the party to the rim of the Parecis Plateau, where the day is cool and free of mosquitoes.
Riding across the high plateau, the party passes the watershed that separates the Amazon basin from the Paraguay's, with rain in the afternoon.
Heading north, Kermit shoots two pampas deer bucks. That night stories go around the campfire while Roosevelt writes; it rains.
The expedition is traveling; nothing else is recorded.
The expedition is traveling; nothing else is recorded.
The expedition travels on through heavy rain.
After a late start the party strikes a telegraph line, crosses the Sacre, and sees the falls at Salto Bello, where the motor road ends. The men go swimming.
Two miles from Utiarity Falls, Roosevelt watches Indians play an unusual form of ball. It rains.
The expedition is at Utiarity Falls in the rain.
Roosevelt's expedition is at Utiarity Falls, where a native village sits beside a station on Brazil's telegraph line.
A live armadillo for the collection

The rain stops though clouds hang on. Roosevelt heads out alone with his rifle and comes back carrying a living armadillo for naturalist Leo Miller, then sits by the falls watching the village men dance.
The expedition splits and heads north

Father Zahm turns back for Tapirapoan with specimens, while Fiala and Lauriado break off to descend the Juruena. Under clearing skies, Roosevelt, Kermit, Rondon, Lyra, Olivera, Cherrie and Miller push on with mules and two ox carts, covering about 15 miles of wilderness.
Biting insects at the Burity River
Fair skies, fierce insects. The party camps on the western bank of the Burity, where the men wash in the river before rain moves in.
Through a downpour the party fords the Burity and camps where the Huatsui River begins, an automobile still traveling with them. Roosevelt studies the Nhambiquara people he meets along the way.
The expedition trims its baggage to travel lighter.
A brief day's march ends at a stream that feeds the Tapajós. George Cherrie returns to camp with bird specimens.
Under clear skies the party covers 20 miles and pulls into Juruena by mid-afternoon, an outpost with a garrison and a telegraph office.
A working rest day at Juruena
The expedition stays put. Specimens are added to the collection, film is developed and journals caught up. Roosevelt watches native dancing as heavy rain falls.
Gibbon and Arsène Lupin by the campfire

Back on the trail in the rain, the soaked party covers 15 miles and crosses the river by ferry. Evenings bring more campfire stories, and Roosevelt reads Gibbon alongside an Arsène Lupin detective tale.
The expedition continues its overland march; no details are recorded.
Roosevelt's party is still marching through the interior. In the United States, his daughter Alice celebrates her 30th birthday.
The party keeps traveling; nothing more is recorded.
The expedition continues north with no further details noted.
Last of the carts at Campos Novos
The party reaches Campos Novos and links up with Amilcar and Mello and the pack train. From here on, everything moves without carts.
The expedition keeps moving and pitches camp in the afternoon.
The party arrives at the telegraph station of Vilhena. Back in the United States, Alice and Nick Longworth mark eight years of marriage.
Another day of northward travel, with nothing else recorded.
First sight of the River of Doubt

After woods give way to open country, the party spots a small brook and recognizes it as the source of the Rio da Dúvida, the River of Doubt. Roosevelt jots notes on local people and their dances; rain falls.
Local people try to make off with things from the expedition's camp.
Through hill pastures to Tres Burity
The march crosses rolling grassland and reaches a ranch at Tres Burity.
At Bonifacio, local Indians show off their skill with bows and arrows for the visitors.

After seven miles the travelers meet Amilcar again and divide. Amilcar, Miller and Mello will follow the Gy-Paraná; Roosevelt, Kermit, Rondon, Lyra, Cherrie and the doctor take the River of Doubt with 16 paddlers, seven canoes and food for 50 days.
The party's camp is plotted at about 12° south latitude, 60° west longitude. Roosevelt writes Robert Bridges about a chapter of his expedition book.
In camp, the expedition's seven canoes are all heavy dugouts hollowed from logs.
Into the unknown on the River of Doubt
Roosevelt's party pushes off down the River of Doubt, a waterway no mapmaker has charted. They survey and measure the river as they paddle.

The survey canoes lead off while Cherrie gathers specimens near camp. Roosevelt and Cherrie follow around midday. Where the Bandeira joins, the river broadens; the team maps 16.5 kilometers. Film footage shows Roosevelt and the party in their canoes.
Ants, bees and monkey for supper

The men wash in the river before dawn, then paddle through heavy rain to map 20.5 kilometers. Stingless bees pester them, ants chew through even their clothing, and a monkey becomes dinner. In New York, Edith takes a hotel room to be near Ethel as her baby's birth approaches.
After 20 kilometers under light rain, the party camps and scouts the rapids ahead, which they name Navaite. Here the river squeezes to under 24 feet across.
The whole day goes into dragging the heavy canoes and supplies overland past the rapids.
The portage continues through pouring rain. The insects are so savage the men smear on 'fly dope,' and termites are devouring clothes and equipment.

The portage wraps up by morning. One dugout goes under and must be hauled back up before the party heads downriver again, faces and hands puffy from bites. They make 12 kilometers and camp among giant ants.

The twisting river yields 19 kilometers. The men gather wild honey and sample the sap of the 'milk-tree.' Rapids ahead mean another portage. After 100 river kilometers, they sit just 55 kilometers, as the crow flies, from the starting point.
A grandson born in New York

On the river, the party moves camp around the rapids while Kermit finds yet another rapid downstream. In New York City, Ethel delivers an eight-pound boy after a 48-hour labor: Richard Derby Jr., Roosevelt's grandson.
While the portage goes on, Roosevelt hunts in the forest without luck. Kermit loans him a volume of French poems.
Another day spent carrying canoes and gear around the rapids.
The canoes travel just 1.5 kilometers but shoot two rapids rather than carrying around them. The pests never let up: ants, termites and biting flies.
Two dugouts tear loose in the night and are wrecked in the current. The party will have to carve replacements.
The men set to hollowing out a huge tree trunk for a canoe. Roosevelt hunts in the forest, while Kermit has better luck finding food elsewhere.
Canoe building goes on from morning until ten at night, the last hours lit by candles.
Racing the rapids to save food

In drenching rain the new canoe is launched near noon and the party moves again. Short on time and food, they run the rapids, bailing after each one, until past 5 p.m., making 16 km and camping in darkness. The Outlook prints his 'South America and the Monroe Doctrine.'

After 6 easy kilometers the party hears rapids. Scouting them, Kermit's canoe is caught by a whirlpool and swept over. Paddler Simplicio is killed; Kermit, pulled under, fights his way out, and his dog reaches shore too. Simplicio is buried before camp.

Under black skies and blinding rain, loads go overland and empty canoes run the rapids. One lost canoe carried the ropes and pulleys, ending heavy portages. Indians kill Kermit's dog. With four canoes and two-thirds of the food left, men will walk the banks, spare clothes are dropped, and quinine is given daily.
Rondon, Lyra, Kermit, Cherrie and nine others hike the bank, while Roosevelt, the doctor and six men, three of them lamed by swollen feet, ride the canoes. They cover 7 kilometers and run two rapids.
The Rio Roosevelt gets its name

A tributary is found joining the river and named Rio Kermit, while the main stream itself gets a new name: Rio Roosevelt. The canoes shoot another set of rapids and slip past an Indian village, covering 8 km.
The men build more canoes. Some go swimming despite piranha in the water, and ants overrun the camp.
As canoe building continues, Roosevelt explores the surrounding forest.
The crew keeps working on canoes. In The Outlook, Roosevelt's 'Chile and the Monroe Doctrine' is published.
With two fresh dugouts, the fleet stands at six. The party gets underway and covers 10 km, though easing the canoes down the newest rapids eats up six hours.
The party makes 13 km, seven hours of it working through a 4-km stretch of rapids. Cherrie talks about his home in Vermont.
With rations shrinking, the men cut palm tops to eat. Big rapids hold progress to 1.5 km.

After bringing the canoes through the rapids, the party names a tributary the Taunay. Half the provisions are eaten, two men have fever, and more rapids rumble ahead. At home, Edith returns from New York and opens Sagamore Hill.
The three most skilled boatmen take the canoes through the rapids. The party discovers carved symbols on rocks.
Three kilometers bring more rapids, which take the whole day. After a ten-minute paddle, still more rapids appear. In heavy rain, the men camp soaked and exhausted.
The canoes shoot rapids and pass a stream the party names the Cherrie River. Kermit finds a perilous three-kilometer cataract downstream, so the loads must be cut further.
The men ease the canoes down rapids inside a steep-sided gorge.
Canoe lowering continues while the cargo is carried up and over the mountain.
One monkey for the whole party

A single monkey is shot, giving each man a few good bites. In heavy rain five canoes come down safely and a sixth breaks. Insects eat Roosevelt's last clothes. At home, Scribners publishes his two-volume natural history of African big game, written with Edmund Heller.
The canoes are finally all lowered, but some of the men are losing heart.
Underway again, the party manages only 3 km, most of the men on foot. Ahead lie more rapids in a deep canyon.

Starting down the rapids, the party loses a canoe; the boots and clothing of Kermit and Lyra are falling apart. Then Julio, one of the paddlers, shoots and kills fellow camarada Paishon. Edith writes Bamie with news.
While working a canoe through the rapids, Roosevelt slams his leg against a rock and comes down with fever. Kermit has dysentery. At home, Ethel marks her first wedding anniversary.
Julio is spotted in the jungle but left alone and never seen again. Roosevelt's fever climbs to 39°C; out of his head, he recites poetry as the party keeps working down the rapids.
Roosevelt asks to be left behind

As the party portages more rapids, Roosevelt urges his companions to go on without him so they can survive. Far away in Bogota, American and Colombian envoys sign a treaty, negotiated under Secretary of State Bryan, that voices regret over the 1903 loss of Panama and promises Colombia $25 million.
The land flattens and the party makes 36 km, passing a large unmapped river that joins the Rio Roosevelt.
Only 5 km today through a chain of rapids; cargo goes around two of them before the canoes are run. Three monkeys and two piranha go into the pot.
The expedition is in camp. At Harvard, Archie celebrates his 20th birthday.
Run, portage, run, more rapids: under 5 km in all. Roosevelt wishes for a light birch-bark canoe instead of the cumbersome dugouts. A toucan, piranha and a turtle feed the party.

Loads are carried down to the base of the rapids, followed by a 30- to 40-minute run before more rapids appear. Roosevelt remains feverish. At Sagamore Hill, Clifford and Teresa Richardson are guests.
On Easter Sunday the party paddles ten minutes and portages for eight hours, but 28 big fish mean everyone eats well for once.
After a day of portaging, a late 15-km run brings the party to a camp where, the roar of rapids is gone for the first time in more than a month.
A 32-km run takes the canoes through a few minor rapids and one portage. The men fall ill after eating nuts and meat.

Still queasy, the men cover 25 km and spot 'J.A.' carved on a post, a rubber tapper's mark. Houses follow, then talk with settlers: they have made it out. Roosevelt's fever lingers; abscesses on his leg need a drain, and Rondon notes erysipelas in the left leg hurt in 1902.
The party makes long runs downstream each day, spending nights at riverside homes.
Roosevelt purchases provisions for the men, ending their need to live off the land.
The trip downstream goes on with Roosevelt still ill.
A guide and a gift from Senhor Barboso
The party engages a rubber worker as guide. Senhor Barboso supplies a canoe and food and will not take payment. Past the mouth of the Rio Branco, they portage rapids; the cook buys a trumpeter bird.

A sun shelter is rigged over the ailing Roosevelt in the lighter canoe they acquired. A stop at a store yields sugar and tobacco, and the party covers 52 km. In Colorado, National Guard troops massacre striking miners at Ludlow.
A good day's run brings the party to the Inferno rapids. At a house they pick up a large boat and a light one, leaving two dugouts behind.
Canoes, boats and gear are worked down the Inferno rapids, a brief run, in the rain.
The canoes cover close to 50 km and shoot the Infernino rapids fully loaded. Night is spent in a grimy house.
Fifty kilometers bring the party to the Carupanan rapids. At a store run by Senhor Caripe, they receive a boat to replace their final dugout.

Guided by Caripe, the party spends a day and a half on the fairly easy Carupanan rapids. Kermit kills a caiman. On the broader river, harsh sun beating down through the trees is hard on the sick Roosevelt.

Past the last dangerous rapids, at 1 p.m. the party reaches the Castanho, where Lieutenant Pyrineus has waited a month, Brazilian and American flags flying. Where the two rivers meet, they form the Aripuanã.

In a small ceremony Rondon lays out the expedition's findings and formally names the river Rio Roosevelt: 750 km in two months by canoe. Leaving Lyra and Pyrineus, the boats reach São João at 1 p.m. in heavy rain, and Roosevelt lodges with Senhor Caripe.
At São João the party abandons boat and canoe and boards Pyrineus's river steamer for a 36-hour trip to Manaus.
The steamer works down the lower Madeira and enters the Amazon in the afternoon. Back home, Corinne marks her 32nd wedding anniversary.

At 1 a.m. the party arrives at Manaus on the Rio Negro and finds Miller. Mr. Robiliard of the Booth Line books passage for Roosevelt and Kermit and pays the camaradas in gold sovereigns. Dr. Cajazeira drains Roosevelt's leg abscess. Roosevelt wires Lauro Müller with results; the naturalists count 2,500+ birds and 500 mammals.

The party sails from Manaus for Belém aboard the Dunstan. Rondon writes that their findings disprove claims made by the explorer Landor, and Roosevelt sends Lauro Müller a complete account of the expedition.
Roosevelt's steamer continues down the Amazon.
Another day steaming toward the sea on the Amazon.
Aboard ship on the Amazon, Roosevelt tells his English friend Arthur Lee about his fever and abscesses and looks ahead to a visit to England.
The party is in Pará, Brazil.

At Belém Roosevelt meets ethnologist William Farabee of the University of Pennsylvania, then boards the Aidan. Fifty-five pounds lighter and leaning on a cane, he bids goodbye to Rondon, Dr. Cajazeira, Lyra and Kermit.
The Aidan leaves Belém bound for Barbados and New York.
Roosevelt is at sea, steaming north toward New York.
Roosevelt is at sea, steaming north toward New York.
Roosevelt is at sea, steaming north toward New York.
When the ship calls at Bridgetown, Barbados, Roosevelt buys 50 books, and he will finish every one before reaching New York.
At sea, Roosevelt works through the stack of books from Barbados.
At sea, bound for New York
Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.
At sea, bound for New York
Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.
At sea, bound for New York
Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.
At sea, bound for New York
Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.
At sea, bound for New York
Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.
At sea, bound for New York
Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.

Roosevelt lands in New York 35 pounds lighter, on a cane, helped by two men, and jokes about his 'big stick.' His wife Edith and sons Ted and Archie are waiting; there are no crowds or parades. Edith and Dr. Lambert have the yacht Joyance carry him to Oyster Bay.
Home one day, Roosevelt meets with Perkins and Pinchot; Frances Kellor, Lillian Wald and Dr. Lambert call. He writes Ruth and Arthur Lee about his exploring, the skeptics, and his new grandson.
Roosevelt sees Robert Bacon at The Outlook, and Oyster Bay holds an official homecoming. He writes General Francis V. Greene that he would raise a cavalry regiment if war with Mexico came.

Roosevelt meets with William Flinn, Pinchot, Wilkinson, Perkins, Oscar King Davis, Robert Bass and Knox. Stoddard, Mark Sullivan and Edmund Heller call. He writes Dan Hanna about the elections and Progressivism and thanks Charles Fairbanks.
Roosevelt talks politics with his nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson, Garfield and Arthur Garford; Regis Post visits. He writes Ambassador Walter Hines Page about his coming British visit.
Roosevelt meets with V. K. Kellogg, Victor Murdock, Perkins, Bourke Cockran and William Loeb. Edith writes Kermit that her husband looks a year younger for each pound lost.
Visitors include John Callan O'Laughlin, Albert Beveridge, Alsop, Schaffer, and Judge Ben Lindsey with Mrs. Lindsey.

In Washington Roosevelt tours the National Museum, attends a Lodge reception, and calls on President Wilson. He meets Progressive members of Congress including Garfield, Murdock, Clapp, Butler, Falconer and Pettigrew, then speaks about Brazil before the National Geographic Society.
At The Outlook Roosevelt sees Felix Frankfurter and Walter Lippmann, then gives testimony to a special commission in a coal miners' lawsuit. Edith writes Ruth Lee.
Roosevelt meets at home with Theodore Douglas Robinson, Perkins, Frank Munsey, Frederick Davenport, Hamlin, Bird and Ransom.
Robinson, Perkins, Davenport, Hamlin and Bird return for discussions, and Alexander P. Moore, Medill McCormick and Albert Shaw call.

After meeting Perkins, Moore and McCormick at Progressive headquarters, Roosevelt boards the Olympic with his daughter Alice and Philip Roosevelt, bound for Spain and Kermit's marriage to Belle Willard, daughter of the American minister there. Edith stays behind.
Roosevelt is at sea on the Olympic, heading for Europe.
Roosevelt is at sea aboard the Olympic on his way to Kermit's wedding.
From shipboard Roosevelt writes George Perkins about demands that he leave the Progressive Party, saying that if Perkins is pushed out, he will go too.
Roosevelt remains at sea on the Olympic.
Roosevelt remains at sea on the Olympic.
Roosevelt comes ashore in France at Cherbourg.
Roosevelt sees the sights of Paris, lunches with Gabriel Hanotaux and calls on President Poincaré. Philippe Bunau-Varilla and T. P. O'Connor visit, and Ambassador Myron Herrick hosts him for dinner.
Roosevelt breakfasts with novelist Edith Wharton and receives Mrs. Cornelius Vanderbilt before he and Alice leave Paris for Madrid.
In Madrid the Roosevelts dine at the American embassy and lodge with the Willards, the family of Kermit's bride.
Lunch with the King of Spain

A couple of hours by motorcar take the Roosevelts to the country palace of Spain's King Alfonso XIII and his queen, Victoria Eugenie, for lunch; Alice recalls the royal pair as very cold. Roosevelt also talks with Spanish journalists.
Roosevelt tours the Prado and travels out to Toledo for its El Greco paintings, then dines at the American embassy.

Roosevelt and Alice witness Kermit's civil wedding to Belle Willard in Madrid, with Philip Roosevelt as best man. Roosevelt writes Edith hopefully about the couple and tells Wolfgang Joerg about the Brazil expedition, then goes back to the Prado.
Roosevelt sets out for London while Alice remains in Europe.
In London, Roosevelt is greeted by Ambassador Walter Hines Page, the Archbishop of Canterbury and his old friend Arthur Lee. He lunches with Page, and geographer J. Scott Keltie calls.
Roosevelt is Arthur Lee's guest at Chequers Court in Buckinghamshire. In America, Ted and Eleanor welcome a son, Theodore Roosevelt III.
Roosevelt lunches with Sir Edward Grey and watches motion pictures of Scott's Antarctic expedition. James Bryce calls, and he dines with Lee and Lord Northcliffe.
Brazil talk to the Royal Geographical Society

After seeing Westminster Abbey and London's natural history museum, and lunching with Lee, Selous, Harry Johnston and Francis Younghusband, Roosevelt addresses the Royal Geographical Society on his Brazilian exploration and dines with the Geographical Club.
The National Gallery and old friends
Roosevelt breakfasts with the Bishop of London, sees the National Gallery, visits Dr. St. Clair Thomson, and lunches with Arthur Balfour, Gilbert Murray and J. B. Bury.
Roosevelt leaves for America aboard the Imperator.
Roosevelt is crossing the Atlantic on the Imperator.
Roosevelt remains at sea while Ted and Eleanor mark four years of marriage.
Roosevelt is at sea on the Imperator.
Roosevelt is at sea on the Imperator.
Roosevelt is at sea on the Imperator.
The Imperator reaches New York, and Roosevelt heads home to Oyster Bay.

A large group of Progressives, including Perkins, Robinson, Hotchkiss, Hamlin, Childs, Davenport, John M. Parker and William Draper Lewis, gather at Sagamore Hill and press Roosevelt to seek the governorship of New York.
Roosevelt meets with Perkins, Medill McCormick, Albert Beveridge, John M. Parker and Holland Duell, and writes Dwight Heard about the Progressive Party.
After talks with Senator Moses Clapp, Wanamaker and Frank Munsey, Roosevelt hears from Dr. Lambert that his larynx cannot stand a speaking tour. He is told to rest for four months.
At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt is at home as news breaks of Archduke Franz Ferdinand's assassination in Sarajevo. Alice, still in Europe, attends the Grand Prix race in France.
Roosevelt rows on the Sound, gives up his editorial post at The Outlook in a letter to Lyman Abbott, and tells Arthur Lee that politics swallowed him the moment he got home.
Back on the stump in Pittsburgh

After a Progressive League banquet, Roosevelt gives his first big speech since 1912 at Exposition Hall, blasting the Republican Old Guard and Wilson's economics. He returns home groggy with jungle fever; Edith and Lambert order months of rest. The family gathers, and Ted joins a Philadelphia investment firm.

Roosevelt lunches at the natural history museum with its president, Henry Fairfield Osborn and has his throat examined by a Manhattan specialist, Dr. H. Holbrook Curtis, who links his slack vocal cords to malaria. Perkins and Governor Hadley call at headquarters. He writes Samuel McCall and Hiram Johnson.
The Mitchels and Judge and Mrs. Ransom are guests at the house.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
For a Fourth of July picnic at Lloyd Neck, Roosevelt rows Edith eight miles out and eight back, while the younger family members drive over.
Roosevelt is at home; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt tells William Allen White he opposes government ownership of the railroads and a ban on liquor.
Letters on Colombia, labor and Barnes
Roosevelt writes Senator Moses Clapp of his anger over Bryan's Colombia treaty, Frank Gilbreth on labor, and Richard Harding Davis about naval promotions and boss William Barnes.
At Progressive headquarters Roosevelt sees Dwight Heard, Cleveland Dodge, I. E. Vernon, Augustus Gardner, Wilkinson and Nettleton. Film shows him rowing at Oyster Bay and at his Outlook desk.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt meets with Joseph Bucklin Bishop and writes William Draper Lewis about the party and his June 30 speech.

Roosevelt writes Senator William Joel Stone that the treaty with Colombia insults the nation, opposes paying $25 million, and asks to testify before Congress. No hearing comes, but the Senate later rejects the treaty.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay with nothing further recorded.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay with nothing further recorded.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay with nothing further recorded.

At Progressive headquarters Roosevelt meets Duell, Robinson, Perkins and other state leaders, and has lunch with representatives of the state's Progressive Service. His physician, Dr. Lambert, stays at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.
Roosevelt holds a reception so Oyster Bay can meet Kermit's new wife, Belle. He writes Ernest Harvier that Chautauqua opinion is running hard against him in the governor's race.
Harvey Hinman and Theodore Douglas Robinson visit.
Roosevelt confers with Robinson, Perkins and Frederick Davenport.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.

After meeting Perkins and Robinson, Roosevelt backs Harvey Hinman as a Progressive-Republican fusion candidate for governor and lashes out at Republican boss William Barnes Jr., calling him as crooked as Tammany's Murphy. Barnes will sue for libel.
Boss William Barnes takes Roosevelt to court for libel, and Austria-Hungary issues its ultimatum to Serbia. Roosevelt promises Franklin D. Roosevelt an article opposing splitting the fleet.
Roosevelt tells Chauncey Hamlin he will not seek the governorship of New York.
Roosevelt writes Royal W. France about possible candidates for governor.
Roosevelt writes California's Governor Hiram Johnson that he would make a good President, and covers New York politics and the Barnes suit.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
While Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill, the Austro-Hungarian empire goes to war against Serbia.
At Progressive headquarters, McHarg and Everett Colby call on Roosevelt.
The Progressive future, in a long letter
Roosevelt sends Hiram Johnson a lengthy letter on California and New York politics, fusion, the party's future and the Barnes suit.
Europe at war, Panama Canal open

Roosevelt receives a Maine Progressive delegation as war spreads across Europe and Alice comes home. The source also records the Panama Canal opening at a cost of $223 million, apart from $40 million to the French company and $10 million to Panama.

As Germany declares war on Russia, The Outlook prints Roosevelt's piece on women and the state constitutional convention. To Arthur Lee he mocks Bryan and Wilson, reports Belle down with typhoid, and touches on Irish home rule and the spreading war.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Germany goes to war with France, and the first vessel moves through the Panama Canal. Roosevelt writes Winfred Denison about the Philippines.
Herbert Croly and Felix Frankfurter lunch at Sagamore Hill on the day Germany invades neutral Belgium and Britain declares war on Germany.
Russian troops cross into Germany and President Wilson proclaims American neutrality. Roosevelt tells Governor Martin Glynn he stands by his corruption charges against the state highway department.
On Edith's 53rd birthday, Roosevelt writes Walter Weyl about labor, civil disorder and the push for a minimum wage for women in New York.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
The Outlook carries Roosevelt's article on the people's right to review judge-made law. He writes Hugo Münsterberg that he won't rush to condemn Germany.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

George Record laments Roosevelt's refusal to lead the Progressives. Roosevelt writes Raymond Robins about Perkins, radicalism, Barnes and fusion, and Frederick Davenport about Barnes, bossism and Hinman.
On Ethel's birthday, Roosevelt explains his own stance and the Progressive Party's in a letter to Henry Wallace.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

Roosevelt attends Gifford Pinchot's marriage to Cornelia Bryce in Roslyn, then leaves for New England and speaks in Hartford. He congratulates Edward Costigan on his Progressive nomination for Colorado governor.
Roosevelt stays in Newfane, Vermont, as the guest of his Brazil expedition companion George Cherrie.
In Boston Roosevelt meets Massachusetts Progressive leaders and speaks for Joseph Walker. Granddaughter Grace turns three, and Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt have a son, Franklin Jr.
Roosevelt gives speeches across Maine, including Lewiston and Portland, and spends the night in Massachusetts.
Roosevelt leaves Massachusetts for Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt meets New York Progressive leaders and withdraws his backing of Harvey Hinman, because Hinman will not commit to a Progressive candidacy should Republicans reject him in the primary.

The Outlook runs Roosevelt's war article about the great powers locked in combat. He writes Arthur Lee that he would protest Germany's handling of Belgium, that Belle is well, and on Wilson, Bryan, Churchill, the fleet and the empires.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt confers with former New York governor William Sulzer.
At Progressive headquarters, William H. Childs calls on Roosevelt.

Writing John Callan O'Laughlin, Roosevelt shifts his support for governor from Hinman to Frederick Davenport and rules out running for President in 1916. He also covers Wilson, Bryan and the Colorado strikes.
Leonard Wood is a guest at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Ethel's husband, Dr. Richard Derby, joins six fellow American surgeons in volunteering at the American Ambulance Hospital in France; Ethel goes with him.
Roosevelt writes the preface for Through the Brazilian Wilderness and sends Emily Carow family news about the war and each of his children.
Roosevelt sees William Sulzer, Theodore Douglas Robinson and Frederick Davenport at Progressive headquarters.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about the war, Lord Kitchener, and the errors of Wilson and Bryan.
Roosevelt sets out for Louisiana, with William Draper Lewis and editor E. A. Van Valkenburg of the Philadelphia North American riding with him to Philadelphia.
Roosevelt is on the way to Louisiana.
Roosevelt campaigns in Louisiana, with speeches including one in New Orleans.
Roosevelt speaks in Franklin, Jeanerette and New Iberia, Louisiana.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.
Roosevelt is at home on Ted's 27th birthday.
Roosevelt visits the Cove School and tells William Allen White he can't speak everywhere he's wanted in the campaign.
Oscar King Davis calls, and Roosevelt attends the christening of Theodore Roosevelt III.
Roosevelt confers with Perkins, Robinson, Bird, Davenport, Hamlin and a Dr. Katherine whose surname is lost.
After a meeting with Charles J. Bonaparte and fellow party leaders, Roosevelt leaves on a western speaking trip. He writes Hungary's Count Albert Apponyi about the war.
Roosevelt travels west on his speaking tour.
A close call with a train in Kansas
Roosevelt speaks in Wichita, to some 6,000 people, and in Hutchinson. His car is nearly struck by a train.
In the Kansas Citys of Kansas and Missouri, Roosevelt stays with editor W. R. Nelson.
In Lincoln, Nebraska, Roosevelt speaks up for woman suffrage. He writes Henry Coonley about his policies and the war.
Iowa stops and a war essay
Roosevelt takes the stump in Iowa at Des Moines and Boone as The Outlook publishes his essay on the tragedies and lessons of the World War.
Roosevelt addresses crowds at Peoria, Galesburg and Rock Island and is the guest of Illinois Governor Edward Dunne.
Roosevelt takes the stump for Raymond Robins in two southern Illinois cities, Marion and East St. Louis.
Roosevelt speaks in Indianapolis and Terre Haute on behalf of Albert Beveridge.
In Ohio Roosevelt stays with James Garfield and receives members of the Belgian commission on atrocities. A war piece by him appears in a New York paper.
Roosevelt campaigns in Cleveland and Columbus for Garfield.
Michigan, and the Brazil book is out
Roosevelt speaks in Bay City, Michigan, staying with Roy Woodruff. The Outlook runs his article on the causes of the war, and Scribners publishes Through the Brazilian Wilderness.
Roosevelt campaigns in Philadelphia for Gifford Pinchot's Senate bid, addressing some 12,000 people packed into the First Regiment Armory, then heads back toward New York City.
Declining a bed at Franklin's house
Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Sara Delano Roosevelt that he had better not stay with her son Franklin, since his upcoming speeches will take aim at the Wilson administration.

Roosevelt writes three letters about the European war: to Cecil Spring-Rice on German anger at his war article and the ultimatum he would have sent Berlin, to Hugo Münsterberg on Belgium, and to Rudyard Kipling on German atrocities.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

Roosevelt opens a campaign swing up the Hudson, speaking in Yonkers, Beacon, Cold Spring, Poughkeepsie and Wappingers Falls before spending the night at Hyde Park. He tells Elbert Baldwin the war leaves him deeply saddened.
Six more stops up the river
The campaign tour rolls on through Kingston, Saugerties, Catskill, Athens and Hudson, ending with a speech at the Music Hall in Troy.
Speaking from Schenectady to Glens Falls
Roosevelt carries the Progressive message north, with speeches at Schenectady, Saratoga, Ballston Spa, Glens Falls and Hudson Falls.
The tour reaches the Champlain country, where Roosevelt speaks at Ticonderoga, Fort Henry, Keeseville and Plattsburgh.
North Country stops near the St. Lawrence
Roosevelt works the far north of the state, speaking at Malone, Potsdam, Canton and Ogdensburg.
Watertown and Utica on Kermit's birthday
Roosevelt speaks at Gouverneur, Watertown and Utica. Back home it is his son Kermit's 25th birthday.
Sunday with his nephew at Jordanville
Roosevelt takes a break from the stump as the guest of his nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson in Jordanville. It is also his niece Eleanor Roosevelt's 30th birthday.
Back on the campaign trail, Roosevelt gives speeches in Herkimer and Gloversville.
Roosevelt's tour passes through Cobleskill, Cooperstown and Oneonta, with a speech at each.
Roosevelt speaks in Syracuse, among other stops on his New York tour.
The campaign brings Roosevelt to Auburn, where he speaks for the Progressive ticket.
Roosevelt addresses audiences in Rochester as the upstate tour continues.
Roosevelt leaves New York for a campaign side trip to Illinois.

In Chicago, Roosevelt dines with physicians from Mercy Hospital. He wires Gifford Pinchot, troubled by Pinchot's plan for a breakneck speaking tour of Pennsylvania. His nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 16.
Roosevelt speaks in Chicago and then crosses into Indiana for a speech in Gary.
Back in New York at Chautauqua
Returning to western New York, Roosevelt speaks at Westfield and Chautauqua.
Another day of New York speeches
Roosevelt keeps up his speaking schedule in New York State; the stops are not recorded.
The tour reaches the Southern Tier, with speeches in Ithaca and Binghamton.
Roosevelt speaks at Liberty, Monticello and Middletown.
The New York swing winds down with speeches at Goshen and Newburgh.
Libel trial moved out of Albany
Roosevelt leaves for Pennsylvania. His lawyers win a change of venue in William Barnes Jr.'s libel suit, moving the trial to Syracuse and away from Albany, the heart of Barnes's political machine.
A windswept day on the stump with Pinchot

Roosevelt and Gifford Pinchot share the platform on a gusty October day across Pennsylvania, from Williamsport and Pottsville through Johnstown, Altoona and Uniontown, with a hop into Morgantown, West Virginia.
Roosevelt spends his 56th birthday making speeches in Pennsylvania.
Roosevelt speaks at Reading, Wilkes-Barre, Hazleton and Lancaster.
Roosevelt gives speeches in Pennsylvania and in New York City.
New Jersey stops and city rallies
Roosevelt crosses into New Jersey to speak at Elizabeth, Princeton and Trenton, then returns for more speeches in New York City.
Roosevelt speaks in New York City as the campaign nears its end, and his account of the South American expedition is published.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Arguing over Belgium on election eve

Roosevelt gives a speech at Oyster Bay. In a letter to Hugo Münsterberg he insists America should have objected when Germany overran Belgium, and he answers Andrew D. White's complaints about his preparedness articles.

Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay on a bad night for his party: Progressives lose across the country. Two bright spots: Hiram Johnson keeps the California governorship, and son-in-law Nick Longworth wins back his House seat.
Praising Quentin's story in The Grot

Roosevelt writes his son Quentin that he enjoyed his story in the school paper, and writes Ethel about her war work in France and her baby, who is staying at Sagamore Hill. To Rudyard Kipling he explains his stand on Belgium.
Roosevelt goes into New York City, where George W. Perkins is among the callers at Progressive Party headquarters.
Tired of reformers, and of him
Roosevelt writes Governor Hiram Johnson about the Progressive drubbing, concluding that voters had simply wearied of reform and of Roosevelt himself.
Sorting out the party's next move

Roosevelt writes to Edmund von Mach, praising the German people while condemning the war on Belgium, and to William Allen White and Charles J. Bonaparte about the Progressive defeat, the Barnes libel suit and where the party goes now.
Roosevelt's essay "The International Posse Comitatus" runs in The New York Times. He also writes Charles McCarthy about Germany.
Roosevelt sends Ernest Harvier a note saying he liked the skit in Harper's.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

Roosevelt writes Kermit that he is happy at home, rowing often and loving his evenings by the fire with Edith. To Cecil Spring-Rice he writes of the war, Wilson, and British searches of American ships.
In a letter to his sister Corinne, Roosevelt cites 2 Timothy 4:3-4, the passage warning of people who turn from sound doctrine to fables.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Roosevelt tells Frederick Selous he is sorry Selous's frontiersmen were not given horses and sent to the front, and assures Morris Jastrow that he has called for preparedness, not war.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
