Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

Roosevelt meets with Herbert Croly and Walter Lippmann. He writes Meyer Lissner about the election's toll on Progressives and urges Hiram Johnson to attend the party's executive committee in Chicago on December 2.

Roosevelt's review of two new books on democracy, Herbert Croly's Progressive Democracy and Walter Lippmann's Drift and Mastery, appears in The Outlook.

Roosevelt tells George W. Perkins he will stay off domestic subjects in print, asks William Sanger about the Swiss army system, and advises Edward Van Valkenburg against Pinchot's proposed Progressive convocation and against further ties with Amos Pinchot and George L. Record.

Roosevelt writes Ethel that she and Dick will sail home in December, and admits he will miss her baby, who has been staying at Sagamore Hill. He also passes on news of Archie.

Roosevelt and Edith hack a path through Smith's field. He writes Henry Ford admiring his labor practices and signs a three-year, $25,000-a-year contract with Metropolitan Magazine. Archie is back from a New Brunswick hunt, bringing a moose and a few deer.
Roosevelt is based at Sagamore Hill this month, making many trips into Manhattan. Naval historian Alfred Thayer Mahan, whose ideas shaped his thinking on sea power, dies.

Roosevelt and Edith mark their 28th anniversary as the Progressive executive committee gathers in Chicago. He writes Archie about military service, the new path in Smith's field and taking better care of his clothes.

Roosevelt confesses to Frederick Selous that he longs to be in the war himself, and writes Bernhard Dernburg about German designs on New York City, America and the Canal Zone.
Roosevelt writes a condolence letter to Ellen Mahan, calling her late husband one of the rare men who leave a lasting mark on history and letters.
Kuno Meyer, a German expert on Celtic history, lunches at Sagamore Hill. A Roosevelt article on Mexico runs in The New York Times.

Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge about violence in Mexico, Wilson and Bryan, and the country's lack of preparedness.

Roosevelt travels into the city to give a Brazil lecture at New York's American Museum of Natural History.
Roosevelt writes Meyer Lissner about Victor Murdock's nomination to chair the Progressive National Committee, about the party's radicals, and about complaints over George W. Perkins.
Roosevelt writes William Dudley Foulke about possible 1916 candidates, Hiram Johnson for President among them, and writes Seth Low about how to give away his Nobel Peace Prize money.

Roosevelt argues in the Times that the Philippines should be independent. He also refuses to sign Mrs. Ralph Sanger's "Hands Across the Sea" appeal for an alliance with Britain, since he rejects divided, hyphenated loyalties.
Roosevelt points Hugo Münsterberg to his refusal of the pro-British appeal the day before, as proof that he treats all sides fairly.
Christmas Eve talk at Christ Church
Roosevelt joins the Christmas celebration at Oyster Bay's Christ Episcopal Church and talks to the gathering about Brazil.
Roosevelt spends Christmas Day at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt goes into Manhattan and shares a meal with Frances Kellor at the city's Municipal Lodging House.

Roosevelt rules in favor of young Harriet Ford, against her father, in a family bet: a teddy bear, he decides, counts as a doll. Around this time Scribner's publishes his America and the World War.
New Year's views on foreign policy
Roosevelt opens 1915 at Sagamore Hill, with regular trips to the city ahead. The New York Times carries his remarks on American foreign policy.

Roosevelt spends the day cutting wood on the Sagamore Hill grounds, wearing a wool army shirt and knickerbockers.
Speaking out on police and Philippines

The Times quotes Roosevelt on Police Commissioner Arthur Woods and on an Independent article titled "Utopia or Hell." He writes W. Cameron Forbes on the Philippines, Winthrop Chanler on a plan for him to lead volunteers against Germany, and William Allen White, promising to ease up on Wilson and Bryan.
Roosevelt writes the British ambassador, Cecil Spring-Rice, about the contraband question.

Roosevelt walks the East Side tenements alongside Miss Pohlman, who investigates cases for the Evening Mail's Save a Home Fund, looking into evictions on East 62nd, 67th, 70th and 81st Streets. He also writes Rómulo Naón to introduce Walter Lippmann, whom he is urging to write about South America.
Roosevelt writes a testimonial for Admiral Charles O'Neil and comments on the Gathmann gun.

Roosevelt writes Charles Washburn that in 1908 Taft promised to keep his cabinet in place, Cortelyou excepted, then reversed himself in 1909, along with a pledge to retain Henry White as ambassador to France.

Roosevelt may have taken a brief New England trip. Riding back from New Haven to New York, he finds William Howard Taft aboard the same train, and declines when reporters try to photograph the two together.
Ted and Alice at the ice races
The Times photo section shows Ted Jr. and Alice at ice trotting races at Glenmore, Robert Goelet's country place. Its front page reports Roosevelt's chance train ride with Taft the day before.

In New York, Roosevelt attends a New York Zoological Society meeting and talks over the eviction problem with Justice Gustave Hartman, who sits on the 6th District Municipal Court.

Roosevelt sends a brief note to Ernest Harvier and tells Rudyard Kipling he has concluded that Wilson has no real policy and cannot be backed.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his older sister Bamie's 60th birthday.
Roosevelt congratulates New York's Short Ballot Organization on its plan to trim the state ballot by making the governor's junior officers appointed rather than elected.
Writing on conservation in The Outlook
An article by Roosevelt on conservation is published in The Outlook.
The New York Times reports that Roosevelt's Nobel Peace Prize fund is being returned to him, with Senator Lodge introducing a bill to dissolve the foundation that held it.
Urging Britain to win over America

Roosevelt writes Sir Edward Grey about relations between the two countries, his support for Britain and the contraband dispute. He tells Cecil Spring-Rice that Britain and France should work harder on American opinion, and writes Charles J. Bonaparte about Wilson, the Dominican Republic and Leslie Shaw.

Taxes, and thanks to his publisher

The Times Book Review takes up America and the World War. Roosevelt writes his cousin Emlen that he backs an inheritance tax and, within limits, an income tax, and thanks Charles Scribner for publishing his book on African game animals.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Calling for a federal jobs bureau

Roosevelt tours city agencies to see how the unemployed are faring, then addresses a packed Metropolitan Opera House meeting called by the Interchurch Committee on Unemployment, urging a federal bureau for the jobless. The same day, Rocky Mountain National Park is established in Colorado.
Writing Kermit on the party's end
The Times covers the previous night's speech on page one. Roosevelt writes Kermit a significant letter on the passing of the Progressive Party and what the 1912 campaign stood for.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Roosevelt writes Dwight Heard that Wilson is a reactionary who does not embody the Progressive ideal, and that the party's prospects for the coming campaign look grim.

Roosevelt writes Senator Miles Poindexter about blocking the Ship Purchase Bill; the measure would let the government buy German merchant ships interned in American ports. He joins Republican senators in the fight to defeat it.

A. S. Cochran and R. P. Perkins stop by Sagamore Hill. "The Panama Blackmail Treaty" appears in Metropolitan Magazine. A garbled note also records Roosevelt pledging $10,000 of his Nobel money to the jobless, alongside collections and ticket sales from the opera house meeting.

Germany rings Britain with a war zone

Germany proclaims the seas around the British Isles a war zone where neutral vessels risk attack. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Alexander Cochran about financial help for the poet Bliss Carman and about Edwin Arlington Robinson.
Roosevelt writes Cecil Spring-Rice about German submarine warfare, the shipping bill in Congress, Wilson and Bryan, and the moral duty of the United States.

Roosevelt stops by the Bundle Day Committee's headquarters in the city. He writes Senator George Norris about beating the shipping bill, comparing Wilson to James Buchanan and calling him untrustworthy, and shares his views on the war with George Otto Trevelyan.

President Wilson declares that Germany will be held to strict accountability if a U-boat torpedoes an American ship. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his daughter Alice's 31st birthday.

Alice and Nick Longworth mark nine years of marriage; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt tells Cecil Spring-Rice that the British and French fight in humanity's cause, and muses on growing old. To Henry Cabot Lodge he unloads: the Wilson administration is the worst he has known, and Wilson is worse even than Bryan.
Roosevelt writes Victor Murdock about the Progressive platform, the party itself and George L. Record.

Rheumatism and a last great journey

In a flurry of letters, Roosevelt opposes required Bible reading in public schools, updates Hiram Johnson on Wilson, Taft and the Barnes suit, and tells his old physician Presley Rixey that rheumatism keeps him from exercise and that the South American trip was the last of its kind for him.

After lunch with Ted and friends at the Brook Club, Roosevelt drives with William H. Childs over the Brooklyn Bridge to Bundle Headquarters on Fulton Street, where jobless New Yorkers make and mend clothing for Belgian relief, then visits several similar shops before heading home.
In the papers on judges and relief
The New York Times reports Roosevelt's views on a judicial appointment and covers his tour of Brooklyn's relief workshops the day before.
What really went wrong in Brazil

Roosevelt writes John Keltie, who has just published his account of the Brazilian expedition in a geographical journal, that many of the trip's mishaps came from the Brazilians' insistence on traveling in comfort.
Roosevelt writes Senator Albert Fall about Mexico.

Relief at not running a party

Barnes answers Roosevelt in the pages of the Times. Roosevelt politely turns down a speaking request from Miss E. J. Giffin and tells E. A. Van Valkenburg how comforting it is no longer to carry responsibility for the Progressives. His Metropolitan article on Mexico appears this month.
Wood's American Legion in the news
The Times reports General Leonard Wood's plan for an "American Legion" of reserve officers. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt writes Count Albert Apponyi about the Magyars, the war and divided loyalties, tells Mrs. John G. Graham how he felt in 1898, and urges Victor Murdock to make national defense the Progressives' theme.

Roosevelt writes William Astor Chanler about taking an independent unit into the fight against Germany, and writes Joseph Dickinson about the American Legion, a preparedness body meant to serve as the nation's first reserves. He sits on its advisory council with Taft, Root, Stimson and others.

Roosevelt testifies to the character of Major Gillette in federal court, and with Mrs. James Speyer and W. H. Childs tours workshops that employ jobless men for Belgian relief, starting at Elbert H. Gary's Fifth Avenue home and ending at the University Settlement. At Salvation Army headquarters he asks reporters to press the public for relief funds.

A front-page Times story reports that Ted's young children, Theodore III and Grace, stand to inherit $4,000,000 from their mother's Alexander relatives. Another item says Denver's Judge Ben Lindsey will seek Roosevelt as a witness.

The Explorers Club gives a luncheon in Roosevelt's honor in New York, where club president Robert E. Peary talks about the Panama Canal. Roosevelt also answers George Viereck's charge that he has been unfair to the Kaiser, advising him to give up being an American and join Germany's army.
Roosevelt has his photograph taken in a studio.
Roosevelt writes Joseph Bucklin Bishop about Wilson and Bryan.

Back door to the Flower Show
Roosevelt goes to the Flower Show in New York; the crowds are so thick he has to be brought in through the kitchen.

Roosevelt writes Munroe Smith about Smith's pamphlet on military strategy and diplomacy, explaining his own work as John D. Long's Assistant Secretary of the Navy. The Times reports he has been called on about the shipping bill.
The Times runs another story on the wealth awaiting Roosevelt's grandchildren Theodore III and Grace.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
The Times quotes Republican leaders naming Roosevelt as a possible 1916 candidate. He writes James Bryce about a world league for peace and about American pacifists who back Wilson and Bryan.
Roosevelt's article "The Need of Preparedness" is published in Metropolitan Magazine.

Roosevelt tells Bamie the Navy has declined since he left office, writes Frederick Selous, now fighting in British East Africa, about the war, and writes Jean Jules Jusserand about a peace built on righteousness. He also drafts a memo on Lady Gregory's idea for an American theater modeled on her Irish one.
A blizzard sweeps over Sagamore Hill.
Easter Sunday finds Sagamore Hill snowbound, the spring storm that hit the day before still blowing. It is also Ethel and Dick Derby's second wedding anniversary.
Roosevelt writes Frederick Whitridge of his frustration with the administration's handling of German ships sitting in American ports.
Roosevelt travels to Philadelphia to speak about Brazil.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his son Archie's 21st birthday.

The Times photo section publishes Roosevelt's March 17 portrait.

In New Haven, Roosevelt helps carry the coffin of Yale's Professor Thomas Lounsbury. William Howard Taft is among the other pallbearers.
Edith undergoes surgery, probably a hysterectomy, and will spend three weeks in the hospital.
An evening at the Park Theater
Roosevelt goes into New York City and attends the Park Theater.
The Times prints on page one Roosevelt's letter to Washington's Mrs. George Rublee, setting out his opposition to the principles of the Woman's Party for Constructive Peace.
Nelson W. Aldrich, the powerful Rhode Island senator Roosevelt dealt with throughout his presidency, dies.

Roosevelt rides into Syracuse on the same train as William Barnes Jr., and is hurried from the depot to the Walnut Avenue home of Horace Wilkinson, a rich steel man and supporter, where he will stay during the libel trial.

The libel suit William Barnes Jr. brought against Roosevelt goes to trial in Syracuse. Justice William S. Andrews refuses the defense's motion to dismiss and the jury is seated. That evening Syracuse University students serenade Roosevelt, and he speaks to them from Wilkinson's front steps.
Three hours on the witness stand
Roosevelt takes the stand for three hours, testifying that Barnes and Thomas Platt pressed him to favor big corporations in legislation.
Roosevelt spends another day testifying in the Barnes trial.
Barnes's lawyer William Ivins cross-examines Roosevelt and revives the 1898 dispute over his tax residence.
Under continued cross-examination, Roosevelt describes Barnes as a Jekyll-and-Hyde figure.
At the Onondaga Hotel, Roosevelt goes over the case with his lawyer John M. Bowers, then goes riding in the afternoon.
Church, a drive, and a cartoon

Roosevelt hears the Rev. John F. Dobbs preach at First Reformed Church, motors into the countryside, and meets his lawyers. A Times cartoon shows him and Barnes hauling an elephant skeleton out of a closet.

Syracuse lawyer William L. Barnum takes over the cross-examination and pins Roosevelt to yes-or-no answers. Letters Roosevelt wrote to Thomas Platt as Governor and as President are read into the record.

Allowed at last to explain himself, Roosevelt lays out his real relationship with Platt and dismantles two days of cross-examination. Bowers resumes direct questioning; Roosevelt has now spent 35 hours on the stand.
Testifying on Tennessee Coal and Iron
Roosevelt testifies about U.S. Steel's 1907 takeover of Tennessee Coal and Iron.
Roosevelt remains in Syracuse for the trial; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt's article "Murder on the High Seas" appears in Metropolitan Magazine.
The Barnes libel case continues in Syracuse with Roosevelt in attendance.
Waiting out the trial in Syracuse
Roosevelt is in Syracuse during the Barnes libel trial; nothing more is recorded for the day.
From Syracuse, Roosevelt tells Victor Murdock he still holds to the principles of 1912 and will not back John W. Weeks or Elihu Root for President.

What he'd do if the Lusitania sank

Roosevelt writes John Callan O'Laughlin about Germany's May 1 warning that ships under British or Allied flags may be destroyed. If the Lusitania is sunk, he says, he would seize every German ship in American waters.
A German submarine torpedoes the liner Lusitania off Ireland, and more than 1,000 people drown. Roosevelt hears the news in Syracuse, in the middle of his libel trial.
Roosevelt gives the press a statement on the sinking of the Lusitania.
Roosevelt releases another statement to the press about the Lusitania.

In Philadelphia, President Wilson declares that a man may be too proud to fight. The same day fifteen men, Ted among them, telegraph Wilson urging preparedness and asking that Leonard Wood start training camps.

A break at home, sick at heart
Roosevelt goes home to Oyster Bay during a pause in the trial. He tells Bamie he is heartsick over how Wilson and Bryan have dealt with Germany.

Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill and returns to Syracuse for the rest of the trial.

Roosevelt warns Bamie the trial may end with a deadlocked jury. To Archie he writes that Wilson rides on the pacifist vote, discusses the Plattsburg training camp Archie and Quentin will attend, and responds to Archie's car accident, after which Archie, who had not been drinking, swears off liquor until he finishes Harvard.
The Barnes case goes to the jury, which comes back 11 to 1 in Roosevelt's favor, but the judge rules the verdict improper.
Victory in the Barnes libel suit
The jury finds for Roosevelt in the libel suit brought by William Barnes Jr. after deliberating 42 hours in all. The fight has cost him about $42,000 for lawyers and other expenses.
With the trial over, Roosevelt returns to Oyster Bay.
An editorial that gets it right
A Times editorial by Charles Willis Thompson explains why Roosevelt has fallen out of political and public favor; Roosevelt considers it accurate.
Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne and her husband Douglas Robinson to thank them for standing by him through the Barnes trial.

Roosevelt tells John St. Loe Strachey that Americans will not look to him again as a leader. He also writes George Otto Trevelyan about the Dardanelles, Judge Charles Amidon about the Lusitania, Richard Child about Louisiana politics, and Lodge about the trial and dual citizenship.
Roosevelt writes the sculptor Gutzon Borglum about Wilson and his pacifist pronouncements.

Roosevelt thanks his daughter-in-law Belle for all she has meant to Kermit. Ted and Eleanor are staying with their two babies; little Grace heads to the beach daily, and Roosevelt checks on Eleanor and young Ted each morning. Metropolitan also runs his article questioning divided American loyalties.

Roosevelt writes Gifford Pinchot about the Lusitania and the Progressives, congratulates David Lloyd George on Britain's new coalition government, and tells Albert Bushnell Hart that Wilson's passivity recalls Jefferson.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
A long letter to Raymond Robins

In a sweeping letter to Raymond Robins, Roosevelt covers foreign policy, Germany, Japan and Russia, leading pacifists, the Barnes trial, prohibition, Catholics and his failed 1910 papal audience, and why he will not run in 1916. He also condemns pacifists in a letter to Hudson Maxim.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill on a trip to the South.
Guest of John Parker on the Gulf
Roosevelt arrives at Pass Christian, Mississippi, as the guest of John M. Parker.

Roosevelt visits the Bird Island bird reservation, joined by Warden Sprinkle and M. L. Alexander. In Washington, William Jennings Bryan quits the State Department to lead a nationwide peace crusade, and Robert Lansing takes his place.
Roosevelt remains at Pass Christian; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is still at Pass Christian, with nothing more noted.
Roosevelt gives reporters a statement about Bryan's resignation.
Roosevelt starts for home, stopping at the Pelican Island and Breton Island bird sanctuaries.
On the way home, Roosevelt stops to speak in Atlanta.
Roosevelt is back at Sagamore Hill for his grandson Theodore Roosevelt III's first birthday.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Last name in the guest book
Alice Longworth signs the Sagamore Hill guest register, the final entry in the book kept since 1887.

Roosevelt tells Arthur Lee he is sick at heart over America's course, and wishes he and his sons were in the trenches beside him. He mentions ribs broken when a horse threw him as he mounted, now nearly mended, and writes editor W. H. Cowles opposing the arbitration treaties.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Edith on a house full of guests
Edith writes Kermit that his father enjoys having the house crowded with all sorts of visitors.
Ted and Eleanor celebrate five years of marriage; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Edith writes her sister Emily that Roosevelt looks better than she has ever seen him and is so full of energy she can barely keep up.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

Roosevelt writes Charles Washburn that John W. Weeks is too standpat to be the Republican nominee and considers others. He writes Owen Wister about pacifists and Wilson, and Julian Street about historical parallels to Wilson.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Roosevelt goes to Gravesend Racetrack to watch mounted and foot police rehearse.

Roosevelt writes Belle about magic and magicians and reports his ribs are mending. He takes Edith rowing for the first time this summer, and a thunderstorm soaks them both. Ethel and Dick have come with the baby, and Archie is home with a Harvard friend.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Ted comes to see his father at Sagamore Hill.
Dreaming of cottages for the family

Roosevelt writes Ted's wife Eleanor that Ethel is staying with her baby Richard, and that he would love to build small houses on the place for his children and grandchildren. He also writes E. A. Van Valkenburg about an international peace conference.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.
Roosevelt begins July based at his Oyster Bay home, making regular trips into Manhattan as the month goes on.
Turning down a welcome for Jane Addams

Roosevelt writes three letters from Oyster Bay: one to Langdon Warner about digs in China and the war, a refusal to help greet Jane Addams home from the Hague peace meeting, and corrections to William Roscoe Thayer's Panama article for Harper's Monthly.
An empty page at Oyster Bay
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no activity is logged for the day.
Fourth of July call for preparedness

At Oyster Bay's Independence Day parade, where New York lawyer Frederick R. Coudert is the featured orator, Roosevelt is called on for a few remarks and uses them to argue that the country must get ready for war.
Britain's envoy to Washington, Cecil Spring-Rice, sits down with Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes to the financier J. P. Morgan Jr. after a pro-German assailant attacked him inside his own house.
Writing Owen Wister about the war
Roosevelt answers his friend Owen Wister about Wister's essay "The Pentecost of Calamity," and turns to the Lusitania sinking and Wilson's response.
In a letter to writer Julian Street, Roosevelt lays out why he objects to Woodrow Wilson, drawing comparisons from history.
Roosevelt is home at Oyster Bay. The record notes nothing else.

Roosevelt sends William Roscoe Thayer more Panama material, tells Frank McCoy how he would organize the cavalry regiment he hopes to raise, and writes William Rainsford about savage newspaper attacks on him.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill and heads west on a long journey to California.
Roosevelt's train carries him west by way of the Canadian Rockies, bound for California.
Rolling west on the Canadian route
Roosevelt is still traveling toward California along the Canadian line through the Rockies.
Mountain miles on the way west
The cross-country trip continues; Roosevelt is in transit through the Canadian Rockies.
Roosevelt remains on the road to California, taking the northern route across Canada.
Another day on the northern route
Roosevelt keeps moving west through the Canadian mountains toward the Pacific coast.
Roosevelt is in transit via the Canadian Rockies, still headed for California.
Last days of the Canadian crossing
Roosevelt continues his westward trip through Canada before turning south toward California.
Meeting Senator Poindexter in the Northwest
Coming down through Portland and Seattle, Roosevelt confers with Senator Miles Poindexter of Washington.
Roosevelt reaches San Francisco, the end of his westward trip.
San Francisco's Panama-Pacific International Exposition marks a day in Roosevelt's honor, and he uses the stage to press his case for national preparedness.
Touring the fair and writing to London

Roosevelt takes in the Exposition grounds, then writes British author Frederick S. Oliver a long letter about Oliver's book on readiness, the division he hopes to lead, Edward Grey, Wilson and Taft, and his own record with Britain as President.
Roosevelt spends a second day walking the grounds of San Francisco's world's fair.
Roosevelt talks to young men enrolled in the War Department's student instruction camp at San Francisco.
Down the coast to Los Angeles
Roosevelt is in Los Angeles; the record gives no other details.

Roosevelt addresses the Panama-California Exposition and huddles with California Progressives. A film camera catches him and Edith pulling up by car and standing on a building's steps.
Roosevelt starts the long trip back east toward New York and Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt is traveling across the country on his way back to New York.
The homeward journey continues, with Roosevelt en route to New York.

Roosevelt is still traveling east. This summer the first Plattsburg camp trains civilians as soldiers, and his sons Archie, Ted and Quentin take part. He is also writing Metropolitan articles calling for preparedness and a harder line on Mexico and Germany.
Roosevelt spends another day on the train heading back to New York.
Back from the West, ready to fight
Roosevelt gets home from his California trip. A New York Times reporter finds him in fine health and spirits.
Settling back in at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; the day carries no other entry.
Roosevelt writes the American novelist Winston Churchill to applaud his book A Far Country, about capital and labor, and shares thoughts on the Socialists.
Roosevelt goes into Manhattan, where Theodore Douglas Robinson and a Mr. McCormick stop by his Metropolitan magazine office, and he has lunch with Robert Bacon.
It is Edith's 54th birthday. Roosevelt writes his English friend Arthur Lee about readiness for war, his scorn for pacifists, and how the fighting is going.
Writing to Russian diplomat Baron Roman Rosen, Roosevelt sketches the course he would have taken in the summer the war began, had he been in the White House.
Sunday at home in Oyster Bay
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt's daughter Ethel turns 24. He is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt and George W. Perkins spend nine hours touring Palisades Interstate Park along the Hudson.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. The day has no other entry.
Ted's daughter Grace Roosevelt celebrates her fourth birthday. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is home at Oyster Bay; nothing more is noted.
While Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill, a German U-boat torpedoes the unarmed British liner Arabic, killing two Americans aboard.
Letters to Selous and on New York politics

Roosevelt writes his old hunting friend Frederick Selous, now a lieutenant with the 25th Royal Fusiliers, about the war, and writes Arthur T. Warner about a possible Democratic-Progressive alliance in New York's upcoming election.
Calling for a break with Germany
Roosevelt tells the press the United States should now cut off diplomatic relations with Germany.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record lists nothing further.
Roosevelt is home on Long Island. No events are recorded.
Home before the trip to Plattsburg
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted for the day.

Roosevelt visits Leonard Wood's training camp at Plattsburg and gives a speech with jabs at President Wilson that infuriate the administration; Wood is officially reprimanded. Archie is commissioned a second lieutenant, Ted is put forward for a major's rank, and Quentin is judged a future lieutenant with more age and seasoning.
A "rational Socialist" and a note to John L. Sullivan
Roosevelt tells writer Reginald Kauffman he counts himself a "rational Socialist," and sends the old heavyweight champion John L. Sullivan good wishes for his lecture tour on temperance.
Roosevelt declares that he alone answers for what he said at Plattsburg, taking the heat off Leonard Wood.
Roosevelt sends his son Kermit news of the Plattsburg camp and his views on Wilson and his policies.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay. The chronology lists no events.
Nothing is recorded for the day; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
The record notes Quentin's entrance into Harvard while Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Henry S. Drinker, president of Lehigh University and a backer of the training camps, to stand by his Plattsburg speech.

Roosevelt writes Archie about the camp, the uproar over his speech, and Winchester rifles and cartridges. A long letter to Arthur Lee covers universal military service, Wilson, German agitation inside America, pacifism, his hoped-for division and Russia.
Roosevelt asks George W. Perkins to keep quiet about the 1916 presidential nomination.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for a holiday at his physician friend Dr. Alexander Lambert's camp in Quebec.
First day in the Quebec woods
Roosevelt is in Quebec Province on his vacation; nothing specific is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Quebec Province. The record gives no details.

Roosevelt's eldest son Ted marks his 28th birthday while his father is in Quebec.

Roosevelt brings down a moose in Quebec, using his Model 1903 Springfield rifle.

With his father in Quebec, Quentin begins at Harvard. A wrenched back from the Arizona hunting trip with his father keeps him out of sports; his interests run to witchcraft, demonology, mechanics and math.
Roosevelt is in Quebec Province; the record lists nothing.
Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 54th birthday as he winds up his Quebec stay.
Nannie Lodge dies; a sardine box for Edith

Anna Cabot Mills "Nannie" Lodge, wife of Roosevelt's close friend Henry Cabot Lodge, dies of heart disease. Roosevelt comes back to New York with a pewter sardine box from Gaspé for Edith, who likes it.
To Boston for Nannie Lodge's funeral
Roosevelt and Edith travel to Boston for the funeral of Nannie Lodge.

Roosevelt and Edith stop at Harvard to see Archie and Quentin, who is reading The Anti-Jacobin, Layard's Nineveh and an English version of a Chinese biography of Genghis Khan, then return home. His essay on hyphenated Americanism appears in the Metropolitan.

Roosevelt writes Kermit's wife Belle that Kermit is unhappy at his bank job in Brazil, and that he understands what his son longs for. Edith is in bed, worn out with nervous fatigue after Nannie Lodge's funeral.
Roosevelt is home at Oyster Bay; no events are entered.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. The record has nothing more.
Shopping an essay on early man

Roosevelt asks Brander Matthews for help placing an essay about early humans and the ancient beasts they lived among. Renamed "How Old is Man?", National Geographic will print it in its February 1916 issue.

Roosevelt stays at his Long Island home. The day has no entry.

Roosevelt tells British editor John St. Loe Strachey that he does not intend to come back into public life.
Roosevelt's son Kermit, working in Brazil, has his 26th birthday.
Roosevelt's niece Eleanor Roosevelt celebrates her 31st birthday.
Roosevelt goes into Manhattan to give the Knights of Columbus a Columbus Day address at Carnegie Hall.
Roosevelt is home in Oyster Bay. No events are listed.
The chronology notes only that Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt sends Perkins a playful letter about the campaign and about Wilson's courtship of Mrs. Galt. To suffragist Ethel Dreier he notes that some of history's mightiest monarchs were women and makes his case for equal rights.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.
No events are entered for Roosevelt, who is on Long Island.
Bamie's son Sheffield Cowles has his 17th birthday. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt is at home. The day has no entry.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is logged for the day.
Ted and his wife Eleanor welcome a son, Cornelius Van Schaack Roosevelt, Roosevelt's newest grandchild.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt asks Charles J. Bonaparte whether he ought to speak out against Washington's recognition of Venustiano Carranza's government in Mexico.
At the movies: The Battle Cry of Peace

In New York Roosevelt watches J. Stuart Blackton's film The Battle Cry of Peace, which pictures an enemy invasion of the city. Based on Hudson Maxim's Defenseless America, it was made with advice from Wood, Garrison and Roosevelt himself.
Roosevelt marks his 57th birthday at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is listed.
No activity is recorded for Roosevelt at his Oyster Bay home.
Roosevelt is home on Long Island. The day passes without an entry.
Making the case for universal service

The Metropolitan carries Roosevelt's essay on what the nation owes its citizens, calling for every American man to train for military service. Alice and her husband Nick Longworth are back in Washington, their political exile at an end.
Roosevelt opens November at Sagamore Hill, often going into Manhattan. He tells Harry V. Osborne he won't take up the cause of the Armenians until he has spoken out for the Belgians.
Casting his ballot in Oyster Bay
On Election Day Roosevelt goes down to the village of Oyster Bay to vote.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

Humorist Finley Peter Dunne, creator of "Mr. Dooley," and Pittsburgh publisher Alexander P. Moore are among the visitors at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt dines with William Allen White and George W. Perkins. He objects to Daniel P. Toomey that the Knights of Columbus printed his Columbus Day speech without its passage on keeping church and state apart, and vows to publish the whole text himself if they won't. He also writes Edwin Lawrence about Catherine the Great and Maria Theresa.
Roosevelt is home; nothing else is noted for the day.
No activity is logged; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
The chronology places Roosevelt at home on Long Island and is otherwise silent.
Roosevelt writes John Rose that President Wilson has at last started moving toward military readiness.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. No events are recorded.
Booker T. Washington, the Tuskegee educator Roosevelt famously hosted at the White House in 1901, dies. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt is home at Oyster Bay; the day carries no entry.
Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence at home.
Thanks for facts on universal service
Roosevelt writes Army Captain George Van Horn Moseley, who had supplied him with material on universal military service.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing else noted.
Roosevelt's youngest son Quentin celebrates his 18th birthday at college in Cambridge.
Civil service, race and a tribute

Roosevelt writes William Dudley Foulke about a plan for competitive exams in New York City government, Charles Washburn about relations between Black and white Southerners and his own record on the question, and James Parsons with warm words about his father.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are listed.

Roosevelt writes Sir Edward Grey to clarify his Metropolitan article, which English readers took as hostile to Britain, and writes Ambassador Spring-Rice about it too. To Richard Gorman he discusses Boston protests against The Battle Cry of Peace.
Roosevelt's sister Bamie and her husband, Admiral William Sheffield Cowles, mark twenty years of marriage.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is noted.
Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge about his own chances of being nominated for President in 1916 and who else might be put forward.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day has no entry.
No events are recorded; Roosevelt is at home.
Pacifists, the Scouts and Henry Ford

Roosevelt tells Boy Scouts chief James West he fears pacifists have taken over the movement. He writes artist Henry Reuterdahl that he may have to go after Henry Ford in print but won't waste time on Oswald Villard, and again defends his Metropolitan articles to James Bryce.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing is recorded.
Anniversary and an immigrant art show

On their 29th wedding anniversary, Roosevelt goes into the city, where George W. Perkins is among his callers at the Metropolitan, and visits "The Immigrant in America" exhibition at Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney's studio.
In the New York Times, Roosevelt condemns Henry Ford's "Peace Ship" voyage to Europe.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day has no entry.
Ernest Thompson Seton steps away from the Boy Scouts, easing Roosevelt's concern that pacifists were steering the organization.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; nothing else is recorded.

Writing Henry Cabot Lodge about possible Republican nominees for 1916, Roosevelt discusses Herbert Hadley and Samuel McCall and is blunt about Charles Evans Hughes, whom he blames for drawing him into the fight with William Barnes and then forgetting it at the libel trial.

Roosevelt addresses Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, a month after Booker T. Washington's death. He also writes a long open letter supporting a fundraising campaign for the Boy Scouts.
Roosevelt gets back to Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt writes Hamlin Garland about readiness and the arms manufacturers, and asks Charles W. Fear to make sure Progressive leaders, himself among them, stand together on the questions facing the 1916 race.
Roosevelt tells philanthropist Julius Rosenwald he supports Robert Russa Moton to succeed Booker T. Washington as head of Tuskegee Institute.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.
Judge Gary's dinner and a threat
In the city, callers at the Metropolitan include a Mr. McCormick, and Judge Elbert H. Gary gives a dinner in Roosevelt's honor. Roosevelt warns he might back the Democratic candidate in 1916.
Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay after his night in the city.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day carries no entry.
Nothing is recorded; Roosevelt is at home.
Roosevelt writes William Knox about how to build public backing for his candidacy in 1916.
Roosevelt is home; no events are listed.

Roosevelt keeps Christmas at his Oyster Bay home.

Roosevelt tells George Miller he prefers California's Hiram Johnson to Philander Knox for the 1916 nomination, given Knox's stance on Mexico. He urges English novelist Mary Ward to explain Britain's view of the conflict.
Roosevelt writes Governor Hiram Johnson of California to say he backs him for the 1916 presidential nomination.
Roosevelt writes Medill McCormick about the rift among Democrats over Wilson's defense program.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day has no entry.
Roosevelt writes Charles J. Bonaparte about what Progressives should stress in 1916. His new Metropolitan article on putting America first attacks Wilson's neutrality and his handling of Mexico.
A foreword for a book of travels
Roosevelt starts the new year at Sagamore Hill, with regular trips to Manhattan, and writes the foreword for his coming collection of outdoor travel essays.

Talking to the American Defense Society
In Manhattan, Roosevelt addresses a joint meeting of the American Defense Society's trustees and advisory board.

George W. Perkins calls at the Metropolitan. Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge about a critic of his portrait of Lincoln in Hero Tales, weighs Root and Lodge as Secretary of State material, and commends both Lodge and Augustus "Gussie" Gardner for what they have done in Congress.
Regulate arms makers, don't own them
Roosevelt tells Gardner Harding the government should oversee private munitions plants rather than take them over, and commends Madeleine Doty for her prison reform work in New York State.

While Roosevelt stays at Sagamore Hill, the Progressive Party's national committee convenes in Chicago.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.

Roosevelt presses Admiral William S. Sims to go before Congress and argue for a stronger navy. He tells Willard Straight that a New Republic piece guessing how he would have handled Germany in 1914 gets it right, though it also repeats tales of his cursing at Santiago.

Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her 61st birthday.
Roosevelt writes Fred P. Barnett that every private arms factory should be under federal supervision.
Philadelphia speech on duty and loyalty
Speaking in Philadelphia for the National Americanization Committee, Roosevelt calls for mandatory military readiness and condemns divided, hyphenated loyalties.
Roosevelt is home after Philadelphia; nothing is recorded.
A member of the Security League
Roosevelt mentions in a letter to his sister Corinne that he belongs to the National Security League, a group campaigning for preparedness.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are entered.
Roosevelt tells Corinne that Judge Albert Nortoni and Robert Bacon have come out to see him. He writes Lawrence Abbott about putting the Chinese indemnity money toward education.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge about the political prospects, the National Security League, readiness for war, and what he sees as Wilson's poor policies.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that her son Sheffield hopes to go hunting over his vacation, and that he and Edith will sail for Barbados and Trinidad in February, a trip he thinks will do Edith good.
Roosevelt writes Franklin Hall to stand up for his record on military readiness.
Telling Henry Ford where he stands
Roosevelt writes Henry Ford to make plain his opposition to Ford's pacifism, and writes Isaac MacVeagh about the upcoming Republican nomination.
Roosevelt gives a talk in Brooklyn at the Academy of Music, sponsored by the borough's Institute of Arts and Sciences.
A new book and a hospital dedication

Roosevelt speaks as the city's Orthopedic Hospital and Dispensary opens its new building. Doran publishes his new book of preparedness writings, named for the Philadelphia speech, and National Geographic runs his essay "How Old Is Man?"
New York Orthopedic Hospital and Dispensary
A luncheon and a YMCA dinner
Roosevelt speaks twice in the city: at a National Americanization Committee luncheon and at a YMCA dinner.
Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt has lunch with Rear Admiral Bradley A. Fiske, and writes Bamie that he sincerely hopes the Republicans pass him over, along with a cutting verdict on Wilson.
Four letters on Wilson and the war

Roosevelt writes Lodge that the papers are casting Root, Stimson and Lodge as supporters of Wilson's preparedness plans. He criticizes Wilson to Charles Bull, thanks Mary T. Bays for standing against pacifism, and writes the Rev. Gustavus Hiller about German-Americans.
A girl raising money for a battleship
Roosevelt writes 13-year-old Marjorie Sterrett of Brooklyn, who is collecting money so the Navy can build a battleship, and tells her about his four grandchildren.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day has no entry.
In New York, Roosevelt is the lunch guest of a group of Jewish New Yorkers from the Lower East Side at the Little Hungary restaurant, and gives a speech.

Roosevelt writes Gifford Pinchot about German-American Progressives who oppose his policies; lays out his views on readiness, the Alaska boundary and Panama to Harvard psychologist Hugo Münsterberg; and writes Willard Straight about a New Republic article on his Philadelphia speech.
Roosevelt writes John Graves about strengthening the Navy and tells Henry Ford again how much he dislikes pacifism.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill the day before sailing; nothing is recorded.
Roosevelt and Edith board ship in New York Harbor for a Caribbean holiday, and he poses on deck for the cameras.
Out to sea on Alice's birthday
Roosevelt is at sea on his daughter Alice's 32nd birthday. Footage survives of the ship pulling away from the pier and passing under the Manhattan Bridge.
Roosevelt and Edith are at sea, bound for the Caribbean.
At sea, Roosevelt receives a note from Edward Huntington, Quentin's Harvard math professor, enclosing some of Quentin's poetry.
While Roosevelt is at sea, Elihu Root tells the New York Republican convention he opposes Wilson's preparedness policies, his first such stand, clearing the way for other moderate Republicans.
A grandson born in Buenos Aires
Kermit and Belle welcome a son, Kermit Roosevelt Jr., in Buenos Aires. His grandfather is at sea.
Roosevelt and Edith reach the West Indies. Back home, Alice and Nick Longworth mark ten years of marriage.
From the West Indies Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about Lloyd George, says he will not be the nominee, and comments on the embargo question.
Roosevelt is in the West Indies; nothing else is noted.
Edith writes Kermit that the whole town in Guadeloupe came out at midnight to see them to their boat, cheering for Roosevelt.
Roosevelt and Edith are in Barbados; the record gives no details.

With Roosevelt in Barbados, the film Shall We Prepare? comes out, including shots of him at Sagamore Hill and at his Metropolitan desk. Scribner's also brings out his new book of outdoor travel essays.
Roosevelt and his wife Edith are away on a winter holiday in the West Indies.

From Trinidad, Roosevelt issues a statement to reporters saying he does not want the Republican nomination for President, and that choosing him would only make sense if the nation were in a heroic frame of mind.

Back to politics, and lunch with Ted
Roosevelt spends the day in the city and at home on Oyster Bay, meeting with George W. Perkins and Horace Wilkinson and lunching with his son Ted.
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt receives visitors, among them his son-in-law Nicholas Longworth.
Praise for a poet's new book

Roosevelt talks politics at Sagamore Hill with Charles Sumner Bird and Augustus Gardner, sends news to his sister Corinne, and writes Edwin Arlington Robinson that he likes the poems in The Man Against the Sky.
Talks with Perkins and Van Valkenburg
Roosevelt meets at Sagamore Hill with George W. Perkins and the Philadelphia editor Van Valkenburg.
Wary of a Wilson with whiskers
Roosevelt meets again with Augustus Gardner and writes George von Lengerke Meyer about his Trinidad statement, Lodge's backing of Hughes, and his wish that Hughes say plainly where he stands.
In New York, Roosevelt addresses a Jewish bazaar at Grand Central Palace, sees callers including Robert R. Moton at the Metropolitan, and confers with Perkins and Wilkinson.
Midday meal with Root, Lodge and Wood

Roosevelt lunches with Elihu Root, Henry Cabot Lodge and Leonard Wood at Robert Bacon's house, then meets Progressives at George W. Perkins's home. The Non Partisan League presses him to run for President.
Visits from Bacon and Wise Wood
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's callers include Robert Bacon and Henry A. Wise Wood.
Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne asking her and some of her friends to lunch at Sagamore Hill.

Joseph Alsop and Gifford Pinchot call at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Matthew Hale he will not be the nominee and holds to his March 9 statement, and writes Governor Hiram Johnson against dual citizenship and about the Progressives.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the third wedding anniversary of his daughter Ethel and Dr. Richard Derby.
Roosevelt meets with George W. Perkins, Horace Wilkinson, Henry L. Stoddard and John C. Shaffer at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes George W. Perkins explaining why he presses for military readiness, pointing to China as a warning, and discussing Germany, Mexico and the errors he believes Wilson made.
Flower show, Burroughs, and a crowd of callers

In New York, Roosevelt meets a long list of politicians, visits John Burroughs, and tours a flower show with General Wood and Ethel. Elihu Root declares for the presidency. Roosevelt writes Frederick S. Oliver praising his book.
Lunch with the Abbotts, and memories of 1912

Roosevelt hosts George Meyer and Charles G. Washburn, then shares a midday meal with the three Abbotts (Lyman, Ernest and Lawrence), the Regis Posts and W. A. Wadsworth, and talks over his 1912 split with Taft.
Off to Boston on Archie's birthday
On his son Archie's 22nd birthday, Roosevelt travels to Boston to stay with William Sturgis Bigelow and has dinner with the Robert Grants, the novelist Owen Wister, and the William Roscoe Thayers.
Harvard overseers and tea with Lowell
Roosevelt sits in on a meeting of Harvard's Board of Overseers, lunches with Archie and some of his classmates, and has tea with President A. Lawrence Lowell.
Roosevelt goes from Boston to Farmington, Connecticut, staying with his sister Bamie and her husband, and dines with Joseph Alsop and Herbert K. Smith.
Back in New York, Roosevelt sees Frederick Davenport and Regis Post at the Metropolitan and lunches with George Cherrie, Frank M. Chapman and Mark Sullivan.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt reads a New York Tribune line casting the coming convention as a choice of national direction, and likens the moment to the choices of the 1890s.
Roosevelt sees William Loeb, Raymond Robins and George W. Perkins at Sagamore Hill and goes to Cold Spring Harbor for F. Hall's funeral.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt writes Dwight Heard about the coming Progressive convention and tells James W. White that more than a thousand letters a week reach him.
At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's callers include William Draper Lewis.
Roosevelt goes into the city, where R. C. Morris and Everett Colby call on him at the Metropolitan.

Roosevelt writes Augustus Gardner asking him to halt the Massachusetts drive Gardner was leading to win Roosevelt the Republican nomination.
In the city, Roosevelt sees Dr. Holbrook Curtis about his throat and meets Judge Albert Nortoni. He tells Julian Street he does not expect to be nominated.
Roosevelt again visits Dr. Holbrook Curtis in New York City.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt addresses a Methodist Social Union dinner in New York and writes his sister Bamie that Americans have yet to rouse themselves.

Roosevelt meets Alice Carpenter of the Women's Roosevelt League, then tells a Congressional Union for Woman Suffrage delegation he supports a constitutional amendment giving women the vote. He leaves that evening for Chicago.
Speech to Illinois lawyers, visit to Jane Addams

In Chicago, Roosevelt sees callers, lunches with McChesney, gives the Illinois Bar Association an address on America's duties at home and abroad, and calls on Jane Addams. It is his sister Corinne's 34th wedding anniversary.
Roosevelt lunches in Chicago with Harold Ickes, Walter L. Fisher, Merriam, John C. Shaffer, La Verne Noyes and Revell.
Roosevelt heads back to New York and Oyster Bay, talking politics on the way with George W. Perkins and Henry L. Stoddard.
Roosevelt writes William Noble that nobody knows what Charles Evans Hughes thinks or where he stands.
Roosevelt jokes to Brooks Adams that the country has as little use for him as for Adams, and writes Henry Fairfield Osborn that William Beebe needs a Ford.
After seeing callers at the Metropolitan, Roosevelt writes that Hughes will likely be the choice though his views are unknown, and that the Chicago convention will pass him over.
Roosevelt gives a talk at the Cove School near home.
Roosevelt writes Charles G. Washburn about the coming Republican national convention.
Roosevelt goes into New York City and spends the night at his daughter Ethel's home.
Roosevelt greets his wife Edith in New York as she returns from Havana, and they go home to Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt sees Bacon and Butler at the Metropolitan, hosts a big lunch of Progressive and Republican leaders, speaks at a memorial for Youngs, and writes Meyer, William Allen White and Foster Brown about the nomination.
Roosevelt writes Guy Emerson of the Roosevelt Non-Partisan League setting out the principles he stands for.
Roosevelt's letter to Guy Emerson laying out his principles runs in The New York Times.

Roosevelt talks to the local Scouts and to a Methodist Bible class while Edith marches up Fifth Avenue in a Preparedness Parade. A four-page Saturday Evening Post ad urges his election, and he thanks Thomas Edison for a kind letter.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Guy Emerson and Desmond, the Non-Partisan League's secretary and treasurer, call at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Guy Emerson again about his principles and tells Frederick Eldridge his support for initiative, referendum and recall is lukewarm, just as in 1912.
At the Metropolitan, Roosevelt sees George Meyer and J. Mayhew Wainwright.
Roosevelt leaves on a speaking trip, after writing William Moody about Root and Pinchot and praising Moody.
In Detroit, Roosevelt speaks for military readiness and regrets the popularity Henry Ford has won with his antiwar views, then starts home.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Callers, then a train to Washington
Roosevelt receives George Meyer, Professor Hiram Bingham, J. Mayhew Wainwright, R. C. Morris and Alexander P. Moore at Sagamore Hill, then leaves for Washington.
In Washington, Roosevelt testifies to the good character of a man named Glover, then returns home. He writes W. Cameron Forbes that the United States should keep the Philippines.
At the Metropolitan, Roosevelt sees Robert Bacon, Lemuel Quigg and August Belmont Jr.
The novelist Mary Roberts Rinehart is among Roosevelt's callers at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt hosts Regis Post and Nassau County Progressives, and writes Franklin D. Roosevelt that he is mistaken: shore staff were not cut to send the battle fleet around the world in 1908-09.

More than 2,000 people turn out for a rally at Sagamore Hill as Roosevelt addresses the Roosevelt Non-Partisan League. He urges Henry Reuterdahl to keep naval engineering strong and tells Brooks Adams he doubts he will be nominated.
Roosevelt leaves New York on a western trip.
In Chicago, Roosevelt meets Butz and other Progressives and writes Charles J. Bonaparte that he might run on a third ticket if the Republicans pass him by.
Roosevelt gives a Memorial Day address in Kansas City and meets with Progressives, writing his sister Corinne beforehand that he hopes she will like the speech.
Roosevelt gives two speeches in St. Louis calling for universal military training and service, scorning "weasel words." The Metropolitan also prints his new article warning against national drift.
Roosevelt speaks at an industrial exhibition in Newark and dines with two former New Jersey governors, John Franklin Fort and Franklin Murphy.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt sends Maurice Egan a copy of A Book-Lover's Holidays in the Open and writes him about the West Indies.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
George Cortelyou calls. Roosevelt writes Major John Parker that he cannot win him the nomination, describing Parker as untested but ambitious.

Roosevelt lunches with General Wood and Simkhovitch, writes Carrie Chapman Catt on woman suffrage, and praises General Pershing's Mexico expedition. Lodge, while expecting Hughes, quietly works to get Roosevelt the Republican nod.

The Republican and Progressive conventions open in Chicago on the same day, with George W. Perkins on a private phone line to Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee on politics and the war, and Thomas Warren on John Hay, books, and the Kaiser's bust of himself.
Roosevelt writes Frank C. Laughlin about Root and wires Senator William P. Jackson urging Republicans and Progressives to join in a shared cause.
With nominations approaching in Chicago, Roosevelt asks his allies there to hold off.
Hughes nominated; Roosevelt turns down the Progressives

After a 3 a.m. call from Nicholas Murray Butler, Roosevelt backs Lodge and refuses the Republican nod for himself. Republicans choose Charles Evans Hughes; the Progressives nominate Roosevelt, and he wires them declining and recommending Lodge.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his son Kermit's second wedding anniversary.
Leonard Wood comes out to Oyster Bay, and Roosevelt meets with William Loeb, Gifford Pinchot, James Garfield and William Draper Lewis.
Roosevelt bars reporters from Sagamore Hill, then meets Perkins, Hiram Johnson, Chester Rowell and Oscar Straus at his daughter Ethel's city home in the city.
A tired Roosevelt at the Langdon
Roosevelt, looking worn, confers at the Hotel Langdon with Raymond Robins, Harold Ickes and Governor Hiram Johnson. His grandson Theodore Roosevelt III turns two.
Roosevelt meets his son Kermit and daughter-in-law Belle at a New York pier, where he needs a doctor's attention, and holds Progressive talks at the Hotel Langdon.
Dry pleurisy, and a pledge to back Hughes

Doctors find Roosevelt has dry pleurisy. Still meeting callers at the Langdon, he writes Bamie, Isaac Russell and William Roscoe Thayer that he will support Hughes, and writes Edgar Lee Masters about his poems.

Roosevelt meets Perkins and Hiram Johnson at the Langdon before going home, and thanks Senator Albert Fall for placing his name in nomination; the Roosevelt demonstration lasted 36 minutes, the convention's longest.
Roosevelt once more asks the press to clear out of Sagamore Hill.

A crowd of Progressive and Republican leaders, Lodge among them, call at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt urges the Progressives to back Hughes. He writes Henry Stimson on the platform and James Bryce on Jutland and the Germans.
Roosevelt meets George Meyer, Charles Bonaparte, Joseph Alsop and H. N. Jackson at Sagamore Hill on his son Ted and Eleanor's sixth wedding anniversary.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Endorses Hughes, ending the Bull Moose era
At the Hotel Langdon, Roosevelt formally backs Charles Evans Hughes. His letter to the Progressive National Committee marks the party's end and calls for defeating Wilson.
Kermit and Belle visit. Roosevelt tells Corinne he is through with national politics, writes Whitmell Martin about Southern Progressives, and urges William Wadsworth to back Hughes.
Chester Rowell and Kirkwood are among callers at Sagamore Hill, Nicholas Longworth is a house guest, and Roosevelt writes T. H. Wanamaker about the Progressives' prospects in Southern states.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. The entry holds only a reading note on the 1916 Progressive convention.
The Progressive committee votes to support Hughes. Roosevelt agrees with Clement Brumbaugh that Harvard is a Democratic school.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt and Charles Evans Hughes patch things up over a three-hour dinner at the Hotel Astor. He also writes Senator Joseph Foraker a warm letter.
Reporters finally leave Sagamore Hill at Roosevelt's repeated urging. He tells Alice Carpenter he has persuaded Hughes to back votes for women, and writes Lemuel Quigg on politics.
Volunteers, a carpet mill, and a houseful of grandchildren

Roosevelt sends Hughes campaign ammunition against Wilson. Offers to join a Roosevelt regiment pour in for Regis Post to handle. Archie has been at a Connecticut carpet mill; he, Quentin and Dick Derby head back to Plattsburg. Five grandchildren fill Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt settles in for the summer at Sagamore Hill, going into New York City often.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Ready to raise a division for Mexico

Roosevelt tells Julian Street he will raise a division if war comes with Mexico. He writes Dwight Heard that the Progressives have split, and tells Lodge about the Cape Cod Canal, his talk with Hughes, Wilson's weakness, and the problems of sending the Guard to Mexico.
Fourth of July in Oyster Bay
Roosevelt joins the Independence Day parade in Oyster Bay and gives a speech. Film of the day survives.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Asks the War Department for a division
Roosevelt writes Secretary of War Newton D. Baker describing the division he wants permission to raise and lead into Mexico should war break out.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

Roosevelt lays out his division plan for Frank R. McCoy: McCoy as chief of staff, Henry Stimson as quartermaster general, Dick Derby and Henry Page on the medical side, plus infantry, cavalry, machine guns, motorcycles, artillery and an air corps.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Pinchot would have been Secretary of State
Roosevelt tells Gifford Pinchot that he would have made him Secretary of State had he won in 1912.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Flinn and Perkins at the office
At the Metropolitan, Roosevelt sees William Flinn and George W. Perkins, and he writes William Willcox about Progressive politics.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

Roosevelt assures a Mrs. Nicholson of Oregon that he trusts Hughes's honesty and patriotism.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt writes Corinne about her son Teddy Robinson's bid for a seat in the state senate at Albany, hoping the family tie to him won't hurt.
A division only if war comes
Roosevelt assures the Army's adjutant general he would raise troops only in wartime, and writes John St. Loe Strachey on his principles and universal service.

Roosevelt tells Bamie his division plans keep him busy, that Archie and Quentin are drilling at Plattsburg, and he is getting fit and enjoying the grandchildren. He questions to James B. Reynolds whether the state Progressive Party should go on.
Roosevelt attends a meeting of Oyster Bay's committee on infantile paralysis.
Roosevelt goes to Fort Terry to speak to a military training camp for schoolboys.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt confers with Senator Albert Fall at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt tells Robert Bass he won't go to France on any diplomatic errand and can't understand Progressives backing Wilson. He tells Julian Street he opposes the Authors' League joining the AFL.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

Roosevelt joins Ted, Robert Bacon and Henry Stimson at Carnegie Hall to hear Hughes formally accept the nomination, his first official Republican gathering since 1912. Hughes speaks for an hour and a half.
Tea for Hughes; a park for Hawaii
Roosevelt goes to a tea for Hughes hosted by the Women's Roosevelt League. The same day, Hawaii National Park is established.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
A worn voice and a visit to Nahant
Roosevelt tells Lodge his voice is in poor shape and suggests meeting at Nahant. He presses Julian Street to make use of his July letter against joining the AFL.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home on his wife Edith's 55th birthday.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

Roosevelt takes in a cowboy show at Sheepshead Bay with a family party: Ted, Kermit and Belle, and Ethel with her husband Richard. He writes Bronson Cutting about a weak Republican slate in New Mexico and John Macrae about E. P. Dutton books.
Lassen Volcanic becomes a national park
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as Lassen Volcanic National Park in California is established.
Roosevelt writes Charles Evans Hughes about the campaign, Wilson, the German-American vote and universal service.
Meeting Bacon at the Harvard Club
Roosevelt goes to the city to talk with Robert Bacon at the Harvard Club.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his daughter Ethel's 25th birthday.

Roosevelt's granddaughter Grace, Ted's daughter, has her fifth birthday.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt goes wading with his grandson Richard Derby Jr. and Belle, and writes James Walsh praising his book The Century of Columbus and discussing history and Spain.
Roosevelt watches his grandson Richard splash a bowl of water on the porch, sailing toy boats and a little swan.

Roosevelt writes William Roscoe Thayer about the ultimatum he says he gave Germany over Venezuela in 1902, tells Dick Derby about Ethel and their son staying at Sagamore Hill, and writes William Willcox about a Maine speech.
Roosevelt writes Charles J. Bonaparte, still torn between Wilson and Hughes, with words of praise for Hughes.
Roosevelt meets Alvin Hert to plan campaign speeches and sends Thayer another letter on the 1902 German ultimatum.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
The National Park Service is born
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as a new law sets up a federal bureau to run the national parks.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt writes Thayer yet again about his 1902 ultimatum to Germany.
Defending Hughes; Italy joins the war on Germany
Italy declares war on Germany. Roosevelt writes Hughes rejecting charges that Hughes favors German submarine warfare.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt confers with Progressives on the way to Boston, breakfasts at the Copley Plaza, then speaks in Lewiston, Maine, assailing Wilson's Mexico policy and championing Americanism.
Roosevelt stays with his sister Bamie and her husband in Farmington, Connecticut.
Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Herbert W. Packard he cannot fathom supporting Wilson, and writes Lyman Abbott about the looming railroad strike.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt writes Edwin Van Valkenburg about his methods and what lies ahead.
Roosevelt writes William Hoster that he thinks Hughes will win, but only on his own strength.
Roosevelt confers with George W. Perkins and Frank H. Hitchcock at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt holds a large strategy meeting at Sagamore Hill with Willcox, Perkins, Colby, Parsons, Robins, Hitchcock, Forbes, Bliss and Reynolds.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt writes Meyer Lissner about California politics, pleased that Republicans chose Governor Hiram Johnson for the U.S. Senate.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt hosts Willcox, Colby, Hitchcock, Forbes, Perkins and Beck for lunch at Sagamore Hill.
On his son Ted's 29th birthday, Roosevelt writes Henry Reuterdahl about the April blunders at Tampico and Veracruz.
Callers and a lunch in town
At the Metropolitan, Roosevelt sees Willcox, Rumely, Halbert, Gardner, Frances Kellor and Perkins, then lunches with Robert Bacon, Cornelius Bliss, Lawrence Abbott and Charles Bonaparte.

Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his sister Corinne's 55th birthday.

Roosevelt writes Henry L. Stoddard about an upcoming encounter with Taft at a club in the city, writes James R. Garfield on Hughes, and congratulates Hiram Johnson on his Senate nomination. Film exists of Hughes speaking near Pittsburgh this day.
Roosevelt leaves New York for Battle Creek, Michigan.
Battle Creek speech on Wilson and labor

In Battle Creek, Roosevelt charges that Wilson fears organized labor and is angling for political gain. His article "The Fruits of Unpreparedness" runs in the Metropolitan, and another piece appears in the Ladies' Home Journal.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt addresses members of the Union League and comes face to face with Taft; the two shake hands and stand side by side, awkwardly. He also confers with Willcox.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt tells Corinne his Western tour on October 25 means skipping lunch with her and Fannie, that he is campaigning for Hughes, and that Teddy Robinson's state senate nomination pleases him.

Roosevelt confers with William R. Willcox at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt is at home on his son Kermit's 27th birthday.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as his niece Eleanor Roosevelt turns 32.
Roosevelt condemns the German submarine U-53 for sinking ships off the American coast, calling it a collapse of international rights.
Roosevelt writes Emmett Scott about immigrants and hard work in America.
Roosevelt delivers a speech in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

Western swing begins, with three reporters
Roosevelt sets out on a campaign tour, stopping in Rochester. Three reporters, Edwin D. Lewis plus Cronin (Sun) and Yoder (UP), ride and dine with him in his car each day.

Moving from Cincinnati to Louisville, where the crowds adore him, Roosevelt also speaks in Paris, Cynthiana, Winchester and Richmond, Kentucky; the reporters act as his bodyguard. His nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 18.
With William Allen White to Emporia
Roosevelt speaks in Missouri and Kansas, and William Allen White rides with him from Kansas City to Emporia.
Phoenix, and nature talk on the train
Roosevelt speaks in Phoenix. On the train he spins stories for the reporters and points out the plants and animals along the way, and he writes Edith that his voice is lasting.
Roosevelt leaves Phoenix for New Mexico.
Roosevelt gives talks around New Mexico, with stops in Albuquerque and Las Vegas. His grandson Cornelius V. S. Roosevelt turns one.
Roosevelt is greeted in Albuquerque in 100-degree heat, a reception caught on film, then gives speeches in Denver.
Roosevelt leaves Denver for Chicago and speaks in Iowa along the way.
Chicago street rally and Assembly Hall

After stops in Iowa and Illinois, a crowd rallies for Roosevelt outside the Congress Hotel and he speaks that evening at Assembly Hall. He wires Alvin Hert that he will not soften his attacks on Wilson.

On his 58th birthday Roosevelt speaks in Indiana, including South Bend. Leaving Buffalo in his Pullman, the three traveling reporters give him a penknife to replace one he lost; he hangs it on his watch chain next to his small gold pencil and Phi Beta Kappa key.
Back in New York, Roosevelt addresses an audience at Brooklyn's Academy of Music.
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.
Roosevelt wires W. H. Gillenwater about what he said while in New Mexico.
Roosevelt's article "Dollar Dove and Vulture" appears in the Metropolitan.
In the last week of the 1916 race, Roosevelt carries his stump tour through Ohio, with stops that include Toledo and Cleveland.
Roosevelt stays on the road in Ohio, speaking again as the presidential campaign nears its end.

Back in New York, Roosevelt addresses a crowd at Thomashefsky's National Theater, then gives his "Shadows of the Tortured Dead" speech at Cooper Union, one of his fiercest attacks on President Wilson. He also fires off a blistering letter to Amos Pinchot.

Roosevelt leaves New York for a Republican rally in Bridgeport, then heads to the Stratford, where Republican leader John T. King has a lamp burning for him and the two talk over party organization. He also wires Murray Cutting about Cutting's backing of Wilson.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Final campaign speech in Oyster Bay
On the eve of the election, Roosevelt speaks in his hometown of Oyster Bay. The journalist John Leary comes to see him.
Election Day: Wilson edges out Hughes

Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay. On election night Charles Evans Hughes looks like the winner, but Wilson pulls ahead as the count goes on, finishing with 277 electoral votes to 254. Many blamed Roosevelt's speeches for the loss, though Hughes did not. Roosevelt also writes Quentin, hoping he can get home for his birthday.

A day of letters after the defeat: Roosevelt tells William Willcox he will always be glad he supported Hughes, tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler the party should have chosen him instead, and asks Dr. Alexis Carrel about his new methods at the front. Edith, writing a friend, calls Wilson a hypocrite she must endure four more years.
New article in Ladies' Home Journal
A Roosevelt article is published in the Ladies' Home Journal.
Roosevelt spends the month based at Sagamore Hill while making regular trips into New York City.
Roosevelt and Edith mark thirty years of marriage. He writes William Allen White about the breakup of the Progressive Party, vowing to hold to the principles he fought for.

Roosevelt sends off his White House records for safekeeping at the Library of Congress: six cases that he and Edith had packed themselves. He also writes Henry Osborn about a possible Polynesian trip for January 1918. In Chicago, former Progressive leaders urge their followers to keep fighting inside the Republican Party.

Roosevelt closes the year at Sagamore Hill. Around this time his papers reach the Library of Congress in six locked cases, and two of his pieces come out: "The Election" in the Metropolitan, which pledges goodwill to Wilson, and "Discipline" in the Ladies' Home Journal.

Roosevelt opens the year with two letters to William Allen White, judging Hughes's campaign and scorning the slogan Wilson's backers ran on about keeping America at peace, and a long letter to the British editor John St. Loe Strachey about Wilson's peace overtures to Europe and a full assessment of Hughes.

At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's old hunting friend Frederick Courteney Selous dies fighting in East Africa at age 66.

Germany's ambassador declares that U-boats will now sink ships without warning and seeks to curb American shipping, and he is sent home with his passport. Roosevelt's article "The League to Enforce Peace" appears in the Metropolitan, and he writes Joseph Morrell about first backing Wilson and then opposing him.

Roosevelt writes Newton D. Baker, the Secretary of War, that he and Edith will give up their Jamaica holiday, and offers the government his own services along with a division he would raise himself.

The United States breaks off diplomatic relations with Germany, and Wilson addresses both houses of Congress. Roosevelt and Edith scrap a Caribbean holiday and an eight-month scientific expedition to Polynesia; he wants to lead a division against Germany. He also writes Elisabeth Cary about German-Americans.

William Howard Taft declares his support for universal military service. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Henry L. Stimson about his battle with Wilson and the pacifists, and writes Secretary Baker again about the division he hopes to raise and about Frank McCoy.

Kermit's son, Kermit Jr., called Kim, turns one. Roosevelt writes Ambassador Jusserand that a volunteer division could be ready in six months, and sends a similar letter to Cecil Spring-Rice.

Roosevelt goes into the city to watch a military drill on Governors Island with General Leonard Wood, on Alice and Nick's 11th anniversary. He writes Hiram Johnson a scathing judgment of Wilson, and other letters to William Allen White and William Patterson.

A visitor named Desmond calls at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt tells Lodge he is beginning to wonder whether anything at all could push Wilson into the war.

Eager for war, and for nature writing

Roosevelt tells Ambassador Jusserand he hopes America will enter the war soon, because he cannot take up arms before his country does. To Wilfred Osgood he wishes C. Hart Merriam and Edward Nelson would publish more on nature.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

Wilson seeks to arm merchant ships
President Wilson appears before Congress to request authority to put guns on American merchant vessels. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
King takes over as political manager; Quentin engaged

John T. King replaces George W. Perkins as Roosevelt's political manager; Roosevelt later backed King for Republican National Committee chairman, though Will Hays won the post. Quentin becomes engaged to Flora Payne Whitney.
Roosevelt, dividing his time between Oyster Bay and New York, travels to Hartford and calls on the nation to strike Germany with full force.
