Belgian Relief rally as Wilson takes the oath
Roosevelt addresses a Belgian Relief meeting in New York on the day Wilson is sworn in for his second term. He also writes Lawrence Abbott recalling how he came to join the staff of The Outlook.

Roosevelt speaks to a huge crowd at Carnegie Hall while Wilson's inauguration ceremonies take place in Washington. He writes geologist Joseph Barrell about climate change, human origins and the apes he saw in Africa.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Gathering facts on machine guns and planes

Roosevelt thanks Frederic Walcott for research on machine guns and aircraft for his planned division, and writes John C. O'Laughlin about the senators, led by La Follette, blocking the arming of merchant ships.
Applauding military drill in California schools
Roosevelt writes California state senator Will Sharkey to praise his push for military training in the state's high schools.

Dinner with Wood, Root and young Franklin
In New York, Roosevelt dines with C. N. Bliss, Morgan, Elihu Root, Meyer, Mayor Mitchel, General Leonard Wood and his cousin Franklin D. Roosevelt.
A provisional government takes power in Russia. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the 1903 treaty with Colombia and the effort to renegotiate it.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Czar Nicholas II of Russia abdicates. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

German submarines send three American vessels to the bottom: the Vigilancia, the Illinois and the City of Memphis. Roosevelt tells Lodge he has held his tongue for weeks and is fed up with talk of standing behind the President.
Roosevelt speaks out in public against Germany's attack on the three U.S. vessels and wires Secretary Baker once more for leave to raise a division.
At the Union League: a state of war exists

Speaking at the Union League Club in New York, Roosevelt argues that Germany's renewed submarine campaign means the two nations are already at war. He talks things over with Choate, Root and Hughes, and writes letters on the Colombia treaty and on a 1914 episode with the German ambassador.
Roosevelt writes John Richeson setting out his thinking on military preparedness.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about the obstacles he keeps hitting with Baker's War Department.
Off to Florida to hunt devilfish

Roosevelt leaves for Punta Gorda, Florida, to go after giant rays, called devilfish, with harpoon expert Russell J. Coles. Before going he writes Secretary Baker again about the division, citing his record as a soldier and former commander in chief.
On his way south, Roosevelt makes a speech in Jacksonville, Florida.
Roosevelt is at Punta Gorda on Florida's Gulf Coast for his devilfish hunt with Russell Coles.

Last day on the Florida waters; "Now We Must Fight"
Roosevelt winds up his devilfish trip at Punta Gorda. His article "Now We Must Fight" runs in the Metropolitan, and Ted and Archie are ordered to Plattsburg for active duty as reserve officers.
Roosevelt starts north, speaking at Punta Gorda and then at Lakeland as he goes.

As President Wilson goes before Congress to seek war against Germany, Roosevelt stops in Washington on his way north and calls at the White House to congratulate him, but Wilson is in a Cabinet meeting. Roosevelt issues a statement praising the President's step.
Roosevelt returns to New York City and goes on home to Sagamore Hill.
Ethel and her husband Dick Derby celebrate four years of marriage; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
In a published statement, Roosevelt calls for American soldiers to be sent to France without delay. He also talks privately with reporters.
Congress formally declares war against Germany. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

It is Archie's 23rd birthday; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.
Asking Wilson in person for a division

Roosevelt and Edith go to Washington, where he has a long White House talk with Wilson and asks to lead a division in France. Wilson gives no firm answer, but Roosevelt will in the end be kept out of the fight. Staying with Alice and Nick, he lobbies Baker, Jusserand, Spring-Rice and others for his plan.

After breakfast with Brigadier General Joseph Kuhn in Washington, Roosevelt goes home and formally breaks up the volunteer division, a ceremony held in his Trophy Room at home. He also writes Don Marquis about writing.
Asking Pershing to take his sons
Roosevelt asks General Pershing to accept his sons as officers. He thanks Secretary Baker for the April 10 meeting and urges Senator George Chamberlain to pass the draft bill.
Roosevelt and Edith set out for Boston. He sends John C. O'Laughlin a detailed account of his meeting with Wilson; Baker had courteously turned the division down.
Roosevelt and Edith watch Archie marry Grace Lockwood at Emmanuel Church in Boston. Quentin is best man, Ted, Kermit and Dick Derby serve as ushers, and Alice and Ethel are there too.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

Governor Charles Whitman offers to make Roosevelt a general in the state's National Guard, and he says no. He tells Cecil Spring-Rice that Quentin is starting flight training and asks whether Britain or France might take his volunteer division.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

Home Guard visit and a Mineola speech
Roosevelt welcomes Oyster Bay's Home Guard to Sagamore Hill. At Mineola he addresses a Farmers Club gathering and speaks for the Reserve Battalion.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Long letter to Baker on the rejection
Roosevelt writes Secretary Baker at length about the refusal of his division, the government's conscription plans and his own military career. He tells Frederick Allen he will not write to Lowell.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Medill McCormick about why he refused a general's commission in the state Guard.
Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is sure the government will never give him a war role. Quentin, meanwhile, has signed up as a sergeant in the Army's flying service.
Roosevelt goes into New York City and leaves for Chicago.
In Chicago Roosevelt speaks at the Stockyards Pavilion for the National Security League, and a parade is held. The same day the Army draft bill clears Congress.
Roosevelt travels back toward New York. It is his sister Corinne's 35th wedding anniversary.

In New York Roosevelt lunches with Count Ilya Tolstoy, wires Warren G. Harding about the draft bill, and writes his old Maine friend Bill Sewall that all four of his sons now wear uniforms. The Metropolitan prints his piece "The Brotherly Court of Philadelphia."
Living at Sagamore Hill and often in town, Roosevelt writes Alexander Moore that American industry must be mobilized for the war, and writes Ilya Tolstoy about the revolution in Russia.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Preparedness talk with Stimson and Choate
In New York Roosevelt joins Henry L. Stimson and Choate at a preparedness meeting held at the Harvard Club.
Secretary of War Baker writes once more to explain why Roosevelt's division cannot be accepted.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt reports that applications to join his proposed division are pouring in at about 2,000 a day.
At Brooklyn's Kismet Temple Roosevelt makes the case for preparedness and sends Secretary Baker another long appeal with details of his division, objecting to reliance on the National Guard.
Roosevelt attends a dinner for the visiting French Mission at Henry Clay Frick's New York home and meets Marshal Joseph Joffre.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Waldorf dinner for the Allied missions
At a Waldorf-Astoria dinner honoring the French and British Missions, Roosevelt talks again with Marshal Joffre. Baker's latest reply holds to the same refusal.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt spends four hours at Sagamore Hill with British statesman Arthur Balfour and Ian Malcolm, a Member of Parliament.
Bat Masterson writes Roosevelt about helping to organize the division for service in Europe.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Call on Governor Whitman in Albany
Roosevelt travels by way of New York City to Albany and calls on Governor Charles Whitman.
Roosevelt tells Bamie he is getting four to five thousand letters a week, likens Wilson to James Buchanan, and says he cannot picture waging the Civil War under so weak a president.
Wire to Wilson: let me raise two divisions

Roosevelt telegraphs Wilson seeking leave to form two divisions and take them straight to the front; Wilson answers that volunteer divisions will not be used. He asks Pershing to take Ted and Archie to France with the first troops, and praises Lodge's Senate attack on Wilson. Quentin is having back trouble.
At the Metropolitan magazine office in New York, Roosevelt sees visitors including A. P. Moore.
Roosevelt writes General Pershing to congratulate him on being picked to lead the American army going to France.
Roosevelt writes a message for the many men who had hoped to serve under him; it will be released on May 25.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes his daughter-in-law Belle that Ethel is visiting. Late in the afternoon in the North Room, he, Ethel, Dick and young Richard put "Garry Owen" on the Victrola and dance.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt formally releases and thanks the men who signed up for his division, which he says could have reached 200,000. He sends Charles J. Bonaparte the full exchange with Wilson from May 18.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
In remarks carried by the press, French leader Georges Clemenceau urges Roosevelt to rethink giving up the volunteer division.
Yale Club talk; a rebuke for White
Roosevelt speaks at the Yale Club in New York and writes William Allen White that he is shocked by White's praise of Wilson.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

At Mineola Roosevelt reviews the Nassau County Sheriff's Reserve Corps and gives a Memorial Day speech. He writes Ted about his efforts to get the boys into the war, and delights in Ted's wife Eleanor and the children, who are staying at Sagamore Hill.

Quentin is accepted at Mineola. Roosevelt's article "Liberal Russia" runs in the Metropolitan, and his message to soldiers is printed in American Bible Society Bibles for the troops. Ted and Archie leave Plattsburg under confidential orders.
Roosevelt writes Captain de Rochambeau of the French 5th Infantry Regiment that the American government will not let him go to France.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells Augustus Gardner he wants to serve, and thanks Georges Clemenceau for his editorial urging Wilson to send Roosevelt to France.
In New York, Roosevelt speaks to the American Medical Association's convention.

In Philadelphia Roosevelt speaks at memorial services held by the Railroad Brotherhood and the Order of Railway Telegraphers.
Kermit and Belle mark three years of marriage; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Nebraska.
In Lincoln, Roosevelt speaks at the celebration of Nebraska's 50 years of statehood. Back east, grandson Theodore Roosevelt III turns three.
Roosevelt travels back east from Nebraska.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Ethel and Dick Derby welcome a daughter, Edith Roosevelt Derby.
Seeking a British post for Kermit
Roosevelt asks Arthur Lee to use his influence to get Kermit into British service in Mesopotamia.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Ted and Archie sail for France

On Ted's seventh wedding anniversary, he and Archie sail for France aboard the Chicago. Ted's wife Eleanor and Alice come to Sagamore Hill, where the British publisher Lord Northcliffe is visiting; through him Roosevelt arranges Kermit's British commission. He tells Arthur Lee his sons should be allowed to fight at the front.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes General Leonard Wood about his choice of sites for training camps in the South. Since April 2 Roosevelt has refrained from criticizing Wilson.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Red Cross meeting and the Italian Mission
Roosevelt addresses a Red Cross gathering, and the visiting Italian Mission calls at Sagamore Hill along with Lloyd Griscom.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.
Against excluding foreign-born from the Red Cross
Roosevelt writes C. A. A. McGee objecting to the barring of people born in enemy countries from Red Cross service in France.
Roosevelt writes Ted's wife Eleanor that he misses her and the children. Quentin and Belle are expected to drive over later.

His latest Metropolitan article, on the kind of peace worth fighting for, is published. Ted and Archie are now officers with Pershing in France; Kermit, now a British officer, is preparing to go to Mesopotamia by way of England; and Quentin has passed his flying exams despite poor eyes and a bad back. Quentin is quietly engaged to Flora Payne Whitney.

Roosevelt writes to thank Marion Couthouy Smith for a poem about him, and sends Kermit a letter on getting ready to ship out, adding that he does not approve of wives following their husbands overseas.
Independence Day speech at Forest Hills

Roosevelt addresses an enormous Fourth of July crowd at Forest Hills, Queens, and reviews the local rifle club; cameras record the occasion. In France the same day, Pershing's American troops parade into Paris.
Roosevelt writes Ralph M. Easley about the behavior of certain German-Americans during the war.
Clash with Gompers at Carnegie Hall

At a Carnegie Hall rally held by American Friends of Russian Freedom, Roosevelt and labor leader Samuel Gompers spar openly on stage over the deadly race riots that had just torn through East St. Louis.

Roosevelt sets aside his objection to wives going overseas and gives his blessing to Ted's wife Eleanor, who is bound for France to work with the YMCA. Lord Northcliffe pays a call, and word comes that Kermit must be ready to go by Tuesday.
Alice tracks Kermit down in Boston
After hours on long-distance calls, Alice finally reaches her brother Kermit in Boston, where John Singer Sargent is drawing his portrait.
Kermit, his wife Belle and little Kim come into New York and share a hotel breakfast with Alice. Roosevelt goes into the city to see Kermit, and Alice heads back to Washington.

Kermit set to sail for Mesopotamia
Kermit, Belle and little Kim are about to leave for Mesopotamia. He telephones Alice, who hurries back to New York.
Roosevelt, his wife Edith and Alice go down to the pier to wave off Kermit, Belle and Kim, who board the Carpathia for England on the way to the war in Mesopotamia.

Writing a labor leader on lawlessness
In a letter to Victor A. Olander, Roosevelt takes up labor, the East St. Louis race riots, the I.W.W. and lawlessness in general, and returns to the Brownsville affair.
The Outlook carries Roosevelt's review of Albert Beveridge's two-volume life of Chief Justice John Marshall.
Roosevelt meets with Mrs. Baker to discuss votes for women.
As Alexander Kerensky takes over as Russia's prime minister, Roosevelt sends a salute to the Russian people through Prince Georgy Lvov, with a like message to Mikhail Tereshchenko.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Edith tucks her youngest, Quentin, into bed one final time before he leaves for France the next morning.

Roosevelt, Edith and Alice say goodbye to Quentin at the 14th Street pier as he boards the Orduna with his school and college friend Hamilton Coolidge. Edith writes Ethel that the house on the hill now stands empty of its boys, borrowing a line from Edwin Arlington Robinson.
Ted's wife Eleanor leaves for France aboard the Espagne to take up YMCA work.
Roosevelt sets out for Pittsburgh. He writes Archibald Coolidge about the Celts, and a newsy letter arrives from Quentin for Edith.
Roosevelt gives a speech in Pittsburgh to the Loyal Order of Moose at its convention.
Back home, Roosevelt writes Augustus Post in favor of air power, and tells George F. Miller that Japan is sending no soldiers to Europe while seizing whatever territory it can in China.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Farmers, Beveridge and the Baker letters

Roosevelt writes Ray McKaig about farmers backing the war and sends Albert Beveridge news and comments on his book. The Metropolitan prints his exchange with War Secretary Newton D. Baker over the volunteer division Roosevelt had hoped to raise.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Sending William Allen White to France

William Allen White is heading to France for the Red Cross, and Roosevelt supplies him with letters of introduction. In the same letter he judges the administration's war preparations harshly and finds fault with Wilson's character.
A party of some 120 students from the West, attending Columbia's summer session, comes calling at Sagamore Hill.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Edith turns 56; a letter on Ireland

It is Edith's 56th birthday. Roosevelt writes the Irish poet George W. Russell that he favors home rule for Ireland, but warns that the Ulster counties cannot be split off from the rest of the island.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

Roosevelt writes Ted that he is delighted his son now has a regular command with the 26th Infantry of the 1st Division. He passes along news of Archie, Quentin and Kermit, reports that grandson Richard Derby Jr. has had his appendix out, and notes that little Gracie is staying for two weeks.
Calling for a ban on German-language papers
Roosevelt issues a public statement urging that German-language newspapers be outlawed in the United States. Quentin, held up for a long spell at Halifax, is at last steaming across the Atlantic.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Quentin's ship docks at Liverpool, and a troop train rushes him and Ham Coolidge to Folkestone to catch a boat across the Channel.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

In New York, Roosevelt speaks at a reception honoring Elihu Root and the American mission just back from Russia, then talks about the war at the Harvard Club. He also writes Lodge about the conflict and what he sees as Wilson's failings.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Gracie turns six; letters on free speech

Granddaughter Grace has her sixth birthday. Roosevelt writes the city's police commissioner denouncing antiwar protesters, objects to Thomas E. Watson about government censorship of The Jeffersonian, and sends his English friend Arthur Lee a sharp assessment of the President.
Quentin is in Paris, lodging at 29 Rue Villejust.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Quentin takes up duties as supply officer at the American flying camp at Issoudun.
Quentin has a motorcycle accident in France.

The Belgian Mission comes to Sagamore Hill along with Coudert and O'Connor, and Roosevelt speaks to the crowd gathered on his lawn. He writes Ted of his pride in his sons. In France, Quentin wrecks a motorcycle for the second time.
Dinner with Perkins; Quentin learns to fly

Roosevelt dines with R. P. Perkins. He confides to Archie how much he dislikes giving rousing "bugle call" speeches, and tells daughter-in-law Eleanor in France about a picnic boat outing with Edith. Quentin is learning to fly at Issoudun, home of the American aviation school.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Quentin explores Bourges, and his command of French makes it easy for him to obtain supplies for the Issoudun camp.
Captain Bertrand Vigne of the Chasseurs Alpins comes to Sagamore Hill for lunch.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt tours the American Museum of Natural History in the company of Coles and Luther. He writes Senator Hiram Johnson about limiting war profits and tells Joel Spingarn which poems he enjoys.
Roosevelt writes William Greenough on two subjects: Woodrow Wilson and Hannibal.
Benefit speech at the Comedy Theater
Roosevelt speaks at New York's Comedy Theater to raise money for the Divisional Headquarters Fund.
Four sons and a son-in-law in uniform

From the Union League Club balcony, Roosevelt reviews a parade of the New York National Guard, and his essay "Must We Be Brayed in a Mortar Before Our Folly Depart From Us?" runs in The Metropolitan. By now Ted commands a battalion of the 26th Infantry in France, Kermit serves with British engineers in Mesopotamia, Archie leads a company in Ted's division, and Quentin handles supplies at Issoudun.
A round of letters to the boys

Roosevelt writes all three sons in France: praise for Ted, a promise to Quentin that he will help him and Archie get started once the war ends, and a note to Archie carrying Edith's first error-strewn try at typing. He adds how much he enjoys having little Gracie in the house.
Camp Mills and a Garden City speech
Roosevelt visits the troops at Camp Mills near Mineola and speaks on military preparedness at Garden City, with film cameras on hand.
Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan; no details are recorded.

In New York, Roosevelt joins Mayor John Purroy Mitchel, Charles Evans Hughes and others to review a parade of newly drafted men, and the scene is filmed. He writes Judge Emory Speer that while he rejects the views of Tom Watson's Jeffersonian, the government has no business barring it from circulation.
Speaking at the Columbia County Fair

Roosevelt is the speaker at Chatham's Columbia County Fair, New York. The Outlook prints his "The Children of the Crucible," a call for Americans to stand together against Germany, along with his tribute to Roger Allier, killed in France. Quentin, meanwhile, is hauling equipment across France through storms and floods.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Rowing with the grandchildren; officers to dinner

Roosevelt and Edith take grandchildren Richard and Edith Derby out in the rowboat, while their mother Ethel remains with Dick. In the evening Major William Donovan comes to dinner with four of his 165th Infantry captains at the house.
Opening the suffrage campaign; four stars

Roosevelt speaks at the launch of New York's second state suffrage campaign. He tells Archie he has hung out a service flag with a star for each of his four sons overseas, and writes Senator Frank B. Kellogg for a graduated tax on war contractors' excess profits.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Asking Gorgas to send Dick to the front
Roosevelt writes Surgeon General William Gorgas asking that his son-in-law Dick Derby be assigned to the front.
A good word for Russell Coles
In a letter to Judge Joseph Buffington, Roosevelt speaks warmly of Russell Coles.

On Ted's 30th birthday, Roosevelt goes to the Mineola flying field with the Hitchcocks and goes up in a Liberty-engine airplane, then writes Ted about his brief flight with the trainee pilots. In France, Quentin joins the 1st Aero Squadron and stays with Eleanor in Paris.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt writes Dr. George C. Dyer about the war. Edith tells Kermit that his absence is harder on his wife Belle than on herself.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
How to rise in the Army
Roosevelt writes Archie about getting ahead as an Army officer.
Roosevelt and Edith set off on a trip west. In France, Quentin is asked to remain with the supply unit at Issoudun.
Roosevelt stops in Chicago on his way west.
Signing on with the Kansas City Star

At the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt signs a $25,000-a-year contract to write for the paper, while keeping his short monthly Metropolitan editorial at $5,000 a year. He and Edith stay with the Star's editor, Kirkwood.
Roosevelt remains in Kansas City; nothing else is noted.
Speeches and a talk with Wood
Roosevelt makes speeches in Kansas City and meets with General Leonard Wood.
Roosevelt leaves Kansas City and travels toward Illinois.
Roosevelt tours Camp Grant at Rockford, Illinois, and speaks for the National Security League. Edith heads home, and writes Ruth Lee that she is well pleased with his Kansas City Star deal.
Fort Sheridan, Great Lakes and Racine
A full day of speaking: Roosevelt addresses audiences at Fort Sheridan, at the Navy's Great Lakes training station and in Racine, Wisconsin. It is his sister Corinne's 56th birthday.
Roosevelt speaks in both St. Paul and Minneapolis, and writes Archie about the Kansas City visit and the training camps on his route.
Roosevelt starts back toward New York, stopping in Chicago.

Roosevelt is the speaker for a Workingmen's Red Cross Sunday program in Johnstown, Pennsylvania. Back at Sagamore Hill, Flora Whitney pays a visit and writes Quentin how much she loves the place, while Edith keeps practicing her typing.
The Foes of Our Own Household published

Doran brings out Roosevelt's new book, The Foes of Our Own Household, its title an idea of Edith's. That evening he speaks in New York for John Purroy Mitchel, who is fighting to keep the mayor's office.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Members of the Japanese Mission visit Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.
Praise for Hoover, complaints to Munsey

Roosevelt addresses the Methodist Episcopal Church's Social Service Commission in New York. He complains to publisher Frank Munsey about the nation's unreadiness and commends Herbert Hoover for his handling of food supply and rationing.
Roosevelt speaks to a patriotic gathering at Madison Square Garden. He tells his sister Corinne he plans a stay in Stamford to drop some weight, and explains why he is backing Mitchel.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt writes his old Maine guide and Elkhorn partner Bill Sewall to introduce Hermann Hagedorn, who later interviewed Sewall for his books on Roosevelt's Badlands years.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Off to Jack Cooper's health farm

Roosevelt heads to Jack Cooper's training camp in Stamford, Connecticut, for a course of diet and exercise meant to trim him down and restore his stamina. Kermit marks his 28th birthday with the British in Mesopotamia.
Roosevelt continues his stay at the Stamford health farm. His niece Eleanor Roosevelt turns 33.
Still at the Stamford health farm
Roosevelt remains at Jack Cooper's camp in Stamford working on his diet and exercise program; nothing else is noted.
Still at the Stamford health farm
Roosevelt remains at Jack Cooper's camp in Stamford working on his diet and exercise program; nothing else is noted.
