Still at the Stamford health farm
Roosevelt remains at Jack Cooper's camp in Stamford working on his diet and exercise program; nothing else is noted.
Writing in the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt insists that the United States declare war on Germany's partners as well. Nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 19.
Still at the Stamford health farm
Roosevelt remains at Jack Cooper's camp in Stamford working on his diet and exercise program; nothing else is noted.

From Stamford, Roosevelt writes Ted about his work for the war effort, and sends daughter-in-law Eleanor an account of life at Jack Cooper's and of romping with her children, telling her how dearly he loves them.
Roosevelt's stay at the Stamford health farm continues; film footage exists for the day.
Home from Stamford, fourteen pounds lighter
Roosevelt comes home from Stamford having shed 14 pounds and three and a half inches around the waist, though Edith sees little real benefit. She writes Ethel that the stay wore on his nerves.
Ted's son Cornelius V. S. Roosevelt turns two while staying with his grandparents at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt speaks on behalf of the Liberty Loan drive.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt writes Ernest E. Smith in anger over Frederic C. Howe's article "Financial Imperialism."
Turning 59 with a houseful of grandchildren
On his 59th birthday Roosevelt writes Ted's wife Eleanor about her children, Gracie, Teddy and Cornelius, who are living with their grandparents while Ted and Eleanor serve in Europe.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt goes into New York to give speeches for Mayor Mitchel's reelection campaign.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

The Metropolitan prints Roosevelt's "The German Kaiser and the German People." Corinne's son, Captain Monroe Robinson, is serving with the 77th Division's ammunition train at Camp Upton on Long Island.
Campaigning for Mitchel; a job for Joe Murray

Roosevelt makes speeches in New York for Mayor John Purroy Mitchel. He asks Grayson Murphy whether his old political friend Joe Murray might be taken on by the Red Cross in France. A letter arrives from Quentin describing French towns and the cathedral city of Chartres.
A school visit and a Hartford rally
Roosevelt inspects Public School 45 in New York, then travels to Hartford to address Connecticut war workers at the State Armory.
In Bridgeport, Connecticut, Roosevelt inspects munitions factories and gives a speech on behalf of S. Merritt.
Dinner with King, Leary and Bridgeport police
Roosevelt dines with John T. King, the reporter John J. Leary, six Bridgeport policemen and others before heading home. Ethel and Dick are staying at Sagamore Hill.
Roosevelt hands out medals to Boy Scouts of Nassau County and sends news to his sister Corinne.
Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay, and son-in-law Nick Longworth wins another term in Congress. He also writes George Dyer about his push for war declarations against Germany's allies.
The Bolsheviks seize power in Russia. Roosevelt writes Ted that Ethel will soon see Dick off to France, and writes Representative Ernest Lundeen about his opposition to the war.
At the Hotel Langdon in New York, Roosevelt lunches with Corinne and his old friend Patty Selmes, and they trade stories of the Dakota days and the Marquis de Mores.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Breakfast for all in New Rochelle
On the drive back to New York from Bridgeport, Roosevelt stops at New Rochelle's Post Road Inn and picks up the breakfast bill for the whole party.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Son-in-law Dick Derby leaves for Europe to serve in the Army Medical Corps.
Roosevelt writes Lodge about embargoes on neutral nations that trade with Germany, advising a careful approach.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

At Princeton, Roosevelt delivers "National Strength and International Duty," talks to the undergraduate battalion, dines with President John Grier Hibben and his wife, and stays for the student smoker.
Still at Princeton, Roosevelt writes Quentin on the anniversary of his engagement to Edith, telling his son he is as much in love with her as ever.
Speaking to the troops at Camp Upton
Roosevelt addresses soldiers at Camp Upton in Yaphank, Long Island.
Quentin marks his 20th birthday in France.
Roosevelt speaks in New York at the state convention of the Woman Suffrage Party.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

Roosevelt sets off for a Canadian speaking tour with Edith, Ethel and Flora Whitney. He tells William Hornaday that teachers who will not sign the loyalty oath should lose their jobs. It is his sister Bamie's 22nd wedding anniversary.
Roosevelt speaks in Hamilton and Toronto, Ontario. He writes James Bryce about the conflict and the upheaval in Russia, and Thomas Nowlin on the Mooney bombing case in California.
Roosevelt returns through New York City to Oyster Bay.
Roosevelt has Smoot and Madden to lunch at Sagamore Hill.

On Thanksgiving, Roosevelt writes Ted that Alice is visiting and Ethel and her children are at the house too, and fills him in on his war speeches. He also writes Kermit, who is now serving in Baghdad as an engineer captain.
Roosevelt's "A Permanent Training Policy" runs in The Metropolitan, faulting the country for failing to prepare before the war.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt and Edith mark 31 years of marriage.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
French Ambassador Jean Jules Jusserand, an old friend, comes to lunch.
Roosevelt gives a talk for the Allied War Bazaar at New York's Grand Central Palace.
The United States declares war on Austria-Hungary, a step Roosevelt had been urging for weeks.
Pennsylvania Society dinner; Quentin takes command

Roosevelt speaks at a Pennsylvania Society of New York dinner. At Issoudun, Quentin is put in charge of the headquarters detachment, some 600 cadets and 40 officers flying Nieuports; a couple of weeks earlier he had nearly been burned in one.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Wartime prohibition and the Mooney case
Roosevelt tells Clarence True Wilson he favors prohibition while the war lasts, and writes Chester Rowell about the Mooney and Billings trials.
Roosevelt commends Senator James Wadsworth for bringing to light the shortages in Army training camps.
Roosevelt travels to Cincinnati, Ohio, and attends a dinner at a businessmen's club.
At Camp Sherman near Chillicothe, Ohio, Roosevelt sees for himself that the troops are short of machine guns and artillery.
Red Cross talk; Quentin falls ill
Roosevelt speaks in Hempstead for a Red Cross campaign. In France, pneumonia forces Quentin to stop training pilots.
Snow covers Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt spends two hours sledding with his grandson Richard.

In the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt stands behind Senator Wadsworth's charges of Army shortages. He writes Dick Derby about Ethel and the children. Quentin is hospitalized in France with pneumonia and will later be nursed by his sister-in-law Eleanor.
Roosevelt writes Felix Frankfurter about the Mooney trial, arguing that the recall of District Attorney Charles Fickert was not justified.
The Kansas City Star runs another Roosevelt editorial on the Army's shortages.
Roosevelt delivers presents to his son Ted's three youngsters, and writes George W. Perkins about William Randolph Hearst and about Japan.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt writes daughter-in-law Eleanor about the gifts he has given the grandchildren and tells her how much he loves the soaps she mailed him.

Alice and Nick join the family for Christmas Eve dinner. Everyone goes to sing carols at Christ Church, where Roosevelt speaks at the Christmas party, and he makes calls on neighbors; the day is captured on film. He also presses Quentin to keep up a steady correspondence with Flora.

Alice and Nick, plus Ethel with her son Richard and infant daughter Edith, come for Christmas dinner while Eleanor spends the holiday with the YMCA in France. Roosevelt sends Christmas wishes to Grace, news to Ted, and tells Kermit how much he values Alice's political judgment.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
In the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt ridicules troops drilling with broomsticks instead of real weapons. The thermometer stands at zero, with Nick and Cousin Laura staying as guests.
Roosevelt tells Archie's wife Grace he is delighted by Archie's promotion and offers money if she needs it. A letter from Quentin reports a joyless Christmas.
A bird under the piazza roof
On a bitter day, Roosevelt steps out the front door to read the thermometer and startles a small bird that had been sheltering on the piazza.
Edith writes Archie about the family's sparse Christmas, with only the two daughters at home to share it.

Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie about the fierce cold. Around this time London recalls its ambassador, Cecil Spring-Rice, John T. King serves as Roosevelt's spokesman in the Midwest and West, Eleanor sets up YMCA centers at Aix and Chambéry, and The Metropolitan prints "Put the War Through."
New Year's Day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt begins 1918 at home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.
Defense groups, suffrage and a doctor's bill

Roosevelt explains to L. B. Hayes how the American Defense Society differs from the National Security League, presses William Willcox to act on woman suffrage, and tells Archie's wife Grace he will cover her doctor's bill.
Roosevelt writes General John Biddle about shortfalls in manpower and training.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Edith sends Kermit a letter about music.
Roosevelt writes Heywood Broun that he likes his articles about the Army.
President Wilson lays out his Fourteen Points for peace in an address to Congress.
Roosevelt speaks at commencement for the Peirce School in Philadelphia.
Roosevelt divides the day between home and Manhattan; no details are recorded.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
In New York, Roosevelt speaks to the Ohio Society.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Roosevelt writes Raymond Robins about Russia and makes plain his dislike of the Bolsheviks.
Recovered from pneumonia, Quentin returns from Paris to the Issoudun camp.
East Side homes and a new grandson

Roosevelt speaks at an American Defense Society trustees' lunch, then tours homes on the Lower East Side with the Community Clearing House to see child malnutrition firsthand. Kermit and Belle's son Joseph Willard Roosevelt is born, and Roosevelt praises Caspar Whitney's reporting on shortages at the front.
Touring the city's child welfare work
With the Community Clearing House, Roosevelt visits an infant welfare station, the Boy Food Scouts at P.S. 40, the neighborhood association at Bowling Green, and the Post Graduate Hospital.
On his sister Bamie's 63rd birthday, Roosevelt writes Belle about her new baby.
Roosevelt speaks to the League for Political Education and at the Society of the Genesee's dinner.
Roosevelt pays tribute to Joseph H. Choate at a memorial service and at a National Security League luncheon.
Roosevelt and Edith leave for Washington, D.C.

Staying with Alice and Nick, Roosevelt receives a stream of senators and congressmen, among them Chamberlain, Hale, Curtis, Wadsworth, Kahn, Lenroot, Madden and Gallivan. He lunches with Senator Hiram Johnson and dines with John T. King, R. K. Hynicka and a dozen lawmakers.
Pinchot lunch and a bad night

Roosevelt confers with politicians and lunches with Gifford Pinchot, then suffers a severe bout of indigestion; a doctor sees him and sends him to bed early. He writes Richard Hurd that Thorstein Veblen ought to be jailed for a book he wrote.
After another round of meetings, a lunch with Senator James Phelan and dinner with Lodge, Roosevelt takes the podium at the National Press Club and lays into the War Department.
Roosevelt breakfasts with New York's members of Congress, calls on Franklin D. Roosevelt, and with Edith and Alice dines with Henry Adams and McCormick before heading back to New York.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Snowed in, fires in the Library

A heavy snowstorm hits; the North Room is shut and fires burn in the Library. Roosevelt writes Quentin that Edith is in Baltimore with Belle Hagner James while he stays home with Ethel. In France, Quentin is weary of camp life but flying more.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Dedicating a hall at Camp Merritt
Roosevelt helps dedicate a new hall at Camp Merritt, New Jersey. In France, Quentin receives a parcel of books from home.
Roosevelt writes Albert Shaw about America's sluggish shipbuilding and Grace Macurdy about the war. The Metropolitan publishes his "The Countrymen of Muhlenberg and Custer."
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Kermit at Tekrit; shoes for Archie's men

Roosevelt is thrilled to learn that Kermit helped capture Tekrit in Mesopotamia the previous November, and writes him and Belle about it, adding news of the children and his views on the Bolsheviks. He tells Archie he will personally pay to put 200 pairs of shoes on the feet of Archie's soldiers.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.
Who should run the Republican committee
Roosevelt attends a private lunch in New York and writes John T. Adams, who hopes to chair the Republican National Committee; the post would eventually go to Will Hays.

While dictating to his secretary Josephine Stricker, Roosevelt is felled when an abscess bursts where he was wounded in the thigh years before; in great pain and losing blood, he faints. He is taken to Roosevelt Hospital, where doctors find infection in both middle ears. He sends Will Hays word on whom to consult while he is laid up.
Roosevelt's ear infection gets worse. Alice stays at his side, and Miss Strand is his nurse.
Mastoid surgery leaves him deaf in one ear
As rumors fly that Roosevelt is near death, surgeons perform a radical mastoid operation on his left ear, which leaves him without hearing on that side.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York; nothing else is noted.
On Alice's 34th birthday, Roosevelt wires Bamie that his illness forces him to cancel his trip, though he still hopes to see her son Sheffield on Friday.
While Roosevelt is still in the hospital, Archie and Grace have a son, Archibald Roosevelt Jr., the eighth Roosevelt grandchild.
Roosevelt's old friend Cecil Spring-Rice, the former British ambassador, dies in Ottawa.
Joseph Bucklin Bishop and George W. Perkins call at the hospital.
On grandson Kim's second birthday, The New York Times reports speculation that plans are afoot for a Roosevelt presidential run in 1920.
Alice and Nick Longworth mark 12 years of marriage while Roosevelt recuperates in the hospital.

Lemuel Quigg, Henry P. Fletcher, William Willcox and George Cortelyou visit. Roosevelt writes George W. Perkins about the talk of a 1920 run, and tells Kermit about the operation and his efforts to get Kermit transferred to the French front.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York; nothing else is noted.
Better not to go to England
From his hospital bed, Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about his surgery and the progress of the war, and concludes it is wiser not to travel to England.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York; nothing else is noted.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York; nothing else is noted.
Joseph Bucklin Bishop, nephew T. D. Robinson and a Major General Allen come to see Roosevelt.
Roosevelt praises Archie, but tells him that a planned article drawn from his letters home is off: they are too political and too critical of the War Department.
Roosevelt meets with Republican chairman Will Hays, and visitors include Bishop, Cortelyou and diplomat Edwin V. Morgan.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York; nothing else is noted.

Word comes that Archie has been severely wounded, his kneecap shattered and his left arm broken with the main nerve severed; he receives the Croix de Guerre. From the hospital Roosevelt writes Grace, Quentin, Martin Hutchens and James Walsh, and The Metropolitan carries his "Service and Self Respect."
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York. No other activity is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt remains a patient at Roosevelt Hospital in New York. No other activity is recorded for the day.
Russia signs a separate peace with Germany
Roosevelt is still in Roosevelt Hospital as Germany and Russia conclude the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, closing the war in the east.

Roosevelt checks out of Roosevelt Hospital and moves into the Hotel Langdon on Fifth Avenue. He writes Will Hays about the Wisconsin Senate seat, asks William Howard Taft for advice on his upcoming Portland speech, and writes Archie about the new baby.
Russell Coles calls at the Langdon
Roosevelt is staying at the Hotel Langdon, where his visitors include Russell Coles.
Roosevelt stays on at the Hotel Langdon in New York. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt leaves New York and goes back to Sagamore Hill. In France, Quentin is learning aerial gunnery at Cazaux, and General Leonard Wood is there too.
A letter about Archie's son and twisted words
Roosevelt writes Archie about the grandson he has not yet laid eyes on, and about remarks of his that were bent to suggest Ted and Archie called the army a "den of iniquity."
Death of George von Lengerke Meyer
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the day George von Lengerke Meyer, who served in his Cabinet, dies.
Roosevelt sends his regrets to Alice Meyer, widow of George von Lengerke Meyer.
Roosevelt tells Kermit he believes the Bolsheviks have wrecked Russia. Edmund Heller had come to see him while he was in the hospital.
Thank-you notes from a mending patient

Roosevelt catches up on mail as he heals. He tells H. Rider Haggard and Henry Stimson he is getting better, hopes to see Henry Clay Frick's new art purchases, and thanks King George V for cabling him in the hospital.
Archie wins the Croix de Guerre

The United Press telephones Sagamore Hill with word that Archie has received the Croix de Guerre. Roosevelt, Edith, Ethel and a friend toast him with Madeira and smash the glasses, and Roosevelt writes Archie with his love.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes William Howard Taft about Taft's ideas for his March 28 speech. Elihu Root and Henry Cabot Lodge have also weighed in.
Roosevelt writes Quentin about Archie and about marrying Flora. To Archie's wife Grace he passes on news of Archie's injuries, hoping they are serious enough to bring him home.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes French premier Georges Clemenceau with harsh words for publisher William Randolph Hearst.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes his English friend Arthur Lee that the two of them see the war and humanity's future much alike. Both grieve the death of Cecil Spring-Rice.
Roosevelt writes Republican chairman Will Hays about the party, the role of women in it, and William Randolph Hearst.
Henry Adams dies; off to Boston
Word comes that Henry Adams has died of a stroke. Roosevelt and Edith travel through New York City to Boston, where they stay with William Sturgis Bigelow.
Speaking to the Maine Republican State Convention in Portland, Roosevelt lays out an updated version of his New Nationalism program. Edith stays behind in Boston.

In Boston, Roosevelt and Edith see Archie's wife Grace and the infant Archibald Jr., again staying with William Sturgis Bigelow. In France, Quentin is back at Issoudun after wrecking his plane; his crew decorates the new one in red, white and blue.
Roosevelt is home again at Sagamore Hill. No other activity is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Archie about meeting the baby. The Metropolitan carries his article about a trip to Manhattan's East Side.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Liberty Loan talk from the piazza
Roosevelt speaks on behalf of the Liberty Loan from the piazza at Sagamore Hill.
Motion-picture film shows Roosevelt out walking near Sagamore Hill.

On Ethel's fifth wedding anniversary, Roosevelt writes William Allen White that his Portland speech points the way the country should now go, and that he wants the Republicans to be a party of reform as in Lincoln's day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Backing more men for the 27th Division
Roosevelt gives his support to raising 3,700 additional volunteers for New York's 27th Division.
Edith has proposed that Quentin bring Flora to France and marry her there, and Quentin thinks it a fine plan.
Roosevelt writes Senator John Sharp Williams that he agrees with the effort to throw Robert La Follette out of the Senate, and adds a word on wartime breads made without wheat.
Archie turns 24 in a French hospital
Archie marks his 24th birthday while recovering from his wounds in France. Roosevelt writes George Otto Trevelyan about Archie's injuries and his four sons at war.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Charles Van Hise about government price controls during the war.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Trying to get Kermit into the U.S. Army
Roosevelt tells Ted he has asked Chief of Staff Peyton March whether Kermit, who has served well with the British in Mesopotamia, can move to the American army in France.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes General Leonard Wood about what Wood saw while touring the lines in France and the shortages Wood found there.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Liberty Loan appeal to the Women's Civic League
Roosevelt speaks to the Women's Civic League in support of the Liberty Loan.
Defending his words on Thomas Paine

Roosevelt replies to a query from W. M. Van der Weyde concerning the line in his Gouverneur Morris biography calling Thomas Paine a "filthy little Atheist," and shares his views on the war with Alfred Holman.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells Kermit's wife Belle that turning his head quickly leaves him dizzy, and writes about Kermit heading to France. To Quentin he sends news of spring and his own doings.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Edwin Van Valkenburg about politics and why some publishers shy away from his sharply worded articles.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt gives a speech at Fort Totten, New York, and writes Royal Cortissoz that Woodrow Wilson has degraded both the nation and morality.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his sister Corinne's 36th wedding anniversary.
Two articles and a visit from Masefield

Roosevelt's The American Museum Journal publishes his "My Life as a Naturalist," and "Lincoln and Free Speech" in The Metropolitan. English poet John Masefield visits Sagamore Hill. Kermit moves from a British armored battery to an American artillery regiment while Quentin keeps training pilots at Issoudun.
Back on the road: Blue Devils and Springfield

Roosevelt picks up his full pace again. At the Harvard Club in New York he greets the Blue Devils, the French Alpine chasseurs, then speaks in Springfield, Massachusetts, for the Hampden County Improvement League.
Liberty Loan speech at the Naval Service Club
In Boston Roosevelt rallies support for war bonds at the Naval Service Club. He writes James Bryce about the war and William Allen White about where the Republicans go next.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Quentin walks away from a crash
News arrives that Quentin has cracked up his plane, steering clear of people on the field and going into some trees. He writes of the funerals of the aces Guynemer and Richthofen.
Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie to arrange a visit to Farmington, and tells Belle that Grace and the baby are staying with them and that Kermit is being moved to France.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Lusitania memorial and a free-press essay
In New York Roosevelt addresses a win-the-war rally and a memorial meeting for the Lusitania. The Kansas City Star prints his editorial on sedition, press freedom and one-man rule.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Cleveland Dodge that the United States ought to declare war on the Ottoman Empire.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Opening the Nassau County Red Cross drive
Roosevelt goes to Garden City to speak at the launch of the Nassau County Red Cross campaign.
Roosevelt writes Sara Greenway a note of remembrance and writes Will Hays about the Progressive Party.
Roosevelt writes Henry Price about sculptor Gutzon Borglum and his probe into the aircraft industry.
A branch of the Needlework Guild
Roosevelt speaks at a meeting called to form a local chapter of the Needlework Guild of America.
Red Cross parade and a Coney Island club
In New York Roosevelt reviews a parade launching a Red Cross drive and speaks as a new service club opens its doors at Coney Island. He writes G. W. Aldridge about politics.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt speaks at Carnegie Hall during a concert held for charity.

Writing to Senator Miles Poindexter, Roosevelt rebuts Postmaster General Albert Burleson, who had disputed his May 7 Kansas City Star charge that the administration was trying to muzzle him. He also lashes out again at Hearst. The letter is published May 27.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt speaks at Wittenberg College in Springfield, Ohio.
In Chicago Roosevelt runs into William Howard Taft at a restaurant. The old friends dine together and talk at length, finding common ground on policy and a shared distaste for Wilson.

Roosevelt gives three talks in Des Moines for the National Security League. He writes Elon Hooker about a governor's primary and sends Henry Bordeaux two letters about Archie's wounds. Quentin is back at Issoudun and Archie is improving.
Roosevelt speaks in Madison, Wisconsin, and passes through Chicago.
Roosevelt makes two speeches in Milwaukee for the National Security League.
Roosevelt delivers a Memorial Day address in Detroit.
Roosevelt gets back to Sagamore Hill. The Metropolitan prints his "Parlor Bolshevism." The old pony Algonquin is still alive, and Gracie has been riding him.
Roosevelt writes Ted that Kermit has won the British Military Cross for gallantry.
Ted, gassed at Cantigny, meets Eleanor in Paris
Ted and his wife Eleanor reunite in Paris; he looks badly worn after being gassed at Cantigny. Quentin turns up too. Ted reads aloud, and after dinner the three go to see Archie in the hospital.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
A dinner for Will Hays, then west

Roosevelt says a few words at a Republican dinner in New York honoring Will Hays, then sets out with Edith on a National Security League speaking tour in the West. He writes Taft about Wilson and Russia and Henry Stimson about the war.
Roosevelt takes his message to audiences in Illinois, Missouri and Indiana.
Roosevelt is traveling west by train. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt speaks in Omaha. Quentin receives orders to Orly.
Roosevelt is on the road toward Missouri.
Roosevelt speaks in Indianapolis on Kermit and Belle's fourth wedding anniversary.
From Indianapolis Roosevelt goes to Bloomington and speaks at Indiana University.
Roosevelt gets back to Sagamore Hill running a high fever, with erysipelas in his left foot.
On grandson Theodore III's fourth birthday, Roosevelt telegraphs Senator Hiram Johnson to cheer his Senate speech asking why Leonard Wood has been denied a command in France.
Roosevelt goes to Farmington, Connecticut, to visit his sister Bamie, staying two more days.
A Sunday sermon at Trinity College
Since it is Sunday, Roosevelt's address at Trinity College in Hartford takes the form of a sermon on a text from First Kings. Quentin is moved to active duty in the Air Service. Edith writes Kermit.

Trinity College gives Roosevelt an honorary Doctor of Science, alongside George Wharton Pepper and J. P. Morgan. He returns to New York for dinner with Russell Coles at the Hotel Langdon, then goes home. Granddaughter Edith Derby turns one.
Quentin gets to the front and joins the 95th Aero Squadron.
Tales of a badly run war
Roosevelt writes Arthur Page about stories of mismanagement in the war effort.
On Ted and Eleanor's eighth anniversary, Roosevelt writes Kermit about his new degree, Russia, and Quentin heading into combat.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Edith writes Kermit about her father, Charles Carow, and explains that her new horse is called Oriole, a name borrowed from a horse Charles once kept.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Quentin glad to be at the front
Word reaches home that Quentin is pleased to be serving at the front.
Roosevelt writes S. Stanwood Menken that he and Elihu Root agree Menken must resign as head of the National Security League after praising Hearst.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Sagamore Hill hosts some hundred Dutch Reformed clergymen and deacons.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

Horace Wilkinson arrives as an emissary of the Republican Party to urge Roosevelt to seek the New York governorship. He writes James Bryce and Taft, and The Metropolitan prints "Don't Spread Patriotism Too Thin." In France, Archie's arm undergoes a second operation.
Roosevelt writes his son-in-law Richard Derby that Ethel and the children are leaving Sagamore Hill for Islesboro that day.
Redirecting the Nobel Peace Prize money

Roosevelt asks Congressman James Gallivan to have the unspent $40,000 of his Nobel Peace Prize money, meant for an industrial peace foundation that never took shape, returned so he can give it to war causes. He also writes George Pepper about a Bastille Day speech and Elihu Root about Menken and the Saratoga convention.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt travels to Passaic, New Jersey, to give an Independence Day speech.
Quentin has his first air fight, but his gun jams and the German plane gets away.
No wartime wedding for Quentin and Flora
John Purroy Mitchel, former mayor of New York, is killed. Roosevelt tells Bamie the government will not let Flora travel to Europe to marry Quentin, and gives news of his other sons' wounds.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

Quentin downs his first German aircraft after taking on three enemy fighters at once. At home Roosevelt writes Leonard Wood about poor appointments and Paul Shimpion about the suffering of the Armenians.
Roosevelt goes to New York to serve as an honorary pallbearer and writes Lioubomir Michailovitch about Serbia. Quentin is quartered in a small French village.
A ride with Edith; Quentin in Paris

Roosevelt writes Ethel about Quentin's victory over a German plane, rides out with Edith, and admits he misses the grandchildren. In Paris Quentin visits Ted's wife Eleanor; they eat at Ciro's and take in the Grand Guignol.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Quentin Roosevelt dies in aerial combat, hit twice in the head; his aircraft falls behind German lines near Cambrai. At home, unaware, Roosevelt writes Archie's wife Grace with news.
Roosevelt congratulates William Howard Taft on his Saratoga speech and tells Loren Palmer what livestock and crops he raises at Sagamore Hill.

As Roosevelt dictates to his secretary Josephine Stricker, AP reporter Phil Thompson carries out a fragment of a cable telling reporters to watch Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt begins to fear that one of his sons has been hurt. In Russia, the Bolsheviks kill Nicholas II and his family.

Phil Thompson returns with an unofficial dispatch: Quentin has been shot down. Roosevelt goes inside to talk with Edith, and together they release a statement to the press. Then he goes back to his desk and dictates until his work is done.

Two days after the news, Roosevelt and Edith travel by way of New York to the unofficial Republican State Convention at Saratoga, where Corinne joins them. His speech rouses the crowd. He meets with Will Hays, Nicholas Murray Butler, Sheffield Cowles and Cocks; Taft, Root and many others urge him to run for governor. He also writes Albert Beveridge about his John Marshall biography.

Roosevelt passes through New York on his way home. In France, Ted reappears in Paris with a bad machine-gun wound in the leg; Dick Derby happens along and persuades him to get to a hospital for surgery.
Roosevelt addresses a delegation from the Japanese Red Cross. A telegram arrives confirming that Quentin is dead.

Roosevelt writes Kermit that Edith has been steadfast, and the two of them go out rowing and swimming together. To Ted he writes that Flora is young and will heal, wishing she had married Quentin. He also writes Archie about his brother.
Roosevelt thanks King George V for his telegram of sympathy on Quentin's death.
The New York Times publishes Roosevelt's statement, framed as a letter to Morgan Lewis, ruling out a candidacy for governor.
Roosevelt urges General Leonard Wood to stay calm in the face of the wrongs done him.
Leaving a house full of memories

Finding Sagamore Hill too full of painful reminders, Roosevelt and Edith decide to join Ethel at Dark Harbor, Maine. He writes Georges Clemenceau about Quentin and tells Taft he will not run for governor.
At Dark Harbor, Roosevelt writes Mary Brown about Quentin and James Ashton about the Pacific islands.
Roosevelt and Edith are staying with Ethel at Dark Harbor, Maine. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt and Edith are staying with Ethel at Dark Harbor, Maine. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt and Edith are staying with Ethel at Dark Harbor, Maine. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt and Edith are staying with Ethel at Dark Harbor, Maine. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is at Dark Harbor. In Paris, Kermit and Belle arrive and find Eleanor, Ted and Archie waiting.
Roosevelt and Edith remain with Ethel at Dark Harbor, Maine. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt and Edith remain with Ethel at Dark Harbor, Maine. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt tells Corinne that Quentin's letters will stay private, that he is enjoying his stay with Ethel, and that grandson Richard has helped soften Edith's ache.
Roosevelt gives a talk to the people of Dark Harbor.
On a rainy day Roosevelt writes Richard Derby that little Richard was devoted to his Uncle Quentin.
Edith turns 57, and Quentin's fiancée, Flora Payne Whitney, comes to Dark Harbor to be with the family.
Roosevelt writes James Bryce about Quentin and the other boys and about subject peoples.
Edith keeps away from the water
Edith writes Corinne that she avoids the water and spends time watching little Richard play with his toy trucks.
Roosevelt and Edith remain with Ethel at Dark Harbor, Maine. Nothing else is recorded.
Back home at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt and Edith find Alice there to greet them. He writes Kermit that Edith will carry this wound for the rest of her life.
Roosevelt sends Belle two letters about Kermit, Quentin's death and Flora, and Ted's and Archie's recovery, tucking in a photograph of himself she had asked for.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Ethel's birthday; praise for Arthur Train
On Ethel's 27th birthday, Roosevelt compliments Arthur Train on his article about Americanism.
Edith writes Corinne how much it meant to have Alice with them.
Too painful to write about Quentin

Roosevelt sends news to Ted and Eleanor, writes Taft about universal military training and Will Hays about Republican politics, and tells Edith Wharton a long account of Quentin would be more than he could manage.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Granddaughter Grace turns seven. Joseph and Corinne Alsop come to Sagamore Hill for lunch.
Roosevelt thanks Corinne for the poem she sent and reports that General Charles Summerall has commended Ted.
Colgate Hoyt proposes an Oyster Bay memorial to Quentin, and Roosevelt gently declines. He thanks General John J. Pershing for his note about Quentin.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Giving away the Nobel Prize money

Roosevelt tells Congressman James Gallivan how he will divide his Nobel Prize fund into 28 gifts of varying size. The Red Cross gets the largest share, $6,900. Ted's wife Eleanor channels $5,000 to the YMCA, the Jewish Welfare Board gets $4,000, Emily Carow passes $1,000 to the Italian Red Cross, and many soldiers' families receive $500 apiece.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
In Springfield, Illinois, Roosevelt speaks at the centennial of Illinois statehood; film catches him speaking and stepping out of a car. He writes Taft about universal military training.
Roosevelt is traveling back toward New York City.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Visitors to Sagamore Hill include Desmond and a group of workers from the Newburgh shipyard.
Roosevelt writes George W. Perkins about Arthur Capper's campaign for the Senate.
Stimson and soldiers from Camp Mills
Henry L. Stimson calls at Sagamore Hill, as do twenty soldiers from Mineola's Camp Mills.
Roosevelt is at home. Across the Atlantic, a recuperating Ted is itching to return to the fighting.
Roosevelt goes up the Hudson to Newburgh to speak as the U.S.S. Newburgh slides down the ways. Ted, meanwhile, earns a promotion to lieutenant colonel.
Roosevelt writes General Leonard Wood about Henry L. Stimson, just back in the United States from Europe.

Archie, discharged because of his wounds, lands in New York. His parents greet him at the Hotel Langdon, where Archie lays eyes on his baby son, now five months old, for the first time. Archie cannot yet move his left arm, and his leg faces more surgery. Roosevelt writes Lodge, now Republican leader in the Senate, about politics and the draft.
George W. Perkins calls. Roosevelt tells Bamie how proud he is of her son Sheffield.
A League of Nations as supplement, not substitute

At Lafayette Day and Marine Day observances in New York, Roosevelt argues that any League of Nations should add to American strength, never replace it. Film shows him waving from the City Hall steps. He writes Gifford Pinchot about Perkins's push for a progressive stand and tells John T. King he could never be named a peace commissioner.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about Quentin's death, his other sons' wounds, and Lee's decision to quit the British food agency.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

Corinne's husband, Douglas Robinson, dies without warning, and Roosevelt and Edith hurry to Henderson House, her place in the Mohawk Valley. He writes Richard Derby about Archie, wires Raymond Benjamin about California Republicans coming back together, and writes Robert Montgomery about poor aircraft materials.
Still at Henderson House, Roosevelt marks Ted's 31st birthday by congratulating him and Eleanor on Ted's fine service. He also backs Truman Newberry over Henry Ford for the Senate from Michigan.
Roosevelt stays on in Mohawk, New York, after Douglas Robinson's death. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt stays on in Mohawk, New York, after Douglas Robinson's death. Nothing else is recorded.
A Jewish homeland and fair draft rules
Back home, Roosevelt writes Julian Miller that it would be right to establish a Zionist state around Jerusalem, and tells James Bates that draftees will get no special favors.
Newspapers carry "The Great Adventure," Roosevelt's tribute to Quentin, with its lines on living fully and facing death without fear.
In New York, Roosevelt helps launch a campaign by New York's National League for Women's Service, a wartime women's group.
Roosevelt writes Corinne about Archie's serious injuries and Elmer Peterson about Wilson's government and the farmers' Non-Partisan League.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes Franklin D. Roosevelt, who is down with pneumonia, wishing him a quick recovery.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells Bamie that President Raymond Poincaré has sent a French government certificate honoring Quentin.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Women for the War Labor Board
On Corinne's 57th birthday, Roosevelt urges Taft to see women named to the National War Labor Board, and thanks General Pershing for his condolence letter and enclosures.
Fourth Liberty Loan opens in Baltimore
At Oriole Park in Baltimore, Roosevelt speaks to launch the Fourth Liberty Loan and greets Cardinal James Gibbons.
Roosevelt speaks in Columbus for the Liberty Loan. The Metropolitan carries an article of his arguing against birth control. He and Edith are enjoying the fall and often go rowing.
Roosevelt is traveling toward Missouri as the Senate votes down the woman suffrage amendment.
Roosevelt continues his trip to Missouri.
In Kansas City, Roosevelt sees General Leonard Wood.
Roosevelt gives a speech in Alliance, Nebraska.
Roosevelt speaks in Billings, Montana, on behalf of the Liberty Loan.
Roosevelt starts back east. Edith writes Kermit about picnicking at Eel Beach under a beautiful sky and seeing an osprey.
Roosevelt is on the train back to New York City.
Roosevelt is on the train back to New York City.
Roosevelt arrives in New York City and goes on to Sagamore Hill.
No talks with Germany until victory
On Kermit's 29th birthday, Roosevelt issues a statement that Wilson ought not to negotiate with Germany before the war is won.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his niece Eleanor Roosevelt's 34th birthday.
Roosevelt makes a speech for the Liberty Loan.
Roosevelt writes Corinne that he is pleased with her son Monroe Robinson, anxious about Bamie's illness, and against Wilson opening preliminary talks with Germany.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Speaking to the Council of Jewish Women

With Archie at his side, Roosevelt speaks for the Liberty Loan at Liederkranz Hall, addressing the Council of Jewish Women's New York section. He thanks Louise Imogen Guiney in England for her sympathy and endorses Selden Spencer for the Senate.
In New York, Roosevelt writes Will Hays about where Republicans should stand on negotiating peace with Germany.
Rhode Island rallies; a nod to Coolidge
Roosevelt speaks for the Liberty Loan in Providence and Newport, and writes the Massachusetts Republican committee backing Calvin Coolidge for governor.
On nephew Sheffield Cowles's 20th birthday, Roosevelt writes John Bartlett in support of New Hampshire's Republican candidates.
Roosevelt explains to Gifford Pinchot why he opposes the Non-Partisan League.
A funny story about Mrs. Vanderbilt
Roosevelt sends Ted and Eleanor an amusing account of Grace Vanderbilt at Newport.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on grandson Cornelius's third birthday.
Roosevelt wires Lodge that the Allies must insist on Germany's unconditional surrender.
Owen Wister and Alice visit. Roosevelt tells Lodge peace must come by force of arms, asks Peyton March that Quentin's body stay in France, and writes Winthrop Chanler about Quentin.
Wilson asks for a Democratic Congress
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as President Wilson openly appeals to voters to return a Democratic Congress.
Roosevelt marks his 60th birthday with letters to Kermit and Corinne, joking that he is now officially as old as he feels and calling himself Methuselah's understudy.
At Carnegie Hall Roosevelt speaks for two hours, sharply attacking Wilson.

After training at Saumur, Kermit joins the 1st Division as an artillery officer. Roosevelt wires Senator Albert Fall his support for reelection. Edith tells Kermit his father thinks of Quentin constantly.
The Kansas City Star runs Roosevelt's "What Are the Fourteen Points?", another broadside at Wilson. He wires Albert Fall again and sends Medill McCormick good wishes for the election.
Roosevelt writes Albert Beveridge that nationalism must come ahead of internationalism. Scribner's brings out his new book, The Great Adventure, a collection of essays on American nationalism.
Taft and Roosevelt call for a Republican Congress

Roosevelt and William Howard Taft jointly appeal for a Republican mandate and Germany's unconditional surrender. With Archie, he speaks at a Boys' Victory Mobilization rally in New York, and wires Stitzel Way his backing for North Dakota's Republican ticket, with words on the I.W.W.
Carnegie Hall for Negro War Relief

Roosevelt speaks at Carnegie Hall to benefit Negro War Relief. He wires Henry Timken his support for Ohio Republicans, writes Charles Bird about John Weeks's Senate race, and tells Julian Street about the Republicans and his dealings with King.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt writes William Potter about a history text titled Medieval and Modern Times.
Out of a sickbed to vote

On Election Day Roosevelt is in bed with swollen joints and a fever of 102, but gets up to cast his ballot in Oyster Bay. Voters turn against Wilson and elect Republicans. Ted is back in battle with the 1st Division.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Roosevelt tells A. T. Volwiler that he owes the presidency to his years in the Badlands.
Kaiser Wilhelm II gives up his throne and flees to Holland.
Flat on his back with gout
Roosevelt sends Ted family news; Edith adds a note that he is laid up in bed with gout.
Armistice Day, back in the hospital

The war ends with the Armistice. Roosevelt, his left foot too swollen for a shoe, is taken back to Roosevelt Hospital with inflammatory rheumatism. Edith will sleep in a nearby corner room for 44 nights, seeing friends, going to plays, and reading him Shakespeare at night. Ted and Eleanor meet at the front, and General Francis Marshall writes TR praising Ted as a soldier.
From his hospital bed Roosevelt tells Robert Pope he has no intention of reading the Non-Partisan League's pamphlets.
Roosevelt is in the hospital. In Paris, Ted and Eleanor have some time together.

Ted heads back to the front, not to see Eleanor for four months. From the hospital Roosevelt writes William Allen White about the peace commission and Lodge about the West's stand against Bolshevism and Weeks's loss, and wires William Davies agreeing with Australia's prime minister in opposing the Fourteen Points.
Nine months of service for every young man

Roosevelt writes Charles Van Hise about universal service and George Haven Putnam about closer ties with Britain, and sketches for Elmer Peterson a plan of nine months' military training for every man between 19 and 23.
Roosevelt writes Senator Miles Poindexter that he opposes Wilson's League of Nations.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
In the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt celebrates the Republican election victory.

Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee a summing-up of the war's tragedy. To James Bryce he writes about the war's causes, his view that America should have fought Turkey, the black republics, Russia, and his three surviving sons.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.

The Kansas City Star publishes Roosevelt's article on freedom of the seas. He tells William Allen White the government should regulate, not own, the merchant marine, and writes Lodge about the Bulgarians.
Roosevelt tells Rudyard Kipling that the first chapter of The Great Adventure is about Quentin, and writes of his other sons, Wilson and the peace talks, Americanism and pacifism.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt is still in the hospital on his sister Bamie's 23rd wedding anniversary.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
One Republican at the peace table
Roosevelt writes Lodge about battle casualties and observes that Henry White is the lone Republican on Wilson's delegation to Versailles.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.

Roosevelt writes Kipling again about The Great Adventure, his opposition to the Fourteen Points, the old rivalry and newer friendship between Britain and America, the Alaska boundary, the Royal Navy, and Wilson. He is also writing a steady run of pieces for the Kansas City Star.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt and Edith mark their 32nd wedding anniversary while he is in the hospital.
Roosevelt writes Ted how proud he is of his war record. Quentin will be left buried in France, and he and Edith hope to visit the grave and set a small stone there.
Wilson sails for the peace conference
President Wilson sets sail on the transport George Washington, bound for the peace conference in France, while Roosevelt is still hospitalized.
Roosevelt tells George Haven Putnam that America and Britain should draw up a universal arbitration treaty, and writes about the navy.

Roosevelt writes Lodge, who is to eulogize Senator Ben Tillman, about the revenue bill. He praises Philander Knox's resolution to keep the League of Nations apart from the German peace and opposes any treaty apologizing to Colombia over Panama. He tells H. Rider Haggard he doubts he will return to public life.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt writes Arthur Balfour to introduce George Wickersham and to set out Republican aims and how they differ from Wilson's. Clemenceau and Lloyd George receive much the same letter.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.

Edith writes Kermit that she has just finished reading Macbeth aloud to Roosevelt. Rheumatism has spread to his left arm, and his wrist is bandaged and splinted. He writes John M. Clark about Wilson using a naval buildup to push Britain toward arms limits.

Roosevelt tells Ted that Eleanor is home and came to the hospital first thing to see him, that Archie will stand in for him at the Cove School Christmas party, and writes about the Mexican oil business.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Archie goes to the Cove School Christmas celebration in his father's place while Roosevelt remains in the hospital.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.
No future for the Progressive Party
Roosevelt writes D. H. Clark that trying to keep the Progressive Party going would be foolish.
Roosevelt remains in Roosevelt Hospital in New York, laid up with inflammatory rheumatism. Nothing else is recorded.

Dizzy from his inflamed ear, Roosevelt still refuses the doctor's help as he walks out of the hospital. At Sagamore Hill he has Christmas dinner with Edith, Archie, Alice, Gracie and Ethel, enjoys watching little Edie Derby dash about the drawing room, and is tired enough by afternoon to be put to bed.
Roosevelt eats breakfast in bed, joins the family downstairs at midday, and dictates while lying on the library sofa, the pattern of his next several days.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

Roosevelt writes Bamie, on paper from his Madison Avenue office, about his rheumatism and sciatica and why he is against the League of Nations. He also writes Henry West about Wilson and the League and Henry J. Haskell about Wilson.
Hoping the family is home soon
Roosevelt writes Ted that he wants them all back home as soon as they can manage.
Edith takes Roosevelt out for a drive of an hour. He writes Madison Grant about where soldiers came from and Richard Derby about Ethel, Ted and Kermit.
Another drive to end the year
Edith again takes Roosevelt out for an hour-long drive.

On a rainy New Year's Day, Roosevelt's leg and hand hurt badly, and he now passes most of each day upstairs, resting on a sofa in what was once the nursery. He writes Russell Coles hoping for another devilfish hunt, consoles Alice Page on her husband's death, and objects to Ogden Reid about calling Wilson an idealist.
Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.
Dictating on the League of Nations

Roosevelt dictates an article on the League of Nations for the Kansas City Star, to run January 13. He writes Richard Hurd about Americanism and sends an Iowa man, Carroll E. Armstrong, a sharp critique of Wilson.
Edith tells Ethel that Dr. Hartwell expects Roosevelt to get well, though not quickly.
Last words: put out the light

On a sunny day Flora Whitney visits. Roosevelt writes Kermit and jots a memo to Will Hays, his last written words. At 11 p.m. he sets down corrected proofs of a Kansas City Star editorial and asks his valet James Amos to turn out the light.

Around a quarter past four in the morning, Theodore Roosevelt dies in his sleep at Sagamore Hill of a coronary embolism. Archie wires his brothers Ted and Kermit in Europe that the old lion is dead. About a hundred dignitaries and Oyster Bay schoolchildren attend a plain funeral, with no music, and he is buried in Youngs Cemetery.
